# Research-Question Charting — Computation-based autism prediction from behavioral data: a systematic review of study design, conduct and reporting

Per-study answers to the 23 prespecified review questions, for all 170 included studies.
Source identifiers (S-nnn) correspond to the study list in the main report; the corpus identifier is given in brackets.

---

## RQ1.1 — Participant groups included and whether each group's presence and size is explicitly reported

_170 of 170 studies charted for this question._

**S-001** [local_76fc33d0] — *Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers*

ASD group (n=23, high-risk siblings later diagnosed) and typically developing low-risk controls (n=20); both explicitly reported with sizes in Table 1. No other-diagnosis group.

**S-002** [local_0dbc5018] — *Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities*

Two groups: ASD (n=15, low-functioning preschool) and typically developing controls (n=15). Both explicitly reported with demographics in Table 1. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-003** [local_dc5fc4bb] — *ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data*

Three groups: ASD (n=18), ADHD (n=30) and typically developing controls (n=13). Group sizes are reported; this is one of the few corpus studies with a non-autistic clinical comparison group. No demographic breakdown beyond mean age.

**S-004** [local_863980f8] — *Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework*

Three groups: ASD (n=29) and two typically developing control groups - chronological-age-matched (n=29) and nonverbal-ability/IQ-matched (n=29). All groups reported with sex ratio, age, nonverbal IQ raw score and AQ. No other-diagnosis clinical group.

**S-005** [local_be8aa62f] — *Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder*

Two groups: adults with ASD (n=27, one non-completer) and typical adults (n=132, two non-completers), the latter reported separately as 45 males and 87 females. No other-diagnosis group - indeed other DSM-IV diagnoses were an exclusion criterion.

**S-006** [local_e404a2a3] — *Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism*

Two groups: children clinically diagnosed with Childhood Autism (n=37 recruited, 35 with usable data) and typically developing controls (n=45). Group composition is reported in unusual detail - 30 'uncomplicated' autism, 1 high-functioning, 2 Asperger's Syndrome, 4 with co-morbid intellectual impairment (2 completing). No non-autistic clinical comparison group, which the authors identify as the key gap.

**S-007** [local_780141fc] — *Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study*

Two groups: autistic adults (16 recruited, 14 analysed after two exclusions for data capture failure) and neurotypical adult controls (n=16). Both group sizes and the exclusion are reported explicitly. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the discussion identifies developmental coordination disorder and ADHD as the comparisons needed next.

**S-008** [local_3a331973] — *Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data*

Four groups: controls (n=18), ASD only (n=22), ADHD only (n=4) and comorbid ADHD+ASD (n=11), totalling 55 adults. Group sizes must be inferred from the classification tables and a bar chart rather than a participant table. The ADHD-only group was explicitly too small (n=4) to train a classifier for, so the reported analyses collapse to controls-vs-condition and comorbid-vs-ASD-only. This is one of very few corpus studies with both a non-autistic clinical group and an explicit comorbid group.

**S-009** [local_7b3e6b3a] — *Earlier identification of children with autism*

Two groups of 10: infants at heightened familial risk (younger siblings of children with ASD) later diagnosed with ASD at 3 years, and typically developing infants from a low-risk population with normal 3-year outcome. Both groups fully specified per subject in Table 1, including vocalisation counts and cross-validation partition assignment - subject-level transparency that is rare in this corpus. No other-diagnosis group.

**S-010** [local_36aa3ace] — *Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative*

Four groups: autism disorders (n=11), PDD-NOS (n=10), specific language impairment (n=13) and typically developing (n=68), totalling 102 children. Group sizes are reported. This is one of the few corpus studies to include a non-autistic clinical comparison group - and notably one (SLI) chosen to probe exactly the specificity question that most ASD-versus-TD studies leave open. It is also one of the few to separate autism disorders from PDD-NOS as distinct classes.

**S-011** [local_44b58f21] — *ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces*

Two groups of 30: children with ASD (all mild category) and typically developing children. Group sizes, mean age, height and body mass are reported for both. Recruitment is split within the ASD group - 14 from the National Autism Society of Malaysia centre and 16 from the local community via parents approached through social media - which is unusually specific. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-012** [local_cb9a5b48] — *Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening*

Two groups of 8: children with ASD and typically developing children, total n=16. Group sizes are reported; no other-diagnosis group. The predecessor study being automated (Soleiman et al.) used 32 children, so this automation paper works on half that sample.

**S-013** [local_40cd7d53] — *Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children*

Two groups of 37: children with ASD recruited from a hospital child mental health outpatient ward, and typically developing children recruited from a local kindergarten. Both groups fully characterised in a demographic table. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-014** [local_5b1d0b36] — *Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday*

Three groups recruited: 18 children diagnosed with ASD, 9 typically developing children, and 8 at-risk children defined as undiagnosed younger siblings of ASD children. Only the 27 with definite TD or ASD status entered the classification experiment; the at-risk group was excluded because undiagnosed, which is handled transparently. Per-subject characteristics are tabulated individually.

**S-015** [local_54954c19] — *Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching*

Two groups: adults with a confirmed clinical diagnosis of high-functioning autism or Asperger's syndrome (18 recruited, 15 analysed) and non-autistic control adults (18 recruited, 15 analysed after 2 data-quality exclusions and 1 random removal to balance classes). All recruitment, exclusion and balancing decisions are reported explicitly, including the random removal. No other-diagnosis group.

**S-016** [local_d8dc996a] — *Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Two groups of 20: children with ASD without accompanying intellectual impairment (18 male), and typically developing children (16 male). One ASD subject (subject 3) was discarded because all their non-corrupted videos came from a single condition, so 39 subjects enter the experiments. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-017** [local_88ddfdd1] — *A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task*

Two groups: 21 individuals with ASD and 23 age- and IQ-matched typically developing controls, total 44. Group sizes, sexes and IQ means are all reported. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-018** [local_361110f1] — *Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features*

Two groups: 20 children with high-functioning autism and 23 age-matched typically developing children. Group sizes are clear. No other-diagnosis comparison group - indeed ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia were explicit exclusions - though the conclusion identifies ASD-versus-ADHD classification as the needed next step.

**S-019** [local_51533de4] — *Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations*

Two groups of 35: children with ASD and typically developing children, plus 22 young adult confederates (19 female) who served as conversation partners and whose speech was also analysed. The confederates are effectively a third participant group whose data enter the model - an unusual design in this corpus. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-020** [local_96c87d36] — *Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking*

Two groups: 23 individuals with ASD (5 later excluded for eye-tracking failure) and 35 typically developing controls, total 58 recruited. Group sizes, sexes and ages are reported, and control status is defined by explicit exclusions. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the discussion proposes extending the paradigm to schizophrenia and ADHD.

**S-021** [local_4b031d44] — *Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine*

Three groups: 55 videos of children with ASD, 50 with speech and language conditions, and 54 typically developing, totalling 159 videos (150 with complete demographic data). The inclusion of a non-autistic clinical comparison group - and the explicit design of a second classification layer to separate ASD from other developmental delay - directly addresses the specificity question that most ASD-versus-typical studies in this corpus leave open. SLC diagnoses are further broken down: 74% had both receptive and expressive language delay, 12% receptive and expressive language disorder, 10% expressive delay alone, 4% receptive delay alone.

**S-022** [local_05ef29e5] — *Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification*

Two groups by dataset label - ASD and typically developing - but the paper reports no participant counts for either group, only image counts (300 training, 100 test). The unit of analysis throughout is the scanpath rather than the person, and subject identifiers are explicitly randomised and inconsistent across images, so participant-level group composition is not recoverable.

**S-023** [local_9528024b] — *Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol*

Two groups: 8 preschool children already diagnosed with ASD and 7 typically developing children, total 15. Group sizes are reported. No other-diagnosis group. Notably the analysis is ultimately regrouped by expert-assessed behaviour rather than by diagnosis, producing four categories (ASD-like behaviour n=5, typical behaviour n=3, ambiguous n=4, session too short n=3) that cut across the original diagnostic grouping.

**S-024** [local_6230fe22] — *Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism*

Two groups are referred to - ASD and typically developing (non-ASD) children - but no participant counts are reported for either group anywhere in the paper. The sample is described only as 'our collected eye movement data set'. This is the only study charted so far that reports classification performance without stating any sample size.

**S-025** [local_785ba418] — *Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis*

Two groups: 24 autistic adults and 22 non-autistic (typically developing) adults, IQ-matched. Both group sizes and sex counts are reported. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-026** [local_fea042be] — *Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual*

Two groups: 29 ASD-diagnosed children and 30 non-ASD children, total 59. Group sizes are reported. For the multi-label experiment the ASD group is further split by CARS severity into Low, Mild and Severe bands, making four classes. No non-autistic clinical comparison group.

**S-027** [local_ba5fbda7] — *Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD*

Two groups of 29: high-functioning autistic adults (ICD-10 F84.0 or F84.5) and typically developed adults. Dyads were composed in three configurations - two typically developed, two autistic, or mixed - which is a design feature no other corpus study uses, since it means each participant's behaviour is measured while interacting with partners of both diagnostic statuses. No other-diagnosis group, though transdiagnostic specificity testing is named as required future work.

**S-028** [local_7b468950] — *Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart*

A planned sample of 760 children aged 30 months to 5 years 11 months across two countries, allocated in a published table: Glasgow 100 autistic, 140 other neurodevelopmental disorder and 180 typically developing; Gothenburg 180 autistic, 60 other neurodevelopmental disorder and 100 typically developing. The composition is the most important feature of the design for this review. Two hundred children with a diagnosed neurodevelopmental condition that is not autism - intellectual disability, non-verbal disability, communication disability, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, Down's syndrome and cerebral palsy - are recruited specifically to test whether the instrument distinguishes autism from other developmental difference rather than only from typical development. Children with subclinical or secondary expressions of autism are excluded from that cohort to keep the contrast interpretable. No participant data are reported, since the protocol was published before data collection closed and the results are embargoed.

**S-029** [local_309e5baa] — *Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns*

Two groups by dataset label - ASD and typically developing - with 14 of each viewing every image. The total number of distinct participants is never stated, only the per-image viewer counts, so the actual sample size is unrecoverable from this paper. No other-diagnosis group.

**S-030** [local_a45f39e9] — *Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time*

The paper does not report participant groups at all. The corpus is described only as 555 videos 'recorded from a mix of children with and without ASD', with no participant counts, no breakdown by diagnostic status, and no indication of how many children contributed the videos. The analytic groups are instead behavioural: 3084 expert-labelled typical time stamps and 5265 atypical time stamps across four video sets. This is a fundamentally different unit of analysis from the rest of the corpus.

**S-031** [local_d587f9cd] — *Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning*

Six children aged 36 to 48 months, each participating in a single session: three described as 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis, but with evidence of risk factors', and three typically developing children serving as the control group, with five boys and one girl in total. The sample is among the smallest in the review and the paper is explicit that it constitutes 'a proof of concept'. The diagnostic status of both groups is undocumented - the risk factors are not enumerated for the index group and no screening procedure is described for the comparison group - so no participant in the study has an established diagnostic classification. That is unusual in this corpus and is stated openly rather than obscured: the phrase 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis' appears in the methods, and the study makes no diagnostic claim on the basis of these children. At 36 to 48 months both groups sit in the age window where identification is typically still under way, so the risk framing is age-appropriate. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is reported.

**S-032** [local_08b8027d] — *SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths*

Two groups by dataset label - ASD and typically developing - with 14 of each viewing every image, though the paper notes 'some of the images have less than 14 scanpaths from the TD or ASD groups' because some children did not look inside the image bounds. The total number of distinct participants is never stated, so the actual sample size is unrecoverable. No other-diagnosis group.

**S-033** [local_c6f1209b] — *Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children*

Preschool children with autism recruited through an integrative kindergarten in Wroclaw, which is named in the acknowledgements. The retrieved text does not state the sample size, ages or sex composition, and no cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is reported. There is no comparison group of any kind - a design feature the authors identify explicitly as their first limitation. The absence of controls means the study cannot support any between-group inference, and it is not presented as doing so: the finding is a within-subject dissociation, where each child's rate of instructed behaviour is compared against their own rate of spontaneous imitation, so every child serves as their own control and the sample size constrains precision rather than validity.

**S-034** [local_83b99e73] — *Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers*

Two groups plus a prospectively emergent third. At enrolment: 45 high-risk infants and 43 typically developing infants, 88 in total, aged 8-23 months. At 24-month follow-up the high-risk group split into 40 confirmed ASD and 5 who no longer met criteria (N-ASD). Classification used the 40 confirmed ASD against the 43 TD. The N-ASD subgroup is the corpus's clearest instance of a genuine clinical comparison group - children who present as high-risk but do not go on to be diagnosed - and the study's inability to classify any of them is the most informative negative result in this record.

**S-035** [local_638860ef] — *Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis*

Two groups totalling 44 adults, split across two independently constituted samples: a development sample of 15 autistic and 15 non-autistic adults, and a hold-out testing sample of 7 autistic and 7 non-autistic adults, each internally matched. Having a pre-specified independent test sample rather than only cross-validation folds is rare in this corpus. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-036** [local_7547db68] — *Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network*

Two groups of ten: 10 autistic children aged 3-6 from Guangzhou Children's Care Center and 10 typically developing children aged 5-8 from Amy Education School in Zhengzhou. A separate group of 16 typically developing Chinese children aged 5-8 (8 boys, 8 girls) supplied 112 training images. No other-diagnosis comparison group. At 20 evaluation participants this is among the smallest clinical evaluations in the corpus, and it is a system test rather than a model validation.

**S-037** [local_878c259f] — *Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach*

Two groups of 25: children with ASD and age-matched typically developing children, total 50. Both groups are characterised in a demographic table with sample size, sex breakdown, body mass, height and age. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though neurological disorders other than ASD were an explicit exclusion for both groups.

**S-038** [local_1579c85a] — *Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through*

Two groups: 5 boys with ASD and 7 typically developing boys, total 12 children. Group sizes, sexes and mean ages are reported. No other-diagnosis comparison group. This is the smallest participant sample in the corpus charted so far.

**S-039** [local_157d6266] — *Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism*

Two groups: 27 children with autism spectrum conditions and 21 typically developing children, total 48. Group sizes are clear and participant characteristics are tabulated with group comparison test statistics, though the values are not recoverable from the extracted text. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-040** [local_8be557e3] — *Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation*

Two groups, 39 infants: 10 diagnosed autistic and 29 typically developing, all recruited as consecutive clinical cases undergoing diagnostic assessment at one hospital between 2016 and 2018. The typically developing group is not a convenience sample - these are infants brought for assessment who were assessed as typical, which makes them a clinically relevant comparison (children of diagnostic concern who turn out not to be autistic) rather than a community control group. Analysis is at the utterance level: 1,125 utterances, 475 autistic and 650 typically developing.

**S-041** [local_c79e100a] — *Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models*

Two groups, 21 subjects: 12 clinically diagnosed autistic and 9 typically developed. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The analysis unit is not the subject but the gait cycle (Dataset A: 167 autistic and 111 typically developed cycles) or the walking trial (Dataset B: 60 and 45), so 21 people generate 278 or 105 data points respectively. The authors themselves note that with a dataset this small 'the impact of variation in the subjects may be magnified due to the large portion of the dataset each subject represents'.

**S-042** [local_4fecbf6d] — *Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network*

One clinically referred cohort of 72 children treated as a severity continuum rather than as contrasting groups: 56 with an ASD diagnosis, 10 referred with suspected autism who received other diagnoses (language or developmental delays), and 6 typically developing children. Including the 10 diagnostically ambiguous referrals is unusual and important - most of the corpus either excludes such children or treats them as noise, whereas here they are the cases that make the prediction problem realistic. All 72 completed the same DSM-5 clinical assessment and ADOS-2.

**S-043** [local_95abe653] — *Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning*

Two groups across two independent collections: 71 adults recruited, 68 retained (28 autistic, 32 control), with 15 per group analysed in Study 1 and 19 per group in Study 2, and 9 participants (6 autistic, 3 control) taking part in both. Exclusions are itemised: in Study 1, three autistic and two control participants for calibration and head-movement problems plus one randomly chosen control to rebalance classes; in Study 2, five controls - one for a high AQ score, three for reported school dyslexia referrals and two for calibration. Adults with high-functioning autism are a substantially under-represented population in this corpus, which is dominated by preschool and school-age children.

**S-044** [local_40168c96] — *Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based*

Two groups: 31 autistic children recruited through the Children Rehabilitation Center at Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital and 43 typically developing children attending mainstream schools in Xi'an. The reported experiments use 30 and 40 respectively (15 + 20 training, 15 + 20 testing), so one autistic and three typically developing children are recruited but unaccounted for in the analysis, with no explanation given. No other-diagnosis comparison group; the authors themselves flag class balance as an issue needing attention.

**S-045** [local_d3852378] — *Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Two groups: 24 autistic children recruited through Red Cenit, a cognitive development centre in Valencia, and 25 typically developing children recruited by a management company through mailings to families. Both groups presented individual assessment reports including ADOS-2 and ADI-R, so the comparison group is instrument-assessed rather than merely unscreened. No other-diagnosis comparison group, and the authors identify this as a specificity limitation, proposing ADHD and intellectual disability comparisons for future work. Note that the results tables imply 22 rather than 24 autistic children were analysed.

**S-046** [local_df438dd2] — *Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening*

Two groups, 41 toddlers: 20 diagnosed autistic and 21 non-autistic, all assessed at the same specialist hospital. The comparison group is therefore clinically referred rather than community-recruited, which makes the discrimination task harder and more clinically realistic than most of the corpus. A separate, non-overlapping group of 54 children under six supplied 15,000 labelled expression clips for training the perception module. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-047** [local_cd9e45eb] — *Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism*

One cohort of 64 children split 32 autistic and 32 non-autistic, with the non-autistic group deliberately heterogeneous - 'typical development, language delay, and other developmental concerns'. This is one of only a few studies in the corpus whose comparison group is a clinically referred mixed-diagnosis sample rather than typically developing children, which raises the difficulty of the task and makes the result far more relevant to real screening. Clinical instrumentation is deep for a subset: ADOS severity, SRS total and Vineland-3 ABC for 30 of the 32 autistic children, and Stanford-Binet IQ for all 64.

**S-048** [local_56237213] — *The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data*

Two groups, 97 children: 49 with confirmed autism diagnoses and 48 typically developing children recruited from a local kindergarten. No other-diagnosis comparison group. At 97 participants this is one of the larger single-site cohorts in the corpus, and the authors note they 'recruited a relatively large sample size for the sake of classification'.

**S-049** [local_f9a5195f] — *Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses*

Two groups: 16 autistic and 17 neurotypical children, from 43 enrolled (23 autistic, 20 neurotypical). Exclusions are itemised with reasons: 4 controls received an early prototype version with visual rather than audio cues and could not read the cues or complete the task; 5 autistic participants received images in a different randomised order because of a stimulus ordering error; and 1 autistic participant had an unrelated health issue mid-session. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The cohort is predominantly high-functioning - only 3 of 16 autistic participants had an abbreviated IQ below 80.

**S-050** [local_16a77fb0] — *Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)*

Two groups in the main study: 37 autistic adults without intellectual disability recruited via the autism outpatient clinic of Charite Universitatsmedizin Berlin, and 43 healthy controls, with one autistic participant excluded from the combined classifier for missing audio. A separate preparatory study used 40 healthy males with facial EMG to select regions of interest before the main analysis - a two-stage design in which feature selection is performed on an entirely different sample, which is stronger than any within-study selection procedure. No other-psychiatric-diagnosis comparison group, though the authors identify testing 'in larger clinical samples with different psychiatric conditions' as necessary since the social interaction deficits targeted are common to many disorders.

**S-051** [local_9c4af7a3] — *Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades*

Two groups totalling 108 participants: 65 with autism and 43 without. No other-diagnosis comparison group. Nothing further is reported about either group, and because the dataset is secondary and unidentified, no additional characteristics can be recovered. The class imbalance (60:40) is never addressed in the modelling, and with accuracy as the only reported metric a classifier predicting the majority class throughout would score 60%.

**S-052** [local_b70dae32] — *An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model*

A single group of 12 autistic children from the Autism Resource Center in Islamabad, split into 8 for training and 4 for the prediction test. There is no non-autistic comparison group and none is intended - the task is severity categorisation within autism rather than case-control discrimination, which makes this one of the few studies in the corpus targeting a graded clinical outcome rather than a binary diagnosis. The analysis unit is the intervention session rather than the child, so 97 sessions arise from 12 individuals and 25 test predictions from 4.

**S-053** [local_51a0af74] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data*

Two groups totalling 86 participants: 56 autistic (38 male, 18 female, aged 5-18, mean 10) and 30 typically developing (20 male, 10 female, aged 3-15, mean 10). The class ratio is 65:35 in favour of autism, which the authors identify as a limitation and address with SMOTE on training folds. No other-diagnosis comparison group. At 86 participants this is among the larger single-site eye-tracking cohorts in the corpus.

**S-054** [local_d8d3037b] — *Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study*

Two entirely separate samples serving different roles. The preliminary experiment used 107 non-clinical adults (49 women, 58 men, mean age 24.84 +/- 5.24) split by AQ score into 52 above-median and 55 below-median. The test experiment used 22 young autistic males (mean age 12.68 +/- 7.61) recruited through the Shenzhen Autism Society, with no comparison group. The two samples differ in age by roughly twelve years on average, in sex composition (mixed versus all-male) and in clinical status (trait-scored general population versus diagnosed), so the second is not a held-out sample from the first population but a different population entirely.

**S-055** [local_991fe435] — *Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task*

Three groups totalling 74 children: 26 high-functioning autistic, 24 low-functioning autistic and 24 typically developing, all age-matched. Splitting the autistic sample by cognitive functioning rather than treating it as homogeneous is the design's defining feature and is argued for explicitly, on the grounds that binary classification 'fails to take into account the heterogeneity in the ASD population' and that low-functioning autistic children may show behaviours confounded with developmental delay and even with 'normal people with autistic traits, such as stereotyped behaviors, aggression, and noncompliance'. No separate developmental-delay or other-diagnosis group.

**S-056** [local_8692a64f] — *Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis*

Two groups: 39 autistic children recruited from the Shanghai Putuo District Zhanyi Children Cultivation Service Center and 53 children described as normal, totalling 92. Nine samples were excluded for partial data loss or non-cooperation, leaving 83 - 33 autistic and 50 typically developing, so 6 autistic and 3 comparison children were removed, a differential exclusion rate of 15% versus 6% that is not commented on. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-057** [local_4d6fac7e] — *Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network*

Two groups of 21 children each, aged 3-6, totalling 42. No other-diagnosis comparison group. Nothing further is reported about either group - no ages beyond the shared range, no sexes, no clinical characterisation - and because no provenance for the dataset is given, nothing can be recovered from a source publication either.

**S-058** [local_30c622f2] — *Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model*

A single clinical population of 88 autistic children and adolescents, split by CARS into 39 severe and 49 non-severe, from 91 recruited. There is no typically developing comparison group and none is intended - the research question is whether severity can be graded within autism, which makes this one of very few studies in the corpus addressing gradation rather than detection. Exclusions were calibration problems, eye-tracking record rate below 80% and age over 17, applied to three participants.

**S-059** [local_bfc088c7] — *Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation*

Two groups: 20 autistic children recruited from the Child Psychiatry Department of Shenzhen Kangning Hospital and 23 typically developing children from local schools, with four excluded for eye-tracking technical problems leaving 19 and 20. No other-diagnosis comparison group, and the authors identify this as a substantive limitation rather than a scope note: 'it remains unclear whether eye-tracking data could effectively detect ASD from other clinical phenotypes (eg, developmental delay and ADHD)'.

**S-060** [local_25e34bbd] — *Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification*

Three groups, but 19 children in total: 6 autistic (3 boys, 3 girls), 6 with Down syndrome (2 boys, 4 girls) and 7 controls (3 boys, 4 girls), contributing 79, 77 and 99 sustained vowel samples respectively. The inclusion of a Down syndrome group is the design's most valuable feature - it is one of only a handful of studies in the corpus with an other-diagnosis comparison rather than only typical development, enabling the differential question the paper poses. But with six children per clinical group the analysis rests on a very small number of individuals however many samples each provides.

**S-061** [local_4917150c] — *Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning*

Two groups of 59 children: 29 autistic and 30 non-autistic, closely matched at 19 males each. The authors explain the age composition candidly rather than presenting it as a design choice - they wanted younger participants for early detection, 'but in our region there were not enough diagnosed children younger than 6 years, and the time it takes to consult a doctor to make a diagnosis can be as long as 2 years'. That is an unusually direct statement of how diagnostic waiting times constrain the very research meant to shorten them. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-062** [local_241ec2c2] — *Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking*

Two groups totalling 106 children and adolescents: 76 autistic recruited from the Psychiatry Institute of the University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine and 30 typically developing. The class ratio of roughly 2.5:1 favouring autism is not addressed by any balancing procedure and matters for interpreting the reported 90% precision. Notably, participants with psychiatric and neurological comorbidities were deliberately retained rather than excluded, with the authors reasoning from co-occurrence prevalence that excluding them would misrepresent the population. No separate other-diagnosis group, though extending to autism-versus-ADHD discrimination is named as a future direction.

**S-063** [local_36617ec5] — *Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis*

Two groups totalling 55 children aged 4-7: 35 autistic recruited from the Red Cenit Neurocognitive Development Center in Valencia and 20 typically developing recruited by a management company through calls and mailings to families. The 35:20 imbalance is not addressed by any balancing procedure. Both groups are stated to have received the same evaluation scales and procedure before the experiment. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the authors name ADHD inclusion as a priority for future work specifically to 'identify with greater precision the degrees of severity in each disorder'.

**S-064** [local_d8e804d6] — *Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms*

Two groups: 20 autistic children recruited from a local psychiatric hospital and 23 typically developing children from nearby communities, with five excluded for camera technical problems leaving 18 and 20. Participants are the same cohort as a companion study by the same group on conversational eye tracking, but the data come from a different conversational session - the yes-no question session rather than the full four-session conversation. No other-diagnosis comparison group. Participants were paid 200 CNY, which is disclosed.

**S-065** [local_712542ca] — *Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset*

Two groups inherited from the source dataset: 30 autistic and 29 non-autistic children, contributing 219 and 328 scanpath images respectively. The analysis operates on images rather than children throughout, and the 59 participants are never treated as the unit of anything. Following k-means partitioning, the effective analysis units become four image clusters of unstated composition - the paper does not report how many images, or how many children, fall in each cluster, nor the class balance within them, which makes the per-cluster metrics difficult to interpret.

**S-066** [local_0ab41681] — *Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder*

Two groups of 13 children each. The autistic group spans three ICD-10 diagnoses - six with F84.9 pervasive developmental disorder unspecified, six with F84.0 autistic disorder and one with F84.5 Asperger syndrome - and includes four children with comorbid mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and one with epilepsy, all reported per participant rather than excluded. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the authors identify developmental coordination disorder and ADHD as necessary additions for establishing whether the motor finding is autism-specific or shared across neurodevelopmental conditions.

**S-067** [local_9ca9b2cc] — *Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment*

Eleven autistic boys recruited from Al Ain Hospital in the United Arab Emirates, all with CARS2 scores between 30 and 36.5 - the mild-to-moderate band - under 16 years of age with a mean of 9.03 years (SD 2.56), and all required to have at least minimal verbal capability, being able to understand verbal communication and answer yes or no. Six of the eleven continued into the long-term study, with no explanation given for the other five. There is no comparison group of any kind, which is consistent with the design: the study measures attention within an intervention rather than discriminating between populations. Two features of the sample are worth recording for the review. Reporting a CARS2 range as an eligibility criterion is more severity characterisation than most included studies provide, and it bounds the population precisely - but because only the range is given rather than per-child scores, within-sample severity variation cannot be related to any outcome. And the eligibility requirements taken together - male, mild to moderate, verbally responsive - define a narrow population, so the system's behaviour with non-speaking or more severely affected children is untested despite the abstract describing the target group as having 'minimal verbal capabilities'.

**S-068** [local_02fa4215] — *Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning*

Two groups of 100 children each: 100 autistic children recruited from the Child Psychiatry Department at Mayo Hospital Lahore and a private autism school, and 100 children described as healthy whose recruitment source is never stated. The comparison group was collected specifically 'to ensure that our model is trained without any class imbalance problem', so its purpose is stated as statistical rather than clinical. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-069** [local_29a3fc54] — *Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism*

Two groups from a single neuroimaging cohort: 104 autistic participants recruited of whom 90 were analysed, and 28 typically developing. All 14 exclusions for poor recording quality came from the autistic group, a differential attrition of 13.5% against 0% that is reported but not discussed - and one that plausibly removes the participants whose speech was hardest to capture, potentially the most severely affected. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The 90:28 imbalance is addressed analytically by repeated undersampling rather than left uncorrected.

**S-070** [local_b7ec3755] — *Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images*

Two groups from the Saliency4ASD benchmark: 14 autistic children and 14 typically developing children, a balanced 28 in total. Both group sizes are reported, but nothing else about either group is. No other-diagnosis or subthreshold comparison group. The autistic and typically developing children are the same in the training and test partitions - the split is over the 400 images (300 train, 100 test), not over participants.

**S-071** [local_684969f6] — *Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data*

Two groups from the Saliency4ASD benchmark: 14 autistic and 14 typically developing children, 28 in total. Every one of the 300 training and validation images was viewed by all 28 children, and the 100 test images likewise, so the three partitions are cuts through the same 28 people - 5542 training scanpaths, 1411 validation scanpaths and 2868 test scanpaths all originate from the same fourteen autistic and fourteen typically developing children. This is stated plainly by the authors and is the fact on which their own closing hypothesis turns. No other-diagnosis or subthreshold group.

**S-072** [local_35004e74] — *Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children*

Three samples, all explicitly sized. Training set: 34 autistic and 34 typically developing children. Testing Set 1: a further 34 and 34, drawn from the same 136-child pool and 'equally distributed' with the training set, matched on diagnosis, age, gender and ADOS module. Testing Set 2: 101 videos from autistic children only, aged 2 to 6.9. The partition is by participant, so the 68 children in Testing Set 1 contributed no data to training - the defining structural strength of the study. Testing Set 2's single-class composition is a real limitation on what it can validate: with no typically developing children, its 80.2% figure is sensitivity alone and cannot detect a model that has drifted toward calling everyone autistic. No other-diagnosis or developmentally-delayed comparison group appears anywhere, so the model is never tested against the discrimination that matters clinically - autism versus other developmental concern - only against typical development.

**S-073** [local_fa91fc18] — *Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities*

Two groups of 30, both explicitly sized: 30 children with a DSM-5 and ADOS-2 diagnosis of autism recruited from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, and 30 typically developing children recruited from a primary school. No other-diagnosis or developmentally-delayed comparison group, which the authors themselves identify as the key gap, noting that the motor signature 'may overlap with other disorders, such as attention deficit disorder, motor coordination disturbance, or general intellectual disabilities'. The two groups come from structurally different settings - a clinic where the autistic children receive ongoing psychomotor and speech therapy, versus a school - so group membership is confounded with familiarity with clinical testing, with the examiner's setting, and potentially with prior therapeutic work on exactly the fine-motor skills being measured. This is not discussed.

**S-074** [local_115dfe8d] — *A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children*

Two groups, both explicitly sized: 40 autistic children and 50 typically developing children, 90 in total, aged 3-6. Typically developing children came from a local kindergarten; the autistic children's site is identified only obliquely as 'the school site' where reliable diagnostic information was limited, which suggests a special-education setting but is never stated. No other-diagnosis or developmental-delay comparison group, so the model is tested only against typical development. The class imbalance (40:50) is handled correctly at the validation level by stratified fold construction, and both classes are large enough that the confusion-matrix decomposition is meaningful.

**S-075** [local_5b7ea7dc] — *AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Two groups, both explicitly sized and accounted for: 50 typically developing children (27 male) and 44 autistic children (22 male), from an initial 50 ASD-suspected recruits of whom 6 were excluded for ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores below 3. Recruitment sources are named - the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Division of Seoul National University Hospital for the clinical group and preschools for the comparison group. All 94 children are allocated across the three partitions without overlap: 40 to training and validation, 36 to test set #1, 18 to test set #2. No other-diagnosis comparison group, which matters here because ADHD and developmental coordination disorder were deliberately excluded rather than recruited as contrast groups - so the model is never asked to make the discrimination that would distinguish autism-specific joint-attention impairment from impairment secondary to attention or motor difficulty.

**S-076** [local_87fe26aa] — *Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Two groups of 40, recruited from special education schools and from regular kindergartens respectively. Both are explicitly sized and their sex composition is identical (33 boys, 7 girls each). No other-diagnosis or developmental-delay comparison group. The recruitment asymmetry is the structural weakness: children attending special education schools and children attending regular kindergartens differ in developmental level, in daily environment, and in familiarity with being assessed, and none of these is measured. With no cognitive or language measure taken, group membership in this study is inseparable from educational placement, and a classifier that separates the two groups at 87.5% cannot be shown to be separating them on autism rather than on the correlates of placement.

**S-077** [local_893ce2fa] — *An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images*

Not answerable from this paper. Groups are described only as image classes - 328 non-ASD images and 219 ASD images, 547 in total - and the number of children contributing them is never stated. The paper's entire treatment of participants is one sentence directing the reader elsewhere: 'For more information about participants diagnosed with ASD and non-ASD, see [44]'. This is the only study in the corpus that reports no participant count at all, in either group. Because the source is the same gaze-path collection Cilia and colleagues assembled - 547 images with roughly nine images per child - the underlying sample is a few dozen children, but nothing in this paper permits that inference, and no participant identifier is available to group images by child.

**S-078** [local_dffe4127] — *Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals*

Two groups, with complete flow accounting. 183 individuals were initially recruited (67 autistic, 20 female, 22 at Caltech; 116 typically developing, 33 female, 34 at Caltech). 176 watched Episode A (62 autistic) and 167 watched Episode B (59 autistic); analyses were restricted to the 166 who watched both (58 autistic). Thirteen were then excluded for eye-tracking data quality - specifically, missing or off-screen gaze for more than half of one or both episodes - leaving 48 autistic and 105 typically developing participants. The exclusion was strongly differential: 10 of 58 autistic participants (17.2%) against 3 of 108 controls (2.8%), a figure reported precisely but not discussed. Its direction matters for interpretation: the analysed autistic sample is the subset whose gaze could be tracked reliably throughout 43 minutes of video, which if anything strengthens rather than weakens the paper's conclusion that classification fails, since the participants most likely to produce noisy data were removed. Participants were split across two independent sites, with 17 autistic and 33 control participants at Caltech and the remainder at Indiana University. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-079** [local_2b766683] — *Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech*

Two groups from a crowdsourced convenience sample: 20 children with a parent-reported autism diagnosis and 38 neurotypical children, 58 in total, contributing 77 videos over four years from 2018 to 2021. Clip counts were deliberately balanced at 425 per class, which means the 20 autistic children contributed roughly 21 clips each against roughly 11 each for the 38 comparison children - so the autistic class is built from fewer children sampled more densely, and each autistic child exerts about twice the influence on the class representation. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The recruitment mechanism is itself distinctive: families downloaded a mobile game, played it at home, and then chose whether to share the recording, so the sample is self-selected among app users willing to disclose a diagnosis and share video of their child.

**S-080** [local_2895bdf0] — *Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection*

Two analytic groups from three clinical ones: 88 autistic participants and 70 non-autistic participants, the latter formed by merging children with ADHD and typically developing children. The merge is justified on two stated grounds and both are substantive - preliminary analyses showed no significant difference between the ADHD and typically developing subgroups on any automated language measure, and 'including a non-autistic clinical group alongside TD participants provided an opportunity to more adequately test for the specificity of the results with respect to the presence or absence of autism'. This is the corpus's clearest instance of a study building the specificity test into its comparison group rather than naming it as future work. Flow accounting is complete: 289 screened, 104 excluded for not meeting strict diagnostic criteria, 10 for failing to complete initial assessment, leaving 175 in the parent neuroimaging study (102 ASD, 45 ADHD, 28 TD); 6 autistic participants excluded for untranscribable ADOS sessions due to poor sound quality or non-compliance; and 11 more excluded for analysis - 6 with undefined um proportion because neither um nor uh occurred in the task, 4 without IQ results, and 1 with an acoustically corrupted file. Note that the exclusions fall disproportionately on the autistic group (14 of 17), and that the 6 excluded for producing no filled pauses at all are plausibly among the least verbally fluent.

**S-081** [local_423b636b] — *Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers*

Three groups identified, two analysed. Of 457 toddlers recruited during well-child checkups at four pediatric primary care clinics, 41 were subsequently diagnosed with autism under DSM-5 and 416 were classified neurotypical. A third group of 12 who screened positive on the M-CHAT-R/F and received a non-autism diagnosis - language delay without autism is the example given - was excluded from analysis because of small sample size. That exclusion is the design's one substantive omission, since those 12 are precisely the children against whom a screening tool must discriminate, and their removal means the reported AUC reflects autism versus typical development rather than autism versus developmental concern. The neurotypical group is nonetheless better ascertained than most comparison groups in this corpus, being formed of two subsets - children with a negative M-CHAT-R/F and no caregiver or physician concern, and children who screened positive or raised concern but were then judged on the ADOS-2 and psychologist clinical judgment to have no developmental or autism-related concerns. The 41:416 ratio is the study's most consequential structural feature: it approximates the base rate a deployed screening tool would encounter, in contrast to the balanced designs that dominate this review.

**S-082** [local_ffa35101] — *Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study*

Four groups across two languages, with recruitment and analysis counts that do not match. Recruited: 55 English-speaking autistic, 39 English-speaking comparison, 28 Cantonese-speaking autistic, 24 Cantonese-speaking comparison. Analysed: 33, 33, 24 and 24 respectively, stated in a parenthesis within the narrative-elicitation section - so 22 of 55 English autistic participants (40%) and 6 of 39 English comparison participants (15%) do not appear in the analysis, with no reason given, no flow diagram, and no comparison between retained and dropped participants. The demographic table reports 28 for the Cantonese autistic group where the analysis text says 24, a further inconsistency. The English participants come from a larger family-genetic study of autism that also enrolled parents and controls; the Cantonese participants were recruited via social media, schools and organisations serving autistic people, and employment programmes for adults previously diagnosed with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism. No other-diagnosis comparison group in either language.

**S-083** [local_81ecbc6f] — *Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings*

Two groups of 25, recruited through a university clinic, diagnostic or therapeutic centres and schools, and 'matched for age, sex and ethnicity, and nearly matched for intelligence quotients'. The autistic group required a prior clinical diagnosis of idiopathic autism from a multidisciplinary team including a psychiatrist under ICD-10 criteria; the comparison group was excluded for personal or family history of autism, history of developmental disorders, and neurological or psychiatric conditions or suspected genetic syndromes. No other-diagnosis comparison group, which the authors identify as a limitation and propose for future work: 'as we compared individuals with ASD and controls with TD, future studies should include individuals with non-spectrum disorders and other psychiatric conditions'. The design's distinguishing feature is that two further comparators operate on the same 50 participants - two standardised instruments and two human raters - so the study contains four independent classification approaches on one sample rather than one model evaluated in isolation.

**S-084** [local_bc62bc4b] — *Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening*

Two groups recruited: 61 toddlers with a clinical DSM-5 autism diagnosis and 72 typically developing toddlers, all aged 26-36 months, from a university-based research centre in Ankara. Recruitment was multi-source for the autistic group - a research centre database, speech and language clinics, and child psychiatrists at accredited hospitals, across both metropolitan and rural areas - and community-based for comparisons. No developmental-delay comparison group, which the authors identify as needed: future work should include 'children with developmental delays'. The critical unresolved issue is that the classification analyses do not appear to use all 133 recruited children. The paper states that 'we used balanced datasets in our study in terms of ASD and TD children distribution... in which all classes had the same number of training samples', and every reported accuracy across all six results tables falls on a 2.5-percentage-point grid while every per-class true positive rate falls on a 0.05 grid - a pattern arithmetically consistent with roughly 20 participants per class and inconsistent with 61 and 72. No exclusion count, flow accounting or subsampling rule is given anywhere, so the number of children behind the headline 87.5% and the basis on which they were selected are both unstated.

**S-085** [local_889d9bd6] — *Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children*

Two cohorts, each with two groups. Toddler cohort: 55 autistic children (aged 1.5-3, including eight aged 1.6-1.8) and 40 typically developing. Preschool cohort: 37 autistic children (aged 3-5) and 41 typically developing. Autistic participants came from the Child Mental Health and Rehabilitation Center of a maternity and child healthcare hospital; comparison children from a local kindergarten or from routine annual check-ups in the same hospital's outpatient ward. No developmental-delay or other-diagnosis comparison group, and the authors identify the consequence explicitly as spectrum bias. The two-cohort structure is the study's design contribution: rather than treating age as a covariate to be adjusted away, the cohorts are analysed both jointly through a diagnosis-by-age-group interaction and separately through cohort-specific classifiers, which is what permits the finding that different areas of interest discriminate at different ages. A discrepancy sits unreconciled between the 37 + 41 = 78 preschoolers reported in the results and the 'N = 74 for preschool' stated in the leave-one-out description, and exclusion counts from the two quality-control steps - calibration failure and off-screen fixation - are not reported for either cohort.

**S-086** [local_361b59fb] — *Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

One consecutively enrolled cohort rather than contrasted groups, with the three-level reference standard producing the comparison structure. Of 711 enrolled, 425 completed both the Device inputs and the specialist evaluation; specialists classified 122 (28.7%) as autism-positive, 263 (61.9%) as autism-negative with at least one other developmental or behavioural condition, and 40 (9.4%) as autism-negative and neurotypical. That composition is the study's decisive structural advantage over every other study in this corpus: the comparison against which the Device is judged is overwhelmingly children with other developmental concerns rather than typically developing children, which is the discrimination a primary care tool actually has to make. Attrition is documented in a flow diagram and its causes disclosed - 126 dropped out before completing Device inputs and a further 160 after completing inputs but before the specialist evaluation, with the COVID-19 national emergency in March 2020 closing 9 of 14 sites, preventing an estimated 100 specialist visits, and the authors estimating the drop-out rate absent COVID at 26.2%. Completers and non-completers are shown to be demographically similar in a side-by-side table.

**S-087** [local_afdb603d] — *Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.*

Two groups of 14, drawn from a homogeneous Tuscan area between Florence, Pistoia and Prato, and matched by construction on group size, age range and sex ratio. The autistic children came from the speech and language therapy service of AUSL Toscana Centro and the Opera Santa Rita foundation, and their recordings were reused from a prior thesis project on discourse and storytelling in autism. The comparison children were recruited separately for this study 'from the same geographical area' with 'the same demographic characteristics'. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The critical structural fact is that the two groups were not merely recruited separately but recorded separately, at different times, by different people, using different equipment, in different environments - a distinction that matters far more for acoustic analysis than for the behavioural comparisons elsewhere in this corpus, and one that the paper discloses fully while underweighting its consequences.

**S-088** [local_4f7e7eb3] — *Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques*

Two groups inherited from the Carette et al. dataset: 29 autistic children contributing 219 images and 30 typically developing children contributing 328 images, 547 images from 59 children in total. This paper is more informative than Gaspar and colleagues on the same data, which reported only image counts, since it restates the participant counts and sex composition from the source publication. But the participant structure is then entirely disregarded in the analysis: the 80/20 partition operates on images, so children are not the unit at any stage and images from the same child necessarily span the training and test sets at roughly nine images per participant. No other-diagnosis or developmental-delay comparison group. The class imbalance of 219 to 328 is addressed by differential augmentation of the training and validation partitions - sevenfold for the autistic class, tenfold for the comparison class - rather than by any participant-level consideration.

**S-089** [local_db6c2d7c] — *Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With*

Two groups from a crowdsourced app population: 68 children with parent-reported autism (53 male, 15 female) contributing 380 videos and 27 neurotypical children (18 male, 9 female) contributing 69 videos, 95 children and 449 videos in total, from approximately 1,000 individuals who downloaded the app. The imbalance is substantial and runs opposite to the direction usual in this corpus - cases outnumber controls by more than two to one at child level and by more than five to one at video level, which the authors identify as the reason for choosing macro- and weighted-average metrics over accuracy. After frame filtering the imbalance is similar (520,536 autistic frames against 99,084), so per-video frame retention was comparable between groups, which is a useful check that the automated quality filters did not operate differentially. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

**S-090** [local_8b5fb23b] — *Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms*

Two groups inherited from the Carette dataset: 29 autistic children contributing 219 images and 30 typically developing children contributing 328 images, 547 images from 59 children. The participant structure is not merely restated but actually used, which distinguishes this paper from the other two reuses of the same data in this corpus: a 'mini batch dataset that encapsulated only single trials from each of 59 participants' is constructed and evaluated separately. That analysis is the study's most valuable output. The main analyses nonetheless proceed at image level, so in the 70:30 split of 547 images and in the augmented analysis of 2,566 images, images from the same child appear in both training and test at roughly 9.3 images per participant. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The class imbalance of 219 to 328 is not corrected in the original analysis and is partly amplified by uniform augmentation, which preserves the ratio at 1,047 to 1,519.

**S-091** [local_6dcefc34] — *Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism*

Two groups from a remotely recruited convenience sample: 28 children with a parent-reported formal autism diagnosis (19 male, 9 female) and 21 neurotypical children (10 male, 7 female, 4 not reporting sex), 49 in total, with data accumulated between April 2017 and February 2021. Recruitment ran through four channels - the app's existing user base, the Hartwell Foundation's KidsFirst autism research database, ResearchMatch.org and Facebook advertisements - which is a more diverse sampling frame than the single-channel recruitment typical here, though all routes select for families with smartphones, internet access and English literacy, and the last two select for research-engaged families. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the diagnostic menu presented to parents included ADHD/ADD, anxiety and speech and language delay, so children with those labels would presumably have been identifiable had they been recruited. The class imbalance is modest (28 to 21) and is handled by SMOTE upsampling applied within each cross-validation split rather than to the whole dataset.

**S-092** [local_65974fc7] — *Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction*

Two groups described only in aggregate: 'more than 80 ASD children and more than 60 normal children', from whom about 4,000 and 3,000 recordings respectively were collected in cooperation with Anhui Medical University, the Anhui Autism Association and special education schools. After quality exclusion 'less than 1/3 of the data was usable', and 511 autistic and 506 comparison recordings were randomly selected for analysis. Participant counts are given imprecisely ('more than'), no exact numbers are stated, and the mapping between children and recordings is never specified - so the analysed sample is roughly six recordings per child but the actual distribution is unknown. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The critical structural fact is that all analysis, splitting and reporting operates on recordings, and children are never used as a unit at any stage.

**S-093** [local_988c462e] — *The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation*

One cohort of 132 children recorded during routine ADOS-2 assessments, partitioned by diagnosis into 105 autistic and 27 non-autistic. The comparison group is the design feature worth noting: it comprises children 'diagnosed with language or developmental delays or were defined as typically developing', so it is a clinically referred population rather than a screened-typical one. That means the model is fitted across the range of children who actually present for autism assessment, and the regression target spans a continuum from ADOS 0 to 30 rather than two discrete classes. The proportion of the 27 who were developmentally delayed rather than typically developing is not reported, which limits how far the specificity claim can be pushed. No exclusion criteria are stated beyond the downstream requirement of at least 20 seconds and 50 vocalisations of child speech, and how many children that requirement removed is not reported.

**S-094** [local_76de1c03] — *The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children*

Ten children aged 5.5 to 6.5 years (mean 6.08, SD 0.4), recruited through the kindergartens they attended in Poland: five diagnosed with autism and five typically developing, each group comprising four boys and one girl. The sample is the smallest in the review, and its composition is nonetheless carefully constructed - exact sex matching, a 12-month age band, and both groups drawn from the same kindergartens, so the recruitment asymmetry that affects nearly every case-control study charted here does not arise. Diagnoses were taken from kindergarten records and had been delivered by a multidisciplinary team of a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a pedagogue, which is genuine clinical ascertainment even though the instruments and criteria are not stated. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is reported. With five children per group, the study can support group-level inference about large effects and cannot support any statement about individual-level discrimination, which is consistent with what it claims.

**S-095** [local_3ba6d25c] — *Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach*

Two groups. Enrolled: 20 ASD and 23 TD. Analysed: 19 ASD and 20 TD, after data from 1 ASD and 3 TD children were dropped for eye-tracking technical failure. Total analysed n = 39. No third or clinical comparison group. The unit of analysis for the model, however, is the gaze behaviour segment, not the child: at 9 s the two groups jointly contribute several thousand segments (exact counts shown only graphically in Fig. 2b), and because ASD sessions were 74% longer on average the ASD group supplies systematically more segments at every window length.

**S-096** [local_70a30e2b] — *A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features*

Three groups recruited, two modelled. Recruited: 28 children with ASD, 18 typically developing children, and 4 children with other disorders (cerebral palsy and fragile X syndrome), total 50, all aged 3-6 years and tested at an autism centre in Tehran. Modelled: 46 subjects, which is exactly 28 + 18, so the four-child other-disorder group is excluded from every classification result without the exclusion being stated. A further subgroup is described but not removed: five of the 28 autistic children 'did not seem interested in playing with the sensorized toy car and neglected it completely', so roughly 18% of the autism group contributed a session of near-zero play. Whether their data were retained is not stated explicitly, but the 46-subject count implies they were, and one of the three selected encoder features is the not-playing ratio.

**S-097** [local_a22f97df] — *A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities*

Two groups of 30, total 60 children aged 5-10 years. ASD group: 30 children, mean age 7 years +/- 1.4, recruited from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center where they were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, all diagnosed under both DSM-5 criteria and ADOS-2, with no existing comorbidities as an inclusion requirement. TD group: 30 children, mean age 6 years 8 months +/- 1, recruited from a primary school, with no confirmed neurodevelopmental disorder and excluded for suspected autism signs, developmental abnormalities, or any current or past psychiatric or neurological history. All 60 had normal vision and no sensory or motor deficits, and any child about whom a clinician or teacher was uncertain was excluded. No attrition or exclusions after enrolment are reported. The modelled dataset, however, is not 60 rows but 1,500: each child contributed 25 task observations (five tasks at each of five difficulty levels), and it is these observations, not the children, that are the unit of the reported cross-validation.

**S-098** [local_c6853fe2] — *A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation*

Thirty children in total: 29 with autism and 1 typically developing, mean age 3.65 years. Selection was by ADOS-2 module - only children assessed with the TM, M1 or M2 modules were included, i.e. children from 12 months upward with little or no fluent oral expression, excluding the M3 and M4 modules used for verbally fluent older children and adults. There is no comparison group in any meaningful sense; the single typically developing participant cannot support a between-group contrast and the paper never attempts one. A second and more relevant unit of analysis exists: 109 individual name-call test events, since each child receives up to five calls (three in natural tone at about 3 s intervals, then up to two reinforced calls by clinician or parent). These 109 events are the denominator for the study's highest reported figure of 98.2%, but they are not independent - they cluster within 30 children and are strongly serially dependent, because a child who ignores the first call usually ignores the remaining four. Table 2 shows the consequence: 17 of the 30 children scored 5, meaning they did not respond to any of the five calls.

**S-099** [local_f1b626c8] — *Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games*

Two groups of 20, total 40 children, all male, aged roughly 4 to 12 years. The autistic group was drawn from the Daily Rehabilitation Clinic for Children with Special Disorders in Tehran, affiliated to the Family Institute of Shahid Beheshti University; the comparison group came from Namjoo public elementary school. Enrolment and attrition are reported for the autistic group only: 25 children with 'high-performance autism' were selected, of whom 5 (20%) were excluded under the study's stated exclusion criteria - refusing to sit on the chair, or failure to calibrate the eye tracker - and their data were never recorded. No exclusions, and indeed no exclusion criteria at all, are reported for the comparison group, so the two groups passed through different filters. The modelled dataset is not 40 rows but 240: arithmetic on the reported training, validation and test percentages fixes the row count exactly (168 + 36 + 36 = 240, with 132 + 24 + 21 = 177 correct and 177/240 = 73.75% matching the reported 73.8% total), so each child contributes six observations to a randomly partitioned dataset.

**S-100** [local_6249bd63] — *Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior*

Forty-four adults enrolled (17 autistic, 27 neurotypical), of whom two were excluded because they had not consented to this particular set of experiments or their data could not be processed, giving a final sample of 42: 15 autistic and 27 neurotypical, i.e. 35.7% autism prevalence. All were native and fluent English speakers. A second sample is central to the design and is reported with equal care: 19 human raters, comprising 8 expert clinicians (doctoral-level, with extensive autism training at the Center for Autism Research) and 11 non-experts (mostly BA-level psychology staff with some familiarity with autism but no specialised training), all of whom rated all 42 videos. A third group also participates without being analysed: 10 conversation confederates (3 male, 7 female, all native English speakers, undergraduate or BA-level research assistants), semi-randomly assigned by availability and clinical judgement, and blind to participant diagnostic status. The unit of analysis for the model is the participant - one 6,272-dimensional vector each - which is why no within-participant leakage is possible.

**S-101** [local_8b9e0e8a] — *Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas*

Two groups, with a corpus considerably larger than most in this review. Total recruited: 333 children aged 3-6, comprising 140 with autism (112 boys, 28 girls; mean age 4.66 +/- 1.00 years) and 193 typically developing (122 boys, 71 girls; mean age 4.77 +/- 0.92 years), all with normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Recruitment was multi-centre, from several hospitals and schools across Shaanxi and Fujian provinces. The evaluation set is 165 subjects - 70 autistic and 95 typically developing - formed by a 50% subject-level random split, with robustness checked over five permutations. The paper explicitly frames sample size as a methodological argument rather than a logistical fact: Fig. 14(a) visualises how group separability degrades as more subjects are added, and the discussion states that 'when the number of subjects is less than 100, the test cannot accurately reflect the performance of the model' - a direct criticism of the small-sample studies that dominate this corpus, and one this study is entitled to make. A second unit of analysis exists and is handled correctly: each child contributes 82 stimulus-based viewing patterns, and these are scored individually before being aggregated to a subject-level decision, but the split is by child so the 82 patterns never straddle training and test.

**S-102** [local_0e476686] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts*

Two groups of Twitter accounts rather than of assessed people: 221 users whose public biography states that they are autistic and 31 users who do not, totalling 252. The imbalance is severe and consequential. Because the modelled dataset was balanced at the tweet level - 45,000 per class from a cleaned pool of 404,627 - each of the 31 comparison users contributes on average about 1,450 tweets while each of the 221 autistic users contributes about 200, a sevenfold difference in per-user concentration. The entire negative class is therefore the writing of 31 individuals. No user was recruited, contacted or aware of the study; the data are historical public posts from 1 January 2017 to 31 January 2022. Cleaning removed 60% of the raw corpus (1,014,723 to 404,627 tweets) by deleting duplicates, retweets, incompletely extracted tweets and cross-platform auto-posts, which is a substantial and appropriately reported reduction, though it is not broken down by user or by group.

**S-103** [local_fbaf69bf] — *Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Four hundred and thirty-six toddlers aged 17-36 months, comprising 40 with autism and 396 typically developing, recruited at four paediatric primary care clinics during routine well-child visits.
