The recruitment route is the defining feature and separates this study from almost every other in the corpus: children were not enrolled as known cases and known controls, but as consecutive clinic attenders who received the M-CHAT-R/F as part of standard care and were referred for ADOS-Toddler evaluation only if they screened positive or if a caregiver or clinician raised a developmental concern. The resulting 9.2% autism prevalence is far closer to a real screening population than the near-balanced designs elsewhere here. Exclusion criteria are stated in full and are practical rather than diagnostic: known hearing or vision impairment, child too upset, caregiver not interested or without time or needing to care for siblings or unable to consent in English or Spanish, child did not complete the procedures, and missing clinical information. The analysed sample varies by movie because only participants with at least 40% valid landmark data for a given movie were included, and those per-movie counts are shown graphically rather than tabulated - the one place where the participant accounting is less transparent than the rest of the paper.

**S-104** [local_74416ba7] — *Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders*

Two independent datasets and three diagnostic groups. Adults: 15 with autism (9 male, 6 female), 15 with schizophrenia (7 male, 8 female) and 16 controls (8 male, 8 female), the latter selected from 26 available controls in order to equalise group sizes, with the selection made by ranking on SRS-2 score in descending order. Children: 15 with autism (13 male, 2 female) and 15 controls (7 male, 8 female), again reduced from 17 by SRS-2 ranking. The presence of a schizophrenia group is what distinguishes this sample from almost every other in the corpus: it supplies a psychiatric rather than merely a neurotypical contrast, and although no autism-versus-schizophrenia classifier is built, the parallel analyses against a common control group produce the study's most useful finding. Note also that the modelled unit is the trial rather than the participant - each adult contributes 21 trials and each child 32 - but the cross-validation splits by participant, so the two levels are handled correctly in the modelling even though the statistical analysis treats trials as independent.

**S-105** [local_7c6a5aa4] — *Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders*

A very large uncontrolled user population with a very small labelled subset. FreeSpeech attracted 6,033 users between January 2012 and May 2014, of whom 5,372 generated enough events to be usable (761 excluded), collectively producing over 2.5 million button presses. Of these, 214 users voluntarily completed an online survey and 180 disclosed a diagnosis - 81 autistic and 99 non-autistic, which is 3.4% of the usable user base. The non-autistic group is itself clinically diverse: Table III lists 32 users reporting no diagnosis, 49 'other', 12 stroke, 4 ALS, 4 dementia, 4 brain injury and 3 ADHD alongside 88 with autism. Two internal inconsistencies should be recorded: Table III sums to 196 and Table II (age bands) to 235, against stated totals of 180 disclosing a diagnosis and 214 completing the survey, and Table III's 88 autistic users does not match the 81 stated in the text. The modelled unit is neither the user nor the session but the window - a fixed-length run of 10 to 100 consecutive key presses - so a heavy user contributes far more pseudo-samples than a light one, and the effective sample size for the classification experiments is never stated. Critically, the headline result is obtained after k-means clustering has assigned pseudo-labels to the roughly 5,192 users who never disclosed anything, so most of the data underlying the 82% figure carry machine-generated labels.

**S-106** [local_8a706eaa] — *Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder*

One hundred and ten children aged 24 to 72 months were screened between 5 August 2021 and 18 July 2022, of whom 95 (86.4%) completed study measures and formed the analytical population: 45 autistic and 50 typically developing. Enrolment criteria were age 24-72 months, ability to sit, and no history of visual or auditory deficits. Recruitment was asymmetric by design - autistic children came from a single national referral centre, the Seoul National University Hospital Child Psychiatry Outpatient Clinic, while comparison children came from day care centres across South Korea, with participants distributed across Seoul (25%), other metropolitan cities (25%) and provinces (50%). The paper states openly that 'conservative inclusion criteria' were applied on both sides 'to select individuals belonging to clinically distinct groups to ensure development of an accurate and precise ASD vs TD classification model' - so the extremity of the contrast is a deliberate design choice, disclosed rather than concealed, and is the single most important fact for interpreting the near-perfect detection results. Each child contributed up to ten IJA clips and five clips per RJA task from a single 10-minute session, and the cross-validation groups by individual so those clips never straddle folds.

**S-107** [local_6b9484ce] — *Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking*

Fifty-nine children contributing 547 scanpath images - the fourth independent reuse of this dataset encountered in this review. The study reports nothing further about who those children were: no counts per group, no ages, no sex, no diagnostic information. The dataset is described purely as two folders, 'TCImages' for typically developing children and 'TSImages' for children diagnosed with autism. The modelled unit is the image, and the split is 382 training, 108 validation and 57 test images with no indication that a child's images were kept together. Because 547 images come from 59 children, each child contributes roughly nine images, so under a random image-level split every test image is accompanied by around eight images from the same child in training or validation. The test-set confusion matrix implies 34 typically developing and 23 autism images among the 57 held out, which is the only class-composition information recoverable anywhere in the paper.

**S-108** [local_c6a4ea7b] — *SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism*

Seventy-six children assembled from three independent corpora in the CHILDES databank: Eigsti (16 autistic, 16 typically developing, aged 3-6, 30-minute free play), Nadig (13 autistic, 25 typically developing, aged 3-7, approximately 10 minutes of parent-child free play) and Flusberg (6 autistic, no comparison children, aged 12-26 months, natural mother-child interaction), giving 35 autistic and 41 typically developing overall. The composition matters more than the totals. Flusberg contributes autistic children only, so corpus membership is partially informative about diagnosis by construction, and it contributes them from an age band - infancy and early toddlerhood - that no comparison child occupies. The three corpora also differ in session length by a factor of three, in conversation partner, and in transcription era and convention. The paper notes that the Eigsti corpus contains a developmental delay group alongside autism and typical development, but that group is not used. No child-level information beyond corpus, group and corpus-level age range is reported anywhere.

**S-109** [local_5c43dffa] — *Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths*

Ninety-nine children were enrolled and 86 had valid eye-gaze data - 54 autistic and 32 typically developing according to Table 1 and the participant text, though the abstract states 55 autistic, an unresolved inconsistency. The 13 excluded participants are not characterised. Participants span the full paediatric age range and are grouped into five bands, with the autistic group distributed 3/11/23/13/4 across 0-1, 2-4, 5-9, 10-17 and 18+ years and the comparison group 5/6/16/5/0. Sex composition differs sharply: 44 male and 10 female among autistic participants (81.5% male) against 15 male and 17 female among comparison participants (46.9% male). The paper states plainly that 'each subject has a different number of recorded ET videos and the data is unbalanced with respect to diagnosis, age, and gender'. The modelled unit is not the child but the scan-path image, one per participant per video clip: 1,012 autistic and 380 typically developing images before augmentation, from 1,414 total clip viewings across 86 children - roughly sixteen images per child, unevenly distributed since Table 6 shows individual clips viewed anywhere from once to 92 times.

**S-110** [local_32da8ede] — *A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths*

Fifty-nine children producing 547 scan-path images - the fifth independent reuse of this dataset encountered in the review. Unlike the other reuses charted here, this paper reports the source participant statistics in a dedicated table: 29 autistic and 30 typically developing children, 38 male (64%) and 21 female (36%), mean age 7.88 years and median 8.1, with CARS mean 32.97 and median 34.50. The image split is 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic, so roughly nine images per child. None of the demographic or clinical variables is broken down by diagnostic group, so it cannot be determined whether the groups were matched on age or sex - the sex ratio of 64% male across the whole sample is compatible with anything from a balanced split to a heavily male autistic group and a balanced comparison group. The 547 images, not the 59 children, are the unit of cross-validation throughout.

**S-111** [local_15ed96cb] — *A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning*

A national population cohort rather than a recruited sample - 780,610 Israeli children born between 2014 and 2019 with at least two years of computerised well-baby records, of whom 775,941 entered the analysis: 1,163 with an autism diagnosis recorded after age two and 774,778 without autism or another pervasive developmental or medical condition. This is by four orders of magnitude the largest sample in the review and the only one drawn from an unselected population. Case ascertainment used two routes and both counts are given: 722 children (56.6%) identified by ICD-9 code and 553 (43.4%) by keyword search of provider free-text notes with manual verification that the reference concerned the child rather than a family member. A further 112 children with autism diagnosed before age two were excluded to preserve the temporal separation between predictors and outcome. Conditions sharing the ASD acronym, notably atrial septal defect, were screened out. Down syndrome was excluded from the comparison group but Fragile X, tuberous sclerosis and other autism-associated aetiologies were deliberately retained, on the reasoning that autism has multiple aetiologies and excluding them would narrow the target condition artificially. The resulting incidence of 0.0015 is roughly a tenth of Israel's reported national rate, and the authors state this openly as a limitation.

**S-112** [local_261afa51] — *AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: &#x201C;A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System&#x201D;*

There are no participants in the ordinary sense - the study analyses 2,836 photographs, 1,418 labelled autistic and 1,418 not, obtained from a public Kaggle dataset. The provenance is stated plainly and is the study's decisive feature: 'the images of autistic children's faces were sourced from online platforms focusing on autism disorder, while the images of non-autistic children's faces were randomly gathered from the internet'. So the two classes are not two groups of children assessed under common conditions but two collections of photographs assembled from different corners of the internet for different reasons. The number of distinct children behind the images is unknown and cannot be recovered, so it is impossible to know whether ten photographs represent ten children or one, or whether the same child appears on both sides of the training-test split. Age is stated as 24-72 months for both classes, but this is a claim in the dataset description rather than a verified attribute of scraped photographs. Nothing else about the children is known.

**S-113** [local_3e88f3ce] — *An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks*

One thousand one hundred and twelve subjects from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange I - 539 autistic and 573 controls - contributed by 17 international sites, each with its own scanner, acquisition protocol and recruitment practice. This is by a wide margin the largest sample in the review apart from the Israeli health-records cohort and the Twitter corpus, and it is the only one that comes with a full clinical phenotype: ADOS totals and subscales, ADOS-Gotham severity, ADI-R social and verbal domain totals, SRS raw totals, and full-scale, verbal and performance IQ. The paper reports none of these as sample characteristics - no age distribution, no sex ratio, no IQ means, no group comparison on anything - because it uses them as model inputs instead. Approximately 65 to 70 phenotype fields enter the classifier. The result is the review's sharpest inversion: the study with the richest clinical characterisation available describes its participants less than almost any other, having redirected that information into the feature vector.

**S-114** [local_5b5f2237] — *Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development*

Forty-three children were recruited - 20 autistic and 23 typically developing - and 41 analysed after data from two typically developing children were lost to technical problems, giving 20 autistic and 21 comparison participants aged 6-13 with at least average non-verbal intelligence. This is the same cohort and the same recordings already charted in this review under a different analysis (Zhao et al., oculomotor gaze entropy), where 19 autistic and 20 typically developing children were retained after four were dropped for eye-tracking failure. The two papers therefore analyse overlapping subsets of one conversation dataset with two different sensors on the same videos - eye tracking in one, whole-body movement extracted from the video in the other - which makes them unusually comparable and means they should not be treated as independent evidence in the synthesis. The unit of analysis here is the participant: each child contributes one 23-dimensional coherence vector, computed from their dyad with the interviewer. A further 21 surrogate dyads were constructed for the chance-level control by pairing children and adults from different videos.

**S-115** [local_13426811] — *Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning*

One hundred and thirty-five participants aged 14 and above, primarily 14 to 20: 64 diagnosed with autism spectrum and 71 non-autistic. The age floor is a reasoned choice rather than a convenience, selected as post-critical-period for language acquisition with reference to Lenneberg's and Newport's hypotheses, so that the linguistic measures reflect settled grammatical competence rather than ongoing acquisition. The comparison group is deliberately compound: 17 individuals who went through the same comprehensive clinical diagnostic process and were determined to have no psychiatric disorder, and 54 recruited as non-autistic, predominantly college students. Every comparison participant received the ADOS-2 and was confirmed non-spectrum against published cut-offs, with group means reported (Module 3 3.17 and Module 4 4.00 for the clinical subgroup; 2.01 and 4.27 for the recruited subgroup). The autistic cohort deliberately includes co-occurring conditions, displayed in a dedicated figure, on reasoning the authors set out explicitly. Recruitment and retrospective record analysis ran concurrently from September 2013 to October 2020.

**S-116** [local_948fa8d0] — *Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms*

There are no participants - 2,936 facial photographs from a Kaggle collection, evenly divided at 1,468 per class, described only as colour images of autistic and non-autistic children. The number of distinct children behind them is unknown and unrecoverable. This is the same publicly scraped 'Autistic Children Facial Dataset' already charted in this review in a companion study which used a 2,836-image version, and the two counts imply different snapshots of a dataset that has been revised. The companion study documents the provenance that this one does not mention: autistic images sourced from online platforms focused on autism, non-autistic images gathered separately from the internet.

**S-117** [local_893dfc22] — *Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed*

There are no autistic participants. The Extended Cohn-Kanade corpus supplies 327 sequences from 118 adult volunteers, of which only the peak frame of each sequence is used, giving roughly 2.8 images per person; the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces corpus supplies posed adult expressions photographed under fixed conditions, with its sample size not stated in this paper. Both are general-population affective-computing resources with no autism component, no autism labels and no clinical ascertainment of any kind. The paper's results section mentions once, in passing, 'the Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression (ASD-FE) dataset and the Extended Cohn-Kanade (CK+) dataset adapted for ASD research', but no such dataset is described, cited, sized or characterised anywhere in the methods and no adaptation procedure is specified, while the experiments reported in the results and figures are conducted on brightness variants of KDEF and on CK+ peak frames. The sample is therefore adult, non-autistic, and posed - three respects in which it differs from the population the study's stated purpose concerns, which is autistic children experiencing spontaneous distress.

**S-118** [local_e7c16f2a] — *Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification*

Twenty children aged 3-6, recruited between 13 February and 21 March 2023: 10 autistic (mean age 4 years, SD 0.94) from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center where they were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, and 10 typically developing (mean 3 years 9 months, SD 0.1) from a pre-primary and primary educational institute in the province of Naples. Inclusion for the autistic group required a clinical diagnosis, age 3-6 and absence of comorbid conditions; the only criterion for the comparison group was parent and teacher report of no neurodevelopmental disorder, with the paper stating explicitly that they were recruited 'without specific assessment of their pre-existing abilities'. The modelled unit is not the child but the trajectory: 738 trajectories were retained after filtering, roughly 37 per child, and a further set of computationally generated trajectories brought the correlation analysis to 932 samples. Twenty children is the smallest sample of any included study in this review, and the discrepancy between 20 participants and 738 modelling units is the central interpretive issue.

**S-119** [local_5a7ab52d] — *Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain*

Not reported. The paper states only that 'different data utilized for the analysis are collected manually, including physical and facial expression data' and that measurements 'are collected from various subjects'. No total sample size, no group sizes, no recruitment route, no eligibility criteria and no setting appear anywhere in the paper. Table 2 displays five individuals as illustrative samples, of whom three are labelled 'Detected' and two 'Not detected', but these are presented as examples of the data format rather than as the study population. A reader cannot determine whether the reported 96.44886% accuracy was computed on tens or thousands of individuals. This is the only included study in the review that reports no sample size at all.

**S-120** [local_8253c2ec] — *Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder*

Two thousand one hundred and fifty-four respondents across four public screening datasets, modelled separately by age band: toddlers aged 18-36 months (1,054 instances, 728 above and 326 below the screening cut-off), children aged 4-11 (292; 141 and 151), adolescents aged 12-16 (104; 63 and 41), and adults aged 17 and over (704; 189 and 515). The datasets originate from autism screening applications and are aggregated on the UCI Machine Learning Repository and Kaggle. Reporting the class distribution for every band, and discussing whether oversampling was warranted, is better practice than much of this corpus - and the counts also make plain what the 'positive' class is: respondents whose summed responses to ten screening items exceeded the instrument's published cut-off. No participant is known to have received any clinical assessment, no age or sex distribution is reported although both fields are present, and no ethnicity, socioeconomic or comorbidity distribution is given although jaundice at birth and family history of autism are among the tabulated fields.

**S-121** [local_1e9d0b71] — *Machine learning’s effectiveness*

One hundred and twenty-six five-year-olds - 64 boys and 62 girls - constituting approximately 99% of the five-year-old residents of Sazacho, Nagasaki Prefecture, assessed during their routine preschool medical examinations. This is a whole-population age cohort rather than a recruited sample, and it is the second study in this review with genuinely population-based sampling, alongside the Israeli well-baby records study. Group assignment used the Social Responsiveness Scale, Second Edition completed by mothers, dichotomised at published sex-specific Japanese cut-offs of 53.5 for boys and 52.5 for girls: 19 children (9 boys, 10 girls) fell above and 107 (55 boys, 52 girls) below, giving a 15.1% above-threshold rate. The groups differ sharply on the defining variable (SRS-2 69.79 +/- 23.66 against 31.24 +/- 11.48, t = -6.956, p < 0.001) and not on age (all five) or sex ratio (p = 0.81). The unit of analysis is the child, with one 16-dimensional feature vector each.

**S-122** [local_b9e05a8f] — *Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network*

There are no participants. The units are images: 2,866 in the Piosenka Kaggle collection, split 1,433 autism-labelled and 1,433 control, described as ages 1-11; and 1,163 face crops extracted with MTCNN from the YTUIA/SSBD video corpus, split after re-clustering into 951 training, 144 validation and 68 test. The number of distinct children behind either figure is unknown and unreported - the paper's own table labels the 2,866 images as 'Total individuals', which is the conflation this review has repeatedly recorded in the image-classification branch. The provenance of each class is stated plainly and is the decisive fact: the autism images were 'taken from websites and Facebook pages that included autism-related content', while the YTUIA positives derive from 100 videos assembled to depict self-stimulatory behaviour, of which 50 came from YouTube and 50 from therapists and professional organisations, with controls being 'YouTube videos featuring kindergarten activities within the relevant age range'. In both corpora, therefore, the class label records where material was found rather than any assessment of the child depicted.

**S-123** [local_0b0960c4] — *Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]*

Seventeen boys: 13 autistic aged 10 to 16 and 4 typically developing aged 9 to 16, drawn from the global autism EEG corpus held by the brain-computer interface group at King Abdulaziz University and used with permission. The comparison group of four is the smallest in the review and is too small to characterise typical variation in any EEG measure, let alone to support a claim about detection. The sample is entirely male, which removes sex as a confound and means nothing reported can be assumed to apply to autistic girls. No age distribution by group is given beyond the two ranges, and none of the descriptors this review usually records - cognitive level, language ability, comorbidity, medication, socioeconomic background - is available. The 13:4 ratio also sets the participant-level majority-class baseline at 76.5%, against which the reported 89-94% should be read and never is.

**S-124** [local_abad69fd] — *Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play*

Two hundred and forty-six children aged 1 to 6, recruited in Beijing between January and August 2022 in a matched 1:1 design: 123 autistic (105 male, 18 female, mean age 54.0 months, SD 9.9) and 123 typically developing (103 male, 20 female, mean age 51.1 months, SD 13.5). The autistic children came from a hospital and from autism intervention service centres; the comparison children from a local kindergarten. Groups were matched and formally tested on age (t(224.10) = 1.90, p = 0.0591) and sex (chi-square = 0.031, p = 0.860), and separated on severity as expected (median CARS-2 37.0 against 15.0, Z = -13.90, p < 0.001). Two sample-definition decisions shape what the study can show. Children with current or previous psychiatric diagnoses other than autism, major physical or neurological disease, or any prior psychotropic medication were excluded, which produces an uncomplicated autism group at the cost of representativeness. And 23 children who met clinical criteria but scored below 30 on CARS-2 were removed, so the autistic group is restricted to the more clearly affected end of the spectrum - a restriction the authors identify themselves and connect explicitly to performance inflation. The unit of analysis is the child throughout, with one 81-dimensional indicator vector each.

**S-125** [local_cd7545e2] — *Predictive model using autism*

Ninety adults recruited from the outpatient and inpatient services of Showa University Karasuyama Hospital in central Tokyo: 40 with schizophrenia (27 men, 13 women, mean age 33.53 years, SD 10.95) recruited between April 2022 and December 2023, and 50 with autism (35 men, 15 women, mean age 33.80 years, SD 8.39) recruited between October 2018 and December 2020. Both groups required a full-scale IQ above 85 and both were diagnosed under DSM-5 by consensus among several psychiatrists with extensive experience in both conditions. Three features distinguish this sample from almost every other in the review. Both groups are clinical, drawn from the same service, so there is no clinic-versus-community recruitment asymmetry and no typically developing comparison group at all. Both are adults with fluent speech and average or above-average measured ability, which is the population in which differential diagnosis is genuinely difficult and in which most of this corpus's paediatric work has nothing to say. And roughly a third of each group is female (30% and 33%), against the heavy male preponderance typical of autism research samples - a consequence of studying adults presenting to psychiatric services rather than children referred to developmental research. Groups did not differ on age, sex or years of education. The unit of analysis is the participant, with one set of ADOS-2 item codes each.

**S-126** [local_3ecb92bf] — *The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech*

Two corpora combined, and the participant accounting is the weakest part of the description. De-Enigma contributes 55 autistic children aged 4 to 10, described as 25 from Serbia and 25 from the United Kingdom - a split that does not sum to 55 - with no control group at all, yielding 5,368 vocalisation samples over 115 minutes. The Child Pathological Speech Database contributes monolingual French-speaking children aged 6 to 18, recruited in Paris, carrying diagnoses of autism, dysphasia or PDD-NOS alongside a typically developing group, yielding 1,722 samples over 62 minutes. The CPSD participant counts cannot be reconciled: the control group is said to consist of 64 typically developing children (52 male, 12 female), while the corpus as a whole is said to have 13 female participants contributing 334 samples and 54 males contributing 1,388 - a total of 67, which would leave three children for the autism, dysphasia and PDD-NOS groups combined. The number of children in each atypical class is never stated anywhere in the paper. This is not a bookkeeping quibble. Speaker-disjoint splitting is the study's stated safeguard against leakage, and its protective value depends entirely on how many speakers each class contains: if the 26 autism, 26 dysphasia and 26 PDD-NOS samples in the diagnosis test partition come from one or two children each, then class membership and speaker identity are nearly the same variable, and disjointness across the split cannot separate them. The sex proportions are also stated inconsistently, as 78% and 81% male in the dataset section and as 95% and 90% male in the limitations. Age distributions per group are not reported for either corpus.

**S-127** [local_4b02df7c] — *Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism*

The largest sample in this review by an order of magnitude, and the least clinically characterised. The autism corpus comprises 3,137,952 tweets from 17,323 users, identified by their use of #ActuallyAutistic in English-language posts between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2022 combined with 'autism', 'autistic' or 'neurodiverse' appearing in their profile description, after which all tweets from those users' timelines were collected. The control corpus comprises 3,377,518 tweets from 171,273 users, obtained by a search query excluding the hashtag and sampling 1,000 tweets per day over the same window. No demographic information of any kind exists for either group - no age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic status, cognitive level or comorbidity - and the location field was discarded as largely missing or uninformative, though the authors note that most of the top 20 stated locations were variants of the United Kingdom. Two structural features of the sample deserve emphasis. The tweet counts are near-balanced while the user counts differ tenfold, because the autism group's entire timelines were harvested while control posts were sampled from the platform's daily stream - so the two classes differ in how their material was selected as well as in who produced it, and this is not discussed. And the autism group is not a clinical population but a self-selected online community organised around a hashtag with an explicit advocacy stance, which the paper describes accurately and which bears on everything downstream.

**S-128** [local_7d7f1fcc] — *Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children*

One hundred and sixty children aged 1.1 to 5.1 years, enrolled in the Geneva Autism Cohort between 25 September 2012 and 10 September 2023: 80 autistic children (48 male, 32 female, mean age 2.68 +/- 0.89 years) meeting DSM-5 criteria with diagnosis supported by gold-standard assessment, and 80 typically developing children (48 male, 32 female, mean age 2.46 +/- 0.98 years) screened for absence of known neurological or psychiatric conditions and for no history of autism in any first-degree relative. Three features of the sample are worth emphasising. Both groups underwent the same ADOS assessment in the same setting, so the recording context is common to both classes - which removes the setting confound that this review has documented repeatedly across the video, audio and image branches, where clinical groups are recorded in clinics and comparison groups in schools, kindergartens or on the internet. Sex is exactly matched at 48 male and 32 female per group, giving 40% girls, which is by a considerable margin the highest female representation of any included study and the only instance of deliberate exact matching on sex. And the matching extends to the analysis: the 50-50 train-test split was itself constructed so that each half contained 40 autistic and 40 typically developing children matched for age, sex and ADOS module, so the held-out set is not merely disjoint but comparable by construction. The unit of analysis is the child, with segments nested within children and never crossing the split.

**S-129** [local_5a331ffe] — *Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning*

Seventy-three children in the autism class, one per video, from 73 of the 75 videos in the Self-Stimulatory Behaviours Dataset - home recordings posted to YouTube by parents and caregivers showing children spinning, head banging or arm flapping, two videos having been dropped for quality. The split is reported by child and by duration: 44 children and 3,214 seconds in training, 15 children and 1,582 seconds in validation, 14 children and 1,496 seconds in test. That per-child reporting is better than the frame-count reporting typical of this branch. What is entirely absent is the other half of the sample. The methods state only that 'in order to have a complete and balanced database to train this model, we extracted the frames featuring the faces of ASD children and gathered facial images of other ASD children and facial images of neurotypical youngsters' - so a non-autistic class exists, but its size, its source, the number of children in it and their characteristics are nowhere given, and the data-distribution table lists SSBD as the sole database for all three splits, which cannot be true if a second class is present. No age, sex, ancestry, cognitive or language information is available for anyone in either class. For a two-class facial image classifier, the composition of both classes is what determines the meaning of the result, and here only one is described.

**S-130** [local_45ef7022] — *A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features*

Thirty male autistic children aged 5 to 15, all attending Don Guanella Special School in Poonamallee, Chennai, contributing 1,500 thermal images distributed across four settings within the school: 500 images from 10 students during outdoor play, 600 from 12 students in the classroom, 200 from 4 students in the dining area and 200 from 4 students on the veranda, plus 20 videos collected for real-time testing that are never analysed. Every image is of an autistic child; the study contains no non-autistic participants and no diagnostic task, since the classification target is a three-level severity grade among autistic children only. Four features of the sample bound what can be learned from it. It is entirely male, so nothing reported can be assumed to apply to autistic girls, and the paper does not remark on this. It is small in the way that matters - 30 children, 50 images each - so image counts overstate the effective sample fiftyfold, and the reported 98.33% must be read against that. The children are drawn from a single residential special school, a setting that selects for higher support needs and makes the sample unrepresentative of the autistic population the framework's medication claim addresses. And the four capture settings differ physically in ways that directly affect the primary measurement: outdoor play in Chennai, a classroom, a dining area and an open veranda produce systematically different skin temperatures for reasons unrelated to autism, and the distribution of severity levels across those settings is never reported.

**S-131** [local_0f5a351e] — *Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

There are no participants. The units are 2,940 RGB images from the Kaggle autistic-children facial dataset, split 1,327 autistic and 1,613 non-autistic, described as children aged 2 to 14, organised into two folders. The number of distinct children behind either count is never stated. The decisive fact is the paper's own description of how the two folders were built: 'The autistic subfolder included images of ASD, while the non-autistic subfolder had images randomly retrieved from web searches.' The class label therefore records the collection route rather than any assessment of the child depicted - the same provenance confound this review has recorded for five other studies on this corpus family, stated here more plainly than in any of them. No age distribution, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is available for either class, and no demographic comparison between them is possible.

**S-132** [local_786b6280] — *Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features*

Sixty-four children aged 3 to 6 - 30 autistic and 34 typically developing - assembled from four archived TalkBank corpora. The autistic children come from ASDBank's Eigsti and Nadig collections; the typically developing children come partly from those same collections and partly from CHILDES's Warren and Kuczaj corpora, added deliberately 'to try to balance demographic (gender and age) representations'. The paper is honest about the residual imbalance, stating that 'most participants are male, and there are more children aged 3-4 than aged 5-6', and it explains the sex imbalance correctly as a consequence of autism being 'almost 4 times as common in boys than in girls'. Numerical age and sex compositions by diagnostic group are not reported, which matters because the paper's own analysis finds that mean length of utterance - the top-ranked predictor - is the only feature that consistently increases with age. Developmentally delayed children present in the Eigsti corpus were deliberately excluded to keep the task binary, which removes the non-autistic clinical comparison group the source data could have supported. The unit of analysis is the child, one transcript and one feature vector each.

**S-133** [local_879ec69b] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning*

Two public corpora used in parallel. The Gait Fullbody Dataset, created by Al-Jubouri and colleagues, contains 100 children aged 4 to 12 - 50 autistic and 50 typically developing - recorded with a Kinect v2 capturing 25 joint coordinates, with each child performing ten walking trials of which one was retained, giving 100 samples. A separate subset of nine children with severe symptoms is available and is not analysed here. The DREAM dataset contains 61 children aged 3 to 7, recorded with Kinect v1 during robot-assisted therapy, yielding 3,121 samples of which 1,833 were used after the non-spectrum class was excluded; only 10 upper-body joints are recorded, since Kinect v1 detects 20 joints and DREAM omits the lower body. No age distribution, sex, cognitive level, language ability or clinical characterisation is available for either corpus. Two structural facts shape everything downstream. In the Gait dataset each child contributes exactly one sample, so cross-validation necessarily partitions children - a property that arises from the data rather than from a design decision, but that gives this study the participant-level split unit most of the video branch lacks. And that single retained sample was chosen from ten trials 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', so the modelled data were selected with knowledge of the outcome.

**S-134** [local_93e5d23d] — *Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]*

Sixty-two children aged 18 to 54 months drawn from the publicly available Khozaei cry corpus collected in Iran: 31 autistic and 31 typically developing, with 24 boys and 7 girls in each group, mean ages 35.6 and 30.8 months. The exact sex matching at 24:7 is a genuine design strength and gives the sample 22.6% girls, higher than most autism research samples in this review. Two features of the sample are less favourable and both are reported without being examined. The mean ages differ by 4.8 months - about 16% of the younger group's mean, in a period of rapid vocal-tract and laryngeal maturation - with no test or adjustment reported, which matters because jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio all vary with vocal development. And the recording settings differ sharply by group: 87.10% of the autistic children's cries were recorded at autism centres and 12.90% at home, while 54.84% of the typically developing children's were recorded at health centres and 45.16% at home. Roughly six cry instances were retained per child (6.10 +/- 5.05 for the autistic group, 5.39 +/- 3.66 for the comparison group), giving an instance-level dataset of around 355 cries from 62 children. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is available.

**S-135** [local_a0d73248] — *Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm*

Seven hundred and four respondents to the AQ-10 adult autism screening instrument, drawn from a public Kaggle aggregation of screening-app submissions. The paper reports the row count and the field names and nothing else: no class distribution, no age or sex composition, no ethnicity breakdown, although age, gender and ethnicity are all among the 21 fields it prints. In the source dataset the positive class comprises 189 of 704, giving a majority-class baseline of 73.2% that the paper never states. No respondent is known to have received any clinical assessment. The population is self-selected users of an autism screening application, which is neither a clinical sample nor a population sample.

**S-136** [local_4ceee075] — *Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics*

One hundred children aged 5 to 9, recruited in Kazakhstan: 50 described as diagnosed with autism and 50 typically developing peers, recorded under a single purpose-designed protocol yielding over 16 hours of video. The sample is balanced 50:50 by group and the acquisition context is common to both, which removes the recruitment and recording asymmetry that affects most of this review's video and image work. Two demographic facts bound what follows. The sex composition differs sharply between groups - the autistic group is approximately 84% male and 16% female, while the comparison group is 52% male and 48% female - a 32-percentage-point gap reported in the results without comment, adjustment or stratified analysis. And no age distribution by group is given, only the shared 5-to-9 range, across which facial proportions, motor coordination and gestural repertoire all change substantially. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is available for either group, and no recruitment source is stated.

**S-137** [local_84bcd4ed] — *Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of*

There are no participants. The units are 2,932 facial images, balanced at 1,466 per class, described in the results as 'collected from platforms such as Kaggle and ASD-related websites'. The number of distinct children behind those images is never stated, and no age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is available for either class - an absence the authors acknowledge directly, noting that 'demographic variables, such as age, gender, and cultural background, were not explicitly controlled'. This is the seventh study in this review built on the Kaggle facial-image corpus family, and the description of the autistic class as sourced partly from autism-related websites places it squarely in the same category as the others: the label records where an image was found rather than any assessment of the child in it. For the paper's second target, gelotophobia, there are not even images with labels - no person was assessed for gelotophobia by any means, so that half of the study has no sample at all.

**S-138** [local_d97673f4] — *Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

There are no participants. The units are 2,940 facial images from the Kaggle autistic-children corpus - the eighth study in this review built on this dataset family - with the number of distinct children never stated and no age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information available for either class. The corpus's construction is the determining fact: its autistic images were harvested from autism-related online sources and its comparison images from elsewhere, so the label records where an image was found rather than any assessment of the child in it. This study does not restate that provenance, but it inherits it.

**S-139** [local_86a67a4f] — *Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children*

There are no participants. The autism corpus comprises 2,886 images partitioned 2,526 training, 280 testing and 80 validation - the standard split of the Piosenka Kaggle autistic-children collection, which this review has now charted in eight other studies - after poor-quality images were discarded. The emotion corpus supplies 703 training and 130 testing images. The number of distinct children behind either count is never stated, and no age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is available for any class. The authors name this directly as their first limitation, observing that 'the absence of demographic information such as gender and ethnicity in the utilized Kaggle datasets might hinder the generalization across different populations' - which is a more explicit acknowledgement than most studies on this corpus offer, and which correctly identifies the consequence without identifying the deeper problem, that the corpus's autistic class was harvested from autism-related online sources so that the label records image provenance.

**S-140** [local_0a39cca9] — *Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy*

Two thousand nine hundred and thirty-six facial images, balanced at 1,468 labelled autistic and 1,468 labelled normal, drawn from two sources - Kaggle and 'data from an autism center in Semarang'. The mixed provenance is what distinguishes this study from the other nine Kaggle-corpus papers charted in this review, and it cuts both ways. Supplementing a web-scraped collection with images from an actual clinical service is in principle an improvement, since clinic-attending children have real diagnoses; but the paper never states how many images came from each source, nor whether the clinic contributed to the autistic class only or to both. If the autistic images are predominantly Indonesian clinic photographs while the comparison images are predominantly international web-scraped ones, the two classes would be separable by ancestry, camera and setting without any facial phenotype being involved - a sharper confound than the pure-Kaggle studies face. The paper's own account of provenance is loose enough to leave this open: the data 'could come from a variety of places, such as clinics, past research, or relevant public statistics'. No age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is reported for either class, and the number of distinct children behind 2,936 images is never stated.

**S-141** [local_7432ffd7] — *Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models*

Two groups from a single archived dataset: 29 children with ASD and 30 typically developing children, 59 in total. The unit actually analysed is not the child but the gaze sample: 1,048,575 rows. That figure deserves attention - 1,048,576 is the maximum row count of a Microsoft Excel worksheet, so the analysed set is almost certainly a spreadsheet-truncated slice of the source recording rather than the complete data, and the paper never remarks on it. Per-child row counts, per-group row counts and per-fold composition are all unreported.

**S-142** [local_8ff20c48] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning*

One group of children aged 2-4 years recruited through Pakistani rehabilitation centres, split by questionnaire outcome rather than by recruitment stream. The paper states 750 participants, but 434 male plus 308 female is 742, and 593 training plus 149 test is also 742; eight children are unaccounted for and the inconsistency is not noted. Class sizes are never stated directly and must be recovered from the test-set support column (106 autistic, 43 non-autistic), implying about 71% positive overall. There is no separate typically developing comparison group in the design sense - both classes come from the same rehabilitation-centre respondent pool, and the questionnaire was described as circulated among trainers and parents of children with autism, which makes the non-autistic class a by-product of scoring rather than a recruited control group.

**S-143** [local_986436f2] — *Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost*

There are no participant groups in any meaningful sense. The unit is the image file: 2,526 images, 1,263 labelled ASD and 1,263 labelled non-ASD, downloaded from a Kaggle re-upload of the web-scraped autism face corpus. The number of distinct children behind those images is never asked, and because the corpus is known to contain multiple images of the same faces, the effective sample is unknown and certainly far below 2,526. An 80-20 split gives 2,020 training and 506 test images, but the headline evaluation is then run on 200 images selected from the test set - and the reported confusion matrix sums to 300 (146 + 141 + 9 + 4), agreeing with neither figure.

**S-144** [local_bb4d1f7a] — *Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models*

Forty children, all with an existing ASD diagnosis, recruited from Dakshinya Autistic School in Guntur, India, and divided into four severity classes of exactly ten each: low, mild, medium and high. There is no typically developing comparison group, which matters because the abstract nonetheless reports that children with ASD exhibit unique and highly individualized gaze patterns when compared to TD children - a comparison the design cannot support. The only TD data in the paper belong to the separate public Saliency4ASD set (14 ASD, 14 TD) used in a side experiment. Two internal inconsistencies affect the count: the introduction states that in the initial training we enrolled a group of 8-10 children aged x years, with the placeholder x left in the published text, and the analysis unit is not the child but the cropped eye image - 50 frames x 2 eyes x 40 children = 4,000 images, which is what the 70:15:15 split partitions.

**S-145** [local_13c1f46d] — *Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism*

No participants. The unit is the image: a stated 2,926 facial samples in two classes, Normal and Autism, downloaded from Kaggle. The number of distinct children is unknown and never raised. The stated total does not survive contact with the results: the confusion matrix at 1,000 epochs reports 1,338 correctly recognised normal and 1,362 correctly recognised autism images, which against the per-class accuracies of 95.57% and 97.29% implies about 1,400 images in each class and about 2,800 overall. Those counts also span essentially the whole dataset, which means the reported confusion matrices are not computed on a held-out subset at all.

**S-146** [local_e771fb69] — *Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data*

Forty-four examples in total - 22 individuals diagnosed with ASD and 22 non-autistic individuals - taken from an open-source movement dataset on Mendeley Data that is neither named nor cited. Nothing else is known about them: not their age band (the introduction discusses both children and adults without saying which these are), not their sex, not their recruitment, not the country, not the year. The 44 examples were divided among three simulated federated clients by an unstated rule, and each client's evaluation rests on nine test cases - a figure that appears nowhere in the text and is recoverable only from the confusion matrices (6 true negatives, 2 true positives, 1 false negative, 0 false positives) and from the fact that every accuracy in Tables 2 through 5 is a multiple of one ninth.

**S-147** [local_945300a5] — *Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network*

Seventy children in two recruited groups: 35 with autism from a Special Elementary School in Banda Aceh and 35 typically developing children from a State Elementary School in the same city. Each contributed 15 photographs (three expressions x five shots), giving 1,050 images split evenly 525/525. The analysis unit throughout is the image, not the child: the 70/20/10 division yields 369/105/51 images per class, and the reported metrics rest on 102 test images drawn from the same 70 children who supplied the training images. This is genuine primary data collection with a real, separately recruited comparison group - which distinguishes it sharply from the twelve Kaggle-corpus reuses charted in this review - but the group difference is confounded with school of origin, since every autistic child comes from one institution and every comparison child from another.

**S-148** [local_ed30e24c] — *Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI*

No groups were recruited. The unit is the questionnaire record: 1,054 cases from the public ASD Toddler dataset (Thabtah, via Kaggle), of which 735 are labelled ASD and 319 non-ASD - a 69.7% positive rate. SVM-SMOTE then expanded the set to 1,456 instances, meaning 402 of the rows subsequently modelled and evaluated are synthetic interpolations rather than children. The 292-case test set (148 ASD, 144 non-ASD) therefore contains an unstated number of synthetic records, and the number of real children behind the reported 100% is never given.

**S-149** [local_b9de0d7f] — *Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques*

No participants were recruited. Two public toddler screening datasets are merged: the Kaggle ASD Toddler set (1,054 instances, 17 columns) and an online questionnaire dataset covering toddlers aged 12-36 months across regions of Saudi Arabia. The size of the second dataset is never given, the size of the merged set is never given, and the size after SMOTE oversampling is never given - so the number of rows behind every table in the paper is unknown, and it cannot be determined how many are real records and how many synthetic. Class counts are likewise absent. The stated motivation for merging - improving diversity by combining two regions - is the paper's best idea and is never exploited: the two cohorts are pooled rather than used as development and held-out sets.

**S-150** [local_14df790d] — *Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach*

No participants. 1,054 records from the public toddler Q-CHAT dataset, 728 labelled autism and 326 control - a 69.1% positive rate that the paper reports and, unusually for this branch, leaves in place rather than resampling. The records were submitted through an ASD screening application by parents and other stakeholders, so neither respondent nor child was verified. The confusion matrices imply a test partition of 317 records, though no split proportion is stated; the row totals also differ across models within the same table (105/212 for LR, KNN and LR-KNN but 110/207 for the ANN), which they should not if all four were evaluated on the same partition.

**S-151** [local_4da2b941] — *Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study*

Two groups of adults recruited into one online survey: 102 autistic adults with a clinician-made diagnosis (72 women, 18 men, 12 non-binary) and 499 non-autistic adults (399 women, 92 men, 8 non-binary), 601 in total. The analysis unit is the person throughout, and the four cross-validation partitions are participant-disjoint by construction - each participant appears in exactly one partition. Exclusions are enumerated with reasons: 12 self-diagnosed respondents and 13 who did not report a gender they identified with. This is the only charted study in which the number of people, the number of analysis units and the number of rows in every reported metric are the same figure.

**S-152** [local_6e7174c0] — *A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach*

No participants. 2,926 images at 224x224, described as curated from public repositories covering diverse demographics and labelled autism or non-autism; the comparison tables identify the source as the same Kaggle facial corpus used by all five of the studies it benchmarks against. The split is 2,526 training, 200 validation and 200 test images. Class counts are never stated for any partition, though the metric arithmetic implies a balanced 200-image test set. The number of distinct children is unknown - and the paper is aware that this matters, because it notes that one cited study cleaned duplicates from the dataset using the MD5 hash algorithm, an acknowledgement that the corpus contains repeated images. No deduplication is performed here.

**S-153** [local_e04bcd32] — *Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network*

No participants. 2,940 images from the Kaggle ASD Children Facial dataset, balanced at 1,470 autistic and 1,470 non-autistic - the fourteenth charted reuse of this corpus in the review. The number of distinct children is unknown and never raised, and the corpus is known to contain repeated images of the same faces. The paper states a split of 2,540 training images (1,270 per class) and 400 test images (200 per class), but the confusion matrix it then reports covers all 2,940 images, so the population behind the headline figure is the whole dataset rather than the held-out 400.

**S-154** [local_183eaef4] — *Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI*

No participants were recruited. The ASD Children Traits dataset was downloaded from Kaggle: 1,985 cases with 28 variables, covering children aged 1-18. Preprocessing then reduced this to 634 cases and 19 variables - 68% of the records and a third of the variables removed as outliers, inconsistencies or erroneous data identified by clinical experts. Neither the raw nor the preprocessed dataset's class balance is reported anywhere, so the number of ASD and non-ASD cases behind every result in the paper is unknown. This matters more than usual because the introduction states explicitly that ASD assessment datasets tend to over-represent ASD cases and that this can bias models toward the majority class - a problem the authors identify and then never quantify in their own data.

**S-155** [local_b6ac2b98] — *Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks*

Ninety-three children aged 32-74 months in three clinically defined groups: 24 with ASD, 25 with developmental language disorder, and 44 typically developing. Both clinical groups were recruited from early childhood intervention centres in Cordoba province and required a formal diagnosis made by a licensed, experienced clinical team. The analysis unit is the child throughout, and each child contributes exactly one row to each of four feature sets. The inclusion of a second clinical group is what distinguishes this study from almost the entire charted corpus: it makes the ASD-versus-DLD comparison possible, and that comparison is where the study's most informative result lies.

**S-156** [local_44d3aef5] — *Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis*

No participants. 547 scanpath images from a public eye-tracking repository, 328 labelled non-ASD and 219 ASD. The abstract converts this image count into a participant count, describing the dataset as scan pathways obtained from 328 characteristically emerging children and 219 children with autism - which would make this one of the larger primary eye-tracking cohorts in the field. The methods section states the correct version, that these are image counts. The source collection is the Cilia/Carette scanpath set, whose originators are cited in the comparison table and in which a few dozen children contributed multiple scanpath images each; the number of distinct children behind the 547 images is never given here. Every reported metric rests on a test partition of 55 images, recoverable only from the support column of the per-class results tables.

**S-157** [local_24fefc5f] — *A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection*

No participants, and no sample size of any kind. The article never states how many records the analysed dataset contains, how many are ASD-positive, or how many are negative - a gap that persists through a results section built entirely on performance curves. The data source is identified only as Autism screening data for toddler, the public Q-CHAT-10 collection. Since no split, test set or fold structure is described either, there is no point in the paper at which a reader can say how many observations any reported number rests on.

**S-158** [local_69b10fe4] — *An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms*

Ninety-four adults in three groups: 31 autistic adults, 32 adults with Parkinson's disease and 31 controls. Both clinical groups required documentary evidence of a formal clinical diagnosis or came from research databases where such evidence had been verified, with mutual exclusion between the two conditions and exclusion of co-occurring movement or developmental disorders. Recruitment order is reported and is itself methodologically informative - the PD group was recruited first as an opportunity sample, autistic adults were then recruited to match it, and controls to match both. The analysis unit is the participant throughout, and the 80/20 classification split partitions people. What limits the classification estimates is size rather than structure: the ASD-versus-PD test partition contains roughly 13 people and the clinical-versus-non-clinical partition roughly 19.

**S-159** [local_af9f4c12] — *An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data*

No participants were recruited. Four public screening datasets from Kaggle and UCI were harmonised into 2,154 records spanning toddlers, children, adolescents and adults, with stratified sampling by age group during merging to preserve cohort proportions. The analysis unit is the record and the cross-validation folds are stratified over records. What is missing is arithmetic: the per-cohort sample sizes, the class counts for the binary screening outcome and the counts for each of the four constructed severity strata are all absent, so the denominator behind every reported accuracy is unknown. The class distribution is characterised only qualitatively, as closely mirroring population-level screening statistics reported in prior paediatric ASD studies.

**S-160** [local_367db0b6] — *An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns*

No participants and no coherent sample. The methods state within four consecutive sentences that the study utilised MRI datasets of newborns comprising 10,000 samples and that the final dataset included 25,000 positive cases and 1200 negative cases, with class balance maintained. Both claims cannot hold: 25,000 positives cannot come from 10,000 samples, and a ratio of nearly 21 to 1 is not balance. Elsewhere the CSBS description reports 500 subjects, and Table 4, labelled Standard dataset, lists the same identifier range 01-1000 five times over with different family relationships (son, daughter, niece) and a different algorithm name in each row, so it is a results table presented as a data description. No consistent count of children exists anywhere in the article.

**S-161** [local_8d43288c] — *Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos*

No participants and no groups. The data are 75 YouTube videos of approximately 90 seconds each from the Self-Stimulatory Behaviour Dataset, uploaded by parents and caretakers, segmented into frame clips by behaviour type using the dataset's original annotations. The number of distinct children is never stated - a consequential omission, since 75 videos may represent fewer than 75 children and the k-fold confusion matrix reports 303 samples, so the analysis unit is the clip. Crucially there is no non-autistic comparison group: all four classes, including normal Behavior, are drawn from videos of autistic children, so the study is a behaviour-recognition problem within one population rather than a diagnostic contrast between populations.

**S-162** [local_5f57ba19] — *Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension*

Forty-five Spanish children from the BeGaze corpus: 19 with an ASD diagnosis made externally by neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists before inclusion, and 26 typically developing children, focused on the 5-8 year preschool-to-primary transition. Each child contributed multiple samples - one per story, under two modality conditions and segmented into three temporal phases - and the cross-validation folds are explicitly participant-independent, so the multiplication of samples per child does not leak across the split. This is the correct handling of a repeated-measures design and it is rare in this corpus.

**S-163** [local_1d856900] — *Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare*

Two datasets with very different standing. Dataset 1 is 1,985 instances with 28 attributes from public ASD screening databases - the same 1,985-record ASD Children Traits collection analysed by local_183eaef4 - and here, unlike there, its class balance is reported: 729 ASD-positive (36.72%) against 1,256 negative (63.28%), with 283 instances carrying missing values. Dataset 2 consists of 100 original clinical samples augmented fourfold to 400, distributed evenly across four severity categories with no non-ASD class at all, and with no source, citation, country or institution given for the original 100. The number of distinct children behind either dataset is never stated.

**S-164** [local_7b19a959] — *Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis*

Two recruited groups of adults: 286 autistic and 266 non-autistic in the final dataset, from 959 initially recruited, with 407 excluded for missing data from at least one contributing experiment (per-study exclusion criteria, technical issues, attrition). Autistic participants came from the Netherlands Autism Register and non-autistic participants principally from Prolific Academic. A second, fully age- and gender-matched subsample of 125 per group was drawn by random selection from the unbalanced sample, and it is this matched analysis the paper reports as its primary result. The analysis unit is the person throughout. The attrition is large and is stated plainly with its causes.

**S-165** [local_d7b6fa00] — *Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath*

Twenty-eight participants, 14 with ASD and 14 typically developing, from a public benchmark eye-tracking dataset released on Zenodo. This is the smallest participant base of any charted study apart from local_e771fb69, and it is the only quantity the paper reports about the people involved - no age, sex, cognitive ability, recruitment source, country or diagnostic procedure appears. Crucially, the analysis unit is the participant: scanpath-level features are aggregated to one vector per person by taking the mean and standard deviation across that person's trials, and the evaluation is described as subject-wise specifically to prevent data leakage. With 28 people and five folds, each test fold holds roughly five or six participants.

**S-166** [local_e54c304c] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models*

No participants. 14,352 annotated facial images of children obtained from the Roboflow platform, labelled autistic or non-autistic and carrying bounding-box annotations. No class counts, no split sizes and no count of distinct children appear anywhere. The scale is worth noting against the branch: the paper's own literature table cites the Kaggle autism face corpus repeatedly, and that corpus contains roughly 3,000 images, so a 14,352-image Roboflow set is most plausibly an augmented export of the same underlying photographs - which the paper's description of Roboflow's built-in augmentation at export time supports but never states.

**S-167** [local_e4c2a776] — *Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images*

No participants. 2,940 images in two balanced classes of 1,470 - the sixteenth charted reuse of the public autism facial-image corpus, identifiable from that exact composition although the paper names only a reference number rather than a repository. The number of distinct children is unknown and never discussed. Results are reported for a 70% training partition and a 30% testing partition with no counts, no seed and no statement of how the split was drawn.

**S-168** [local_231757c7] — *SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers*

One hundred and nine children from a public Kinect V2 dataset: 50 typically developing, 50 moderate ASD and 9 severe ASD. The composition is uneven in a way that determines everything else about the study - the nine severe-ASD children have no Kinect recordings at all, only 2D phone video, because the original collectors could not set up Kinect V2 in controlled laboratory settings for children with severe autism. The severe class in the analysis therefore contains no real motor measurements from any child; its feature vectors were synthesised by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise. The analysis unit is the child, one 463-dimensional vector each, and the paper reports this structure openly rather than presenting three comparable groups.

**S-169** [local_1b457442] — *Screening autism spectrum*

Eighty-six children across two independently collected public corpora. Eigsti et al.: 48 children aged 3-6 in three balanced groups of 16 - typically developing, developmental delay and ASD - each recorded in a 30-minute free-play session, with ethnic composition reported (39 White, 3 LatinX, 6 African-American). Nadig and Bang: 38 children, 26 typically developing and 12 with ASD, sampled at three time points over a year in parent-child interactions. The analysis unit is the child throughout, and the two corpora are analysed separately, merged, and - for Eigsti - as a three-class problem. The presence of a developmental-delay group is the design's most valuable feature and is the reason this study can say something the rest of the speech branch cannot.

**S-170** [local_b26db2f2] — *Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches*

Twelve children aged 3-6 years - six with a clinical ASD diagnosis and six without, matched across the same age bands - who together completed 640 game sessions over three months in their own school setting. The recruitment structure is documented in unusual detail: three inclusive-education professionals were recruited with stated inclusion and exclusion criteria, trained on the tool, and supervised the children's use of it, with guardians absent during play. The gap between the number of children and the number of analysis rows is the study's decisive feature: 640 sessions from 12 children is roughly 53 per child, and the dataset is partitioned by session rather than by child.

Clinical and health-economic, and unusually precise about the problem being solved. The diagnostic argument is specific rather than dismissive: 'Diagnosis currently relies on specialist medical expertise with diagnostic instrumentation dependent on subjectively rated scores during child observations, parent interviews and testing' - an accurate description that identifies subjectivity of scoring as the issue rather than impugning clinical judgement, and the protocol's stated ambition is to be 'an attractive and useful addition to the assessment and diagnostic toolbox', explicitly alongside ADOS-2 and ADI-R rather than in place of them. Early identification is framed in terms of what it enables for families - 'opportunity to adjust' and access to healthcare intervention and children's services - rather than in terms of treatment or cure. No autistic person or organisation is reported as involved in the design.

Standard clinical framing of the period, with 'individuals suffering from ASD' and 'children in risk of suffering from ASD' recurring - phrasing that treats autism as an affliction and is less careful than the corpus's better examples. The abbreviation CwASD (children with autism spectrum disorder) is used throughout. Against this, the paper's account of the clinical problem is precise and non-dismissive: diagnosis 'is usually performed through several sessions of behavioral observation, exhaustive screening, and manual coding behavior', signs may be observable before ten months while reliable diagnosis is possible only at 18 or 24 months, and the delay between the two is what the technology addresses. The stated purpose throughout is to 'assist and enhance the traditional practice' and to 'help the clinicians', with the therapist retaining control of the protocol - so the technology is positioned as instrumentation for a clinician rather than as a substitute. No autistic person or family organisation is reported as involved.

Clinical and engineering registers combined, with the paper's distinctive framing being that autism assessment is a joint design problem. Terminology is standard for the period ('children with autism', 'autistic children', 'autistic population'), and the language of 'abnormal social interactions' and 'abnormal interaction patterns' is used in the abstract. The theoretical framing is theory of mind and mentalisation, which locates the construct in social cognition rather than in deficit enumeration. No autistic person is reported as involved, though the group's 2022 follow-up names children among the target users to be consulted.

**S-052** [local_b70dae32] — *An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model*

**S-053** [local_51a0af74] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data*

**S-054** [local_d8d3037b] — *Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study*

The taxonomy given in the background is also outdated, listing Rett syndrome and childhood disintegrative disorder as ASD subtypes, which DSM-5 removed. Against that, the paper is careful to distinguish trait detection from diagnosis in its framing, positioning the work as identifying high autistic traits 'before making a definite diagnosis'.

The framing is developmental and mechanism-oriented, discussing superior temporal sulcus activation and intention inference rather than burden or deficit.

**S-056** [local_8692a64f] — *Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis*

**S-057** [local_4d6fac7e] — *Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network*

**S-058** [local_30c622f2] — *Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model*

The framing is clinical and severity-oriented, describing autism as classifiable by severity 'based on the degree of impairment in social communication, repetitive and restricted behavior patterns and also according to the need for support', and motivating the work by the claim that 'the categorization of individuals with ASD into levels contributes to the intervention, which directly impacts the prognosis'.

**S-059** [local_bfc088c7] — *Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation*
