DSM-5 diagnosis confirmed by a research diagnostic team comprising an experienced child psychiatrist and a clinical psychologist using best-estimate procedures after reviewing both videos and scored protocols of standardised assessments. ADOS-2 Module 3 administered by staff trained to research reliability level. ADI-R administered to caregivers of the autistic group by trained interviewers and integrated into the best-estimate procedure. Autism actively ruled out in comparison participants using ADOS-2 and SRS supplemented by expert clinical review. An extensive medical and psychiatric exclusion list applied to both groups, including current psychoactive medication - a control that matters directly for voice measures and that almost no other speech study in the corpus applies.

**S-070** [local_b7ec3755] — *Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images*

Nothing. No diagnostic instrument, clinical criterion, clinician role or diagnostic setting is mentioned at any point. The autism label is treated as an attribute of the dataset file, and even the source dataset's diagnostic procedure is not summarised or cited. Under the review's classification this is dataset-label-only ascertainment, in the weakest form encountered - some other benchmark-reuse papers here at least restate the original cohort's ADOS or CARS procedure.

**S-071** [local_684969f6] — *Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data*

Not reported. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role or setting is named; the label is an attribute of the released dataset. The paper cites the source collection for its recording parameters (Tobii T120, 17-inch monitor, 3-second presentations) but not for its ascertainment procedure. Under the review's classification this is dataset-label-only. The omission is more conspicuous here than in most benchmark-reuse papers because the author list includes established autism-research investigators and the work is funded by an NIMH R01, so the expertise to characterise or question the labels was present.

**S-072** [local_35004e74] — *Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children*

Clinical diagnosis under DSM-5, corroborated by gold-standard instruments (ADOS-G or ADOS-2) administered as part of an established longitudinal cohort study, with cohort recruitment procedures documented in three cited prior publications. Comparison children were screened not only for known neurological or psychiatric illness but also for autism in any first-degree relative - a criterion stricter than nearly any other study in this corpus, since it excludes children carrying familial liability who might show subthreshold features and thereby blur the contrast. Ethics approval from the Faculty of Medicine of Geneva University, written informed parental consent for all children, and separate explicit consent for the identifiable figure images.

**S-073** [local_fa91fc18] — *Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities*

Among the better ascertainments in the corpus for a study of this size. Diagnosis required both DSM-5 clinical criteria and the ADOS-2, and was made by 'qualified doctors and professionals in the sector' who 'have no affiliation with our laboratory or our research' - an explicit assertion of independence between the diagnosing clinicians and the research team that almost no other study here makes, and which forecloses the possibility of diagnostic classification being influenced by knowledge of the study hypothesis. Comparison children were excluded for suspected autism signs, developmental abnormalities, or current or past psychiatric or neurological disorder, though the screening was by clinician or teacher judgement rather than a standardised instrument, and any child about whose diagnosis or health a clinician or teacher was uncertain was excluded outright. The one waste is that the ADOS-2 was administered but its severity scores are never reported or used.

**S-074** [local_115dfe8d] — *A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children*

The study's weakest element, and unusually, the authors say so themselves. Diagnosis is stated to have been confirmed under DSM-5, but the very next sentence concedes 'we had limited access to reliable information in the school site' and explains that the children were therefore assessed using parent report on four instruments - the Autism Behavior Checklist, Social Communication Questionnaire, Social Responsiveness Scale and Clancy Behavior Scale. None is an observational or clinician-administered diagnostic instrument; all four are screening or symptom-report scales. No ADOS, ADI-R, CARS or direct clinical observation is reported. The consequence for interpretation is specific: the label the classifier is trained to predict is grounded in parent report, so a demonstration that a model recovers it at 95.56% shows agreement with parent-reported symptomatology, not with clinically established diagnosis. The comparison group is better handled - ABC, SRS and SCQ completed by teachers, with no child reaching any cut-off - so negative cases are screened on three instruments even though positive cases lack observational confirmation.

**S-075** [local_5b7ea7dc] — *AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Strong for a four-page conference paper. Diagnosis was made under DSM-5 criteria. The ADOS-2 was administered by two experienced professionals to all children referred for suspected autism, and because different modules were used according to age and language level, raw scores were converted to calibrated severity scores - total, social affect and restricted/repetitive - which is the correct procedure for comparing across modules and is done in only a minority of studies here. The paper states the CSS interpretation bands explicitly (1-3 non-spectrum, 4-5 ASD, 6-10 Autism) and applies them: 6 of the 50 initially recruited ASD-suspected children scored below 3 and were excluded, leaving a group with a mean CSS of 6.00, in the 'Autism' band. The Korean CARS was also administered with its 25.5 high-risk cut-off, and comparison children averaged 15.5 against 30.9 for the autistic group. The ascertainment therefore combines DSM-5 criteria, a module-calibrated observational instrument, a rating scale, and an explicit exclusion rule applied to borderline cases.

**S-076** [local_87fe26aa] — *Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

The weakest ascertainment in the 2022 cohort. Autism is established by 'the criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition' with nothing further: no ADOS, ADI-R, CARS, SRS or any other standardised instrument; no statement of who applied the criteria, with what training, or in what setting; and no indication whether diagnosis was made for this study or taken from school records. Comparison children were 'screened to exclude any with psychiatric or neurological disorders, including ASD', again with no instrument named and no cut-off stated. Under the review's classification this is clinical-diagnosis-only in its least documented form, and it means the reference standard cannot be independently evaluated.

**S-077** [local_893ce2fa] — *An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images*

Nothing. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role or setting, and no summary or citation of the source dataset's ascertainment procedure beyond a pointer to the source paper. The class labels are treated as properties of image files. This matters more than usual because the study reports 98.8% accuracy against a reference standard whose nature is entirely unspecified within the paper.

**S-078** [local_dffe4127] — *Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals*

Thorough and site-specific. Caltech required three conditions jointly: a prior diagnosis by a qualified clinician holding an MD or PhD; confirmation via clinical interview with the participant, and a parent where available, conducted by a named licensed clinical psychologist among the authors; and ADOS-2 Module 4 scores meeting a precisely stated criterion - at or above cutoff on at least two components of the original algorithm and within one point on the third, or within one point of the total cutoff under the Hus and Lord revised algorithm with Social Affect plus Restricted Repetitive Behaviors >= 7. Indiana University required a prior community diagnosis of ASD, autism, Asperger's syndrome or PDD-NOS, plus ADOS-2 Module 4 administered by research-reliable administrators meeting the same revised-algorithm criterion. Naming the exact scoring algorithm and the tolerance around cutoffs, and stating that the two sites differed in whether independent clinical confirmation was additionally required, is more precise ascertainment reporting than any other study in this review provides. The comparison group was characterised with the AQ rather than by exclusion alone.

**S-079** [local_2b766683] — *Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech*

Parent report alone, and the authors state the limitation directly: 'while we require parents to disclose their child's clinical diagnosis by choosing from options not widely known to those who have not received a clinical evaluation, these labels are self-reported and thus unverified'. No standardised instrument, no clinician involvement, no medical record check. The safeguard offered - that the diagnostic labels presented in the app are unfamiliar to families who have not been through an evaluation - is a reasonable heuristic against casual mislabelling but does nothing to establish which diagnosis a child actually received, when, by whom, or against what criteria. The comparison group's neurotypical status likewise rests on parental assertion with no screening instrument. This is the weakest reference standard in the corpus alongside the benchmark-reuse studies, and it is a consequence of the crowdsourcing design rather than an oversight: a fully remote app-based collection cannot verify diagnoses without a separate clinical pathway.

**S-080** [local_2895bdf0] — *Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection*

Among the strongest ascertainments in the corpus and comparable to its companion paper. Diagnosis was confirmed by experienced child psychiatrists and clinical psychologists who directly assessed every participant in the autistic and ADHD groups under DSM-IV-TR criteria, followed by a research diagnostic team reviewing 'results of the standardized diagnostic assessments (both videos and scored protocols)' and applying best-estimate procedures. ADOS-2 Module 3 was administered to all participants by research assistants or a senior clinical psychologist trained to research reliability level. Autism was actively ruled out in both comparison subgroups using the ADOS, clinical interview and parent-completed autism questionnaires - so negative cases are excluded on three independent sources rather than assumed. The screening list is extensive and clinically targeted, excluding seizure disorder, cerebral palsy, paediatric stroke, chemotherapy history, sensorimotor handicaps, closed head injury, thyroid disorder, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, current major depressive episode, fetal alcohol syndrome, Tourette's disorder, severe vision impairment, Rett syndrome, current psychoactive medication, non-English speakers and IQ below 70. That 104 of 289 screened participants were excluded 'for not meeting strict diagnostic criteria' indicates the criteria were applied stringently rather than nominally.

**S-081** [local_423b636b] — *Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers*

A genuine prospective screening pathway, which is rare in this corpus and is the study's principal methodological asset. Every participant received the M-CHAT-R/F as part of routine clinical care. Referral for diagnostic evaluation was triggered by a total score of 3 or more initially, 2 or more after follow-up questions, or developmental concerns raised by the pediatrician or parent. Referred children received the ADOS-2 Toddler Module from research-reliable licensed psychologists who determined DSM-5 status, supported by the Mullen Scales of Early Learning. Diagnosis therefore followed rather than preceded enrolment, and the mean interval between diagnosis and app administration was 0.7 months, so the behavioural measurement and the diagnostic determination are close in time. The comparison group's status is partly instrumented rather than assumed, since screen-positive children judged to have no concerns are retained in it. The one gap is that children with a negative M-CHAT-R/F and no raised concern were not directly assessed, so the neurotypical group will contain some proportion of children whose autism was not detected by screening - which biases toward underestimating the group difference rather than inflating it.

**S-082** [local_ffa35101] — *Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study*

ADOS-2 with research-reliable administration and scoring, using Overall, Social Affect and Restricted and Repetitive Behavior calibrated severity scores. This is a real observational instrument correctly administered, but it is the only diagnostic evidence described - there is no ADI-R, no DSM criterion application, no clinician best-estimate procedure and no statement of who made the final determination. For a subset of the Cantonese sample recruited through 'employment programmes particularly designed for adults previously diagnosed with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning Autism', the original diagnosis was made elsewhere under unknown procedures and the ADOS-2 serves as confirmation. The comparison groups are handled more stringently than in most studies here, screened for personal or family history of autism or related genetic disorders such as fragile X - a criterion that follows from the English cohort's family-genetic origins and that excludes the broader autism phenotype in relatives. General exclusions of brain injury, major psychiatric disorder, known genetic syndrome and other neurodevelopmental disorders were applied to all participants.

**S-083** [local_81ecbc6f] — *Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings*

Two-stage and well structured. Entry required a prior clinical diagnosis of idiopathic autism made by a multidisciplinary team including a psychiatrist under ICD-10 criteria - so ascertainment is clinical and independent of the research team. For the study itself, ADOS-2 was administered by research-reliable clinicians under the supervision of an author who is an ADOS-2 trainer, and parents completed the SCQ. The critical design detail is stated explicitly: 'Prior to this study, participants were not evaluated using SCQ and ADOS-2 measures.' That independence is what makes the instruments usable as comparators rather than as circular confirmations - though not entirely, since group membership was determined by the prior clinical diagnosis and the instruments are then evaluated against that same clinical determination. The Polish versions of both instruments have published psychometric validation, and the SCQ's reported agreement with clinical diagnosis (kappa 0.84) and with ADI-R (kappa 0.81) is cited. The comparison group's negative status is established by three separate exclusions plus fresh ADOS-2 and SCQ administration.

**S-084** [local_bc62bc4b] — *Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening*

Clinical diagnosis by licensed child psychiatrists under DSM-5 criteria, established before study entry and applied as an eligibility criterion, with subsequent exclusion of comorbid conditions including seizure disorder, known genetic disorder and uncorrectable sensory impairment. No observational diagnostic instrument - no ADOS, ADI-R or CARS - was administered, so ascertainment rests on clinical judgement whose procedures are not described beyond the practitioners' qualification. The M-CHAT-R/F was administered and its distribution reported by group (55 high risk and 6 medium risk among autistic participants; all 72 comparisons at no risk), which provides useful confirmation that the groups separate on a standardised screener but is not itself a diagnostic instrument, and the authors are clear-eyed about its limits, citing evidence of 'low to moderate accuracy' and explaining their use of it on the practical ground that it 'is the only available standardized screening instrument in the participants' native language'. The comparison group's negative status is established more stringently than the autistic group's positive status: no autism in any first- or second-degree relative, and no sibling with developmental, behavioural or emotional symptoms.

**S-085** [local_889d9bd6] — *Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children*

DSM-5 diagnosis by experienced physicians with a CARS score above 30 required for children aged 2 and over, described as 'in line with the ADOS standard'. The absence of an observational instrument is stated as the study's first limitation together with its cause - limited access to ADOS and ADI-R in China - which is a candid acknowledgement of a resource constraint rather than a methodological choice. The comparison group is screened more thoroughly than in most studies here: three instruments (the Ages and Stages Questionnaires Chinese Version, the Chinese children warning signs checklist, and the Developmental Screening Parent Questionnaire for Children Aged 0-6) covering communication and language, physical ability, social skills, problem solving and intelligence, administered by a study physician through onsite assessment and parent interview, with exclusion of any psychiatric or neurological history. The authors nonetheless flag the asymmetry: 'we did not assess the CARS in TD Children', so comparison participants were screened on general development but never on autism-specific symptomatology with the same instrument used to establish the cases.

**S-086** [local_361b59fb] — *Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

The strongest reference standard in the corpus, and the one against which others should be judged. Diagnosis was made by board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrists, child neurologists, developmental-behavioural pediatricians or child psychologists with more than five years of autism diagnostic experience, using structured clinical observation (comprising conversation or free play, symbolic interactive play and sensory stimulation), clinician interview and examination, medical and developmental review, and standardised assessment instruments, to reach a DSM-5 determination. That determination was then independently reviewed by a blinded second specialist working from standardised medical history, physical examination findings and video of the initial assessment, with a third specialist adjudicating disagreements and the majority decision defining the standard. The stated purpose is to reduce 'confirmation bias, deindividuation, and homogenized group thinking'. Crucially, the paper also quantifies the reference standard's own reliability rather than treating it as ground truth: the first reviewer agreed with the diagnosing specialist 79% of the time; of the 21% requiring a third opinion, the third sided with the diagnosing specialist 43% of the time and the first reviewer 57%; and diagnosing specialists reported being 'completely certain' only 67% of the time when diagnosing autism, 74% when ruling it out in favour of another condition, and 95% when the child was neurotypical. Reporting the imperfection of one's own gold standard is rare and consequential: it places a ceiling on what any device validated against it can be shown to achieve.

**S-087** [local_afdb603d] — *Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.*

One sentence: 'The diagnosis was made by a neuropsychiatrist according to DSM-5 criteria.' No standardised observational instrument such as ADOS, no interview such as ADI-R, no rating scale, no statement of when the diagnosis was made, whether it was made for this study or taken from clinical records, or what the diagnostic procedure comprised. Recruitment through a speech and language therapy service and a disability foundation indicates that all participants were receiving services, but nothing further is established. The comparison group's status is asserted rather than screened - no instrument, no exclusion criteria, and no statement about family history or developmental concerns. This is among the weakest ascertainments in the corpus and is not acknowledged as a limitation.

**S-088** [local_4f7e7eb3] — *Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques*

Nothing. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role, setting or timing is reported, and the source dataset's ascertainment procedure is not summarised even in a sentence. The class labels are treated as file attributes throughout. Under this review's classification this is dataset-label-only ascertainment in its least documented form. The omission is compounded by the paper's framing, which repeatedly describes the systems as tools for 'diagnosis' and 'early diagnosis' and proposes that they 'could help experts and autism treatment centres in the early detection of autism in children' - claims about diagnostic utility made against a reference standard whose nature is entirely unknown to the reader.

**S-089** [local_db6c2d7c] — *Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With*

Parent report alone. Parents who chose to share videos 'completed a survey to provide the age, sex, and diagnostic status of their children'. No instrument, no clinician involvement, no record verification, and no description of how diagnostic status was elicited. The companion study from the same group using the same app for speech analysis concedes this directly, noting that such labels 'are self-reported and thus unverified' and describing the mitigating design of offering diagnostic options unfamiliar to families who have not been evaluated. Neither the concession nor the mitigation appears here, and the limitations section does not mention the reference standard at all. Comparison-group status likewise rests on parental assertion with no screening.

**S-090** [local_8b5fb23b] — *Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms*

Not reported for the analysis. The literature review does note that the source group 'developed a four-level severity-based classifier model for ASD, with classes such as TD, low, medium, and severe based on Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) score', which establishes that CARS scores accompany the source dataset - so this paper is aware that a severity instrument exists and does not use it. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role or setting is stated as applying to the participants analysed, and the class labels are treated as image attributes. Under this review's classification this is dataset-label-only ascertainment, though better documented in its literature review than in its methods.

**S-091** [local_6dcefc34] — *Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism*

Parent report, with a described mitigation that is more substantive than most. Caregivers were required to confirm that the diagnosis 'came from a formal medical assessment', to select a diagnostic label from a menu including several distinctions that a family without evaluation experience would be unlikely to navigate - Autism Spectrum Disorder, Autistic Disorder, PDD-NOS, Asperger Syndrome, ADHD/ADD, anxiety, speech and language delay - and to report the specific therapies their child was receiving, on the reasoning that 'this information requires a specialized understanding of the autism diagnosis and subsequent treatment prescriptions'. That is a coherent design: it uses the specificity of diagnostic and treatment vocabulary as an indirect check on whether a formal evaluation occurred. It remains parent report, with no instrument, clinician contact or record verification, and the therapy information collected as part of the check is never described or analysed. Comparison-group status rests on parental assertion with no screening at all.

**S-092** [local_65974fc7] — *Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction*

Nothing. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role, setting or timing is reported anywhere in the paper. The only relevant information is the recruitment route - cooperation with a medical university, an autism association and special education schools - which establishes that participants were engaged with autism services but not how their diagnoses were made or verified. The comparison group's status is likewise unestablished, with 'normal children' asserted and no screening described. The paper's introduction observes that 'ASD diagnosing can be difficult because there are no standard and quantified medical tests like blood tests to diagnose the disorder', which makes the absence of any account of how the reference labels were obtained more conspicuous rather than less.

**S-093** [local_988c462e] — *The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation*

The reference standard is the ADOS-2 itself, administered by a clinician with ADOS-2 research reliability, and it functions here as a continuous outcome rather than a categorical label - raw scores on the 0-30 scale are the regression target. That is a defensible use of the instrument and is more demanding than binary classification, since it requires the model to track a graded clinical judgement rather than a dichotomy. Two caveats. The categorical diagnoses used to describe the groups - autistic versus language delay, developmental delay or typical development - are stated without describing who assigned them or under what criteria, so the group composition rests on unspecified clinical judgement even though the regression target does not. And using a single instrument as both the sole clinical characterisation and the prediction target means the system is validated against one clinician's scoring on one occasion, with no second rater, no test-retest interval and no independent confirmation of the score's stability.

**S-094** [local_76de1c03] — *The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children*

Multidisciplinary clinical diagnosis by a team comprising a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a pedagogue, recorded in kindergarten files. This is real clinical ascertainment and places the study well above the folder-membership, hashtag and questionnaire-threshold labels charted elsewhere in this review - the diagnoses were made by qualified clinicians working together, which is closer to best practice than a single-instrument threshold. Two limitations attach. The instruments, criteria and dates behind those records are not stated, so the standard cannot be characterised further. And the diagnoses were obtained from records rather than confirmed for the study, which means they were known in advance to whoever recruited and, potentially, to the raters - and rater blinding is nowhere addressed, in a study where every measurement is a human judgement.

**S-095** [local_3ba6d25c] — *Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach*

Diagnosis was clinical and consensus-based rather than instrument-based, and the paper is candid about why: 'Due to a limited access to established ASD diagnostic instruments such as ADOS and ADI-R, the accuracy of the ASD diagnosis in the present study was assured through a variety of other rigorous procedures.' Those procedures were DSM-IV criteria applied by a licensed psychiatrist with at least five years' experience, re-evaluation by a senior psychiatrist, and adjudication by at least two further senior psychiatrists if they disagreed. Additional gates: non-verbal IQ >= 70 on Raven's APM, absence of schizophrenia or ADHD, no medication at the time of the experiment, and adequate conversational ability judged by a speech-language psychologist. TD children were community-recruited, Raven-screened to IQ > 70, self/parent-reported free of physical or mental disorder, and with no ASD/ADHD in first-degree relatives. Note the DSM edition: DSM-IV, not DSM-5, in a study published in 2022. Multi-psychiatrist consensus is a defensible reference standard and better than the single-clinician or registry labels used elsewhere in this corpus, but it is unblinded to everything the clinicians already knew about the child, is not quantified for reliability, and yields no severity gradation.

**S-096** [local_70a30e2b] — *A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features*

Not reported at all - this is the study's most serious gap. The paper never states how any child's autism diagnosis was established: no DSM or ICD criteria, no ADOS, ADI-R, CARS, GARS or M-CHAT, no named clinician or team, no date of diagnosis, no inclusion or exclusion criteria for either group. The only clue is the recruitment site, an autism centre, so the ASD label is presumably the child's existing service-eligibility status. TD status is equally unspecified: the typically developing children are not described as having been screened for autism or developmental delay by any instrument, and their recruitment route is not given. The four children in the other-disorder group are labelled with CP and fragile X, again with no source. The result is that the study's target variable - the thing the 85.56% accuracy is accurate about - is undefined. This places it at the weakest end of reference-standard reporting in this corpus, below even the studies that use a single unblinded clinician's DSM judgement, because here there is no statement of any process at all.

**S-097** [local_a22f97df] — *A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities*

Among the better-specified in this corpus. Autism required satisfaction of two independent criteria - DSM-5 clinical criteria and the ADOS-2 - with diagnoses made by 'qualified doctors and professionals in the sector', and the absence of comorbidity was an explicit inclusion requirement. This is a dual-criterion standard including a gold-standard observational instrument, which places it above the single-clinician, registry-label or unspecified approaches seen elsewhere here. Typically developing status was established negatively rather than by instrument: no confirmed neurodevelopmental disorder, no suspected signs of autism, no developmental abnormality, no psychiatric or neurological history, plus an unusual and sensible catch-all whereby 'any child whose clinician or teacher was uncertain about the child's diagnosis or health was excluded'. That conservative rule reduces the risk of undetected autistic traits in the control group, though no screening instrument (SCQ, SRS, CAST) was administered to confirm it. Three details limit the standard's usefulness. The ADOS-2 module, algorithm scores and comparison scores are never reported, so the instrument is used as a gate and then discarded as data. Diagnosing clinicians are described only generically. And there is no statement of the interval between diagnosis and testing.

**S-098** [local_c6853fe2] — *A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation*

Two distinct reference standards operate in this study and the paper does not clearly separate them. For group membership, the 29 autistic children were assessed by professional clinicians using ADOS-2 at the Department of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics of a university teaching hospital, with module assignment reported; but no ADOS-2 score, no DSM or ICD criteria, no diagnosing-clinician description and no diagnostic date are given, and the single typically developing child's status is not characterised at all. For the study's actual outcome, the reference is an experienced clinician's 0-5 response-to-name score, assigned during the same session under an explicitly stated rule set. This second standard is well defined operationally - the rule tree in Fig. 2 is unambiguous - and it is the appropriate comparator for what the system does. Its weaknesses are that a single clinician scored each child, that this clinician was necessarily unblinded (they were conducting the assessment and calling the child's name), that no second rater or reliability statistic exists, and that the score is therefore an individual judgement rather than a consensus. Since response to name is exactly the kind of item where a clinician standing behind a child must judge in real time whether a head turn counted as a response with eye contact, the absence of any inter-rater reliability is a real gap: the paper's headline number is agreement with one person's uncorroborated judgement.

**S-099** [local_f1b626c8] — *Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games*

Weak and under-specified. Autistic status rests on admission to the recruiting clinic, where 'the children were admitted into this clinic based on the diagnosis made by a pediatric psychiatrist and a pediatric clinical psychologist and underwent a comprehensive evaluation', restated in the inclusion criteria simply as 'the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorders made by specialists'. Two clinicians of different disciplines is better than one, and the involvement of a psychiatrist and a clinical psychologist is a reasonable clinical standard, but no diagnostic instrument is named, no DSM or ICD version is cited, the 'comprehensive evaluation' is not described, no diagnosis date or interval to testing is given, and no reliability is quantified. The comparison group is weaker still: children were recruited from a mainstream public elementary school and are called 'normal' and 'healthy', with no screening instrument administered, no exclusion criteria listed and no statement that autism or developmental concerns were ruled out - so undetected autistic traits or other neurodevelopmental conditions in the comparison group cannot be excluded. The autistic group additionally passed two functional gates that shape who was studied: a therapist's judgement that the child had 'relative perception of people's faces', and the ability to sit at a computer and attend to images. Both are defensible for a face-processing task but both further narrow an already high-functioning sample.

**S-100** [local_6249bd63] — *Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior*

The strongest reference standard encountered in this review. Diagnostic status was 'confirmed as part of this study' - established prospectively rather than inherited from records - using the Clinical Best Estimate process, informed by ADOS-2 Module 4 and adhering to DSM-5 criteria. Clinical Best Estimate is the accepted research gold standard precisely because it integrates a standardised observational instrument, developmental history and clinical judgement rather than resting on any single source, and Module 4 is the correct ADOS-2 module for verbally fluent adolescents and adults. Neurotypical status was not merely the absence of a diagnosis: controls were 'recruited specifically as neurotypical controls', and raters were told they were 'clear cases of individuals without autism'. That framing is a genuine strength for a benchmark study - it means the human raters' 80.3% accuracy is not depressed by ambiguous controls - but it is simultaneously the study's central external-validity limit, since the two groups are drawn from the well-separated ends of a distribution that a real screening population fills continuously. The authors say so themselves in the conclusion. Two further points: the ADOS-2 was administered but no calibrated severity score is reported, so the autistic sample's position on the spectrum is unquantified; and the conversation confederates were blind to diagnostic status and unaware of the dependent variables, so the elicitation itself was not differentially shaped by knowledge of group membership - a control that few conversational studies in this corpus implement.

**S-101** [local_8b9e0e8a] — *Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas*

Not described. This is the study's most serious reporting gap and it sits oddly alongside the sophistication of everything else. The Data Acquisition section states only that 140 children with autism and 193 typically developing children were recruited and that all had normal or corrected vision; no diagnostic instrument, no DSM or ICD criteria, no clinician, no assessment procedure and no diagnostic date appears anywhere in the main text for either group. Two clinical co-authors are affiliated with the Children Healthcare Department of the Affiliated Hospital of Northwest University and the Children Rehabilitation Center of Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital, so clinical diagnosis is clearly implied, and the multi-centre recruitment from hospitals suggests service-identified children - but none of this is stated. The irony is sharpened by Table IV, in which the authors tabulate the diagnostic instruments used by comparator studies in the literature - Autism Behaviour Checklist, M-CHAT, ADOS, ADI-R - as a characteristic worth reporting, while leaving their own blank. Typically developing status rests on school recruitment with no screening instrument reported. Supplementary material was not retrieved and may contain more; on the main text alone, the quantity the model predicts with 96.73% accuracy is not defined.

**S-102** [local_0e476686] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts*

Self-disclosure in a public social-media biography, with no clinical component of any kind. Users were located by keyword search over biographies for 'Autism', 'ASD', 'Asperger', 'Aspie', 'Autistic' and 'ActuallyAutistic', and each candidate profile was then reviewed by hand and discarded if it belonged to an organisation or society, to someone describing themselves as an 'ASD advocate', or to a family member using phrasing such as 'father of an ASD kid' or 'mother of an ASD kid'. That filtering is thoughtful, is described in enough detail to repeat, and removes the most obvious sources of false positives - it is the best-executed part of the study. What it cannot do is establish that anyone is autistic. There is no diagnosis, no instrument, no criterion, no date and no verification, and the authors themselves note that biographies may contain false information and that tweets may be written by someone other than the account holder. The comparison label is weaker still and is not described at all: the paper never states how the 31 non-autistic users were found or chosen, whether they were sampled at random or selected for any property, or whether any effort was made to exclude autistic people who simply do not disclose - which, given that undiagnosed and undisclosed autism is common, means the negative class is defined by the absence of a public statement rather than by the absence of the condition. What the models therefore predict is whether a tweet came from an account whose biography contains an autism keyword.

**S-103** [local_fbaf69bf] — *Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Among the strongest in this review, and structurally different from the case-control norm because the diagnostic pathway is the clinical one rather than a research recruitment. Every toddler received the M-CHAT-R/F, a validated caregiver screening instrument, as part of routine well-child care. Children screening positive, and children about whom a caregiver or clinician expressed developmental concern, were then evaluated by a child psychologist using the ADOS-Toddler module, the age-appropriate observational gold standard. Mean ADOS-T total in the autistic group was 7.64 +/- 1.69. Two features deserve particular credit. The comparison group is screened rather than assumed: 396 typically developing toddlers all completed M-CHAT-R/F, so undetected autism in the comparison group is reduced (though not eliminated, since M-CHAT-R/F sensitivity is imperfect and only screen-positive or concern-flagged children received ADOS-T). And the single discordant case is reported explicitly - one typically developing child screened positive, was evaluated with ADOS-T, and was not diagnosed - a level of transparency about the reference-standard pathway that no other study charted here provides. The limitation is the one intrinsic to a two-stage design: children who screened negative and prompted no concern did not receive ADOS-T, so the comparison group's status rests on a screening instrument rather than on the diagnostic one.

**S-104** [local_74416ba7] — *Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders*

Among the strongest in this review, and the only one applying condition-specific re-evaluation to two different diagnoses. Diagnoses were determined according to DSM-5 research criteria and then re-evaluated with the appropriate instrument: ADOS-2 for the autistic participants, with the adult group's mean total raw score reported (46.5 +/- 11.9), and the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale for the schizophrenia group (67.1 +/- 13.0). Controls were not merely assumed neurotypical but were actively screened - 'physicians and psychologists interviewed them and excluded' anyone with learning delays or communication problems, and no control had a history of psychiatric disorder, drug abuse or epilepsy. So all three groups have an explicit ascertainment procedure, the two clinical groups have quantified symptom measures, and the control group has a stated exclusion protocol applied by clinicians. The residual gaps are minor by comparison: no inter-rater reliability is reported for the ADOS-2 or PANSS administrations, no interval between diagnosis and testing is given, and the ADOS-2 figures are total raw scores rather than calibrated severity scores, which limits comparability with other studies.

**S-105** [local_7c6a5aa4] — *Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders*

The weakest reference standard in this review alongside the social-media study. Diagnosis is voluntary self- or proxy-report through an optional online survey embedded in a free commercial app: users 'were asked to disclose their reason for using the application', 214 of 6,033 chose to respond, and 180 named a diagnosis. There is no clinical assessment, no diagnostic instrument, no clinician involvement, no verification, no date of diagnosis, and no record of who completed the survey - the AAC user, a parent, a spouse or a speech-language therapist, each of which would be plausible for a device used by people with communication impairments spanning early childhood to advanced dementia. Because 'refusal to answer the survey did not cause denial of service', respondents are self-selected on unknown characteristics, and they represent 3.4% of usable users. The 'no diagnosis' category (32 users) is particularly ambiguous, since a person using a speech-generating device while reporting no diagnosis may be a therapist, a family member, a curious downloader or someone with an undisclosed condition. The comparison group's composition is simultaneously the study's most interesting feature and a further source of uncertainty: contrasting autism against other communication-impaired populations rather than against typical development is exactly the differential framing this literature usually avoids, but here the comparison group is a convenience aggregate of eight loosely specified categories, one of which is literally labelled 'other' and accounts for half of it.

**S-106** [local_8a706eaa] — *Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Strong, staged and transparently described, though with an important detail about which instrument supplies which label. All caregivers completed the Korean Childhood Autism Rating Scale II, a 15-item instrument scored 15 to 60. Children whose scores indicated autism risk, or about whom a caregiver expressed concern, were referred to a child psychiatrist at Seoul National University Hospital for diagnostic evaluation, and the Korean Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule II was administered to those receiving a clinical diagnosis - so the autism label rests on the conjunction of clinician diagnosis and an above-cutoff score on a criterion-standard observational instrument, with calibrated severity scores reported (total CSS 6.07 +/- 1.6, social affect 6.62 +/- 1.8, restricted and repetitive behaviour 6.16 +/- 2.2). Comparison status rests on a below-cutoff K-CARS-2 score together with no parent-reported history of developmental delay or psychiatric condition, so the comparison group is screened rather than merely assumed - though with a caregiver-completed instrument rather than a clinician assessment. Two qualifications matter. The paper states plainly that these conservative criteria were adopted specifically to produce 'clinically distinct groups', so the reference standard is being used to construct maximal separation rather than to sample a clinical spectrum, which the authors disclose but do not connect to their near-ceiling accuracy. And the severity prediction target is derived from K-CARS-2 bands (under 30 non-autism, 30-36 mild or moderate, 37-60 severe) rather than from the K-ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores that were collected and reported - so the clinician-administered severity measure is available in the paper but is not what the severity model predicts.

**S-107** [local_6b9484ce] — *Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking*

Absent. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician or process is reported for the 59 children, and the labels are taken directly from the folder structure of the downloaded dataset. The introduction does contain a description of how autism is diagnosed in general practice - initial concern about developmental milestones, paediatrician assessment, referral to a psychologist, child neurologist, speech and language pathologist or developmental paediatrician, then behavioural observation, child and parent interviews, questionnaires and the CARS rating scale - and it correctly observes that 'there are no standard definitive tests like blood test to identify the condition'. But none of this is connected to the actual data. The target being predicted is therefore whichever folder an image sits in, and the study inherits without examination whatever ascertainment the source dataset applied. For a review comparing studies partly on the strength of their reference standards, this is the floor.

**S-108** [local_c6a4ea7b] — *SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism*

Absent as a described procedure. The paper's entire statement on this point is that it 'considered the binary classification problem of classifying a child as having ASD or not, as all three datasets had binary labelling of the clinical status' - so the labels are inherited from three separately assembled research corpora with no account of how autism was diagnosed in any of them, by whom, against which criteria or in which era. Given that the Flusberg corpus records children aged 12-26 months, its labels must derive from a very different ascertainment process from corpora recruiting 3-7 year olds, and pooling them without comment means the target variable is heterogeneous in an unexamined way. ADOS is invoked repeatedly, but as the source of the behavioural constructs the features are designed to mirror - echolalia, back-and-forth interchange, building on statements - rather than as an instrument administered to these children. That is a legitimate and rather elegant use of a diagnostic instrument as a specification for feature engineering, and it should not be confused with having a reference standard.

**S-109** [local_5c43dffa] — *Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths*

Not described. The retrieved text contains no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician, procedure, date or setting for either group; participants are simply designated ASD or TD. This is a notable omission for a study from a group closely associated with the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials, whose tasks the paper says its battery resembles, and it sits awkwardly with an introduction that criticises clinical assessment for being subjective and providing 'minimal information about the underlying mechanism of the disorder'. Whatever the actual ascertainment - and given the authorship it was very likely rigorous - the paper as published does not state it, so the target being predicted is undefined from the report alone.

**S-110** [local_32da8ede] — *A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths*

Inherited and thinly reported, though better specified than in the other reuses of this dataset. The autistic children 'were evaluated in specialized clinics, and the level of autism in each child was gauged using the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS)', while typically developing children were recruited from mainstream French schools. Two distinctions matter. CARS is described as gauging the level of autism rather than establishing the diagnosis, so it functions here as a severity measure applied after specialist clinic evaluation - and that evaluation is named but not described, with no diagnostic criteria, DSM or ICD version, clinician discipline or procedure given. And the comparison group's status rests on school recruitment with no screening instrument reported, so undetected autistic traits in that group cannot be excluded. For the present study these are inherited rather than authored deficiencies, but they define the target being predicted and the paper does not flag them as open.

**S-111** [local_15ed96cb] — *A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning*

Routine clinical diagnosis recorded in the health record after age two, ascertained by ICD-9 code for 56.6% of cases and by verified keyword search of provider free-text notes for the remaining 43.4%. There is no research instrument - no ADOS, ADI-R or equivalent - and the well-baby protocol contains no autism-specific screening tool, which the paper states explicitly and which is part of its motivation. Three features of the ascertainment are handled better than the norm in this corpus. The temporal separation is enforced by design: predictors are capped at 24 months and outcomes restricted to diagnoses recorded after 24 months, adopted specifically 'to develop a model that minimizes data leakage from diagnosis to predictors' - a form of leakage control that most studies here do not have to think about and that this one does. Acronym collisions were checked and excluded, and free-text mentions were manually verified to concern the child rather than a relative. And the resulting label noise is quantified rather than glossed: the authors state that 'based on the national incidence of ASD, the true positive ASD group is at least 10 times higher in the examined population', so most autistic children in the cohort sit in the comparison group. That is an unusually candid acknowledgement, and it has an implication the paper does not draw out - that a large share of the flagged false positives may be correctly identified children whose diagnosis was simply never recorded, so both specificity and positive predictive value are understated. The 43.4% of diagnoses ascertained from free text also introduces provider-dependent recording variation, which the authors flag as warranting research into inter-rater differences.

**S-112** [local_261afa51] — *AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: &#x201C;A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System&#x201D;*

There is none, and the substitute is source of retrieval. An image is labelled autistic because it appeared on a website about autism and non-autistic because it did not. No diagnosis, criterion, instrument, clinician or verification underlies either label. Both directions of error are unbounded: an autism-website photograph may depict a sibling, a parent, a stock model or a child whose diagnostic status is unstated, while a randomly gathered photograph may depict an autistic child. Because the label is a property of where a file was found rather than of the person depicted, the quantity the model predicts is image provenance, and the paper's reported 95% accuracy is best read as a measure of how distinguishable the two collections are. That distinguishability has many possible sources - camera type, resolution, JPEG compression, lighting, background, pose, cropping convention, the tendency of advocacy imagery towards particular framings - none of which is examined.

**S-113** [local_3e88f3ce] — *An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks*

The strongest reference standard in the review, and the study's principal problem is what it does with it. Diagnosis at the ABIDE-I contributing sites rested on clinical judgement supported by ADOS and ADI-R - the field's two gold-standard instruments, administered by trained clinicians - so the labels are as sound as any charted here. The difficulty is that the scored output of those instruments is then supplied to the classifier as input. GAMI-Net ranks ADOS_TOTAL first among behavioural contributors at 0.278; the final SHAP analysis ranks ADOS_Gotham_Total first at 0.234; and ADI_R_SOCIAL_TOTAL_A, ADOS_COMM, ADOS_GOTHAM_SEVERITY, SRS_RAW_TOTAL and ADI_R_VERBAL_TOTAL_BV all appear in the top ten. In ABIDE-I these instruments are administered to the autism group as part of establishing the diagnosis and are largely absent for controls, so two mechanisms operate simultaneously: the recorded values encode the clinician's diagnostic judgement, and the presence or absence of a value is itself label-informative. A model with access to this stream will reproduce the diagnosis on any partition, however carefully constructed. This is the clearest instance of target leakage in the corpus, and it differs in one respect from the questionnaire-dataset studies charted alongside it: there the label was an arithmetic function of the features, here it is the clinical judgement that the features summarise, which is less mechanical but no less circular.

**S-114** [local_5b5f2237] — *Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development*

Clinician consensus under DSM-IV, described in the same terms as the group's companion paper on this cohort: initial diagnosis by a licensed psychiatrist with at least five years' experience, evaluation of that diagnosis by a senior clinician, and, where the two disagreed, involvement of two further senior clinicians to confirm. No standardised diagnostic instrument was administered - no ADOS, ADI-R, CARS or SRS - and the companion paper on this cohort explains why, stating that the group had 'limited access to established ASD diagnostic instruments'. Typically developing children were recruited from local communities and reported no diagnosis of any psychiatric, motor, vision or other physical disorder, but no autism screening instrument was applied to them. Multi-clinician consensus is a reasonable clinical standard and better than a single unblinded judgement, but it yields no quantified severity, no reliability statistic, and no dimensional measure against which the coordination findings could be checked. The use of DSM-IV rather than DSM-5 in work published in 2024 also reflects the age of the underlying recordings rather than current practice.

**S-115** [local_13426811] — *Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning*

The most thorough reference standard in the review alongside the joint-attention study, and the only one that applies a gold-standard instrument to both groups. Autism diagnosis followed DSM-5 criteria applied by experienced clinicians specialising in neurodevelopmental disorders, with ADOS-2 as the primary confirming instrument administered by someone holding research reliability certified through Western Psychological Services, and supported by a full battery: SRS-2, age-appropriate Wechsler IQ testing, Vineland-II, AQ and PARS-TR caregiver interview. What distinguishes it further is the comparison group. Every non-autistic participant received the ADOS-2 and was confirmed non-spectrum against the published cut-offs, which are quoted (6 or below on Module 3; combined communication and social interaction of 7 or below on Module 4), with group means reported separately for the clinically assessed and the recruited subgroups. Almost every other study in this corpus establishes comparison status by absence of a diagnosis or by parent report; this one administers the same instrument to both sides. The inclusion of co-occurring conditions in the autistic cohort is also a deliberate and well-argued choice rather than an oversight. Two qualifications remain: the diagnosing clinicians were not blind to anything and no inter-rater reliability is reported beyond the administrator's certification, and the language samples analysed come from the same ADOS-2 sessions that generated the labels.

**S-116** [local_948fa8d0] — *Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms*

Absent. The labels are the names of two subdirectories in a downloaded folder, and the methods section describes exactly this: features are extracted 'by traversing through the directory structure', with 'a label column added to denote the class label (autistic or non_autistic)'. No diagnosis, instrument, criterion, clinician or verification underlies either class. The quantity the models predict is therefore which folder an image was filed in, and given that the folders were populated from different parts of the internet, the reported accuracies are best read as measures of how distinguishable the two source collections are as image sets.

**S-117** [local_893dfc22] — *Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed*

None is required by the task as executed, since no autism classification is attempted - the labels are posed emotion categories, which are a strong ground truth for emotion recognition and carry no information about autism. The consequence for this review is that the study cannot contribute evidence on any of the diagnostic questions. Its relevance is instead to the review's treatment of how autism framing attaches to work containing no autism data: a reader relying on the title, abstract, keywords and conclusion would record this as an autism study, and it is not one.

**S-118** [local_e7c16f2a] — *Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification*

Solid for the autistic group and absent for the comparison group. Autism required a clinical diagnosis confirmed with the ADOS-2, and the paper states something few in this review do: the diagnoses were made 'by healthcare professionals and industry experts who were independent of our research laboratory and study'. Explicit independence between the diagnosing clinicians and the research team removes one route by which knowledge of the study could influence the reference standard, and is worth crediting. Against this, no ADOS-2 score of any kind is reported, so the severity range the autistic group is said to span cannot be characterised; comorbidity was excluded by criterion, narrowing the sample relative to the clinical population; and typically developing status rests entirely on parent and teacher report of no neurodevelopmental disorder, with no screening instrument administered and no assessment of abilities - so undetected autistic traits or developmental difficulty in the comparison group cannot be ruled out.

**S-119** [local_5a7ab52d] — *Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain*

None. The label is a binary 'Detected' or 'Not detected' for a combined 'autism and visual SPD' construct, with no diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician, assessment or source described. Two features of the labelling deserve specific note. First, the target conflates two distinct conditions - autism and visual sensory processing disorder - into a single undifferentiated binary, so even if the label were valid it would not identify which condition a positive prediction refers to, and the paper nowhere addresses how a model trained on a merged label could support either diagnosis. Second, the dataset section asserts that 'a new dataset named AQ10 is developed based on autism screening performed in individuals and holds 20 features', which conflates a dataset with the AQ-10, an existing published autism screening questionnaire, and in any case none of the AQ-10 items appears among the eleven variables the paper actually shows. The quantity being predicted is therefore undefined.

**S-120** [local_8253c2ec] — *Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder*

None, and its absence is structural rather than incidental. The class variable in the UCI and Kaggle autism screening datasets is not a clinical diagnosis: it is computed by summing the A1 to A10 item responses and applying the instrument's published cut-off, so it is a screening outcome derived arithmetically from the same fields supplied to the model. The paper describes the scoring rule itself - 'each question is scored as either 0 or 1 based on the individual's response. Only responses that indicate autistic traits are given a score of 1' - without drawing the consequence. Two facts follow. No respondent in any of the four datasets is known to have undergone diagnostic assessment, so nothing here is validated against autism as clinically established. And because the label is a deterministic function of the modelled inputs, the classification task has no uncertainty in it: 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC across all four age bands simultaneously is the expected output of the arrangement, obtainable by a single summation and comparison, and no optimisation, architecture or validation scheme bears on it. This is the second study in the review resting on these datasets, and the pattern is identical in both.

**S-121** [local_1e9d0b71] — *Machine learning’s effectiveness*

There is none in the diagnostic sense, and the study is explicit about this. Group membership rests entirely on maternal completion of the SRS-2 and application of published sex-specific screening cut-offs; no child received a clinical assessment, ADOS, ADI-R or diagnostic evaluation of any kind. The authors state the consequence directly, recommending that the method form 'part of a comprehensive assessment process that includes clinical evaluation and other standardized measures' and that 'integrating more robust diagnostic tools for ASD, such as clinical assessments or standardized behavioral tests, alongside the SRS-2, would improve the reliability of the screening process'. This places the study in a different category from the diagnostic studies charted elsewhere in this review: what is predicted is whether a mother's questionnaire responses about her child exceed a threshold, which is a legitimate screening target but not autism. Three specific consequences follow. Single-informant report carries known biases and no second informant or reliability statistic is available. A dichotomy imposed on a continuous scale creates borderline cases whose classification is arbitrary, which matters for a model reporting perfect separation. And the 19 above-threshold children are a screening-positive group of whom, at a population SRS-2 cut-off, a substantial proportion would not receive an autism diagnosis on assessment.

**S-122** [local_b9e05a8f] — *Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network*

There is none. No child in either corpus is known to the authors to have received a diagnostic assessment. In the Piosenka dataset the positive label means an image was found on a website or Facebook page with autism-related content; in the YTUIA dataset it means a video was collected into a corpus of self-stimulatory behaviour, half from YouTube and half from therapists and professional organisations. Neither carries a clinician judgement, a diagnostic instrument, a medical record or any documented ascertainment. The paper cites no reference standard, does not identify the absence as a limitation, and describes the positive class throughout as 'individuals diagnosed with ASD' - a description the data cannot support. The YTUIA positives at least depict a behaviour that is associated with autism, which places them a step above pure provenance labelling; but the modelling target is the face crop rather than the behaviour, so even that association does not transfer to what the model is trained on. This is the same reference-standard failure recorded for the other Piosenka-based papers in this review, and it bounds every figure the paper reports.

**S-123** [local_0b0960c4] — *Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]*

None described. The 13 autistic participants are stated to be 'diagnosed with ASD' with no instrument, criteria, clinician qualification, setting or date, and no screening procedure is reported for the 4 comparison children. The labels derive from the originating corpus and this paper transmits none of its documentation. The consequence is the same as for several studies in this review: the quantity the models predict is a label of unknown provenance, and no reported figure can be located relative to any clinical standard.

**S-124** [local_abad69fd] — *Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play*

Among the stronger reference standards in this review. Diagnosis was made by senior child and adolescent psychiatrists as a best-estimate clinical judgement against DSM-5 criteria, corroborated by CARS-2 with the instrument's psychometric properties cited from the literature (internal consistency 0.93, meta-analytic alpha 0.90, sensitivity 88%, specificity 86%). The corroboration is real clinical assessment rather than a questionnaire threshold standing in for one, and it is applied by clinicians qualified to make it. Two qualifications matter. First, the CARS-2 floor of 30 was applied as an exclusion: 23 children with a clinical diagnosis but a score below 30 were removed from the study. This converts the reference standard from 'clinically diagnosed autism' into 'clinically diagnosed autism of at least moderate severity', truncating exactly the part of the spectrum on which a screening tool would be hardest and most useful. The authors state the consequence directly - selection bias toward more pronounced characteristics, with the model's performance therefore possibly overestimated - which is the correct inference and one that few papers here draw about their own inclusion rules. Second, whether the video coders knew each child's group is not stated, and because the autistic children were recruited from hospitals and intervention centres while controls came from a kindergarten, group membership may have been inferable from the recordings independently of any behaviour coded.

**S-125** [local_cd7545e2] — *Predictive model using autism*

The strongest reference standard in the review for the specific question at hand, and its strength lies in what was deliberately left out of it. Diagnoses in both groups were made under DSM-5 by consensus among several psychiatrists with extensive experience in both conditions, drawing on interactions during diagnostic assessment and on prior psychiatric and medical histories. The paper then states the crucial fact: 'ASD diagnosis was a good clinical estimate, as neither the ADOS-2 nor the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R) was employed in the assessment process.' Because ADOS-2 items are the index test, any contribution of ADOS-2 to the diagnosis would have made the analysis circular - the model would be predicting a label partly derived from its own inputs, which is the failure this review has documented in the questionnaire-item studies where the class label is an arithmetic function of the modelled features. Here the separation is explicit and deliberate, and it is what makes the headline negative finding meaningful: when the ADOS-2 algorithm labels 45% to 52% of schizophrenia patients as autistic, that is a genuine disagreement with an independent clinical judgement rather than an artefact of shared information. Two qualifications. Best-estimate consensus diagnosis is the accepted standard in adult psychiatry but has no external criterion, so disagreement between algorithm and clinicians is evidence about the algorithm only if the clinicians are taken as correct. And whether the ADOS-2 administrators were blind to the established diagnosis is not stated, which matters more here than in an automated study because every item code is a clinician's judgement.

**S-126** [local_3ecb92bf] — *The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech*

Absent as an independent element and inherited without description. De-Enigma children are stated to be 'diagnosed with ASD' and CPSD children to carry diagnoses of autism, dysphasia or PDD-NOS, but neither corpus's diagnostic process is described - no instrument, no criteria, no clinician qualification, no date. The typically developing group is characterised only by absence: 'no prior history of difficulties with learning, speech, hearing or general learning', which is a screening statement rather than an assessment. Two features compound this. The CPSD categories are pre-DSM-5, since PDD-NOS was eliminated as a diagnosis in 2013, so the labels encode a superseded nosology whose boundaries with autism were themselves contested - and the four-class task therefore asks a model to reproduce a distinction that the diagnostic system has since abandoned. And the atypical and typical children were recorded in different physical settings, clinic and school respectively, so the label is confounded with the circumstance of recording independently of whatever the diagnoses mean. The paper does not treat the reference standard as a topic at all.

**S-127** [local_4b02df7c] — *Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism*

None, and the paper's handling of this is the most precise in the review. The positive label is use of #ActuallyAutistic plus autism-related keywords in the profile description - self-identification within an online community. The authors do not claim otherwise at any point: their own conclusion states that the models predict 'use of the #ActuallyAutistic hashtag, an imperfect proxy for self-reported autism', and their first limitation is that 'while we focused on individuals who self-identified as autistic, there is no clinical validation for their diagnosis'. They then reason about contamination in both directions. Users of the hashtag might be parents, caregivers or advocacy organisations rather than autistic people, which they judge rare 'due to the negative social connotations of using #ActuallyAutistic without a diagnosis' - an appeal to community norms rather than evidence, but an informed one, since the hashtag's function within the autism rights movement is precisely to mark first-person testimony. And autistic users who do not self-identify will contaminate the control group, which they bound at roughly the population prevalence, arguing that 'with autism having a prevalence rate of <3%, the model performance should not degrade by more than 3%' - a bound that assumes population prevalence transfers to Twitter's user base and that non-self-identifying autistic users write like non-autistic ones, neither of which is established. What the paper does not consider is that its label might be a design choice rather than a defect: undiagnosed self-identifying autistic adults are precisely the population an access-oriented screening tool would most want to reach, and treating their self-identification as noise assumes that clinical ascertainment is the only valid criterion in a study whose framing elsewhere questions exactly that assumption.

**S-128** [local_7d7f1fcc] — *Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children*

Strong in substance and incompletely reported in one respect that matters. Autistic children met DSM-5 clinical criteria with the diagnosis 'further supported by employing gold standard diagnostic assessments', within an established longitudinal cohort staffed by a clinical psychiatry department - so this is genuine clinical ascertainment, not a questionnaire threshold or a dataset label, and it stands among the better reference standards in this review. The comparison group was actively screened rather than merely assumed typical: absence of known neurological or psychiatric conditions, and no first-degree relative with autism, which excludes the elevated-likelihood siblings who would otherwise blur the contrast. The unresolved issue is independence. The model's input is the ADOS recording, and 'gold standard diagnostic assessments' in a paediatric autism cohort ordinarily means ADOS, so the same session that supplied the model's training data may have contributed to the diagnostic label it is trained to predict. That is a circularity of the same family as the questionnaire studies excluded from this review, though far milder in degree - the model sees raw pose and audio rather than the clinician's coded items, so it must rediscover from signal what the clinician judged, rather than reproducing an arithmetic function of its inputs. Still, it means the label is not independent of the material, and the fix would be one sentence: another study in this review states explicitly that neither ADOS nor ADI-R entered its diagnostic process, which is exactly the statement needed here and is absent. The main text also defers the specific instruments to supplementary material, so a reader cannot check.

**S-129** [local_5a331ffe] — *Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning*

None, and the paper's account of why is the most candid statement of provenance-based labelling in this review. SSBD videos were 'posted by parents/caregivers on YouTube', collected and annotated for stimming behaviour, and the authors reason: 'Therefore, and in the way the dataset is described, the data only concerns ASD children ... We are also confident in the reliability of the parents who uploaded these videos, and we, therefore, consider that the youngsters presented as the main subject of these videos are all autistic.' The autism label thus rests on two inferences - that a family posting a video of their child stimming implies a diagnosis, and that families are reliable reporters of that diagnosis - and on an explicitly stated act of trust. No clinical assessment, diagnostic instrument, medical record or clinician judgement exists for any child in the corpus. The comparison class is worse still: no basis whatever is offered for the non-autistic label, because the class itself is never described. Two structural consequences follow. Because the positive class comprises children whose families filmed and published their stereotypies, it is drawn from the visibly and severely affected end of the phenotype rather than from any representative spectrum. And because the paper elsewhere lists 'existing datasets are not necessarily trustworthy' as a limitation while simultaneously declaring confidence in these particular uploads, the two statements sit uneasily together.

**S-130** [local_45ef7022] — *A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features*

There is none for diagnosis and none stated for severity, and the second gap is the more damaging. All 30 children are described as autistic on the basis of attending a special school; no diagnostic instrument, clinician judgement or record is cited for any of them. The classification target is severity level 1, 2 or 3, and the origin of those labels is nowhere given - not in the dataset description, not in the methodology, not in the results. The Aberrant Behavior Checklist is discussed at length in the introduction as the 58-item instrument clinicians use to grade severity and guide dosage, and it is the obvious candidate, but the paper never states that it was administered to these children, by whom, when, or with what training. Two consequences follow. First, what the classifiers predict is simply unknown, so the 98.33% cannot be interpreted even setting aside the splitting problem. Second, the paper's central comparative claim becomes incoherent: it reports that the machine learning methods 'outperform the clinical ABC method' in classifying severity levels and presents a table comparing their accuracies. If the ABC supplied the labels, a model can at best reproduce it and cannot exceed it, and any apparent excess is measurement of the model's agreement with its own training signal; if some independent criterion existed against which both were scored, the paper does not say what it was. A claim to beat the clinical standard, in a paper proposing to adjust medication, requires the standard to be specified, and it is not.

**S-131** [local_0f5a351e] — *Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*
