None. The autism label means an image was placed in the autistic subfolder of a Kaggle collection; the non-autistic label means an image was returned by a web search. No child in either class is known to have been assessed, no diagnostic instrument or clinician judgement is cited, and the paper does not identify the absence as a limitation - it reports the folder structure factually and moves on. This is the sixth study in the review resting on this corpus, and the position is unchanged: whatever separation the models achieve, it is a separation between two collections of internet images, and the paper supplies the description that makes this plain.

**S-132** [local_786b6280] — *Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features*

Inherited from the source corpora and not transmitted. Children are designated autistic or typically developing by the original Eigsti and Nadig investigators, but this paper reports no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician qualification or assessment date. The labels are nonetheless in a different class from those in the web-scraped branches of this review: ASDBank and CHILDES are established research archives whose contributing studies performed documented clinical ascertainment, so the underlying labels are real diagnoses rather than folder membership or hashtag use. The specific weaknesses are that the paper does not tell the reader what those diagnoses rested on, and that the typically developing designation for the Warren and Kuczaj children means only that those corpora were collected from typically developing populations, without any screening described in this paper.

**S-133** [local_879ec69b] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning*

Inherited and undescribed for both corpora - no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician qualification or assessment date appears anywhere. The Gait Fullbody Dataset carries binary autistic and typically developing labels from its creators; DREAM carries a three-level label - non-spectrum, ASD and AUT - of which the non-spectrum class was discarded, following the prior study whose architecture this work extends. Discarding the non-spectrum group has a consequence the paper does not draw: the DREAM experiment is then a discrimination between two autism-related categories rather than between autism and non-autism, so its 70.19% is not comparable to the Gait dataset's autism-versus-typical task and the two figures cannot be read as measurements of the same thing. The reference-standard issue that most affects validity, however, is procedural rather than definitional. The methods state that in the Gait dataset each child performed ten walking trials and 'the most optimal trial was selected based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation'. Selecting which of a child's trials enters the dataset on the basis of that child's diagnosis is selection on the outcome: it means the 100 modelled samples are not a random sample of each child's walking but the trial a clinician judged most suitable given what the child was known to have. Whatever separation the models achieve is conditioned on that choice, and no splitting scheme downstream can undo it.

**S-134** [local_93e5d23d] — *Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]*

Among the stronger ascertainment procedures in this review and described with unusual completeness for a secondary analysis. The process ran in four stages: the Gilliam Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition completed by parents; a caregiver interview conducted against DSM-5 criteria; direct evaluation and observation of the child by two child clinical psychologists holding doctorates; and separate confirmation of the diagnosis by at least one child psychiatrist in a different setting. Independent confirmation by a second clinician working in a different setting is a real safeguard against single-assessor error and appears in almost no other study charted here. The authors also state plainly why ADOS was not administered - 'the official version of Autism Diagnostic Observational Schedule (ADOS) is not available for Farsi' - and repeat it in their limitations rather than leaving the omission unexplained. Two qualifications remain. The GARS-2 is a parental questionnaire, and its position at the front of the process means the pathway begins with parental report; and the typically developing group's status is not described as having been screened by any instrument.

**S-135** [local_a0d73248] — *Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm*

None. The 'Class/ASD' variable in this dataset is not a clinical diagnosis but a screening outcome, computed by summing the A1-A10 item responses and applying the AQ-10 cut-off. No respondent underwent diagnostic assessment, and no instrument, clinician or record is cited. The distinctive feature of this particular study is that the derivation is visible in its own methods: the paper prints the complete field list - 'A1 Score, A2 Score, A3 Score, A4 Score, A5 Score, A6 Score, A7 Score, A8 Score, A9 Score, A10 Score, age, gender, ethnicity, jundice, austim, contry of res, used app before, result, age desc, relation, Class/ASD' - which contains both the ten items, their sum ('result'), and the thresholded outcome ('Class/ASD'). The model is therefore asked to predict a variable that is a deterministic function of another variable it is given.

**S-136** [local_4ceee075] — *Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics*

None described. The 50 children are stated to be 'diagnosed with ASD' and nothing further is given - no instrument, no criteria, no clinician, no setting, no date - and no screening procedure is reported for the 50 comparison children. For a prospective study that designed its own acquisition protocol, recruited 100 families and recorded over 16 hours of video, this is a striking omission, and it contrasts sharply with the care taken over the technical description: the paper specifies the MediaPipe landmark counts, the composition of the 1,639-value feature vector, the dropout rate, the L2 coefficient and the early-stopping patience, while saying nothing at all about how autism was established in the children whose data those numbers describe. The consequence is that the label the model predicts is undefined, and the study's reported 85-90% cannot be located relative to any clinical standard.

**S-137** [local_84bcd4ed] — *Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of*

None for autism and none for gelotophobia, with the second absence being the more remarkable. The autism label reflects folder membership in a public image collection assembled partly from autism-related websites; no diagnostic instrument, clinician judgement or medical record is cited for any image, and the paper does not identify this as a limitation. For gelotophobia the position is stronger still: the ethics section states that the GELOPH<15> questionnaire 'was not directly administered to participants in this study; it was used solely as a reference from previously validated research' and that 'no direct contact with human participants occurred'. This directly contradicts the abstract, which says that in ambiguous cases 'the GELOPH<15> questionnaire, consisting of 15 items, was administered to confirm the diagnosis'. Taking the ethics statement as authoritative - as its specificity and its consistency with the study's design require - no person in this study was ever assessed for gelotophobia, so the system's gelotophobia outputs were never compared with anything. The conclusion nonetheless states that the study 'demonstrates the effectiveness of combining deep learning techniques with validated diagnostic tools for detecting gelotophobia'. This is the clearest instance in the review of a headline claim resting on no measurement whatever, and it is distinct in kind from the label-quality problems recorded elsewhere: those studies have bad ground truth, this component has none.

**S-138** [local_d97673f4] — *Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

None. The autism label reflects folder membership in a public collection whose positive class was harvested from autism-associated online content; no child is known to have received a diagnostic assessment, no instrument or clinician judgement is cited, and the paper does not identify the absence as a limitation. This is the eighth study in the review on this corpus family and the position is unchanged across all of them: whatever the models separate, they separate two collections of internet images.

**S-139** [local_86a67a4f] — *Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children*

None. The autism labels reflect folder membership in a public collection whose positive class was assembled from autism-associated online content; no child is known to have received a diagnostic assessment, and no instrument, clinician judgement or record is cited anywhere. The paper describes the corpus as 'large, well-labelled public data promoting reproducibility', which conflates consistent labelling with valid labelling - the labels are consistent in that every image in the autistic folder carries the same tag, and they are not diagnoses. This is the ninth study in the review resting on this corpus family and the position is unchanged. The emotion labels are category assignments from the source corpus and are adequate for what they measure, though nothing establishes that they were assigned by raters familiar with autistic facial expression, which is the very phenomenon the paper says general-population models miss.

**S-140** [local_0a39cca9] — *Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy*

None described for either source. For the Kaggle portion the labels are folder membership in a collection whose autistic class was harvested from autism-associated online content - the position documented across nine other studies in this review. For the Semarang autism-centre portion, children attending a clinical service would ordinarily carry clinical diagnoses, and this is the one point at which the study could have improved on its predecessors; but no instrument, criteria, clinician, assessment date or procedure is reported, and the paper's provenance sentence explicitly leaves the sources open, saying the data 'could come from a variety of places, such as clinics, past research, or relevant public statistics'. The opportunity to anchor part of the corpus in real diagnoses is therefore present and unrealised.

**S-141** [local_7432ffd7] — *Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models*

Not confirmed by this study. Labels are inherited wholesale from the figshare dataset. The presence of a CARS_Score field implies that the original collectors administered the Childhood Autism Rating Scale, but this paper reports no cut-off, no administrator qualification, no ADOS or ADI-R, no DSM or ICD criterion, and no statement of who made the diagnoses or when. The TD group's status as non-autistic is likewise asserted rather than evidenced - no screening instrument is named.

**S-142** [local_8ff20c48] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning*

Not confirmed for any participant. This is the defining feature of the study: there is no clinical diagnosis anywhere in the pipeline. The label Class/ASD Traits is generated by the Q-CHAT-10 scoring function applied to the same ten items that supply the features. What is modelled is therefore a scoring rule, not a condition. The one screening instrument used is a caregiver checklist completed variously by parents, caregivers, medical staff or clinicians - and the field recording which of those it was was deleted during preprocessing as irrelevant, discarding the only available indicator of measurement heterogeneity.

**S-143** [local_986436f2] — *Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost*

No diagnostic confirmation of any kind. The class labels are Kaggle folder names on images gathered from the open web. No clinical assessment, no instrument, no assessor, no date, and no record of who the children are. The paper does not mention this once, and instead treats the labels as ground truth adequate to support claims about automated ASD screening.

**S-144** [local_bb4d1f7a] — *Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models*

Well handled and honestly reported. Diagnoses were made by experienced physicians applying DSM-5 criteria together with CARS scores, and the paper states plainly why gold-standard instruments were not used: ADI-R and ADOS evaluations are not widely available in India. That candour about a real infrastructural constraint compares favourably with the many studies in this corpus that simply assert diagnosis or inherit labels from a download. What undermines it is the severity banding rather than the diagnosis: eligibility required CARS >=30, yet Table 3 assigns ten children to a Low class defined as CARS <=20 and ten more to a Mild class spanning 20 to 40, and a High class defined as CARS >60 when the scale's maximum is 60. The four equal groups cannot have been generated by the stated rule, and the actual CARS distribution is never shown.

**S-145** [local_13c1f46d] — *Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism*

None. Labels are Kaggle folder names on photographs of unknown origin. No clinical assessment, instrument, criterion, assessor, date or provenance record exists for a single image, and the paper does not acknowledge the issue at any point - including in its ethics statement, which cites the dataset's public availability as the reason no ethical review was required.

**S-146** [local_e771fb69] — *Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data*

Not described. Labels come as a binary field in the downloaded dataset (1 autistic, 0 non-autistic). No diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor, setting or date is reported for either group, and the source dataset's own procedures are not summarised. The comparison group's non-autistic status is likewise asserted with no screening evidence.

**S-147** [local_945300a5] — *Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network*

None. Group membership is determined by school: the autism group is the set of children attending a Special Elementary School, the comparison group the set attending a State Elementary School. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor, date or record is reported for a single child, and the typically developing children were not screened with any instrument. The study's exclusion of intellectual disability, cerebral palsy and Down syndrome implies some clinical information was available, but its source is never described. School placement is a proxy for diagnosis that also carries administrative, geographic and socioeconomic structure into the label.

**S-148** [local_ed30e24c] — *Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI*

None. The outcome is Class/ASD_Traits, the Q-CHAT-10 screening result, and no clinical diagnosis exists for any case. The paper describes this as 735 cases diagnosed with ASD, which overstates what the dataset contains: the ASD label here records that a caregiver's ten checklist answers summed above a cut-off, not that a clinician assessed the child. No assessor, criterion, instrument beyond Q-CHAT-10 or date is reported.

**S-149** [local_b9de0d7f] — *Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques*

None, and the paper states the label rule plainly enough that this is not in doubt: a 1 is scored for each Q-CHAT-10 item answered Always, Usually or Sometimes, and a total above 3 indicates the presence of potential ASD traits. That threshold is the outcome variable. No clinician, diagnostic instrument, criterion or assessment date exists for any record in either dataset, and the online questionnaire origin of the Saudi data means the respondents were not verified either.

**S-150** [local_14df790d] — *Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach*

None. The outcome is the Class/ASD traits field, the Q-CHAT-10 screening result, applied to app-submitted responses with no clinical assessment, no clinician, no instrument beyond the checklist and no verification of who completed it. The paper's title and abstract are accurate about this - it predicts autism traits, not autism - and that accuracy distinguishes it from several neighbours in the corpus that describe the same label as a diagnosis.

**S-151** [local_4da2b941] — *Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study*

Self-reported but with real safeguards, and honestly characterised. Participants were asked about a clinically based diagnosis and about which professional made it; the 12 who reported self-diagnosis were excluded; and respondents were instructed to report only clinician-confirmed diagnoses and not diagnoses based on personal feelings of distress. The authors then name the residual uncertainty as a limitation and recommend clinician-based confirmation in future work. No diagnostic instrument was administered by the research team. Importantly, diagnosis is not the prediction target here - it is a covariate tested for incremental value - so the study's central claims do not rest on label accuracy in the way the rest of this corpus does.

**S-152** [local_6e7174c0] — *A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach*

None. Labels are the folder assignment of a public image corpus. No clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for a single image, and unlike several of its neighbours the paper does not even describe the labelling process in passing. The comparison table's premise - that the models being compared share a common foundation because they use the same dataset - makes this the shared and unexamined weakness of the whole benchmark line.

**S-153** [local_e04bcd32] — *Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network*

None. Labels are Kaggle folder names on photographs of unknown provenance. No clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for a single image. The paper opens by observing correctly that there is no medical screening or test like a blood test or scan for ASD and that diagnosis requires developmental history and behavioural assessment - and then treats folder labels on downloaded photographs as sufficient ground truth for a diagnostic classifier.

**S-154** [local_183eaef4] — *Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI*

None. The dependent variable is ASD_traits, a binary yes/no field in a Kaggle spreadsheet. No clinical assessment, diagnostic instrument administration, criterion, assessor or date exists for any case, and the originating collection procedure is not described at all. The paper nonetheless frames the task as ASD diagnosis throughout, titles itself Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics, and opens by criticising clinician-administered instruments for introducing variability and potential bias - a criticism made in favour of a label whose provenance is entirely unknown.

**S-155** [local_b6ac2b98] — *Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks*

Clinically ascertained and honestly qualified. Diagnosis of ASD or DLD was made by a licensed, experienced team of clinicians following DSM-5 and international diagnostic manual guidelines, independently of this study and as a precondition of enrolment at an early intervention centre. Typically developing children are defined by the absence of such enrolment. The authors then add two caveats that few in this corpus offer: that their diagnostic tools could have been supplemented with further assessments but were the only ones available at the time, and that diagnoses at early ages are provisional and may evolve over time, so the findings should be interpreted with caution.

**S-156** [local_44d3aef5] — *Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis*

None. Labels are inherited from a public image collection with no diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date reported, and the originating study's diagnostic procedure is not summarised. The paper's opening argument is that conventional ASD assessment relies on subjective criteria and lacks objectivity - a criticism advanced in favour of a label whose ascertainment it never examines.

**S-157** [local_24fefc5f] — *A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection*

None, and the paper states the substitute rule explicitly: if the Q-CHAT-10 score is higher than 3 then the class value is allocated as YES which implies ASD traits potential; if not, NO is allocated. The outcome is therefore a threshold on the sum of the ten checklist items that also constitute the feature set - the seventh instance of this structure in the review, after local_8253c2ec, local_a0d73248, local_8ff20c48, local_ed30e24c, local_b9de0d7f and local_14df790d. No clinician, instrument administration or diagnostic criterion enters at any point.

**S-158** [local_69b10fe4] — *An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms*

Clinically ascertained with documentation, and honestly bounded. Participants had to supply evidence of a formal clinical diagnosis such as a clinician's letter, or be drawn from databases where that evidence had been verified. The limitations section then names the two residual problems precisely: absence of a diagnosis does not exclude undiagnosed cases, and the PD and control participants belong to a generation in which autism diagnoses were not prevalent, so undiagnosed autistic people may sit in the comparison groups. That second observation is a genuine insight about ascertainment in older cohorts that appears nowhere else in this corpus.

**S-159** [local_af9f4c12] — *An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data*

None, and the paper is explicit rather than silent about this. The abstract states that reliable severity stratification remains challenging due to the absence of explicit clinician-annotated severity labels; the methods then construct severity labels from the A1-A10 items themselves; and the scope paragraph states that because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the subsequent prediction task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting. The one external anchor is the weight calibration, in which domain weights were optimised to maximise agreement with independent expert assessments on a randomly sampled subset, achieving Cohen's kappa 0.72 (95% CI 0.69-0.76) - and the paper immediately qualifies this as supporting the internal consistency of the labeling heuristic while not implying external diagnostic validity. Neither the number of expert-labelled records, the identity or qualification of the experts, nor the instrument they used is reported.

**S-160** [local_367db0b6] — *An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns*

None. No diagnostic instrument administration, criterion, assessor or record is described for any dataset. The named sources - ASQ, CSBS, PEDS, M-CHAT and STAT - are developmental screening instruments, not diagnoses, and the paper does not describe how any label was assigned. One results passage categorises outcomes as yes (Y), random (R) - indicating a 50% probability of yes and a 50% probability of no - and not detected (N), which introduces a coin-flip category into what is presented as a diagnostic output.

**S-161** [local_8d43288c] — *Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos*

None, and not required by the task as executed - but required by the task as described. The videos are annotated for when a behaviour occurs, not for whether the child has a diagnosis; no clinical assessment, instrument or assessor exists for anyone in the dataset. The paper's title nonetheless places the work in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder and its abstract states that the approach facilitates quick, accurate and effective screening of ASD. Those claims do not follow from a four-way discrimination among arm flapping, head banging, spinning and other movement in videos of children who are all autistic.

**S-162** [local_5f57ba19] — *Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension*

Independent and clinician-made: diagnostic classification was conducted externally by qualified specialists (neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists) prior to inclusion in the corpus, with the SCQ administered separately as a symptomatology measure. The label therefore predates and is unrelated to the gaze data - the property that separates this study from the checklist-threshold and folder-label branches of this review.

**S-163** [local_1d856900] — *Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare*

None for either dataset. Dataset 1's target is a binary ASD-traits field with no diagnostic procedure described, and the dataset's own feature list includes the Autism Spectrum Quotient, Social Responsiveness Scale, Q-CHAT score and Childhood Autism Rating Scale - four instruments used to determine autism status, supplied as predictors of it. This is the same instrument-inclusion leakage documented in local_183eaef4, which used the same 1,985-record dataset and reached accuracy 1.0000. Dataset 2's four severity categories are asserted with no instrument named; clinical experts are said to have verified annotation consistency at Cohen's kappa 0.92, but what they were rating and against what standard is not stated.

**S-164** [local_7b19a959] — *Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis*

Self-reported formal diagnosis by a registered clinician, with participants drawn from a national research register (NAR) rather than a convenience sample, and non-autistic participants reporting no autism diagnosis. Diagnosis therefore predates and is independent of the task data. The population is explicitly characterised as late-diagnosed, which the paper treats as a strength for the research question - it is precisely the group that existing screening instruments miss - rather than glossing over it.

**S-165** [local_d7b6fa00] — *Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath*

Not described. Labels are inherited from the public dataset with no diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date reported, and the originating collection's ascertainment procedure is not summarised. This is the study's largest unforced omission, since two of its authors are clinicians - one at a psychiatric hospital and one at a clinical medicine school - and a paragraph characterising the source cohort would have been straightforward.

**S-166** [local_e54c304c] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models*

None. Labels are annotations attached to a Roboflow dataset. No clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for a single image, and the originating collection is not described. The paper's introduction gives an accurate account of how ASD is actually diagnosed - paediatricians or psychologists using developmental history, behavioural observation and instruments including CARS for severity - and then treats platform annotations on downloaded photographs as an adequate substitute.

**S-167** [local_e4c2a776] — *Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images*

None. Labels are the folder assignments of a public image corpus, with no clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date for any image, and no description of how the collection was assembled. The introduction gives a conventional account of ASD as requiring thorough clinical testing and then treats folder labels as sufficient ground truth for a system offered as a diagnostic aid in clinical settings.

**S-168** [local_231757c7] — *SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers*

Inherited from the original collection and not independently established. The three-level grouping (typical, moderate, severe) is used as the classification target and the instrument behind the moderate/severe distinction is not named in the extracted text. What the paper does establish clearly is the provenance chain: ethics approval was obtained by the original collectors from their institutional review board before collection, guardian consent was given, and this study is a secondary analysis of de-identified public data.

**S-169** [local_1b457442] — *Screening autism spectrum*

Inherited from two peer-reviewed developmental-language studies, whose own diagnostic procedures are cited but not summarised. Governance is handled by reference to TalkBank's contribution requirements, which oblige contributing researchers to obtain informed consent from participants or guardians and the necessary ethical approvals before sharing. That is a reasonable basis for secondary analysis of a curated academic repository and is stated rather than assumed - a different situation from the web-scraped and platform-hosted collections elsewhere in this review.

**S-170** [local_b26db2f2] — *Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches*

Clinical diagnosis is an inclusion criterion - children with a diagnosis form the ASD group and children without form the control group - but the diagnosing procedure, instrument and assessor are not described. The framing is honest about why this matters in context: the study's motivating problem is that a significant number of children with ASD in Brazilian early and primary education remain without an appropriate clinical diagnosis, which leaves educators without information to tailor teaching. The tool is proposed for exactly those undiagnosed children, and is trained on children whose diagnostic status is already known.

---

## RQ1.5 — Cognitive, severity and related measures reported

_170 of 170 studies charted for this question._

**S-001** [local_76fc33d0] — *Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers*

Standardized developmental and language tests are mentioned as part of the cohort protocol but no cognitive, linguistic or adaptive scores are reported for the analysed sample. Comorbidities not described; other non-ASD language disorders explicitly absent from the sample.

**S-002** [local_0dbc5018] — *Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities*

Yes - IQ and mental age assessed with the Griffiths Mental Development Scales for all participants; ADOS Social/Communication and Stereotyped Behavior and Restricted Interests subscores reported for the 7 children who received ADOS. Comorbidities: participants were drug-naive with normal/corrected vision; other neurodevelopmental conditions were excluded from the design and flagged as future work.

**S-003** [local_dc5fc4bb] — *ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data*

No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive-functioning measures reported. ASD participants are described as high-functioning and older than the low-functioning samples in prior work, but no IQ figures are given. Comorbidities are not described, and it is not stated whether ASD-ADHD co-occurrence was excluded - a material omission given the three-group design.

**S-004** [local_863980f8] — *Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework*

Nonverbal IQ measured with the Combined Raven Test (CRT-C2) for all participants and used to construct the ability-matched control group; AQ-Child reported for all three groups. No language or adaptive-functioning measures. Comorbid conditions are not described or excluded.

**S-005** [local_be8aa62f] — *Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder*

Yes, extensively: full-scale, verbal and performance IQ, Wechsler Memory Scale, Autism Quotient, Inventory of Interpersonal Problems, SCL-90 and Social Adjustment Scale reported for all groups. Comorbidity was actively excluded via SCL-90 screening, and the authors use verbal IQ, vocabulary subsection and WMS as covariates to show the semantic effect is not explained by structural language ability.

**S-006** [local_e404a2a3] — *Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism*

A questionnaire on level of intellectual and social functioning and on prior mobile-device experience was administered to clinicians (autism group) and teachers (control group), but no scores are reported. IQ was explicitly not controlled - the authors state they 'were unable to exclude intelligence as a potential confounder' and mitigate by noting most children were clinician-classified as average (n=29) or high functioning (n=4), with only 2 low-functioning children contributing final data. Comorbidity is reported at the individual level (intellectual impairment in 4).

**S-007** [local_780141fc] — *Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study*

Full-scale IQ measured with the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence and reported for both groups (118.5 vs 119.8) and used as a matching variable - one of the few corpus studies to match and verify on IQ. No language or adaptive-functioning measures, no autism trait or severity scores (no AQ, ADOS or equivalent), and no comorbidity information.

**S-008** [local_3a331973] — *Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data*

No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive-functioning measures are reported for any group. ASRS and AQ-10 are used only as control-admission gates and their scores are never reported for the ASD, ADHD or comorbid groups. Comorbidity, by contrast, is handled seriously - ADHD+ASD co-occurrence is a defined group and the subject of the second classification task, motivated by the observation that treatment differs across the three clinical groups.

**S-009** [local_7b3e6b3a] — *Earlier identification of children with autism*

Speech-language developmental level was annotated using the Stark Assessment of Early Vocal Development-Revised (SAEVD-R), recording whether each infant produced vocalisation types more complex than single canonical syllables - 4 ASD and 4 TD infants did, so the groups were comparable on this measure. No cognitive, adaptive or IQ measures are reported, and comorbid conditions are not described. Pacifier use during recording is noted for three infants, and one misclassified TD infant is flagged as having used one - an unusually granular disclosure of a potential acoustic confound.

**S-010** [local_36aa3ace] — *Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative*

Lexical abilities and academic grades are named as matching variables for the patient groups, but no scores are reported for any group and they are not used in modelling. All children are stated to have communicative verbal skills - an important inclusion constraint that excludes minimally verbal autistic children. Comorbidities are not described beyond the exclusion of learning disorders from the TD group.

**S-011** [local_44b58f21] — *ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces*

None. No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive-functioning measures are reported for either group, and no autism severity instrument underlies the 'mild category' description. The only functional criteria are physical - no history of lower-extremity injury and ability to walk independently. Comorbidities are not otherwise described.

**S-012** [local_cb9a5b48] — *Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening*

None reported. No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive measures for either group, and no autism severity instrument. Functioning level enters only as a post-hoc anecdote - two misclassified autistic children are described as 'high-functional in autism range' - which is used to explain errors rather than as measured data.

**S-013** [local_40cd7d53] — *Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children*

The Gesell Developmental Scale (Chinese version) was administered to the ASD group, with adaptation, large motion, fine motion, language and personal-social subscores all reported - one of the fuller functional characterisations in the corpus. However the authors themselves list the absence of IQ and adaptive behaviour measures as their second limitation, and no GDS or other functional data were collected for the control group. Comorbidities are not described for the ASD group.

**S-014** [local_5b1d0b36] — *Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday*

None reported. No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive-functioning measures, no autism severity instrument, and no comorbidity information for any group. The reading materials are drawn from the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, so a standardised articulation instrument supplies the stimuli, but it is not scored as an assessment. The authors note narratively that 'some non-verbal children may not able to finish the reading test' but no verbal-ability data exist.

**S-015** [local_54954c19] — *Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching*

Years of formal education reported for both groups; web-use frequency assessed for all participants (all daily users); familiarity with each of the six stimulus websites surveyed to rule out over-familiarity confounds. No IQ, language or adaptive-functioning measures, and no autism severity score for the autistic group. Comorbidity handled only by excluding formally diagnosed intellectual disability, which bounds the sample to high-functioning adults.

**S-016** [local_d8dc996a] — *Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Full Scale IQ measured by WISC-IV for both groups and used as a matching variable; executive function assessed in both groups by the Tower of London test with no significant difference (TD 29.35 +/- 3.54, ASD 29.35 +/- 2.80, t38 = 0, p = 0.999); handedness assessed by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (all but two children right-handed). Comorbidity is handled by explicit exclusion of pharmacological treatment, dyslexia, epilepsy and any other neurological or psychiatric condition. This is unusually thorough functional characterisation for a computer-vision paper.

**S-017** [local_88ddfdd1] — *A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task*

Intelligence measured with the Wechsler Scales for all participants, with group means reported (109.4 and 112.3) and a minimum threshold of 85 applied as an inclusion criterion - so IQ is both measured and controlled by restriction and matching. Vision was normal or corrected-to-normal and neurological conditions excluded for all subjects. No language or adaptive measures, and ADOS-2 severity scores are not reported despite the instrument being administered.

**S-018** [local_361110f1] — *Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features*

Non-verbal IQ assessed by Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices and used as an inclusion criterion (average ability), so cognitive level is controlled by restriction rather than by matching or covariate adjustment. No language or adaptive-functioning measures and no autism severity instrument. Comorbidity is handled by exclusion: ADHD, mental retardation and schizophrenia ruled out for the ASD group; controls reported no physical or mental disorders.

**S-019** [local_51533de4] — *Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations*

Full-scale, verbal and non-verbal IQ measured with the WASI-II for both groups and used as matching variables with all comparisons tested. ADOS-2 Calibrated Severity Scores (overall, social affect, restricted and repetitive behaviour) and SCQ lifetime scores reported for both groups with group comparisons. All participants were native English speakers. Comorbid conditions are not described.

**S-020** [local_96c87d36] — *Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking*

IQ score range (58-137) reported for the ASD group only, with no mean, SD or control comparison, and not used as a covariate despite the authors' own introduction noting that eye-tracking results 'can be impacted by sample size, age, developmental level and IQ'. No language or adaptive measures. Comorbidities not described for the ASD group; controls screened by exclusion of psychiatric history, developmental delay and special education.

**S-021** [local_4b031d44] — *Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine*

MCHAT total scores and ADOS subscores (social affect, restricted and repetitive behaviour, composite) reported for the assessed subset. Additional health and social indicators are reported that no other corpus study collects: preterm birth, stunted growth, family income band, urban/semiurban/rural residence, and religion. Stunting information is missing for the entire TD cohort, which prevents its use as a covariate. No IQ, language or adaptive-functioning scores.

**S-022** [local_05ef29e5] — *Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification*

None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures, and no comorbidity information - consistent with the complete absence of participant metadata in the source dataset as used here.

**S-023** [local_9528024b] — *Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol*

None reported. No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive measures, no severity instrument, and no comorbidity information. Mental age is used for matching but its values are not given. The one clinically relevant characteristic reported is that all ASD-group children were undergoing intervention and trained on similar tasks almost daily - which the authors correctly identify as a confound affecting their behaviour toward the robot.

**S-024** [local_6230fe22] — *Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism*

None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures for either group. The workflow specifies that a therapist collects patient information and medical history in the pre-analysis phase, so such data are presumably gathered, but none is reported or used.

**S-025** [local_785ba418] — *Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis*

IQ matching is claimed but no IQ values are reported for either group, and no language, adaptive-functioning or autism-trait measures are given. Comorbidities are not described. This is unusually sparse given that the paper is otherwise meticulous about its analysis.

**S-026** [local_fea042be] — *Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual*

No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive measures are reported for either group, and no comorbidity information. CARS is the only clinical instrument, reported as a sample-level mean and median with a box-plot distribution.

**S-027** [local_ba5fbda7] — *Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD*

Extensive neuropsychological examination is stated to have supplemented the diagnostic interviews for the autistic group, but no scores are reported and none are used in analysis. No IQ, language or adaptive measures for either group, no autism severity instrument, and no comorbidity information.

**S-028** [local_7b468950] — *Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart*

Planned and comprehensive. The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, the ESSENCE Questionnaire and the Adaptive Behavior Assessment System-3 or Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-II are all administered to parents of children in the autistic and other-neurodevelopmental-disorder cohorts. That combination gives a behavioural-difficulty measure, a neurodevelopmental symptom-breadth measure and an adaptive-functioning measure alongside the diagnostic label, which is the apparatus needed to ask whether the instrument's output tracks severity or only category - the analysis this review has repeatedly found missing in completed studies whose data would have supported it.

**S-029** [local_309e5baa] — *Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns*

None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures, and no comorbidity information - consistent with the absence of participant metadata in the challenge dataset as used here.

**S-030** [local_a45f39e9] — *Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time*

None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures and no comorbidity information for any participant.

**S-031** [local_d587f9cd] — *Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning*

None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for any participant.

**S-032** [local_08b8027d] — *SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths*

None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures and no comorbidity information.

**S-033** [local_c6f1209b] — *Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children*

None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure was obtained.

**S-034** [local_83b99e73] — *Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers*

Comprehensive by corpus standards. Gesell Developmental Scale developmental quotients across five domains (adaptive, gross motor, fine motor, language, personal-social) for all participants; CSBS-DP with three factor scores and total, CARS, and ABC for symptom severity in the high-risk group. All were used analytically - correlated against behavioural indicators - not merely tabulated. The requirement that the mother be the primary caregiver is also a stated inclusion criterion for both groups, controlling a variable that matters for a mother-infant interaction paradigm.

**S-035** [local_638860ef] — *Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis*

IQ is reported for all four subgroups and used as a matching variable with statistical verification, and handedness is also matched. No language, adaptive-functioning or autism-severity measures are reported, and no comorbidity information. IQ means of 122-126 indicate a sample well above population average.

**S-036** [local_7547db68] — *Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network*

None. No IQ, developmental quotient, language, adaptive functioning, symptom severity or comorbidity measure is reported for either group. Severity grading is named only as future work.

**S-037** [local_878c259f] — *Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach*

No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or autism-severity measures are reported. Anthropometrics (height, body mass) are measured and reported for both groups, which is the relevant covariate set for postural biomechanics. Comorbidity is handled by explicit exclusion of neurological disorders other than ASD, chronic medical disorders, visual impairments and physical impairments affecting balance - a well-targeted exclusion list that removes the most plausible competing explanations for balance differences.

**S-038** [local_1579c85a] — *Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through*

None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures for either group, and no comorbidity information.

**S-039** [local_157d6266] — *Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism*

Extensive. Full-scale and index IQ measured with WISC-V and used as an inclusion criterion; general motor ability measured with the Movement Assessment Battery for Children-2 explicitly to separate imitation-specific from general motor differences; ADOS-2 and SRS-2 administered and used quantitatively in correlational analyses of symptom severity. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are deferred to a supplement. This is among the fullest functional characterisations in the corpus.

**S-040** [local_8be557e3] — *Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation*

K-CARS, SRS and SCQ were administered and could have supported severity analysis, but no severity, cognitive, language or adaptive scores are reported and no severity-stratified result is given. The five-category vocalisation labelling (single syllable, canonical babbling, non-syllabic babbling, first word, atypical voice) functions as a developmental-stage descriptor and is the only developmental characterisation reported, given per group as proportions of total vocalisation time.

**S-041** [local_c79e100a] — *Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models*

None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure is reported, and no comorbidity information. Nor are the anthropometric variables that directly determine gait phase durations - height, leg length, body mass - which for a gait study is a substantive omission independent of clinical characterisation.

**S-042** [local_4fecbf6d] — *Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network*

ADOS total, SA and RRB scores are the severity characterisation and are used analytically throughout, including a separate correlation analysis per subscale. No IQ, language, adaptive or cognitive measures are reported, which matters because ADOS module assignment already encodes language capacity and so the cohort spans a language range that is not otherwise quantified. Comorbid language and developmental delays are present in 10 children and identified as such but not scored.

**S-043** [local_95abe653] — *Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning*

Intellectual disability and reading disorder were formal exclusions, and three control participants were excluded for school dyslexia referrals, so reading ability is controlled at the eligibility level for a task that depends on reading. Vision not correctable by glasses or lenses was also excluded. No IQ, AQ score (for the autistic group), symptom severity or adaptive functioning measure is reported; functional level is characterised by employment, housing and education instead, which is arguably more informative for an adult cohort though not comparable across studies.

**S-044** [local_40168c96] — *Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based*

None. No IQ, developmental quotient, language, adaptive functioning or symptom severity measure is reported for either group, and no comorbidity information. Grading severity is named only as future work.

**S-045** [local_d3852378] — *Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

None reported, and their absence is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation. ADOS-2 and ADI-R were administered and yield severity indices in social affect and restricted/repetitive behaviour domains, but no scores appear and no severity-stratified analysis is performed. No IQ, cognitive, language or adaptive measure, and no motor comorbidity screening despite the outcome being motor.

**S-046** [local_df438dd2] — *Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening*

None. No IQ, developmental quotient, language, adaptive or symptom severity measure is reported, and no comorbidity information. The six behaviour scores function as a within-protocol profile but are not related to any external severity measure.

**S-047** [local_cd9e45eb] — *Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism*

The most complete clinical characterisation in the corpus for a subset of participants: ADOS severity (autism symptom severity), SRS total (reciprocal social behaviour), Vineland-3 ABC across communication, daily living skills and socialisation (adaptive functioning), and Stanford-Binet IQ for the full cohort. Critically, these are not merely tabulated but used as regression targets, which is what allows the paper's central negative finding - that eye-tracking features predict IQ but not autism severity or adaptive functioning.

**S-048** [local_56237213] — *The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data*

None reported. PEP-3 yields developmental scores that could have supported severity or functioning analyses, but no scores appear and no stratification is performed. This is a substantive gap given the paper's own explanation for inconsistent EEG findings in the literature - that 'autism can be divided into low function and high function according to behavioral ability' and that heterogeneity is why 'using only EEG evaluation may be insufficient'. Having advanced that argument, the study is unable to test it in its own data.

**S-049** [local_f9a5195f] — *Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses*

Complete. SCQ, SRS-2 total and Stanford-Binet ABIQ for every participant in both groups, plus itemised comorbid psychological conditions and current medications for those who completed the survey. Uniquely in this corpus, the medication data are reported at drug level rather than as a summary count, which matters because several of the drugs listed - methylphenidate, guanfacine, aripiprazole - have documented effects on attention and eye movement.

**S-050** [local_16a77fb0] — *Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)*

ADOS scores for 35 participants, Autism-Spectrum Quotient for all participants in both groups, and Wortschatztest verbal intelligence as an inclusion screen. The ADOS data are used substantively: the classifier's predicted class probability correlates with ADOS score at rs = 0.48, p < 0.0001, establishing that the model's output tracks symptom severity and not merely group membership. No full-scale IQ, adaptive functioning or comorbidity scores are reported.

**S-051** [local_9c4af7a3] — *Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades*

None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure, and no comorbidity information. Given the paper's opening claim that autism symptoms 'range from completely debilitating to manageable', the absence of any severity characterisation means nothing can be said about where on that range the classified sample sits.

**S-052** [local_b70dae32] — *An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model*

CARS severity category only, as minimal or mild. No CARS total scores, no IQ, no language or adaptive measures, and no comorbidity information. The two performance measures the model consumes - joint attention and imitation success rates - are themselves clinically meaningful and are tabulated per child, but they are the model's input rather than an independent characterisation.

**S-053** [local_51a0af74] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data*

CARS scores for both groups, reported as ranges and a group mean. The autistic range of 33-45 spans mild-to-moderate through severe on standard CARS bands, so the sample covers meaningful severity variation - but this is never exploited. No severity-stratified analysis is performed, no relationship between CARS score and classifier output is examined, and no IQ, language or adaptive measure appears. Given that the discriminative signal is in anticipatory gaze during joint attention, which plausibly varies with severity, relating classifier confidence to CARS would have been a straightforward and valuable analysis.

**S-054** [local_d8d3037b] — *Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study*

AQ total scores for the preliminary sample only, with the five subscale domains described but never analysed. No severity, IQ, language, adaptive or comorbidity measure for the diagnosed test participants, and no AQ administered to them - so it is not possible to establish whether the diagnosed group would even have scored above the study's own trait threshold.

**S-055** [local_991fe435] — *Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task*

The most complete cognitive characterisation in the corpus. Combined Raven's Test for nonverbal and PPVT-R for verbal mental intelligence, plus SCQ, administered to all three groups with means and standard deviations tabulated and all pairwise comparisons tested. These are not merely reported but used structurally - they define the functioning subgroups, they establish that the high-functioning and typically developing groups are matched on both intelligence measures, and they support the interpretation that visual-orienting performance tracks cognitive level. No adaptive functioning or comorbidity measures.

**S-056** [local_8692a64f] — *Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis*

None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure, and no comorbidity information for either group.

**S-057** [local_4d6fac7e] — *Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network*

None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure, and no comorbidity information for either group.

**S-058** [local_30c622f2] — *Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model*

Strong for a severity study. CARS for all participants with group ranges and means; Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales and the Repetitive Behavior Scale-Revised administered 'when possible'. The Vineland result is used substantively - significantly lower adaptive functioning in the severe group corroborates the CARS-based split from an independent instrument, which is the correct way to validate a severity dichotomy. The absence of IQ is acknowledged as a limitation and proposed as a future model feature.

**S-059** [local_bfc088c7] — *Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation*

Nonverbal IQ via Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices for both groups, with at least average intelligence required for inclusion in the autistic group. No autism severity measure of any kind, which the authors state candidly: severity 'was not specifically measured in our study' and the sample 'could be viewed as representing individuals with minor severity'. No language, adaptive functioning or comorbidity scores. The IQ data are reported but, unusually, the significant group difference they reveal is not carried into the analysis.

**S-060** [local_25e34bbd] — *Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification*

None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure, and no comorbidity information for any of the three groups.

**S-061** [local_4917150c] — *Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning*

CARS for severity and ECSP for social communication, both in French versions, administered to both groups by psychologists. CARS is used analytically in the correlation analysis rather than merely tabulated. ECSP is reported but not used, and its near-identical group means at what appears to be a ceiling limit its informativeness. No IQ, adaptive functioning or comorbidity measures, and ADI-R and ADOS-G scores were inaccessible.

**S-062** [local_241ec2c2] — *Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking*

Among the better-characterised samples in the corpus: CARS for all participants, plus WISC intelligence, Repetitive Behavior Scale and Vineland adaptive behaviour for autistic participants where obtainable, all deposited per participant. The limitation is that none of these measures is used analytically - there is no severity-stratified analysis, no relation between CARS or IQ and classifier output, and no examination of whether comorbidity status affects classification, despite comorbid participants having been deliberately retained.

**S-063** [local_36617ec5] — *Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis*

ADOS-2 and ADI-R administered but with no scores reported and no severity-stratified analysis. No IQ, cognitive, adaptive or language measures, and the authors identify the absence of IQ and cognitive matching as a limitation requiring attention in future work. The only functional indicator available is the choice of ADOS-2 module 1.

**S-064** [local_d8e804d6] — *Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms*

Nonverbal IQ via Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices, used both as an inclusion criterion and, importantly, as a covariate in the feature-discrimination models. No autism severity measure, which the authors acknowledge in calling for future samples with 'different behavioral presentations'. No language or adaptive functioning measures.

**S-065** [local_712542ca] — *Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset*

None used. CARS is mentioned as having been applied in the source study but no scores are reported, no severity stratification is performed, and no cognitive, language or adaptive measures appear. Since the source dataset's accompanying publication reports CARS and ECSP scores, the omission is a choice of this reanalysis rather than a constraint of the data.

**S-066** [local_0ab41681] — *Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder*

ADOS total scores individually reported for all 26 participants with the module used, plus ICD-10 diagnostic subtype and comorbid diagnoses per child. Severity is used analytically rather than descriptively - correlated against all four kinematic outcomes - which is what produces the paper's key dissociation. The acknowledged gap is intellectual functioning: no IQ or developmental level was measured, and the authors state that future research 'will have to evaluate intellectual disability, which is an important source of inter-subject variability in ASD that seems to impact motor planning and coordination'.

**S-067** [local_9ca9b2cc] — *Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment*

CARS2 is used as an eligibility range rather than as a per-child variable, so no severity gradient is available for analysis - a missed opportunity, since relating attention trajectories to baseline severity across six children in a seven-week course would have been the natural individualisation question and the data existed to ask it. The study's own outcome measure, the automated attention score, functions as a repeated within-child measure and is used that way: its whole design rationale is that assessment could be 'repeated more frequently to trace the severity and development of symptoms'. That is a severity-tracking argument, and it is the clearest statement in this review of why continuous behavioural measurement might matter clinically for reasons other than diagnosis.

**S-068** [local_02fa4215] — *Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning*

None. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive measure. Family history of cognitive disability is collected as a predictor rather than as a characterisation.

**S-069** [local_29a3fc54] — *Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism*

The most complete clinical characterisation of any speech study in the corpus. ADOS-2 Social Affect, Restricted and Repetitive Behavior, total and Calibrated Severity Scores; SRS total t-scores; WISC-IV short-form full-scale IQ from Information, Block Design and Vocabulary subtests; and the Children's Communication Checklist-2 yielding both a General Communication Composite and a Social Interaction Difference Index designed so that more negative values indicate autism. All are reported with group means and p-values, and the ADOS-2 CSS, SRS, GCC and SIDI are used analytically as correlates of the selected voice features, with partial Spearman coefficients adjusted for IQ.

**S-070** [local_b7ec3755] — *Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images*

None. No IQ, language, adaptive functioning, comorbidity or medication information for either group, and no exclusions described. Nor is there any severity measure, so the model's outputs cannot be related to any clinical gradient.

**S-071** [local_684969f6] — *Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data*

None. No IQ, adaptive functioning, language measure, comorbidity or medication information, and no exclusion criteria. Consequently nothing links model output to any clinical gradient, and the frequently cited possibility that IQ rather than diagnosis drives gaze differences cannot be examined.

**S-072** [local_35004e74] — *Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children*

Comprehensive and, unusually, used analytically rather than descriptively. ADOS calibrated severity scores for total, social affect and restricted/repetitive behaviour; VABS-II Adaptive Behavior Composite with communication, socialisation, daily-living and motor subdomains; and a Best Estimate IQ constructed to combine 'the most representative cognitive functioning measures for each child', since instruments varied with age and with each child's ability to attend demanding tasks - a pragmatic solution to a real problem in toddler cognitive assessment, and one that is documented rather than glossed. All three feed the validation analyses. Comorbidities are not described for the autistic group.

**S-073** [local_fa91fc18] — *Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities*

Partial. IQ was assessed with the Leiter-3, a nonverbal intelligence test appropriate for this population and administered in its original form for the assessment, but reported only as a range per group. Comorbidity was handled by exclusion rather than measurement: 'no existing comorbidities' was an inclusion criterion, no specific comorbidity was reported, and all participants were required to have normal vision and no sensory or motor deficit - the last a genuinely relevant control for a study whose outcome is a fine-motor measure, and one that also narrows the sample away from the substantial proportion of autistic children who do have motor impairment. No adaptive functioning measure, no language level, and no ADOS severity scores despite the instrument being used for diagnosis. Medication is not reported, though ongoing psychomotor and speech therapy is.

**S-074** [local_115dfe8d] — *A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children*

No cognitive, language or adaptive measure of any kind for either group - a significant omission in 3-to-6-year-olds, where developmental level varies enormously and both resting EEG spectral power and social gaze allocation are strongly age- and ability-dependent. No comorbidity information and no exclusions described. Four symptom instruments (ABC, SCQ, SRS, CABS) were administered to the autistic group and three to the comparison group, and their scores are tabulated, so a severity gradient exists in the data; it is used only to characterise the sample and is never related to the model's continuous output, missing the opportunity to test whether the classifier's confidence tracks symptom level - the analysis that would have provided clinical anchoring.

**S-075** [local_5b7ea7dc] — *AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

IQ was measured for every child using an age-appropriate instrument - Korean WPPSI-IV for older children, Korean Bayley Scales-II for younger - and combined into a best-estimate figure, which is the right approach for a sample spanning 24 to 72 months. The result is the study's central confound rather than a control. Comorbidity was handled by exclusion and the exclusions are mechanistically reasoned: because joint attention depends on 'perception, attention, and motor coordination', children were required to have normal or corrected vision and normal hearing and were excluded for pharmacological treatment, developmental coordination disorder, ADHD, and any other neurological or psychiatric condition. This is a more thoughtfully constructed exclusion set than most in the corpus, since each element removes a plausible non-autism cause of failing the specific target behaviour. No adaptive functioning or language measure is reported.

**S-076** [local_87fe26aa] — *Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

None whatsoever. No IQ, developmental quotient, language level, adaptive functioning measure, severity score, comorbidity list or medication information for either group. This is the most complete absence of clinical characterisation among the studies in this corpus that nonetheless report high accuracy, and it compounds the recruitment asymmetry: with children drawn from special education schools versus regular kindergartens and no cognitive measure taken, there is no way to determine whether the classifier separates autism or separates developmental level.

**S-077** [local_893ce2fa] — *An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images*

Nothing. No IQ, language, adaptive functioning, comorbidity, medication or severity data, and no exclusions described. Consequently there is no possibility of relating model output to any clinical gradient, and no way to assess whether developmental level rather than diagnosis distinguishes the classes.

**S-078** [local_dffe4127] — *Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals*

Comprehensive and used analytically rather than descriptively. Full-scale IQ was measured in both groups and reported with range and test statistic; the AQ was administered to both groups; and ADOS-2 Overall Calibrated Severity Scores derived by the Hus and Lord algorithm were obtained for the autistic group with a full range of 3 to 10, meaning the sample spans the severity spectrum rather than clustering at one end. Severity was then correlated against all four gaze features, with the finding that none reached significance - a negative result that matters, since it means the gaze measures that do differentiate groups on average do not index how autistic an individual is. Comorbidity handling is deliberate and unusual: depression, anxiety and ADHD were permitted rather than excluded on the grounds that they are common in autism, with only moderate-to-severe depression (BDI-II >= 25) and antipsychotic medication ruled out. The authors then list this inclusiveness among their own limitations, noting it leaves open how much comorbidity contributed to the findings - a rare instance of a design decision being defended and then flagged as a threat in the same paper.

**S-079** [local_2b766683] — *Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech*

None. No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity measure for either group, and no comorbidity or medication information. This matters more than usual for a speech study, since expressive language level directly determines what a child produces in a 90-second game and would be expected to differ between a median-5-year-old autistic group and a median-9.5-year-old comparison group on both developmental and diagnostic grounds. Nothing in the data allows that to be examined, and no exclusion criteria of any kind are described.

**S-080** [local_2895bdf0] — *Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection*

Complete and used analytically throughout. IQ was estimated from a three-subtest WISC-IV short form (Information, Block Design, Vocabulary) with the Sattler and Dumont formula, and the authors note honestly that separate verbal and non-verbal estimates cannot be derived from this short form. The Children's Communication Checklist-2 was completed by parents, with its structure described in detail - ten subscales, the first four averaged into a Structural Language scale and four more into a Pragmatic scale, with the last two measuring behaviours characteristic of autism. ADOS-2 Social Affect and Restricted and Repetitive Behavior scores were computed under the Gotham et al. algorithm. Three objective language-output indices were additionally computed from the task itself: total c-units, total words and activity time. All of these then serve as predictors in the misclassification analysis, which is the paper's most original contribution - they are not merely descriptive but are the variables through which the complementarity of the two modalities is established.

**S-081** [local_423b636b] — *Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers*

Comprehensive for the autistic group and absent for the comparison group. ADOS-2 Toddler Module calibrated severity scores average 7.56 +/- 1.67 across a range of 2-10, so the sample spans the severity spectrum. The Mullen Scales of Early Learning provide an Early Learning Composite of 63.64 +/- 10.17 alongside Expressive Language (T = 28.08), Receptive Language (T = 23.14), Fine Motor (T = 34.11) and Visual Reception (T = 33.94) T-scores - all substantially below average, indicating a group with considerable developmental delay, and the Fine Motor score is directly relevant since the outcome is a motor measure. The Mullen composite is used analytically, correlated against all three head movement measures. Because no Mullen data exist for the neurotypical group, the cognitive difference between groups cannot be estimated or adjusted, and the authors list this among their limitations: 'The autistic and neurotypical group differed in cognitive ability and, thus, it is not clear the degree to which differences in cognition contributed to our findings.' Comorbidity is not otherwise characterised, and the 12 children with non-autism diagnoses were removed.

**S-082** [local_ffa35101] — *Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study*

IQ was measured in every participant, but with different instruments by language group: the WASI, WAIS-III/IV or WISC-IV for English participants and the TONI-4 for Cantonese participants. The TONI-4 is a nonverbal reasoning measure while the Wechsler scales yield full-scale IQ incorporating verbal subtests, so the two sets of scores are not interchangeable and cross-language comparison of cognitive level is not possible. Within each language group the comparison participants score higher (111.03 versus 104.13 in English; 115.08 versus 108.54 in Cantonese). ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores are reported for both autistic groups (7.02 English, 6.00 Cantonese) with full ranges spanning 3-9.5 and 3-10, so both samples cover the severity spectrum. No language ability measure was administered, and the authors identify this as a limitation that matters specifically for their outcome: 'future studies should employ more comprehensive assessments of language abilities for group matching, since baseline language ability may covary with age and autism severity, influencing prosody and pitch in particular'. No adaptive functioning or comorbidity data.

**S-083** [local_81ecbc6f] — *Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings*

Both verbal and non-verbal IQ measured in every participant using age-appropriate Wechsler scales - the WISC-R for those aged 6.0-16.11 and the WAIS for those older - with means, standard deviations, ranges and t-tests reported for both. Reporting verbal and non-verbal IQ separately is appropriate and uncommon, and matters directly for a narrative-language outcome. Non-verbal IQ of 80 or above was an inclusion criterion, so the sample is confined to participants without intellectual disability, which the authors identify as limiting generalisation: 'our study included only fluently speaking participants with ASD with no intellectual disability and might not apply to everyone on the autism spectrum'. ADOS-2 overall and SCQ overall scores characterise severity in both groups. No adaptive functioning or language-specific standardised measure was administered, and no comorbidity information is reported beyond the idiopathic-autism inclusion requirement.
