Main findings: US-trained classifiers transferred to Bangladeshi videos at maximum AUC 0.75 (SD 0.06) against 92% accuracy on US videos; retrained stacked classifiers with rater-adaptive weighting achieved AUC 76% (SD 3%) and sensitivity 76% (SD 4%) for atypical versus typical, and AUC 85% (SD 5%) and sensitivity 76% (SD 6%) for ASD versus other developmental delay; and feature importance differed by culture, with eye contact more prominent for Bangladeshi videos and social participation and stereotyped speech more prominent for US videos.

**S-022** [local_05ef29e5] — *Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification*

Goal: identify ASD from visual behaviour during image viewing, developed for the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge. Main findings: accuracy 59.30%, recall 68.43%, specificity 50.56%, F1 61.64%, precision 56.96%, AUC-ROC 59.50% on the organiser's held-out test set. The authors describe this as promising with room for improvement, and attribute the limitation primarily to the absence of age information and to the age-dependence of ASD fixation behaviour.

**S-023** [local_9528024b] — *Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol*

Goal: enable a humanoid robot to reason about a child's unobservable state during an ADOS-derived diagnostic protocol and to select tasks adaptively, addressing the reported problem of inter-clinician disagreement arising from the need to simultaneously observe, code and interpret many behaviours. Main findings: belief distributions separated expert-assessed ASD behaviour clearly and typical behaviour less decisively; behaviour experts judged ambiguous was assigned to high-functioning ASD; and sessions too short for expert assessment produced near-uniform beliefs (approximately 0.27-0.43), correctly signalling insufficient information. No accuracy figure is reported.

**S-024** [local_6230fe22] — *Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism*

Goal: early screening via an Arabic automated gaze-based system integrating eye tracking with machine learning, to speed up diagnosis and reduce dependence on subjective clinical observation. Main findings as reported: accuracy 88.6%, specificity 92.31%, sensitivity 86.63%, AUC 0.96. The authors claim the AUC is the best among comparable models and argue this means it 'works well regardless of the class distribution', which is an overstatement of what AUC guarantees.

**S-025** [local_785ba418] — *Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis*

Goal: predict autism diagnosis at the individual level from a short simple motor task, with the stated methodological aim of producing unbiased performance estimates. Main findings: 71% accuracy (75% sensitivity, 66% specificity, p=0.021) with t-test feature selection and 70% with ReliefF, while SVM-RFE (62%) and mRMR (60%) did not reach significance; autistic participants moved more slowly but pointed about twice as accurately; and large group-level effect sizes did not translate into high classification accuracy.

**S-026** [local_fea042be] — *Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual*

Goal: assistive diagnosis supporting early detection, achieved by converting scanpaths into images so the problem becomes image classification. Main findings: neural networks exceeded AUC 0.90 (best approximately 0.92 with a single 200-neuron hidden layer) against approximately 0.70 for Naive Bayes, logistic regression, SVM and random forests on the same data; increasing model depth or width gave no further gain; and a four-class CARS-severity model reached approximately 83% overall but performed at least 20% worse on ASD categories than on non-ASD, particularly for severe ASD.

**S-027** [local_ba5fbda7] — *Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD*

Goal: proof-of-principle demonstration that full-body non-verbal behaviour from naturalistic interaction can classify autistic adults, alongside a methodological argument for cross-validation standards. Main findings: 75.9% accuracy, 96.6% sensitivity, 55.2% specificity, AUC 0.71, with 28/29 autistic participants correctly identified but 13/29 controls misclassified. The authors present 75.9% as a deliberately conservative estimate produced by a rigorous validation procedure.

**S-028** [local_7b468950] — *Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart*

The aim is to test, under phase III conditions, whether a tablet-based serious game can identify autism in preschoolers - specifically whether the 93% accuracy obtained in an 82-child Polish pilot survives prospective, blinded, multi-site evaluation against clinical diagnosis. The primary outcome is sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing autistic from typically developing children; the secondary outcome is accuracy in distinguishing autistic children from those with other neurodevelopmental disorders. No results are reported: the trial is registered as NCT03438994 with status 'Pre-results' and 'the results are blind until data collection is complete'. The protocol's substantive contribution to this review is therefore methodological, and it is considerable - it is the only study in the corpus that locks its algorithm before seeing the evaluation data, separates the analysts from the developers, prespecifies sensitivity and specificity as primary outcomes, powers the study to detect underperformance, recruits a non-autistic clinical comparison group, registers prospectively and publishes the protocol in advance.

**S-029** [local_309e5baa] — *Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns*

Goal: an easy-to-use ASD screening tool for infants and toddlers, motivated by the gap between early symptom emergence and a mean US diagnosis age above 4 with fewer than 25% diagnosed before age 3. Main findings: internal validation accuracies of 61.62-65.41% with AUC 0.63-0.69, falling on the organiser's blind test set to 53.88-55.13% with AUC 0.545-0.553 and specificity as low as 0.282. The 492-parameter model performed best on validation and was matched by the 11.3-million-parameter CNN on the blind test.

**S-030** [local_a45f39e9] — *Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time*

Goal: automatic prediction of ASD-related atypical behaviour from home video, with the stated design constraint that any practical algorithm be cost-efficient and unobtrusive enough for long-term monitoring in the child's natural environment. Main findings: 0.72 accuracy, 0.72 precision, 0.92-0.93 recall and 0.66 AUC for the pose-based approach, against 0.66 accuracy and 0.62 AUC for an RGB single-frame baseline; retraining the pose estimator on child poses improved frame annotation rates by 9-14%; and imputation method made essentially no difference to performance.

**S-031** [local_d587f9cd] — *Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning*

The aim is a robot-assisted framework that automates the behavioural coding on which autism diagnosis depends, addressing the delay between when signs are observable and when diagnosis becomes reliable. The technical contribution is an unstructured, scalable network of RGBD sensors on ROS, each node performing local face analysis and publishing head pose and gaze as navigation messages, with a central node fusing them and computing visual focus of attention through a Hidden Markov Model, coupled bidirectionally to a robot whose gaze shifts, facial expressions and sound rewards adapt to the child's performance. The behavioural finding, from six children in single sessions, concerns initiation of joint attention across a within-session transition from therapist to robot mediator: all three typically developing children initiated joint attention toward the therapist, then across the transition, then toward the robot, whereas the three at-risk children initiated only toward the therapist during the transition. The authors describe this as 'a clear difference of behavior pattern' usable 'as evidence to improve the ASD diagnosis'. No classifier is trained, no accuracy is computed, and the evaluation is labelled a proof of concept.

**S-032** [local_08b8027d] — *SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths*

Goal: objective scanpath-based ASD screening, motivated by the observation that comprehensive ASD evaluation 'requires the assessment from well-trained specialists, which is not available in less-developed regions'. Main findings: 74.22% validation accuracy; 55.66-57.90% on the organiser's blind test set, which the authors attribute to overfitting; performance peaked at 1024 visual features and degraded at both 512 and 2048; and per-image accuracy varied widely with images containing people, particularly looking at the camera, classified better than natural scenes without faces.

**S-033** [local_c6f1209b] — *Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children*

The stated aim is twofold and unusual: to test whether play with a social robot reveals abnormal interaction patterns in autistic preschoolers, and simultaneously to collect user requirements and evaluation criteria for designing such a robot. The psychological finding is specific and well constructed: autistic children performed significantly more behaviours when the robot instructed them to than they performed spontaneously in imitation of the robot (Wilcoxon signed-rank W = 21, p = 0.028), from which the authors conclude that 'autistic children have more deficits among automatic turn-taking (spontaneous, without instruction) as compared to intentional turn-taking (after being instructed)'. That is a dissociation within the construct rather than a difference in its overall level, and it is exactly the kind of claim that a paired within-subject design can support and a between-group design at this scale could not. The engineering finding - a set of requirements and evaluation criteria for robot design derived from the experimental experience - is presented as a co-equal output, which no other study in this review does.

**S-034** [local_83b99e73] — *Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers*

Goal: determine whether still-face paradigm social behaviours differ before 24 months and whether machine learning on them can screen for autism prospectively. Main findings: high-risk infants showed less eye contact, social smiling and active social engagement in free interaction, and less eye contact and active social engagement under the maternal still face; negative-emotion behaviours did not differ; SVM reached 83.35% for the still-face episode and 81.18% for free interaction, with the still-face episode superior for all three algorithms; still-face behaviours correlated with CSBS-DP symptom severity while free-interaction behaviours did not; and the model misclassified all five children who resolved off the spectrum.

**S-035** [local_638860ef] — *Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis*

Goal: predict autism diagnosis from imitation kinematics and gaze, with methodological reliability as the explicit primary focus. Main findings: 73% accuracy from kinematics, 70% from eye movements, 78% from combined features; development and independent-test accuracies comparable, demonstrating that nested cross-validation controlled overfitting; the general instruction block outperformed the attention instruction block across all data types; t-test feature selection outperformed SVM-RFE, ReliefF and mRMR on both accuracy and stability; and seven of ten selected kinematic features came from the elevated-amplitude condition, where autistic adults imitated with lower vertical amplitude and earlier peak acceleration.

**S-036** [local_7547db68] — *Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network*

Goal: build a deployable hospital information system that diagnoses autism from facial expression imitation using deep CNNs, reducing subjectivity and physician time and extending early diagnosis to underserved regions. Main findings: mean expression recognition rate of 81.4% in typically developing children versus 34.3% in autistic children; a proposed 60% threshold below which a child is said to show a tendency toward autism; recognition errors in typically developing children concentrated on disgust and surprise; and in autistic children happy and sad were best recognised while neutral and disgust were worst.

**S-037** [local_878c259f] — *Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach*

Goal: develop and validate automated identification of ASD postural control patterns, framed around the open question of whether postural sway can serve as a diagnostic biomarker. Main findings: all six classifiers exceeded 0.800 accuracy; naive Bayes achieved 0.900 accuracy with 1.000 specificity, 1.000 precision, 0.898 F1 and 0.826 sensitivity; k-nearest neighbour was second at 0.860. The underlying group difference is greater sway magnitude in ASD across displacement, distance and area, with no group difference in sample entropy complexity.

**S-038** [local_1579c85a] — *Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through*

Goal: behavior-based risk detection to streamline standard diagnostic procedures through rapid detection and clinical prioritisation of at-risk children. Main findings: CNN 0.8846 accuracy, 0.8912 precision, 0.8853 recall; random forest 0.8852/0.8876/0.8856; KNN 0.8874/0.8920/0.8878 - all three within 0.003 of one another; false negative rate 0.1787. The authors conclude that simpler methods suffice at this scale and that the method is not ready for standalone diagnostic use.

**S-039** [local_157d6266] — *Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism*

Goal: develop an objective, continuous, scalable measure of motor imitation, validated on four fronts - construct validity, test-retest reliability, diagnostic discrimination, and clinical association. Main findings: CAMI classified diagnostic groups at 87.2% versus 74.4% for human observation coding; a single one-minute trial reached 84.6%; CAMI-HOC correlations r = .69-.87; test-retest r = .73-.86; poorer imitation in ASC (p < .005); and poorer imitation correlated with greater symptom severity on SRS-2 (r = -0.50 total) and ADOS-2.

**S-040** [local_8be557e3] — *Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation*

Goal: determine whether auto-encoder-based learned features, jointly optimised with the classifier, improve automated autism detection from infant vocalisations under small, unbalanced, unrefined data conditions. Main findings: the jointly optimised AE+BLSTM outperformed vanilla BLSTM and SVM on accuracy (0.6818), F1 (0.5457) and UAR (0.6509); Mann-Whitney-based selection of 54 eGeMAPS features degraded rather than improved performance; t-SNE shows eGeMAPS-88 and eGeMAPS-54 spaces nearly identical and heavily overlapped while the auto-encoder space is visibly redistributed; and at the categorical level autistic infants produced proportionally fewer first words and more atypical vocalisation.

**S-041** [local_c79e100a] — *Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models*

Goal: determine how the choice of data representation - individual gait cycles versus trial averages - affects autism classification performance, as a methodological question in its own right. Main findings: averaging reduced intra-subject variance, most for subjects with the greatest initial variance; random forest improved from 68.75% to 76.67% accuracy; decision tree and KNN showed little accuracy change but substantial F1 loss; the SVM degenerated into an always-autistic predictor; autistic subjects showed visibly greater intra-subject gait variability than typically developed subjects; and the benefit of variance reduction depends on classifier suitability, dataset size and class balance.

**S-042** [local_4fecbf6d] — *Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network*

Goal: estimate continuous autism severity (ADOS total) from speech recorded during the ADOS itself, and compare regression and deep architectures for the task. Main findings: 21 of 60 features correlated significantly with ADOS total; higher and more variable pitch and higher ZCR with greater severity, fewer vocalisations and turns with greater severity, and shorter rather than longer response latency; RRB scores tracked acoustic and prosodic features while SA scores tracked conversational features; a CNN on a 100 x 48 sub-sample matrix achieved mean R = 0.72 and RMSE 4.65 across 50 balanced splits, beating SVR (0.51) and linear regression (0.36); and matrix-input models were far more stable across splits than vector-input ones.

**S-043** [local_95abe653] — *Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning*

Goal: test whether gaze during ordinary web-page use detects high-functioning autism in adults, and whether the effect holds across independent participants, stimuli and tasks. Main findings: all four tasks produced a discrimination signal, with best accuracies of 0.75 (Search), 0.74 (Browse, 120 s), 0.73 (Synthesis) and 0.65 (Browse, 30 s); capping browse time showed the groups differ in browsing strategy and not only in time spent; increased task complexity did not increase separability; AOI content and granularity both affect accuracy, with the 2 x 2 grid consistently worst; and page visual complexity and participant gender contribute nothing.

**S-044** [local_40168c96] — *Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based*

Goal: identify autism from the dynamic structure of saccadic scanpaths rather than from static fixation statistics, using learned representations. Main findings: 93.15% mean subject-level accuracy across five participant-level permutations (94.29% maximum), with sensitivity 94.66% and specificity 92.00%; accuracy increases monotonically with aggregation from pieces (87.16%) to scanpaths (88.03%) to subjects (93.15%); CNN features contribute most and high-level semantic features next in ablation; and errors concentrate on typically developing children, attributed to distraction producing uninformative gaze.

**S-045** [local_d3852378] — *Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Goal: determine whether body movement during multimodal VR imitation tasks discriminates autistic from typically developing children, which body regions carry the signal, and which sensory conditions best elicit it. Main findings: 15 joints differed significantly with autistic children moving more in 13 of them, concentrated in head and legs; best classification 89.36% (all joints, visual condition; and head joints, visual-auditory-olfactory condition); head is the most consistent region and improves with increasing sensory load; whole-body accuracy declines with increasing sensory load; the all-joints all-conditions model performs worst at 70.21%; and every model needed three or fewer features.

**S-046** [local_df438dd2] — *Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening*

Goal: automate scoring of the responsive social smile, one element of clinical screening that lacks clear behavioural benchmarks, and use the resulting scores for autism classification. Main findings: 85.20% agreement with three-clinician consensus stimulus scores; 80.49% autism classification accuracy with 85.00% sensitivity and 77.27% specificity from a decision tree; substituting clinicians' own stimulus scores raises this only to 82.93%, locating the performance ceiling in the protocol rather than the perception pipeline; 92.60% smile classification after fine-tuning on a purpose-built children's expression database; and most residual scoring errors are correctly detected smiles that clinicians judged spontaneous rather than socially responsive.

**S-047** [local_cd9e45eb] — *Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism*

Goal: select a parsimonious subset of eye-tracking stimuli that preserves discriminative and predictive power, treating selection as a grouped variable problem. Main findings: 11 of 109 stimuli retained 78.13% accuracy and 82.91% AUC; SGIN was the only method achieving sparsity and accuracy together, with lasso 15 points worse at comparable sparsity and group lasso behaving near-bimodally; Dyadic Bids was the most-retained paradigm and Social Referencing the most-discarded; and the features predicted IQ (r = 0.54) but failed above chance for ADOS severity, SRS and Vineland.

**S-048** [local_56237213] — *The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data*

Goal: test whether fusing resting-state EEG spectral power with face-viewing gaze features improves autism identification over either modality alone. Main findings: EEG alone 68%, gaze alone 75.89% (AUC 0.865) combining own- and other-race faces, and fused 85.44% with AUC 0.93 at 32 selected features; autistic children fixated the background far more (19.4% versus 3.3%) and the face, nose and mouth less; own-race faces classified better than other-race faces; and EEG showed differences in theta, beta and gamma but not delta or alpha.

**S-049** [local_f9a5195f] — *Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses*

Goal: test the feasibility of wearable gaze tracking during an emotion recognition task and whether the resulting data distinguish autistic from neurotypical children. Main findings: autistic children showed a higher mean distraction ratio (0.0433 versus 0.0139) but not significantly at the participant level (P = .12); the full classifier reached 71.0%, exactly matching an age-and-gender-only baseline; gaze features alone reached 83.9% but did not survive Bonferroni correction; performance was best on trial 1 before feedback and worst on trial 2 during audio cueing; and the authors conclude the differences are too subtle and the data too noisy for reliable machine exploitation.

**S-050** [local_16a77fb0] — *Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)*

Goal: build and validate a standardised, automatically scored measure of social interaction behaviour capable of supporting autism diagnosis in adults. Main findings: combined AUC 0.78 with 73% accuracy, 67% sensitivity and 79% specificity; voice was the strongest modality (0.77), facial expression next (0.74), gaze weakest (0.63) with no differences surviving correction; autistic adults showed less social smiling and less mimicry and higher fundamental frequency; the classifier beat a majority vote and matched eight clinical experts whose own accuracy ranged from 0.56 to 1.00 and scaled with experience; and predicted probability correlated with both ADOS severity (rs = 0.48) and age (rs = 0.35), the latter identified as a confound.

**S-051** [local_9c4af7a3] — *Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades*

Goal: build a machine-learning classifier on saccade features to shorten and simplify autism diagnosis. Main findings: a Two-Class Boosted Decision Tree reached 88% accuracy (88-91% per the abstract); mutual-information filtering selected six of sixteen attributes, including mean primary saccade amplitude, absolute saccade error and latency; and descriptively, autistic participants showed comparable mean saccade latency but greater trial-to-trial variability, larger and more variable absolute saccade error amplified at higher target amplitudes, and lower peak velocity with longer time to reach it.

**S-052** [local_b70dae32] — *An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model*

Goal: use performance data already generated during robot-mediated therapy to categorise autism severity level without requiring a therapist to do the categorisation. Main findings: an HMM over binned joint attention and imitation categories matched clinician CARS categories in 19 of 25 test sessions (76% accuracy) with moderate agreement (kappa 0.52, p = 0.009); average joint attention success across all children was 65.47% and imitation 76.19%; and most children fell in the delayed joint attention and moderate-to-full imitation bands.

**S-053** [local_51a0af74] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data*

Goal: build gaze trajectory features that can represent the joint attention paradigm computationally, using semantically tracked floating regions of interest, and classify autism from them. Main findings: 75% accuracy, 87% sensitivity, 53% specificity and 0.82 F1 from an ensemble using three of nine video segments; the informative segments correspond to the therapist's gaze resting, shifting to the object, and returning; no single segment exceeded 75% alone; and regions containing the eyes outperformed those containing the pointing hand.

**S-054** [local_d8d3037b] — *Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study*

Goal: build a rapid VR-based gaze screening method for high autistic traits, deployable where clinical resources are limited. Main findings: an ensemble of seven classifiers reached 0.73 accuracy, 0.81 recall and reported AUC 0.90 on the median-split adult sample and recalled 77% of 22 diagnosed autistic participants; continuity of looking at the figure and animal regions was the most important feature family across tree-based models; and individual model recall shifted markedly between the two experiments, which the authors read as evidence that the two populations differ.

**S-055** [local_991fe435] — *Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task*

Goal: classify three groups defined by diagnosis and cognitive functioning from raw gaze during a visual-orienting task, and test whether less-social directional cues also discriminate. Main findings: 81.08% three-class accuracy rising to 93.24% for binary autism versus typical development; success rates ranked 74.7%, 29.1% and 5.7% across typically developing, high-functioning and low-functioning groups; deficits appeared for arrow and finger cues as well as gaze cues, with removing either cue family costing accuracy; and cross-group tests showed a model trained on typically developing versus high-functioning children identified 100% of unseen low-functioning children while the reverse transfer achieved only 53.85%.

**S-056** [local_8692a64f] — *Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis*

Goal: build an auxiliary autism diagnostic method from structured, interpretable eye-movement features rather than unstructured data. Main findings: cubic-kernel SVM achieved 0.93 accuracy, 0.80 sensitivity and 1.00 specificity; Gaussian naive Bayes 0.90/0.80/0.96 and KNN 0.80/0.60/0.92; gaze at untrackable regions and head-eye co-movement were the most label-correlated feature families; and the hypothesis that autistic children would show more head-eye co-movement was refuted, the correlation running in the opposite direction.

**S-057** [local_4d6fac7e] — *Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network*

Goal: fuse EEG and eye-tracking features through a graph convolutional network over a covariance-derived feature graph, improving on simple feature- or decision-level fusion. Main findings: 95% accuracy for the fused model against 79% for gaze alone and 74% for EEG alone; 81% for a conventional mRMR-plus-SVM pipeline and 70% for ResNet18 on concatenated features; gaze alone outperformed EEG alone; and covariance analysis revealed cross-modal relationships between EEG synchronisation and entropy features and face, joint attention and social interaction gaze paradigms despite asynchronous recording.

**S-058** [local_30c622f2] — *Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model*

Goal: test whether autism severity can be classified from gaze via a visual attention model, and whether semantic top-down attentional guidance degrades with severity. Main findings: mean ROC AUC 0.85 with sensitivity 87% and specificity 60%; presence of face and presence of skin were selected as predictive features only for the non-severe group; the non-severe model retained more features overall (15 versus 12); and the CARS severity split was corroborated by significantly lower Vineland scores in the severe group.

**S-059** [local_bfc088c7] — *Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation*

Goal: determine whether gaze during live face-to-face conversation classifies autism, and whether combining fixation features with conversation duration improves on either alone. Main findings: 92.31% accuracy with SVM using three combined features against 84.62% for either feature family alone; total conversation length alone achieved 79.49%; autistic children fixated less on mouth, face and body but not differently on the eyes; and the three misclassified autistic children fell within the typically developing range on all selected features.

**S-060** [local_25e34bbd] — *Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification*

Goal: detect autism and Down syndrome from sustained vowel phonation and discriminate between them, comparing three acoustic feature families. Main findings: MFCC and RASTA-PLP achieved 100% accuracy for autism detection and Down syndrome detection; MFCC and harmonics-to-noise ratio achieved 100% for autism-versus-Down-syndrome discrimination; perturbation and noise measures performed worse throughout; combining feature families reduced performance in almost every condition; and the feed-forward network outperformed SVM and naive Bayes comparators on the same features.

**S-061** [local_4917150c] — *Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning*

Goal: represent eye-tracking scanpaths as velocity-coloured images so that autism screening becomes an image classification problem. Main findings: approximately 90% accuracy with image-level splitting and approximately 71% with participant-level splitting; a maximal information coefficient of 0.79 between CARS score and average gaze velocity; and a working demonstration application linking eye tracking, visualisation and prediction through a hosted model.

**S-062** [local_241ec2c2] — *Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking*

Goal: replace region-of-interest annotation with learned per-group visual attention models over video stimuli, and classify individuals by adherence to those models. Main findings: AUC 0.822 with 90% precision, 93% specificity and 69% sensitivity; genetic algorithm selection retained distance-to-centre and biological movement only for the autistic model and colour only for the typically developing model; selection improved the neural network's fold-to-fold stability far more than its mean AUC while degrading the SVM substantially.

**S-063** [local_36617ec5] — *Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis*

Goal: determine whether gaze in an immersive virtual environment distinguishes autistic from typically developing children and which parameters do so. Main findings: 86% accuracy with 91% sensitivity and AUC 0.91 using all features; autistic children looked at social elements in more frames than typically developing children, contrary to most prior work; they also attended more to static non-social items; people-versus-items contrasts discriminated best at 84% while adults'-faces-versus-bodies discriminated worst at 66%; and the model restricted to the 13 statistically significant features was less accurate but the most stable across iterations.

**S-064** [local_d8e804d6] — *Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms*

Goal: determine whether head movement dynamics discriminate autistic from typically developing children, and which kinematic features do so. Main findings: 92.11% accuracy with a decision tree on two features, with all five classifiers above 81% using three features or fewer; head nodding, shaking and non-use frequencies did not differ between groups; but rotation range and amount of rotation per minute were significantly greater in autistic children in all three rotational axes after adjusting for age, IQ and gesture frequency.

**S-065** [local_712542ca] — *Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset*

Goal: improve classification on an existing scanpath image dataset by clustering it first into more homogeneous subgroups. Main findings: best accuracy of 88.89% with a multilayer perceptron in cluster 1, against 74.2% for the best classifier on the pooled dataset; the other three clusters reached 70.7%, 75.8% and 77.8%; and the authors conclude that clustering produced groups in which classes were more separable.

**S-066** [local_0ab41681] — *Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder*

Goal: test whether motor synergies - the co-control of redundant degrees of freedom - are impaired in autism, and relate this to symptom severity. Main findings: autistic children moved faster with more symmetrical velocity profiles, showed greater trial-to-trial spatial variability, and showed significantly reduced variance accounted for by the first three principal components across nine joint angles; only the synergy measure correlated with ADOS severity (rho = -0.650, p = 0.016); and leave-one-subject-out SVM classification reached AUC 0.947 with 0.846 sensitivity and 0.923 specificity at the optimal operating point, on trial-level accuracy of 0.739.

**S-067** [local_9ca9b2cc] — *Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment*

The aim is a robot-mediated therapy and assessment system that measures a child's attention automatically, adapts its own interaction scenario to that measurement, and thereby increases engagement over a course of sessions. Two results are reported. The automated attention score agreed with the treating therapist's assessment on 28 of 34 sessions, giving 82.4%, which the conclusion describes accurately as 'matching over 80% of therapist assessments'. And attention scores rose across a seven-week course in most of the six children who continued, from which the authors draw an explicitly hypothetical conclusion - 'our hypothesis is that a properly designed robot intervention system can increase the attention levels'. Neither claim concerns autism detection: all participants are autistic, there is no comparison group, and no classification is attempted. For this review the study contributes a different kind of evidence - a demonstration that an automated behavioural measure can track a clinician's judgement of the same construct well enough to be usable in a therapy loop, which is the closed-loop application that most of the corpus's detection-oriented work does not consider.

**S-068** [local_02fa4215] — *Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning*

Goal: build the first autism prediction model for Pakistan from a purpose-collected questionnaire and identify commonly associated background factors. Main findings: 95% best accuracy across several algorithm-and-selection combinations, with 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity in the best confusion matrices on a 40-child test set; and a set of narrative single-group observations about birth order, sex, family history, sensory reactivity, maternal vaccination and parental smoking, none accompanied by control comparison or statistical test.

**S-069** [local_29a3fc54] — *Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism*

Goal: quantify prosodic abnormality automatically and test whether voice alone predicts diagnosis better than chance, and whether ADOS-2 tasks differ in discriminative value. Main findings: prosodic features reached 82.23% AUC against a 49.90% chance baseline; articulation features alone reached only 67.98% and combining the two was worse than prosody alone; friends and marriage conversation was the single best sampling context at 83.04% with no gain from combining tasks; pitch and loudness formed the optimal subset and both correlated with independently rated severity after IQ adjustment; and an IQ-matched 28-pair subsample reproduced the result at 88.27% AUC.

**S-070** [local_b7ec3755] — *Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images*

Goal: build a classifier that combines image-content features with viewing-behaviour features, on the argument that competing entries modelled scanpaths without reference to what was being looked at. Main findings: 0.59 accuracy, 0.68 recall, 0.50 specificity on the challenge test set, tied for best of eight entries; performance concentrated on images where mean fixation duration separated the groups (88.5% on the best five images, 46.2% on the worst five); autistic children showed more brief fixation clusters under 100 ms (24% versus 15%) and fewer beyond 500 ms (21% versus 35%); and the authors conclude that age-conditioned feature selection is needed but unavailable.

**S-071** [local_684969f6] — *Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data*

Goal: extend the authors' ICME 2019 challenge submission by testing whether a generative neurotypical scanning baseline (STAR-FC) improves classification and whether a holistic image-plus-fixation network beats it. Main findings: best test performance 62.13% accuracy and 0.667 AUC (ResNet50), best of five compared methods; substantial improvement over their own challenge entries (53.88% to 61.39% and 55.13% to 61.45%); the STAR-FC synthetic saccade contributes nothing across four paired comparisons; validation-optimal and test-optimal configurations differ in both pipelines; and, decisively, scanpath-only input matches scanpath-plus-image everywhere, which the authors attribute to systematic per-child gaze bias in a 28-participant pool and support with a large group difference in total scanpath duration.

**S-072** [local_35004e74] — *Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children*

Goal: test whether a network trained purely on non-verbal social interaction, represented as skeletal motion, can differentiate autistic from typically developing children - explicitly framed against prior digital phenotyping that focused on 'relatively isolated behaviors elicited by largely controlled prompts'. Main findings: 80.9% accuracy (precision 0.784, recall 0.854, specificity 0.765, F1 0.818) on 68 held-out children; 80.2% on a further 101 autistic children; ~70% from 10 minutes of video, with 100% within-child prediction consistency from a random 10-minute segment for half the autistic sample; robustness to different rooms, examiners and cameras; ASD probability correlated with ADOS severity (total 0.451, social affect 0.509, repetitive behaviours 0.409), inversely with adaptive functioning (-0.444) and IQ (-0.283); and 15 of 27 ADOS items significantly related after Bonferroni correction, predominantly non-verbal, confirmed by a permutation-tested PLS-C latent component (p = 0.001).

**S-073** [local_fa91fc18] — *Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities*

Goal: determine whether the kinematics of a simple dragging movement, recorded incidentally during a digital cognitive assessment, can classify autism, and describe the motor features that differentiate the groups. Main findings: 88 +/- 3% accuracy under ten-fold cross-validation with five repetitions, and 93% accuracy with sensitivity 0.87 and specificity 0.98 for the best fold model; classification degraded only gradually as features were removed, reaching 78% with five features and chance with one; speed and acceleration measures dominated the importance ranking over straightness and directional change; and autistic trajectories were shorter, less straight, more frequently redirected and far more variable in speed and acceleration.

**S-074** [local_115dfe8d] — *A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children*

Goal: determine whether learned fusion of an internal neurophysiological modality and an external behavioural modality outperforms either alone, and whether hierarchical latent-space fusion beats naive feature concatenation. Main findings: MMSDAE reached 95.56% accuracy, 92.5% sensitivity, 98% specificity and AUC 0.984 under subject-independent stratified ten-fold cross-validation, improving on eye tracking alone (86.67%) by 8.89 points and EEG alone (81.11%) by 14.45; both fusion variants beat both unimodal models, and two-stage fusion beat naive concatenation; the modalities are complementary in a specific and demonstrated way, with EEG stronger on autistic children (82.5% versus 77.7%) and gaze much stronger on typically developing children (94% versus 80%); and the behavioural modality alone outperformed the neurophysiological one.

**S-075** [local_5b7ea7dc] — *AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Goal: build a screening tool whose input is raw video and whose target behaviour is one that clinicians already regard as diagnostically meaningful, addressing two named shortcomings in prior work - that the Cognoa-derived system feeds human ratings rather than video into the model, and that Zunino's grasping-kinematics approach targets a gesture 'not generally considered an indication of ASD behavior by most mental health specialists'. Main findings: 0.916 accuracy, 0.900 precision, 0.945 recall and 0.922 F1 on a subject-disjoint raw-video test set of 36 children; 0.918 accuracy on a second, background-reduced test set of 18 children; and an attention analysis showing that typically developing children produce a distinct attention peak coinciding with an observed triadic gaze shift while autistic children produce flat attention profiles, with fewer than 1% of autistic children showing both.

**S-076** [local_87fe26aa] — *Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Goal: compare the discriminative power of eye fixation, facial expression and EEG collected simultaneously, and test whether hybrid fusion - behavioural feature fusion followed by weighted decision fusion with the physiological stream - outperforms any single modality. Main findings: EEG most discriminative (83.75% best, 74.69% average), facial expression next (77.50%, 71.56%), eye fixation weakest (73.75%, 67.50%); hybrid fusion 87.50% against 85.00% for behavioural data alone and 83.75% for physiological data alone; modalities fail in opposite directions, with EEG best on autistic children (90.0%) and facial expression best on typically developing children (92.5%); and theta power elevated in the autistic group across five of six brain regions.

**S-077** [local_893ce2fa] — *An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images*

Goal: demonstrate the Giza Pyramids Construction metaheuristic as an optimiser for Kernel Extreme Learning Machine parameters, benchmarked on autism classification from gaze-path images. Main findings: GPC-KELM reached 0.9881 accuracy, 0.9859 precision, 0.9843 sensitivity, 0.9906 specificity, 0.9752 MCC and 0.9851 F1, with sub-0.0015 standard deviations across 30 runs; it beat PSO, ABC, ALO, BA and HHO variants (0.9736-0.9800) with Wilcoxon p-values below 1.1e-11; and it beat a multilayer perceptron (0.8179), naive Bayes (0.7306) and logistic regression (0.7243) on the same data, with AUC 98.18 against 79.17 and 66.55. Optimal parameters were C = 26.644 and gamma = 23.603, converging by the sixth of ten iterations.

**S-078** [local_dffe4127] — *Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals*

Goal: determine whether the excess behavioural variability of autistic participants reflects within-individual unreliability or between-individual heterogeneity, by testing three mutually exclusive hypotheses. Main findings, in the order they eliminate hypotheses: within-individual reliability was high and statistically indistinguishable between groups at every epoch duration (Spearman's rho > 0.635, between-group difference p > 0.333), and individuals were identifiable from their own gaze at 35% against a 3-6% chance level from as little as 2 minutes of video, ruling out hypothesis 1; the autistic and typically developing reference heatmaps were correlated at r = 0.966 and autistic individuals matched the autistic reference less well than controls did, and unsupervised clustering split the autistic group nearly in half rather than separating it from controls, ruling out hypothesis 3; supervised classification reached 0.618 against an empirical chance level of 0.607 with 22 of 48 autistic adults reliably misclassified, confirming hypothesis 2. Group differences themselves were moderate and robust: Cohen's d 0.60-0.82, replicated across two episodes and detectable from 2-minute epochs.

**S-079** [local_2b766683] — *Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech*

Goal: test whether autism can be detected from self-recorded home speech captured on ordinary smartphones, removing the specialised equipment and centralised recording locations that the authors argue make prior work undeployable. Main findings: a purpose-built 8.7-million-parameter CNN over mel spectrograms reached 79.3% accuracy and 0.822 AUROC; a fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 reached 76.9% and 0.815; a random forest over conventional acoustic features reached 69.7% and 0.740; folds were constructed child-disjoint to block recording-idiosyncrasy leakage; all three models covaried across folds, suggesting the folds are too small; an ImageNet-pretrained Inception v3 underperformed the smaller purpose-built CNN; and the whole result rests on 115.5 minutes of audio from 58 children.

**S-080** [local_2895bdf0] — *Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection*

Three explicit aims, each addressed. First, replicate the voice model of Asgari et al. (2021) and the language model of Salem et al. (2021) and compare their discriminant validity using the same methodology in the same sample - achieved, with language (AUC 0.8748) significantly better than voice (0.7800, DeLong p = 0.036), the difference lying in specificity (0.83 versus 0.69). Second, quantify the gain from combining them - the combined model reached AUC 0.9205, significantly better than voice (p < 0.001) and language (p = 0.033), with accuracy 0.8671, sensitivity 0.8977 and specificity 0.8286; the entire gain is in sensitivity while specificity is unchanged. Third, characterise which participants each model detects - the language model caught children with poorer structural and pragmatic language, less output and one year younger; the voice model caught children with better language profiles and showed no association between language measures and classification success; only nine autistic participants (10.2%) escaped the combined model, and these had the highest IQ and most language output of any subgroup.

**S-081** [local_423b636b] — *Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers*

Goal: replicate a prior head-movement-rate finding in a larger sample with redesigned stimuli, and extend it to acceleration and multiscale-entropy complexity, testing whether differences are more pronounced for social content and whether the measures can be combined for classification. Main findings: autistic toddlers showed significantly higher rate (F(1,427) = 42.48), acceleration (F(1,427) = 38.65) and complexity (F(1,427) = 29.68), all p < .0001, with medium to large effect sizes for social movies and small to medium for nonsocial; a significant main effect of movie type with no group-by-type interaction; neurotypical toddlers modulated all three measures by content while autistic toddlers did not; classification reached AUC 0.85 for acceleration across the four social movies and 0.80 for entropy, with the eight-dimensional combination performing worse at 0.73; and neither age nor missing data affected the group comparisons.

**S-082** [local_ffa35101] — *Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study*

Goal: identify prosodic differences in autism that span typologically distinct languages and those shaped by language-specific properties, by comparing rhythm-relevant and intonation-relevant acoustic feature classes within English, within Cantonese and across both combined. Main findings: rhythm classified successfully in English (median AUC 0.900), Cantonese (0.962) and combined (0.886), all p < 0.001; intonation classified significantly only in English (0.695, p = 0.007), failing in Cantonese (0.620, p = 0.507) and falling near chance when combined (0.559, p = 0.509). The dissociation is attributed to the phonological role of pitch in tone languages and is used to reconcile the conflicting f0 literature, where higher f0 and wider range are reported in English but lower f0 range in Thai and Japanese.

**S-083** [local_81ecbc6f] — *Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings*

Goal: evaluate deep neural text encoders for detecting autism from narrative transcripts and compare them against standardised instruments and human expert judgement on the same participants. Main findings: best computational configurations reached sensitivity 0.72 and specificity 0.68; two psychiatrists reading identical transcripts achieved 0.56-0.60 sensitivity and 0.60-0.64 specificity, close to chance; ADOS-2 achieved 1.00 sensitivity and 0.92 specificity and SCQ 0.92 and 0.96 on the same sample; page-level representation with zero vectors for skipped pages outperformed whole-narration representation; and ELMo and USE reached identical top scores despite different architectures, suggesting representation granularity matters more than encoder choice.

**S-084** [local_bc62bc4b] — *Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening*

Goal: develop and test a decision support system for early autism screening in toddlers, and determine whether toys or animations are the more effective non-social competitor in a preferential-viewing paradigm. Main findings: best accuracy 87.5% with ROC area 0.888 (random forest and SVM with ReliefF features on the animation dataset); animations outperformed toys across most configurations, with mean looking times showing autistic toddlers viewing animations for 6.06 s against 3.20 s for comparisons and people for 5.68 s against 10.37 s; diversion duration, net dwell time and first fixation duration on the social area of interest were selected as discriminative by all three feature-selection algorithms; multivariate feature sets beat net dwell time alone (78.12% and 84.37% against 70.67% and 79.17%); and 12.5% of autistic toddlers were false negatives even in the best model.

**S-085** [local_889d9bd6] — *Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children*

Goal: determine whether eye-tracking differences between autistic and typically developing children are the same in toddlers and preschoolers, and identify which paradigms discriminate at which age. Main findings: reduced fixation time percentage in nine of ten areas of interest with a main effect of diagnosis, but a main effect of age group on only one area; significant diagnosis-by-age interaction on the eye area, where toddlers did not differ (p = 0.93) but preschoolers did (p = 0.006); single-area classification rankings that largely invert between cohorts, with mouth, upright walking, moving dot and baby face discriminating toddlers and eyes, duck, infant face and fan discriminating preschoolers; full-model accuracy of 80% in toddlers and 71% in preschoolers; only preschool comparison children showing the expected preference for upright biological motion; and no association between any fixation measure and CARS severity.

**S-086** [local_361b59fb] — *Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

Goal: test whether an AI-based diagnostic aid can allow primary care clinicians to diagnose autism directly, reducing referral load and diagnostic delay. Main findings: for the 31.8% of children on which the Device rendered a verdict, PPV was 80.8% and NPV 98.3%, with sensitivity 98.4% and specificity 78.9%; if abstention were removed, sensitivity across all completers would fall to 51.6% and specificity to 18.5%; 91% of the children the Device declined to classify had at least one neurodevelopmental disorder; all 15 false positives had a non-autism developmental condition and none were neurotypical, with one specialist judging a third of them autistic; there was a single false negative; the mean age at which an autism-positive output was rendered was 2.81 years against a national average diagnosis age above 4; and no performance differences were detected across sex, race and ethnicity, income or education, though the study was not powered to test them.

**S-087** [local_afdb603d] — *Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.*

Goal: establish whether acoustic markers of autism reported for English and other languages also appear in Italian, using a standard clinical parameter set, with classification as a check on whether the selected features carry signal. Main findings: 16 of 88 eGeMAPS parameters differed significantly, spanning voice quality (jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio), loudness, pitch dynamics and spectral distribution; best classifiers reached 83% accuracy on a six-sample test set with SVM most consistent across ten runs at a mean of 79.8%; jitter and shimmer were higher on average but less variable in the autistic group, matching a pattern reported in Italian-language-independent adult work; and mean pitch was higher though not significantly, which the authors use to argue against the monotone-speech stereotype.

**S-088** [local_4f7e7eb3] — *Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques*

Goal: compare three artificial-intelligence approaches - shallow neural networks on hand-engineered texture features, transfer-learned CNNs, and CNN-plus-SVM hybrids - for classifying autism from gaze-path images. Main findings: FFNN and ANN on concatenated LBP and GLCM features reached 99.8% overall accuracy (98.7% at test phase); ResNet-18 reached 97.6% and GoogleNet 93.6%; the hybrids reached 95.5% and 94.5%; and the hand-engineered pipeline was concluded to be 'the best performance amongst the proposed systems'. No behavioural finding, group difference or gaze characteristic is reported.

**S-089** [local_db6c2d7c] — *Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With*

Goal: determine whether gaze fixation and visual scanning differences associated with autism can be detected from unstructured home video on consumer phones, without eye trackers, manual annotation or structured tasks. Main findings: one of 16 gaze regions (BC, p < .001) and one of 61 transition pairs (BB-BC, p < .001) differed significantly after Bonferroni correction across 100,000-permutation tests, with comparison children making 13% of transitions between these regions against 9.4% for autistic children; an LSTM on the discretised gaze sequences reached macro-averaged recall 0.598 and weighted-average recall 0.656 on a child-disjoint held-out set, described by the authors as mild predictive power; and the entire pipeline operated without any human viewing participant video.

**S-090** [local_8b5fb23b] — *Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms*

Goal: identify an accurate model for autism screening from scan path images and determine whether performance survives restriction to one image per child. Main findings: conventional classifiers performed at or near chance on the original images (deep SVM AUC 51.50%, decision jungle 60.40%, boosted decision tree 67.60%); the convolutional network reached AUC 78.00% on the same images; rotation augmentation raised the network to AUC 97.00%, which the authors attribute to data contamination; and the participant-level subset of 59 images evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation yielded 72.88% accuracy with sensitivity 58.62% and specificity 86.67%.

**S-091** [local_6dcefc34] — *Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism*

Goal: determine whether the GuessWhat game generates a signal separating autistic from neurotypical children using only objective gameplay metadata, as a step toward an easily deployed remote screening tool. Main findings: AU-ROC 0.745 with recall 0.769 for the best model (random forest on duration features); duration features significantly more important than accuracy features (t = 5.15, p = 1e-5); accuracy features uninformative because they cluster at ceiling in both groups; three of four classifiers improved or held when accuracy features were removed; and disgust, surprise and sadness prompts carried the most importance among duration features.

**S-092** [local_65974fc7] — *Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction*

Goal: compare three acoustic feature constructions derived from time-frequency ICA for distinguishing autistic from comparison children's speech. Main findings: unmixing-matrix features reached 98.51% accuracy with SVM and 95.59% with CNN; separated frequency-point sequences reached only 59.71% and 55.19%, this being the best of 256 sequences; cepstral features on separated signals reached 91.00-92.89% with SVM, with PLP best and MFCC worst; and SVM outperformed CNN under every condition, which the authors attribute to the small dataset.

**S-093** [local_988c462e] — *The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation*

Goal: build an end-to-end system that locates child speech within a full ADOS recording and estimates autism severity from it, and determine whether automatic diarization can replace manual annotation. Main findings: MFCC-plus-pitch diarization achieved a 26.91% diarization error rate against x-vectors' 89.84% child-segment accuracy; severity estimation reached Pearson R 0.606 +/- 0.099 with NRMSE 0.248 with automatic diarization, against 0.567 +/- 0.120 and 0.261 with manual segmentation; and automatic diarization therefore matched or slightly exceeded manual annotation, which the authors attribute to imperfect manual labelling of quiet child speech in a reverberant room.

**S-094** [local_76de1c03] — *The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children*

The aim is to test whether a dyadic game with a social robot can elicit and reveal turn-taking deficits, as a step toward a robot-enabled diagnostic aid. Five autistic and five typically developing preschoolers each played 'Touch me' and 'Dance with me' with a NAO robot for about five minutes per game, and six raters from special education scored their behaviour from video on a purpose-built scale. Autistic children produced significantly fewer turn-taking behaviours in both scenarios, and group differences also appeared on interest in the robot and on additional movements. Inter-rater reliability was satisfactory (Kendall's W = 0.65, p < 0.001) with subscale alpha 0.77. The study's contribution is the paradigm and its validation rather than a detection result: no model is fitted, no child is assigned a predicted class, and no accuracy is computed or claimed. The authors state the intended use precisely - 'If a specialist has a sense of how a typical child plays with NAO, then they will be able to see possible deficits in the turn-taking of a child with autism by observing him/her' - which is a claim about calibrating human observation, not about automating it.

**S-095** [local_3ba6d25c] — *Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach*

Two stated goals: first, to test whether gaze behaviour segments produced by autistic and TD children can be classified by machine learning; second, to test whether children themselves can be classified from the proportion of their segments the model labels ASD-like. The framing is explicitly novelty-driven - the authors assert that prior eye-tracking ML studies all extracted features from visual fixation patterns and that 'no study has been found to identify ASD with oculomotor behavior', drawing a conceptual distinction between where attention is directed (fixation) and how the eyes move in the sockets (oculomotor). Findings: segment classification peaked at 74.15% (9 s windows, single feature: entropy of gaze allocation in the x-y plane, sensitivity 75.45%, specificity 72.51%), above the majority-class baseline at every window length; child classification peaked at 87.18% (7 s windows, 46% threshold, sensitivity 89.47%, specificity 85.00%). Feature-level statistics show entropy differences significant at every window length from 1 to 10 s (all p <= .006 for the x-y plane), while range differences are significant only at the shortest windows and fall away beyond 4 s - so the discriminative signal is the irregularity of gaze allocation, not its spatial extent. Secondary observation of substantive interest: ASD children took 191 s to complete the same six-question session against 110 s for TD children (U = 48, p < .01).

**S-096** [local_70a30e2b] — *A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features*

Goal: to extend the group's existing accelerometer-only sensorized toy car by adding wheel shaft encoders, testing whether autistic children's documented interest in rotating objects can be captured as a second sensing modality and whether fusing it with movement features improves screening accuracy. The comparison is deliberately internal - the authors state they do not wish to compare their accuracy against other modalities in the literature, only against their own version 1. Findings: the reimplemented accelerometer-only baseline achieved 71.11% accuracy on the new data (lower than the 85% reported for version 1, attributed to different data, different collection setup and a from-scratch reimplementation); adding encoder features gave 78.61%; adding new roll/pitch acceleration features instead gave 75.83%; adding both gave 85.56% with sensitivity 81.67%, specificity 81.00% and precision 87.67% - the claimed improvement of more than 10 percentage points over baseline. Of the ten features surviving two rounds of backward elimination, three came from the encoders: the ratio of wheels-only play to total playtime, the not-playing ratio, and the total wheel turn rate. A secondary and arguably more informative finding is that random forest on the full feature set gave lower accuracy (80.83%) but the best sensitivity and specificity of any configuration (85.48%, 83.67%), which the authors flag as a reason a deployer might prefer it - a rare instance in this corpus of explicitly preferring a model on error-profile grounds rather than on headline accuracy.

**S-097** [local_a22f97df] — *A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities*

Goal: to move beyond descriptive comparison of touchscreen motion features - which the group's own earlier work (Simeoli et al., 2020) had found insufficient to distinguish the groups significantly - by using a variational autoencoder to learn a low-dimensional latent distribution of movement, and then to interrogate that latent space to identify which kinematic features drive classification and at what values. The framing is explicitly dual: not merely a diagnostic classifier but 'a new quantitative method to assess ASD', with the theoretical grounding in embodied cognition and predictive coding and the claim that motor abnormality is an underrated defining feature of autism. Findings: task-level cross-validated accuracy 91.2% +/- 5.6%; a latent space in which the two groups occupy distinct, approximately Gaussian regions, with cleaner separation when participants are plotted as the mean of their 25 tasks than task by task; latent structure stable across initialisations up to rotation; and, from Monte Carlo perturbation of one feature at a time, the finding that sdSpeed, MaxAcceleration, MinAcceleration and sdAcceleration have the largest capacity to move a participant across the latent space and reverse their classification, while sdDC, MeanSpeed, MaxSpeed and MeanLength map preferentially into the TD region and are judged marginal. The fitted class densities give signed rules - higher MaxAcceleration and sdAcceleration, and lower MaxSpeed and MinAcceleration, increase the probability of ASD assignment - which the authors offer to clinicians as candidate threshold values.

**S-098** [local_c6853fe2] — *A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation*

Goal: to automate the judgement of response to name during real clinical ADOS-2 assessments, by combining automatic speech recognition (to timestamp the name calls) with human pose tracking (to measure shoulder rotation) and head pose estimation (to measure head yaw), and to show that adding body pose to the head-pose-only approach used in prior work improves agreement with clinicians. Three contributions are claimed: a four-camera multi-view capture rig; a 'Response to name Dataset' drawn from live ADOS-2 screening rather than a controlled laboratory protocol, with more natural child behaviour and an unrestricted number of accompanying parents; and the finding that combining shoulder rotation angle, head pose and response duration improves accuracy over pose alone. Findings: shoulder pose alone agreed with the clinician for 25 of 30 children (83.3%) and 104 of 109 calls (95.4%); adding head pose raised this to 28 of 30 (93.3%) and 107 of 109 (98.2%), with sensitivity 84.6% and specificity 100% under an inverted convention in which the 'positive' class is non-response. The two residual participant-level errors are diagnosed concretely: one child responded too slowly to accumulate the required 10 frames above the shoulder threshold and was also wearing a mask, which blocked the facial-landmark fallback; the other turned their head too fast for 8 frames of yaw to be detected. The score-level confusion matrix shows the modal outcome to be clinician 5 / predicted 5 in 17 children.

**S-099** [local_f1b626c8] — *Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games*

Goal: to classify autistic from non-autistic children by analysing eye-tracking data captured while they play a purpose-designed computer game, motivated explicitly by the shortage of diagnostic specialists relative to a growing autistic population and the wish for a system 'easily applicable by not-so-expert users'. The game was designed with expert guidance around two objectives drawn from picture-exchange practice: face recognition and facial-expression matching. Findings as reported: precision 76.6% and accuracy 73.8% with all 18 features, which the paper presents as the best of four nested feature subsets and describes as 'a suitable diagnostics system'. Findings as they should be read: those numbers are the TOTAL column of Table 5, pooling training, validation and test rows, and the held-out test values in the same table are precision 66.7%, accuracy 58.3%, sensitivity 57.1% and specificity 60.0% - between 6 and 10 points above a 50% chance level on 36 observations. Across all four feature subsets the pattern is identical and consistent: total accuracies of 65.0-73.8% concealing test accuracies of 52.8-58.3%, with training accuracies of 67.9-78.6%. The gap between training and test performance is present in every configuration and is never remarked on. Two subsets also show unstable held-out behaviour, with test sensitivity of 33.3% for 'around FIGs' and test specificity of 33.3% for 'on FIGs'.

**S-100** [local_6249bd63] — *Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior*

The stated goal is not primarily to build a better classifier but to answer a prior question the field has left open: how do AI predictions correspond to human ones? The framing is explicit and is the paper's organising logic - 'the utility of an AI algorithm would be negligible if it provides little information beyond what clinicians can readily infer' - so the study is designed as a benchmark rather than a demonstration. Nineteen raters (8 doctoral-level autism experts, 11 non-experts) and a computer-vision pipeline were given the same 3-minute silent videos of 42 adults in casual conversation. Findings: AI accuracy 80.5%, expert clinicians 83.1%, non-experts 78.3%, all humans 80.3% - so the model performs at approximately expert level on this evidence. The operating characteristics show why accuracy alone is misleading: PPV 0.86, NPV 0.79, specificity 0.95 and sensitivity 0.55, meaning the classifier is highly conservative and detects only just over half the autistic adults. The paper's real result is the error analysis. Of five participants misclassified by a majority of human raters, four were correctly classified by the model, including the hardest case, which only 21% of raters got right. Per-participant accuracy of humans and AI correlated at just rho = 0.35, falling to 0.19 once the participants nearly all raters got right are removed, and the lower-left quadrant of the scatter - hard for both - is essentially empty. Feature weights point to head pose and its coordination with eye movement, and to mouth-related coordination, as the dominant signal, with both categories over-represented in the top-weighted features relative to their share of the feature pool.

**S-101** [local_8b9e0e8a] — *Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas*

The goal is explicitly infrastructural rather than merely methodological: to build a screening method that works where the constraints are affordability, child-friendliness and the absence of professionals, which the authors identify as the three barriers to autism screening in remote areas. The technical contribution is the dynamic viewing pattern - gaze treated as an ordered trajectory over both viewing time and the stimulus set, rather than as a static distribution of fixations - together with a pipeline that encodes each fixation semantically via an autoencoder, scores each stimulus sequence with an LSTM, and aggregates 82 stimulus scores into a subject decision. Findings: subject-level accuracy 96.73% with sensitivity 96.85% and specificity 96.63% on 165 test children, stable above 95.76% across five random subject-level splits. The supporting analyses are more informative than the headline. Conventional hand-crafted features reproduce the expected group differences - autistic children make fewer fixations with longer saccades, look less at faces and other salient objects, take longer to notice them, and dwell more on background and on the grey mask - but the authors state plainly that these differences are 'not sufficiently significant to directly use these hand-crafted features for classification'. A time-delay embedding analysis then shows that between-group distance grows with the length of the pattern section used and with the number of stimuli included, and that for sections shorter than five fixations the within-autism variability exceeds the between-group difference - a quantitative argument that separability is manufactured by using more temporal and more stimulus context, not merely asserted. Ablation confirms both feature families contribute (semantic 94.85%, low-level 93.33%, combined 96.73%) and that sequence modelling beats fixation-histogram and stacked-fixation baselines.

**S-102** [local_0e476686] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts*

The stated objective is to build models 'capable of diagnosing ASD through the analysis of texts posted by users who disclose their condition in their biographies', motivated by the scarcity of specialists and the value of early diagnosis. Three contributions are claimed: a new Twitter dataset of 404,627 tweets from 252 users of whom 221 disclose autism; application of several machine-learning techniques to build predictive models; and comparison of classical machine learning against deep learning. Findings: BERT-base-multilingual-cased, used untuned, reached 84.3% accuracy and F1 0.84, outperforming XGBoost at 71.6% (F1 0.74), decision trees at 61.2% (F1 0.72) and k-nearest neighbours at 60.8% (F1 0.67), all three of which were hyperparameter-tuned by grid search. The authors present this as the paper's headline - that a default deep model beats optimised classical ones - and describe the result as 'quite astonishing'. The confusion matrices they report, to their credit, reveal more than the accuracies do: the decision tree produced 11,229 true positives against just 41 false negatives, meaning it labelled nearly every tweet autistic and achieved 99.6% sensitivity at 22.6% specificity - close to a degenerate classifier, which its 61.2% accuracy and 0.72 F1 conceal. BERT's counts correspond to sensitivity 82.1% and specificity 86.5%. No user-level result is reported for any model.

**S-103** [local_fbaf69bf] — *Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Three questions, stated as hypotheses in advance. Whether the complexity of facial landmark dynamics differentiates autistic from typically developing toddlers; whether that complexity is higher specifically in the eyebrow region, on the basis of prior work on eyebrow raising in this cohort, and the mouth region, on the basis of atypical vocalisation literature; and whether the complexity measure adds information beyond the group's own previously published affect-based analysis or merely duplicates it. Findings: autistic toddlers showed significantly higher multiscale entropy in both regions, with a clear social/non-social gradient - during social movies p < .0001 with large to very large effect sizes (r = .51-.82), during non-social movies still significant but only medium (r = .32-.40). Integrated entropy over the first 20 scales gave p < .00001 with large or very large effects for all social movies. Eyebrows and mouth did not differ from each other (p > .05, r < 0.1), so the hypothesis of regional specificity was not supported in the sense of one region dominating. The autistic group also showed a significantly wider range of integrated entropy across the six movies (eyebrows p = .001, r = .33; mouth p = .0002, r = .39), meaning their facial responsiveness varied more between contents. On the third question, correlations between integrated entropy and positive-affect energy were moderate for two movies and negligible for four, and adding affect to the classifier did not improve on entropy alone - while affect alone performed worse - so the measures are largely independent and the complexity measure is the more informative of the two. Classification with a decision tree on social movies gave 76.6-78.3% accuracy with entropy alone; logistic regression gave odds ratios up to 1.8 for entropy against 0.8 for affect.

**S-104** [local_74416ba7] — *Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders*

The stated aim is to test whether modelling the specificity of gaze to particular facial expressions improves classification, on the premise - supported by prior basic research but not previously operationalised - that groups differ in gaze for some emotions and not others. The proposal is to classify each of the 21 or 32 FEIT images separately and then aggregate the per-image decisions with a random forest that learns which images matter, rather than by unweighted voting. Findings, all reported with binomial tests against chance and none oversold. For autistic adults versus controls the weighted CNN reached 0.710 accuracy (sensitivity 0.733, specificity 0.688), significantly above chance and 10 points above the unweighted CNN. For autistic children the weighted models reached 0.667 (weighted CNN sensitivity 0.600, specificity 0.733), significant and 16.7 points above the unweighted CNN, with the weighting raising sensitivity from 0.286 to 0.600. For schizophrenia the best models reached 0.645, only marginally above chance (p = 0.052), and weighting produced no improvement at all. The statistical analysis explains why the method behaves differently across conditions and is the more interesting result: in adults, reduced fixation at the eyes distinguished the schizophrenia group from controls for every one of the seven emotions, but the autistic group from controls for only two (anger and neutral), while scan-path length distinguished autism from controls for six of seven emotions. So the classic reduced-eye-looking signature was present uniformly in schizophrenia and only selectively in autism - which is exactly the condition under which per-image weighting helps for one and not the other. In children, almost no gaze feature reached significance at all, yet the weighted models still exceeded chance.

**S-105** [local_7c6a5aa4] — *Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders*

Two goals, and the paper is clearer about the first than the second. The first is to demonstrate that the dense telemetry generated by digital AAC systems is worth analysing at all, which the authors argue has been almost entirely neglected: 'with the exception of one prior report, no efforts have been made to use the dense streams of data collected by digital AACs to derive insights of clinical importance'.
