The second is the classification question, posed precisely and unusually well: 'can we distinguish individuals with ASD from individuals without ASD (but who have need for AAC systems), based solely on patterns of use?' - the parenthesis matters, because it commits the study to a differential rather than an autism-versus-typical contrast. Findings: conventional usage statistics separate nothing. Session length was 2.14 versus 2.10 minutes (p = 0.86), word selects per use 5.6 versus 4.31 (p = 0.166) and word-select frequency 2.99 versus 2.28 per minute (p = 0.147), none significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction, and the authors present this explicitly as motivation for more advanced modelling. The prior analysis of the same data reached 47-61% across sequential, temporal and spectral views - sequential SVM peaking at 58% at window size 40, temporal at 60%, spectral at 61% with LogitBoost - which is at or barely above chance. Accuracy rose to 70% with sequential modelling only after k-means pseudo-labelling enlarged the training set, and to 82% in the present study with stacked autoencoders at window size 40. Descriptively the study also reports that use spanned the whole lifespan with heaviest engagement among under-10s, that autistic users had the highest average number of app accesses, and that the commonest phrases concerned food, sleep, sport and greetings.

**S-106** [local_8a706eaa] — *Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Two objectives, both clinically framed. First, to train deep learning models to distinguish autism from typical development using video of joint attention behaviours; second, to differentiate autism symptom severity from the same data. The motivating argument is precise and is worth recording because it diagnoses the corpus's own problems: prior video-based models are said to be unsuitable for tool development 'due to a lack of automation, the requirements for specialized and expensive equipment, calibration, trained personnel, dependence on human rating of autistic behaviors, and low precision and recall', and the authors attribute that low precision and recall to 'a lack of targeted behavioral biomarkers that can readily discriminate ASD from TD' and to the absence of methods for quantitatively measuring hallmark autism behaviours. Their response is to instrument an existing validated clinical construct rather than to search for a statistical signature. Findings: detection AUROC of 99.6% for IJA, 99.8% for low-level RJA and 99.5% for high-level RJA, with accuracy 97.6-98.8% and confidence intervals throughout. Severity prediction was markedly lower and task-ordered: IJA 90.3% AUROC, low-level RJA 84.4%, high-level RJA 84.2%, with precision falling to 68.6% for high-level RJA. The IJA advantage for severity is interpreted substantively - initiation reflects motivation to share attention and so captures nuance that responsiveness tasks miss - and is corroborated by the cluster maps, where IJA attention-weight trajectories separate the three severity classes more cleanly than the RJA ones. The compliance analysis adds a behavioural finding independent of the models: both groups habituated after ten IJA or five RJA repetitions, but autistic children showed comparable initial interest to comparison children in IJA before declining, while showing 'contrasting uninterest in the social cue presented at the beginning of RJA tasks'.

**S-107** [local_6b9484ce] — *Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking*

The stated aim is to use eye-tracking scanpath images 'as a biological indicator to identify children with autism' and to compare a transfer-learning-plus-classical-classifier pipeline against an end-to-end custom CNN. Findings: the custom CNN reached 71.9% accuracy, InceptionV3 features with logistic regression 78.9%, and InceptionV3 features with an MLP 81.0%. The per-class analysis is the substantive result and the authors present it properly rather than resting on accuracy. The custom CNN's confusion matrix shows 30 of 34 typically developing images correct against only 11 of 23 autism images - class-wise recall of 0.88 versus 0.48, F1 of 0.79 versus 0.58 - so a model reported at 71.9% accuracy is in fact detecting fewer than half the autism cases, and the authors say so: its 'ability to classify the people affected by ASD was not upto the mark'. The transfer-learning models are markedly more balanced, with class-wise F1 of 0.82/0.75 for logistic regression and 0.84/0.76 for the MLP, and the authors conclude on that basis rather than on the accuracy difference alone. The conclusion attributes the modest overall performance to the small dataset and proposes augmentation and dataset expansion.

**S-108** [local_c6a4ea7b] — *SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism*

The stated objectives are threefold: to automatically extract semantic and pragmatic language features including echolalia, semantic coherence and repetitive language usage; to compare them systematically and identify the most significant; and to build an interpretable assessment system on that basis. The gap the paper identifies in the literature is specific and fair - prior work on semantic-pragmatic features for autism has examined individual measures such as echolalia or pronoun usage in isolation, and 'the cumulative effect of the features and how they complement the lexical, syntactic and other text-based features in the diagnosis of autism has not been analysed'. Findings: the best classifier, an RBF SVM on all 63 retained features, reached 94.1% accuracy with 94% macro F1 against a majority-classifier baseline of 56.4% accuracy and 32% macro F1. The feature-set ablation is the substantive result and is reported in full: morphosyntactic baseline 70.59%, syntactic complexity alone 70%, part-of-speech frequencies alone 82%, semantic-pragmatic features alone 82.3%, part-of-speech plus semantic-pragmatic 88.2%, and all three families 94.1%. So the semantic-pragmatic set matches the lexical set on its own and the three families are complementary rather than redundant, which is exactly the claim the study set out to test. SHAP attribution places the number of distinct word roots first, with unexpected words and both child-child and child-partner discourse coherence in the top ten, and the authors relate each to prior findings on vocabulary extent and on global coherence in autistic conversation.

**S-109** [local_5c43dffa] — *Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths*

The stated objective is to test whether scan-path images - spatial representations of gaze - can stratify autism from typical development, and then whether they also capture the age and sex variation that makes autism biomarkers hard to generalise. The two contributions claimed are incorporating temporal information into scan-path images and infusing gaze velocity into them. Findings, in the paper's own summary order: spatial scan-paths separate autism from typical development at 74.4% test accuracy (AUC 0.68-0.72); scan-paths separate 2-4 year old from 10-17 year old autistic children at 80.5% (AUC 0.868); scan-paths separate male from female autistic children at 78.0% (AUC 0.850); and within the 5-9 year autistic subgroup they separate male from female at 98.8%. Temporal windowing shows the first three seconds of viewing discriminate best (76.3%) with a monotone decline to 70.2% by 12-15 seconds. Velocity-based colour coding raises the 3-6 second window from 71.74% to 80.25% (AUC 0.839), the paper's headline representational result. Per-clip ablation ranks the contribution of individual videos, with Theory of Mind and Dyadic Bid clips mattering most. The authors read the age and sex results as evidence that scan-paths capture heterogeneity; they can equally be read as evidence that the diagnostic result is confounded, since the two groups differ substantially on both variables.

**S-110** [local_32da8ede] — *A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths*

The stated aim is to build an enhanced convolutional deep network for autism identification from eye-tracking scan-path images, with an explicit methodological claim distinguishing it from prior work: 'we addressed the issue of working with a dataset containing a small number of images without utilizing augmentation. Whereas many earlier studies depended on augmenting image data to improve outcomes, we maintained the original image count and achieved superior performance.' That is a defensible and welcome position, since augmentation on a 547-image corpus split at image level compounds dependence between training and test data, as another study in this corpus demonstrates directly. Findings: 95.59% accuracy for greyscale images with two hidden layers of 300 and 150 neurons, kernel size 3, stride 1, Adam optimiser and 20% dropout; 94.69% with colour. Comparators on the same data reach 61.3% for k-nearest neighbours, 67.7% for decision tree, 69.60% for random forest and 94.69% for a multilayer perceptron. Optimiser choice dominates everything else: Adam and Nadam give 81-95%, RMSprop and AdaMax 85-94%, while SGD and Adadelta collapse to 56-62% - a 35-point spread that indicates the result is highly sensitive to optimisation rather than robustly present in the data. The decisive problem is that the same results table reports sensitivity 77.60% and specificity 79.91% alongside the 95.59% accuracy, and those three figures cannot describe the same classifier: with 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images they imply an accuracy near 79%.

**S-111** [local_15ed96cb] — *A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning*

The aim is to build and evaluate a machine learning model predicting later autism diagnosis from routinely collected well-baby records, so that providers can be alerted during ordinary checkups to administer an autism-specific screening tool - the Israeli protocol containing none. Findings: average test AUC 0.86 (SD 0.009) with sensitivity 0.75 and specificity 0.81, against a training AUC of 0.88 that the authors flag as indicating slight overfitting. At the Youden threshold, 18.6% of the cohort (144,632 children) were classified high risk, capturing 874 of 1,163 cases - an autism incidence of 0.006 in that group against 0.001 in the cohort, a 4.3-fold enrichment. The seven most important milestone predictors, all confirmed by independent Fisher's exact tests at p < 0.001, are strikingly ordinary clinical observations: vocabulary over ten words, building a tower from cubes, giving a kiss, eating independently with a spoon, knowing at least one body part, composing two-word sentences and saying 2-3 words. Four are language milestones, two personal-social, one fine motor, and all fall between 12 and 24 months. Other key predictors are male sex, parental developmental concern, non-nursing, older maternal age, lower gestational age and atypical growth percentiles. The most instructive result is the method comparison: logistic regression achieved exactly the same AUC of 0.86 with marginally better sensitivity (0.77 versus 0.75), random forest 0.84 and naive Bayes 0.83 - so gradient boosting gained nothing over a linear model on 59 features, which bears directly on the assumption running through this corpus that model sophistication is where performance comes from.

**S-112** [local_261afa51] — *AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: &#x201C;A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System&#x201D;*

The aim is an AI-powered mobile application that identifies autistic children from facial photographs, combined with a facial expression recognition module, intended for use by families and psychiatrists. Findings: MobileNet reached 95% validation accuracy with sensitivity 0.97 and specificity 0.93, alongside 100% training accuracy; Xception 94% (sensitivity 0.92, specificity 0.95); InceptionV3 89% (sensitivity 0.95, specificity 0.83). The expression module reports precision 0.988 and mAP50 0.991 for the proposed variant - against 0.992 and 0.99 for the smallest YOLOv8 baseline, so the proposed model is marginally worse than the lightest comparator on its own task, a result the paper presents as demonstrating 'a good balance of accuracy and efficiency'. The two modules are never combined, tested against each other, or shown to inform one another, despite the paper's claim to provide 'a more complete picture of a child's condition'. What no result in the paper addresses is what the autism classifier is responding to. Given that the two image classes were assembled from different internet sources, the reported accuracy is consistent with a model that has learned to distinguish autism-website photographs from general internet photographs, and no analysis in the paper can rule that out.

**S-113** [local_3e88f3ce] — *An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks*

The stated aim is an interpretable, personalised multimodal framework that combines structured behavioural phenotypes with structural MRI, addressing what the authors identify as two gaps in prior work: the absence of principled fusion strategies and insufficient attention to explainability and personalisation. The architecture is genuinely thoughtful - GAMI-Net for transparent additive modelling of tabular clinical data, a CNN-GNN pair to capture both voxel-level structure and inter-region relationships over the Harvard-Oxford atlas, an autoencoder to fuse into a shared 32-dimensional space rather than concatenating naively, and a hypernetwork generating subject-specific classifier weights so that decision boundaries adapt per individual. Reported results are 99.40% accuracy, 100% precision, 98.84% recall and 99.99% ROC-AUC on a held-out split, and 98.56% accuracy with 99.62% ROC-AUC under five-fold stratified cross-validation. The explainability analysis identifies ADOS_TOTAL and ADOS_Gotham_Total as the dominant predictors. Read together, these findings say that a model given the diagnostic instrument scores reproduces the diagnosis nearly perfectly, which is what one would expect and which the architecture's sophistication does not alter. The paper's own contributions section states a different and lower figure - 96.4% accuracy and AUC 0.92 - that is not reconciled with the abstract anywhere.

**S-114** [local_5b5f2237] — *Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development*

Two objectives: to quantify interpersonal motor coordination, described as 'an omnipresent yet least studied behavioral characteristic in ASD', and to test whether coordination features can classify autistic from typically developing children. The methodological rationale for cross wavelet analysis is stated explicitly and is the paper's reason for existing: the group's earlier analysis of these same recordings used complexity matching to quantify overall coordination across the conversation and 'failed to find significant differences in IMC between the ASD and TD children', whereas cross wavelet analysis resolves coordination at separate movement frequencies and so 'could provide a more detailed picture', while also generating many candidate features for classification. Findings: coherence was significantly lower in the autistic group at six of 23 time scales, all at the faster end (0.1-0.9 s), with both groups exceeding the pseudo-pair chance level, so real coordination was occurring in both and differed in degree. Classification on original coherence features reached 85.37% (specificity 95.24%, sensitivity 75.00%) with five features, of which four were among the significantly different ones. Constructing 57 derived features by summing subsets of the six significant coherences raised the best result to 92.68% (specificity 95.24%, sensitivity 90.00%) with a decision tree using three of them. The specificity is identical across both conditions, so the whole improvement is a rise in sensitivity from 75% to 90% - three additional autistic children out of twenty.

**S-115** [local_13426811] — *Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning*

The study begins from a specific and well-evidenced clinical problem rather than from a technical opportunity: ADOS-2, the gold standard, has documented limitations for adolescents and adults, because it does not clearly separate autism from ADHD or from the negative symptoms of schizophrenia and other psychiatric comorbidities, and because masking, compensation and camouflaging can conceal impairment. The proposed remedy is a comprehensive mapping of pragmatic impairment through lexicogrammatical analysis, which the authors note has not previously been attempted - prior linguistic work examined single grammatical areas such as modality, relative clauses or syntax, leaving 'the overall picture of the impairment... uncharted'. Findings: on interview transcripts the combined text-plus-tag Bi-LSTM reached 0.82 accuracy (95% CI 0.75-0.89) with AUC 0.90 under automatic annotation, and 0.80 (0.73-0.87) with sensitivity 0.73 and specificity 0.87 under manual annotation. The tag-only linear model reached 0.78 and the text-only model 0.80, and McNemar tests found no significant differences between them on the interview task. The substantive result is the task contrast: every model performed better on interviews than on picture-book recounting, where the linear model fell to 0.60-0.64 and the best model reached 0.78. The authors interpret this as evidence that the discriminative signal lies in socially interactive language use rather than in narrative production generally, which is exactly what a pragmatic-impairment account predicts and is a stronger form of evidence than a single accuracy figure.

**S-116** [local_948fa8d0] — *Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms*

The stated aim is to improve autism detection accuracy from facial images by combining transfer-learned deep features with handcrafted image descriptors, and to identify the best classifier and feature combination. Findings: handcrafted features alone gave 78.0-84.5% across five classifiers, with random forest best; adding ResNet features raised the range to 84.4-90.2%, with SVM best; and adding Inception features gave 83.2-94.6%, with SVM best at 94.6%. The reported progression - handcrafted alone, then fused with each backbone - is a systematic ablation and is the paper's substantive content. What it cannot establish is what the improvement means, because no evaluation protocol is stated: the words 'split' and 'validation' appear nowhere, no cross-validation is described, and no train-test partition is specified for any of the eighteen reported accuracies. Whether these are held-out figures, training figures, or something else is not determinable from the paper.

**S-117** [local_893dfc22] — *Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed*

The stated aim is to improve recognition of altered facial expressions in autistic people, on the argument that conventional systems misread the nuanced cues that autistic faces produce - a real and under-addressed problem, and the strongest idea in the paper. The executed work is six-way emotion classification on KDEF and CK+, reporting 99.8% accuracy, 99.8% precision, 100% recall and 94% specificity, with significance tests against CNN, linear SVM and k-nearest-neighbour baselines at p < 0.01. The gap between the two is the study's defining feature. The paper's own introduction supplies the reason the executed task cannot address the stated aim, observing that 'research indicates a lack of studies utilizing static or dynamic facial stimuli displaying real, spontaneous emotions' and that 'staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones' - after which the evaluation uses only staged emotions from instructed adult volunteers. A separate study charted in this review tests the transfer question directly and finds that affect models trained on neurotypical faces perform poorly on autistic children and improve substantially only after fine-tuning on autistic data, which is the evidence this study would have needed and did not seek.

**S-118** [local_e7c16f2a] — *Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification*

Two objectives, both methodological rather than clinical. First, to test whether raw motion trajectories alone - unprocessed x and y coordinates - carry enough information to classify autistic from typically developing children, or whether derived kinematic features are needed; the comparison is motivated by the group's own prior work, which had found that maximum and minimum acceleration and standard deviations of speed and acceleration were the leading contributors in a feature-based model. Second, to test the specific role of acceleration by generating synthetic trajectories with systematically varied acceleration and observing how the models respond. Findings: the four-feature model reached 0.90 accuracy against 0.76 for the two-feature model, with a consistently higher fold-wise distribution and a better ROC curve, so derived features help substantially. But the simulation analysis complicates the simple reading: acceleration correlated with the two-feature model's predictions at r = 0.69 despite that model never receiving acceleration as an input, and with the four-feature model's at r = 0.82, both at p < 0.001 over 932 samples, with higher acceleration increasing the probability of an autism prediction in both. So the information is present in the raw coordinate sequence and the four-feature representation makes it easier to use rather than supplying something new - a conclusion the authors reach and state, writing that their findings 'support the potential of raw data analysis in objectively assessing motor behaviors related to autism' while the four-feature model 'excels'.

**S-119** [local_5a7ab52d] — *Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain*

The stated aim is a detection model for autism and visual sensory processing disorder that combines facial expression data with heart rate and body temperature, using a purpose-designed hybrid optimisation algorithm to select features and tune network parameters. Findings: the proposed method reached 96.44886% accuracy, 96.2963% sensitivity, 96.50485% specificity and 91% precision. Four metaheuristic comparators using the identical network architecture clustered within one percentage point (95.45-95.74%), and four conventional classifiers were substantially lower (81.5-86.6%). The tight clustering of the metaheuristic variants is the most interpretable result in the paper: it indicates that the choice among optimisation algorithms contributes about one accuracy point while the network architecture contributes about ten, which somewhat undercuts the paper's central claim that the novel optimiser is the contribution. Against this, the results cannot be evaluated because the dataset on which they were computed is never described, and the two accounts of the validation scheme - a variable learning-percentage split illustrated at 65/35, and 5-fold cross-validation defined among the evaluation measures - are not reconciled or tied to the reported figures.

**S-120** [local_8253c2ec] — *Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder*

The stated aim is to improve the precision and speed of early autism diagnosis by optimising one-dimensional convolutional networks with the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator across four age-specific datasets, and to deploy the result as an interactive diagnostic tool. The methodological argument is coherent and specific: prior work on these datasets relied on predefined hyperparameters or on exhaustive grid search, which the authors correctly characterise as 'computation-intensive and inefficient', and an adaptive Bayesian alternative is a sensible remedy. The result reported is 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC-ROC in every age band, attributed to the optimisation. The alternative explanation is complete and requires nothing of the model: the class label in these datasets is the summed item score thresholded at the instrument's cut-off, the items are among the inputs, and the sum itself is among the tabulated fields, so the model is being asked to reproduce a deterministic function of its own predictors. On that reading the baseline models' shortfall reflects optimisation difficulty rather than any information limit, and the optimised models' perfection reflects the arithmetic. The paper's own literature review is consistent with this: it tabulates the subliterature at 97.15% to 100% on these datasets, and notes one comparator - using physical fitness tests, brain scans and severity assessments on recruited participants - reaching 77.99%, roughly twenty-two points lower.

**S-121** [local_1e9d0b71] — *Machine learning’s effectiveness*

The aim is to test whether machine-learning analysis of movement during the one-legged standing test can identify five-year-olds with high autistic traits, motivated by a specific timing gap: autism can be detected at 14 months and diagnosed reliably by two years, yet over 70% of affected children are not diagnosed until after 51 months, so screening before elementary school entry is needed. Balance is chosen because prior behavioural work reports that autistic children show smaller centre-of-pressure shift, more repetitive centre-of-pressure patterns and less complex postural control in both static and dynamic states, and because the one-legged standing test is already a standard clinical assessment - so the measurement can be added to a routine examination at essentially no cost. Findings: accuracy, sensitivity and specificity all reached 1.000 for the study's proposed variable set (correlations between centre-of-pressure and shoulder, right trunk and right knee angles) and for the combined set, while the conventional variable set based on prior literature performed less well on accuracy and sensitivity though it also achieved specificity of 1.000. SHAP attribution identified shoulder, hip and trunk as the dominant contributors. And SRS-2 total correlated positively with predicted probability across all three variable sets. The substantive claim is therefore not that balance differs in magnitude but that the coordination between upper body and the shifting base of support differs - the conventional sway measures are the weaker predictors and the novel correlation measures are what produce the separation.

**S-122** [local_b9e05a8f] — *Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network*

The stated aim is to improve facial-image-based autism detection by combining squeeze-and-excitation channel attention, multiscale feature fusion and convolutional networks with automated hyperparameter search using the white shark optimisation algorithm, motivated by four claimed gaps in prior work: limited modelling of long-range dependencies by CNNs, insufficient local inductive bias when images are treated as token sequences, weak interpretability, and inadequate splitting strategies. The headline finding is 95.36% accuracy, 92.62% precision and 95.5% F1 - a triple that is arithmetically consistent with a recall of 98.6% and a specificity of 92.2% at the reported 1:1 ratio, which is worth noting because internal inconsistency is common in this branch. Three secondary findings carry more weight than the headline. The ablation shows that the paper's own multiscale fusion contribution reduces accuracy relative to squeeze-and-excitation alone when the hyperparameter search is removed (0.85 against 0.89), and the authors state this plainly rather than burying it. The leakage investigation on the video-derived corpus found a maximum training-test cosine similarity of 0.9714 before intervention, which is direct evidence that naive frame-level splitting of that dataset - the standard practice in the papers it is drawn from - leaks. And bidirectional cross-dataset evaluation reached 89-90%, which the paper presents as robustness and which is better read as evidence that whatever the model has learned is common to two corpora built by the same web-scraping principle.

**S-123** [local_0b0960c4] — *Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]*

The aim is to compare a broader range of neural architectures on EEG-derived features than prior work has done, on the argument that existing studies have explored a limited set of models and feature combinations. Four architectures were fitted to eleven linear and non-linear time- and frequency-domain features: a custom neural network reached 94.02% accuracy, an LSTM 93.83%, a deep neural network 91.98% and a convolutional network 89.02%, with precision, recall, specificity and F1 reported for each. The comparison is even-handed and includes the lowest performer rather than only the winner. What the study cannot establish is what those figures mean. With 17 participants the accuracies must have been computed over EEG epochs rather than people, no validation scheme of any kind is described, and with four control children a participant-disjoint evaluation would leave at most one control in any held-out set. The paper's own comparison table is the most useful thing in it for this review, and its pattern is discussed below.

**S-124** [local_abad69fd] — *Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play*

The aim was to measure functional and imaginative play together with other core autistic traits during a brief free play task, characterise the group differences, and build from them a clinical prediction model capable of screening children aged 1 to 6 - explicitly extending prior work that had examined play behaviours alone. Directional hypotheses were stated in advance, including the prediction that repetitive behaviour frequency would not differ between groups because the session would be too short for it to emerge. The findings: autistic children showed less functional and less imaginative play, and reduced eye contact, facial expression and vocalisation. Restricted and repetitive behaviours did not separate the groups, exactly as predicted - the reported odds ratios for stereotyped language use, repetitive hand and body movements and unusual sensory seeking are numerically enormous with confidence intervals spanning zero to infinity and p-values near 1, the signature of behaviours almost never observed in a 90-second window. Stepwise regression retained five predictors, all in the protective direction: duration of socially oriented vocalisations (OR 0.940), total counts of functional play (OR 0.639), and play time with miniature or representational toys (OR 0.985), cause-and-effect toys (OR 0.973) and construction toys (OR 0.958). The nomogram reached AUC 0.826 (95% CI 0.776-0.877) with sensitivity 85.4% and specificity 68.3% at a cut-off of 0.399. The confirmed negative prediction about repetitive behaviour is worth as much as the positive findings: it demonstrates that the task samples the social-communication and play dimensions of the phenotype and not the restricted-repetitive dimension, which bounds what any model built on it can claim to detect.

**S-125** [local_cd7545e2] — *Predictive model using autism*

The aim was to identify similarities and differences in the symptoms of schizophrenia and autism, establish a more objective method of differential diagnosis, and characterise autistic features in schizophrenia - motivated by a clinical problem the introduction sets out at length: the two conditions co-occur, cluster in families, share genetic risk and produce overlapping presentations, while the features that distinguish them (the content and duration of delusions, self-disturbance, developmental timing) are precisely the ones that become unavailable when verbal expression is poor, when symptoms are concealed, or when a high-functioning autistic adult's characteristics did not surface until adolescence. The findings answer that question in three parts. The ADOS-2's own algorithms failed: 45.0% and 52.5% of the schizophrenia group screened positive on the original and revised algorithms, AUCs were 0.562 and 0.569, and no domain score of either algorithm carried significant predictive value. An item-level model built on six items - A7 reporting of events, A10 emphatic or emotional gestures, B1 unusual eye contact, B6 comments on others' emotions or empathy, B8 responsibility, B9 quality of social overtures - reached apparent accuracy 86.6% and AUC 0.938, significantly outperforming both algorithms by DeLong's test, but dropped to 65.3% under holdout validation. And the autistic-looking features in schizophrenia proved to be negative symptoms: ADOS-2 scores correlated with the PANSS negative scale, cut-off-positive patients had higher negative-symptom scores than cut-off-negative patients, and cut-off positivity was predicted by the negative scale alone. The negative finding is the durable one. The positive finding is a promising direction whose own validation shows it is not yet ready.

**S-126** [local_3ecb92bf] — *The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech*

The aim is to test whether deep transfer learning can compensate for the scarcity of labelled child speech data in autism recognition, by comparing two fine-tuning strategies - discriminative fine-tuning pre-trained on a related child corpus, and Wav2Vec 2.0 fine-tuning pre-trained on 960 hours of unrelated adult speech - across a binary typicality task and a four-class diagnosis task, with fairness testing by gender. The findings are best read against the study's own comparison tables, which the authors supply. On binary typicality, D-FT reached 94.8% unweighted average recall and W2V2-FT 91.5%, against a stated baseline of 94.1% and prior published results of 90.7% and 93.6% on the same corpus - an improvement of 0.7 points over baseline. On four-class diagnosis, D-FT reached 60.9% and W2V2-FT 54.3%, against a baseline of 62.4% and prior results of 67.1% and 69.4% - so both proposed models fall below the baseline and below prior work on the task that actually requires separating autism from other conditions. And the fairness analysis shows that the binary headline does not survive subgroup evaluation: D-FT sensitivity falls from 94.8% on the mixed-gender test set to 43.6% on the female set and 61.5% on the male, with W2V2-FT falling from 92.3% to 24.4% and 53.8%. Publishing a benchmark table showing one's own model below baseline on the harder task, and a fairness table showing a fifty-point sensitivity collapse, is a level of candour this review has encountered in very few papers.

**S-127** [local_4b02df7c] — *Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism*

The stated objective was 'to study the feasibility of autism screening from Twitter data and discuss the ethical implications of such models' - the ethics being a co-equal aim from the outset rather than an appended caveat, which is unique in this corpus. The technical finding is modest and honestly reported: a tweet-level classifier reached 73% accuracy, AUC 0.728 and F1 0.71 using word2vec representations with logistic regression, and a user-profile classifier reached AUC 0.78 and F1 0.805 using an attention-based bidirectional LSTM. Aggregating a user's full timeline improved discrimination over single tweets, as expected if the signal is a property of a writer rather than of a post. Exploratory analysis found that sentiment polarity was nearly unchanged between the raw and profanity-censored corpora, and that autism-related discussion rose across 2014-2022. The conclusion the authors actually draw is not about accuracy: having demonstrated feasibility, they restrict the legitimate use of such models to 'a broader cross-sectional level' rather than individual prediction, enumerate the misuse scenarios the artefact would enable, delete the data and the models, and caution researchers against building comparable systems without explicit consent and participatory community-centred design. That is the study's contribution and it is a real one.

**S-128** [local_7d7f1fcc] — *Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children*

The aim is broad automated screening rather than detection of a single symptom, achieved by combining two neural networks trained on the video and audio channels of the same semi-standardised assessment, and by then asking which clinical features each modality is sensitive to. The performance findings are modest and are not oversold: video alone 80.0% accuracy on the held-out 80 children, audio alone 78.8%, and the best ensemble 82.5% with sensitivity 0.775 and specificity 0.875. Alternative combination rules trade these off - an OR rule reaching sensitivity 0.90 at specificity 0.75, an AND rule reaching specificity 0.925 at sensitivity 0.60 - and the authors present all five variants in one table rather than only the best. The fusion result is honestly negative in the accuracy sense and the authors say so, identifying 'the inability of the simple ensemble model to outperform the individual modalities' as an important limitation; what fusion does provide is complementary errors, with both networks simultaneously wrong on only 8.75% of cases, and operating-point control. The more interesting findings are interpretive. Video confidence tracks initiation of joint attention, quality of social overtures, unusual eye contact and pointing gestures - a coherent nonverbal social-communication cluster. Audio confidence tracks showing behaviour, pointing, unusual sensory exploration and hand mannerisms - which are not vocal constructs, leading the authors to propose that ambient non-vocal sound from object manipulation contributed to the audio classification, and to note prior evidence that examiners' prosody adapts to child severity such that a full-band model may partly be reading the adult. Those two admissions are the study's most valuable output for this review.

**S-129** [local_5a331ffe] — *Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning*

Two aims are pursued in one pipeline: classify autism from face images, then estimate continuous affect in the identified autistic children, with a view to a longitudinal monitoring platform. The autism classification result is modest and stable - 74.5% accuracy with F1 73.7% and recall 73.2% at a 10% test split, 74.8% at 20%, and 75.2% under 5-fold cross-validation. The affect results are where the substance lies and they are structured as a genuine comparison across conditions: 93.7-98.4% for discrete affect on laboratory-controlled CK+, falling to 57.3-62.2% on in-the-wild AffectNet, with continuous-affect concordance correlations on AffectNet of 0.342-0.513 for arousal and 0.373-0.661 for valence. The finding the paper is built around, and the one worth carrying into the synthesis, is the transfer result: a model trained solely on AffectNet - neurotypical faces - performs poorly on autistic children, while fine-tuning it on the newly annotated autistic data produces 'noticeably superior outcomes', leading the authors to conclude that 'it is preferable to have a dataset where the data obtained relates to ASD children and not neurotypical subjects, specifically, when the task is to predict the values for valence and arousal'. That is an empirical demonstration that affect-recognition tools built on neurotypical populations do not transfer to autistic faces, which has direct implications for every deployed emotion-recognition system and for the several studies in this corpus that apply generic affect models to autistic children.

**S-130** [local_45ef7022] — *A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features*

The aim is a framework for continuous thermal monitoring of autistic children that classifies severity and thereby informs psychiatric medication dosing, motivated by the argument that the ABC's brief administration cannot capture daily behavioural variation and that imprecise dosing risks adverse effects the paper lists as including cardiac arrest, kidney failure, irregular heartbeats and high blood pressure. Three results are reported. The denoising pipeline, combining a non-decimated wavelet transform with a DnCNN, outperformed comparison filters on PSNR and SSIM. The DN-FME facial-mood network reached 96.39% accuracy across five categories - neutral, anger, sadness, fear, happiness - with two properly conducted ablations showing dropout at 0.2 outperforming 0.5 (0.9639 against 0.9521) and batch normalisation adding four points (0.9639 against 0.9378). And the severity classifiers reached 98.33% for Random Forest and SVM with AUCs of 0.9878 and 0.9865, against 90.00% for KNN. The paper then reports that its classifiers outperform the clinical ABC method and presents a severity-to-dosage mapping. The engineering components are competently executed and reported; the clinical components rest on labels of unstated origin, an image-level split that allows the classifiers to identify individual children, and a comparison against a clinical standard that is very likely the source of the labels themselves.

**S-131** [local_0f5a351e] — *Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

The stated aim is to evaluate deep transfer-learning architectures for distinguishing autistic from non-autistic children from facial images, motivated by the cost and delay of conventional assessment and by the premise that autism has a distinct facial phenotype. Results: Inception-V3 98% accuracy, VGG-19 97%, ResNet50 96%, each with per-class precision and recall of 96-98% and confusion matrices on 588 evaluation samples. Two internal inconsistencies bear on how these should be read. The abstract names ResNet50, Inception-V3 and VGG-19 with Inception-V3 best; the introduction names 'ResNet, VGG16, and VGG19' and states that VGG19 achieved the superior 98%, contradicting the paper's own results tables. And all three result tables are headed 'Validation results', with the confusion matrices described as validation-stage - so the headline figures come from the partition used for model selection, while the 10% test partition defined in the methods is never reported on. The paper's own comparison table places this subliterature at 80.05% to 96% across ten prior studies on the same corpus, so a 98% validation figure sits above every published test figure for the same data.

**S-132** [local_786b6280] — *Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features*

The stated aim is to compare classical machine learning against deep learning for autism detection from linguistic features, using more than one data source and paying attention to how features differ across age and sex - three gaps the paper identifies in prior work, the second of which ('all previous studies based their research on a single data source') is a fair criticism of much of this literature. Findings: the convolutional network reached 84% accuracy and the multilayer perceptron 83%, against 77-80% for logistic regression, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbours and random forests, and roughly ten points lower for Gaussian naive Bayes; mean length of utterance was the top-ranked feature for both models that supply importances, confirming one prior study and contradicting another on total number of words; and the demographic analysis found MLU rising with age, a reversal of the sex gap between the 3-4 and 5-6 bands, and a sex-by-diagnosis interaction on mean length of turn. The performance figures are modest, honestly reported, and benchmarked against three prior studies at 70-80%, which places them in a credible range for this task and in sharp contrast to the 95-100% figures elsewhere in this review. What the study cannot establish is what the models detect: its leading feature is a developmental language index, no independent language measure exists, and the age composition of the two groups is unreported.

**S-133** [local_879ec69b] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning*

The aim is to optimise a dual-stream skeleton architecture for autism detection, replacing the vision transformer of a prior design with a convolutional backbone to test whether CNN-based models capture gesture features effectively, and comparing MSG3D against a Stack Transformer in the temporal stream. The headline results are 95.4% on the Gait Fullbody Dataset and 70.19% on DREAM. The more informative findings are in the ablation tables. Across six image backbones the Gait results span 93.2% to 95.4% and the DREAM results 68.92% to 70.19% - so architecture choice moves accuracy by around two points on one dataset and one point on the other, while the gap between the two datasets is 25 points. That is a clean demonstration that in this branch the data determine performance and the model barely matters, which is a useful corrective to a literature organised around architectural novelty. The paper also reports that substituting a Stack Transformer for MSG3D lowered accuracy, and it reports its own reference implementation (ViT-B at 94.8%) alongside the alternatives rather than only the winner. What the study does not establish is what the 25-point gap means: the two corpora differ in sensor generation, joint coverage (25 full-body against 10 upper-body), task (walking against robot-assisted therapy), label structure (autism versus typical against two autism-related classes) and splitting unit (child against sample), and no analysis separates these.

**S-134** [local_93e5d23d] — *Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]*

Two aims: to identify acoustic differences between autistic and typically developing children's cries, and to test whether deep learning can classify them. The statistical result is coherent and physiologically interpretable - significantly higher jitter (p < 0.01) and shimmer (p < 0.01) and significantly lower harmonics-to-noise ratio (p < 0.0001) in the autistic group, which together describe greater cycle-to-cycle instability in both pitch and amplitude and a noisier, less periodic voice signal, consistent with less stable laryngeal and respiratory control. The direction replicates prior cry work the authors cite. The classification result was 90.28% accuracy with AUC 90.83%, sensitivity and specificity both 88.64%, precision 95.12% and F-score 91.75%. The two halves of the study are of very different evidential weight. The acoustic comparison is a straightforward group contrast on prespecified clinical measures and stands or falls on the confounds - age, recording setting, cry cause - none of which is adjusted. The classification figure additionally rests on a validation-set maximum selected across 2,000 epochs with no held-out test partition and no participant-level splitting, so it carries essentially no information about performance on a new child, and the paper does not connect the network's behaviour to the interpretable acoustic features it identified.

**S-135** [local_a0d73248] — *Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm*

The stated aim is to improve autism prediction with a Bayesian-optimised Random Forest, motivated by the subjectivity and slowness of conventional assessment. The reported result is 0.9890 accuracy, described as highly promising and as providing 'recommendations for a verified diagnostic technique when implemented'. The alternative explanation is complete: the class variable is the summed AQ-10 item score thresholded at the instrument's cut-off, the ten items are inputs, and the sum itself is printed among the study's own feature list with no removal step described - so the model is recovering a threshold rule from its own predictor, a task a single decision stump would solve. The paper attributes the accuracy to Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation of the ensemble.

**S-136** [local_4ceee075] — *Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics*

The aim is an automated method for detecting autism from facial and motor features extracted from video, motivated by the subjectivity of expert observation, the weakness of early behavioural signs, and a shortage of specialists. The pipeline extracts 1,639 numerical parameters per frame using MediaPipe face mesh, pose and hands, adds a mouth aspect ratio and per-region motion energy, and models the sequence with a hybrid CNN+LSTM. Reported results: 90% accuracy on training data, 85-90% on validation, recall 0.95 and AUC above 0.9042, with the hybrid significantly outperforming single-architecture baselines at p < 0.05 by paired t-tests across folds. Heat map and movement-energy analyses showed group differences in motor activity and facial expression. The performance is modest and in a credible range for this task, and it is benchmarked against external comparators rather than presented in isolation. What the study cannot establish is what the separation reflects: the autistic group is 84% male against 52% in the comparison group, and the inputs are facial and body geometry, so sex is a live alternative explanation that no reported analysis excludes.

**S-137** [local_84bcd4ed] — *Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of*

The stated aim is a dual diagnostic framework detecting both autism and gelotophobia, motivated by evidence that gelotophobia affects around 6% of neurotypical people but up to 45% of autistic people, with prevalence reaching 41.98% in adolescents with high-functioning autism - a genuine and under-studied comorbidity, and the identification of it as a target is the paper's most interesting idea. The reported findings are 92% overall accuracy for autism identification using DeepFace features and a multilayer perceptron, with 10-fold cross-validation on the training portion, and qualitative statements for gelotophobia: the system classified it successfully where facial expressions were clear, DeepFace alone was insufficient where cues were ambiguous, and adding the questionnaire improved reliability. The evidential standing of the two halves is entirely different. The 92% is a real number from a real classification experiment, subject to the provenance and splitting problems that this review has recorded for six other studies on the same corpus. The gelotophobia statements are descriptions of an intended workflow, since no gelotophobia assessment was performed on any person and no metric of any kind is reported for that task.

**S-138** [local_d97673f4] — *Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

The aim is autism detection from facial images alone, using pretrained convolutional networks as feature extractors with a simple downstream classifier. Five extractors - MobileNet, Xception, VGG16, VGG19 and EfficientNet - were compared across three preprocessing configurations, with augmentation applied, and the best combination reached 88.33% accuracy on test data, supported by a confusion matrix. The figure is the second-lowest among the eight Kaggle-corpus studies charted in this review, which range from 81.0% to 99.8%, and the architecture is the one least able to memorise: frozen pretrained extractors with a logistic-regression head have far fewer fitted parameters than the end-to-end fine-tuned networks used elsewhere on the same images. Whether the lower figure reflects that restraint or simply a different split cannot be determined, because no validation scheme is described.

**S-139** [local_86a67a4f] — *Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children*

Two aims are pursued. The first is autism prediction from facial images using a hybrid architecture, justified by the argument that 'a single CNN is utilized within most studies which limits generalization. Therefore hierarchical features with fine grains are not obtained' - so combining ResNet50V2 and InceptionV3 should capture features at multiple granularities. The second, and the paper's better idea, is emotion recognition trained specifically on autistic children's faces, on the reasoning that existing systems are 'primarily trained for healthy ones and consequently missing abnormal facial movements'. The reported results diverge sharply in credibility. The emotion model reached 73.33% on six classes against a VGG16-plus-Random-Forest baseline at 57.33%, with precision 72.26, recall 73.33, specificity 83.90 and F1 70.38 - a modest, internally coherent figure on a genuinely hard task, and one consistent with the difficulty another study in this review documents for affect recognition in autistic children. The autism model's reported set is not coherent: 'accuracy = 95, precision = 0.96, sensitivity/recall = 0.94, Specificity = 42.5, F1 = 0.95 and AUC = 78'. On a balanced 280-image test set, recall 0.94 with specificity 0.425 yields roughly 68% accuracy, not 95%; precision 0.96 is impossible alongside specificity 0.425 at a 1:1 ratio, where the implied 80 false positives against 132 true positives would give precision near 0.62; and an AUC of 0.78 is incompatible with an accuracy of 0.95. The figures cannot all be right and no reconciliation is offered.

**S-140** [local_0a39cca9] — *Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy*

The aim is to identify a lightweight CNN ensemble that classifies autism from facial photographs accurately enough for deployment on mobile or edge devices. Five pairings were compared - MobileNetV2 with EfficientNetB0, B5 and B7; ResNet50 with EfficientNetB0; VGG16 with EfficientNetB0 - combined by probability averaging or majority voting. The best, MobileNetV2 with EfficientNetB0, reached accuracy 0.8299, precision 0.8514, recall 0.8182 and F1 0.8344, an internally consistent set and among the lower figures in this branch. Two aspects of the reporting are better than the branch norm. The precision-recall trade-off is interpreted in screening terms: ResNet50 with EfficientNetB0 achieved 'higher precision but lower recall, making them less useful for finding all ASD cases', which correctly identifies that a screening instrument's priority is not missing cases. And the learning curves are read substantively for stability and overfitting rather than displayed decoratively, with some pairings noted to show 'slower learning with more fluctuations, indicating less stable models that might struggle with generalization'. The comparison table places the result against two prior studies at 0.7500 and 0.8050 - modest comparators, and the study does not claim to have exceeded the high-nineties figures reported elsewhere in the branch.

**S-141** [local_7432ffd7] — *Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models*

The stated goal is to implement deep learning on eye-tracking data from social attention tasks to diagnose ASD, and to identify the feature-selection strategy that lets the model reach high accuracy. Note that maximising accuracy is written into the objectives themselves - one of the listed research questions asks for the feature selection strategy that can assist the deep learning model in achieving high accuracy, which is a statement of intent to optimise the reported number rather than to estimate a diagnostic property. The headline finding is CNN-LSTM accuracy 99.78% (SD 0.11%), reported as outperforming previous studies and showing promise for clinical application.

**S-142** [local_8ff20c48] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning*

The stated goal is to apply automated machine learning (TPOT) to a locally collected Pakistani dataset to determine the likelihood of ASD in children at early stages and to speed up diagnosis, with an explicit framing as one of the first uses of AUTOML for ASD detection on real-world non-high-income-country data. Headline findings: TPOT selected a BernoulliNB plus RandomForest ensemble; autistic-class precision 0.83, recall 0.90, F1 0.86; non-autistic-class precision 0.68, recall 0.53, F1 0.60; accuracy 0.83 in the results tables but reported as 78% in the abstract; micro-ROC 0.87, macro-ROC 0.81.

**S-143** [local_986436f2] — *Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost*

The stated goal is to overcome the failure of 2D face scans and eye tracking to capture subtle facial asymmetries by performing 3D facial landmark localisation with a CNN plus active shape appearance model, encoding inter-landmark geometry as a Euclidean graph, and classifying with Randomized-Trees-guided XGBoost. Headline findings at 500 epochs: accuracy 0.985, precision 0.975, recall 0.987, F1 0.925, AUC 0.98, detection accuracy 0.99, miss rate and fall-out both 0.07, and landmark localisation error 0.9 mm. The central problem is that the premise and the data do not meet: the entire methodological argument is about depth information that 3D scans obtain and 2D images lack, while the actual input is a Kaggle folder of 2D web photographs processed with Dlib's 2D 68-point detector at 224x224. A localisation error quoted in millimetres cannot be established from such images at all, since they carry no scale reference and no metric ground truth.

**S-144** [local_bb4d1f7a] — *Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models*

The stated goal is to replace largely manual, unscalable eye-tracking analysis with an automated scanpath-based method that classifies autism severity into four levels, and to characterise how gaze features vary across those levels using DTW and MultiMatch similarity. Headline findings: CNN-RNN with features (x, d, y) reaches accuracy 97.00%, recall 98.24%, F1 97.04%, against GRU 92%, 2-LSTM 92%, XGBoost 80.25% and RFC 80.80%. The more interesting finding is the feature ablation: velocity contributes least, and the authors conclude that it is the continuous attention process, as opposed to the transition phases, that reflects atypical visual behaviour - with differences concentrated in attention duration and vertical gaze distribution.

**S-145** [local_13c1f46d] — *Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism*

The stated goal is to distinguish facial images of individuals with ASD from normal controls with an ensemble pipeline: Gabor filtering, MobileNetV2 feature extraction, an ensemble of LSTM, deep belief network and hybrid-kernel extreme learning machine, and Crested Porcupine Optimizer hyperparameter selection. Headline findings: average accuracy 96.43%, precision 96.44%, recall 96.43%, F-score 96.43% and G-measure 96.43% at 1,000 epochs, against literature-quoted comparators between 89.55% and 92.64%. The Gabor ablation - the paper's one genuinely executed experiment - gives 96.43% with filtering against 92.80% without, at less than half the training time.

**S-146** [local_e771fb69] — *Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data*

The stated goal is a secure, privacy-preserving ASD diagnostic framework combining multimodal kinematic and eye-movement data, deep neural networks, federated learning with FedAvg, and SHAP-based explanation, evaluated in two scenarios (all features versus SHAP-selected features) across three clients and three rounds. The reported headline is that L_General gives the best results with an accuracy of 99.99% and F1 of 99.99%, described as flawless classification performance. The substantive finding, once the tables are read, is different and more interesting: performance is wildly unstable. Across the four feature subsets and three clients, accuracies in the all-features scenario range from 0.01 to 0.88, and SHAP-based feature selection helps some client-subset combinations and badly hurts others (Client 2 on K_General rises from 0.22 to 0.66 while Client 2 on K_Attention falls from 0.55 to 0.33). The paper reports this variability but attributes it to data heterogeneity rather than to the estimator's variance at n=9.

**S-147** [local_945300a5] — *Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network*

The stated goal is to address the limited variation and representativeness of existing autism facial-image datasets by building a new dataset with broader variation in facial characteristics, lighting and social context, and to refine a CNN classifier on it. Headline findings: accuracy 0.90, precision 0.92, recall 0.88, F1 0.90 on 102 test images, with 47 and 45 correct classifications against 4 false positives and 6 false negatives. The conclusion attributes the result principally to the choice of a 1:1 aspect ratio and 224x224 image size, which is a claim about preprocessing conventions rather than about autism.

**S-148** [local_ed30e24c] — *Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI*

The stated goal is to improve early ASD detection for toddlers aged 12-36 months by combining chi-square feature selection with six machine learning classifiers, SVM-SMOTE balancing, Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation and SHAP explanation, claimed as the first study to combine all four. Headline findings: chi-square selection improved every classifier (DT 0.938 to 0.969, KNN 0.959 to 0.973, LGBM 0.976 to 0.980, ET 0.986 to 0.990, MLP 0.993 to 0.997), and SVM reached 1.000 on accuracy, precision, recall and F1 both before and after selection, with all 292 test cases classified correctly - zero false positives and zero false negatives, reported as 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity and as confirming suitability for reliable clinical screening applications.

**S-149** [local_b9de0d7f] — *Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques*

Two goals. Phase I: identify ASD from merged toddler screening data using seven classifiers plus a proposed RF-XG voting ensemble, under three feature-selection schemes. Phase II: recommend an appropriate teaching method for each child from their physical, verbal and behavioural performance. Headline findings: RF-XG reaches 0.94 on original features, 0.92 with Bi-Directional Elimination, 0.98 with Boruta and 0.99 with ML-based feature selection; 10-fold cross-validation averages 0.986; and Phase II predicts the teaching-method label at 0.9917. The comparison table separately claims 99.99%, a number that appears in none of the results tables and exceeds every figure the study actually reports.

**S-150** [local_14df790d] — *Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach*

The stated goal is to identify a minimal feature subset for ASD trait screening in toddlers through systematic feature selection and hyperparameter tuning, and to map Q1-Q10 and the Q-CHAT total onto DSM-5 behavioural domains. Headline findings: using Q1-Q10 alone (a 41% feature reduction) gives the best performance across all classifiers, with the LR-KNN ensemble at accuracy 0.99, precision 1.00, specificity 1.00 and MCC 0.98, followed by ANN 0.98, LR 0.97 and KNN 0.94. Q9, Q6 and Q5 rank consistently highest across chi-squared, tree-importance and correlation methods; Q8 and Q10 lowest.

**S-151** [local_4da2b941] — *Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study*

The stated goal is to evaluate whether machine learning on self-reported camouflaging behaviours can predict dimensional autistic traits and anxiety/depression symptoms, and whether knowing a person's gender or autism diagnosis improves that prediction. Headline findings: correlations between true and predicted scores of R=.85 for Aloofness, .82 for Pragmatics and .75 for Rigidity (strong by the pre-specified Colton criterion), against .58 for Depression and .54 for Anxiety (moderate); and adding gender and/or diagnosis changes R by at most .03, from which the authors conclude that this information is already implicit in the camouflaging items. The stated implication is a possible screening aid for people whose autistic traits are masked or subthreshold and whose diagnosis is unclear or not yet established, regardless of gender identity.

**S-152** [local_6e7174c0] — *A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach*

The stated goal is to overcome the limitations of prior facial-image ASD classifiers - computational cost, pose sensitivity, poor generalisation across demographics - with HyVit-ASD, a hybrid combining a pre-trained ResNet convolutional block, a pre-trained ViT with a custom residual ReAttention mechanism, and an Attention-Based Augmentation Layer. Headline findings: test accuracy 91%, sensitivity 94%, specificity 88%, AUC 95.67%, F-measure 90.99%, G-mean 90.95%, fall-out 0.12, miss rate 0.06, against six models the authors fitted (71-80% validation accuracy) and five literature figures on the same corpus (68-90%).

**S-153** [local_e04bcd32] — *Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network*

The stated goal is to make facial-image ASD screening robust to poor image quality by adding a deblurring stage and a joint denoising-classification network with metaheuristic parameter tuning. Headline findings: accuracy 96.94%, precision 97.28%, recall 96.62%, F-measure 96.95%, against five literature figures between 92.0% and 96.63%; and, for the deblurring stage, 91.22% blur removed with PSNR 32.75 dB and SSIM 0.96 against Deepblur, Wiener filtering and blind deconvolution.

**S-154** [local_183eaef4] — *Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI*

The stated goal is to combine explainable AI with a rigorous, clinically guided preprocessing pipeline to make ML-based ASD diagnosis both accurate and interpretable, and to provide practical R-based guidelines for non-expert clinicians. Headline findings: under 10-fold cross-validation the neural network reached accuracy, precision, recall and F1 of exactly 1.0000, with GBM and XGBoost at 0.9984 and logistic regression at 0.9858; Wilcoxon and Friedman tests confirmed significant differences between models; and PFI, LIME and SHAP all identified the A1-A10 behavioural items as dominant with demographic variables contributing little.

**S-155** [local_b6ac2b98] — *Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks*

The stated aim is to apply explainable machine learning to eye-tracking data from a social attention task in children with ASD, DLD and typical development, to assess classification accuracy across all group combinations and to identify which variables best differentiate the groups. Headline findings: F1 0.912 for DLD versus TD, 0.88 for pooled ASD+DLD versus TD, 0.86 for ASD versus TD, and 0.63 for ASD versus DLD; broad social versus non-social areas of interest carried the signal while finer decompositions by facial region and emotion did not improve accuracy; naive Bayes and logistic model trees performed best; and mean duration of visits to objects emerged as a candidate disorder-specific marker.

**S-156** [local_44d3aef5] — *Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis*

The stated goal is to automate ASD categorisation from eye-tracking data using deep learning, in response to the cost, delay and subjectivity of conventional assessment. Headline findings: MobileNet reached 100% accuracy with perfect precision, recall and F1 for both classes and ROC 100%; VGG19 92%; DenseNet169 78%; the proposed model is ranked above three prior studies on the same dataset (87%, 90%, 79%). The paper attributes its advantage explicitly to preprocessing - our model achieved high accuracy because we have used a different preprocessing approach from improving dataset.

**S-157** [local_24fefc5f] — *A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection*

The stated goal is a hybrid deep-learning method for ASD detection in three stages: Yeo-Johnson transformation to remove noise and artefacts, DeSEHO (Double Exponential Smoothing integrated into the Elk Herd Optimizer) for feature selection, and MEResNeXt (Moments Embedding Network combined with ResNeXt) for classification. Headline findings: accuracy 95.3%, sensitivity 96.5%, specificity 94.8%, described as performing better than traditional models.

**S-158** [local_69b10fe4] — *An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms*

Two aims, one confirmatory and one applied. First, to test directly whether autistic and parkinsonian movement resemble each other - a comparison previously possible only by juxtaposing separate studies with different designs and demographics. Second, to assess whether kinematic features can classify clinical versus non-clinical status and, within the clinical groups, ASD versus PD. Findings: autistic participants differed from both PD and controls in speed modulation and sub-movements, and from PD in reaction time; classification reached a best mean test accuracy of 0.73 for clinical versus non-clinical and 0.93 for ASD versus PD, in both cases from kinematics combined with questionnaires; and, most importantly, no kinematic feature was found to be similar between ASD and PD while also differing from controls. The anecdotal likeness between autistic and parkinsonian movement is not supported.

**S-159** [local_af9f4c12] — *An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data*

The stated goal is a single-stage framework performing joint screening-level ASD identification and four-level ordinal severity stratification, under an explicitly controlled labelling paradigm, with a bidirectional LSTM as representation learner and a chaotic optimiser for training stability. Headline findings: accuracy 99.10% for toddlers, 97.10% children, 98.50% adolescents and 98.10% adults with AUROC above 0.99, a 3-6 point gain over the authors' own baselines (SVM 0.911, logistic regression 0.902, random forest 0.928, MLP 0.944, unidirectional LSTM 0.932). The framing of these results is the study's distinguishing feature: they are presented as evidence of the model's effectiveness in approximating a deterministic behavioural severity-scoring function rather than independent clinical diagnostic performance.

**S-160** [local_367db0b6] — *An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns*

The stated goal is a machine-unlearning-integrated explainable AI framework for early ASD and brain-disability detection in newborns, motivated by a genuinely important argument: once a newborn's data is used in training, most models provide no mechanism to remove it if parents withdraw consent, which raises ethical and legal problems under GDPR and HIPAA. Headline findings: a 23% reduction in error rates, reduced false positives, accuracy improved to 98%, and reduced processing time. The results are described as simulation results.

**S-161** [local_8d43288c] — *Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos*

The stated goal is to classify four behaviour categories - arm flapping, spinning, head banging and normal behaviour - from naturalistic, unstructured video, using a CNN-GRU architecture, in order to help clinicians monitor behavioural trends. Headline findings: CNN-GRU reaches k-fold accuracy 0.9294 +/- 0.0038 and validation accuracy 0.96, outperforming MobileNet (0.9193), 3D-CNN+LSTM (0.8912), EfficientNet-B7 (0.8808) and VGG16, with paired t-tests significant against all four at a corrected threshold of 0.0125. Per class, the two clearly distinct repetitive behaviours (arm flapping, head banging) reach F1 0.98 while spinning and normal behaviour reach 0.94 and 0.93.

**S-162** [local_5f57ba19] — *Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension*

The stated goal is to investigate eye-tracking-based ASD detection during audio-visual storytelling using traditional but explainable machine learning, and to identify which gaze features and which phases of speech carry discriminative information. Headline findings: best performance 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC (logistic regression, audio-visual speech phase); around 55% F1 in the speech phase across both modalities; a statistically significant advantage for audio-visual over audio-only stimuli in the pre-speech phase but not during or after speech; and convergent feature-importance and SHAP evidence that mouth fixation time and revisits across facial areas of interest are the most informative features. The abstract states in its second-to-last sentence that performance remains modest.

**S-163** [local_1d856900] — *Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare*

The stated goal is an ensemble framework that is both accurate and interpretable enough for clinicians to trust, evaluated on a behavioural dataset and a multimodal one. Headline findings: 97.6% accuracy on behavioural data from a regularised neural network (ROC-AUC 0.998) and 98.2% on multimodal data, with all other models above 93%; and an ablation showing accuracy rising from 89.40% (no feature selection, no resampling) through feature selection, SMOTE and ensemble fusion to 97.60% with neural-network regularisation.

**S-164** [local_7b19a959] — *Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis*

The stated goal is to test whether online performance-based measures can predict adult autism diagnosis, whether they add to the most widely used screening questionnaire, and which behavioural variables carry the predictive signal. Headline findings on the age- and gender-matched sample: objective task measures alone reach 74% accuracy (sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 79.2%, F1 73.5%); the AQ alone reaches 83%; the two combined reach 92%. On the unmatched full sample the objective measures reach 81.8%, which the paper states is inflated by including age and gender as features. A label-randomised control performs at chance. Several variables with no significant group difference under Bonferroni correction nevertheless contributed predictive value in combination.

**S-165** [local_d7b6fa00] — *Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath*

The stated goal is a hybrid ensemble integrating bagging, boosting and stacking that operates directly on raw scanpath features rather than on scanpath images, so as to reduce preprocessing overhead and improve interpretability for real-time screening. Headline findings: the stacking ensemble reached accuracy 0.9600 (SD 0.0800), precision 0.9750, recall 0.9500 and F1 0.9524, above every base learner (AdaBoost 0.9267, KNN 0.8867, random forest 0.8533, decision tree 0.8200, gradient boosting 0.7800), and comparable to image-based deep learning models on the same dataset at a fraction of the preprocessing cost.

**S-166** [local_e54c304c] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models*

The stated goal is real-time ASD screening from facial images using object detection, with YOLOv8n compared against YOLOv9c to identify the more effective solution. Headline findings: YOLOv8n reached precision 91.95%, recall 92.77%, F1 92.36% and mAP@0.5 94.76%, against YOLOv9c at 91.29%, 90.29%, 90.79% and 93.32%; YOLOv8n showed higher true-positive rates for both classes with fewer misclassifications into the Background class; and, in an out-of-distribution probe, YOLOv8n rejected non-human inputs while YOLOv9c classified a dog as Autistic and a leaf as Nonautistic.

**S-167** [local_e4c2a776] — *Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images*

The stated goal is a computationally efficient, privacy-preserving and optimised framework for ASD detection from facial images, combining Gaussian Gabor filtering, fused deep features from VGG16, DenseNet-121 and XceptionNet, a wavelet neural network classifier tuned by the chimp optimisation algorithm, and Grad-CAM++ for visual interpretation. Headline findings: average accuracy 98.42% with precision 98.40%, recall 98.42%, F-measure 98.41% and AUC 98.42% in the 30% testing phase, against quoted comparators from 92.10% to 97.76%.

**S-168** [local_231757c7] — *SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers*

The stated goal is objective classification of three ASD severity levels from 3D motor features, identification of the contributing motor biomarkers through SHAP, and evaluation across multiple validation strategies. Headline findings: 84.6 +/- 10.9% accuracy under 5-fold cross-validation and 86.4% on the held-out sets; 100% on the severe class (4 of 4) with a 95% confidence interval of 39.8% to 100.0%; and wrist movements, knee trajectories and elbow-to-foot distances as the leading biomarkers. The abstract itself states that the severe-class result is a methodological proof-of-concept rather than clinical validation because the severe features were synthetically generated.

**S-169** [local_1b457442] — *Screening autism spectrum*

The stated goal is to test whether privacy-preserving machine learning on speech transcripts can screen for ASD, on the argument that structured text avoids identifiable biometric data such as raw audio or video.
