Headline findings: ROC-AUC 0.93 on Nadig and 0.87 on Eigsti binary with logistic regression, approximately 0.96 on the merged data with TabNet, accuracy above 86% on both binary datasets, and a four-feature model reproducing nearly the same 86%. The result the authors themselves flag as important is the three-class Eigsti task, where the best ROC-AUC falls to 0.71.

**S-170** [local_b26db2f2] — *Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches*

The stated goal is a serious-game tablet application combining inclusive-design requirements with machine learning, to give educators a playful, non-invasive ASD screening aid usable inside the school day. Headline findings: random forest reached 96% accuracy, MLP, deep MLP and SVM 94%, KNN 90%, logistic regression 82% and naive Bayes lower, with learning curves showing training accuracy above validation accuracy and no abrupt decline.

## RQ2.2 — Study setting and data provenance

_170 of 170 studies charted for this question._

**S-001** [local_76fc33d0] — *Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers*

Clinic setting (videotaped ADOS assessments). Existing data: a subset of the ongoing Canadian Infant Sibling Study database, analysed retrospectively.

**S-002** [local_0dbc5018] — *Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities*

Clinical/laboratory setting at an Italian research hospital. Newly collected data (ASD group recruited over 18 months; controls via pediatricians and kindergartens); no existing dataset used.

**S-003** [local_dc5fc4bb] — *ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data*

Clinic setting - a child and adolescent psychiatry outpatient department. Newly collected application-log data; stimuli drawn from the existing public Cohn-Kanade facial-expression database.

**S-004** [local_863980f8] — *Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework*

Laboratory eye-tracking setting. Existing data - the study is an explicitly secondary machine-learning analysis of the eye-movement dataset collected for Yi et al. (2016), which had analysed it with a conventional area-of-interest approach.

**S-005** [local_be8aa62f] — *Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder*

Clinic/research setting - an academic outpatient developmental neuropsychiatry program plus advertisement and advocacy-group recruitment, with instruments delivered through a computer-based program. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used.

**S-006** [local_e404a2a3] — *Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism*

Applied real-world settings - specialist therapeutic centres for the autism group and standard kindergartens for the controls, explicitly chosen over a university laboratory because laboratory motion-capture paradigms with reflective markers 'under the watchful gaze of curious scientists' are difficult for autistic children and may invalidate the data. Newly collected data; commercially available games were adapted with logging code.

**S-007** [local_780141fc] — *Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study*

Laboratory setting at the University of Manchester. Existing data - the study is an explicitly secondary machine-learning re-analysis of an imitation experiment previously analysed with mean-based statistics on only five kinematic parameters. Its contribution is analytic rather than new collection, though it does newly release the dataset.

**S-008** [local_3a331973] — *Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data*

A controlled recording setting with a screen and Kinect camera, with clinical recruitment via an NHS Asperger and ADHD service. Newly collected data - the study contributes the KOMAA dataset and no existing dataset is used.

**S-009** [local_7b3e6b3a] — *Earlier identification of children with autism*

Laboratory setting - a closed recording room with ceiling-mounted cameras, deliberately arranged so parents would play as they would at home and with study personnel absent during recording. Existing data: retrospective analysis of recordings collected within the EASE (Early Autism Sweden) longitudinal high-risk sibling study.

**S-010** [local_36aa3ace] — *Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative*

Mixed clinic and school setting - patients recruited in two Paris university child and adolescent psychiatry departments, controls from elementary schools. Existing dataset: the Child Pathological and Emotional Speech Database (CPESD), used entirely as secondary data; no new collection.

**S-011** [local_44b58f21] — *ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces*

Laboratory setting - a dedicated human motion gait analysis laboratory with force plates embedded in an instrumented walkway. Data were newly collected within a larger institutional research project but are reused here from the authors' earlier published work, so this paper is a secondary analysis of an in-house dataset rather than a new collection.

**S-012** [local_cb9a5b48] — *Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening*

Clinic setting - the Center for Treatment of Autistic Disorders (Tehran Autism), with the robot placed in a cage and cameras positioned overhead and beside it. Newly recorded interaction data, but building directly on an existing robot-screening platform and protocol from the same research group.

**S-013** [local_40cd7d53] — *Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children*

Clinic setting for testing (a dark, soundproof room with fixed viewing geometry) with clinical recruitment from a hospital outpatient ward and control recruitment from a kindergarten in the same city. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used.

**S-014** [local_5b1d0b36] — *Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday*

Home setting, and uniquely so in this corpus - devices were mailed to families and all collection occurred inside children's homes with no professional supervision, deliberately to emulate real deployment of child-specific smart devices. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used.

**S-015** [local_54954c19] — *Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching*

Laboratory setting with a controlled eye tracker and fixed viewing distance. Existing data - the eye-tracking corpus was originally collected to investigate web-searching difficulties experienced by autistic users, and the authors are explicit that 'the data used in this study was not collected with this objective in mind', treating this as a limitation on achievable accuracy.

**S-016** [local_d8dc996a] — *Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Laboratory setting - a quiet room with fixed table and chair geometry and a standardised start posture - with clinical recruitment from a hospital child neuropsychiatry unit and control recruitment from primary schools. Newly collected data, released as the first public video dataset of ASD/TD gestures.

**S-017** [local_88ddfdd1] — *A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task*

Laboratory setting with a chinrest, fixed viewing distance and periodic data-quality monitoring. The data were collected by the authors across two experiments, with Experiment 1 data also used in a separate publication on information extraction - disclosed transparently on the grounds that 'recruiting ASD subjects and validating their diagnoses is extremely costly'.

**S-018** [local_361110f1] — *Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features*

Clinical recruitment (hospital child psychiatry department) with laboratory-style testing on a desktop LeapMotion apparatus. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used.

**S-019** [local_51533de4] — *Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations*

Clinic/research setting at a hospital autism centre. Newly collected data; the design deliberately departs from the field's reliance on ADOS-derived or highly structured speech samples in favour of naturalistic conversation with a non-expert partner.

**S-020** [local_96c87d36] — *Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking*

Mixed clinic and community setting - recruitment spanned university clinics, websites, registries, local advertising and the 2015 Minnesota State Fair, with testing at more than one location using different displays and different eye trackers. Newly collected data; the face stimuli come from the existing Cohn-Kanade database.

**S-021** [local_4b031d44] — *Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine*

Home setting for data capture - parents recorded brief videos on mobile phones - combined with clinical setting for diagnosis and recruitment at a Dhaka children's hospital, and remote US-based rating. Newly collected data. The design deliberately exploits Bangladesh's 95% mobile phone subscription rate as the deployment substrate.

**S-022** [local_05ef29e5] — *Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification*

Setting not reported - this is entirely secondary analysis of an existing benchmark dataset (Saliency4ASD, IEEE ICME 2019 Grand Challenge), with no data collection by the authors and no description of the original acquisition conditions.

**S-023** [local_9528024b] — *Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol*

Laboratory setting - a purpose-built examination and observation suite with a two-way mirror, fixed camera position and overhead microphone, with a therapist in the room and a second therapist plus robot operator behind the mirror. Newly collected session data; no existing dataset used.

**S-024** [local_6230fe22] — *Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism*

Intended clinical setting - autism centres or hospitals in Saudi Arabia, with a therapist-operated workflow. Newly collected data, though nothing about the collection setting, session structure or conditions is described.

**S-025** [local_785ba418] — *Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis*

Laboratory setting at a UK university. Newly collected data using motion tracking; no existing dataset used.

**S-026** [local_fea042be] — *Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual*

Laboratory setting - a quiet university room with white barriers to reduce visual distraction, children seated alone or on a parent's lap at approximately 60 cm. Newly collected data, with the resulting image dataset released publicly on Figshare and described in more detail in an earlier publication by the same group.

**S-027** [local_ba5fbda7] — *Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD*

Laboratory setting with standardised lighting and fixed camera and seating geometry, but with naturalistic unscripted conversation content. The data come from an existing study on interpersonal coordination in dyadic interactions by the same group, so this is a secondary analysis for classification purposes.

**S-028** [local_7b468950] — *Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart*

Two sites, Glasgow and Gothenburg, with recruitment through NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde Specialist Children's Services, other specialist children's centres, nurseries and schools, and via two streams for the clinical cohorts - children receiving a positive diagnosis following an NHS clinic assessment, and children already diagnosed. Multi-site international recruitment is itself a design feature aimed at the pilot's acknowledged weakness, that a sample drawn from 'a small number of specialist day-care centres in Poland' is 'prone to selection bias and site-specific effects'. The assessment is intended for use 'in the home, clinic or classroom', so the deployment envelope is broad and the trial's setting is the referral pathway rather than a research laboratory. The residual limitation, not stated, is that recruitment through specialist services and existing diagnoses means predictive value at population prevalence will still not be directly estimable.

**S-029** [local_309e5baa] — *Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns*

Setting not reported - entirely secondary analysis of the Saliency4ASD benchmark. The source dataset used a Tobii T120 eye tracker with a 17-inch monitor, but no room, distance, calibration or session details are given.

**S-030** [local_a45f39e9] — *Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time*

Home setting - videos recorded by parents during the child's daily activities and submitted through a commercial remote assessment platform. Existing data: the NODA corpus was collected and expert-annotated by Behavior Imaging and provided to the authors, so this is secondary analysis of industry data. A manually annotated children's pose dataset was newly created by the authors for retraining the pose estimator.

**S-031** [local_d587f9cd] — *Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning*

An in-clinic setup with the therapist, the robot and a caregiver all present in the room, the caregiver instructed not to help the child perform the task. The multi-person setting is what necessitates one of the pipeline's design decisions - face recognition is used specifically to 'differentiate the child's face from other faces detected and found in the scene', since a system measuring a child's gaze in a room containing two adults must first establish which face is the child's. That is a practical requirement of clinical deployment which laboratory single-subject setups do not encounter, and its explicit handling is a strength.

**S-032** [local_08b8027d] — *SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths*

Setting not reported - entirely secondary analysis of the Saliency4ASD benchmark, with no description of the original acquisition conditions, viewing durations, eye tracker or calibration.

**S-033** [local_c6f1209b] — *Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children*

An integrative kindergarten in Wroclaw, named in the acknowledgements. Assessing children in their own everyday setting, with a portable robot brought to them, is the deployment scenario the work envisages, so the pilot data were collected under the conditions in which the method would be used. Integrative kindergartens in Poland enrol autistic and typically developing children together, which is also the setting that would make the group's stated next step - comparison against typically developing peers - straightforward to arrange without changing anything else about the protocol.

**S-034** [local_83b99e73] — *Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers*

Outpatient clinic of the Child Mental Health Research Center, Nanjing Brain Hospital Affiliated to Nanjing Medical University, with typically developing controls recruited from the Nanjing area over the same period (December 2017 onward). Prospectively registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry as ChiCTR-OPC-17011995.

**S-035** [local_638860ef] — *Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis*

Laboratory setting at a UK university. The data come from an experimental protocol previously published by the same group, so this is a machine-learning analysis of an existing behavioural dataset rather than a new collection.

**S-036** [local_7547db68] — *Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network*

Testing was conducted in quiet classrooms at two cooperating institutions - Amy Education School in Zhengzhou for the typically developing group and Guangzhou Children's Care Center for the autistic group. System requirements were developed through repeated consultation with physicians at Hubei Maternal and Child Health Hospital, Wuhan Children's Hospital and Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center, including direct observation of how they administer the diagnostic scales.

**S-037** [local_878c259f] — *Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach*

Laboratory setting - a biomechanics laboratory with force-plate instrumentation. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used.

**S-038** [local_1579c85a] — *Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through*

Laboratory setting with robots on a table and children standing or seated around it. Newly collected data from a user study; no existing dataset used.

**S-039** [local_157d6266] — *Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism*

Research centre setting at a neurodevelopmental research institute, with community and school recruitment. Data were collected as part of a wider study of imitation skills in autism, so this is a focused analysis within a larger programme rather than a standalone collection.

**S-040** [local_8be557e3] — *Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation*

Retrospective secondary analysis of audio extracted from video recordings of clinical autism diagnostic sessions conducted at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital between 2016 and 2018, under IRB approval for use of fully anonymized data from an existing study. Recording conditions are reported: two clinical rooms of stated dimensions with ambient noise around 40 dB.

**S-041** [local_c79e100a] — *Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models*

Not stated. Author affiliations span Ulster University (Northern Ireland), Bangor University (Wales) and the University of Colombo (Sri Lanka), but no collection site, recruitment route, period or setting is identified, and no ethics approval or consent statement appears.

**S-042** [local_4fecbf6d] — *Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network*

The National Autism Research Center of Israel in Beersheba, a collaboration between Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and Soroka University Medical Center. Recording used a fixed setup in a dedicated ADOS room - an AKG CHM99 microphone 1-2 m from the child feeding a TASCAM US-16x08 interface at 44.1 kHz, downsampled to 16 kHz. Funded by the Israel Science Foundation (grant 961/14) and the BGU Research Authority, with the centre itself funded by the Israeli Ministry of Science and Technology.

**S-043** [local_95abe653] — *Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning*

A quiet room at the University of Wolverhampton with only researcher and participant present. Autistic participants recruited through a UK autism charity and the university's Enabling Centre; controls by snowball sampling in the Birmingham area. Ethical approval obtained from the University of Wolverhampton Ethics Committee before collection began.

**S-044** [local_40168c96] — *Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based*

A therapy room with at most two people present besides the child. Autistic participants came from the Children Rehabilitation Center at Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital, Xi'an; typically developing participants from mainstream Xi'an schools. Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the China Postdoctoral Science Foundation and the Natural Science Foundation of Shaanxi Province.

**S-045** [local_d3852378] — *Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

A three-surface CAVE of 4 x 4 x 3 m at the Institute for Research and Innovation in Bioengineering, Polytechnic University of Valencia. Autistic participants came from Red Cenit, a Valencia cognitive development centre; controls were recruited by a management company through family mailings. Funded by the Spanish Ministry of Economy, Industry and Competitiveness ('Immersive virtual environment for the evaluation and training of children with autism spectrum disorder: T Room'), the Generalitat Valenciana REBRAND project, and ERDF Valencian Community funds.

**S-046** [local_df438dd2] — *Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening*

A standardised low-cost room setup deployed at the collaborating Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, with a fixed seating layout for child, clinician and parent and a single camera positioned to record the child's frontal face. Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Key Research and Development Program of Jiangsu Province, the Six Talent Peaks project and a Guangzhou municipal livelihood science and technology plan.

**S-047** [local_cd9e45eb] — *Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism*

Laboratory eye-tracking at Seattle Children's Research Institute and Yale University, with acquisition protocols aligned to a published multi-site standard and a delivery system providing embedded 5-point calibrations and the ability to insert video breaks for behavioural management. Funded by NIH awards K01 MH104739, R21 MH103550 and R03 MH092618, an NSF Expedition in Socially Assistive Robotics, and a Simons Foundation award.

**S-048** [local_56237213] — *The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data*

A shielded room for EEG recording and a separate eye-tracking station, with autistic children recruited clinically and typically developing children from a local kindergarten. Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the National Key Research and Development Program of China.

**S-049** [local_f9a5195f] — *Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses*

In-lab at Stanford University, with families recruited between 25 February 2015 and 26 January 2016 through the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Research Registry, referrals to the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Clinic, the Developmental Behavioral Unit of Lucile Packard Children's Hospital, and academic presentations. Funded by NIH grants 1R01EB025025-01 and 1R21HD091500-01 plus multiple foundation and Stanford programme grants. The senior author declares founding Cognoa, a company building digital child-health solutions.

**S-050** [local_16a77fb0] — *Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)*

A quiet laboratory with constant lighting at Humboldt-Universitat zu Berlin, with participants recruited through the autism outpatient clinic of Charite Universitatsmedizin Berlin. The experimenter left the room before the task began, so the participant was alone with the screen. Ethics approval from the Charite ethics committee, Helsinki conformity, written informed consent from all participants and separate consent for figure publication.

**S-051** [local_9c4af7a3] — *Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades*

Not stated. No collection site, period, recruitment route or ethics approval appears, because the data are secondary and their origin is never identified. All modelling was performed in Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio.

**S-052** [local_b70dae32] — *An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model*

The Autism Resource Center, Islamabad, with the study approved by the centre's autism specialist and director board and parental consent obtained. Two robots were placed in an arc approximately 1 m from the child, who sat for the joint attention module and stood for imitation, with a Kinect behind the robots. The authors state that the participant setting is illustrated 'to make the intervention replicable'. No external funding was received.

**S-053** [local_51a0af74] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data*

Laboratory eye tracking with participants recruited through the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Sao Paulo's School of Medicine, in collaboration with the School of Arts, Sciences and Humanities and the bioinformatics postgraduate programme. Funded by CNPq, FAPESP/INCT-MACC, CAPES and PRONAS/PCD. No ethics approval statement appears.

**S-054** [local_d8d3037b] — *Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study*

Laboratory sessions at Tsinghua University's Shenzhen International Graduate School, with diagnosed participants recruited through the Shenzhen Autism Society. Funded by Shenzhen Humanities and Social Sciences Key Research Bases, the Guangdong Natural Science Foundation, the National Philosophy and Social Sciences Foundation of China and a Tsinghua SIGS foundation. IRB approval from the Department of Psychology, Tsinghua University (No. THUDP20) covering both experiments.

**S-055** [local_991fe435] — *Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task*

Laboratory testing at Peking University, with autistic participants recruited from a preschool specialised for autistic children in Beijing. Funded by multiple National Natural Science Foundation of China grants, an NSFC/DFG collaborative research centre, a Guangdong key project on autism diagnosis and treatment tools, and a Beijing municipal science and technology grant. No conflicts of interest declared.

**S-056** [local_8692a64f] — *Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis*

Autistic participants were recruited from the Shanghai Putuo District Zhanyi Children Cultivation Service Center; no setting is stated for the comparison group and no laboratory conditions, lighting or viewing distance are described. Acknowledged support from two university research teams at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Shanghai University of Engineering Science. The first author is affiliated with a Shanghai high school.

**S-057** [local_4d6fac7e] — *Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network*

EEG recorded in a shielded room and eye tracking conducted subsequently; ethics approval indicates Beijing Normal University while the analysis was conducted at Wuhan University's School of Computer Science. No recruitment route, period or clinical setting is described.

**S-058** [local_30c622f2] — *Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model*

The Psychiatry Institute of the University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine, with acknowledgement to the Autism Spectrum Disorder Program of the Clinics Hospital (PROTEA-HC). Funded by CAPES and the Brazilian National Program to Support Health Care for Persons with Disabilities. Ethics approval from the School of Medicine research ethics board under protocol 17556019.8.0000.0068.

**S-059** [local_bfc088c7] — *Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation*

A laboratory dyadic setup at Shenzhen University with participants seated 80 cm from the interviewer, autistic children recruited from Shenzhen Kangning Hospital's Child Psychiatry Department and comparison children from local schools. Funded by seven Shenzhen and Guangdong municipal, medical-discipline and provincial research programmes. No conflicts declared.

**S-060** [local_25e34bbd] — *Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification*

Recording in an unspecified 'noise free location' using consumer audio editing software on a laptop, at two engineering colleges in Tamil Nadu. No recruitment route, clinical setting or collection period is described, and no funding or ethics information appears.

**S-061** [local_4917150c] — *Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning*

A quiet room at the University of Picardy Jules Verne with white barriers to reduce visual distraction, in an interdisciplinary collaboration between psychology and artificial intelligence research units. Children were recruited regionally, with autistic participants diagnosed at multidisciplinary specialty clinics. Supported by a university research quality bonus; no conflicts declared.

**S-062** [local_241ec2c2] — *Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking*

Laboratory eye tracking with autistic participants recruited from the Psychiatry Institute of the University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine, in collaboration between computing, psychiatry and bioinformatics units. Ethics approval from the University of Sao Paulo under protocol 57185516.9.0000.5390.

**S-063** [local_36617ec5] — *Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis*

A three-wall CAVE of 4 x 4 x 3 m at the Institute for Research and Innovation in Bioengineering, Polytechnic University of Valencia, with autistic participants from the Red Cenit Neurocognitive Development Center and comparison children recruited by a management company. Funded by the Spanish Ministry of Economy, Industry and Competitiveness project 'Immersive Virtual Environment for the Evaluation and Training of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: T Room'.

**S-064** [local_d8e804d6] — *Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms*

A laboratory dyadic setup at Shenzhen University with the child seated 80 cm from a 33-year-old female interviewer blinded to group membership and required to behave and speak identically across participants; autistic children recruited from a local psychiatric hospital, comparison children from nearby communities. Funded by seven Shenzhen and Guangdong municipal, medical-discipline and provincial programmes.

**S-065** [local_712542ca] — *Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset*

No data collection. The source data were gathered from schools in Hauts-de-France; all analysis here was performed in Google Colaboratory using scikit-learn, by authors at institutions in Bangladesh and Australia.

**S-066** [local_0ab41681] — *Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder*

Laboratory motion capture at the University of Ferrara and the Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia's Center for Translational Neurophysiology of Speech and Communication, with autistic children recruited from a local outpatient neurodevelopmental clinic and comparison children from a local kindergarten. Funded by two Italian Ministry of Health young-researcher grants and an EU H2020 project. No competing interests declared.

**S-067** [local_9ca9b2cc] — *Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment*

An autism rehabilitation centre, with participants recruited from Al Ain Hospital - a clinical service setting, and the same setting in which the system would be deployed. That alignment between study setting and intended use setting is shared by only a few studies in this review. The clinical framing is specific: the authors note that assessment is typically performed at enrolment and repeated during long-term therapy, and that if it 'could be repeated more frequently to trace the severity and development of symptoms, then therapists could implement more efficacious diagnostic and therapeutic options' - so the setting defines the problem, which is the cost in expert time of repeated assessment.

**S-068** [local_02fa4215] — *Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning*

The Child Psychiatry Department at Mayo Hospital Lahore, described as the only government-run child psychiatry department in Pakistan and seeing on average two patients daily, together with a private school for autistic children in Lahore. Questionnaires were administered on paper at the school and via Google Forms otherwise. No setting is described for the comparison group.

**S-069** [local_29a3fc54] — *Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism*

Oregon Health and Science University, with participants recruited by community outreach and referral from OHSU specialised clinics into a neuroimaging study, and speech extracted from videotaped ADOS-2 administrations conducted as part of that study's screening. IRB approval from OHSU.

**S-070** [local_b7ec3755] — *Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images*

Not reported. The eye-tracking sessions belong to the Saliency4ASD collection and the authors describe neither the room, the tracker, the viewing distance, nor the country. The only settings named are the two Italian universities where the analysis was performed. For a study whose entire signal is fixation duration, the absence of the acquisition sampling rate and calibration procedure is a substantive reproducibility gap rather than a formality.

**S-071** [local_684969f6] — *Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data*

Not reported for the data collection - the setting belongs to the Saliency4ASD source study. The acquisition conditions are partially restated: Tobii T120 eye tracker, 17-inch monitor, each image presented at original full resolution for 3 seconds. This is more than the companion paper on the same data provides but still omits room conditions, viewing distance, calibration procedure and sampling rate, all of which matter for a signal whose dominant discriminator turns out to be total fixation duration.

**S-072** [local_35004e74] — *Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children*

University of Geneva, Switzerland, within an ongoing longitudinal study of early autism development. The assessments were not staged for this analysis - they are the cohort's routine clinical ADOS sessions, conducted 'in several different rooms', by 'different examiners', and 'filmed with different camera systems'. That heterogeneity is the study's most under-appreciated methodological asset: where other work in this corpus achieves high accuracy under a single fixed acquisition setup and therefore cannot distinguish diagnostic signal from site signature, here the acquisition varies within both classes, so camera, room and examiner cannot serve as proxies for group. The authors report classification robustness to this variability explicitly in supplementary analysis and treat it as evidence for generalisability rather than as noise to be apologised for.

**S-073** [local_fa91fc18] — *Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities*

Naples, Italy, across two different settings by group: autistic children at the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, which provided 'the clinical ward for the experimentation' and where those children also receive ongoing psychomotor and speech therapy; comparison children at a primary school. The physical arrangement is specified precisely and identically for both - child seated at a table 65-70 cm high adjusted for age, experimenter opposite, tablet within 20 cm of the table edge - which controls posture and reach geometry, the most obvious physical determinants of drag kinematics. What is not controlled is the setting asymmetry itself. Recruiting cases from a therapy centre and comparisons from a school means group membership is entangled with familiarity with clinical assessment and with prior therapeutic exposure to fine-motor practice, either of which could shift drag dynamics independently of diagnosis.

**S-074** [local_115dfe8d] — *A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children*

Beijing, China. Comparison children were recruited from a local kindergarten; the autistic children came from a school site whose identity is not given and where the authors report limited access to reliable diagnostic information. Both recordings took place under controlled conditions - EEG in a quiet room with the child in an armchair usually accompanied by a caregiver, eye tracking at a fixed ~60 cm viewing distance following a five-point calibration that had to pass with small error vectors before proceeding. Recruiting the two groups from different institutional settings is a structural feature the paper does not discuss, and it carries a specific risk for the eye-tracking modality here: the stimulus is Tiger Qiao Hu, a widely broadcast Chinese children's programme, so prior familiarity with the characters could differ systematically between children in a mainstream kindergarten and children in a special-education setting, and familiarity affects where a viewer looks.

**S-075** [local_5b7ea7dc] — *AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Seoul, South Korea. The clinical group came from the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Division of Seoul National University Hospital and the comparison group from preschools - a recruitment asymmetry of the kind that elsewhere in this corpus introduces setting confounds, but mitigated here because the paradigm itself is identical for both groups and highly constrained: same quiet room arrangement, same height-adjustable chair, same 70 cm toy placement, same 45-degree examiner offset, same ten toys, same 30-second waits. The paper also states that videos 'were acquired at different locations with various background noises' and treats the model's robustness across them as evidence for generalisability - which the train-on-segmented, test-on-raw result supports more directly than the assertion alone would.

**S-076** [local_87fe26aa] — *Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

China, with the two groups drawn from different institutional settings - special education schools for the autistic children and regular kindergartens for the comparison children. Recording conditions are described only obliquely and only in the limitations, where the authors note that 'the recording environments are changing' and that 'across-day variability exists in recording conditions'. That acknowledgement is candid but incomplete: if recording conditions varied across days and the two groups were recruited from different institutions, sessions may have been clustered by group, in which case environmental variation is partially confounded with diagnosis. The paper does not report whether recordings were interleaved across groups.

**S-077** [local_893ce2fa] — *An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images*

Not reported. The recordings belong to the source dataset and the paper describes neither the room, the country, the recruitment route nor the acquisition protocol. The only setting information is the hardware on which the experiments were computed - an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X with 16 GB RAM, a GTX 1050 Ti and a 250 GB SSD - which is specified more precisely than anything about the children.

**S-078** [local_dffe4127] — *Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals*

Two independent sites - Caltech and Indiana University - using 'otherwise identical eye trackers and video stimuli', with the two-site design adopted explicitly 'to optimize generalizability'. Recruitment was through flyers distributed at outpatient treatment programmes, community support groups and community locations including college campuses and YMCAs, so the sample is community-recruited rather than clinic-referred - which matters for representativeness, though the authors note the sample 'is not representative of ASD in general'. Site membership is carried through the analysis and displayed in every figure by marker shape, so site effects remain visible rather than being pooled away. This is the only multi-site study in the corpus.

**S-079** [local_2b766683] — *Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech*

Participants' own homes, with no researcher present, no controlled acoustics and no equipment standardisation - the design's defining property and its explicit purpose. The authors' argument is twofold and both parts are worth noting. Logistically, prior speech studies used directional microphone arrays or multiple wireless microphones at a hospital, which 'pos[es] significant barriers to the widespread availability of automatic diagnosis tools', reinforced by the observation that 83.86% of American counties have no autism diagnostic resources at all and that the delay from first consultation to diagnosis averages over two years. Behaviourally, the authors argue that 'interacting with unknown adults in foreign environments could be stressful and possibly affect the behavior of children with autism, thus leading to observations that are not generalizable to the real world' - a validity argument for home recording rather than merely a convenience one. The consequence embraced rather than lamented is heterogeneous audio quality, which the paper treats as fidelity to deployment conditions.

**S-080** [local_2895bdf0] — *Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection*

Oregon Health & Science University, with participants recruited through community outreach and referral from OHSU specialty clinics into an fMRI study - so the sample is a research cohort rather than a consecutive clinical series. Recording arrangements are described precisely and with their rationale: 'The microphone was suspended in a cage and placed on a table approximately 3 feet from where the child sat. This allowed the recording to accurately capture the child's language, even if, as is common in ADOS Module 3 administrations, the child sometimes moved around the room before being reminded to sit down.' That sentence does two things few papers here manage - it specifies the acquisition geometry and it explains the specific behaviour the geometry was designed to accommodate. The authors nonetheless flag microphone quality and placement as insufficiently controlled and recommend tightening it in future work to reduce reliance on denoising.

**S-081** [local_423b636b] — *Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers*

Four Duke pediatric primary care clinics during routine well-child checkups - the only truly point-of-care setting in the corpus. The description of environmental control is unusually honest: a quiet room with few distractions was identified at each clinic, but 'although it was quiet and without a lot of distraction, it was not otherwise controlled as in a laboratory setting', with the four rooms noted as similar in size, lighting and presence of distractions. The social arrangement is specified in detail and matters for the measurement: the caregiver held the child on their lap with no instructions on how to do so, sat quietly, and was asked not to guide the child's behaviour or give instructions, while siblings and the administering assistant stayed behind both caregiver and child to reduce distraction. The tablet sat on a tripod approximately 60 cm in front of the child. That the caregiver's holding is uninstructed is a deliberate choice for ecological validity and an uncontrolled source of variance for a measure of postural movement.

**S-082** [local_ffa35101] — *Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study*

Two sites in different countries with different recruitment routes - a research setting in the United States, where participants came from an established family-genetic study of autism, and community recruitment in Hong Kong through social media, schools, autism organisations and employment programmes. The recording setting itself is described minimally: pages presented on a computer monitor with narration audio recorded, and no information about room, microphone, distance or recording equipment in either site. For a study whose primary features are the amplitude envelope and its spectral structure, the absence of any acoustic-recording specification is a genuine reproducibility gap, and it is compounded by the two-site design: if recording conditions differed systematically between the United States and Hong Kong, that difference would be absorbed into the envelope features. The combined-language model would be sensitive to this, though the fact that rhythm classification succeeds within each language separately - where recording conditions are presumably homogeneous - substantially mitigates the concern.

**S-083** [local_81ecbc6f] — *Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings*

Poland, with participants contacted through a university clinic, diagnostic or therapeutic centres, or schools, and assessed as part of a research evaluation. The narratives themselves come from ADOS-2 administrations conducted by research-reliable clinicians, so the elicitation context is a standardised clinical assessment rather than a naturalistic setting. This has the same double edge noted in the OHSU studies: the standardisation makes narratives comparable across participants and the data are a by-product of an assessment already being conducted, but the assessment is specifically designed to elicit autism-related behaviour, so performance may not transfer to spontaneous narration. The authors raise the related point about narrative context, citing evidence that 'participants with ASD exhibit lower performance in less structured tasks (i.e., narratives of personal experiences, conversation) than more structured picture book tasks' - which implies, though the authors do not draw the inference explicitly, that a less structured elicitation might yield stronger rather than weaker classification.

**S-084** [local_bc62bc4b] — *Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening*

A purpose-built eye-tracking laboratory at a university research centre for children with special needs, with lighting described as optimised for tracking. The acquisition arrangement is described with the care a toddler paradigm requires: children sat approximately 60 cm from the screen either alone or on a parent's lap, screen distance and height adjusted individually, a researcher accompanying each parent-child pair throughout, a five-point calibration using a crying cartoon as the attention-catching target, and calibration repeated for each child until deviation in both x and y fell below one degree. Repeating calibration to a stated tolerance rather than accepting the first attempt is a discipline few studies here report. The setting is a controlled laboratory rather than a clinic or home, which the authors implicitly acknowledge as a limitation of the field when they call for 'less intrusive screening instruments that do not require tightly controlled environments' - a requirement their own paradigm does not yet meet.

**S-085** [local_889d9bd6] — *Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children*

A hospital-based child mental health and rehabilitation centre in Shenzhen, with testing conducted in 'a dark and soundproof room' at a fixed 65 cm viewing distance with the child's centre of vision aligned to the monitor centre. This is a tightly controlled laboratory environment rather than a point-of-care setting, which suits the measurement but limits the deployment claim - a dark soundproof room with a calibrated remote tracker is not a paediatric waiting area. The recruitment asymmetry is present but mitigated: autistic children came from the hospital's rehabilitation centre while comparison children came either from a local kindergarten or from routine check-ups at the same hospital's outpatient ward, so a proportion of the comparison group was recruited within the same institution.

**S-086** [local_361b59fb] — *Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

Fourteen sites across six US states, recruiting children 'representing a population of patients that HCPs would see in their primary care practice' - so the sampling frame is the referral population the tool is intended for, not a research cohort. The participating clinicians are equally representative: 15 physicians trained in general pediatrics or family medicine, spanning 1 to 38 years of post-residency experience, and explicitly 'not recruited on the basis of any special interest or experience of ASD diagnosis, beyond what was delivered as part of their standard training'. That last detail matters more than it might appear: a diagnostic aid evaluated only with enthusiastic autism-interested clinicians would not establish that ordinary primary care physicians can use it. Thirteen point nine percent of clinician assessments were conducted by telemedicine rather than in person, with 'no evidence of performance degradation' when done remotely - an incidental finding produced by the COVID-19 disruption that speaks directly to rural and low-access deployment.

**S-087** [local_afdb603d] — *Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.*

Two entirely different settings, and this is the study's defining problem. Autistic children were recorded in June 2019 by a designated speech therapist, in the room where they usually play, during a session that 'started with activities generally done during the treatment session so the child would act in the most spontaneous way', with 'a video camera placed on a tree-legged support'. Comparison children were recorded later by their own parents at home on the parents' phones, because 'due to the COVID-19 pandemic, it was impossible to collect the data in situ'. The clinical setting was designed carefully for the autistic children's comfort, which is good practice for eliciting natural speech and simultaneously guarantees a fixed, distant, uncontrolled microphone position in a room with unknown reverberation. A parent holding a phone produces a close-miked, low-noise, high-signal recording. Since the paper's entire yield is acoustic, the recording chain is not a nuisance variable but a direct competitor for every reported effect.

**S-088** [local_4f7e7eb3] — *Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques*

Not reported. The paper describes neither the room, the country, the recruitment route, the eye tracker nor the acquisition protocol for the source recordings. The only settings named are the four institutions where the analysis was carried out and the hardware on which it ran - a fifth-generation i5 processor with 8 GB RAM and a 4 GB GPU, specified more precisely than anything about the children.

**S-089** [local_db6c2d7c] — *Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With*

Participants' own homes with no researcher present, no environmental control and no equipment standardisation - and the paper's positioning depends on this. The related-work section is unusually specific in critiquing prior computer-vision studies on precisely this point, noting that Hashemi and Chang 'controlled the room lighting and distance of the camera from the participant's face' and concluding that 'the ability of these techniques to translate to natural nonclinical environments and unstructured tasks remains to be explored'. The consequences are then reported rather than hidden: 'excessive camera movement and poor lighting conditions rendered some frames in our data set too blurry for use', and 'other adults or siblings would often join in gameplay, resulting in multiple faces in the frame'. Roughly 43% of frames were discarded by the automated quality filters. This is the most uncontrolled acquisition setting in the corpus and the paper treats that as its subject rather than as noise.

**S-090** [local_8b5fb23b] — *Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms*

Not reported for the data collection. The literature review states, summarising the source publication, that recordings used 'an SMI RED series mobile eye tracker' while participants 'watched a series of videos to stimulate eye movement across the screen', but nothing about the room, country, recruitment or protocol is restated in the methods. The only settings named are the two analysing institutions and the compute environments - Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio Classic, Google Colaboratory, and a specified Dell laptop.

**S-091** [local_6dcefc34] — *Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism*

Participants' own homes with no researcher present, no equipment provision and no environmental control - 'this study was conducted remotely' - which is the design's entire point. The equity argument is developed at length and with specifics rather than as a gesture: prevalence is similar in rural (0.9%) and urban (1.0%) areas but rural communities face limited access to identification and intervention services; up to 80% of US counties lack sufficient diagnostic resources; and existing questionnaire-based screening 'require[s] literacy and perform[s] worse with non-white and lower education caregivers', so digitising those questionnaires 'risks exacerbating current disparities'. The proposed alternative - deriving signal from behaviour rather than from caregiver report - would in principle be insensitive to caregiver literacy, though the game itself still requires a smartphone, internet access and English.

**S-092** [local_65974fc7] — *Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction*

China, with collection organised through Anhui Medical University, the Anhui Autism Association and special education schools. The recording environment is not described in text at all - a figure is referenced showing the collection setup, but no room, distance, microphone or channel configuration is stated. This gap is not merely a reporting deficiency here but a methodological one, because time-frequency ICA is a multichannel technique: it requires at least two observation channels to separate sources, and which two signals constitute those channels determines entirely what the unmixing matrix represents. Without the recording configuration the paper's central feature construction cannot be reconstructed or evaluated.

**S-093** [local_988c462e] — *The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation*

The ADOS examination room at a national autism research centre, with recording conditions described honestly rather than idealised: a single microphone 1-2 metres from the child, in an environment with 'background noise, reverberation, and overlapping speech', and with both child and therapist free to move during the session. The resulting average signal-to-noise ratio of child speech is reported as 12 +/- 5 dB and named as a limitation. The authors position this deliberately against better-equipped prior work, noting that another group 'applied a diarization method for speech signals using four microphones, including a beamforming algorithm that improved their recordings' SNR' and that 'even though our proposed diarization methods achieved higher DER values, we used only one distant microphone recorded in a noisy environment'. Accepting worse acquisition in exchange for deployability in an ordinary clinic room is a defensible trade and is argued as such.

**S-094** [local_76de1c03] — *The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children*

The kindergartens the children attended, with a maximum of three children assessed per visit. Both groups were assessed in the same settings under the same protocol, which removes the clinic-versus-school recruitment asymmetry that this review has documented as a confound across the photograph, audio and thermal branches. Bringing a portable robot to a child's own nursery is also the deployment scenario the work envisages, so the data were collected under the conditions in which the method would be used - a property shared with only a few studies in this corpus, notably the population-based one-legged-standing study and the routine-examination work.

**S-095** [local_3ba6d25c] — *Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach*

Single site in Shenzhen, China. Autistic children were recruited from a first-class mental health centre (Shenzhen Kangning Hospital / Shenzhen Mental Health Center, the affiliation of the child-psychiatry co-author); TD children came from nearby communities. The recording setting is a controlled but not screen-based one: a face-to-face structured conversation with an interviewer at a fixed 80 cm distance, with the child wearing eye-tracking glasses. This is a clinic-adjacent laboratory setting, not a naturalistic home or classroom setting and not a primary-care setting, so the recruitment path guarantees a spectrum-narrow, already-diagnosed autistic sample facing an unselected community control group - the classic case-control geometry whose accuracy does not transfer to a screening population.

**S-096** [local_70a30e2b] — *A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features*

Single site: an autism centre in Tehran, Iran. Children played in a 3 x 4 m room at the centre for 3-5 minutes, alone or accompanied by a parent or therapist, with a child psychologist from the centre supervising. This creates a gap between the study as conducted and the study as framed: the paper's central argument is for a home-based IoT device usable 'at homes, daycares, or clinics' in natural settings without expert involvement, and it repeatedly criticises fMRI, EEG and robot-based approaches for requiring specialised centres - yet all the reported data were collected at a specialised centre under psychologist supervision. The recruitment geometry is also the standard case-control one: an already-identified autistic group from a service setting against a typically developing comparison group, at 61% autism prevalence, which is roughly 60 times the population base rate the device is proposed to screen at.

**S-097** [local_a22f97df] — *A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities*

Two sites in Campania, Italy, and the pairing is itself a confound. Autistic children came from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, which is also the employer of two of the four authors, and were undergoing psychomotor and speech therapy there. Typically developing children came from a mainstream primary school. Testing conditions were standardised across both groups - the same tablet, a table 65-70 cm high with the tablet within 20 cm of the edge, the examiner seated opposite, the same instruction protocol - so the acquisition chain does not differ by group in the way it does in some other studies in this corpus. But the recruitment geometry is the classic case-control one at 50% prevalence, and it carries a specific extra risk here: the autistic group's ongoing psychomotor therapy is an intervention directed precisely at the motor system whose kinematics constitute the study's entire feature set. Whether that therapy makes autistic movement more or less like typical movement, it makes the two groups differ in motor training history as well as in diagnosis.

**S-098** [local_c6853fe2] — *A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation*

Single site: the Department of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics, The First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, with engineering from Jilin University's School of Communication Engineering. The setting is the study's most distinctive feature and is used deliberately rather than incidentally. Recording took place during actual ADOS-2 screening sessions rather than in a purpose-built experiment, with four fixed cameras installed in the assessment room and the clinical protocol left untouched: the clinician stands where the protocol requires, calls in a natural tone, repeats and reinforces as the manual specifies, and an unspecified and varying number of parents may be present. The authors argue explicitly that this yields 'less laboratory control, more realistic child response, and a flexible number of accompanying parents', and they are right that this is the correct target distribution for a tool meant to sit inside a clinic. It also creates the engineering problem the pipeline is built to solve - the scene contains multiple adults, so person re-identification is needed simply to know which skeleton belongs to the child. The countervailing point is that the sample is a referred clinical series at a tertiary hospital with 29 of 30 children already autistic, which is the opposite of the community screening population the conclusion invokes when it proposes deployment 'in remote areas with underdeveloped medical care'.

**S-099** [local_f1b626c8] — *Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games*

Single-city, two-source recruitment in Tehran, with testing centralised at one laboratory. Autistic children came from the Daily Rehabilitation Clinic for Children with Special Disorders, a specialist service affiliated to the Family Institute of Shahid Beheshti University; comparison children came from Namjoo public elementary school. All eye tracking took place on one stationary system at the Faculty of Education and Psychology, Shahid Beheshti University, so unlike some studies in this corpus the acquisition chain is identical for both groups and no equipment confound arises. The recruitment geometry is nonetheless the standard clinic-versus-school case-control arrangement at 50% prevalence, and here it is compounded by asymmetric filtering: the autistic group faced five inclusion criteria and two exclusion criteria that removed 20% of those approached, while no criteria at all are stated for the school-recruited comparison group. The children who could not tolerate sitting at the computer or could not be calibrated - plausibly those with greater sensory or attentional difficulty - are precisely those absent from the analysed autistic sample.

**S-100** [local_6249bd63] — *Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior*

Single site: the Center for Autism Research at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, with the University of Pennsylvania. This is a specialist research centre, and both arms of the study reflect that - the participants are a research-registry sample assessed by Clinical Best Estimate on site, and the 19 raters are the centre's own doctoral clinicians and BA-level staff. The rater sample is therefore an unusually strong human benchmark (these are people who assess autistic adults professionally) and simultaneously a narrow one (they share an institution, a training culture and, plausibly, prior exposure to similar video material). The recording setting is a laboratory room with a floor-standing dual-camera device between the two conversation partners, and the paradigm is a semi-structured assessment rather than a clinical encounter. The recruitment geometry is case-control at 35.7% prevalence with deliberately clear-cut controls, which the authors flag as the key generalisation limit. Against that, the paradigm itself is deliberately designed for scalability outside such settings: the conversation partner is a non-clinician, the interaction lasts three minutes, and the only equipment is a camera - which is the basis for the claim that this could serve as a screening procedure.

**S-101** [local_8b9e0e8a] — *Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas*

Multi-centre, and deliberately so: children were recruited from multiple hospitals and schools in Shaanxi and Fujian provinces, chosen because 'medical conditions are relatively poor' there. This is one of only a few studies in this corpus with genuine site diversity, and the framing is consistent throughout - the paper's entire motivation is that screening in remote and low-income areas is understudied, and the design constraints follow from that premise rather than being retrofitted to it. Recording took place in a therapy room with the child 0.5 m from the monitor and at most two other people present, the mother and one researcher, which is a realistic community-clinic arrangement rather than a laboratory. The counterweight is the usual one: recruitment pairs hospital- or rehabilitation-identified autistic children against school-recruited comparison children at 42% prevalence, so the geometry remains case-control and the accuracy does not transfer to a community screening population. The authors do not compute what their operating point would mean at population prevalence, which for a proposed universal screening tool is the omission that matters most.

**S-102** [local_0e476686] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts*

There is no setting in the usual sense. No participants were recruited, contacted, assessed or informed; the study consists of harvesting five years of public posts from 252 identifiable Twitter accounts through the developer API and classifying them offline. The research group is at Universidad de Leon in Spain, and the compute is a single desktop workstation. Two features of this design deserve comment for the review. It is the only study in the corpus with no acquisition protocol at all, which means it is free of every acquisition confound that troubles the video and audio studies here - no equipment differences, no examiner effects, no laboratory artificiality - and simultaneously free of every control those protocols provide, since nothing about who wrote what, when, why, or to whom is known or standardised. And it is the only study here whose data subjects are neither aware of nor consenting to their participation, on a topic they disclosed publicly about themselves, which raises governance questions the paper does not engage with at all.

**S-103** [local_fbaf69bf] — *Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Four paediatric primary care clinics in the Duke Children's Primary Care network, with data captured during routine well-child visits. This is the study's most consequential design property and it addresses the corpus's most pervasive external-validity problem. Because recruitment is by clinic attendance rather than by diagnostic status, the sample is not a set of specialist-clinic cases contrasted with community controls but a screening cohort in which autism is identified prospectively at 9.2% prevalence. The measurement is embedded in the visit rather than added to it: the child sits on the caregiver's lap, an iPad is placed at 60 cm, and the movies play for a few minutes while the front camera records. Practical constraints of the setting are reported honestly as exclusion criteria - the child was too upset, the caregiver had no time or needed to mind siblings, consent could not be given in English or Spanish - which is a realistic account of what limits deployment in primary care and is more informative than a laboratory study's silence on the same issues. The one respect in which the setting is not fully representative is socioeconomic: 82.8% of caregivers held a college degree, which is far above the US population and reflects the catchment of an academic health system.

**S-104** [local_74416ba7] — *Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders*

Single-country, clinic-linked laboratory testing in Nara and Osaka, Japan, with participants recruited through the psychiatry department of Nara Medical University School of Medicine and Osaka Psychiatric Medical Center and tested on equipment at the Nara Institute of Science and Technology. The setting is a controlled screen-based assessment at a fixed 65 cm viewing distance rather than a naturalistic or point-of-care one, and no deployment scenario is proposed. Recruitment geometry is the standard clinical case-control arrangement, with the important qualification that both clinical groups come from psychiatric services and both are contrasted against the same actively screened control group, which is what makes the parallel comparison meaningful. One setting-related feature is unaddressed: the FEIT is a Western instrument and the participants are Japanese, so every trial involves other-race face processing, in a task whose entire outcome is where on a face the participant looks. Cross-cultural differences in face-scanning are well documented and the paper does not mention them.

**S-105** [local_7c6a5aa4] — *Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders*

There is no research setting: the data are telemetry from a free commercial iPad app used by people at home and in daily life across at least three continents over two and a half years, transmitted automatically to a backend server. This is the most naturalistic dataset in the corpus by a wide margin, and the authors are right that it represents a kind of scale that conventional autism research cannot reach - approximately 200 new users per month even at the end of the app's life, and around 1,800 in the busiest month. The corresponding losses are total. Nothing about the context of any interaction is known: whether the user was communicating with a person or exploring the interface, whether a therapist was present, whether the device was being used for its intended purpose, whether the account holder was the person using the screen. The logs were not designed for research and the authors say so plainly - collected 'for developers' debugging purposes and general system usage statistics', with 'little attention... given to the data structure and representation during the app development'. So the study inherits both the reach of consumer telemetry and its complete absence of experimental control, and it is candid about the latter in a way that makes the work easier to appraise.

**S-106** [local_8a706eaa] — *Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Multi-site in the sense that participants were drawn from across South Korea - Seoul, other metropolitan cities and self-governing provinces in equal-ish thirds - but recruitment channels differ completely by group. Autistic children came exclusively from the Child Psychiatry Outpatient Clinic of Seoul National University Hospital, described as receiving referrals of children at high risk of autism from throughout the country; comparison children came from day care centres. This is the standard case-control geometry, and here it is compounded by the deliberate selection of clinically distinct groups. The testing environment itself is standardised and low-tech - a quiet room, a height-adjustable chair, a table, a single consumer camera on a front-facing tripod - and this is presented as a feature, since the protocol is designed to be replicable without specialised equipment, calibration or trained raters. The claim that the setup is 'amenable to computer vision and DL and applicable to a wide range of neuropsychiatric conditions' is credible on the acquisition side; what it does not address is that the model was trained on children drawn from the extreme ends of a clinical distribution.

**S-107** [local_6b9484ce] — *Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking*

There is no study setting: all work was performed on Google Colab using a downloaded public dataset, at Vellore Institute of Technology in India, on images collected elsewhere. No children were recruited, tested, observed or consented for this work. This matters for how the study should be weighted in the review: it contributes no new evidence about autistic children and no new data, and its value lies entirely in being an additional independent modelling attempt on a dataset that several other included studies also use - which makes it a comparison point rather than a primary source.

**S-108** [local_c6a4ea7b] — *SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism*

No study setting: this is a computational reanalysis conducted at IIIT Delhi on transcripts collected years earlier in North American research laboratories. The three source settings are described only briefly and differ substantially - 30-minute free play sessions in one corpus, roughly 10 minutes of parent-child play in another, and natural mother-child interaction with 12-26 month olds in the third. That heterogeneity is the study's central unexamined problem, because it is not random with respect to the label: one corpus supplies autistic children exclusively. Any systematic difference between the corpora - transcription conventions, how disfluency and unintelligibility were marked, who the partner was, how long the session ran, what era the recording belongs to - is therefore partially aligned with diagnosis. Length-dependent features are normalised over conversation length, which handles the most obvious component, but transcription and partner effects are not addressable by normalisation and are not discussed.

**S-109** [local_5c43dffa] — *Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths*

Described only as a naturalistic study with a battery of eye-tracking video stimuli; no site, room, equipment or procedure is given in the retrieved text. The authorship spans seven United States institutions including the Yale Child Study Center and Seattle Children's Research Institute, and the paper notes that its paradigm 'share similarities with recent studies of autism biomarker Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT)', which locates the work within a serious clinical-research programme even though the report itself supplies no setting detail. The recruitment geometry cannot be assessed because recruitment is not described.

**S-110** [local_32da8ede] — *A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths*

No study setting: a computational reanalysis at two universities in Amman, Jordan, of images collected in France. The source acquisition setting is described in more detail than in the other reuses of this dataset and is worth recording, because it bears on what the scan-paths represent: a quiet room at university premises, physical white barriers erected to reduce visual distraction, the child seated alone or on a parent's lap approximately 60 cm from the screen, and all interaction conducted in French, the participants' first language. Typically developing children came from schools in the Hauts-de-France region and autistic children from specialised clinics - the standard clinic-versus-school case-control geometry, inherited rather than chosen.

**S-111** [local_15ed96cb] — *A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning*

The Israeli national well-baby surveillance programme, Tipat Halav, operating across 503 Ministry of Health clinics and covering 75% of the population, with the remaining quarter followed by two health maintenance organisations under identical national guidelines. Services span immunisation, growth monitoring, developmental surveillance and risk detection for mother and child, delivered by nurses with specific maternal and child health training alongside a developmental paediatrician, across approximately eleven visits from birth to age six. This is the only study in the review whose setting is the deployment setting: there is no recruitment, no research protocol, no laboratory and no case-control geometry, and the model is trained on exactly the data that would be available at the moment of use. The equity implication is drawn out explicitly - because the surveillance system is universal and free, a model built on it inherits multi-cultural representativeness that a recruited cohort could not, which the authors contrast with 'disparities in healthcare screening resources and in provider awareness' as barriers to detection. The counterweight is that the model's transferability depends on a health system that most countries do not have, and the authors say so, calling for cross-cultural validation covering 'the expression of signs, parental recognition, interpretation, and reporting levels'.

**S-112** [local_261afa51] — *AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: &#x201C;A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System&#x201D;*

No study setting exists. Images were downloaded from Kaggle and processed in Google Colab. The absence of a setting is not incidental: because the photographs were captured by unknown people, with unknown devices, in unknown circumstances, for unknown purposes, there is no acquisition chain to standardise and no way to establish that the two classes were photographed comparably. Every other study in this review that uses cameras controls the device, the distance, the lighting or at least the protocol; this one controls nothing, and the two classes are known to come from different sources.

**S-113** [local_3e88f3ce] — *An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks*

No study setting; ABIDE-I aggregates 17 sites internationally. Multi-site aggregation is the dataset's principal strength and its principal hazard: it provides scale and population diversity, and it introduces systematic between-site differences in scanner hardware, field strength, pulse sequence, head coil and recruitment practice that are well documented to support above-chance autism classification on their own.
