Participants were deliberately not told the glasses recorded gaze, with a post-experiment interview confirming none had realised; this is methodologically well motivated for behavioural naturalness but the deception is not discussed as an ethical consideration.

**S-060** [local_25e34bbd] — *Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification*

Cross-sectional; multiple phonations per child in a single session with no follow-up. Data are voice recordings of identifiable children with clinical diagnoses. No ethics committee approval, parental consent procedure, anonymisation statement or data-handling policy appears anywhere in the paper - a complete absence rather than a partial omission, and one that matters given the population.

**S-061** [local_4917150c] — *Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning*

Cross-sectional; a single session of approximately 10 minutes per child with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates rendered as abstract scanpath images and released openly. Governance is fully reported and its regulatory basis explained: informed written consent from parents or guardians after explanation of objectives, tasks and the right to withdraw; assent from every child; parents permitted to remain in the room; Helsinki conformity; and an explicit statement that ethics committee authorisation was not required under French recommendations for psychological research. Explaining why approval was unnecessary, rather than simply omitting the matter, is better practice than the silence found in much of the corpus.

**S-062** [local_241ec2c2] — *Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking*

Cross-sectional; a single 54-second viewing session per participant with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates over video stimuli. Governance is complete and detailed: named ethics committee approval with full protocol number, informed consent from participants or legal guardians, Helsinki conformity, and separately obtained consent for publication of identifying images from the individuals appearing in the stimulus videos - the last being a consideration almost never addressed elsewhere in this corpus.

**S-063** [local_36617ec5] — *Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis*

Cross-sectional; a single 24-minute session per child with no follow-up. Data are first-person video of identifiable children moving through a monitored environment. Governance is properly reported: informed consent from relatives after explanation of objectives and procedure, separate explicit consent to video recording of the child, ethics committee approval at the Polytechnic University of Valencia, and Helsinki conformity. A researcher remained present to monitor the child but 'attempted to intervene as little as possible (only in situations of device failure or cybersickness)' - the only mention of cybersickness in the corpus and a real consideration for immersive paradigms with children.

**S-064** [local_d8e804d6] — *Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms*

Cross-sectional; a single conversational session per child with no follow-up. Data are frontal and side video of identifiable children. Governance is partially reported - Helsinki conformity and written caregiver informed consent, with payment of 200 CNY disclosed - but no ethics committee approval or reference number is given.

**S-065** [local_712542ca] — *Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis of publicly released images. No ethics statement appears, which is largely defensible for reuse of open data, though the paper does not discuss the terms of that reuse. The Figshare repository is cited with its URL, and the originating study is credited.

**S-066** [local_0ab41681] — *Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder*

Cross-sectional; two sessions per child with no follow-up. Data are numeric marker trajectories, with per-participant clinical data published in tabular form but no identifiers. Governance is complete: written informed consent from parents or legal guardians, Helsinki-compliant design, and local ethical committee approval with a full reference number.

**S-067** [local_9ca9b2cc] — *Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment*

Longitudinal in design - a seven-week course of sessions per child, with 34 sessions contributing to the agreement analysis - which distinguishes it from the almost uniformly cross-sectional remainder of this review. Repeated measurement within children is the study's methodological point rather than an incidental feature. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the Social Sciences Research Ethical Committee of UAE University and by Al Ain Hospital, with signed parental consent letters. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text. Attrition is substantial and unexplained: 6 of 11 children completed the long-term study.

**S-068** [local_02fa4215] — *Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning*

Cross-sectional; a single questionnaire per family with no follow-up, though the items ask retrospectively about the perinatal period and early childhood. Data include maternal substance use, antidepressant use and miscarriage history - sensitive material about identifiable families collected partly through a commercial web form. No ethics committee approval, consent procedure, anonymisation policy or data-handling statement appears anywhere in the paper.

**S-069** [local_29a3fc54] — *Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism*

Cross-sectional; one ADOS-2 administration per participant with no follow-up, though the stated application as a treatment outcome measure would require longitudinal demonstration that the measures capture change, which the authors identify explicitly. Data are audio from videotaped clinical assessments. Governance is reported: informed written consent or assent from all participants and their parents, who also had to be fluent in English, and IRB review and approval at OHSU.

**S-070** [local_b7ec3755] — *Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a released benchmark; no follow-up. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere - a defensible position for public challenge data, but the paper never states that position, nor does it point to where the original approvals were obtained. A competing-interests declaration is present, though it declares only a domain-based conflict.

**S-071** [local_684969f6] — *Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis; no follow-up. No ethics, consent or IRB statement anywhere, despite acknowledged NIMH funding (R01MH121344-01) and a full competing-interests declaration - so the omission is not a matter of the paper lacking front-matter sections. Data are public challenge material, which mitigates but does not remove the expectation of a statement about the source approvals.

**S-072** [local_35004e74] — *Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children*

Cross-sectional analysis of data acquired within a longitudinal cohort; no longitudinal modelling is performed here, though the parent study follows children over time and the authors position the measure as suitable for tracking development. Ethics are reported in full: approval by the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Medicine of Geneva University, methods stated to conform to that institution's guidelines and regulations, informed written consent obtained from a parent or legal guardian for every child, and separate explicit consent for publication of identifying images from both the adults and the guardian of the child appearing in Figure 1. The privacy engineering is stronger still: reducing video to skeletons on a black background was adopted partly 'to ensure de-identification of the persons involved', so the analytic representation is itself the anonymisation - among the few instances in this corpus where sensitive video data are handled by design rather than by assurance.

**S-073** [local_fa91fc18] — *Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities*

Cross-sectional, one session per child, no follow-up, though the authors state a future aim of applying the method to younger children. Ethics are reported: approval by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities, University of Naples Federico II, with written informed consent from legal guardians obtained before the study. The data are coordinate streams rather than video or audio, so re-identification risk is intrinsically low, and a data availability statement commits to sharing raw data 'without undue reservation'.

**S-074** [local_115dfe8d] — *A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children*

Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. Ethics approval from the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee of Beijing Normal University, with informed consent obtained from all children with parental permission before enrollment. Funding sources are itemised (NSFC grants 62003228 and 61761166003, a Beijing Municipal Education Commission project, and a National Key R&D programme grant). No data availability statement, no data sharing plan and no discussion of how the EEG and gaze recordings are stored or protected - though both modalities are lower-identifiability than the video and audio data used elsewhere in this corpus.

**S-075** [local_5b7ea7dc] — *AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. Ethics are reported in full for a conference paper: approval by the Yonsei University IRB under number 4-2021-0845, conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and written informed consent from parents 'after receiving a detailed description of the study'. The data are identifiable video of young children, and although semantic segmentation removes background it retains faces; two children appear in published figures identified by participant codes. No data availability statement, no code release and no description of how the video corpus is stored or protected.

**S-076** [local_87fe26aa] — *Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: approval by the Institutional Review Board of Pingdingshan University under protocol code 068 dated 20 October 2020, conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and informed consent from all subjects involved. A data availability statement commits to sharing 'from the corresponding author on reasonable request'. Facial video of identifiable preschoolers is collected and no statement about its storage, retention or de-identification appears.

**S-077** [local_893ce2fa] — *An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a public dataset; no follow-up. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere, and no pointer is given to where the source dataset's approvals were obtained - an omission that is common for benchmark reuse in this corpus but is not acknowledged here either. A competing-interests declaration and a CRediT contribution statement are both present, so the absence of an ethics statement is not a matter of missing front matter.

**S-078** [local_dffe4127] — *Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals*

Cross-sectional with two measurement blocks on the same day separated by a break, drawn from a larger study that also included extensive behavioural assessment and neuroimaging. The authors identify the temporal limitation themselves as their second main limitation: 'we collected only two [blocks], both close in time and for similar (but distinct) video episodes', and argue that longer-term longitudinal data with dense state measures such as sleepiness and mood would be needed to distinguish measurement error from genuine state-dependent within-individual change. No ethics or consent statement appears in the extracted text, though the study is embedded in an established multi-site research programme. Copyright constraints on the sitcom prevented reproducing stimulus frames, and a royalty-free substitute image was used for the segmentation figure.

**S-079** [local_2b766683] — *Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech*

Cross-sectional, with data accumulated opportunistically over four years from 2018 to 2021 rather than in a defined recruitment window; no follow-up. Parental consent to share each recording is built into the app flow - families view the video after each session and choose whether to send it - which is a stronger form of ongoing consent than a single upfront authorisation, though no IRB approval statement appears in the extracted text. Privacy is treated substantively rather than as boilerplate, with a dedicated Discussion subsection arguing that the models' small size permits on-device inference and privacy-preserving federated learning, motivated explicitly by autism's stigmatisation and by parents who want a diagnostic signal but are unwilling to share video. A senior author declares founding Cognoa, a company developing digital paediatric health solutions.

**S-080** [local_2895bdf0] — *Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection*

Cross-sectional; one assessment per participant, with the intended application being longitudinal outcome measurement rather than cross-sectional classification. The authors are explicit that the reliability evidence needed for that application does not yet exist: 'we do not yet know the reliability (test-retest) and short-term stability of the measures we generated from transcripts and audio recordings', though they state they are currently undertaking those studies. This is an important self-limitation, since an outcome measure without demonstrated test-retest stability cannot distinguish treatment effect from measurement noise. Ethics reporting is complete: IRB review and approval at OHSU, with informed written consent or assent obtained from all participants and their parents at the initial visit. A data availability statement offers de-identified data on request and gives a public GitHub URL for the analysis code.

**S-081** [local_423b636b] — *Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers*

Cross-sectional in analysis but embedded in a prospective screening pathway, with diagnosis ascertained after app administration at a mean interval of 0.7 months (range -0.1 to 5.9). No longitudinal follow-up of the measures themselves, and the authors identify the developmental course of head movement differences as a future direction. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: written informed consent from caregivers and approval by the Duke University Health System Institutional Review Board under two named protocol numbers. Conflicts of interest are declared at length and are substantial: five authors developed technology related to the app which has been licensed, with both they and Duke University benefiting financially; the senior clinical author sits on four scientific advisory boards, consults for three companies including Apple and receives book royalties; both senior authors have invention disclosures and patent applications registered with Duke's licensing office; and the senior engineering author is affiliated with Apple, with a note that the work was done before and independently of that affiliation. The disclosure is exemplary in its completeness, and the commercial interest in the app is relevant context for a paper reporting the app's discriminative performance.

**S-082** [local_ffa35101] — *Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study*

Cross-sectional, one narration per participant, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is adequate but generic: informed assent and consent from all participants and guardians as applicable, approval by each institution's ethics committee, and conformity with the Declaration of Helsinki, without naming the committees or protocol numbers. Data sharing is a genuine strength and rare in this corpus - 'The minimal dataset and analytic scripts are available from the OSF database' with a working URL, so the analysis is independently verifiable even though raw audio is not shared, which is the appropriate handling of identifiable speech. A competing interest is declared: one author owns a startup company supported by a Hong Kong government technology scheme, with a statement that the reported research is not associated with it.

**S-083** [local_81ecbc6f] — *Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings*

Cross-sectional, one narration per participant, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is complete and unusually granular on consent, which was obtained separately from three parties as applicable: parents of participants under 16, parents of participants aged 16 and older, and the participants themselves - a structure that respects the assent of older adolescents and adults alongside parental consent. Approval came from the Faculty of Psychology, University of Warsaw Research Ethics Committee, with Declaration of Helsinki conformity stated. Data are withheld from public deposit on an explicit and appropriate privacy rationale - narrative transcripts of identifiable clinical assessments 'containing information that could compromise the privacy of the research participants' - with availability on request from the named authors. No competing interests, with Polish National Science Centre and University of Warsaw funding declared.

**S-084** [local_bc62bc4b] — *Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening*

Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. The most conspicuous reporting omission in the paper is ethical: no ethics committee approval, protocol number, consent or assent statement appears anywhere in the extracted text, despite the participants being toddlers with clinical diagnoses recruited through hospitals and clinics. Funding by the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey is acknowledged and a conflict-of-interest declaration is present, so the absence is not a matter of missing front matter. Against this, data sharing is handled well: an open practices statement provides a URL at which 'the study data for all machine learning experiments are available', which is more than most studies here offer and which would in principle allow the sample-size discrepancy to be resolved externally.

**S-085** [local_889d9bd6] — *Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children*

Cross-sectional with two age cohorts sampled independently rather than followed longitudinally - so the developmental claim rests on a cross-sectional age contrast, which the design cannot distinguish from cohort effects, though this is a standard and reasonable compromise. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the Ethics Committee of Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital, written informed consent from legal guardians, and separate written consent obtained specifically for publication of potentially identifiable images or data. Partial overlap with a prior publication by the same group is disclosed rather than concealed: 'A portion of preschool data using paradigm (video clip) data had been used in a previous study... However, this study used more comprehensive paradigms and the findings presented in this study have never been published before.' Raw data are offered on request.

**S-086** [local_361b59fb] — *Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

Prospective and prospectively registered (NCT04151290) before initiation, conducted August 2019 to June 2020, with each child assessed once by the Device and once by specialists. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: centralised IRB review by IntegReview under protocol number Q170886, approved 19 July 2019, with the subsequent acquisition by Advarra noted, and informed consent from all caregivers. The COVID-19 disruption is disclosed in detail rather than smoothed over - the date of the national emergency, the number of sites closed (9 of 14), the reduced availability of those remaining, the estimate that 100 specialist visits could not be completed, the 97 that were completed afterwards, and the estimated drop-out rate absent the pandemic (26.2%). Data are withheld from public release on patient-sensitivity grounds but offered to qualified researchers under a data-sharing agreement, with the full protocol public on ClinicalTrials.gov. The code is proprietary and not available.

**S-087** [local_afdb603d] — *Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.*

Cross-sectional, one recording per child, with the two groups recorded at different times separated by the onset of the pandemic. Ethical reporting is incomplete: written consent from caregivers is stated for the autistic group, but no consent statement appears for the comparison group and no ethics committee approval is reported for either. Data are not shared. The analysis code, however, is publicly released on GitHub, which is rare in this corpus and materially improves verifiability of the computational steps even though the recordings themselves are unavailable.

**S-088** [local_4f7e7eb3] — *Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a public dataset; no follow-up. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere, and no pointer is given to where the source dataset's approvals were obtained. A data availability statement supplies the figshare URL for the source images with an access date, funding is acknowledged from the Najran University Scientific Research Deanship under a named grant, and a conflict-of-interest declaration is present - so the absence of an ethics statement is not a matter of missing front matter but of the section not being written.

**S-089** [local_db6c2d7c] — *Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With*

Cross-sectional, with videos accumulated opportunistically as families played and chose to share; no follow-up. Ethics approval from the Stanford IRB under a named eProtocol number, with parental consent to share each recording built into the app flow. Privacy is treated as a design constraint rather than a compliance step, and is one of the paper's three stated contributions: annotation was performed entirely computationally so that no human annotator ever viewed the footage, and the discussion explicitly contrasts this with prior manual-annotation work that 'may compromise the privacy of participants by providing annotators with access to video footage'. The senior author declares founding Cognoa and a co-author declares part-time consulting for the same company.

**S-090** [local_8b5fb23b] — *Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a public dataset; no follow-up. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere, and no pointer is given to the source dataset's approvals - an omission that is common for benchmark reuse in this corpus but is not acknowledged. Funding is not declared in the extracted text. The dataset is described throughout as publicly available but no URL or accession is given in the extracted portion.

**S-091** [local_6dcefc34] — *Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism*

Cross-sectional, with data accumulated opportunistically across nearly four years as families played and shared. Stanford Institutional Review Board approval is stated, though without a protocol number, and recruitment channels are named. The privacy position is a genuine design property rather than a claim: because the analysis uses only four event fields per trial - start time, end time, correct flag, skip flag - no imagery, audio or identifiable content is involved at all, which the authors present as enabling screening 'in a privacy-preserved manner' and contrast with computer-vision approaches where 'privacy concerns are at the forefront'. Among the three GuessWhat studies in this corpus, this is the only one whose modality raises no confidentiality question.

**S-092** [local_65974fc7] — *Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction*

Cross-sectional, with recordings accumulated over roughly two years and no follow-up. No ethics committee approval, consent statement or institutional review is mentioned anywhere, despite the study having purpose-collected approximately 7,000 speech recordings from more than 140 children recruited through special education schools and an autism association. Funding from two Anhui provincial science programmes is acknowledged. The dataset is presented as a contribution, with the authors noting that 'currently, there is no available public speech dataset for ASD children, which creates a big obstacle for related research', but no release, access route or sharing commitment is offered.

**S-093** [local_988c462e] — *The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation*

Cross-sectional, one recorded session per child, with no follow-up and no test-retest assessment of the severity estimate's stability. The absence of any ethics, consent or institutional review statement is the most conspicuous reporting gap: the study analyses audio recordings of clinical diagnostic assessments involving young children, their parents and clinicians, manually labelled by researchers, and no approval is mentioned in the extracted text. Funding from the Israel Ministry of Science and Technology is acknowledged with a grant number. No data availability statement and no code release.

**S-094** [local_76de1c03] — *The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children*

Cross-sectional, single session per child, with no follow-up or test-retest - the last being a real gap for a five-minute protocol proposed as a diagnostic aid, since the stability of a six-year-old's engagement with a novel robot across occasions is unknown and is exactly what a supplementary assessment tool would need. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: approval from the local research ethics committee at the University of Lower Silesia; legal guardians acquainted with the research aims and procedures; and signed consent forms covering both participation and, separately, the filming of the study. Separate consent for video recording is reported by very few studies in this review. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text.

**S-095** [local_3ba6d25c] — *Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach*

Cross-sectional; no longitudinal component, no follow-up, no repeat testing, no test-retest reliability for the entropy features. Ethics reporting is the weakest element of the paper: the retrieved full text contains no institutional review board statement, no Declaration of Helsinki statement, and no description of parental consent or child assent, despite the study involving minors, a clinical population, and a deliberate withholding of the device's true purpose from participants. The parent study (Zhao et al., 2021c) may carry the approval, but a secondary analysis reusing identifiable behavioural recordings should restate it. What is declared is a conflict-of-interest statement (none) and a detailed funding list of eight grants.

**S-096** [local_70a30e2b] — *A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features*

Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, no test-retest reliability for any feature - which matters for a device intended for repeated home use. Ethics reporting is unusual and problematic. Consent is handled well: parents were informed of the study, its goals, the procedure and their rights, informed consent was obtained in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, a child psychologist supervised, and data were stored under anonymous participant IDs without names or personal information. But formal ethics review was not obtained and the Institutional Review Board Statement argues that it was not needed: the proposal was accepted by the University of Tehran's School of ECE 'considering the privacy of participants and non-intrusiveness of the screening nature of the work', and the authors assert that 'this is a non-intrusive screening that does not require ethics approval as long as the privacy of the participants is considered', supplemented by the autism centre's own guidelines. A departmental engineering-school sign-off plus site guidelines is not equivalent to ethics-committee review of research on 3-6 year old children with developmental disabilities, and the non-intrusiveness of the measurement does not remove the need for review of recruitment, consent and data handling in a vulnerable population.

**S-097** [local_a22f97df] — *A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities*

Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, no test-retest reliability for any kinematic feature - which matters for a proposal to use feature values as clinical thresholds, since a threshold is only useful if the measurement is stable within a child across occasions. Ethics reporting is complete and appropriate: the study was reviewed and approved by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities, University of Naples Federico II, and written informed consent was obtained from participants' legal guardians. The conflict-of-interest statement discloses that two authors were employed by Neapolisanit S.R.L., the rehabilitation centre from which the autistic participants were recruited - a material disclosure, correctly made. Funding is not reported.

**S-098** [local_c6853fe2] — *A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation*

Cross-sectional single session with no follow-up and no test-retest assessment. Since the pipeline is proposed as a clinical scoring aid, the absence of any repeat measurement means nothing is known about whether the same child assessed twice would receive the same automated score. Ethics reporting is minimal but present in both required elements: 'these experiments have passed an ethical review', with no committee, institution or approval number named, and informed consent obtained from the children's parents before each session. A privacy measure is also implemented and disclosed - participants' faces are mosaicked in the published figures, with the authors noting that this may obscure the facial joints they wish to illustrate - and the data are declared confidential rather than released. For video recorded on preschool children with disabilities during clinical assessment, the consent and privacy handling is appropriate; the ethics statement is thinner than the norm and would not satisfy most journals' current reporting requirements.

**S-099** [local_f1b626c8] — *Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games*

Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, no test-retest reliability. Ethics reporting is the strongest element of the paper's governance: approval was obtained from the Research Ethics Committee of Islamic Azad University, Tehran Science and Research Branch, with the approval identifier IR.IAU.SRB.REC.1401.152 stated in a dedicated Ethics subsection and repeated in the declarations - a named committee and a verifiable reference number, which most reports in this corpus do not provide. Consent is handled less completely: parental consent appears as an inclusion criterion for the autistic group only, with no consent statement for the school-recruited comparison children and no mention of child assent. Funding (none received) and competing interests (none) are declared.

**S-100** [local_6249bd63] — *Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior*

Cross-sectional, single session per participant, no follow-up and no test-retest assessment of the coordination features. Ethics governance is well handled: the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, and consent was evidently granular rather than blanket, since two of the 44 enrolled participants were excluded specifically because of 'their lack of consent for this particular set of experiments' - a per-experiment consent regime that is a positive marker of data governance in a study involving identifiable facial video. Confederates were blinded to diagnostic status. The human raters were not blinded in the ordinary sense - they were told that every participant was either a confirmed autism case or a deliberately recruited clear control - which is appropriate for calibrating a benchmark but does mean their task was easier than a real screening decision. Funding from four NIH grants is fully itemised. No competing-interests statement appears in the retrieved text, which is a gap given that the work develops a potential clinical tool.

**S-101** [local_8b9e0e8a] — *Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas*

Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, and no test-retest reliability - which is a real gap for a tool proposed for repeated community screening. The nearest thing to a temporal analysis is Fig. 8, which tracks how the sample and the classification results evolved across the four quarters of 2021, showing 2-4 misclassified cases in an initial 40-child phase and stable results thereafter; this is a development log rather than a validation, but it is unusually transparent about how the model matured alongside the dataset. Ethics reporting is complete for approval and thin for consent: the study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Northwestern Polytechnical University under protocol 202002032, with all procedures conducted in accordance with the latest revision of the Declaration of Helsinki - a named committee and a protocol number, better than most reports here - but no parental consent or child assent statement appears, despite the participants being 3-6 year olds. Funding from three National Natural Science Foundation of China grants is itemised. No competing-interests statement appears.

**S-102** [local_0e476686] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts*

Cross-sectional in analysis though the data span five years, with no temporal modelling: tweets from 2017 and 2022 are pooled and classified independently, so nothing is learned about stability or change over time, and no test-retest or within-user consistency is examined. Ethics is the study's most serious deficiency and is entirely absent. There is no institutional review board approval, no ethics committee, no research-ethics statement, no consent, and no discussion of the ethics of the enterprise. The data are health-related disclosures made by identifiable individuals about themselves, harvested without their knowledge and used to train a classifier whose stated purpose is to identify people who may be autistic. The only privacy measure described is the redaction of username, location and date of birth from two example biographies reproduced as a figure, done 'in compliance with Twitter's policies' - a platform-terms consideration rather than a research-ethics one. The paper does not consider whether the autistic Twitter community, which is organised and vocal, would regard such a classifier as acceptable; whether a model that infers autism from public text could be used against the people it identifies; or whether public availability implies availability for this purpose. Given that several of the search keywords are terms this community coined for itself, the omission is conspicuous.

**S-103** [local_fbaf69bf] — *Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, and no test-retest reliability of the entropy measure - which matters for a biomarker proposed for treatment monitoring, since sensitivity to change requires knowing the measurement's stability. Governance is exemplary by the standards of this corpus. The study was approved by the Duke University Health System Institutional Review Board under two protocol numbers (Pro00085434, Pro00085435), written informed consent was obtained from caregivers or legal guardians, and inability to consent in English or Spanish is disclosed as an exclusion criterion rather than passed over. Funding from eight sources including four NIH grants and four technology companies is itemised, with an explicit statement that 'the funders had no direct role in the study design, data analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript'. The competing-interests statement is the longest in this corpus and is unusually forthcoming: several authors developed technology licensed to Apple and have benefited financially, one is CEO of a company and holds a granted patent plus three applications alongside numerous advisory and consulting relationships, and another was affiliated with Apple at publication. Crucially, a structural mitigation is described rather than merely asserted: 'Data analysis for this project is constantly independently reviewed by Scott Compton, who has no conflict of interest related to this work', and Compton is a named co-author. Given the commercial stakes attached to a tablet-based autism screening app, an independent analysis reviewer is the right safeguard and is worth noting as a practice other groups could adopt.

**S-104** [local_74416ba7] — *Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders*

Cross-sectional, single session per participant, no follow-up and no test-retest reliability for any gaze feature. The two datasets are age-stratified rather than longitudinal - adults and children are separate samples, not the same people at two ages - although the introduction motivates the design partly by an interest in 'the developmental trajectory in processing emotional stimuli in neurodevelopmental conditions', and the parallel analysis does permit a cautious comparison across age groups, which the discussion makes: anger is highly weighted in both the adult and child autism models, suggesting a possible common specificity. Ethics reporting is complete for approval and consent: the data collection was approved by ethics committees at both Nara Medical University and Nara Institute of Science and Technology, the procedure was explained at the start of recording and informed consent obtained, and the formal ethics statement records written informed consent from participants' legal guardian or next of kin. Funding from a single CREST grant is stated, and competing interests are declared as none.

**S-105** [local_7c6a5aa4] — *Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders*

Longitudinal in data span and cross-sectional in analysis: usage covers January 2012 to May 2014 with per-month user and event counts charted, but the classification treats windows as exchangeable and models nothing about change over time. This is a striking missed opportunity, since AAC usage is expected to develop as a user learns the system and, in the acquired-condition groups, may decline with disease progression - and the conclusion identifies 'the stability of predictions over time' as future work. Ethics is the study's most serious deficiency and is entirely absent. There is no institutional review board approval, no ethics committee, no research-ethics statement and no consent process for research use of the telemetry, which was gathered automatically for debugging from a commercial product. The only safeguard reported is that 'all the recorded data were encrypted and de-identified', and the only choice offered to users concerned the optional survey. The population includes 75 users aged 10 or under and a further 20 aged 11-18 among survey respondents alone, plus an unknown number among the roughly 5,192 unlabelled users, and every one of them is a person with a communication impairment whose attempts to speak are the data. Retrospective research use of consumer telemetry from disabled children, without consent or ethical review and without any discussion of either, is a governance gap that a four-page conference format does not excuse. No competing-interests statement appears despite three commercial or industry-lab affiliations among the authors and the app itself having been a commercial product.

**S-106** [local_8a706eaa] — *Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Prospective and cross-sectional: children were enrolled and assessed over an eleven-month window, but each contributed a single 10-minute session with no follow-up, no repeat testing and no test-retest reliability for the model's output - a gap for a system proposed as a severity-assessment tool, since severity assessment implies sensitivity to change. The nearest thing to a temporal analysis is the within-session compliance study across repeated trials, which is genuinely informative about habituation but says nothing about stability across days. Governance is complete and well documented. The study was approved by the Yonsei University Health System Institutional Review Board, caregivers gave written informed consent, and the report follows the STARD reporting guideline for diagnostic accuracy studies - one of very few studies in this corpus to adopt a formal reporting standard, and the reason its participant table, flow accounting and confidence intervals are as complete as they are. Funding is from a Korean government physician-scientist training programme with an explicit no-role statement. The competing-interests disclosure is material and full: two authors hold issued patents on the method and apparatus for diagnosing developmental disability and its severity in toddlers based on joint attention, a third has a patent pending, two report non-financial support from LumanLab Inc, one is affiliated to that company, and the acknowledgements thank LumanLab's administrative, regulatory and data management staff. So the method is patented by its developers and a commercial entity participated in data management - disclosed properly, but without any independent-analysis safeguard of the kind reported by the Duke group elsewhere in this corpus.

**S-107** [local_6b9484ce] — *Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking*

Cross-sectional by inheritance; the study performs no temporal analysis and could not. No ethics statement of any kind appears, which for a secondary analysis of published de-identified images is defensible in substance but is still a reporting omission - the source dataset's approvals are not referenced. No funding statement and no competing-interests declaration appear either. The paper is a four-to-six page conference contribution and these omissions are typical of that format, but they are omissions nonetheless.

**S-108** [local_c6a4ea7b] — *SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism*

Cross-sectional by inheritance, with one session per child and no temporal analysis. The pooling of corpora spanning 12 months to 8 years creates something that looks like developmental range but is not a developmental design, since age is confounded with corpus and with label. No ethics statement appears, which is defensible for a secondary analysis of a public research corpus but is still an omission - the CHILDES databank operates under its own conditions of use and no reference to the source studies' approvals is made. Funding from an Indian government start-up research grant with partial industry-linked centre support is acknowledged; no competing-interests statement is provided.

**S-109** [local_5c43dffa] — *Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths*

Cross-sectional with no follow-up and no test-retest assessment. The study is nonetheless the most thorough in this corpus on within-trial temporal structure: gaze is analysed in successive non-overlapping 3-second windows across the first 15 seconds, and separately in 1-second sub-windows, revealing that discrimination is highest in the first three seconds (76.3%) and declines steadily thereafter (71.7%, 69.3%, 71.0%, 70.2%). That is a substantive finding about when social attention differentiates, and it has a practical implication the paper does not draw out - that a shorter protocol may lose little. No ethics approval, consent statement, or competing-interests declaration appears in the retrieved text, which for a study of children including infants is a significant reporting omission whatever the underlying governance. Funding from an NIH K01 award and a Simons Foundation grant is stated.

**S-110** [local_32da8ede] — *A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths*

Cross-sectional by inheritance, with no temporal analysis. Ethics is handled by reference to the source study: procedures 'were conducted following the ethical standards set by the institutional and/or national research committee, as well as in compliance with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its subsequent amendments'. Citing the originating study's ethical basis is appropriate practice for a secondary analysis and is more than most dataset-reuse papers in this corpus do. No funding statement and no competing-interests declaration appear in the retrieved text.

**S-111** [local_15ed96cb] — *A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning*

Genuinely longitudinal in structure and, by the standards of this review, exemplary in its handling of time. Predictors are drawn only from measurements taken up to 24 months and the outcome only from diagnoses recorded after 24 months, an ordering imposed deliberately 'to develop a model that minimizes data leakage from diagnosis to predictors'. Mean age at recorded diagnosis was 37.5 months (SD 13.3), so the model predicts on average more than a year ahead of the clinical event. Follow-up varies by birth cohort, and the authors address this both by noting the smaller autism proportion among 2019 births and by fitting a sensitivity model excluding that year. Within-child longitudinal structure is nonetheless collapsed - milestones are binarised to ever-passed versus only-failed - which the authors name as their first limitation and as a target for future work. Governance is complete: Ministry of Health Helsinki committee approval with number and date, consent waived on anonymisation grounds, extraction and anonymisation performed by dedicated Ministry personnel, access only through a secure platform, funding stated, and no competing interests declared.

**S-112** [local_261afa51] — *AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: &#x201C;A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System&#x201D;*

Cross-sectional in the trivial sense that photographs have no time dimension. There is no ethics statement, no consent, and no discussion of either. This is the most serious governance failure in the review, and it is worth stating precisely why. The dataset consists of identifiable photographs of children, obtained without their knowledge or their families' consent, in which one class was collected specifically because those images appeared in autism contexts - so the dataset itself asserts a health status about identifiable minors. Training on that dataset propagates the assertion; publishing a mobile application built on it would extend the assertion to new children photographed by whoever downloads it. None of this is acknowledged. No funding statement and no competing-interests declaration appear either.

**S-113** [local_3e88f3ce] — *An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks*

Cross-sectional analysis of a cross-sectional repository, with no longitudinal element - although ABIDE-I's phenotype records include age at scan across a wide range, so age is present as a covariate rather than as a design dimension. No ethics statement appears in the retrieved text; ABIDE-I contributing sites obtained their own approvals and consents, and secondary analysis of the public release conventionally proceeds without fresh approval. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text.

**S-114** [local_5b5f2237] — *Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development*

Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up and no test-retest reliability for the coherence measures. The temporal dimension that is analysed is within-conversation frequency rather than change over time: cross wavelet analysis decomposes coordination across 23 time scales from 0.1 to 10 s, which is a genuine and well-motivated use of temporal structure and locates the group difference specifically at the faster scales. Ethics reporting is complete: the protocol conformed to the Declaration of Helsinki, written informed consent was approved by the local ethics committee and signed by caregivers, and a separate declaration confirms Helsinki 2013 conformity, consent, and removal of identifying details. Participants were paid 200 CNY, which is disclosed. Funding from seven Chinese sources is itemised.

**S-115** [local_13426811] — *Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning*

Cross-sectional in analysis, though the corpus was assembled over seven years, with prospective recruitment and retrospective record examination running concurrently. No follow-up, no repeat sampling and no test-retest assessment of the linguistic measures - which matters for an instrument proposed as a diagnostic aid, since stability across occasions is unestablished. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: approval by the Hirosaki University Committee on Medical Ethics under IRB 2013-142, subsequently updated to 2018-168 with the previous number 2015-055 also given; the committee's information security guidelines followed; written consent from participants aged 20 and above and from both participants and guardians for those 19 and under; and anonymisation by alphanumeric identifier with identifiable utterances removed from transcripts. The last of these is a specific privacy measure appropriate to a corpus of personal spoken narratives and is not standard practice in this corpus. Funding from two JSPS KAKENHI grants is itemised and competing interests are declared as none.

**S-116** [local_948fa8d0] — *Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms*

Cross-sectional in the trivial sense. No ethics statement, consent, funding declaration or competing-interests statement appears anywhere. As with the companion study, the dataset consists of identifiable photographs of children obtained without their families' knowledge, with one class assembled specifically because those images appeared in autism contexts - so the collection asserts a health status about identifiable minors, and training and publishing on it propagates that assertion. None of this is acknowledged.

**S-117** [local_893dfc22] — *Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics statement appears, which is conventional for secondary use of two established consented affective-computing corpora. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text.

**S-118** [local_e7c16f2a] — *Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification*

Cross-sectional, single session per child, with recruitment compressed into five weeks. No follow-up and no test-retest reliability for any kinematic measure - which the authors identify as a limitation and address directly, recommending that 'the sample should be expanded and observed longitudinally'. Governance is complete: approval by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities at the University of Naples Federico II, written informed consent from parents of all participants described as guaranteeing full understanding, funding from two named sources with an explicit statement that the funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, publication decision or manuscript preparation, and a declaration of no competing interests. The data are deposited in a public GitHub repository, which is the only open data release among the included studies in this review.

**S-119** [local_5a7ab52d] — *Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain*

Cross-sectional as far as can be determined; no temporal structure is described. There is no ethics approval statement, no ethics committee, no consent statement and no governance description of any kind, for a study that reports manual collection of physiological measurements - heart rate and body temperature - and facial data from human subjects. This is the most complete governance absence among included studies that involve primary data collection. No funding or competing-interests statement appears either.

**S-120** [local_8253c2ec] — *Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis of public repositories, with no longitudinal element. No ethics statement, consent statement, funding declaration or competing-interest declaration appears in the retrieved text. Secondary use of public tabular repositories conventionally requires no fresh approval; the absence of a competing-interest statement is more notable given that the study's output is a deployed public-facing diagnostic tool.

**S-121** [local_1e9d0b71] — *Machine learning’s effectiveness*

Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up and no test-retest reliability. The absence of repeat measurement is a real gap for a proposed screening instrument, since a threshold decision on a single brief balance trial requires knowing how stable that trial is within a child. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the Ethics Committee of Nagasaki University under number 22051204, procedures conducted in accordance with institutional and national standards and the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its amendments, and written informed consent obtained from both the children and their guardians after a comprehensive explanation - the participants section specifies 'all subjects and their guardians provided written informed consent', so assent as well as parental consent. Funding from two JSPS Grants-in-Aid, JST MIRAI and JST CREST is itemised, and competing interests are declared as none.

**S-122** [local_b9e05a8f] — *Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network*

Cross-sectional and retrospective, with no longitudinal element and no repeat measurement. The ethics reporting is the notable gap: the paper contains no ethics statement, no institutional review board approval and no consent statement of any kind - a full-text search returns no occurrence of 'ethic' or 'consent'. Analysis of public datasets frequently proceeds without fresh approval, and PeerJ's declaration structure elicited funding, competing-interests, author-contribution and data-availability statements from these authors, so the omission is specific to human-subjects considerations. The data are identifiable photographs and video frames of children, harvested from personal websites, Facebook pages and YouTube, whose families posted them to seek support or raise awareness and did not consent to their use as training data for an autism classifier. The paper's conclusion envisages clinical deployment of a model built on that material without touching the question. Funding from King Faisal University grant KFU250488 is declared with a no-role statement, competing interests are declared as none, and the authors disclose that generative AI was used to correct the English.

**S-123** [local_0b0960c4] — *Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. The ethics declarations read in full: 'For this type of study, statement of human rights is not required' and 'For this type of study, informed consent is not required.' The data are EEG recordings of identifiable children obtained from another institution's research group with permission, so the declaration concerns secondary use rather than the original collection - but the paper does not distinguish the two, gives no reference to the originating approvals, and states the exemption in absolute terms. The data provider is acknowledged by name with the corpus URL, and competing interests are declared as none.

**S-124** [local_abad69fd] — *Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play*

Cross-sectional with a single session, no follow-up and no test-retest. The absence of repeat measurement matters for a proposed screening instrument built on a 90-second sample of a young child's behaviour, since day-to-day variation in a toddler's play is substantial and unquantified here. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the institute's ethics committee (anonymised in this version for blind review), conformity with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki, and written informed consent from primary caregivers before the study began. The competing-interest declaration is more informative than most and deserves recording: six of the eleven authors declare two patent applications arising from this research (202310300588.1 and 202310315701.3) while five declare none, and four authors are affiliated with ALSOLIFE, a Beijing autism-services company, alongside the Peking University Sixth Hospital group. The paper states it received no funding of any kind. The patents are declared without their claims being described, which is the relevant detail when the paper proposes the coding scheme and model as a deployable clinical tool.

**S-125** [local_cd7545e2] — *Predictive model using autism*

Cross-sectional with a single assessment session per participant and no follow-up, though the schizophrenia group's clinical characterisation includes age at onset and duration of illness, giving a longitudinal dimension to the covariates if not to the design. No test-retest data. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the Medical Ethics Committee of Showa University School of Medicine, conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and with local legislation and institutional requirements, and written informed consent from the participants themselves - who, being adults with measured IQ above 85, consented on their own behalf rather than through proxies, which is true of very few studies in this review. The authors declare no financial support of any kind and no competing interests, and acknowledge a named colleague for teaching them ADOS-2 administration and an editing service for language.

**S-126** [local_3ecb92bf] — *The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element and no repeat measurement. The ethics reporting is the thinnest of any included study that reports any at all: approval is attributed to 'The Child Pathological Speech Database and De-Engima Project administrations' - the dataset custodians rather than a named research ethics committee - and written informed consent was 'not required from the participants or the participants' legal guardians/next of kin in accordance with the national legislation and institutional requirements'. The contrast with the paper's own introduction is worth noting, since that section reflects specifically on research ethics committees and institutional review boards as safeguards for child data and presents transfer learning as a response to the difficulty of obtaining such data - the topic is raised seriously in the argument and handled formulaically in the declaration. The study received no funding and declares no competing interests, and author contributions are itemised.

**S-127** [local_4b02df7c] — *Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism*

Cross-sectional in analysis but drawing on nine years of longitudinal record, since users' full timelines from 2014 to 2022 were collected - a temporal depth no other included study approaches. That depth is used only descriptively, to show a rising trend in autism-related discussion, and no within-user temporal modelling is attempted. Ethics reporting is by a distance the most thorough in this review. The study holds University of Hawaii Institutional Review Board approval 2023-00248 under expedited review and passed a separate institutional data governance review that deemed it exempt 'due to the inherently public nature of the study data'. The authors then describe measures 'not required by the Institutional Review Board': encrypting user IDs to reduce reidentification risk, and anonymising user mentions and personal information such as email addresses within tweet text. They engage with the consent question substantively rather than resting on the public-data exemption, citing survey evidence that 84% of users were not or only slightly concerned about university research use while observing that 'this leaves a considerable portion of the population who remains concerned', and noting that privacy policies are 'long, with complex legal terms that the users may fail to understand or authorize'. They call for large-scale consent procedures and a regulatory framework for social media data mining. And they act: 'the data set and the model that we built using those data have been deleted. When the data set did exist, it was never shared outside of the original authors.' Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text.

**S-128** [local_7d7f1fcc] — *Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children*

The classification analysis is cross-sectional, but the participants are drawn from a longitudinal cohort explicitly established to study early development in autism, and the recruitment window spans eleven years - the longest in this review. No longitudinal modelling or follow-up outcome is reported here. Ethics reporting is complete and in one respect exceeds every other included study: approval by the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Geneva; written informed consent from a parent or legal guardian for all children; and separately, specific consent obtained from the child depicted in a figure, from their legal guardian and from the examiner for publication of identifying images in an open-access article. That last item is a detail no other paper here reports, and it stands in sharp contrast to the studies charted nearby that train on identifiable photographs of children scraped from support pages without any ethics statement at all. Six funding sources are itemised with grant numbers and a no-role statement, and competing interests are declared as none.

**S-129** [local_5a331ffe] — *Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element, despite the stated goal being a longitudinal monitoring platform. There is no ethics statement, no institutional review board reference and no consent statement anywhere in the paper - a full-text search returns no occurrence of the word. The data are identifiable home videos of children, published by their families for reasons of their own, from which faces were cropped and then annotated frame by frame for emotional state by five raters in order to build an autism classifier. Whether families posting a video of their child's stimming for a community of other parents thereby consent to its use as autism training data, and whether a child depicted at two or three years old has any interest in the matter, are questions the paper does not raise. The one place the authors do discuss the trustworthiness of their data concerns label accuracy rather than the ethics of use. Funding under the Malaysia-France Bilateral Research Grant IF040-2021 is declared, competing interests are declared as none, and the data availability statement reads in full: 'The authors do not have permission to share data' - which means the annotations offered as the paper's dataset contribution cannot be obtained.

**S-130** [local_45ef7022] — *A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features*

Cross-sectional despite being framed as continuous monitoring - no child is followed over time, no repeat measurement is analysed, and the 20 videos collected 'for real-time testing to assess the algorithm's performance in dynamic settings' are mentioned once and never reported on. Longitudinal study appears only as future work. The ethics position is the most serious in this review and is stated in five words: 'Ethical Approval. Not required.' There is no institutional review board reference, no ethics committee, no consent statement and no assent statement anywhere in the paper. The participants are 30 disabled children aged 5 to 15, resident at a named special school whose full postal address is printed in the article, thermally photographed during play, lessons and meals, in a study whose declared purpose is to automate adjustment of their psychiatric medication. Who authorised the imaging, whether guardians consented, and whether the children were told what was happening are all unaddressed. This exceeds the ethics gaps recorded elsewhere in this review for the web-scraping studies, because the data here were collected prospectively and in person from a dependent institutionalised population rather than harvested from material families had already made public. The study declares no funding; competing interests are not stated; and the data - identifiable thermal images of these children - are offered to anyone who asks.

**S-131** [local_0f5a351e] — *Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. The retrieved text terminates within the discussion section before the declarations, so ethics, funding, data-availability and competing-interest statements could not be assessed from what was available. What can be said is that the paper contains no discussion anywhere in its main text of the ethics of the underlying material - identifiable photographs of children aged 2 to 14, collected from the internet without their families' knowledge or consent, one class specifically from autism-related sources. The introduction does raise the ethical hazards of autism identification in general terms, naming labelling, effects on self-esteem and social relationships, and overdiagnosis, which is more than the rest of this branch offers; it does not extend that concern to the provenance of its own training data.

**S-132** [local_786b6280] — *Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis of archived transcripts, one session per child, with no follow-up. The ethics position is stated briefly and is defensible: 'The data used in this research is from a publicly available database. The information was gathered with informed consent. This research will not involve any personal information.' Unlike the web-scraping and institutional-imaging studies charted elsewhere in this review, the underlying material was collected for research purposes with consent obtained at source and archived under a governance framework designed for reuse, so a secondary analysis of it raises materially different questions from harvesting children's photographs from support pages or thermally imaging pupils at a special school. Funding and competing interests are not stated.

**S-133** [local_879ec69b] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics statement appears, which is conventional for analysis of two public corpora collected under their originators' governance. The paper does address a related concern substantively, and its argument deserves recording: it notes that prior eye-tracking work 'raised concerns about ensuring anonymity' and identifies 'the issue of privacy protection associated with gaze data', then positions skeleton representation as the answer. Joint coordinates carry no face, appearance, clothing, room or lighting information, so a skeleton corpus is inherently less identifying than the video or photograph corpora that dominate this branch. That is a real privacy property of the modality, argued as a motivation rather than noted as a side effect, and it aligns with the same reasoning that led the Geneva group charted elsewhere in this review to render pose as skeleton-on-black and to release a de-identified pose subsample when raw video could not be shared. Funding from the University of Aizu Competitive Research Fund is declared, competing interests are declared as none, and both datasets are identified with public locations.

**S-134** [local_93e5d23d] — *Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element, though the paper argues that the modality would support one - cry 'allows for longitudinal assessment, enabling researchers to track developmental changes over time', which is a real advantage of a signal that can be captured repeatedly at home at no cost. Ethics reporting is complete for the original collection: approval by the ethics committee of Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences and Health Services in Tehran, with 'comprehensive informed consent ... acquired from the parents or legal guardians' before enrolment, specified as covering objectives, procedures and possible advantages and risks. The competing-interest declaration is the fullest in this review and is itemised by individual: two authors are employed by Zoundream AG, a commercial infant-cry-analysis company, one of them being a co-founder holding stock; a third received compensation as a member of its scientific advisory board; the fourth declares none; and the company funded the research alongside four public and quasi-public funders. Naming employment, founder status, equity and advisory compensation separately is exactly what a commercially sponsored diagnostic-technology study should do, and it allows a reader to weigh the translational claims accordingly.

**S-135** [local_a0d73248] — *Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a public tabular repository, with no longitudinal element. No ethics, consent, funding or competing-interest statement appears in the retrieved text; secondary use of a public tabular dataset conventionally requires no fresh approval.

**S-136** [local_4ceee075] — *Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics*

Cross-sectional, single session per child, with no follow-up or test-retest. The ethics position is the study's most serious reporting failure. There is no institutional review board reference, no ethics committee, no consent statement and no assent statement anywhere in the paper - a full-text search returns no occurrence of the word 'consent'. The only appearance of ethics is in the data availability statement, which cites 'privacy and ethical considerations' as grounds for withholding the data, so the authors evidently regard the material as ethically sensitive while documenting no approval for having collected it. This is a prospective study that recruited 100 children including 50 autistic children and recorded more than 16 hours of video of them, so unlike several other studies in this review the omission cannot be attributed to secondary-data status. Competing interests are declared as none; funding is not stated in the retrieved text.

**S-137** [local_84bcd4ed] — *Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of*

Cross-sectional secondary image analysis with no longitudinal element. The ethics reporting is better than most of this branch and deserves credit: approval by the Faculty of Computers and Information Research Ethics Committee with a stated approval code (2024 01 004), conformity to the Declaration of Helsinki, and explicit reference to 'ethical standards regarding data privacy and the responsible use of AI in health-related research'. Very few studies in the facial-image branch obtain or report any approval at all. Two features of the statement are nonetheless questionable. It describes the images as coming from 'a publicly available, anonymized dataset on Kaggle, ensuring no personally identifiable information was used' - but a photograph of a face is among the most directly identifying data types that exists, and the same study processes those photographs with a face-recognition library whose purpose is to establish identity from them; calling such a corpus anonymised misstates what it is. And the claim that 'no direct contact with human participants occurred' is accurate and is precisely what makes the gelotophobia component unevaluable, since it means no one was ever assessed for the condition the system claims to detect. The study declares no funding and no competing interests, and supplies the GELOPH<15> as a supplementary appendix.

**S-138** [local_d97673f4] — *Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics or consent statement appears anywhere in the paper, in work whose training data are identifiable photographs of children collected from the internet without their families' knowledge. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text.

**S-139** [local_86a67a4f] — *Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children*

Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics or consent statement appears anywhere, for work whose training data are identifiable photographs of children collected from the internet without their families' knowledge. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text.

**S-140** [local_0a39cca9] — *Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy*

Cross-sectional secondary and clinic-sourced analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics or consent statement appears anywhere in the paper. This is a more serious omission than for the purely Kaggle-based studies charted elsewhere in this review: part of the corpus consists of facial photographs of children attending an autism centre in Semarang, so identifiable images of clinically attending children were obtained and used with no reported institutional approval and no consent process. Funding and competing interests are not stated.

**S-141** [local_7432ffd7] — *Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models*

Cross-sectional, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is absent entirely - no approval statement, no committee, no consent statement, and the word ethic does not appear in the article. This is a study of clinically labelled disabled children published in a medical journal with a full data-availability statement and no ethics statement of any kind. Only the public status of the source dataset is offered, which addresses data access, not the ethics of the analysis or of the diagnostic claim being made.

**S-142** [local_8ff20c48] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning*

Cross-sectional, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is among the better examples in this corpus in form: Declaration of Helsinki compliance, named committee, protocol number BUIC/H11/SE/46113 with an approval date of 3 April 2023, informed parental consent as an inclusion criterion, and exclusion of children with comorbid neurological disorders. The reviewing body is a Software Engineering Department ethical review committee rather than a clinical or psychological board, which is a mismatch given that the study collects health data on disabled children and advertises a diagnostic use.

**S-143** [local_986436f2] — *Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost*

Cross-sectional. Ethics reporting is absent: the declarations section contains only a conflict-of-interest line. There is no approval, no consent statement, and no consideration of the fact that the corpus consists of photographs of identifiable children scraped from the web and redistributed with an autism label attached.
