Reported by the authors: very small sample; classifier highly specific to the training sample (preschool, low-functioning); need for females, high-functioning children and adults; no ADOS on the full sample; no other neurodevelopmental comparison groups; predictive value constrained by population base rate. Identifiable in review: strong male skew (25/30 male); chronological-age and IQ imbalance between groups confounded with diagnosis; single-site recruitment; maximum-over-feature-subsets accuracy reporting; feature selection not demonstrably nested within the LOO loop.

**S-003** [local_dc5fc4bb] — *ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data*

Reported by the authors: class imbalance across groups, attributed to 'technical problems' and corrected by random oversampling to 30 per group. Identifiable in review: very small control group (n=13); no gender data at all, so sex bias cannot be assessed in a literature where ASD samples are typically male-skewed; no age matching; single-site outpatient recruitment; no reported handling of ASD-ADHD comorbidity despite a three-way design; post-hoc selection of the best-performing class grouping and classifier; oversampling apparently applied before rather than within validation; and no validation scheme reported, so all accuracies are of unknown optimism.

**S-004** [local_863980f8] — *Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework*

Reported by the authors: sample prevalence (33% ASD) far exceeds population prevalence (~1%), so positive predictive value in practice would be much lower; face-scanning is age- and culture-adapted so the model may not transfer across ages or cultures; ASD sample characteristics such as symptom severity and cognitive function may drive scanning patterns; sample size is small for pattern classification. Identifiable in review: strong male skew (25/29, ~86% male, replicated across all groups); single-country Chinese sample with race-specific face stimuli; diagnosis confirmed by questionnaire (AQ-Child) rather than ADOS/ADI-R; cluster number K and decision threshold tuned for maximum accuracy on the same data; K-means quantisation fitted on all participants including the held-out test participant, a subtle transductive leak; and the direction of the discriminative-region effects is stated inconsistently between Results and Discussion.

**S-005** [local_be8aa62f] — *Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder*

Reported by the authors: small patient sample, especially few female participants with ASD, with an explicit note that male and female ASD participants may differ in language patterns; the model omits word ordering and phrase-level effects; the prompted format may not capture core language-generation deficits; mechanisms are not disambiguated. Identifiable in review: group sizes are very unequal (27 vs 132) and gender is imbalanced in opposite directions between groups (85% male ASD vs 66% female typical) while gender is not matched - a serious confound for a language-production measure; the ASD group is also on average 7-12 years older; the sample is high-functioning adults (IQ >= 70, mean verbal IQ ~107) so results cannot extend to the wider spectrum; no statement that LSI was refitted within cross-validation folds; and 59% White in the ASD group with no other ethnicity analysis.

**S-006** [local_e404a2a3] — *Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism*

Reported by the authors, unusually thoroughly: IQ was not controlled and could confound; recruitment from particular specialist institutions gives only a subgroup of the spectrum and this 'inherent selection bias in our autism group may have facilitated machine learning differential power'; machine learning is sensitive to sample size so wider recruitment and larger numbers are needed; and the comparison is against children with no concern for ASD rather than against the clinically relevant ASD-versus-ASD-like contrast. Identifiable in review: 247 features against 82 children; feature importance assessed univariately by KS distance rather than from the models; the reported AUC is the best of four algorithm variants across two games plus their average; and two authors are affiliated with the commercial developer with explicit commercialisation ambitions, disclosed by affiliation but not as a competing-interests statement.

**S-007** [local_780141fc] — *Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study*

Reported by the authors: small sample size is named as the study's limitation; ASC heterogeneity means generalisation to a wider population 'remains to be tested'; and comparison against other motor-deficit groups (developmental coordination disorder, ADHD) is needed to know whether the profile is autism-specific. Identifiable in review: no diagnostic instrument is reported for the ASC group at all; both groups have mean IQ near 119, so the sample represents only high-IQ verbally able adults; sex counts are never given despite sex-matching being claimed; 6% of ASC trials and 2% of control trials were excluded for recording or imitation errors, an asymmetry that is disclosed but not analysed; and the reported 86.7% is the best cell of a grid spanning three feature-selection methods, four-plus classifiers and eight conditions, so some selection optimism survives even the nested validation.

**S-008** [local_3a331973] — *Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data*

No limitations section exists, so nothing is acknowledged by the authors beyond the ADHD-only group being too small to model. Identifiable in review: severe class imbalance (18 controls vs 37 condition) reported only as accuracy, where always predicting 'condition' would already score 67%; group sizes of 4 and 11 in two of the four cells; ages and genders never reported numerically and never matched or tested, so demographic confounding cannot be assessed at all; a very high-dimensional feature vector (six feature families x 12 segments) against 55 subjects with greedy forward selection not stated to be nested inside the leave-one-subject-out loop - the single most likely explanation for 37/37 and 22/22 perfect recall on the majority classes; single-site recruitment; and no ethnicity data.

**S-009** [local_7b3e6b3a] — *Earlier identification of children with autism*

Reported by the authors: the small number of subjects limits the impact of the results, and a genuine performance difference between SVM and deep learning 'might only become evident on a dataset with a considerably higher number of vocalisations'. They also note that a proportion of ASD infants' vocalisations carry no acoustic atypicality, and disclose pacifier use as a possible source of error for one misclassified control. Identifiable in review: n=20 makes the 75% subject-level figure equivalent to 15/20 correct with a very wide confidence interval; the headline 75% uses per-fold optimised thresholds rather than the fixed 0.5 threshold (70%); vocalisation counts are unbalanced between groups (259 ASD vs 425 TD) and per subject (9 to 98), so subject-level ratios rest on very different amounts of evidence; 54 of 88 features are declared significant with no multiple-comparison correction, so a substantial share are likely false positives; and the high-familial-risk sibling design means the ASD group is not representative of general-population screening.

**S-010** [local_36aa3ace] — *Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative*

Reported by the authors: small corpus size in ASC research generally is the paper's motivating problem, and they cite prior work warning that high accuracies on small datasets 'may lead to potential confounds'. Identifiable in review: severe class imbalance (68 TD versus 11 AD children, 4547 versus 149 test-set utterances by the confusion matrices) with the reported UAR concealing near-floor autism recognition; no age or sex data reported at all, so demographic bias cannot be assessed; matching is asserted without numbers; single-country, monolingual, verbally able children only, which excludes minimally verbal autistic children entirely; evaluation is at utterance rather than child level; and the best-layer selection differs between feature sets in a way that suggests the layer choice is being read off test performance rather than validation - the eGeMAPS validation UARs are essentially flat across layers (39.33-40.92%) while the test UARs vary by more than a point.

**S-011** [local_44b58f21] — *ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces*

Reported by the authors: only that evaluation on a larger dataset is needed to confirm the observations - there is no limitations section as such. Identifiable in review: feature selection by SWDA used group labels on the full dataset before cross-validation, and the exhaustive hyperparameter grid search (three SVM kernels, six C values, three polynomial degrees, 21 gamma values, 50 ANN hidden-layer sizes) was likewise performed outside the folds, so 93.3% is not an unbiased generalisation estimate; the reported figure is also the best of four classifier configurations; no gender data at all, so sex bias cannot be assessed in a literature with strong male skew; groups differ by ~0.9 years in mean age with no matching test, and gait matures with age; body mass SD is large and unequal; ASD recruitment is split across a specialist centre and social-media outreach with no comparison between subgroups; only one stance phase of one limb from one trial represents each child, so within-subject gait variability - itself a reported feature of autistic movement - is entirely discarded.

**S-012** [local_cb9a5b48] — *Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening*

Reported by the authors: the limited number of cases is explicitly named as a limitation, with a stated plan to run on more children; and the method is acknowledged to fail on shy typically developing children, which the authors address by arguing it should be combined with other screening methods rather than used alone. Identifiable in review: control age range (2.11-7.6 years) roughly doubles the ASD range (2.1-4.1) with no matching, confounding age with group in a spatial-approach measure; no gender data despite a strongly sex-skewed condition; no diagnostic instrument; the best of five classifiers across three feature configurations is reported with no nesting of that selection inside the 8-fold cross-validation; the stacking layer degrades four of five classifiers, so the 81.3% may reflect a fortunate combination rather than a real gain; and post-hoc explanations of the four first-layer errors (shyness, high functioning) are unmeasured narrative rather than data.

**S-013** [local_40cd7d53] — *Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children*

Reported by the authors in an explicit five-point limitations list: ADOS/ADI-R unavailable so diagnoses rest on DSM-5 and CARS alone; no IQ or adaptive-behaviour measure of functional level; relatively small sample requiring larger-sample validation; unknown whether findings are specific to the 4-6 age group; and no direct comparison against or combination with other eye-tracking paradigms. Identifiable in review: gender is imbalanced in practice (89% vs 73% male) despite a non-significant chi-square on n=74; the control group has no GDS or functional data so the correlational analysis cannot be contrasted across groups; single-site recruitment with an ethnically homogeneous sample viewing an Asian female face, leaving cross-cultural transfer untested; whether AOI selection was nested inside the five-fold cross-validation is unstated; and the paper reports two mutually inconsistent sets of accuracy figures for the same analysis.

**S-014** [local_5b1d0b36] — *Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday*

Reported by the authors, unusually thoroughly for a conference paper: large variance in data volume per subject (4 to 1968 recordings) driven by device-usage preference rather than condition; real-life data errors including interrupted tests and parents completing tests on the child's behalf, which would overestimate development level; varying background noise across subjects; absence of speaker diarization so child and parent speech cannot be separated; ASR error rates that increase precisely when child speech is atypical, undermining the linguistic features; and misclassification associated with low data volume for two of the three errors. They also deliberately excluded age and gender as features because 'in the subject recruitment process, it is possible that age and gender information have some implicit connection with the label'. Identifiable in review: that same recruitment confound is not addressed at the sample level - ages span 3 months to 17 years with toddlers over-represented in the ASD group and teenagers among the TD group, entirely unmatched, so acoustic maturation is confounded with diagnosis; 18 ASD versus 9 TD with only 27 analysed; no diagnostic instrument whatsoever; no ethics or consent statement; and the 17-month longitudinal structure is collapsed to a single averaged vector, discarding the developmental information the design was uniquely placed to capture.

**S-015** [local_54954c19] — *Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching*

Reported by the authors in a dedicated Limitations subsection: the 0.75 accuracy compares unfavourably with the 71-86.7% range reported for fMRI classifiers, which they attribute partly to the data not having been collected for classification; web-searching tasks are unsuitable for the very young children in whom early detection would be most valuable, so a different task would be needed to reach them; and the sample is not large, though they note it exceeds the 12-per-group benchmark study they compare against. Identifiable in review: no diagnostic instrument is named, with verification delegated to the recruiting charity; formally diagnosed intellectual disability is an exclusion criterion so results apply only to high-functioning adults; control education exceeds autistic education by 2.3 years, undiscussed; the headline is selected across two tasks, two AOI schemes, four feature sets and multiple page subsets - though every alternative is reported with confidence intervals, making the selection auditable; and the participant-level aggregation rule (majority vote over behaviours) is a design choice whose sensitivity is not explored.

**S-016** [local_d8dc996a] — *Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

There is no limitations section, so nothing is formally acknowledged, though the authors do report the difficulty candidly in the results - the large per-subject standard deviation is presented as evidence that 'finding a very general pattern in the video, that could be unique in distinguishing autistic subjects, is a challenging task', and TD subjects being classified better than ASD ones is read as 'evidence of the fact that autistic spectrum disorders comprise indeed a very wide spectrum of variability'. Identifiable in review: n=39 makes 0.82 equal to 32 of 39 children; the ASD group excludes intellectual impairment and is IQ-matched to controls, so results cannot extend to the broader spectrum; both groups are 80-90% male; the per-subject table shows several ASD children classified confidently wrong (subjects 7, 17 and 20 at 0.15, 0.16 and 0.31), which a single aggregate figure would conceal; the 0.5 threshold on averaged frame probabilities is a lenient decision rule and performance collapses below chance above a 0.9 threshold; and single-site recruitment with one fixed camera viewpoint leaves transfer entirely untested.

**S-017** [local_88ddfdd1] — *A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task*

The paper has no dedicated limitations section, since it is framed as a methods demonstration. It does report transparently that Experiment 1 data were reused from a companion paper and why. Identifiable in review: the absolute accuracies of 53.9% and 55.5% are barely above chance and correspond to a 1.6 percentage point improvement, so while the temporal claim is statistically supported the practical discriminability is negligible - a fact the paper does not emphasise; the unit of analysis is a single two-second trial rather than a person, so no participant-level diagnostic estimate exists; the ASD age range extends to 29 against a control maximum of 21 despite matched means; both groups are heavily male on very small female counts; all participants have IQ above 85, so the sample excludes much of the spectrum; and trials with no AOI transitions in either eye were excluded, which may remove disproportionately many ASD trials given the noted tendency toward stray fixations.

**S-018** [local_361110f1] — *Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features*

Reported by the authors in a dedicated Limitations section that is notably candid: only high-functioning children were recruited to ensure task compliance, and whether low-functioning patients could perform the task 'remains an open question'; and 'obviously, this motor task would not work for children less than 2 years old, which suggests that this motor task would not function for the early screening of ASD' - an explicit concession that the method cannot serve early screening, which almost no other corpus study makes. They further note that motion-capture approaches can quantify low-level stereotyped movement but not higher-level RRB such as circumscribed interest. Identifiable in review: the t-test screen from 18 to 9 features used the full labelled dataset before cross-validation, and forward feature selection then selected the combination maximising classification accuracy, so 88.37% is a maximum over a search using the evaluation criterion; the best of five classifiers and four k values is reported; sensitivity and specificity are reversed between abstract and discussion; the direction of the velocity features carrying most of the signal is not reported; exclusion of ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia makes the discrimination easier than the clinical task; and demographic detail resides in a table that is not reproduced in the running text.

**S-019** [local_51533de4] — *Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations*

Reported by the authors: performance is limited by 5-minute samples and generic topics compared with ADOS evaluations designed to elicit ASD-like features; human raters outperformed the model, which the authors read as evidence that the feature set fails to capture topicality, relevance, appropriateness and conversational flow at a turn-by-turn level; ASD is harder to predict than TD because of phenotypic heterogeneity; and the approach 'is not yet valuable as a method for diagnosing ASD, which still needs to be diagnosed by expert clinicians'. Identifiable in review: the demographic table's sex counts sum to 25 rather than 35 in both groups; the confederate features that are among the most consistently selected mean part of the signal is an interlocutor's response to the child rather than the child's own behaviour, which limits transfer to any self-administered or partner-free screening context; all participants were native English speakers at a single site, with no ethnicity or socioeconomic data; confederates were 19 of 22 female, so partner-sex variation is minimal; and n=70 makes 75.71% equal to 53 of 70 children.

**S-020** [local_96c87d36] — *Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking*

No dedicated limitations section. The introduction acknowledges at field level that eye-tracking results 'can be impacted by sample size, age, developmental level and IQ, variation in stimuli, and task effort and objective', but the study does not then control for these. Identifiable in review: the two eye trackers are confounded with group - all ASD subjects used the 300 Hz TX300 while 29 of 35 controls used the 60 Hz X2-60 - and the most important model features (fixation frequency, fixation duration, fixation time, saccade amplitude) are exactly the measures a fivefold sampling-rate difference would bias, yet the authors dismiss this in one sentence; five ASD subjects were excluded for eye-tracking capture failure with no controls excluded, a group-dependent attrition that could itself reflect the behaviour being measured; control ages extend to 34 versus an ASD maximum of 17, with a control SD more than double the ASD SD; IQ is reported only as an ASD range and never controlled; two display sizes were used; and the reported equations define sensitivity in terms of TN and specificity in terms of TP, inverting the standard definitions.

**S-021** [local_4b031d44] — *Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine*

Reported by the authors in a dedicated limitations section that diagnoses the transfer gap in three specific ways: the source classifiers were trained on clinical scoresheets rather than features obtained from live video; those scoresheets came from formal clinical assessments of US children and 'do not capture a culturally diverse set of behavioral nuances'; and the classifiers were built to separate typical development from autism whereas this dataset contains other delays including SLCs. They also hypothesise that raters sharing the children's linguistic and sociocultural background would improve performance. Identifiable in review: sex is markedly imbalanced between the ASD and SLC cohorts (72% versus 46% male), directly confounding the second classification layer; family income differs sharply across groups (96% of ASD families above 30,000 taka versus 26% of TD families), as does residence; stunting data are missing entirely for the TD cohort; ADOS covered only 28 of 50 ASD children; the demographic table's gender percentages are inconsistent with their counts; and the senior author founded a company developing paediatric digital health solutions, disclosed as a conflict of interest.

**S-022** [local_05ef29e5] — *Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification*

Reported by the authors, and unusually thoughtfully for a four-page workshop paper: ASD fixation behaviour changes with age, with toddlers, young children and grown-up children differing markedly and adults with ASD showing no visible difference in fixation duration between objects and non-objects, so 'the ASD subject age is very important for detecting the condition' - yet age was unavailable in the dataset; and fixation behaviour also depends on image content, since young ASD children do not differ from TD children on scenes containing both faces and objects of circumscribed interest, so 'ASD condition cannot be generalized over age, fixation behaviour, and image content' whereas the model generalises all features over all subjects. Identifiable in review: specificity of 50.56% is chance level and the model is therefore near-useless for ruling out ASD, which the summary framing of '60% accuracy' obscures; no participant counts, ages or genders exist at all; subject identity is not consistent across images so subject-independent evaluation is impossible and the same person's scanpaths can appear in both training and test sets; the unit of analysis is a scanpath not a person, so this is not a person-level diagnostic result; and no feature importance is reported despite the model providing it natively.

**S-023** [local_9528024b] — *Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol*

Reported by the authors, with notable candour: the sample size 'is not large'; because each task runs once the robot makes only three decisions, which 'does not necessarily warrant a use of POMDP'; social cue detection algorithms are 'not accurate enough for fully autonomous execution' so the robot is only semi-autonomous with an operator supplying critical observations; not all children completed all tasks, some because of robot failures and some through fear or refusal; in four cases robot failure ended the session because children would not continue; and crucially, typically developing children 'sometimes exhibit autistic behavior, and vice versa', which the authors attribute to the ASD group being in daily intervention and unafraid of the robot while typically developing children were shy and wary. Identifiable in review: no ages, genders or diagnostic instrument; no ethics or consent statement despite two-way-mirror video of preschoolers; observation probabilities elicited by clinician survey rather than estimated from data; no quantitative performance metric whatsoever; and the confidence-scaling parameter was tuned until 'more appropriate' belief values emerged, which is a judgement call rather than a fitted value.

**S-024** [local_6230fe22] — *Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism*

Reported by the authors: only that the model should be replicated with larger datasets to validate performance, and that other classification techniques should be compared. No limitations section exists. Identifiable in review: no sample size is reported, so the precision of the four performance figures is unknowable; no ages, genders or diagnostic procedure, so demographic and ascertainment bias cannot be assessed; no stimulus, ROI or feature specification, so the measurement cannot be evaluated; methods sections are written partly in the future tense, suggesting the system was planned rather than fully executed at time of writing; the claim that a high AUC means the model 'works well regardless of the class distribution (i.e. when data are new/unknown)' conflates class-distribution invariance with generalisation to new data; and the study is framed around screening before age 2 while never reporting the age of any participant.

**S-025** [local_785ba418] — *Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis*

No dedicated limitations section, but the paper's entire framing is a limitation critique aimed at its own field: prior kinematic studies achieving 86.7-96.7% 'used K-fold Cross-Validation, which was demonstrated to produce overoptimistic performance estimates, especially when a sample size is small' and did not assess whether performance differed significantly from random guessing. The conclusion adds that large parametric effect sizes 'do not necessarily translate to high ML classification performance'. Identifiable in review: no diagnostic instrument named; IQ matching claimed without values; no age standard deviations or ranges; adults only; n=46 so 71% is roughly 33 of 46 correct, with no confidence interval reported though accuracy distributions are plotted; the best of four pipelines is highlighted, though all four including the two non-significant ones are reported in full; and outlier replacement with group means (1.4% of data points) uses group information, a minor leakage route not discussed.

**S-026** [local_fea042be] — *Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual*

Reported by the authors in a brief limitations section: the relatively small number of participants, and the fairly short duration of the video scenarios, with longer scenarios possibly allowing a richer visual representation. Identifiable in review and more consequential: the unit of analysis is the image not the child, with 547 images from 59 children plus 2,735 augmented synthetic derivatives, and no statement that cross-validation was participant-independent - so images and their own augmented near-duplicates can span the training and test folds, which would inflate the reported AUC substantially; no per-group age or sex data at all; the qualitative observation that the ASD exemplar looked toward the bottom of the screen where the eye tracker was physically located raises the possibility of apparatus-driven signal; the multi-label experiment predicts CARS bands from data collected on children whose diagnosis was itself characterised by CARS, which is partly circular; and the work was funded by a commercial healthcare IT company, acknowledged but not declared as a competing interest.

**S-027** [local_ba5fbda7] — *Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD*

Reported by the authors: the sample size is 'rather limited', so the next step must be applying the algorithm to a completely new and larger dataset; transdiagnostic specificity across psychiatric conditions is untested; and Motion Energy Analysis retains 'a subjective component' because regions of interest are drawn manually, even though pixel-change detection is automatic. The paper also criticises the wider literature for circularity where classifiers are trained on clinician-derived features. Identifiable in review: no participant ages, sexes or matching information are reported in this paper at all; specificity of 55.2% means the model misclassifies nearly half of controls, so the headline accuracy rests on an unbalanced error profile; the dyadic design means each participant's synchrony was measured while interacting with partners of differing diagnostic status, a potential source of variance that is not analysed; one entire task was dropped because a single dyad misunderstood instructions; and the sample is high-functioning adults only.

**S-028** [local_7b468950] — *Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart*

The protocol's account of its predecessor's limitations is the most methodologically literate passage in this corpus, and it names both failure modes that this review has documented repeatedly. On selection: the pilot's 82 children came from 'a small number of specialist day-care centres in Poland. Such limited subject recruitment is prone to selection bias and site-specific effects and precludes assessment of predictive value in population-based settings.' On evaluation: 'the pilot study employed the same dataset to train and test the machine learning algorithm. It did so with 10 repetitions of a 10-fold cross-validation procedure that is not prone to overfitting. Nevertheless, it only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset.' That second sentence is important - it concedes that repeated cross-validation, which most studies in this review treat as sufficient, does not establish generalisation beyond the dataset it is computed on. Both concerns are then addressed structurally rather than rhetorically. Two design points remain unstated: recruitment through specialist services means population-prevalence predictive value will still not be directly estimable, and the algorithm remains a commercial black box, so a positive result would show that the instrument works without showing what it measures.

**S-029** [local_309e5baa] — *Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns*

Reported by the authors only briefly: 'The performance gap may be caused by the imbalanced distribution of training and test dataset and lacking of training images'. They also note, when citing the prior 92% adult result, that it 'may not be directly applicable to gaze patterns from children' - a caution about transfer that few corpus papers offer about their own antecedents. Identifiable in review: the internal split is partitioned by image, not by participant, so the same child's scanpaths appear in both internal training and validation, which is the most likely reason internal accuracy exceeds blind test accuracy by 6-11 points; the number of distinct participants is never stated; no control ages, no genders, no diagnostic information; specificity on the blind test collapses to 0.282-0.471, meaning the models achieve their apparent sensitivity largely by over-calling ASD; and the unit of analysis is the scanpath rather than the person, so no person-level estimate exists.

**S-030** [local_a45f39e9] — *Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time*

No dedicated limitations section. The authors note only that the approach could be improved by combining RGB and audio modalities and by moving to 3D trajectories. Identifiable in review and more consequential: the classification target is episode-level expert-labelled behaviour rather than participant diagnosis, so the reported figures are not diagnostic accuracy despite the paper's 'ASD prediction' framing; no participant counts, ages, genders or diagnostic status are reported, so the corpus composition and any demographic confounding are unknowable; the train/test partitioning basis is unstated with 8349 episodes from 555 videos, making episode-level leakage across the split highly likely; class imbalance (5265 atypical to 3084 typical) is unaddressed and is consistent with the 0.92 recall against 0.66 AUC, indicating a majority-class-biased classifier; the imputation ablation shows three conditions performing identically on accuracy, precision and recall yet the text claims 'the classifier benefits a lot from interpolation'; multiple expert annotators are mentioned with no inter-rater agreement reported; and there is no ethics or consent statement for home video of children.

**S-031** [local_d587f9cd] — *Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning*

There is no dedicated limitations section, but the paper's self-description is honest at the points that matter: the evaluation is labelled 'a proof of concept', the index group is described as 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis', and the vision pipeline's occlusion failures are reported rather than omitted. The introduction also identifies the gap in prior work accurately - early robot-assisted diagnostic systems 'have primarily been open loop and remotely operated systems. However, these approaches are unable to perform autonomous feedback to enhance the interaction' - which is the specific deficiency the closed-loop architecture addresses. What is not addressed: six children in single sessions cannot support a behavioural claim, and no statistical test, effect size or uncertainty estimate accompanies the reported difference; neither group has documented diagnostic status; the mediator order is not counterbalanced, confounding the key finding with order, fatigue and novelty; no ethics approval is reported; no developmental measure was obtained in three-year-olds, so general developmental level cannot be separated from autism risk; and the behavioural finding rests on automated visual-focus-of-attention estimates with no reliability check against human coding, in a pipeline whose occlusion problems the paper itself reports.

**S-032** [local_08b8027d] — *SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths*

Reported by the authors: the blind-test performance 'is much lower than that of the validation dataset, which could indicate the submitted models being overfitted', with a call to further investigate the structure of visual attention to mitigate this. They also note candidly that SalGAN was trained on SALICON, 'collected from subjects over a large age range and thus not perfectly reflected the saliency distribution of the children', and that no public large-scale child saliency dataset exists to retrain it. They further acknowledge that the influence of saliency prediction quality on final classification has not been exhaustively tested. Identifiable in review: the internal split is partitioned by image, not participant, so the same children appear in both training and validation; model selection across two CNN variants, three feature dimensionalities and two normalisation settings was performed on that same validation set, compounding optimism; no participant counts, ages, genders or diagnostic information exist; the unit of analysis is the scanpath rather than the person; and blind-test precision of 0.5319-0.5684 with recall up to 0.8771 for model A indicates the best-recall model achieves it by over-calling ASD.

**S-033** [local_c6f1209b] — *Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children*

Two limitations are stated and both are correctly identified. The first is the absence of a comparison group - 'we observed only autistic children interacting with the robot' - with the remedy given as comparison against typically developing children, which the group subsequently carried out. The second is more valuable and is rare in this corpus: 'the especially challenging task is to differ autism from other similar disorders. Thus, the other direction of our future studies is to observe the interactions performed by the robot and the children with other disorders.' Committing to a non-autistic clinical comparison is a commitment almost no study in this review makes, and the one included study that does test autism against another clinical population found the field's gold-standard observational instrument achieving an AUC of 0.562 - which is the evidence that this stated priority is the right one. What is not addressed: sample size and participant characteristics are unreported; no diagnostic ascertainment is described; inter-rater reliability is not quantified for this study; rater blinding to the hypothesis is not discussed; and no developmental measure separates general cognitive level from autism as an explanation for reduced spontaneous imitation.

**S-034** [local_83b99e73] — *Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers*

Two limitations are stated: the groups could not be age-matched because autistic children generally have delayed development, so matching on age would unmatch developmental level; and the sample was small. The N-ASD failure is discussed candidly - 'the 5 N-ASD was not classified correctly', attributed to class imbalance and to only ten indicators per sample, with identifying N-ASD from ASD named as a goal for future work. The contrary finding on negative emotion is also flagged as needing further validation. Identifiable in review but not acknowledged: the verification step is largely circular, since 40 of the 45 high-risk children used to verify the SVM were in its training set; the age gap coincides with significant differences in four of five developmental quotients, so group separation may partly reflect developmental level rather than autism; features were selected by group-difference t-tests computed on the full dataset before cross-validation, which leaks label information into the feature set; and the reported accuracies do not exactly match the tabulated confusion matrices.

**S-035** [local_638860ef] — *Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis*

The paper's framing is itself a critique of prior work's limitations rather than only its own. On the field: prior kinematic ML studies 'had small sample sizes and achieved high classification accuracy', but 'models developed with small sample/high dimensional data are prone to fit noise and not necessarily an underlying pattern separating classes', and those studies 'did not avoid pooling training and validation data while developing their ML models and did not take other steps to control for the fitting of random noise', were 'not tested with independent data', and did not assess statistical significance. On their own work they acknowledge the difficulty of small-sample high-dimensional pattern recognition requiring careful handling of both validation and feature selection. Identifiable in review: 44 adults total with a 14-participant test set means 78% is roughly 11 of 14 correct; the diagnostic ascertainment is entirely absent from this paper; both samples are high-IQ adults; the reported headline is the best across several feature-selection variants; and the marked sex-composition difference between samples, while turned into a generalisation argument, also means the independent test provides limited evidence about performance in a comparably composed sample.

**S-036** [local_7547db68] — *Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network*

The authors acknowledge that the algorithm 'is affected by the environment and light' and that accuracy suffers accordingly, noting that two typically developing children scored 57.1%; that errors concentrate on disgust and surprise because those expressions involve only minor local facial change and some participants produced them weakly; and that more real samples are needed. They do not acknowledge the design's central problems. No model is trained on autism labels, so a proxy task's failure rate is being treated as a diagnostic signal, and the design cannot separate non-imitation, atypical imitation, developmental immaturity and out-of-distribution faces from autism. The groups differ in age (3-6 versus 5-8) and are fully confounded with recruitment site. The supplementary training images came from typically developing 5-8 year olds, the control group's own population, which biases the classifier toward recognising control-group faces. The 60% threshold is fitted to the same 20 children it is evaluated on. And the abstract's 81.4% is the expression recognition rate in typically developing children, not a diagnostic accuracy, yet is presented as 'the accuracy of facial expression recognition of this system'.

**S-037** [local_878c259f] — *Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach*

Reported by the authors only briefly, in the abstract and conclusions: 'By increasing the sample size and analyzing more data/features of postural control, a better classification performance would be expected'. There is no dedicated limitations section. Identifiable in review: n=50 with five-fold cross-validation means roughly 10 children per test fold, so 0.900 accuracy is about 45 of 50 correct and the exact 1.000 specificity and precision reflect zero false positives among 25 controls - values that will not be stable at this scale; the headline is the best of six algorithms evaluated on the same cross-validation with no nested selection or external validation; no diagnostic instrument is named; inclusion criteria requiring comprehension of instructions and task performance restrict the ASD sample to more able children; sex is not matched (56% versus 40% female); and the negative sample entropy result contradicts two prior studies cited in the introduction without the discrepancy being discussed in the extracted text.

**S-038** [local_1579c85a] — *Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through*

Reported by the authors, and unusually directly for the format: the work 'is limited by the number of participants, the inclusion of a single gender and the exclusive use of behaviors available from video data', and given the 0.1787 false negative rate 'this method cannot be claimed to be ready to be used singularly as a diagnostic tool for ASD'. Identifiable in review and more consequential: the evaluation unit is the 1-second data window rather than the child, with approximately 18,597 data points per subject and a single 80/20 split whose partitioning level is unstated - so windows from the same child are almost certainly split across training and validation, making the reported accuracy a within-child figure rather than a person-level detection estimate; 12 children cannot support a person-level estimate regardless; no diagnostic instrument is reported; ages are unmatched with markedly unequal variances; validation and test sets are not distinguished; and no feature-level interpretation is offered so nothing is learned about what distinguishes the groups behaviourally.

**S-039** [local_157d6266] — *Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism*

Reported by the authors, and addressed unusually rigorously rather than merely acknowledged. On sample size, they concede that 27 ASC and 21 TD 'can be considered relatively small' given phenotypic heterogeneity, then argue quantitatively that the method does not suffer from a sample size problem: invoking the 1-in-10 rule for the three-variable metric learning (30 samples needed, approximately 90 used), and applying Raudys's formula for SVM expected error with p=3, delta=3.83 and n=13 per class to derive a 5.9% expected error against a 2.8% infinite-sample floor. They also note their parameter-to-sample ratio is more favourable than two named prior autism motor studies (40 parameters from 30 subjects, and 7 parameters from 30 subjects). On scalability they concede that Kinect imperfections 'require some manual processing that can be time-consuming'. Identifiable in review: 48 children means 87.2% is roughly 42 correct; the headline is the better of two scoring methods evaluated on the same folds; IQ at or above 80 and ages 8-12 bound generalisability; and the demographic table is not recoverable from the extracted text so matching cannot be verified.

**S-040** [local_8be557e3] — *Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation*

Explicitly acknowledged: the data set is insufficient, dispersed and unbalanced; performance is 'relatively poor in comparison to the general classification tasks based on deep learning'; the improvement from joint optimisation is 'only marginal'; the BLSTM was deliberately kept small (eight cells) to match prior work rather than to maximise performance; and comparison with the prior study is only indirect because feature selection did not reproduce. Not acknowledged: the near-disjoint age distributions between groups, on the variable that most strongly governs infant vocalisation; the inverted sex ratio; the utterance-level rather than infant-level splitting, which allows the same child's voice into both training and evaluation folds; and the transposed precision and recall labels in the results table. Reading the confusion matrices directly also shows that autistic-class sensitivity is only 45.3% even for the best model, a figure the accuracy and UAR headline numbers obscure.

**S-041** [local_c79e100a] — *Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models*

Acknowledged with unusual directness in one respect and not at all in others. The authors state that training and testing folds 'can both contain data points from the same subject and even from the same trial', judge the impact 'potentially limited', and choose 10-fold over leave-one-out on that basis - naming the leakage and then reasoning past it rather than eliminating it by splitting on participants. They also acknowledge the small dataset, the class imbalance, that averaging reduces the data available for training, and that the SVM's apparent 100% recall was a degenerate single-class predictor with 'no use in real world applications'. Not acknowledged: that grid search selected hyperparameters on the same cross-validation whose scores are reported, so every figure is optimistically biased; that no participant characteristic is reported, so nothing rules out age, sex or stature as the discriminated variable in features that are all durations; that no diagnostic instrument is named; and that no ethics approval is stated. The paper describes itself as a 'preliminary investigation', which is a fair self-assessment.

**S-042** [local_4fecbf6d] — *Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network*

Acknowledged: that speaker labelling was manual and that automatic diarization is needed for a fully automated system; that recordings are short clinic sessions rather than naturalistic home recordings; that the shorter-response-latency finding contradicts prior English-language work and needs replication; that feature utility may change with age and requires longitudinal testing; and, implicitly but importantly, that single-split results overstate robustness. Identifiable in review but not stated: RMSE 4.65 on a 0-30 scale is a large absolute error against which the phrase 'remarkably accurate prediction' sits uneasily; architecture and hyperparameters were selected by trying combinations, apparently outside the 50-split evaluation, so the reported means carry model-selection optimism; only 6 typically developing children means the low end of the severity range is thinly sampled, which inflates correlation through range restriction at one end and thin support at the other; and no ethics approval is reported for full clinical session audio.

**S-043** [local_95abe653] — *Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning*

Acknowledged: that web-searching tasks are unsuitable for very young children; that the sample is small, 'comparable with those of state-of-the-art fMRI studies for autism detection but smaller than the number needed for large validation studies'; that the design cannot explain why some pages discriminate better than others, nor why the harder Synthesis task did not outperform Search; that testing on independently collected data is not currently feasible because the data are task-specific and no comparable independent dataset exists; and, in a footnote, that the better accuracy under the longer browse limit might reflect the different pages and participants rather than the time limit itself. Identifiable in review but not acknowledged: the headline accuracies are maxima over a large configuration space - task, AOI definition, feature set, split ratio and every page subset - selected on the same 100 splits that produce the reported means, so the confidence intervals describe split variability but not selection uncertainty; and the control group's visibly higher educational attainment is left unadjusted in tasks that are fundamentally reading and search tasks.

**S-044** [local_40168c96] — *Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based*

Acknowledged and unusually specific: the sample of 31 and 43 children is small and needs large-scale replication; class balance 'is also a problem that needs attention in the validation of our machine learning based model'; severity subdivision is not addressed; and data validity is limited because distracted typically developing children 'may generate meaningless eye movement', which the error analysis identifies as the reason specificity trails sensitivity. Not acknowledged: the Otsu threshold is computed on the score distribution being classified, including at test time, so the decision boundary uses test data and would not be available when assessing a single child; the abstract's 94.28% is the best of five permutations rather than the average; comparisons against Liu and Jiang and Zhao are across different datasets and cannot establish superiority; age differs between groups in mean, spread and range without any test or adjustment; sex is unreported; the control group is unscreened; and no ethics approval is stated.

**S-045** [local_d3852378] — *Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Acknowledged with unusual candour: the sample is small and precludes a genuine test set; autism's heterogeneity means larger training groups would be needed for generalisation; other neurodevelopmental comparison groups are absent, so the classifier may separate neurodevelopmental difference generally rather than autism specifically; the groups were not matched on IQ, cognitive ability or motor comorbidities, which the authors say directly limits attributing the differences to autism; and the stimulus order was not counterbalanced. Not acknowledged: the Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a paired test applied here to independent groups, where Mann-Whitney U is required, so the reported per-joint significances are unverified; 24 models were built and hyperparameters tuned to maximise kappa on the same leave-one-out estimate reported as the result, making 89.36% a best-of-many figure on 47 children where one child is worth 2.13 points; the sex distributions differ substantially on a motor outcome; the analysed sample appears to be 47 not 49; and the quantity called 'frequency' throughout is mean displacement, a magnitude.

**S-046** [local_df438dd2] — *Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening*

Acknowledged: that a single protocol is insufficient - 'using the responsive social smile score alone cannot give a very comprehensive ASD classification' - and that fusing multiple protocols is needed; that autistic children are heterogeneous, making single-aspect screening hard; and, through the failure case study, that most residual errors are smiles that occurred but were not responses to the designed stimulus. Not acknowledged: that group-wise ages and sexes are never reported, so age and sex confounding cannot be excluded in a 12-32 month cohort; that the diagnostic reference standard is a bare DSM-IV clinical judgement with no instrument; that 80.49% is the best of four classifiers on 41 children where one child is worth 2.4 points - the same size as the gap the human-score ablation reveals; that stimulus scoring is evaluated at the trial level so the same child appears across folds; and that no ethics approval is reported.

**S-047** [local_cd9e45eb] — *Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism*

Acknowledged with unusual directness: 'We acknowledge that the validation performance might be over-optimistic and does not represent real-world performance for ASD/non-ASD classification'; only 64 participants with just 30 having full ADOS, Vineland and SRS measurement; limited power to characterise autism heterogeneity; results possibly specific to the school-age period; selected paradigms not guaranteed stable across runs because the p > n problem may have no unique optimum; and that much remains before eye tracking can be used practically for treatment optimisation or long-term outcome prediction. Identifiable in review but not stated: group-wise ages, sexes and IQs are asserted as balanced but never tabulated, which matters greatly given that IQ is the one variable the features do predict; the sparsity operating point, the hyperparameters and the identification of SGIN as best were all determined against the same 10-fold estimate; and the non-autistic group's heterogeneity, while a design strength, means the classifier's target is 'autism versus other developmental presentations', which is not the same construct as 'autism versus typical development' and complicates comparison with the rest of this corpus.

**S-048** [local_56237213] — *The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data*

Acknowledged: that the cohort begins at age 3 and that 'diagnosis of autism at earlier ages is a pressing clinical need', with a stated plan to recruit children aged 2 or younger; and that more features should be extracted from both modalities. The paper also usefully concedes a limitation of its own EEG modality, noting that 'no differences in EEG were found in some previous studies, especially for high functioning autism' and concluding that 'using only EEG evaluation may be insufficient to identify children with this complex disease'. Not acknowledged, and decisive: no validation scheme of any kind is described, so the reported accuracies have no established out-of-sample interpretation; mRMR uses class labels with no indication of nesting within any resampling; the headline 85.44% is the maximum of a curve swept over one to forty-five features, so the operating point was selected on the reported data; the identity of the selected features is never given; recruitment routes differ systematically between groups; and no severity or functioning measure is reported despite heterogeneity being central to the paper's own argument.

**S-049** [local_f9a5195f] — *Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses*

The most complete limitations section in the corpus, with five named items. Age range 6-17 'is not representative of children who are in critical periods of development for cognition and speech'. Gender imbalance of 13:3 in the autistic cohort against 9:8 in controls, with the authors noting that gender differences exist on emotion recognition and gaze tasks and 'may have been exacerbated by our imbalanced cohorts'. Limited spectrum coverage, since only 3 of 16 autistic participants had ABIQ below 80 so 13 are high-functioning. A chinrest added after the first four participants because of head movement, with the explicit admission that 'more ASD subjects took part in the study later on. This confound may be exploited by the classifiers'. And nonstandard eye tracking - the custom system was never evaluated against a standard tracker, the mount shifted requiring recalibration and extensive manual annotation, and it 'occluded roughly 15% of the field of view in the lower region for most participants, which may have had a greater distracting effect on participants in the ASD group with tactile sensitivities'. The discussion adds an ethological caution: static 6-second photographs are 'quite divergent from real-life social interactions with moving children and fleeting displays of facial emotion', and the field 'does not have enough information to know how divergent our experimental data might be from the ecologically valid situations'.

**S-050** [local_16a77fb0] — *Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)*

Acknowledged with unusual thoroughness. On the age bias: 'older participants in both groups were more often labeled as autistic than young participants by the machine-learning classifiers, as the classifier was probably picking up a tendency of higher age in the ASD group. This age bias points to the strong need of careful testing for confounders and biases in training data for all kind of machine-learning diagnostic methods.' On gaze: the null result is attributed to appearance-based estimation being 'not sensitive enough to detect the subtle gaze dysfunctions present in ASD', with a caution that the null 'has to be interpreted with caution'. On the paradigm: the prerecorded actress cannot adapt to answer length, and future versions should provide tailored responses and partners matched on gender, age or ethnicity since similarity enhances mimicry. On the HNR finding: interpretation 'is not straightforward, given the lack of reference studies', with conflicting prior findings acknowledged and the possibility raised that groups differ in speaking-to-pause ratios. On multiplicity: the authors note that automated analysis 'allows the comparison of many different aspects of behavior' so 'the problem of multiple testing remains', which is why they favour the multivariate machine learning approach. Not acknowledged: the reported direction of the HNR effect contradicts the tabulated medians, which are lower rather than higher in autism; and the age confound, though identified, is not adjusted for in the headline accuracy.

**S-051** [local_9c4af7a3] — *Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades*

Acknowledged: that only 108 individuals were used and more would produce a more diverse and robust classifier with better performance on edge cases; that restricting to six features may have cost accuracy; and that Azure ML Studio prevented direct hyperparameter tuning. Not acknowledged, and decisive: mutual-information feature selection was applied to the full dataset before splitting, so supervised selection sits outside the cross-validation loop; no participant characteristics are reported so no confound can be excluded; the dataset's provenance, diagnostic basis and collection ethics are entirely unstated; only accuracy is reported for a proposed diagnostic test, with no sensitivity or specificity and an unlabelled ROC curve; the 60:40 class imbalance means a majority-class predictor scores 60%; the abstract's 88-91% range is unexplained against the text's single figure of 88%; the comparator set includes regression methods that are not binary classifiers; and every descriptive group difference is asserted without a statistic.

**S-052** [local_b70dae32] — *An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model*

Essentially none. The paper has no limitations section, and the only self-critical remark is a defence of the sample size on the ground that 'the presented work is based on previous research that also uses a similar number of subjects'. Identifiable in review and unaddressed: Table 2 assigns each test child a single autism type (one mild, three minimal) while Table 4 records 12 mild and 13 minimal actual categories across 25 test sessions, which cannot be reconciled without an unexplained within-child change in CARS category, and until resolved makes the reported accuracy and kappa uninterpretable; the kappa treats 25 sessions from 4 children as independent, inflating the effective sample about sixfold; the two observables are binned to three levels each using thresholds set with the therapist who also supplied the labels; the conditional independence assumption is contradicted by the design, since the imitation module is activated by joint attention; the severity labels 'minimal' and 'mild' are never mapped to the DSM levels the introduction describes; and the claim that no therapist is needed is undercut by the fact that every training label comes from a therapist's CARS assessment.

**S-053** [local_51a0af74] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data*

Acknowledged: the dataset is imbalanced and synthetic sampling is a stopgap pending more real data; region demarcation still requires a therapist and automatic identification would make the method faster; and accuracy could be improved with other methods such as genetic algorithms for meta-classifier construction. The low specificity is noted and defended rather than treated as a limitation - the authors argue that 'our major goal is to capture all possible individuals with the disorder' and that highly sensitive tests suit early rule-out. Not acknowledged: the reported 75% is the maximum over 511 classifier subsets, three ensemble strategies, swept thresholds, five balancing methods and per-segment hyperparameter grids, all selected on the same 10-fold estimate with no outer validation loop, so the figure is optimistically biased and the segment-1-3-8 finding is a selection outcome rather than an independent result; the practical consequence of 53% specificity - referring roughly half of typically developing children onward - is not discussed; ages span 3-18 with different ranges per group and no adjustment; CARS scores are collected but never related to model output; and no ethics approval is reported.

**S-054** [local_d8d3037b] — *Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study*

Acknowledged: aGlass stability and accuracy are insufficient; VR was rejected by some autistic participants; small samples in both experiments make bias inevitable; not all scenes containing social stimuli discriminate, so scene design should involve a specialist psychologist and several scenes should be compared. Most valuably, the authors report and interpret the recall instability across experiments, concluding that 'the data patterns of the adults we recruited in the preliminary experiment are somehow different from those autistic adults'. Not acknowledged: that the preliminary positive class is a median split of a general-population trait distribution well below the AQ clinical cut-off, so the models were never trained on autism; that Table 2's group AQ means are transposed; that age and sex are model features while the test sample differs sharply from the training population on both; that the test experiment has no negative cases so specificity is unmeasured and recall alone cannot distinguish a good model from one biased toward positive prediction; that the ensemble's AUC of 0.90 is inconsistent with constituent AUCs of 0.57-0.68; and that outlier replacement by the mean is unspecified in both criterion and timing.

**S-055** [local_991fe435] — *Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task*

Acknowledged with four specific limitations: still rather than dynamic directional cues, whereas dynamic cues predominate in daily life; the attention-sustaining phase distinguishes this paradigm from conventional visual-orienting tasks and may itself drive the group differences, so future work should test whether the algorithms can separate autism from attention deficits; too few girls to test sex-specific performance, with the specific rationale that 'autistic girls exhibit more typical social attention than do autistic boys'; and that 'the predictive power of automatic classification techniques is constrained by the base rate of ASD in the population', so direct comparison against current diagnostic methods requires caution. The absence of ADOS and ADI-R is disclosed with its reason. Identifiable in review but not stated: the low-functioning group's 5.7% success rate means these children largely failed the task, so their classification may reflect general non-engagement rather than a visual-orienting deficit specifically; and the criterion for assigning children to that group included failure to complete the Raven's test, which partly conflates cognitive level with capacity to complete a structured assessment of the same general kind as the outcome task.

**S-056** [local_8692a64f] — *Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis*

Acknowledged: the dataset is limited so 'comparisons cannot be simply drawn with other existing diagnostic methods, and more samples are needed for further analysis'; the clap-prediction feature 'needs to be further justified' given its weak correlation; and the hyperparameters were empirically set with the explicit note that 'different values could be set to gain a better performance'. The refutation of hypothesis 2 is reported clearly and the interpretation revised. Not acknowledged: no diagnostic instrument or criteria are reported for either group; no ethics approval; groups differ substantially in age (4-10 versus 2-15) and sex (74% versus 51% male) with no test or adjustment; validation is a single random split with no cross-validation or repetition, so the 40-child result carries wide sampling uncertainty; the correlation analysis validating the feature hypotheses used the full dataset including the test half; exclusion rates differ between groups (15% versus 6%); and the most predictive feature family, area0, is defined by the tracker's failure to resolve gaze, conflating attentional signal with equipment dropout.

**S-057** [local_4d6fac7e] — *Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network*

Essentially none. The paper has no limitations section and offers no caveats on sample size, generalisability or validation design. Identifiable in review: the reported accuracies are arithmetically incompatible with a participant-level 80/20 split of 42 children and correspond instead to 19 of 20, 14 of 19 and 15 of 19 samples, which combined with 4-second EEG epoching implies segment-level splitting and hence leakage across the train/test boundary; no diagnostic instrument or criteria are reported for either group; age and sex matching is asserted with no figures; the t-tests and covariance thresholds defining the graph structure were computed on the full dataset including test samples; validation is a single unrepeated split with no confidence intervals; and the reduction from 128 to 8 electrodes is justified only computationally.

**S-058** [local_30c622f2] — *Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model*

Acknowledged: that the saliency-map approach needs testing with different visual inputs 'in order to validate the relevant features'; that the age range is restricted to 3-16 while autism is lifelong; that the sample is small; and that the sex imbalance between groups is a limitation. Analysing IQ as an additional feature is proposed. Not acknowledged: the reported accuracy of 88% is inconsistent with the reported error rate of 25% and with the reported sensitivity and specificity, and coincides exactly with the separately reported maximum ROC AUC; ReliefF feature selection is not stated to be nested within cross-validation folds, so the group-specific feature sets that constitute the paper's main finding may have been chosen using all the data; and the 20-frame decision threshold was fitted by Youden index on the same ROC used for evaluation.

**S-059** [local_bfc088c7] — *Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation*

Acknowledged extensively and specifically: the sample excludes severe presentations and children below 6 or above 13, so the work is 'proof-of-concept research'; only four girls participated, and autistic males and females differ across behavioural, cognitive and emotional domains; severity was not measured; head-mounted eye tracking may itself affect autistic children's behaviour and contactless methods are needed; only fixation percentage was computed while counts, entropy, revisits and oculomotor measures were available; only autism versus typical development was tested, leaving discrimination from other clinical phenotypes unknown; and live interaction introduces uncontrollable subjective factors, with the honest observation that 'no human being can be expected to behave exactly the same way when interacting with different people'. Not acknowledged: forward feature selection maximises the same leave-one-out accuracy that is reported, so the headline is not an unbiased estimate, and the maximum is quoted across 21 feature counts, four classifiers and three feature sets; and IQ differs significantly between groups with no adjustment, despite the leading feature being conversation duration.

**S-060** [local_25e34bbd] — *Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification*

None. There is no limitations section and no caveat anywhere on sample size, validation design, generalisability or the absence of clinical characterisation. The nearest approach is the acknowledgement that hidden neuron counts have no exact formula and were fixed by trial. Identifiable in review: 255 samples derive from only 19 children with roughly 13 samples each, and the 70/15/15 partition operates over samples with no statement that speakers were kept together, which alone would explain the perfect accuracies; hidden neuron counts were tuned to maximise the reported accuracy for each feature set and task; no diagnostic instrument is reported for either clinical group; ages are given only as a collective 5-14 range in a domain where voice changes with maturation; no ethics or consent statement exists; and the sustained vowel task cannot express the prosodic properties the paper itself identifies as characterising autistic speech.

**S-061** [local_4917150c] — *Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning*

Acknowledged: the small participant count as the primary limitation; the inability to access ADI-R and ADOS-G scores, which 'limits the interpretation of our results'; the short duration of video scenarios, since 'perhaps longer scenarios might have allowed for a richer representation of the gaze behavior'; the restricted age group; the absence of a benchmark dataset in the autism literature making cross-study comparison difficult; and hardware and software costs as barriers to clinical adoption. The performance decline under participant-level splitting is reported as expected rather than hidden. Not acknowledged: the MIC of 0.79 is computed per image rather than per child, so 547 observations derive from 59 individuals; and because every non-autistic child scores the CARS floor of 15 with zero variance, that correlation largely reflects the between-group difference rather than a severity gradient within autism. Also unremarked: augmented copies of an image share its participant, which would compound leakage in the image-level condition, and three training epochs is very few.

**S-062** [local_241ec2c2] — *Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking*

Acknowledged with unusual directness on one point. The authors anticipate the objection that using the same video for training and diagnosis constitutes contamination, state it themselves - 'although it could be interpreted as contamination and biasing of learning' - and describe their mitigation: only 700 sampled pixels per map enter learning, 50 frames are withheld entirely for diagnosis, and negatives are randomly drawn, which they argue 'approximates a scenario of usage of different videos'. They also note the optical-flow threshold is stimulus-specific, identify dataset construction as the field's binding constraint, and flag intent to release data. Not acknowledged: sensitivity of 69% is not discussed at all despite being the weakest metric and the one that matters for screening; the 2.5:1 class ratio inflates precision and is unaddressed; genetic algorithm selection is not stated to be nested within folds although the selected feature sets are the paper's main interpretive claim; the 28-vote threshold was fitted by Youden on the reported ROC; and no group-wise ages are given across a 3-18 year span.

**S-063** [local_36617ec5] — *Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis*

Acknowledged with unusual completeness. The sample is small, the feature count high, and 'the models were not applied to an independent sample'; the authors state directly that 'data from all participants were used to validate the model; therefore, the reported results correspond to the cross-validation process', offering the 20 iterations and low standard deviations as partial mitigation. Groups were not matched on sociodemographics, IQ or cognitive ability. The macro-level area-of-interest approach 'presented some limitations in terms of recognition of specific eye gaze patterns related to specific areas, such as face areas (i.e., eyes and mouth)'. Eye-tracking glasses may not be accepted by young children and both they and the CAVE are expensive, limiting clinical deployment. Training took about 20 hours even parallelised. Not acknowledged: the feature subset and model were both chosen on the same repeated cross-validation that produces the reported metrics, across five algorithms and ten datasets, so the headline is a maximum over roughly fifty fits; participant sex is never reported; and the minimally verbal composition implied by ADOS-2 module 1 may bound the generality of the reversed social-attention finding.

**S-064** [local_d8e804d6] — *Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms*

Acknowledged: the small sample, attributed to 'the great difficulty of recruiting a large sample of ASD participants and having them complete the motor tasks', with leave-one-out cross-validation and the small number of retained features offered as mitigation against overfitting; autism's heterogeneity requiring larger and more varied samples; and the age range of 6-13 being 'much older than the mean age at diagnosis', so the study 'could only be viewed as an initial examination of social head behaviors in an older sample to establish proof of concept'. The instructed-gesture confound is also raised directly as an explanation for the frequency null. Not acknowledged: the exhaustive search evaluated 63 feature subsets across five classifiers on the same leave-one-out estimate that is reported, so the headline is a maximum over 315 fits; the abstract and results disagree on which two features produced it; and OpenFace tracking failure was fifteen times higher in the autistic group (3.46% versus 0.23%), which is reported but never examined as a possible source of the group difference.

**S-065** [local_712542ca] — *Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset*

None. There is no limitations section and no caveat on sample size, validation design, cluster interpretation or generalisability. Identifiable in review: ten-fold cross-validation operates over 547 images from 59 children with no statement that a child's images were confined to one fold, and the source study demonstrated on these same images that participant-level splitting reduces accuracy from approximately 90% to approximately 71%; k-means clustering was performed on the full image set before classification, so cluster membership was determined using test images; the headline is the best of 45 cluster-by-classifier cells with no multiplicity correction or confidence intervals; the abstract quotes 87% against the table's 88.89%; several reported cells are near-degenerate single-class predictors that are not flagged; and no clinical or behavioural interpretation of any result is offered.

**S-066** [local_0ab41681] — *Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder*

Acknowledged: the sample was 'relatively small and likely not able to capture the full heterogeneity of ASD'; intellectual disability was not measured despite being a known source of variability affecting motor planning and coordination; and only autism and typical development were contrasted, whereas motor difficulties occur across neurodevelopmental disorders so additional diagnostic classes would 'facilitate a dimensional acknowledgment of atypical development'. Practical constraints are also disclosed, including that left-arm markers could not be placed on three autistic children due to compliance problems. Not acknowledged: the abstract reports 0.947 as classification accuracy when it is the subject-level AUC, with trial-level accuracy being 0.739; the sensitivity and specificity are taken at an operating point optimised on the same ROC used to characterise performance; the sex imbalance of 38% versus 69% female is tabulated but never tested or discussed; and the severity correlation rests on 13 observations with a visibly influential high-ADOS point.
