Larger-sample validation; extension to other populations, particularly young infants, where early detection would matter most; determination of whether the effect is age-group specific; direct head-to-head comparison of this short paradigm against established longer paradigms; and combination of the short paradigm with other paradigms. The authors also state a general principle rather than a research step - that current ASD biomarkers including eye tracking are supplementary and not replacements for clinical assessment.

**S-014** [local_5b1d0b36] — *Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday*

Develop a speaker diarization algorithm suited to everyday monitoring conditions, named as important future work because the absence of diarization degrades both acoustic and linguistic analysis; incorporate age and gender to enable age- and gender-dependent fine-grained inference; and extend beyond screening to evaluating intervention effectiveness and tracking child development over time.

**S-015** [local_54954c19] — *Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching*

Design tasks specifically intended to amplify visual-processing differences between groups, since the present stimuli were repurposed; explore capturing the same differences without an eye tracker at all, using operation logs, mouse clicks, task accuracy and miss rate, so that screening could run on ordinary hardware; develop a serious game for large-scale accessible screening; extend the gaze-classifier approach to other conditions with visual attention differences such as dementia, schizophrenia and ADHD; and confront the ethical implications of profiling for clinical conditions from web behaviour.

**S-016** [local_d8dc996a] — *Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Exploit the intention labels already in the dataset to test whether intention classification itself is altered in ASD, which could provide an additional diagnostic cue; and refine the spatial attention model to more finely inspect the kinematic discriminants in the gestures. Both are concrete and grounded in the existing data rather than generic calls for larger samples.

**S-017** [local_88ddfdd1] — *A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task*

No autism-specific future work is proposed. The methodological conclusion is that the technique 'could be used in other problems in which one needs to compare two sets of eye movement sequences in terms of their temporal features', positioning the contribution as a general tool for eye-movement research rather than an autism screening development.

**S-018** [local_361110f1] — *Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features*

Extend classification from ASD-versus-TD to ASD-versus-other-conditions, specifically ADHD; apply machine learning to adjacent problems such as engagement evaluation; integrate genetic, neurological, psychological and kinematic features toward automated objective diagnosis, while acknowledging the open problem of selecting relevant features from a very large pool; and develop ways to quantify higher-level restricted and repetitive behaviour such as circumscribed interest, which accelerometer and Kinect approaches to stereotyped movement cannot capture.

**S-019** [local_51533de4] — *Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations*

Engineer features that directly capture semantic and pragmatic appropriateness turn by turn, since that is what human raters used and the model lacked; enlarge the dataset to improve performance and enable real-world deployment; and test whether longer conversations (10 rather than 5 minutes) and designated topics improve performance. All three are grounded in specific observed shortfalls rather than generic.

**S-020** [local_96c87d36] — *Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking*

Extend to more subjects across a wider span of developmental ages; build a multimodal classifier incorporating demographic information, autonomic nervous system measures, functional MRI and other methodologies; and apply the same paradigm to schizophrenia and ADHD, which also show altered gaze patterns in visual tasks - a differential-diagnosis direction that addresses the specificity question left open by ASD-versus-TD designs.

**S-021** [local_4b031d44] — *Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine*

Expand to larger samples across Bangladesh and other low-resource settings; recruit raters who share the children's linguistic and sociocultural background, hypothesised to close the performance gap with US results; accumulate a large annotated video corpus so that convolutional and recurrent networks can learn features directly from raw video and audio rather than from human annotations; and use location-tagged videos to generate epidemiological prevalence estimates that could inform policy and resource allocation - a public-health framing of future work that is unique in this corpus.

**S-022** [local_05ef29e5] — *Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification*

Incorporate object semantics - the type of object fixated rather than merely whether a fixation fell on an object - motivated by evidence that ASD subjects look at the mouth rather than the eye region of faces; and study in depth which areas of fixation coverage ASD subjects miss, on the argument that what fails to attract attention may be as diagnostic as what attracts it. The discussion additionally implies, without stating it as a formal direction, that features must be adapted by participant age.

**S-023** [local_9528024b] — *Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol*

Run more clinical sessions to obtain data on child engagement and verbal activity during robot-administered tasks, which would enable richer reward models, permit evaluation of the robot's task-selection policy, and allow belief-based classification to be compared against conventional classifiers that currently cannot be trained for lack of data; continue developing social cue detection toward full autonomy; increase the number of protocol tasks; and investigate whether children behave differently when diagnostic tasks are administered by a robot rather than a human examiner - a question that bears directly on whether robot-administered protocols measure the same construct as clinician-administered ones.

**S-024** [local_6230fe22] — *Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism*

Replicate with larger datasets to validate the machine-learning performance, and apply and compare other classification techniques against SVM. Both are generic; no specific validation design, population extension or deployment study is proposed.

**S-025** [local_785ba418] — *Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis*

Extend the approach to kinematic data from more complex movement imitation tasks, with preliminary results described as promising - which is exactly what the same group's 2020 Scientific Reports paper in this corpus goes on to do; and validate the models on newly collected independent data to establish robustness, directly addressing the absence of external validation.

**S-026** [local_fea042be] — *Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual*

No dedicated future-work section. The limitations imply that longer video scenarios should be tested, and the conclusion suggests the scanpath-visualisation approach may generalise to comparable diagnostic problems and to other psychological disorders. No proposals for participant-level validation, larger or independent samples, or addressing the demographic reporting gaps.

**S-027** [local_ba5fbda7] — *Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD*

Apply the trained algorithm to a completely new and larger dataset, and test transdiagnostic specificity across different psychiatric disturbances; combine multiple non-verbal communication parameters with clinical data such as questionnaires to improve prediction and detect cross-domain associations; extend to eye-gaze and facial expression; and move toward fully automated computer-vision pose and gaze estimation to remove the manual region-of-interest step - while cautioning that such tools' validity against standard motion capture is not yet demonstrated and that they vary in susceptibility to tracking failure and in the video types they support.

**S-028** [local_7b468950] — *Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart*

Completion of recruitment and comparison of the blinded classifications against medical diagnosis, with dissemination through peer-reviewed publication and conferences. For the review, the protocol's value is that it specifies in advance what a credible answer would look like, which makes any eventual result interpretable in a way that retrospective studies cannot be.

**S-029** [local_309e5baa] — *Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns*

None proposed. The paper closes by noting the validation-to-test performance gap and its possible causes without setting out future work, consistent with its four-page challenge-entry format.

**S-030** [local_a45f39e9] — *Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time*

Combine RGB and audio modalities alongside pose to improve accuracy; and develop a 3D-trajectory version of the PoTion representation to add spatial information to the pipeline. Both are technical extensions; no validation, population-characterisation or participant-level evaluation work is proposed, despite these being the study's principal gaps.

**S-031** [local_d587f9cd] — *Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning*

Extension of the framework to the other behavioural features the paper names as within its reach - 'eye contact, stereotyped movements of the head, concentration and excessive interest in objects or events' - and continued development of the reasoning module that closes the loop between measurement and robot behaviour. The steps the study most needs are counterbalancing the mediator order, establishing diagnostic status for both groups, validating the automated attention estimates against human coding, and a sample capable of supporting a statistical claim.

**S-032** [local_08b8027d] — *SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths*

Investigate and integrate attention mechanisms into the architecture; explore incorporating additional image features; and - notably - 'a thorough investigation on the differences in the scanpaths between ASD and TD children will also be conducted', an explicit acknowledgement that the model was built and evaluated without establishing what behavioural difference it is exploiting.

**S-033** [local_c6f1209b] — *Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children*

Three directions, two of them named as limitations and one as an engineering output. Compare autistic children's robot interaction against that of typically developing children - subsequently done. Observe interactions with children who have other developmental disorders, to address the differential-diagnosis problem the paper identifies as the hardest. And apply the collected user requirements and evaluation criteria to robot design, which the paper treats as a research product in its own right.

**S-034** [local_83b99e73] — *Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers*

Expand the sample, especially the N-ASD group, to verify the model on children who resolve off the spectrum; make identifying N-ASD from ASD an explicit objective; develop more effective machine-learning models; repeat the analysis under controlled physiological and psychological ages to address the age-matching problem; and develop the still-face paradigm into a convenient, objective and standardised self-screening mode usable at home.

**S-035** [local_638860ef] — *Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis*

Not set out as a discrete future-work section in the extracted text. The introduction's framing implies the priority - the paper notes that adult diagnostic instruments 'have only been validated for use with children', that with adults 'clinicians rarely rely on standardised diagnostic methods making diagnosis less accurate, more subjective and lengthier', and that researching adult diagnostic criteria is listed among the top ten priorities by a UK autism research charity. The work positions itself as contributing quantitative tests to supplement current qualitative ones in that under-served context.

**S-036** [local_7547db68] — *Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network*

Test the system in a large number of cooperating hospitals; collect far more facial expression data from both typically developing and autistic children and build a dedicated children's facial expression database, since existing databases are built mainly from adults and children have rounder faces, larger eyes and less prominent bones that make their features harder to recognise; extend the system to recognise physical movement so autism can be assessed from multiple perspectives; and add severity grading into severe, moderate and mild.

**S-037** [local_878c259f] — *Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach*

Increase the sample size and analyse more postural control data and features, with the expectation of better classification performance. No proposals for external validation, comparison against other developmental conditions, or clinical deployment are made.

**S-038** [local_1579c85a] — *Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through*

Increase participant numbers and add repeated interaction sessions, which the authors expect will grow the dataset rapidly and may then favour the CNN over simpler classifiers; incorporate physiological, eye gaze and vocal data to represent ASD behaviours more comprehensively and improve network reliability; and extend the approach to other naturalistic interactions such as play at home, where much larger datasets could be obtained - a direction the authors argue is enabled specifically by the absence of obtrusive sensors and movement restriction.

**S-039** [local_157d6266] — *Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism*

Improve scalability by exploring capture technologies beyond Kinect, whose motion-tracking imperfections currently require time-consuming manual processing. The authors also frame CAMI as a candidate biomarker 'for defining biologically meaningful ASC subtypes and guiding intervention', and note it can 'track performance during interventions designed to improve social-communicative function through imitation training' - positioning it as a measurement instrument for intervention research rather than only a diagnostic tool.

**S-040** [local_8be557e3] — *Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation*

Increase the volume of infant speech data; refine the acoustic features and the auto-encoder architecture; adopt deeper and more current model structures, since the authors expect the auto-encoder's redistributed feature map to pay off more in complex models than in the deliberately small BLSTM used here; extend the approach to children aged 3-4 who can produce several sentences, adding linguistic features to acoustic ones; and generalise beyond autism to the detection of developmental delay.

**S-041** [local_c79e100a] — *Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models*

Include objective measures of intra-subject gait variance directly in the feature vectors, on the basis of the observed greater variability in autistic subjects; pair variance reduction with synthetic data generation for the minority class to counter the imbalance that averaging exacerbates and the overfitting seen in the SVM; and examine more generally when the loss of dataset size outweighs the gain from reduced variance.

**S-042** [local_4fecbf6d] — *Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network*

Incorporate automatic speaker diarization to remove the manual annotation step and enable a fully automated system; extend from clinic recordings to long home recordings of the kind LENA collects; adopt a longitudinal design testing which speech features are informative at which developmental periods; and reassess the anomalous finding that more severely affected children responded faster rather than slower.

**S-043** [local_95abe653] — *Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning*

Develop a serious game that captures visual processing differences without a dedicated eye tracker; move to behavioural data collected in natural environments; test whether aggregating more simple Search tasks beats designing more complex ones, since complexity did not help; and apply the approach to other conditions with atypical attention patterns - dementia, schizophrenia, ADHD. The authors frame three prerequisites: what makes a good discriminating task, how to record outside the laboratory, and how to do so ethically.

**S-044** [local_40168c96] — *Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based*

Larger-scale replication with attention to class balance; extension from binary identification to severity scoring; protocol improvements to hold children's attention and increase the proportion of valid data; incorporation of fixation duration, which the authors observe 'most identification models have ignored'; replacement of fixed-length piece encoding with recurrent networks able to consume variable-length scanpaths directly; and transfer of the framework to other recognition tasks including other diseases, gender and age.

**S-045** [local_d3852378] — *Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Larger samples permitting a held-out test set and better coverage of autism's heterogeneity; comparison groups with other neurodevelopmental conditions involving movement impairment - ADHD and intellectual disability are named - specifically so that 'taking also into account different neurodevelopment conditions could improve the specificity of the classifiers for ASD rather than for neurodevelopment disorders in general'; matching on IQ, cognitive ability and motor comorbidity; and counterbalanced stimulus orders stratified by functioning level.

**S-046** [local_df438dd2] — *Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening*

Fuse scores and features from multiple complementary automated protocols - response to name and joint attention are named as the natural partners - to move from a single-aspect indicator to a composite screen, and address the distinction between spontaneous and socially responsive smiling that accounts for most remaining scoring error.

**S-047** [local_cd9e45eb] — *Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism*

Extend group sparsity to bi-level, hierarchical, tree-structured and overlapping group definitions so that paradigms can be organised into nested subgroups; replace expert-annotated event windows with data-driven identification of the informative time periods within stimuli; expand the sample to characterise heterogeneity, since limited power constrains severity prediction; design stimuli specifically for predicting ADOS, SRS and Vineland rather than reusing paradigms built for group separation, and develop modelling techniques suited to those outcomes; and test the robustness of selected stimuli on larger unseen data.

**S-048** [local_56237213] — *The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data*

Recruit younger children, aged two years or under, to address the clinical need for earlier diagnosis; and extract additional features from both EEG and eye tracking, since 'multi-modal, multi-feature fusion will likely improve classification accuracy further'.

**S-049** [local_f9a5195f] — *Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses*

Move acquisition into the home, with four named prerequisites: large-scale in-home data acquisition, augmented reality platforms with robust native eye tracking, game design for at-home analysis platforms, and clearly defined measurable experimental parameters. Extend feasibility testing to younger children. Balance cohorts for age and gender. And solve a human-computer interaction problem the authors state precisely - producing 'appropriate user interfaces and games that homogenize use in ways so as to lower the natural variability of measurement', since follow-up Superpower Glass studies showed heterogeneity in less-restricted collection. They also note that later generations of the system dropped the eye tracker entirely because of bulkiness and calibration issues, and expect native gaze tracking in commercial AR devices to resolve this.

**S-050** [local_16a77fb0] — *Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)*

Compare SIT behaviour against a live face-to-face condition with the same topic and script to validate the simulation; make the actress's responses adaptive to participants' answer lengths; provide interaction partners matched on gender, age or ethnic background since similarity enhances mimicry; add automated camera and microphone checks and evaluate accuracy in home settings, since self-administration often diminishes accuracy; use state-of-the-art eye tracking to establish whether gaze carries information in this paradigm; and test sensitivity and specificity in larger clinical samples spanning other psychiatric conditions, since social interaction deficits are common to psychosis, depression, bipolar disorder and substance use disorders.

**S-051** [local_9c4af7a3] — *Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades*

Retain more than six input features, since filtering may have discarded useful signal; move the model out of Azure ML Studio to permit tuning of node count, leaf count and tree depth; and expand beyond 108 participants for a more diverse and robust classifier better able to handle edge cases.

**S-052** [local_b70dae32] — *An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model*

None stated. The conclusion asserts the model's usefulness without identifying required replication, larger samples, per-child validation, or the reconciliation of its own tables.

**S-053** [local_51a0af74] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data*

Enlarge the dataset so that class balance can be achieved with real rather than synthetic samples; automate region-of-interest identification to remove the therapist from the loop and speed the method; and explore alternative machine learning approaches including genetic algorithms for meta-classifier construction. The authors also note the approach generalises to any joint attention video provided a therapist marks the first and last frame of each region.

**S-054** [local_d8d3037b] — *Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study*

Improve the accuracy and stability of the eye-tracking hardware and address VR acceptability among autistic participants; enlarge both samples to reduce small-sample bias; involve a specialist psychologist in scene construction since social stimuli do not automatically discriminate; and design multiple scenes and select the most discriminative.

**S-055** [local_991fe435] — *Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task*

Test dynamic directional cues; establish whether the method distinguishes autism from attention deficits, given that the attention-sustaining phase may be doing much of the work; recruit balanced numbers of girls and boys to test sex-specific performance; and treat base-rate constraints seriously when comparing automated classification against clinical diagnosis.

**S-056** [local_8692a64f] — *Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis*

Collect more samples to permit meaningful comparison against existing diagnostic methods, and establish whether the clap-prediction feature is genuinely diagnostic given its weak observed correlation.

**S-057** [local_4d6fac7e] — *Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network*

None stated beyond the general remark that the approach 'holds potentials in the applications when concerning fusing much more data sources'.

**S-058** [local_30c622f2] — *Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model*

Test the method with different visual inputs to validate which features are genuinely relevant rather than paradigm-specific; extend the age range beyond 3-16 given that autism is lifelong; enlarge the sample and address the sex imbalance; and incorporate intelligence quotient as an additional model feature.

**S-059** [local_bfc088c7] — *Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation*

Validate on a larger autistic sample varying in severity with balanced sex ratio; include other clinical conditions such as developmental delay and ADHD; recruit younger children, citing a meta-analytic mean diagnosis age of 60.48 months overall and 43.18 months among children aged 10 or under; develop contactless calibration-free gaze recording, citing recent webcam-plus-computer-vision work whose accuracy was comparable to manual coding; generate richer gaze features including fixation counts, entropy, revisits and oculomotor performance; and combine eye tracking with kinematic, EEG and neuroimaging data.

**S-060** [local_25e34bbd] — *Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification*

None stated.

**S-061** [local_4917150c] — *Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning*

A larger cohort spanning different ages with analysis of socio-cognitive and cognitive profiles alongside gaze; autism-specific data augmentation methods; longer video scenarios for richer gaze representation; adaptation of more recent deep network methodologies; and, more broadly, transfer of the approach to other neurodevelopmental disorders. The authors also identify the field-level need for a benchmark dataset, which their own open release partly addresses.

**S-062** [local_241ec2c2] — *Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking*

Continue building the dataset toward public release, with the observation that assembling eye-tracking signals alongside expert clinical evaluation 'is not a trivial task'; evaluate further machine learning techniques and additional features; and extend from case-control comparison to discrimination between two disorders, specifically naming autism versus ADHD - the differential question the corpus almost never addresses.

**S-063** [local_36617ec5] — *Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis*

Larger samples with testing on an independent dataset; treatment of sociodemographics, IQ and cognitive ability as moderators; refinement of areas of interest to include eyes and mouth, and adoption of a bottom-up data-driven definition rather than predefined macro-areas; development of a portable system with integrated remote eye tracking to replace glasses that young children may reject and a CAVE that is prohibitively expensive to assemble; and inclusion of other neurodevelopmental conditions such as ADHD to sharpen discrimination and characterise severity gradations.

**S-064** [local_d8e804d6] — *Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms*

Larger and more behaviourally varied samples given autism's heterogeneity; investigation of unintentional rather than instructed head nodding and shaking, to test whether reduced gesture use appears only in spontaneous contexts; and extension to younger children, with the argument that constraint-free computer vision is particularly suited to early screening since data can be collected in natural settings without worn devices or task instructions.

**S-065** [local_712542ca] — *Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset*

None stated.

**S-066** [local_0ab41681] — *Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder*

Measure intellectual disability as a source of inter-subject variability affecting motor planning and coordination; include developmental coordination disorder and ADHD comparison groups to test whether impaired synergies represent 'a common pathogenetic mechanism for these conditions' rather than an autism-specific marker; and extend the synergy framework to speech and language, on the argument that 'speech and language coordination share key similarity with upper limb action' and that language difficulties are common in autism.

**S-067** [local_9ca9b2cc] — *Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment*

The authors propose sharing assessment data 'locally, within the same team or clinic, or globally as integrated clinical dataset sharable by professionals in different places through interoperable systems', and continued development of semi-autonomous adaptive robots that recognise behavioural cues and respond accordingly. The steps the study most needs are a control condition to separate intervention effect from familiarisation, an account of attrition, a chance-corrected agreement statistic with clustering adjustment, and reliability data for the therapist ratings.

**S-068** [local_02fa4215] — *Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning*

Expand the dataset; build a mobile application for clinicians; maintain historical records and raise mental health awareness; and strengthen trait correlations with more data. The authors add two cautions that function as recommendations - that the model requires professional supervision in use, and that the dataset is local and should not be transferred to other populations without consultation.

**S-069** [local_29a3fc54] — *Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism*

Compare voice-only against language-only analysis on the same participants and test whether combining them helps, building on the group's parallel work applying natural language processing to ADOS-2 transcripts from this same sample; develop these measures as treatment outcome measures given 'a recognized dearth of outcome measures available for treatment research in autism', which requires longitudinal demonstration of sensitivity to change; and extend to preverbal toddlers at risk and to young children with minimal or no language, where the authors note identification of atypical voice patterns 'might enhance diagnostic procedures'.

**S-070** [local_b7ec3755] — *Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images*

Two directions, both specific. Condition the feature set on participant age, given the age-dependence documented in the Discussion - though this requires demographic metadata the benchmark does not supply. And invert the analytic target by studying the regions of an image that autistic viewers fail to cover rather than those they fixate, on the reasoning that this 'might provide an insight on what does not attract the attention of a person with ASD'. The second is a genuinely different framing from the rest of the eye-tracking literature in this corpus, which almost uniformly models where gaze goes rather than where it does not.

**S-071** [local_684969f6] — *Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data*

One explicit direction: produce explainable features by mapping the learned representations back to interpretable scanpath properties, which the authors state is 'left for future studies'. One implicit: enlarge the participant pool, since small subject count is their own explanation for the anomalous scanpath-only result. Neither is elaborated, and notably the paper does not propose participant-wise partitioning, which is the direct remedy for the mechanism it identifies.

**S-072** [local_35004e74] — *Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children*

Two concrete and well-motivated directions. Add a spatio-temporal attention mechanism 'to allow knowledge on the specific elements in space and time used to inform the diagnosis process in the network' - which, if it also resolved which person's skeleton drives the decision, would address the study's main unexamined confound. And perform fine-grained annotation along the non-verbal continuum for the behaviours that contributed most, specifically 'the precise annotation of the incidence of communicative gestures, shared affective states, atypical social overtures', to establish what the network learned and to build a measure more sensitive than a 3- or 4-point clinical scale. The broader agenda is finer-grained digital phenotyping able to process data 'at the spatio-temporal resolution that is off limits to human coding', to uncover manifestations not previously evidenced and to define subtypes for more precise clinical action.

**S-073** [local_fa91fc18] — *Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities*

Four directions, three of them named by the authors and one clearly implied. Replicate on a larger sample and determine whether the trained model transfers without retraining - a transfer question rather than a sample-size platitude. Control IQ explicitly as an independent variable rather than relying on task selection to suppress its influence. Include other neurodevelopmental conditions - ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, intellectual disability - to establish whether the signature is autism-specific rather than a general marker of atypical development; the authors give the mechanistic reason, that sensory integration dysfunction is not autism-specific. And extend the method to younger children, where earlier identification would matter most, which is where the motor-precursor literature they review predicts the signal should already be present.

**S-074** [local_115dfe8d] — *A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children*

Two directions, both about model efficiency rather than about validity. Replace the three-model pipeline with convolutional or attention architectures to reduce computational cost; and, more interestingly, develop fusion that can operate 'even especially in the absence of one modality during the model training', which would address the practical barrier that the current design requires both an EEG net and an eye tracker for every child - a genuine obstacle to the scalability the paper claims. A third, briefer aim is to explore additional autism-related features via advanced signal processing. Absent from the agenda: external validation, direct diagnostic confirmation, developmental-level control, or any analysis of which features drive the result.

**S-075** [local_5b7ea7dc] — *AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Two directions, both well chosen. Replicate with IQ-matched cohorts - which follows directly from the acknowledged confound and is the single analysis that would establish whether the result is about autism or about developmental level. And extend from binary classification to continuous prediction of social-function deficit severity, to serve 'as an objective assessment tool that can be used in conjunction with currently available symptom severity measurement questionnaires and clinical scales'. The second is well supported by data already in hand, since ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores, CARS totals and human-rated IJA scores were all collected and none was related to model output; the severity-regression analysis is available in this dataset and simply was not run.

**S-076** [local_87fe26aa] — *Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Two directions, both modest. Enlarge the sample to improve accuracy and stability. And address non-stationarity by 'adopting detection models over time' given the across-day variability in recording conditions - which points toward domain adaptation and is a sensible response to the consumer-EEG constraint the study operates under. Absent from the agenda: any proposal to strengthen diagnostic ascertainment, to measure developmental level, to recruit comparison children from comparable settings, or to validate on an external cohort.

**S-077** [local_893ce2fa] — *An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images*

Two lines are proposed, neither addressing the study's weaknesses. First, 'the enhancement and democratization of eye-tracking technologies' - an infrastructure aim rather than a research one. Second, improving the classifier 'by incorporating multi-class information such as medical records or clinical evaluations', which would move the work toward the multimodal designs elsewhere in this corpus but would require exactly the clinical data this study does not have. Notably absent: any proposal to validate at participant level, to obtain participant metadata, to test on an independent cohort, or to separate augmentation from evaluation.

**S-078** [local_dffe4127] — *Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals*

The agenda follows directly from the findings and is unusually specific. Scale up via internet-based (WebGazer) and smartphone-based eye tracking to obtain the sample sizes needed to identify subtypes, which the authors argue is now feasible and is made more so by their own finding that 2-minute epochs suffice. Collect longitudinal data with dense state-dependent measures - sleepiness, mood - to separate measurement error from genuine within-individual variation across weeks or years, and to assess intervention efficacy while revealing what an intervention changes ('gaze to faces but not to other features might change throughout training'). Design stimuli with specifically chosen visual features to maximise within-individual reliability and between-individual differences, which 'possibly... could also improve the classification analyses'. And integrate with neuroimaging and genetics, on the reasoning that systematic gaze differences 'would be expected to translate to differences also in evoked BOLD-fMRI activations' and 'may be an endophenotype reflecting substantial genetic effects'. The through-line is that establishing individual-level reliability was a prerequisite for all of these, which is the paper's framing of its own contribution.

**S-079** [local_2b766683] — *Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech*

Five directions, with the most substantive being technical. Collect more data across a wider selection of both groups, argued from the observation that 115.5 minutes already sufficed. Replace manual splicing with automatic blind source separation - the authors are realistic about this, calling it 'an exceptionally challenging task' while noting it is 'possibly a necessary hurdle to overcome to develop widely available and consistently effective autism machine learning diagnosis resources', which correctly identifies the bottleneck for any home-recording pipeline where parents and children speak simultaneously. Explore wearable collection through devices such as Google Glass, building on the group's prior work delivering social cues through wearables. Add crowdsourced human annotation of audio features. And combine audio with computer-vision quantification of hand stimming, upper-limb movement and eye contact toward an interpretable multimodal system. Notably absent: any proposal to verify diagnoses, to match on age, or to characterise what acoustically distinguishes the groups.

**S-080** [local_2895bdf0] — *Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection*

Seven directions, each traceable to a stated limitation. Extend to adults and younger children, and to lower-IQ and minimally verbal participants who cannot complete Module 3. Test each component feature systematically to establish individual predictive power. Determine which voice features drive the voice model's false positives, with a specific and testable hypothesis - 'it could be that loudness is a general non-specific feature of young children interviewed on sensitive topics (as those covered by the Friends task) in an unfamiliar setting; if so, removal of these non-contributory features might improve the classification performance of voice-only models'. Control microphone quality and placement to reduce dependence on denoising. Establish test-retest reliability and short-term stability, which are prerequisites for the intended outcome-measure application. Sample naturalistic conversation outside the clinic, 'aiming at minimizing interference by strangers and capturing naturally occurring conversations in the ecological niche of the participants'. And replace manual transcription with automatic speech recognition, with the explicit caveat that 'future studies based on ASR transcription will need to re-evaluate performance of the models relying on ALMs' - recognising that ASR errors would propagate into disfluency and maze measures that depend on precise transcription.

**S-081** [local_423b636b] — *Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers*

Three directions, each following from a stated limitation. Explore the developmental course of head movement differences and 'elucidate their nature and neurobiological basis', with several concrete hypotheses already advanced - that the movements modulate sensory information generally rather than social perception specifically, that they reflect postural control difficulties that increase with sensory demand, or that like some repetitive behaviours they serve a regulatory function when stimuli are arousing. Extend the computer vision beyond the face to the trunk and shoulders, following directly from the observation that the movement is not confined to the head. And combine head movement 'with other behavioral biomarkers such as gaze, facial dynamics, and response to name' toward a multimodal digital phenotyping tool - which is the group's programmatic direction and is supported here by the demonstration that a single behavioural channel reaches AUC 0.85 in a prevalence-realistic sample.

**S-082** [local_ffa35101] — *Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study*

Five directions, four of them well grounded. Larger samples covering both sexes and wider age ranges. Comprehensive language-ability assessment for group matching, with the mechanism stated. Extension to further typological classes, with named candidates chosen for their position relative to the two languages studied - German and Dutch as rhythmically similar to English, Japanese as distant from both. Neurophysiological investigation of prosody production across language groups, building on existing findings of increased right inferior frontal gyrus and right caudate activation during prosody comprehension in autism, with the observation that such findings 'would be particularly compelling if replicated in individuals with ASD who are speakers of languages other than English'. The fifth is a proposal to examine the ASPM gene as a marker for prosodic differences, on the basis that most Han Chinese people carry a T allele favouring linguistic pitch processing which 'may implicate a role of genetic factors in contributing to cross-linguistic differences of ASD phenotypes'. This last is speculation built on a population-genetic association applied to a null classification result, with no genetic data collected in the study, and it is the one place where the paper's interpretive discipline lapses - it offers an ancestry-based genetic explanation for a language-based finding when the language explanation the authors themselves give (that lexical tone constrains f0) is sufficient.

**S-083** [local_81ecbc6f] — *Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings*

Six directions, each following from a stated limitation. Larger samples permitting stratification by age, sex and IQ. Inclusion of non-spectrum and other psychiatric groups. Other narrative contexts, with the specific prediction that less structured elicitation may behave differently. Model explanation techniques applied to word-level contributions, with the goal that 'giving meaning to collections of important words may lead to discovering new dimensions of language relevant to ASD' - which frames explainability as a route to linguistic discovery rather than only to trust. Combination of text with speech and extra-linguistic features, citing Asgari and colleagues and Fusaroli and colleagues. And automatic speech-to-text to eliminate the transcription bottleneck. The authors also express a clear preference between their own representations for translational purposes: 'the single vector approach, rather than the pages approach, seems to have the greatest possible clinical utility', because page segmentation is ambiguous and manual whereas the single vector 'enables full automation and objectification of the measurement' - choosing the marginally worse-performing option on deployability grounds, which is the right kind of reasoning and rare in this corpus.

**S-084** [local_bc62bc4b] — *Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening*

Five directions, the first two substantive. Recruit a developmental-delay comparison group alongside autistic and typically developing children - the specificity test that the paradigm currently cannot support, and which matters particularly for a preferential-viewing task since developmental delay would be expected to affect social attention. Test at true population prevalence rather than balanced classes, to establish deployment performance. Characterise the symptom profiles of false-negative children, on the hypothesis that the 12.5% miss rate reflects clinical heterogeneity - though this requires severity data the study did not collect. Address the sex imbalance with reference to the established prevalence gap. And develop the system into 'an off-the-shelf and ready-to-use software package'. The last sits uneasily against the preceding four: a system that has not been tested at realistic prevalence, against developmental delay, or with characterised failure modes is not ready for packaging, and the paper does not sequence these.

**S-085** [local_889d9bd6] — *Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children*

Five directions, tightly tied to the stated limitations. Validate on independent datasets. Recruit 'a broad spectrum of the ASD and non-ASD participants' to address spectrum bias - the direct remedy for the acknowledged overestimation. Add developmental assessment alongside chronological age. Resolve the biological motion inconsistency, where their toddler comparison group failed to show a preference that prior work reports, with the authors noting that 'the age range for our study is between 1.5 and 3, while the previous study focused only on 2-year-olds, so we cannot exclude the possibility that the discrepancy is due to age range difference'. And exploit the age-specific paradigm rankings: 'elucidating the role of different paradigms in ASD classification across different stages may shed light on developing paradigms for earlier ASD detection, particularly for toddlers between 1.5 and 3 years old or even younger' - which is the concrete translational implication of the study's central finding.

**S-086** [local_361b59fb] — *Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

Six directions, all operationally concrete. Reduce dependence on human video analysts in future algorithm generations - the scalability bottleneck. Determine what training primary care clinicians need to use the Device confidently in practice, which is a human-factors question the trial did not address since it used a study protocol rather than routine deployment. Run a registrational study monitoring the stability of Device results against diagnosis over time, 'including establishing a diagnosis later in children who at the time of initial evaluation did not meet diagnostic criteria for ASD' - the follow-up that would establish whether indeterminate and negative outputs remain correct as children develop, and the single most important missing evidence for a tool used at 18-72 months. Power future studies for demographic subgroups. Confirm performance across intellectual levels. And obtain cost and reimbursement data to establish whether deployment would be equitable, with explicit reference to Medicaid sustainability and to families without smartphones or insurance.

**S-087** [local_afdb603d] — *Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.*

Five directions, of which two are unusually well targeted. Redesign the recording process so that intensity and pitch can be analysed at all, with the concrete specification that all participants should wear a microphone at a fixed mouth distance - the authors note this must be balanced against 'the necessity of maintaining some environmental comforts for the patients in a clinical condition', which correctly identifies the tension between naturalistic elicitation and acoustic control. Adopt common feature sets across studies so results are comparable across languages, citing De La Fuente and colleagues - a standardisation argument that this review's cross-linguistic study (Lau and colleagues) makes in a different form. The remaining three are larger datasets with feature-subset comparison to build a standard acoustic set for autism; investigation of how voice features relate to speaker age, sex and height; and testing whether the jitter and shimmer pattern seen here in children and reported by Kissine and Geelhand in adults persists across the lifespan, which the authors suggest would be 'a turning point in the early diagnosis'.

**S-088** [local_4f7e7eb3] — *Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques*

One direction: 'to extract features using CNN models and combine them with features extracted by LBP and GLCM algorithms into a single feature vector for each image and classify it using all three ANN, FFNN and SVM algorithms.' This proposes more feature concatenation on the same 547 images with the same split, and addresses none of the study's substantive weaknesses. No proposal is made to group by participant, obtain demographic or diagnostic metadata, validate externally, interpret the features behaviourally, or test on an independent dataset.

**S-089** [local_db6c2d7c] — *Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With*

Four directions, of which two are unusually practical. Expand the population and correct the class imbalance by augmentation. Analyse additional motion features such as limb movements and coordination, which the charades format would support naturally since the child is acting out prompts with their whole body. And - the most substantive - 'performing qualitative human-centered investigations or pragmatic randomized controlled trials to evaluate clinical usability' and 'evaluating the real-world diagnostic capabilities of our approach across diverse environmental settings'. Proposing a pragmatic randomised trial and human-centred usability work as the next step, rather than a larger dataset or a better architecture, is a translational rather than technical research agenda and is rare in this corpus.

**S-090** [local_8b5fb23b] — *Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms*

Four directions. The first follows directly from the stated limitation and is the right one: obtain a dataset of single trials from a large group rather than multiple images from few participants. The second concerns collection quality - ensuring attention to the tracker and a distraction-free environment. The third proposes electrooculography as an alternative signal. The fourth is a deployment proposal that outruns the evidence considerably: 'a mobile app with an incorporated DNN-based ASD classifier and an extensive ET dataset of children aged 6 to 24 months may assist parents in independently screening their toddlers for ASD using a mobile device' - proposed for an age band entirely outside the analysed data, using a modality that requires an eye tracker, on the basis of a participant-level sensitivity of 58.62%.

**S-091** [local_6dcefc34] — *Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism*

Four directions, two of which would directly test the study's own weaknesses. Reproducing the paradigm with an examiner who is neither the parent nor informed of the diagnosis would isolate the child's contribution to the duration measure from the parent's and would blind the labeller - addressing the confound and the unblinding in a single design change, and it is the right experiment. Expanding recruitment to permit demographic subgroup validation follows directly from the equity framing that motivates the study, since a tool proposed to reduce disparities must be shown not to perform differentially across the groups it is meant to serve. The remaining two are extending prompts beyond CAFE images to video, and investigating how the parent-child dyadic relationship shapes the signal - the latter framed as scientific rather than merely methodological.

**S-092** [local_65974fc7] — *Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction*

One direction: 'One of our main tasks in future is to further enrich the dataset', motivated by the observation that the CNN needs more labelled data than are available. No proposal is made to group by child, characterise the participants, document the diagnostic procedure, describe the recording configuration, or validate on independent data.

**S-093** [local_988c462e] — *The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation*

No dedicated future-work section, but both stated limitations imply directions and one is developed comparatively. Improving acquisition - the authors' contrast with a four-microphone beamforming setup indicates that better signal-to-noise ratio is the obvious lever, though it would trade against the deployability that a single-microphone setup buys. And relaxing the 20-second, 50-vocalisation minimum, which is framed as a constraint of the deep-learning architecture and which currently excludes the least verbal children. The paper also positions its result against two prior severity-estimation studies - one on Japanese-speaking adolescents using support vector regression and one on English-speaking children achieving a correlation of 0.634 in 33 children - and notes that it achieves 'a similar correlation value (0.606) while using a larger dataset of 132 children', which implicitly frames sample size as the axis along which the field should progress.

**S-094** [local_76de1c03] — *The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children*

Improve and further develop the game scenarios in close cooperation with target users, explicitly including children alongside psychiatrists, psychologists and therapists; identify scenarios attractive to children; and extend toward a human-robot-interaction-enabled system that supports differentiation of autism symptoms beyond turn-taking. The inclusion of children themselves among the users to be consulted is the only participatory-design commitment in this corpus. The obvious additional steps, not proposed, are blinded rating, a larger sample, a developmental-level covariate, and test-retest assessment.

**S-095** [local_3ba6d25c] — *Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach*

Fuse oculomotor with visual fixation features, since the authors' own earlier work on the same children reached 84.62% from fixation alone and 92.31% with fixation plus conversational length; build a representative ASD oculomotor template on the model of Eraslan et al.'s scan-path trend analysis and classify by similarity to it; pursue the neural basis of gaze irregularity; push the age range down towards the 43-month mean diagnostic age, motivated by evidence of atypical oculomotor behaviour in infants later diagnosed; test against developmental delay and ADHD rather than TD alone; extend to children with more severe presentations and a balanced sex ratio; and separate inherent oculomotor function from visual-attention allocation in unconstrained settings. The last of these is the most interesting, because it is an admission that the paper's central conceptual claim - that it measures oculomotor behaviour rather than attention - is not established by its own data.

**S-096** [local_70a30e2b] — *A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features*

Three concrete directions, the first two of which address real gaps. Test on a wider population and on a variety of cognitive deficits to determine whether the device can differentiate autism from other conditions rather than only from typical development - which is precisely what the four excluded CP and fragile X children could have begun to address. Investigate how the toy car's size, shape and colour affect children's engagement with it and therefore the extracted features - a design-sensitivity question rarely raised in this literature and directly relevant to whether a play-based screen generalises across devices. And position the device as one component of a larger multimodal screening system rather than standalone, on the argument that different autistic children present different symptoms so a single modality will always miss some.

**S-097** [local_a22f97df] — *A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities*

Four directions. Enlarge the dataset in both size and feature relevance so that the latent space organises without supervision, which is the authors' stated ambition and would remove their reliance on clinical labels as ground truth. Generate as many candidate features as possible so a globally optimal feature set for autism identification can be determined, citing Zhao et al. (2021). Collect more clinical data so the latent space is more densely covered and new participants are less likely to fall into unvisited regions - a coverage argument that follows directly from their decision to classify by fitted density rather than by the predictor network. And combine these kinematic measures with traditional behavioural and cognitive scales into a multimodal risk indicator supporting clinicians rather than replacing them. Absent from the list, and more pressing than any of these, are participant-level validation, an independent cohort, a clinical comparison group, and test-retest reliability for the features proposed as clinical thresholds.

**S-098** [local_c6853fe2] — *A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation*

No future-work section is provided. The conclusion's forward-looking claims are about deployment rather than research: that the method reduces the professional-knowledge requirement for assessment, provides efficient and objective computer-aided screening, and could support early autism screening in remote areas with underdeveloped medical care. Judged against the evidence, the research steps that would need to come first are clear and unstated: evaluation on children not used to train the detector; a balanced sample containing a meaningful number of non-autistic children so that the item score's discriminative value can be assessed; a second, blinded clinician rater with reported reliability so the reference standard is not one person's judgement; chance-corrected agreement statistics appropriate to an ordinal score; and threshold selection on a development set separate from the evaluation set. The wider point this study raises for the review, and does not itself pursue, is whether automating individual ADOS-2 items one at a time is a viable route to instrument automation - it is the only paper in this corpus attempting it, and the answer depends on error rates the paper cannot currently estimate.

**S-099** [local_f1b626c8] — *Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games*

Three directions are stated. Enrich the feature set derived from the eye-tracking graph in order to improve precision and accuracy - a reasonable ambition, and one the study has itself left unexploited, since the introduction develops a graph-theoretic framing of fixations as vertices and saccades as edges but no graph metric is ever computed. Extend the classifier to include conditions that overlap with autism so that differential diagnosis becomes possible - the most valuable of the three, and an acknowledgement that separating autistic children from unscreened schoolchildren does not establish clinical utility. And note that a system trained on children will not transfer to adults without retraining. Not mentioned, and more pressing: participant-level validation, reporting held-out rather than pooled performance, an independent cohort, culturally matched stimuli, inclusion of girls, and any cognitive covariate.

**S-100** [local_6249bd63] — *Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior*

Five directions, all following directly from what the study found. Examine which behaviours drive a predicted diagnosis, framed not as a nicety but as a precondition for clinical use - 'clinicians should understand how the AI algorithm makes a prediction before taking this prediction into account' - and requiring more granular expression models than the current localised basis provides. Extend to younger participants, since early diagnosis is where the developmental benefit lies. Move from monadic to dyadic analysis by incorporating the confederate's behaviour, which the recording setup already captures and the paradigm's interactive nature makes theoretically apt. Test on neurodiverse samples rather than autism-versus-neurotypical, the authors' own diagnosis of their key external-validity gap. And conduct user research to determine whether clinician decisions actually improve when AI assistance is available - the step that would convert a demonstrated non-overlap of errors into demonstrated clinical value. Absent from the list: raising sensitivity, external validation on an independent cohort, and analysis of the bored condition.

**S-101** [local_8b9e0e8a] — *Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas*

Four directions, all substantive. Collect data from other age bands both to extend the model beyond 3-6 years and to characterise how dynamic viewing patterns change developmentally. Investigate diversity and individuality within the autistic group through subcategory classification and, notably, through explicit comparison of children who have and have not undergone rehabilitation training - which would convert the study's incidental finding about trained attention into a proper analysis. Predict stimulus discriminability directly with deep models, so that screening image sets can be designed rather than curated, building on the study's own demonstration that 60 well-chosen images match the full 82 while 60 random ones do not. And fuse gaze with fMRI, EEG, facial expression and observation-scale scores, described as an important and understudied challenge. What is missing from the list is the step that would matter most for the stated purpose: prospective evaluation in an unselected community population at realistic prevalence, with a described diagnostic reference standard.

**S-102** [local_0e476686] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts*

Two directions, both narrow: tune BERT's hyperparameters, since it was deliberately left at defaults and might improve further; and train additional deep and classical models 'to ensure that no high-performing models are overlooked'. Both extend the leaderboard rather than test the finding. The steps that would matter are absent from the list: splitting by user rather than by tweet, masking autism-related vocabulary to separate topic from style, describing and expanding the comparison group, reporting user-level performance, and obtaining any form of clinical validation for the label. So is any consideration of research ethics or of engagement with the community whose posts constitute the dataset.

**S-103** [local_fbaf69bf] — *Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Four directions, each following from a specific gap. Study complexity and coordination of facial dynamics during live interpersonal interaction rather than passive viewing, motivated by evidence that autistic people have difficulty with affect coordination in social exchange - the natural extension of a measure built on temporal predictability. Apply the same complexity analysis to head motion as an index of postural control, exploiting data the pipeline already produces. Pursue the preliminary supplementary finding that integrated entropy may separate autism from developmental or language delay, which is the differential-diagnosis question most of this corpus avoids. And combine the facial-complexity biomarker with gaze indices, response to name, motor signatures and other measures before any automated decision tool is deployed - stated as a precondition rather than an aspiration. Absent from the list, and worth adding: test-retest reliability, prospective external validation, and the relationship between entropy and ADOS-T severity.

**S-104** [local_74416ba7] — *Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders*

Three directions, each tied to a specific finding. Collect more data to establish validity, the standard response to a small sample. Develop a method that works for participants whose gaze barely moves - which follows directly from the error analysis and is a real methodological problem rather than a generic wish, since a gaze-based classifier that fails on 17% of children because they use peripheral vision has a systematic blind spot that more data alone will not close. And obtain actual IQ values and other individual characteristics so that the relationship between the model and the heterogeneity of the conditions can be examined - an acknowledgement that a high-functioning sample of 15 cannot speak for a spectrum. Not proposed, and worth noting: a direct autism-versus-schizophrenia classifier, which the dataset already supports and which would be the natural differential-diagnosis test; and validation on an independent cohort.

**S-105** [local_7c6a5aa4] — *Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders*

Three directions, all in the conclusion and all reasonable. Examine the stability of predictions over time - the obvious next step for a dataset spanning two and a half years that is currently analysed cross-sectionally. Predict quantitative traits of clinical relevance such as adaptive skills and the severity of the autism presentation, which acknowledges that the present labels are binary and unverified. And develop 'next generation digital markers and fingerprints for understanding change, variation, and opportunities for growth' - a framing oriented towards monitoring and personalisation rather than diagnosis, which is the more defensible use of this kind of data. Not proposed, and more pressing: obtaining any clinically verified labels, adjusting for or matching on age, reporting user-level rather than window-level performance, evaluating without pseudo-labelling, and addressing the ethical basis for research use of the telemetry.

**S-106** [local_8a706eaa] — *Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder*

External validation in larger, IQ-matched cohorts is named as the priority and is the correct one. Beyond that, the authors propose that the standardised video acquisition setup could support large-scale collection of behavioural biomarker datasets 'applicable to a wide range of neuropsychiatric conditions', and offer a concrete protocol recommendation derived from their compliance analysis - that a joint attention-driven model should be trained on the first five to ten repetitions of a task, since both groups habituate beyond that point. Not proposed, and needed: a clinical comparison group so that autism-specificity can be separated from general developmental difference; a within-autism-only severity analysis using the K-ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores the study already holds; reporting of specificity; and test-retest assessment for a system intended to track severity.

**S-107** [local_6b9484ce] — *Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking*

Two directions, both aimed at the sample-size constraint the authors identify: use data augmentation, specifically generative adversarial networks, to synthesise additional scanpath images, and expand the dataset itself. The first should be flagged as a hazard rather than a solution in this specific setting - generating synthetic scanpath images from a 547-image corpus and then evaluating on an image-level split would compound rather than mitigate the dependence between training and test data, and would do so invisibly. Expanding the dataset is the sound recommendation. Not proposed: splitting by participant, reporting participant-level accuracy, characterising the children, or examining what the models learn.

**S-108** [local_c6a4ea7b] — *SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism*

Two directions, both apt: identify autism severity from speech, and explore differential diagnosis using speech-based analysis. The second is the more important and is unusually actionable, because the Eigsti corpus the study already uses contains a developmental delay group alongside autism and typical development. Distinguishing autistic children from children with developmental delay on pragmatic features - rather than from typically developing children on measures dominated by general language level - is the clinically meaningful version of this study's claim, and the material for it was in hand. Not proposed, and needed: leave-one-corpus-out validation, which the three-corpus structure makes available and which would test whether the model generalises across settings rather than learning corpus identity; adjustment for age and language level; and nesting of feature selection.

**S-109** [local_5c43dffa] — *Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths*

No future-work section. The conclusion restates the finding that velocity-infused spatio-temporal scan-paths capture patterns associated with age, sex and their interaction, framed as progress on the heterogeneity problem. The steps the study's own results most clearly call for are absent from the paper: subject-disjoint evaluation, augmentation applied only within training folds, and - most importantly - a diagnosis classifier stratified or matched on age and sex, since the paper has itself established that both are strongly encoded in the representation and both differ substantially between its diagnostic groups.

**S-110** [local_32da8ede] — *A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths*

No dedicated future-work content in the retrieved text beyond the conclusion's framing that early-detection tools should be 'brief, easily understandable for parents, and easy to administer by healthcare professionals' and that eye tracking suits that purpose. Absent, and needed: reconciliation of the reported metrics, participant-level cross-validation, a held-out confirmation of the selected hyperparameter configuration, a majority-class baseline, and use of the available CARS scores to test whether classification tracks severity.

**S-111** [local_15ed96cb] — *A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning*

Five directions, all specific and all following from a stated limitation. Model each child's milestone performance pattern over time rather than collapsing to binary attainment, which would restore the delay-trajectory information the current representation discards. Add early signs not currently in the national protocol, with three concrete candidates named. Incorporate paternal age and family history of autism, both known risk factors absent from routine collection. Replicate with a later and more stable outcome label to reduce the label noise the authors quantify. And conduct direct cross-cultural validation before transferring the approach, covering not only sign expression but 'parental recognition, interpretation, and reporting levels' - an acknowledgement that a model built on parent-reported concern and clinician recording is embedded in a particular culture of help-seeking and documentation. The list is notable for containing no proposal to improve the algorithm.

**S-112** [local_261afa51] — *AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: &#x201C;A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System&#x201D;*

None is proposed. The introduction states an intention to test the model on images of children below 36 months 'to assess its efficacy in early detection', and no such analysis is reported. The conclusion contains no future-work content beyond restating the results.

**S-113** [local_3e88f3ce] — *An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks*

The paper proposes validation on larger multi-site datasets under different partitioning schemes. The more informative next steps, all available within ABIDE-I: refit with the ADOS, ADI-R and SRS fields removed, which would establish what the imaging and demographic streams contribute on their own; run leave-one-site-out evaluation to quantify the site confound; report an age-and-IQ-only baseline; and correlate the model's output probability with ADOS severity rather than consuming severity as input. The first of these would convert the study from a demonstration of circularity into a genuine test of multimodal fusion, and the architecture is well built enough to make that test worth running.

**S-114** [local_5b5f2237] — *Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development*

Larger samples with a balanced sex ratio and a wider severity range. The discussion adds a deployment argument rather than a research direction, positioning the approach as economic, contactless and calibration-free and therefore suited to early objective identification. Not proposed, and needed given the study's own results: nesting the feature construction within the cross-validation to establish whether the derived-feature gain survives, adjusting for the IQ and age differences, relating coordination to severity dimensionally, and directly reconciling the cross wavelet result with the group's own null complexity-matching finding on the same recordings.

**S-115** [local_13426811] — *Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning*

Three directions, all concrete. Comprehensive verification with a substantially larger and more diverse participant pool, with the logistical difficulty of achieving this acknowledged rather than waved away. Improvement of the automatic annotation system, particularly for te-clauses, either by sharpening category definitions or by expanding training data - a specific and testable target derived from the study's own error analysis. And extension to other languages through transfer comparison, the same method used to build the Japanese system network, which the authors argue makes the annotation scheme 'applicable to any language'. That last is an unusually ambitious but well-grounded claim, since it rests on a documented linguistic methodology rather than on an assumption that features transfer. Not proposed, and needed: cognitive assessment of the comparison group, and analysis relating model output to the SRS-2, AQ, Vineland-II and ADOS-2 data already collected.

**S-116** [local_948fa8d0] — *Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms*

None proposed. The conclusion restates the method and the comparison without identifying any next step.

**S-117** [local_893dfc22] — *Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed*

None stated.
