Without that decomposition, an accuracy of 98.33% is consistent with the model reading affective state, with it reading ambient temperature at the moment of capture, and with it reading individual identity across an image-level split - and the study provides no means of distinguishing them.

**S-131** [local_0f5a351e] — *Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

None. A single image modality throughout, with no fusion of any kind.

**S-132** [local_786b6280] — *Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features*

None across modalities - text only, with no acoustic, prosodic or visual information. The ratio features constitute a form of dyadic fusion in that they combine the child's output with the investigator's within a session, which is conceptually similar to the interaction-level modelling in the pose-based studies charted elsewhere in this review and is more than most transcript-based work attempts. Its vulnerability is that the investigator's behaviour is not standardised across the four source corpora, so the denominator of every ratio feature varies by protocol.

**S-133** [local_879ec69b] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning*

Two representational streams over one sensor, aligned by a pairwise Euclidean distance loss during training and then tested separately. Stream one encodes skeleton sequences as Skepxels for an image backbone; stream two embeds relative joint angles and applies MSG3D, combining graph convolution over the skeletal topology with temporal convolution over time. The design rationale is stated clearly - the loss 'minimises the distance between the Skepxel embedding, which captures spatiotemporal features, and the GCN embedding, which models structural joint relationships', promoting co-learning of complementary representations - and the ablation supports the graph component, with a Stack Transformer substitution lowering accuracy. This is representational rather than sensor fusion, but it is a coherent idea coherently tested. What is missing is a decomposition of how much each stream contributes to the final figure, which would be the natural complement to the architecture ablation that is reported.

**S-134** [local_93e5d23d] — *Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]*

None. A single acoustic modality, with two analysis routes over the same signal - Praat-derived perturbation measures for the statistical comparison and spectrogram images for the network. The two routes are never joined: the paper does not test whether the network's confidence relates to jitter, shimmer or harmonics-to-noise ratio, which would have connected its interpretable finding to its opaque one and is the single most useful additional analysis the existing data would support.

**S-135** [local_a0d73248] — *Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm*

None. A single tabular modality.

**S-136** [local_4ceee075] — *Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics*

Three landmark streams from one camera, concatenated at the feature level and modelled jointly - within-camera multimodal fusion rather than multi-sensor fusion. The breadth is a genuine advantage: face, posture and hands are rarely combined in one model in this literature, and doing so at 30 frames per second with temporal modelling gives the network access to how expression, posture and gesture co-vary. The paper argues this explicitly, proposing a model that 'simultaneously analyzes facial expressions, head movements, hand gestures, and posture over time, combining spatial and temporal learning'. What is missing is any decomposition: no ablation reports performance with each stream removed, so the relative contribution of face, pose and hands is unknown. That omission is more costly here than usual, because the three streams carry very different confound exposure - facial mesh geometry is strongly sex-linked, hand motion energy much less so - and the study's 32-point sex imbalance between groups makes the distinction decisive for interpreting the result.

**S-137** [local_84bcd4ed] — *Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of*

None empirically. The proposed architecture is a two-stage fusion of facial expression analysis with questionnaire response, with the questionnaire invoked when facial cues are ambiguous - a sensible design in principle, since it routes the hard cases to the instrument actually validated for the construct. But the questionnaire was never administered to any person, so no fusion occurred on any data, and the claim that 'incorporating the GELOPH<15> questionnaire improved diagnostic reliability and consistency' describes an expected property of the design rather than an observed result.

**S-138** [local_d97673f4] — *Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

None. A single image modality throughout.

**S-139** [local_86a67a4f] — *Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children*

Architectural rather than modal fusion. The autism model combines ResNet50V2 and InceptionV3 at the feature level, with the rationale that single-network approaches fail to obtain 'hierarchical features with fine grains'. Combining backbones whose receptive-field structures differ - residual depth against inception-module width - is a coherent argument for multi-granularity feature capture, and it is stated rather than assumed. No ablation isolates what each backbone contributes, so whether the hybrid outperforms its components is not established, and given the inconsistency in the reported metric set the comparison could not be evaluated in any case.

**S-140** [local_0a39cca9] — *Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy*

Decision-level ensembling rather than modality fusion. Two CNNs classify independently and their outputs are combined by probability averaging or majority voting, with the stated rationale that this 'makes the system more reliable and accurate by lowering the chance of errors from a single model and making it better at generalizing new data'. Five pairings are compared, which gives real architectural breadth, and the pairings deliberately combine a lightweight backbone with an EfficientNet variant of differing scale. No ablation reports single-model performance against the ensembles, so the claimed ensembling gain is asserted rather than demonstrated.

**S-141** [local_7432ffd7] — *Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models*

No fusion of behavioural modalities - eye tracking only. There is, however, an undeclared fusion of a different kind: the clinical instrument score (CARS) is concatenated with the behavioural features into a single input vector. That is not multimodal behavioural fusion; it is the insertion of the outcome's own measurement instrument into the predictor set. Multimodal work is named as future rather than present.

**S-142** [local_8ff20c48] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning*

No fusion - a single questionnaire modality, augmented by four static fields (age, sex, jaundice, family history). The study belongs to the corpus's questionnaire-tabular branch alongside local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 rather than to any sensor-based branch.

**S-143** [local_986436f2] — *Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost*

No fusion - a single image modality. The architecture stacks several representations of the same photograph (CNN features, shape-appearance model, landmark graph, boosted trees), which the paper presents as integrating multiple facial features but which is pipeline depth rather than multimodality. Genuine multimodal fusion with voice, gaze and movement is deferred to future work.

**S-144** [local_bb4d1f7a] — *Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models*

No multimodal fusion - eye tracking alone. There is a within-modality fusion of two representations of the same recording (scanpath sequences for the RNN path, cropped eye images for the CNN path), which is what the hybrid designation refers to. The Gesell Developmental Scale was collected and could have supported a genuine behavioural-clinical fusion, but no GDS result is reported.

**S-145** [local_13c1f46d] — *Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism*

No fusion of modalities - a single image source. What the paper calls an ensemble is three classifiers (LSTM, DBN, HKELM) over one shared MobileNetV2 feature vector from one photograph. The LSTM's inclusion is unexplained: there is no temporal or sequential structure in a single still image for a recurrent model to exploit, and the paper never addresses this.

**S-146** [local_e771fb69] — *Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data*

This is one of the few charted studies with genuine cross-modal structure, and its fusion design is worth recording precisely. Two local models operate on separate files, one specialising in kinematic features and one in eye-movement features; their outputs are merged and passed to a global model with its own dense layers and dropout. That is late fusion at the model level, in contrast to the feature-concatenation fusion used elsewhere in the corpus. The design is sound in outline. What it cannot support is inference: with 44 examples divided among three clients and evaluated on nine cases, no comparison between the unimodal and fused configurations is distinguishable from noise, and the paper never makes that comparison explicitly in any case.

**S-147** [local_945300a5] — *Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network*

No multimodal fusion - a single photographic modality. The introduction reviews thermal-imaging work at length (ResNet-50 on facial skin temperature across emotional states) and a thermal branch would have been a natural pairing with this acquisition setup, given that the protocol already controls room temperature and includes a body-temperature acclimation period. Only RGB photographs are collected.

**S-148** [local_ed30e24c] — *Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI*

No fusion - a single questionnaire modality plus static demographic covariates. Multimodal extension with genetic and neuroimaging data is proposed as future work only.

**S-149** [local_b9de0d7f] — *Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques*

No modality fusion. The only fusion is the merging of two questionnaire datasets from different regions, which is dataset pooling rather than multimodal integration - and, as noted, the regional structure created by that merge is then discarded rather than used for cross-cohort validation.

**S-150** [local_14df790d] — *Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach*

No fusion - a single questionnaire modality with demographic covariates. The systematic subset comparison is a study of feature configurations within one modality, not multimodal integration.

**S-151** [local_4da2b941] — *Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study*

No modality fusion - a single self-report modality throughout. The nearest analogue is the input-configuration comparison, which tests whether adding gender and/or autism diagnosis to the CAT-Q-ES items improves prediction and finds that it does not. The authors themselves identify observational measurement of camouflaging as the modality this study lacks and recommend adding it.

**S-152** [local_6e7174c0] — *A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach*

No fusion of modalities. The hybrid designation refers to combining two vision backbones (ResNet and ViT) over the same image. The introduction reviews multimodal neuroimaging and EEG-plus-eye-tracking work and dismisses both on cost and complexity grounds.

**S-153** [local_e04bcd32] — *Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network*

No fusion of modalities - a single image source. The pipeline stacks three processing stages (deblurring, denoising, classification) over one photograph, which is depth rather than multimodality.

**S-154** [local_183eaef4] — *Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI*

No modality fusion - a single tabular source. There is, however, a fusion of instrument types within the feature vector that is the study's defining characteristic: AQ-10 item responses, an AQ-10 total, a Q-CHAT-10 total, an SRS score and a CARS severity rating all sit in the same 19-variable input alongside the ASD_traits label they are designed to determine.

**S-155** [local_b6ac2b98] — *Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks*

No multimodal fusion - eye tracking alone. What the study does instead is a granularity comparison within one modality: four nested feature sets ranging from 24 broad variables to 158 fine-grained ones. The result is a clean negative finding that broad social/non-social area-of-interest variables carry the discriminative information while adding specific facial features and emotion categories does not improve accuracy. Multimodal extension with behavioural, cognitive or neurophysiological measures is named as the next step.

**S-156** [local_44d3aef5] — *Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis*

No fusion of modalities - one image source. The hybrid model combines two ImageNet backbones over the same image, which is architectural ensembling rather than multimodality.

**S-157** [local_24fefc5f] — *A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection*

No fusion - a single questionnaire modality. The hybrid designation refers to combining two convolutional architectures over the same tabular input.

**S-158** [local_69b10fe4] — *An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms*

Genuine and declared multimodal fusion, and the study's most useful applied finding. Kinematic features and self-report questionnaire scores are combined in an explicit grid of predictor configurations - kinematics alone, questionnaires alone (ASD, PD, or both) and their combinations - and the combination outperforms either alone for both classification problems (0.73 clinical versus non-clinical; 0.93 ASD versus PD). Because the questionnaire sets are named and separated, the contribution of each modality is visible rather than buried, and the finding that both trait questionnaires together beat either individually is directly interpretable.

**S-159** [local_af9f4c12] — *An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data*

No fusion - a single questionnaire modality. What the study does perform is dataset harmonisation across four age cohorts into a common 15-attribute schema with stratified merging, which is cross-cohort integration rather than multimodal fusion. Multimodal extension with prosody and gaze is named as future work, and the absence of such cues is acknowledged as a constraint of the current data.

**S-160** [local_367db0b6] — *An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns*

Multimodal fusion is the framework's structural claim: each modality is partitioned, processed by per-partition CNNs, aggregated into a modality representation, and fused into a single feature vector for a softmax classifier. The claim cannot be evaluated. The modality set differs between sections (MRI, video, audio, text and EEG versus MRI, video and text); no dataset is characterised well enough to know what any modality contains; the fused feature vectors are printed as illustrative example numbers; and no ablation isolates any modality's contribution except a reference to an MRI-only ablation whose results are not shown in the extracted text.

**S-161** [local_8d43288c] — *Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos*

No fusion - video only. The CNN-GRU combination is spatial-plus-temporal modelling within one modality, and the architectural rationale is stated properly: convolutional layers extract spatial features from single frames while autism-related behaviour is a temporal phenomenon requiring sequence modelling across frames. That is a correct justification for a recurrent component, unlike the several studies in this corpus that apply LSTMs to single static inputs.

**S-162** [local_5f57ba19] — *Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension*

Modality is manipulated experimentally rather than fused computationally, which is a different and arguably more informative use of the term. By presenting the same storytelling task audio-only and audio-visually and comparing gaze features across the two, the study isolates what the visual speech channel contributes to group discrimination - and finds that it contributes most before speech onset. That is a designed contrast producing an interpretable answer, in contrast to the corpus's several studies that concatenate modalities and report only the combined figure.

**S-163** [local_1d856900] — *Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare*

Dataset 2 is presented as genuine four-modality fusion - image, audio, motion and physiological features concatenated into a 4,220-dimensional vector - and the ablation attributes the final gain from 97.80% to 98.2% to multimodal integration. Three things make that uninterpretable. There are 4,220 features for 400 samples, of which only 100 are original. The 400 include augmented copies split across training and test, so the multimodal gain is measured on partly duplicated data. And no modality-level attribution is reported: SHAP and LIME are applied to Dataset 1 only, so the paper cannot say what any modality contributed. A 0.4-point accuracy gain on a 40-sample test set is a single case reclassified.

**S-164** [local_7b19a959] — *Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis*

Genuine, declared and quantified multimodal fusion, and the study's central result. Objective task measures and the AQ questionnaire are evaluated separately and together on the same matched sample: 74% for tasks alone, 83% for the AQ alone, 92% combined. Because each configuration is reported, the increment attributable to fusion is visible (9 points over the questionnaire alone), and because the feature-importance profile is very similar with and without the AQ, the authors can argue that the two data types contribute information in different ways rather than merely duplicating each other. This is the only study in the charted corpus to report all three configurations and thereby make the fusion claim checkable.

**S-165** [local_d7b6fa00] — *Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath*

No modality fusion - eye tracking alone. What is fused is classifiers rather than data: bagging, boosting and stacking are combined within one architecture, with base learners selected by a stated diversity criterion to promote complementary decision boundaries.

**S-166** [local_e54c304c] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models*

No fusion - a single image modality. The paper's own literature table lists no multimodal analysis as a limitation of a cited prior study and does not apply it to itself.

**S-167** [local_e4c2a776] — *Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images*

No modality fusion - a single image source. The paper's fusion is across three ImageNet backbones (VGG16, DenseNet-121, XceptionNet) applied to the same photograph, which is representational concatenation rather than multimodality, and no ablation isolates any backbone's contribution.

**S-168** [local_231757c7] — *SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers*

No modality fusion - 3D skeletal motion alone. The study's most interesting observation is instead about modality availability: the severe-ASD group could not be captured with the same sensor as the other two, so the modality itself is unavailable for the group whose severity the study most wants to classify. That is a genuine finding about the deployability of depth-sensor assessment and it applies well beyond this paper.

**S-169** [local_1b457442] — *Screening autism spectrum*

No modality fusion - text alone, deliberately. The paper's argument is that excluding audio and video is the point, since transcripts avoid identifiable biometric data, and it acknowledges the cost: prosodic features indicative of atypical speech cannot be captured in text. Its future-work proposal to add limited prosodic cues while preserving text-level privacy is an explicit privacy-information trade-off, which no other study in this corpus formulates.

**S-170** [local_b26db2f2] — *Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches*

No modality fusion - game telemetry alone. The behavioural anamnesis questionnaire completed by guardians is collected and not used as a predictor, which keeps the model's inputs clean of parent-report information but also leaves an available modality unexploited.

---

## RQ4.1 — Model paradigms

_170 of 170 studies charted for this question._

**S-001** [local_76fc33d0] — *Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers*

Supervised learning. Algorithms: support vector machine with RBF kernel, and probabilistic neural network (Parzen-window Bayes network).

**S-002** [local_0dbc5018] — *Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities*

Supervised learning. Algorithm: linear-kernel support vector machine, with Fisher discriminant ratio feature ranking as the selection step.

**S-003** [local_dc5fc4bb] — *ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data*

Supervised learning. Algorithms: decision tree, random forest, support vector machine, k-nearest neighbour and AdaBoost, each evaluated with and without ReliefF feature selection across eight class-grouping definitions.

**S-004** [local_863980f8] — *Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework*

Supervised learning. Algorithm: RBF-kernel support vector machine, preceded by unsupervised K-means clustering used purely as a quantisation/feature-construction step.

**S-005** [local_be8aa62f] — *Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder*

Supervised learning with unsupervised dimensionality reduction. Algorithms: linear discriminant, quadratic discriminant and RBF-kernel SVM; latent semantic indexing (an SVD-based technique related to PCA) provides the representation. Graph-theoretic network analysis (local clustering coefficient) is used descriptively alongside the classifiers.

**S-006** [local_e404a2a3] — *Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism*

Supervised learning with decision-tree ensembles: ExtraTrees, Random Forest and Regularized Greedy Forest (plus an RGF variant without demographics). The authors explicitly rejected SVMs and gradient boosting machines as overfitting-prone given more features than observations and strong inter-feature correlations - a deliberate model-selection rationale that is rare in this corpus.

**S-007** [local_780141fc] — *Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study*

Supervised learning, with unsupervised PCA used only for feature selection. Algorithms: Naive Bayes, SVM with linear and RBF kernels, decision tree C4.5 and random forest. The choice of Naive Bayes first is explicitly motivated by anticipated SVM overfitting given 40 features and 30 samples, and the paper reports the informative finding that Naive Bayes performed comparably to SVM even on a quarter of the features, speculating that the independence assumption may genuinely hold for these kinematic parameters.

**S-008** [local_3a331973] — *Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data*

Supervised learning. The diagnostic classifier is an RBF-kernel SVM with greedy forward feature selection. A deep CNN (a modified dynamic deep-learning AU architecture) is used upstream as a pre-trained facial action unit detector. The authors explicitly reject end-to-end deep learning on raw pixels because the small training set would cause severe overfitting - a deliberate and well-reasoned choice to use deep learning for representation but not for diagnosis.

**S-009** [local_7b3e6b3a] — *Earlier identification of children with autism*

Supervised learning. Algorithms: linear-kernel SVM (Weka SMO) as the baseline, chosen for robustness and insensitivity to feature overfitting, and a one-layer bidirectional LSTM neural network with eight cells as the deep-learning alternative. The comparison is reported as effectively a tie, which the authors attribute to sample size rather than to the architectures.

**S-010** [local_36aa3ace] — *Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative*

Unsupervised deep representation learning combined with supervised classification. Algorithms: a generative adversarial network whose discriminator acts as a non-linear feature extractor, with hidden-layer activations fed to a linear-kernel SVM. Baselines: linear SVM, RBF-kernel SVM and a four-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron. Notably the GAN is used purely for representation learning, not for the data augmentation that the introduction motivates - the generator's synthetic samples are never used to enlarge the training set.

**S-011** [local_44b58f21] — *ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces*

Supervised learning. Algorithms: a three-layer feed-forward artificial neural network trained by scaled conjugate gradient backpropagation, and support vector machines with linear, polynomial and RBF kernels. Stepwise discriminant analysis serves as a statistical feature-selection stage. The authors note that comparative studies often favour SVM, which makes their ANN result a departure from expectation.

**S-012** [local_cb9a5b48] — *Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening*

Supervised learning. Algorithms: decision tree, k-nearest neighbours, Gaussian-kernel SVM, linear discriminant analysis and logistic regression, each evaluated on both feature families and on the stacked combination. Gaussian SVM was selected as the final model. Statistical hypothesis testing (t-test, ANOVA) is used alongside classification to establish that the features carry group information.

**S-013** [local_40cd7d53] — *Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children*

Supervised learning with a single algorithm: support vector machine, described as discriminant analysis. No comparison against alternative classifiers, which is unusual for this corpus and arguably a strength - it removes the best-of-many selection optimism that inflates other studies here.

**S-014** [local_5b1d0b36] — *Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday*

Supervised learning. Algorithm: binary SVM optimised by stochastic gradient descent with a hinge loss objective, preceded by correlation-based feature subset selection. No deep learning, and no comparison against alternative classifiers - the paper's contribution is the data collection and fusion scheme rather than the model.

**S-015** [local_54954c19] — *Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching*

Supervised learning. Algorithm: logistic regression in R, chosen after testing several classification algorithms. The deliberate choice of a simple linear model with a small feature set, rather than a high-capacity model on 30 participants, is consistent with the paper's general conservatism about overfitting.

**S-016** [local_d8dc996a] — *Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Supervised deep learning: a pre-trained GoogLeNet CNN as frame feature extractor feeding a recurrent LSTM with a learned soft spatial attention mechanism and a binary softmax classifier. A handcrafted alternative (dense trajectories with HOG/HOF and VLAD encoding) is included specifically as a baseline and is reported to perform at chance - an informative negative comparison that most corpus studies omit.

**S-017** [local_88ddfdd1] — *A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task*

Supervised learning with unsupervised embedding: gradient boosted decision trees (LightGBM) over t-SNE embeddings of a ScanMatch similarity matrix. The Needleman-Wunsch sequence alignment underlying ScanMatch is a classical bioinformatics algorithm repurposed for gaze. A benchmark condition substitutes Levenshtein distance and Kruskal's non-metric multidimensional scaling for the ScanMatch/t-SNE pair.

**S-018** [local_361110f1] — *Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features*

Supervised learning with a broad classifier comparison: SVM, linear discriminant analysis, decision tree, random forest and k-nearest neighbour with k in {1,3,5,7}. KNN with k=1 - effectively a nearest-neighbour lookup, the highest-variance choice available - gave the best result, which on 43 participants with four selected features warrants caution the paper does not express.

**S-019** [local_51533de4] — *Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations*

Supervised learning: a Gradient Boosting Classifier from scikit-learn. Principal Component Analysis is used unsupervised for dimensionality reduction. No comparison against alternative classifiers, which removes best-of-many selection optimism but also leaves the algorithm choice unjustified empirically.

**S-020** [local_96c87d36] — *Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking*

Supervised learning: random forest with bootstrap sampling, majority voting and balanced class weights. A pre-trained deep convolutional network (OpenFace, 37 layers in 8 Inception blocks) is used upstream as a frozen feature extractor without fine-tuning, on the stated grounds that the LFW training set is sufficiently general.

**S-021** [local_4b031d44] — *Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine*

Supervised learning. Random forests per rater with softmax ensemble weighting for the main classification; logistic regression with elastic net regularisation and balanced class weights for the cross-cultural transfer analysis. The choice of a two-layer stack is motivated conceptually - layer one optimised for sensitivity so no atypical case is missed, layer two optimised for both sensitivity and specificity to separate ASD from other delays - which links model design to intended clinical use more explicitly than most of the corpus.

**S-022** [local_05ef29e5] — *Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification*

Supervised learning. Algorithm: random forest via MATLAB TreeBagger with 128 trees and bootstrap aggregation, selected on the stated grounds that it performs well on all-numeric feature sets with a numeric class label. Mean-shift clustering is used unsupervised as a feature-construction step. No alternative classifiers are compared.

**S-023** [local_9528024b] — *Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol*

Not machine learning in the supervised sense. The method is probabilistic sequential decision-making: a hierarchical POMDP with task-level and protocol-level models, solved by the SARSOP point-based value iteration solver. Model parameters are specified rather than learned - transition matrices for child states are identity (robot actions cannot change the child's condition, and no data existed on their effect on engagement or verbal activity), and observation probabilities were elicited from a clinician survey. The authors themselves note that comparison against trained classifiers is not yet possible for lack of data.

**S-024** [local_6230fe22] — *Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism*

Supervised learning. Algorithm: support vector machine only, selected because it is used in the cited literature and is a capable binary classifier. No paradigm comparison, no alternative algorithms, and no kernel specification.

**S-025** [local_785ba418] — *Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis*

Supervised learning. Algorithm: SVM with RBF kernel, with C and gamma grid-searched. Four feature-selection strategies are compared as complete pipelines: SVM recursive feature elimination (embedded), two-sample t-test (filter), ReliefF (filter with neighbour interactions) and mRMR (filter with redundancy penalty). The finding that the two simplest filters outperformed the two more sophisticated methods is reported without embellishment.

**S-026** [local_fea042be] — *Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual*

Supervised learning, with the problem deliberately recast as image classification. Conventional baselines (Naive Bayes, logistic regression, SVM, random forests) are compared against feed-forward artificial neural networks of increasing capacity (single layer with 50, 200 or 500 neurons; two layers of 80 and 40), trained with 100 epochs and 20% dropout. PCA provides unsupervised dimensionality reduction. Notably no convolutional architecture is used despite the image framing, since PCA-compressed grayscale vectors are fed to fully connected layers.

**S-027** [local_ba5fbda7] — *Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD*

Supervised learning: linear-kernel support vector machine, with PCA used unsupervised for dimensionality reduction. A single algorithm with no best-of-many comparison, consistent with the paper's methodological conservatism.

**S-028** [local_7b468950] — *Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart*

A commercial third-party classifier, Play.Care, described as an adaptation of the algorithm developed and published from the pilot study. Its internals are not restated in the protocol, and for the trial's purposes this is by design: the point of a phase III evaluation is that the instrument is locked and applied unchanged to new data, so the algorithm's specification belongs to the development phase rather than to the evaluation. The trade-off is that the trial can establish whether the instrument works without establishing what it measures - a limitation the protocol does not name.

**S-029** [local_309e5baa] — *Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns*

Supervised deep learning throughout. Fully connected networks of two capacities for the synthetic saccade approach, and a dual-branch convolutional architecture built on pretrained ResNet-18 for the image-based approach. STAR-FC, a computational saliency and saccade generation model, is used upstream as a reference generator rather than as a classifier. No conventional machine-learning comparators are included.

**S-030** [local_a45f39e9] — *Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time*

Supervised deep learning throughout, in a three-stage pipeline: a retrained Mask R-CNN detector for pose estimation, a classical particle filter for state estimation of missing keypoints, and a convolutional binary classifier over the resulting motion images. A conventional video-classification approach (Inception V3 on single frames with majority voting) serves as a baseline, which is a genuine comparator rather than a strawman since it represents standard practice.

**S-031** [local_d587f9cd] — *Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning*

No model is trained on the study's own data. The neural components are pretrained and used as instruments: Dlib's CNN face detector and ResNet face recogniser, and OpenFace's CLNF landmark and gaze estimator, integrated into ROS nodes with the neural model made an attribute of the node class and evaluated on each topic callback. The only inference component developed here is the Hidden Markov Model for visual focus of attention, which infers the attention target from the fused pose and gaze sequence. For a review of computational approaches this is the measurement-infrastructure end of the field: the machine learning does the perceptual work that a human coder would otherwise do frame by frame, and the clinical inference remains with the therapist. The paper's stated purpose supports this reading - automated video coding is intended to 'help the clinicians to reduce the delay of ASD diagnosis' by removing the manual coding burden, not to produce a diagnosis.

**S-032** [local_08b8027d] — *SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths*

Supervised deep learning combining convolutional and recurrent architectures: shallow CNNs for per-patch visual encoding and a two-layer LSTM for sequence modelling, with a pretrained generative adversarial saliency model (SalGAN) used upstream as a frozen feature source. No conventional machine-learning comparators are included, and no ablation isolates the contribution of the saliency map versus the raw image.

**S-033** [local_c6f1209b] — *Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children*

None. No computational or machine-learning model is fitted. The analysis is a Wilcoxon signed-rank test on paired within-subject proportions, which is the correct choice for small-sample paired ordinal data and is used appropriately. For a review of computation-based approaches, the study sits immediately upstream of the modelling work: it establishes that a robot-delivered paradigm produces a measurable and theoretically interpretable behavioural dissociation, which is the finding that a subsequent automated system would need to reproduce.

**S-034** [local_83b99e73] — *Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers*

Three classical supervised classifiers compared on identical tabular features: support vector machine, Gaussian naive Bayes and random forest, all from scikit-learn. No deep learning, which is appropriate at n = 83 with 10 features. The three algorithms perform within about three percentage points of each other, which is itself informative: with this feature set the choice of classifier matters far less than the choice of elicitation episode.

**S-035** [local_638860ef] — *Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis*

Supervised learning with SVM-RBF as the fixed classifier, so that the experimental variable is feature selection rather than model family. Four established selectors are benchmarked (t-test filter, SVM-RFE, ReliefF, mRMR) and three variants developed (ensemble, bagging, wrapped t-test). Holding the classifier constant while varying selection is a clean design that isolates the contribution the paper is actually studying.

**S-036** [local_7547db68] — *Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network*

Deep supervised learning: VGG-19 and ResNet-18 convolutional neural networks for seven-way facial expression classification. The paper argues explicitly for deep over traditional approaches, on the grounds that handcrafted features (oriented gradient histograms, Gabor filters, local directional patterns, enhanced local binary patterns) are 'artificial design, time-consuming and laborious' and work well only on small image sets, whereas end-to-end deep models combine feature extraction and classification. Critically, neither network is trained on an autism label - the diagnostic layer is a hand-set threshold on classification agreement, not a learned model.

**S-037** [local_878c259f] — *Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach*

Supervised learning with an unusually broad comparison: discriminant analysis, k-nearest neighbour, naive Bayes, decision trees, support vector machine and random forest, each briefly explained with a citation. The rationale is stated explicitly - because features, sample sizes and data structures differ, 'no one algorithm works best for every dataset', so researchers usually implement several and explore the best. The authors also note that basic supervised algorithms are chosen because they are 'computationally efficient and relevant to small sample sizes'.

**S-038** [local_1579c85a] — *Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through*

Supervised learning with a deliberate depth comparison: a 1D convolutional neural network chosen for its suitability to ordered temporal data, benchmarked against random forest and k-nearest neighbour, which the authors describe as having 'simpler structures than a deep CNN with fewer hyperparameters that require fine-tuning'. Reporting a null result from this comparison - that all three perform equivalently - is a strength.

**S-039** [local_157d6266] — *Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism*

A hybrid of classical algorithm and learning: dynamic time warping provides temporal alignment, metric learning determines how the three derived features combine, and a support vector machine performs diagnostic classification. The design rationale is stated explicitly - the authors deliberately impose structure to reduce learnable parameters using expert-derived guidance, arguing that 'using expert knowledge to guide the features improved CAMI's interpretability, while deviance from HOC as a result of automatized learning processes improved CAMI's diagnostic discriminative ability'.

**S-040** [local_8be557e3] — *Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation*

Four models compared on identical data: a linear-kernel SVM baseline, a vanilla eight-cell BLSTM on 88 features, the same BLSTM on 54 statistically selected features, and a stacked auto-encoder jointly optimised with the BLSTM. The auto-encoder is semi-supervised, carrying an auxiliary binary ASD/TD softmax head on its latent layer so that the representation is shaped by the diagnostic target rather than by reconstruction alone. Joint optimisation of representation and classifier is the paper's actual contribution, and holding the BLSTM fixed at eight cells across conditions is what isolates it.

**S-041** [local_c79e100a] — *Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models*

Four classical supervised classifiers held as the experimental variable: SVM, KNN, random forest and decision tree, each optimised by grid search so that comparisons are between best-configured models rather than arbitrary defaults. The selection rationale is stated per classifier - KNN as a simple baseline suited to small data, SVM as the field's default for small datasets and for autism classification specifically, and random forest and decision tree for their handling of non-linearly separable data. No deep learning, appropriately for 105 or 278 data points with eight features.

**S-042** [local_4fecbf6d] — *Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network*

Six models spanning linear regression, kernel regression and three deep architectures, all on identical data, which makes the comparison genuinely informative. The decisive variable turns out to be input structure rather than model family: the same 100 x 48 matrix input produces the two best models (FC-DNN 3 and CNN) while the same sub-sampled features presented as independent 48-vectors (FC-DNN 2) produce the worst model of all six. The authors draw the right conclusion - that architectures exploiting multiple simultaneous samples of a child's speech have a large advantage, and that the non-linear models' margin over linear regression and SVR shows 'the optimal ADOS prediction model is not likely to be linear'.

**S-043** [local_95abe653] — *Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning*

Logistic regression, chosen after testing a set of standard classification algorithms in R with the comparison deposited publicly. A deliberately simple model, appropriate at 30-38 participants, and consistent with the paper's emphasis on characterising the signal and the data representation rather than on architecture. The experimental variables are the task, the AOI definition and the feature set, not the learner.

**S-044** [local_40168c96] — *Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based*

A hybrid: a pretrained two-stream CNN as a fixed feature extractor (not fine-tuned on this data), scale-specific SVM regression models via LIBSVM, and Otsu thresholding for the final decision. Using a frozen pretrained CNN is a sensible response to 74 participants, avoiding the overfitting that end-to-end deep training would invite, and the SVM stage operates on a much larger effective sample because each child contributes many scanpath pieces. The multi-scale design - one model per piece length from 1 to 5 fixations - is the architectural contribution, and is explicitly contrasted with the alternative of zero-padding variable-length scanpaths to a fixed size.

**S-045** [local_d3852378] — *Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

A conventional and appropriately conservative pipeline for 47 participants: PCA at 95% variance retention, then C-SVM with a Gaussian kernel, with nonlinear SVM-RFE including correlation bias reduction as a wrapper inside each training fold. No deep learning is used for classification - OpenPose supplies the deep component as a fixed, externally trained pose estimator, which is the right division of labour at this sample size. Hyperparameters were searched over seven logarithmically spaced values of cost and gamma between 0.1 and 1000.

**S-046** [local_df438dd2] — *Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening*

A cascade rather than a single model: pretrained ASR, pretrained face detection, a fine-tuned two-branch expression network, and a shallow classifier over six binary scores. The design is well matched to the data regime - deep components are trained on large external corpora (AISHELL-2, Oulu-CASIA, and the purpose-built 15,000-clip children's database) while the only model fitted to the 41-child cohort is a decision tree over six features. Four classifiers are compared, with the decision tree best by a wide margin (80.49% against 70.73% for SVM), which for a six-dimensional binary feature space is plausible.

**S-047** [local_cd9e45eb] — *Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism*

Three sparsity-inducing methods compared on identical splits - lasso, group lasso and the paper's SGIN - against a panel of non-sparse baselines (linear and RBF SVM, decision tree, random forest, linear and logistic regression) run 100 times each. SGIN extends group l1 regularisation to a multi-layer non-linear network by penalising the Frobenius norm of the parameter block connecting each input group to all first-hidden-layer neurons, and introduces a Stochastic Blockwise Coordinated Gradient Descent optimiser that converges faster and finds more sparse groups than plain SGD. The comparison is informative precisely because the winner is not the most accurate model: non-sparse linear baselines reach about 84% accuracy against SGIN's 78-80%, but they remove nothing, so they cannot shorten the battery at all.

**S-048** [local_56237213] — *The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data*

A single linear SVM throughout, preceded by mRMR feature selection based on mutual information, chosen for jointly maximising relevance to the class label and minimising redundancy among features. No model comparison is performed - the experimental variable is the modality and the number of selected features, not the learner. This is a defensible focus given the paper's question, but it means there is no evidence about whether the linear SVM is the right choice for these features.

**S-049** [local_f9a5195f] — *Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses*

Elastic net as the primary classifier, chosen explicitly for the data regime: 219 features per trial against 33 participants means 'regularization was important to prevent model overfitting', and elastic net combines lasso and ridge penalties. Logistic regression with grid-searched l1 or l2 regularisation serves as an ablation comparator, included on the technical grounds that elastic net optimisers can be unstable at the edge cases where one penalty vanishes. Elastic net outperformed logistic regression in most tasks, which the authors read as confirming 'a need for regularization in this dataset'. No deep learning, correctly - the discussion notes that a larger, more balanced corpus 'would also enable the use of more complex statistical models, such as artificial neural networks', which is a statement of what the data cannot currently support.

**S-050** [local_16a77fb0] — *Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)*

A single random forest of 1,000 trees with maximum depth and minimum samples per leaf tuned over seven values each, applied identically to each modality and to the combination. Model choice is deliberately conservative given 80 participants, and an earlier conference paper by the same group compared alternative approaches. The more consequential modelling decision is what enters the model: features were restricted 'strictly to features based on domain-knowledge or on the EMG preparatory study' for the primary analyses, which is a principled constraint that sacrifices accuracy for interpretability and is quantified by the parallel all-action-unit result.

**S-051** [local_9c4af7a3] — *Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades*

A Two-Class Boosted Decision Tree, selected after comparing linear regression, logistic regression, multiclass neural networks, support vector algorithms and quantile regression models within Azure ML Studio. The stated justification - that ensemble boosting suits small tabular data better than the bagging of random forests or the hierarchical structure of neural networks - is reasonable in outline, and choosing a shallow tabular model over deep learning at n = 108 is the right instinct. But no performance figure is given for any comparator, so the selection cannot be assessed, and including linear and quantile regression in a binary classification comparison indicates the model set was not well matched to the task.

**S-052** [local_b70dae32] — *An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model*

A two-state Hidden Markov Model with the severity level as the hidden state and the two binned behavioural categories as observables. The choice is defensible for an intrinsically sequential intervention series with a latent clinical state, and the model is inherently interpretable. But the temporal structure that motivates an HMM is not actually exploited - sessions are treated as independent observations rather than as a sequence within child, no state transitions over the course of therapy are examined, and the reported posterior computation is a static Bayes calculation over two conditionals rather than a sequential inference. In effect the model functions as a naive Bayes classifier over nine input cells, with the HMM framing adding formalism rather than capability.

**S-053** [local_51a0af74] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data*

Random forests, one per video segment, combined into an ensemble by weighted voting - a design that mirrors the temporal structure of the stimulus rather than flattening it. Three combination strategies are compared systematically, and the exhaustive variant testing all 511 subsets is thorough as an exploration but constitutes a very large selection space when evaluated on the same cross-validation used for reporting. No deep learning, which is appropriate at 86 participants, and no single-model baseline over concatenated features is reported, so the benefit of the segment-wise decomposition itself is not isolated.

**S-054** [local_d8d3037b] — *Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study*

Seven classical classifiers plus an ensemble, with each model's assumptions and their consequences discussed individually - PCA applied before logistic regression because of multicollinearity and before naive Bayes because of its independence assumption, normalisation before KNN because distance is scale-sensitive, standardisation before SVM for convergence. This model-by-model reasoning is more careful than most of the corpus. The ensemble is then justified on generalisation rather than accuracy grounds, which is the right argument and is the one the test experiment supports.

**S-055** [local_991fe435] — *Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task*

k-nearest neighbours, deliberately simple, chosen for the low intrinsic dimensionality of gaze coordinates, for tolerance of overlapping class distributions and for small-sample performance. The single hyperparameter k was fixed by piloting on a different published dataset rather than tuned on the present data - so the entire model specification is set outside the evaluation, which removes the model-selection optimism that affects most of the corpus. No comparison against alternative classifiers is reported, which is a minor gap, but the choice is consistent with a paper whose stated aim is to avoid optimising anything on the evaluation data.

**S-056** [local_8692a64f] — *Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis*

Three classical classifiers compared on identical features: KNN with Euclidean distance, Gaussian naive Bayes and a cubic-kernel SVM. The choice is appropriate for 83 samples and 43 features, and the paper's stated rationale for the whole approach - preferring structured interpretable features over unstructured deep learning inputs - is coherent and is followed through. The cubic kernel is an unusual choice, more prone to overfitting than the standard RBF at this sample size, and no justification for the polynomial degree is given.

**S-057** [local_4d6fac7e] — *Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network*

A graph convolutional network over a feature graph, with random forest for upstream gaze feature selection, compared against an SVM-based feature-engineering pipeline and a ResNet18. The GCN choice is well matched to the stated problem - modelling relationships between features across modalities where no explicit correlation exists between the raw signals - and using features rather than subjects as graph nodes is an unusual and defensible formulation. That the much deeper ResNet18 performs worst supports the argument that architecture matched to the fusion problem matters more than capacity at this sample size.

**S-058** [local_30c622f2] — *Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model*

An unusual architecture for this corpus: rather than training one discriminative classifier on participant-level features, the paper trains one small generative model per severity group - each a ten-neuron single-hidden-layer network with Bayesian regularisation, predicting whether a pixel was fixated by that group - and then classifies a new participant by which group's saliency map their own fixation map more closely resembles. This is a nearest-prototype scheme in saliency space. It has two consequences worth noting: the model is small enough to be well conditioned on the available data, and the comparison of the two fitted models is itself the scientific output, which is why the feature-selection difference is reported as the main finding rather than as an ablation.

**S-059** [local_bfc088c7] — *Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation*

Four classical classifiers - SVM, linear discriminant analysis, decision tree and random forest - each wrapped in forward feature selection, with the paper giving a short rationale for each including the observation that decision trees offer 'strong interpretability, but it is prone to overfitting'. The model comparison is informative in one respect: random forest needed sixteen features to reach 84.62% while SVM reached 92.31% with three, which speaks to how concentrated the signal is. The wrapper design is also what creates the study's main methodological weakness, since the selection criterion is the reported metric.

**S-060** [local_25e34bbd] — *Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification*

A single-hidden-layer feed-forward network trained by scaled conjugate gradient, chosen for its lack of user-dependent parameters and avoidance of line search, compared against RBF-kernel SVM and naive Bayes on identical features. The comparison is systematic and the network wins in every condition, though the margins - 100% against 78.5% for SVM and 91.2% for naive Bayes on the same MFCC features for autism detection - are large enough to be suspicious, since a shallow network and an RBF SVM on the same low-dimensional features would not normally diverge this far unless one is exploiting something the other is not.

**S-061** [local_4917150c] — *Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning*

A convolutional network with four convolutional layers, four pooling layers, two fully connected layers and dropout, trained for three epochs. The architectural choice follows directly from the representation decision: having converted gaze to images, the natural learner is a CNN, and the authors describe the whole approach as recasting diagnosis as 'a typical task of image classification'. No comparison against alternative classifiers or against engineered-feature baselines is reported, though the authors note this study builds on their own earlier work using fixation and saccade event features.

**S-062** [local_241ec2c2] — *Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking*

Two small neural networks, one per group, each acting as a generative model of where that group looks, plus a similarity-vote decision rule - the same architecture as the severity study from the same laboratory but applied to diagnosis. SVM was tested as an alternative learner and performed worse (0.775 against 0.818 without selection). The comparison table across six classifier-and-selection combinations is genuinely informative: genetic algorithm selection raised the network's mean AUC only from 0.818 to 0.822 but cut its standard deviation from 0.053 to 0.015, while the same selection dropped the SVM from 0.775 to 0.695. Reporting a case where feature selection helps stability rather than accuracy, and helps one learner while harming another, is more nuanced than most of the corpus manages.

**S-063** [local_36617ec5] — *Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis*

Five classifiers - naive Bayes, XGBoost, kNN, random forest and SVM - trained on each of ten datasets, with the best per dataset reported. Default hyperparameters were used throughout, a decision the authors justify explicitly as avoiding an additional layer of search complexity. That is defensible and unusually candid, though it means the algorithm comparison reflects default behaviour rather than tuned potential, and different algorithms win on different datasets (SVM on two, kNN on two, naive Bayes on two, random forest and XGBoost on one each), which is what one would expect when nothing is tuned and sample sizes are small.

**S-064** [local_d8e804d6] — *Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms*

Five classifiers compared on identical features, each with a short rationale and stated weaknesses, including the acknowledgement that decision trees are 'prone to overfitting' and that random forest 'could well address the overfitting problem of the DT algorithm' - which makes it notable that the decision tree nonetheless produced the highest accuracy, a pattern consistent with the exhaustive search finding a favourable split on a small sample. Reporting that all five classifiers exceeded 81% with three features or fewer is more informative than the single maximum, since it shows the signal is not classifier-specific.

**S-065** [local_712542ca] — *Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset*

Nine classifiers spanning trees, ensembles, kernel methods, neural networks and probabilistic models, applied uniformly across all five datasets. Breadth is the only principle - no rationale is given for any individual choice, no hyperparameters are reported, and the winning algorithm differs by cluster (multilayer perceptron in cluster 1, random forest in clusters 3 and 4, three classifiers tied in cluster 2), which at these sample sizes is consistent with noise rather than with any property of the clusters.

**S-066** [local_0ab41681] — *Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder*

A single radial-basis-function SVM with hyperparameters grid-searched at each leave-one-subject-out iteration. No model comparison is reported, which is appropriate given that classification is explicitly secondary to the mechanistic question and the paper makes no claim about optimal architecture. The design decision that matters is aggregation: the classifier operates on trials, and subject-level inference is obtained by taking each participant's proportion of positive trial responses as an estimate of diagnosis probability, from which the ROC is built.

**S-067** [local_9ca9b2cc] — *Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment*

No model is trained. The system is rule-based throughout: off-the-shelf Haar cascade classifiers perform face and ear detection as measurement infrastructure, and the attention score is accumulated by hand-specified increments with operator-adjustable constants. There is no training set, test set, cross-validation or fitted parameter anywhere. For a review of computational approaches this is a useful boundary case, because it shows what can be achieved without learning: a transparent, adjustable, real-time measure that tracks a clinician's judgement on 82.4% of sessions and closes a therapy loop. The corresponding limitation is that the constants are asserted rather than derived, so the score's calibration rests on the operator's judgement rather than on evidence.

**S-068** [local_02fa4215] — *Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning*

Nine classifiers spanning probabilistic, instance-based, linear, tree, ensemble and kernel families, each described in a sentence with no rationale for inclusion and no hyperparameters. Breadth substitutes for justification. That six of the 27 cells reach 95% while the rest cluster between 90% and 92.5% - a spread of two test cases - indicates the comparison is not resolving real differences between algorithms.

**S-069** [local_29a3fc54] — *Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism*

A single linear SVM with L1 regularisation, chosen after the non-linear variant underperformed and justified by L1's property of zeroing uninformative coefficients - appropriate for a high-dimensional feature space built by summarising frame measures across statistics, regions and activities. The more important modelling decision is the inclusion of an explicit chance classifier that randomly assigns participants, run through the same pipeline and reported in every results table at 49.90% AUC with its own confidence interval. That baseline is what converts the reported figures from numbers into evidence, and its presence distinguishes this study from most of the corpus.

**S-070** [local_b7ec3755] — *Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images*

A bagged decision-tree ensemble over 30 hand-engineered features - deliberately classical rather than deep, and justified by the comparison table showing that no classifier family separated meaningfully from any other. The spread across all 23 candidates is 59.3% (fine KNN) to 68.5% (TreeBagger), roughly nine points across decision trees, discriminant analysis, logistic regression, naive Bayes, six SVM kernels, five nearest-neighbour variants and five ensembles. That flatness is itself an informative negative result: when every model family lands within a few points of every other, the limiting factor is the feature representation and the data, not the learner - which supports the authors' focus on features and undercuts any claim that a deeper model would help.

**S-071** [local_684969f6] — *Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data*

Five architectures compared directly on the same data: baseline MLP, branched multi-encoder MLP, CNN over fixation maps, ResNet18/ResNet50 two-branch image models, and a 5-layer LSTM. The spread on the blind test set is 52.53% (CNN-SP-STAR) to 62.13% (ResNet50) - about ten points across shallow and deep, feedforward, convolutional and recurrent families - and the two best (62.13% and 61.39%) come from opposite ends of that range, a deep image model and a shallow MLP on raw coordinates. As in the companion paper on the same benchmark, the flatness across architecture families indicates that the limiting factor is the data rather than model capacity. The authors also note a specific failure mode with a plausible cause: the CNN over fixation maps performed worst, which they attribute to 'the mismatch between the fixation image maps and the CNN networked pretrained on natural images' - a sparse synthetic input passed through an ImageNet backbone.

**S-072** [local_35004e74] — *Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children*

A CNN-LSTM action-recognition architecture - VGG16 for per-frame spatial encoding, a 512-unit LSTM for temporal dependency within 5-second windows - selected because it 'previously showed a good performance in video-based action classification'. The choice matches the construct: if what distinguishes the groups is the temporal coordination of non-verbal behaviours rather than their static configuration, a model without temporal structure could not capture it. The authors report that the final architecture 'was obtained upon testing various configurations', with the alternatives shown in supplementary Figure S2, and that 5-second segments beat 10- and 15-second segments on validation loss - so architecture and segment length were both selected on the internal validation split rather than on the held-out children, which is the correct separation.

**S-073** [local_fa91fc18] — *Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities*

A single small feedforward network - 17 inputs, one hidden layer of five tanh units, two softmax outputs - chosen for the stated reason that neural networks handle 'complex and nonlinear relationships between variables', which matches the paper's explicit epistemic position that no individual movement variable need differ between groups and that what is categorisable is 'the dynamic interaction of these features'. That position is argued rather than assumed, with a citation to Yarkoni and Westfall on prediction versus explanation, and it justifies choosing a predictive framework over group-difference testing. Model selection was equally restrained: a descending grid search from 10 hidden units found comparable accuracy down to 5 and degradation below, and 5 was chosen on the explicit principle that fewer hidden units reduce overfitting. Deliberate simplicity of this kind is rare in this corpus and is the right instinct for a 60-participant dataset; the difficulty is that it was verified against a cross-validation that does not hold participants out.

**S-074** [local_115dfe8d] — *A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children*

Stacked denoising autoencoders used hierarchically - two for unimodal representation learning, a third for fusion - with greedy layer-wise unsupervised pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning. The choice is well matched to the problem: 221 hand-engineered features from 90 children is a regime where supervised deep learning would overfit immediately, and unsupervised pre-training exploits the input data without consuming label information, while the denoising objective with zero-masking corruption prevents the identity mapping and encourages robustness. The paper justifies the choice by precedent in Alzheimer's diagnosis, ADHD classification and machinery fault diagnosis. The architecture is also deliberately shallow - two hidden layers per model, compressing 125 to 50 and 96 to 50 - which is appropriate for the sample size, though the t-SNE analysis reveals a cost the authors acknowledge: learned EEG features separate the classes less well than raw ones in the visualisation, which they attribute to dimension reduction discarding useful information.

**S-075** [local_5b7ea7dc] — *AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

CNN-LSTM with soft attention over raw video - a standard action-recognition architecture, applied without modification and without comparison to alternatives. Only one model is reported: no baseline, no ablation over architecture, no simpler comparator such as a frame-averaged CNN or a hand-engineered gaze-shift detector, and no chance or trivial baseline. The architectural choices are nonetheless well reasoned for the task. The last convolutional layer of VGG-16 is retained specifically because it 'preserves the spatial information' as a 7x7 grid of 512-dimensional vectors rather than a globally pooled summary, which matters when the discriminative event is a head turn at a particular image location. The LSTM supplies temporal structure, necessary because the target behaviour is a sequence - object, then person, then object - not a static configuration. And the attention module is included not for performance but for inspectability, which is how it is actually used.

**S-076** [local_87fe26aa] — *Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Deliberately conventional classifiers - random forest, SVM and K-nearest neighbour - with all three applied to every modality, and both best and average accuracy reported. Running the full grid rather than reporting one model is informative: the spread on EEG features runs from 65.00% (SVM) to 83.75% (random forest), an 18-point range on identical inputs, and SVM is the weakest learner on all three modalities. That variability is a caution about single-classifier results generally, and its reporting here is more transparent than the corpus norm. The modelling novelty sits in the combiner rather than the base learners: an attribute-weighted naive Bayes whose weights are computed from training-set counts, with the formula given and its zero-avoidance property noted. No deep model is used for classification, which is appropriate given 80 participants, though a CNN is used upstream for facial expression recognition.

**S-077** [local_893ce2fa] — *An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images*

A Kernel Extreme Learning Machine - a single-hidden-layer feedforward network with randomly assigned input weights and an analytically computed output layer, kernelised with an RBF - chosen for computational economy over deep models, with the paper explicitly excluding deep learning from comparison 'since they require many computational resources and time for training'. The KELM has exactly two tunable parameters, C and gamma, and the entire modelling contribution is how they are chosen. The Giza Pyramids Construction algorithm searches that two-dimensional space via a metaphor of workers pushing stone blocks up a ramp, with gravity, ramp angle, kinetic friction and a worker-substitution probability as parameters. It is worth stating plainly that a two-parameter search over a grid of powers of two from 2^-7 to 2^7 does not require a population-based metaheuristic - exhaustive enumeration of 225 combinations would be cheaper than 10 iterations of a 10-member population - so the algorithmic apparatus considerably exceeds the difficulty of the problem it is applied to. The convergence result reported (optimal values found by iteration six) reflects this.

**S-078** [local_dffe4127] — *Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals*

The modelling is deliberately simple and the choice is argued: a Gaussian naive Bayes classifier on four features, because the study's question is whether diagnostic information exists in the gaze data at all, not how much a flexible model can extract from 153 participants. The complementary unsupervised analysis uses a variational Bayesian Gaussian mixture model, which learns the number of clusters from the data rather than being told it - an important property here, since forcing two clusters would have guaranteed a partition that could be compared against diagnosis, whereas learning the number allows the data to indicate no meaningful split. It returned predominantly two clusters (25 of 33 windows) and was robust to initialisation at 5, 10 or 20 components. Pairing a supervised classifier with an unsupervised clustering that asks the same question from the opposite direction, and finding that both fail to recover diagnosis, is stronger evidence than either alone.

**S-079** [local_2b766683] — *Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech*

Three families compared on identical folds - an ensemble tree model on hand-engineered features, a convolutional network on spectrograms, and a fine-tuned self-supervised transformer on raw waveforms - which spans the realistic design space for a small audio classification problem. The comparison is conducted honestly: alternatives that lost are named rather than omitted (logistic regression, Gaussian naive Bayes, AdaBoost for the shallow family; Inception v3 for the deep one), and the winning CNN is the smallest deep model tried. Full hyperparameters are given for the random forest and described as 'manually chosen', with no tuning procedure stated - which leaves open whether the shallow model was tuned as carefully as the deep ones and hence whether the ten-point gap partly reflects unequal effort. The fold-to-fold correlation across all three models is the most thoughtful analytic observation in the paper: 'each model appears to perform well on fold 2 while performing relatively poorly on fold 3. This suggests that the data in each fold may be too limited', which correctly attributes the variance to the data partition rather than to model instability.

**S-080** [local_2895bdf0] — *Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection*

Linear-kernel SVMs throughout, chosen deliberately over more flexible alternatives and justified by prior use in speech-and-autism work. Non-linear SVMs and formal hyperparameter tuning were run and relegated to supplementary material with the linear configuration reported in the main text - which is the correct ordering when the goal is validating interpretable measures rather than maximising accuracy, though it does mean the reported soft-margin constants (C = 10, 1 and 100 for the three models) were selected on performance. The restraint is consistent with the study's stated purpose: 17 interpretable features, a linear classifier, and an emphasis on which participants are detected rather than on how high the number can be pushed. The mSVM-RFE analysis then delivers a genuinely useful negative result - the optimal eight-feature subset (0.9344) did not significantly outperform the full 17-feature model (0.9235, p = 0.1592), so feature selection bought nothing, and the authors report this rather than promoting the higher figure as their headline.

**S-081** [local_423b636b] — *Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers*

A single SVM with RBF kernel on two or three interpretable features, chosen because it 'is popular when used on relatively smaller datasets' and paired with leave-one-out cross-validation explicitly 'to minimize the risk of overoptimistic classification', citing Vabalas et al.
