The one unresolved representational question is aggregation: features are described as computed 'for a single session of gameplay' while the sample is 49 children, and the paper does not state whether a child playing several sessions contributes several rows. If it does, the nested cross-validation would not be child-disjoint and the estimates would inherit the within-subject leakage that the paper is otherwise careful to avoid.

**S-092** [local_65974fc7] — *Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction*

Three representations of the same recordings, differing in where they intercept the ICA pipeline, and the choice among them is the paper's contribution. Method 1's representation is the unusual one and the one carrying the headline: the coefficients of the 2x2 unmixing matrix at each of 256 frequency points, concatenated. These are not properties of the child's voice in any direct sense - they are the parameters of a linear demixing operator estimated from the observation channels - and their interpretation depends entirely on what those channels are, which the paper does not establish. Method 2's representation is the separated component sequences, one per frequency point, of which the single best-performing was reported. Method 3's is conventional: MFCC, LPCC and PLP computed on reconstructed audio, and the authors note that separation 'eliminates the influence of certain noises and makes the speech data more pure', while sensibly cautioning that speech processing 'need not overly pursue the complete elimination of noise' since aggressive denoising distorts speech.

**S-093** [local_988c462e] — *The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation*

The representation choice is the study's most considered technical decision. Rather than reducing each recording to a single averaged feature vector - which is what most speech studies in this corpus do - the system builds a 100x48 matrix per child, where each row summarises 48 features over a randomly drawn run of 10 sequential vocalisations. This preserves within-session variability, which matters for a construct like prosodic atypicality that is expressed as inconsistency rather than as a shifted mean, and it supplies a two-dimensional input that a convolutional architecture can exploit. Because the matrix is the input and one prediction is produced per recording, the unit of analysis remains the child despite the internal resampling, so no leakage arises from the 100 correlated rows. The design also implicitly handles variable session length: a child with more vocalisations contributes more distinct draws, but every child yields the same fixed-size matrix.

**S-094** [local_76de1c03] — *The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children*

Rater-assigned counts of movement activities and 0-5 severity scores per defined position, aggregated into turn-taking indicators for each game. Every value is traceable to a named behaviour with a published definition, so the representation is fully auditable - the opposite end of the interpretability spectrum from the 100,352 DeepFace features or 1,639 landmark values used elsewhere in this review, and a reminder that the constructs those studies attempt to learn were originally defined by exactly this kind of manual specification.

**S-095** [local_3ba6d25c] — *Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach*

Six hand-crafted scalar features per fixed-length window of the raw gaze coordinate stream: entropy_x, entropy_y, entropy_xy, range_x, range_y, range_xy. The window length is itself a modelled hyperparameter, swept from 1 to 10 s. The binning that defines the entropy is spatial and fixed to the scene camera resolution (10 px cells), which means the features are defined in the wearer's own head-centred frame rather than in a world or face-referenced frame - an appropriate choice given head-mounted tracking, but one that makes the features depend on the geometry of where the interviewer sat. No normalisation, standardisation or per-participant centring is described, so between-child differences in absolute gaze spread enter the model directly - the same property that makes segment-level pooling risky.

**S-096** [local_70a30e2b] — *A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features*

A single 54-dimensional hand-crafted feature vector per child, reduced to 10 by feature selection. The 44 inherited acceleration features are per-axis means, variances, the five dominant frequencies and their amplitudes, signal energies, pairwise inter-axis correlations, a jolt count and the playing-time duration - i.e. a mix of time-domain statistics and coarse spectral descriptors computed over the whole session. The 10 new features are of two kinds: seven state-occupancy ratios derived from the joint encoder/accelerometer signature (fractions of total and of interactive playtime spent not playing, on wheels only, on the ground and in the air) plus the total wheel turn rate, and two tilt-count features (about X and about Y) obtained by short-time Fourier transform of the acceleration signal to recover the car's roll and pitch during wheel play. The representation is therefore entirely aggregate: no temporal ordering, no sequence, no windowing, and no per-episode analysis, so a child who spins the wheels once for ninety seconds and one who spins them thirty times for three seconds each are indistinguishable. The final selected set was seven acceleration features (Y-direction jolt, tilt about Y, X-direction energy, X-Y acceleration correlation, the fourth-highest X frequency, the fifth-highest Z frequency, and the relative amplitude of the highest Y frequency) and three encoder features (wheels-only play ratio, not-playing ratio, total wheel turn rate).

**S-097** [local_a22f97df] — *A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities*

Twelve hand-crafted scalar features per task observation: four speed statistics (mean, max, min, SD), four acceleration statistics (mean, max, min, SD), and four path-geometry descriptors (STH straightness, DC directional change, sdDC directional-change variability, MeanLength). Features are computed per trajectory - one dragging movement from first tap to finger lift - using the R traj package, then averaged across the trajectories within a task, giving one 12-vector per child per task and 1,500 rows overall. The 40 Hz raw coordinate stream is therefore reduced twice before the network sees anything: once to per-trajectory summary statistics, once again by averaging across trajectories. No sequence model, no raw-signal input, no learned front end, and no representation of within-task variability across trajectories except through the SD features. The bottleneck is 10 latent dimensions at training, reduced to 2 for analysis after PCA showed the first two components carried 95% of the latent variance - so the effective representation of a child's movement on a task is a point in a plane.

**S-098** [local_c6853fe2] — *A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation*

Two scalar angle time series per 3 s response window, each sampled at 25 fps and therefore up to 75 frames long, reduced to threshold-crossing frame counts before the decision. The shoulder rotation series is computed frame by frame as theta_t = arccos(v_0 . v_t / |v_0||v_t|) converted to degrees, where v_t is the vector from the right to the left shoulder joint at frame t and v_0 is the same vector at the first frame after the name call - so the measurement is self-referenced to the child's posture at call onset rather than to any absolute frame, which is a sensible choice that removes dependence on how the child happened to be sitting. The head series is the OpenFace yaw Euler angle, accompanied by an implicit binary of whether a face was detected at all by the relevant rear camera. Both series are then summarised only by counting frames that satisfy a threshold, so the representation discards the shape of the movement entirely: peak angular velocity, smoothness, whether the turn was completed or aborted, and whether the child returned to the toys are all invisible. Nothing is learned from the raw joint coordinates, and no representation of the temporal profile of orienting survives into the decision.

**S-099** [local_f1b626c8] — *Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games*

An 18-dimensional vector of region-based fixation statistics per observation. The stimulus space, 1024 x 768, was augmented beyond its true extent to accommodate out-of-range gaze samples, then partitioned into named regions: on FIG 1, FIG 2 and FIG 3; on the Reference FIG; around each of these; and two OUT regions below the outer figures. Fixations were clustered by location of node aggregation and two quantities extracted per region - the number of fixation nodes and the fixation time. Four nested subsets of this matrix were evaluated separately: around the figures, on the figures, on and around the figures, and all features. The representation carries no temporal information: no scan-path order, no saccade amplitudes or directions, no transition probabilities between regions, no within-trial dynamics, and no trial-to-trial evolution across the 240 images. This is a notable gap given the introduction's extended development of a graph-theoretic view in which fixations are vertices and saccades are edges - Fig. 6 even displays such a graph for one autistic child - because every quantity that graph representation would naturally yield (degree distribution, edge weights, path structure, transition entropy) is left uncomputed, and the model receives only vertex-region tallies.

**S-100** [local_6249bd63] — *Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior*

A single 6,272-dimensional vector per participant, built in three steps. First, frame-wise 3D morphable model fitting via 3DI, which jointly models identity, pose and expression so that the person's facial identity is estimated and removed rather than left to confound the expression signal - the authors cite identity bias explicitly, and this is one of very few studies in this corpus that treats individual identity as something to be subtracted rather than as an accidental source of accuracy. Second, replacement of the model's default PCA expression basis with 60 purpose-built localised components, of which 53 are retained (nose and cheek discarded), so that each dimension corresponds to a nameable facial region; concatenated with yaw, pitch and roll, this gives a 56 x T matrix per video. Third, windowed cross-correlation on every ordered pair of the 56 series, using 50% overlapping windows of length Tw and permitting only forward lag on the second series so that direction is preserved and the (i,j) pair differs from (j,i); each pair contributes the mean and standard deviation of its maximal cross-correlation across windows. The representation is therefore about temporal relationships rather than about static or averaged expression content, and it deliberately discards absolute expression magnitude, which is exactly the quantity most vulnerable to identity and recording differences. The dimensionality - 6,272 features for 42 participants - is extreme, mitigated by a linear model, fixed regularisation, no feature selection and participant-level nested cross-validation.

**S-101** [local_8b9e0e8a] — *Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas*

Per fixation: a c-bit semantic code obtained by locating the fixation's SLIC superpixel, resizing that superpixel's bounding box to d x d and passing it through the pretrained autoencoder, concatenated with four low-level descriptors - normalised position, duration, saccade amplitude and saccade orientation. A viewing pattern of m+1 fixations on one stimulus becomes a length-m sequence of these vectors, and each child yields 82 such sequences. The defining property is that no aggregation precedes the model: sequences enter the LSTM in their original order and length, in deliberate contrast to the histogram baseline (which discards order entirely) and the stacked-feature baseline (which fixes the fixation count at 10 by zero-padding or truncation). The authors' analysis of the minLength parameter is a good illustration of how carefully this was handled - raising the minimum sequence length from 2 to 4 fixations improves nothing and causes 'significant data loss in the ASD group', because autistic children produce fewer fixations, so filtering by pattern length would systematically discard the very participants the model must detect. Recognising that a preprocessing threshold interacts with the group difference it is meant to measure is a subtlety absent from most of this corpus. One reported negative result adds to the representation's credibility: using a fixed patch at each superpixel's centre performed worse than the resized full bounding box.

**S-102** [local_0e476686] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts*

For BERT, subword tokens and contextual embeddings from the multilingual cased checkpoint, applied to one tweet at a time. For the three classical models, unspecified - the paper says natural language processing techniques were used but names no tokenisation, vectorisation or feature scheme, so the representation those models consumed is unknown. In every case the unit is a single tweet treated independently: no thread context, no reply structure, no temporal ordering, no user-level aggregation, and no metadata. The maximum sequence length is not stated, which matters because tweets in the 2017-2022 window span both the 140- and 280-character limits. Nothing was masked or normalised beyond the four corpus-cleaning steps, so hashtags, mentions, URLs, emoji and autism-related vocabulary all remain in the text the models see - the last of these being the reason the results cannot be read as evidence about communication style.

**S-103** [local_fbaf69bf] — *Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Two scalar features per participant per movie: integrated entropy of the eyebrow region and of the mouth region, each being the cumulative sum of sample entropy across the first 20 coarse-grained scales of the landmark time series. The pipeline that produces them is where the work sits. Forty-nine landmarks are tracked at 30 fps; the child's face is isolated from those of caregiver, siblings and clinicians by facial embedding; eye-corner and nose landmarks drive an affine transform to a canonical face so that head motion is removed rather than confounded with expression; head-pose angles are estimated separately; signal above 15 Hz is filtered as noise on the physiologically motivated grounds that a facial expression takes at least 260 ms; non-attending intervals are excised; and the remaining landmark points within each region are averaged into a single time series. Sample entropy uses m = 2 and r = 0.15 sigma, both taken from prior literature with an appendix showing insensitivity to the choice. The missing-data rule is stated with a worked numerical example: only embedding vectors free of missing points contribute to the counts, because concatenating across gaps would inflate Cm without inflating Cm+1 and so bias the entropy. A minimum 40% valid-data requirement per movie applies. The representation deliberately discards expression identity, amplitude and timing, retaining only predictability - which is what makes it complementary to the affect measure rather than a variant of it.

**S-104** [local_74416ba7] — *Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders*

Two parallel representations, compared directly. The baseline uses three interpretable scalars per trial: number of fixations, number of saccades and scan-path length. The CNN uses a spatial representation: gaze sample positions are set to 1 in an otherwise zero image, blurred with a Gaussian kernel of sigma 10, centre-cropped and downscaled to 34 x 34 greyscale, then paired with the stimulus image so the model sees both where the person looked and what was there. Two observations about this representation. It discards temporal order entirely - a heat map is a spatial density, so the sequence in which regions were visited, which the paper's own scan-path measure partly captures, is unavailable to the CNN. And the aggressive downscaling to 34 x 34 from a 1920 x 1080 display means each pixel spans roughly 56 x 32 display pixels, so the representation can distinguish eyes from mouth but not, say, one eye from the other or the pupil from the eyelid; this is a reasonable trade for a dataset of this size but bounds what the model can learn. One reporting inconsistency: fixation counts of 200-300 in a five-second trial exceed the number of possible fixation events at 120 Hz, so these are gaze samples classified as fixation rather than discrete fixation events, and the label is used loosely throughout.

**S-105** [local_7c6a5aa4] — *Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders*

Fixed-length windows over a pseudo-semantic numeric encoding of the key-press stream. All events and keys across the corpus were enumerated - 69 unique ones despite users being able to add vocabulary - and partitioned into normal keys, complex keys, normal app events and complex app events, with each category assigned a non-overlapping range of integer identifiers so that a value's category is recoverable from its magnitude. That design is a genuine thought: it gives an otherwise arbitrary integer encoding a coarse semantic structure that a model can exploit. The stream is then cut into non-overlapping windows of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 or 100 consecutive presses, each becoming a pseudo-sample; overlapping windows were tested and gave 'no tangible improvement'. Temporal modelling substitutes inter-press intervals for identifiers, and spectral modelling replaces windows with per-session frequency counts. Two properties of this representation matter for interpretation. Users contribute pseudo-samples in proportion to how much they used the app, so heavy users dominate and the effective sample size is never reported. And lexical content is discarded: what a person said is reduced to a category-preserving integer, even though the paper's descriptive analysis shows content to be both recoverable and group-discriminating.

**S-106** [local_8a706eaa] — *Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Raw RGB video frames at 224 x 224, in sequences of 300 (IJA) or 150 (RJA) - a fully end-to-end representation with no intermediate abstraction whatsoever. This is a stronger commitment to learned representation than any other study in this corpus, most of which extract landmarks, poses, gaze coordinates or hand-crafted statistics before modelling. It has two consequences that pull in opposite directions. It removes an entire class of failure - no landmark detector to fail on a child who turns away, no gaze estimator to calibrate, no feature engineering to bias - and it is what allows the same pipeline to work on a task where the child physically turns around, which a face-based method could not handle. But it also means the model has access to everything in the frame: the child's appearance, clothing, posture, the examiner, the room, and anything that co-varies with recruitment site. With autistic children recruited exclusively from one hospital clinic and comparison children from day care centres, and with a 44-50 point IQ difference between groups, an end-to-end model on raw frames has many routes to near-perfect separation that have nothing to do with joint attention. The Grad-CAM analysis is the study's answer to this, and it is a good one as far as it goes - the heatmaps localise to faces and eyes and the described behaviours match the constructs - but it is illustrative rather than systematic, and no quantitative check on background or appearance confounds is reported.

**S-107** [local_6b9484ce] — *Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking*

A rendered scanpath image, resized either to 100x100 greyscale (custom CNN) or 299x299 RGB with pixel values normalised to [-1, 1] (InceptionV3). The greyscale conversion for the CNN is described candidly as an empirical choice: RGB training was slow and 'converting the images to grayscale proved to significantly reduce the training time and an improvement in classification accuracy was also noticed'. That is honest reporting of a decision made partly on observed accuracy, and it is worth noting that if the source rendering used colour to encode anything - fixation order, duration, or which eye - greyscale conversion would discard it, and the paper cannot say whether it did, because the rendering scheme is never described. The deeper representational point is that all temporal information in the original gaze data survives only as visual geometry: sequence order, fixation duration and saccade velocity are recoverable from a drawing only to the extent the renderer encoded them, and the model receives no time series at all.

**S-108** [local_c6a4ea7b] — *SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism*

One fixed-length vector per child summarising an entire conversational session, comprising 45 part-of-speech tag frequencies, 23 syntactic complexity measures and 9 semantic-pragmatic measures, reduced from 77 to 63 by SHAP-guided elimination that removed non-informative tags such as SYM and MD and an um-propagation artefact. Count-based features - echolalia, unintelligible units, unexpected words - are normalised over conversation length, which is a necessary and correctly applied step given that source sessions range from about 10 to 30 minutes. Two of the features are computed with contextual embeddings rather than surface statistics: child-child and child-partner discourse coherence are cosine similarities between BERT representations of consecutive sentences, which is a reasonable operationalisation of topic maintenance and is more sensitive than lexical overlap would be. The representation discards temporal structure beyond that local coherence, so trajectory across a session - whether a child warms up, disengages, or shifts topic progressively - is not represented.

**S-109** [local_5c43dffa] — *Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths*

A 100 x 100 image per participant per video clip, produced by drawing the gaze trajectory on a 1680 x 1050 black background and downsampling. The downsampling is aggressive - each output pixel spans roughly 17 x 11 input pixels - so fine spatial structure such as whether gaze fell on an eye or a cheek is not preserved, and what survives is the coarse geometry of the trajectory: its extent, its density, how many times it crosses itself. Three enrichments are then tested. Temporal restriction to 3-second or 1-second windows, which encodes time by segmentation rather than within the image. Velocity colour coding, which maps average speed between consecutive points - Euclidean distance over time interval - onto a colour scale with stated thresholds. And rotation-based augmentation, which generates additional images and is applied at three levels in one experiment. Two properties of this representation matter for interpretation. Because the image is a drawing, incidental graphical characteristics such as total ink and plotted extent are available to the network alongside behavioural ones, and no analysis distinguishes them. And because velocity depends on sampling rate, which is never stated, the velocity encoding cannot be reproduced or compared across studies.

**S-110** [local_32da8ede] — *A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths*

A 100 x 100 greyscale image flattened to a 10,000-element vector, with a parallel colour variant. Three transformations separate the raw gaze data from the model input, each discarding information: rendering the coordinate time series as a static drawing removes temporal order, fixation duration and saccade velocity; downscaling from 640 x 480 to 100 x 100 means each output pixel spans roughly 6 x 5 source pixels, so fine spatial resolution of where on a face gaze landed is lost; and flattening removes spatial adjacency. What survives is the coarse geometry and density of the drawn path. The greyscale conversion is reported to work slightly better than colour, which is consistent with colour carrying no information in these renderings - but the rendering scheme is not described, so whether colour originally encoded anything (order, duration, which eye) cannot be determined.

**S-111** [local_15ed96cb] — *A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning*

A tabular feature vector per child, built from 100 candidate variables reduced to 59 on clinical-relevance grounds before any modelling - a reduction made a priori rather than by data-driven selection, which the paper states explicitly and which removes a source of optimism that data-driven feature selection would introduce. The central representational decision concerns milestones, and it is reasoned carefully. Records vary in the timing of checkups and contain multiple entries per milestone per child, so each milestone was reduced to a binary of 'ever passed' versus 'only failed', chosen specifically 'to avoid attributing a-priori developmental assumptions' to never-tested and late-tested records. The cost is stated in the same paragraph: children who passed after several attempts cannot be distinguished from those who passed immediately, so the pattern of delay - arguably the most diagnostically informative aspect of milestone data - is discarded. Stating a representational trade-off, its motivation and its cost in three sentences is better practice than anything comparable in this corpus. Longitudinal structure within a child is otherwise collapsed, and modelling performance patterns over time is named as the first priority for future work.

**S-112** [local_261afa51] — *AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: &#x201C;A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System&#x201D;*

Cropped facial photographs, resized (to 96 x 96 in one passage and 224 x 224 x 3 in another) and rescaled to [0, 1], with an extensive augmentation list: rotation, horizontal and vertical flipping, zooming and cropping, brightness and contrast adjustment, noise injection, shearing and scaling. Two elements deserve comment. Vertical flipping produces upside-down faces, which has no rationale for a task premised on facial landmark geometry and would be excluded by anyone reasoning about the construct rather than reaching for a standard augmentation set. And brightness, contrast and noise augmentation are described as helping the model generalise across imaging conditions - which is the right instinct but addresses only the appearance of the problem, since systematic imaging differences between the two source collections would remain available through resolution, compression and framing regardless.

**S-113** [local_3e88f3ce] — *An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks*

Voxel volumes and Harvard-Oxford region graphs for imaging; approximately 65-70 tabular clinical fields for the phenotype stream; a 32-dimensional fused latent vector. The phenotype representation is where the study's problem is located and where its transparency is greatest - because GAMI-Net decomposes contributions feature by feature, the paper is able to report exactly which fields drive the prediction, and it does so honestly. The top ten are ADOS_TOTAL, ADI_R_SOCIAL_TOTAL_A, FIQ, AGE_AT_SCAN, SRS_RAW_TOTAL, ADOS_COMM, ADOS_GOTHAM_SEVERITY, VIQ, PIQ and ADI_R_VERBAL_TOTAL_BV - six diagnostic-instrument scores, three IQ measures and age. Not one is a measurement of behaviour, and six of the ten are the assessment whose result is the label.

**S-114** [local_5b5f2237] — *Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development*

A 41 x 23 matrix: one row per participant, one column per time scale of cross wavelet coherence, with scales spanning 0.1 s to 10 s. Each value is the coherence between the child's and the interviewer's whole-body movement time series at that scale, computed from motion energy analysis of a single side-view video. Two properties are worth recording. The representation is inherently relational - no value describes the child alone - and it is inherently frequency-resolved, which is what allowed the group difference to be localised to the fast scales where a summary measure had found nothing. A second representation of 57 derived features was then built by summing subsets of the six significant coherences: all 15 pairs, 20 triples, 15 quadruples, 6 quintuples and the single six-way sum. These are transparent linear combinations of the originals and add no new information about movement, only a re-weighting chosen with reference to the group difference.

**S-115** [local_13426811] — *Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning*

Two representations, both derived from the same transcripts. Tags come from a Systemic Functional Linguistics annotation scheme built for Japanese through transfer comparison, comprising four system networks and eleven or more lexicogrammatical headings each with multiple tag types - modality, te-clauses with eight subtypes, twelve negotiating particles, explanative mood and others. For the linear model the input is a tag-frequency vector normalised by total word count, which discards order. For the Bi-LSTM variants the input is the ordered sequence of tag sets, with each word represented by the sum of the embedding vectors of its tags, giving 300-dimensional tag embeddings; the text model uses 300-dimensional word embeddings; and the combined model concatenates the two at each time step. Annotation was performed both manually and automatically, with both evaluated in parallel throughout, and the automatic annotator achieving a mean F of 0.88 against manual - so the study reports both the ceiling achievable with perfect annotation and the performance obtainable in a setting where manual annotation is impossible.

**S-116** [local_948fa8d0] — *Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms*

A 3,315-dimensional concatenation per image: 3,000 activations from one backbone plus 100 HOG, 50 LBP, 50 ORB, 65 PHASH and 50 SIFT features. The handcrafted component is worth characterising because it determines what a source-provenance confound would look like. HOG encodes gradient distributions, which depend on image sharpness; LBP encodes local texture, which depends on resolution and compression; PHASH is a whole-image fingerprint, which encodes global tone and layout; SIFT and ORB encode keypoint structure, which depends on contrast and focus. Every one of these is a property of the photograph rather than of the face, and all differ systematically between images collected from different sources. That this feature set alone achieves 84.5% is therefore the paper's most diagnostic result, and it is reported without comment.

**S-117** [local_893dfc22] — *Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed*

Grayscale cropped faces at 120x110 for Gabor filtering and 100x100 for convolutional processing, after normalisation, histogram equalisation, face detection and realignment. KDEF images are additionally pre-standardised by the corpus creators so that eyes and lips occupy fixed coordinates, which removes pose and scale variation entirely - a property that raises accuracy and reduces the relevance of the result to any uncontrolled setting.

**S-118** [local_e7c16f2a] — *Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification*

A rotation-normalised sequence of 20-69 points per trajectory. The rotation step is the representational contribution and is worked out carefully: because targets sit at eight positions 45 degrees apart, raw trajectories to different targets are not comparable, so the angle between consecutive points relative to the origin is computed with atan2, mapped from the atan2 range into 0-360 degrees, and applied as a rotation - with all three steps written out as numbered equations and the resulting endpoint coordinates given. This makes trajectories to any target directly comparable while preserving their shape, and it is the kind of preprocessing that reflects thought about the construct rather than convention. The two-feature model then receives only these rotated coordinates and the four-feature model adds velocity and acceleration. Crucially, unlike the group's companion study on a different sample - which averaged twelve kinematic features across a task to give one vector per child - this study preserves the full temporal sequence, so the model sees the unfolding of the movement rather than its summary. The 20-69 point length window standardises comparability at the cost of discarding both very brief and very extended drags.

**S-119** [local_5a7ab52d] — *Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain*

A tabular vector of eleven variables per individual, reduced by the optimisation-based selection stage to an unnamed subset. The fitness function combines correlation, data variance and inter- and intra-class cosine similarity, which is a reasonable multi-objective formulation for filter-style selection but depends on class labels and is therefore a candidate leakage route if applied outside training folds - a question the paper does not address. No temporal, sequential or image representation is used, so whatever dynamics the underlying facial or physiological recordings contained are absent from the model input.

**S-120** [local_8253c2ec] — *Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder*

A 17-dimensional tabular vector per respondent, retained from 19 or 21 available fields after dropping two judged irrelevant. Ten of the seventeen are the binary screening item responses. The critical structural fact is that the outcome is computed from those ten by summation and thresholding, and that the sum is itself present among the fields in these datasets - so the representation contains the answer twice over, once implicitly across the items and once explicitly in the total.

**S-121** [local_1e9d0b71] — *Machine learning’s effectiveness*

A 16-dimensional summary vector per child. Time-series pressure and pose data are compressed into scalar descriptors: path length, mean speed, entropy and convex-hull area for centre-of-pressure; longest-trial duration for overall balance; and ten joint-wise correlations plus the centre-of-mass to centre-of-pressure difference for the body-pressure relationship. This is aggregation rather than sequence modelling, so the temporal unfolding of a stance is not represented except insofar as entropy and correlation capture it. The correlation features are nonetheless well chosen for the construct: a correlation between a joint angle and centre-of-pressure position is inherently relational and cannot be computed from either stream alone, and it summarises coordination in a single interpretable number. Every variable is named, categorised and explained, with the rationale and calculation method for each given in supplementary material.

**S-122** [local_b9e05a8f] — *Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network*

RGB face crops, normalised to [0, 1], obtained by third-party cropping in dataset 1 and by MTCNN detection with alignment, cropping and resizing in dataset 2. No landmark coordinates, no morphometric derivations, no temporal sequence. The representation therefore cannot express any of the specific craniofacial or expression-dynamic constructs the introduction invokes, and it retains every source-dependent property of the image - resolution, compression, illumination, pose, background - that is free to vary with class given how the two classes were harvested.

**S-123** [local_0b0960c4] — *Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]*

An eleven-dimensional vector of linear and non-linear time- and frequency-domain descriptors per EEG segment. The features are individually interpretable and have an established electrophysiological literature, which makes the absence of any feature-importance analysis a real loss - identifying which descriptors and which electrode positions separate the groups would have produced a transferable finding independent of the classification accuracy. The number and duration of segments and their distribution across participants are not reported, which is the missing information needed to judge the sample structure.

**S-124** [local_abad69fd] — *Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play*

An 81-dimensional vector per child of counts, durations and proportions, derived arithmetically from human coding of a 90-second video with onset and offset times on a timeline. Every element is directly interpretable and directly auditable - a coder's judgement about a named behaviour, aggregated by a stated rule. The final representation is five numbers: one speech duration and four play quantities. The proportion indicators are a thoughtful design element, since normalising socially oriented vocalisations by total vocalisations, or word-use vocalisations by total vocalisations, separates the social direction of speech from the amount of speech - and indeed the proportional versions had the strongest univariate odds ratios in the vocalisation family (0.367 and 0.345). It is notable that stepwise selection nonetheless retained the raw duration measure rather than a proportion, which leaves the model's strongest predictor confounded with how much the child spoke at all, and thus with expressive language level, which was never measured.

**S-125** [local_cd7545e2] — *Predictive model using autism*

Two representations, compared directly. The instrument's own algorithm domain scores - communication and reciprocal social interaction under the original algorithm, social affect and restricted repetitive behaviour under the revised - which aggregate item ratings into totals against published cut-offs. And a binary per-item vector recording whether each of the 32 items received a non-zero score. The dichotomisation is the more interesting choice and is justified on psychometric rather than convenience grounds: for several items a higher rating denotes a different presentation rather than a more severe one, and the paper works through item B11, quality of social response, where a rating of 1 describes limited, awkward or inconsistent reactions and a rating of 2 describes odd, stereotyped or contextually inappropriate ones - 'there was no clear difference between scores 1 and 2 regarding the severity of ASD symptoms, and the differences were considered to be limited to phenotypic differences in symptoms'. Treating such a scale as ordinal and summing it is exactly what the algorithms do, and the collapse to presence-or-absence of atypicality is part of why the item-level analysis recovers information the totals lose.

**S-126** [local_3ecb92bf] — *The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech*

Raw waveform segments per vocalisation, encoded by learned representations - either the discriminatively fine-tuned model's features or Wav2Vec 2.0 context representations. No hand-crafted acoustic descriptors are used in the study's own models, though the ComParE feature set is discussed as background. Sample durations are not stated but can be inferred at roughly 1.3 seconds for De-Enigma and 2.2 seconds for CPSD from the reported totals. Short segments are a real constraint on a prosodic claim: intonation contour, pitch range and expressive variation are properties of utterances and turns rather than of one- to two-second fragments, so the representation may not span the timescale on which the hypothesised difference lives.

**S-127** [local_4b02df7c] — *Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism*

TF-IDF vectors and word2vec embeddings at tweet level; a self-trained embedding layer feeding an attention-based BiLSTM over a concatenation of all of a user's preprocessed tweets at profile level, restricted to users with at least five tweets. The representation is the product of aggressive normalisation - profanity masking, removal of non-alphanumerics, links, mentions and HTML, lowercasing, stop-word removal, stemming and lemmatisation - which strips much of the paralinguistic texture of social media writing (capitalisation, punctuation, emoji, elongation) that might itself carry the signal of interest. The most consequential representational decision is the removal of sixteen autism-related tokens including the hashtag that defines the label, on the explicit ground that they 'could introduce bias and lead to model overfitting'. That is a target-leakage control, correctly reasoned, and it is the same failure mode this review documents in the questionnaire-item studies where the label is an arithmetic function of the features - handled here rather than left in place.

**S-128** [local_7d7f1fcc] — *Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children*

The video representation is the study's most important technical decision and functions as a designed confound control. Rather than modelling raw frames, the authors apply OpenPose and plot the resulting skeletal keypoints over a plain black background at 320x240, 'hence preserving a visual gist of the social interaction between the examiner and the child'. This removes face, expression, clothing, body habitus, skin tone, room, furniture, lighting and every other appearance cue - so a classifier operating on it cannot be exploiting the identity and setting confounds that this review has documented throughout the image-based branch, where models trained on photographs may be recognising where an image came from rather than who is in it. Here the confound is architecturally excluded, not merely unmeasured. It also makes partial data sharing possible, which is why a de-identified pose subsample could be deposited on Zenodo when the raw video could not. The audio representation is the mirror image: the full band with no diarisation, retaining child voice, examiner voice and ambient sound, summarised as time-averaged MFCCs, Mel spectrogram, chromagram, spectral contrast and tonal centroid over 10-second windows. Time-averaging discards temporal structure within each window, so prosodic contour is only weakly represented - consistent with the finding that the audio model's predictive items are gestural and sensory rather than vocal.

**S-129** [local_5a331ffe] — *Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning*

RGB face crops produced by a Haar cascade, with only frames in which the child's face is observable retained and the number of frames per video varying accordingly. No landmark geometry, no morphometric derivation, no body pose and no temporal sequence for the classifier. Two consequences. Cropping to the face discards the stereotypies that define the corpus, so the classifier cannot use the behaviour that identified these children as autistic in the first place - which the authors implicitly acknowledge by proposing gesture analysis as future work. And retaining only frames with a visible face introduces a selection that could differ systematically between classes, since a child spinning or flapping presents their face to a home camera less consistently than a child photographed for a curated corpus would.

**S-130** [local_45ef7022] — *A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features*

Denoised thermal face images at 160x160 for the mood network, and a concatenation of learned mood output with measured skin temperature for the severity classifiers, whose dimensionality is never stated. Two representational points matter. Absolute skin temperature is only meaningful relative to ambient conditions, and no normalisation or ambient reference is applied, so the same child at the same physiological state would yield different feature values outdoors and indoors. And each image is treated as an independent observation despite 50 coming from each child, so the representation carries no notion of within-child variation - which is exactly what a continuous-monitoring framework should model and what the paper's own critique of the 15-minute ABC assessment implies it should measure.

**S-131** [local_0f5a351e] — *Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

RGB face images at 224x224x3 with pixel values rescaled to [0, 1], augmented by 10% shear, 10% zoom and horizontal flip. No landmark geometry and no morphometric derivation, so the craniofacial constructs invoked as motivation are not represented at all, and every source-dependent property of the image is retained.

**S-132** [local_786b6280] — *Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features*

A vector of at most twelve interpretable linguistic values per child, reduced after a first round comparing the child-alone and ratio forms of each feature. This is the most parsimonious representation in the review and is well matched to the sample: every dimension is a quantity with a published psycholinguistic literature, computed by documented rules from a public archive, so the representation is auditable end to end. Its limitation is that transcript-level aggregation discards everything about how the speech unfolded - no sequence, no timing, no prosody - so constructs such as turn-taking latency or intonation, which the wider literature associates with autistic speech, are outside its reach.

**S-133** [local_879ec69b] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning*

Three-dimensional joint coordinate sequences, re-expressed two ways - as Skepxel images and as angle-augmented graph sequences. The skeleton representation functions as a designed confound control of the same kind used by the Geneva pose study charted elsewhere in this review: face, expression, clothing, body habitus, room, lighting and background are all absent by construction, so a classifier operating on it cannot exploit the appearance and setting confounds that dominate the photograph branch. It also carries the privacy property the paper argues for, since joint coordinates do not identify a child by appearance. The limitation is coverage: 25 full-body joints in one corpus against 10 upper-body joints in the other, so the two experiments do not measure the same thing, and the paper's own figure contrasting the joint layouts makes this visible without drawing the inference for the 25-point performance gap.

**S-134** [local_93e5d23d] — *Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]*

Two representations. For the statistical analysis, Praat-derived scalar features per cry pattern - jitter as the mean absolute difference between consecutive pitch periods, shimmer as the amplitude analogue, and harmonics-to-noise ratio - each with a clinical interpretation and an established literature. For the classification, 128x128 single-channel spectrogram images per cry instance. The spectrogram representation retains time-frequency structure that the scalar perturbation measures discard, which is the right complement in principle; but because each cry instance is treated as an independent observation and roughly six come from each child, the representation also carries whatever is idiosyncratic to an individual voice, which is what an instance-level split allows the model to exploit.

**S-135** [local_a0d73248] — *Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm*

A tabular vector per respondent drawn from 21 fields, with the retained subset unspecified after a feature-engineering stage. The decisive representational fact is that both the ten AQ-10 items and their summed total appear in the enumerated field list, and no removal of the total is described.

**S-136** [local_4ceee075] — *Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics*

A per-frame vector of 1,639 values comprising a timestamp, 99 pose landmark coordinates, 63 coordinates for each hand, facial mesh coordinates, the mouth aspect ratio and per-region motion energy, formed into sequences for temporal modelling. Reducing video to landmark coordinates before any learning is a deliberate confound control of the same kind used by the pose-based studies elsewhere in this review: skin tone, clothing, background, lighting and room are all discarded, so none can drive the classification, and this is a substantive advantage over the whole-image approaches in the photograph branch. The residual exposure is facial mesh geometry, which retains craniofacial morphology and therefore retains the sex- and age-linked variation that the sample does not control.

**S-137** [local_84bcd4ed] — *Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of*

A 100,352-dimensional DeepFace feature vector per image. Whole-image transfer through a pretrained face model retains every source-dependent property of the photograph, and the identity-encoding character of the embedding makes the representation particularly ill-suited to a corpus split at image level with an unreported number of distinct children. No landmark geometry, morphometric measurement or temporal information is used, so no specific facial construct is operationalised.

**S-138** [local_d97673f4] — *Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Preprocessed face crops in one of three configurations - resize plus normalisation; resize plus normalisation plus CLAHE; resize plus normalisation plus greyscale plus CLAHE - encoded as pretrained CNN embeddings, with augmentation by zoom (1.0 to 1.2) and brightness (0.7 to 1.3). The augmentation parameters are explained rather than merely listed, which is good reporting; the concern is that zoom and brightness variants of one photograph are near-duplicates, so if augmentation preceded splitting the evaluation is compromised, and the paper does not say which order was used.

**S-139** [local_86a67a4f] — *Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children*

Normalised and augmented face images, filtered to require a visible frontal face with eyes, nose and mouth. The quality filter is a genuine and unusual step for this branch, since web-scraped corpora contain profile shots, partial faces and heavy occlusion that add noise without adding signal - but it also selects a subset whose class balance is unreported, and if image quality differs systematically between two folders drawn from different online sources then the filter itself could shift the composition.

**S-140** [local_0a39cca9] — *Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy*

Resized and normalised face images augmented by rotation, flipping and contrast adjustment. Contrast adjustment is worth noting because it partially normalises a property that would differ systematically between image sources; whether it is sufficient to remove a source signal is untested, and no source-wise analysis is performed.

**S-141** [local_7432ffd7] — *Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models*

A 16-element tabular vector per gaze sample: trial and stimulus identifiers, Tracking_Ratio, Point_of_Regard right/left X and Y, six gaze-vector components, Category_Right, Category_Left, #Stimulus, and CARS_Score. Min-max scaled to [0,1], reshaped to (1,16). Two of these deserve separate note. CARS_Score is a clinician-administered autism severity instrument: within this dataset it is effectively a monotone function of the label, so its inclusion is direct target leakage and by itself can account for a near-perfect result. Tracking_Ratio is a signal-quality index that plausibly differs systematically between groups for reasons of compliance rather than social attention. Stimulus and trial identifiers encode session structure.

**S-142** [local_8ff20c48] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning*

A nine-field tabular row per child: five binary Q-CHAT items plus age in months, binary sex, binary jaundice and binary family history. The feature-selection step is the analytically decisive move and it runs in an unexpected direction. Items A1, A2, A6, A8 and A9 were removed because they correlated highly with the Q-CHAT-10 score - but the Q-CHAT-10 score is the sum of exactly those items, so high correlation is arithmetic necessity, not redundancy. Deleting them does not remove noise; it removes half of the summands that define the label. The reported 0.83 is thus an estimate of how well five items reconstruct the threshold on all ten, which is why this study lands in the low 80s while local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248, which retained all items, reach 100%.

**S-143** [local_986436f2] — *Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost*

Nominally a 3D landmark graph; actually a 2D landmark configuration from Dlib applied to 224x224 web photographs, with rotation and scaling augmentation. The depth channel that the entire introduction argues is essential does not exist in the data. This mismatch propagates into the results: the reported landmark localisation error falling from 2.5 mm at 100 epochs to 0.9 mm at 500 epochs is a physical measurement that no part of the input can support, since the images have neither metric calibration nor ground-truth 3D landmark positions.

**S-144** [local_bb4d1f7a] — *Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models*

Two representations. (i) Variable-length scanpath sequences over four features - x, y, fixation duration d, velocity v - padded to maximum length with a masking mechanism, evaluated in four combinations. (ii) 4,000 cropped eye images at 416x416, fifty frames per child times left and right eye, each labelled with subject ID, frame number, severity band and eye side. The image-level representation is what the 70:15:15 split partitions, and it is where the validity problem originates: with a fixed 100 images per child, the split cannot separate participants even in principle.

**S-145** [local_13c1f46d] — *Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism*

Gabor-filtered RGB face crops at an unstated resolution, passed through MTCNN detection, median denoising and Z-score channel normalisation, then encoded as MobileNetV2 features. Augmentation adds rotation, horizontal flip, cropping and brightness variation, described as a preprocessing stage rather than as a training-time operation. Class weighting is applied on the stated grounds of imbalance, although the source Kaggle corpus is balanced by construction and the paper's own confusion matrices imply near-equal class sizes.

**S-146** [local_e771fb69] — *Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data*

Tabular vectors of 120 kinematic or 48 behavioural/eye features per instructional segment, organised into four named subsets (K_General, K_Attention, L_General, L_Attention). Preprocessing includes one step that deserves separate note: missing values and anomalies were replaced with the mean value of each respective class - imputation conditioned on the outcome label, computed over the whole dataset before any split. Where a feature has missing values at different rates in the two groups, that step writes the label into the feature matrix directly, and it is a sufficient mechanism to produce a nine-of-nine result on its own.

**S-147** [local_945300a5] — *Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network*

224x224 RGB face crops at 1:1 aspect ratio, rescaled to [0,1], with training-time augmentation by rotation to 20 degrees, width and height shifts to 0.2, shear 0.2, zoom 0.2 and horizontal flip. Noise removal and contrast enhancement are mentioned without method. The conclusion treats the 1:1 ratio and 224x224 size as the study's principal finding, which places a preprocessing convention where an empirical result should be.

**S-148** [local_ed30e24c] — *Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI*

A tabular row per toddler: ten binary Q-CHAT-10 items plus sex, ethnicity, jaundice, family history, region, respondent and age, label-encoded and min-max scaled. Two features of this representation matter. First, the ten items are the constituents of the Q-CHAT-10 score whose threshold defines the label, so the predictor set arithmetically determines the outcome - the same structure as local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 (which reach 100% on six metrics) and the inverse of local_8ff20c48 (which deleted five of the ten items and consequently fell to 0.83). Second, ethnicity and region are nominal categories converted to ordered integers by label encoding, imposing an artificial ordering that the paper does not remark on.

**S-149** [local_b9de0d7f] — *Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques*

Tabular rows of ten binary Q-CHAT-10 items plus demographic and history fields, SMOTE-augmented and feature-selected. The ten items are the constituents of the Q-CHAT-10 total whose threshold defines the Phase I label and whose bands define the Phase II label, so in both phases the predictor set arithmetically determines the outcome.

**S-150** [local_14df790d] — *Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach*

Standardised tabular vectors in five configurations: the default 19-attribute set; Subset 1 (chi-squared, ordered by Q1-Q10 with Q9, Q5, Q6 top); Subset 2 (tree importance, retaining both Qchat-10-Score and Q1-Q10); Subset 3 (correlation-based: Qchat-10-Score, sex, jaundice, age, family history, ethnicity, respondent); Subset 4 (minimal: Qchat-10-Score, age, sex, jaundice); and Q1-Q10 alone. The configurations are the study's real object, and their comparison is where its diagnostic value lies - Subsets 3 and 4 keep the Q-CHAT total and drop the items; Q1-Q10 keeps the items and drops the total; Subset 2 keeps both.

**S-151** [local_4da2b941] — *Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study*

The 25 raw CAT-Q-ES Likert items, in four configurations: items alone, items plus gender, items plus autism diagnosis, and items plus both. Subscale scores were tested as an alternative input and did not improve accuracy - a negative result the paper reports rather than suppresses.

**S-152** [local_6e7174c0] — *A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach*

224x224 RGB face crops from the public corpus, with unspecified preprocessing and augmentation plus a proposed Attention-Based Augmentation Layer applying unnamed non-destructive transformations. Neither the augmentation set nor its placement relative to the split is stated.

**S-153** [local_e04bcd32] — *Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network*

Resized, deblurred and denoised RGB face images at unstated resolution. Resizing is described as adjusting the facial image for ratio and resolution with the loss of pixels - an unusual admission that information is discarded before the pipeline whose purpose is to recover information begins.

**S-154** [local_183eaef4] — *Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI*

A 19-field tabular row containing, together: the ten AQ-10 behavioural items, the AQ10 total score, the Q-CHAT-10 score, the Social Responsiveness Scale score, the CARS severity rating, seven comorbidity flags and demographics - with ASD_traits as the target. This is the review's most concentrated instance of target leakage by instrument inclusion. CARS is a clinician-administered autism severity scale; SRS measures social impairment severity; AQ10 and Q-CHAT-10 are autism screening totals whose thresholds define exactly the kind of traits-present label being predicted; and the ten AQ-10 items are the summands of the AQ10 total. Four separate measurements of the target condition, plus the item-level constituents of one of them, are supplied to the model as predictors of that condition. A perfect neural-network score under this arrangement is the expected outcome, not an anomaly - and it explains why even logistic regression, a linear model on 19 variables, reaches 0.9858.

**S-155** [local_b6ac2b98] — *Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks*

Four nested tabular feature sets per child: full (158 variables), secondary (72), prior (60) and basic (24), differing in how finely stimuli and areas of interest are decomposed. All variables derive from the eye-tracking record; no clinical instrument score, demographic variable or diagnostic measure enters the feature set - a point worth stating explicitly, because it is exactly what separates this study from the corpus's leakage cases. With 93 children and up to 158 variables, three of the four datasets have more variables than participants.

**S-156** [local_44d3aef5] — *Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis*

640x480 scanpath images, enhanced, converted to arrays and normalised to [0,1], with rotation, shifting and flipping augmentation applied during training only. Augmentation of a scanpath image is worth a separate note: flipping and rotating a gaze trace changes its spatial relationship to the stimulus that produced it, so the augmented examples correspond to no possible viewing behaviour - a transformation that is standard for photographs and semantically incoherent for scanpaths.

**S-157** [local_24fefc5f] — *A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection*

A tabular vector of Q-CHAT-10 items and individual characteristics, Yeo-Johnson transformed and then reduced by the DeSEHO metaheuristic. Two observations. First, Yeo-Johnson is a variance-stabilising power transformation for continuous skewed variables; applying it to binary checklist responses to remove noise and artefacts, and justifying that choice at length against Box-Cox on the ground that it accommodates negative values, is a category error about the data. Second, the ten items are the summands of the score whose threshold defines the label, so whatever subset DeSEHO retains, the target remains an arithmetic function of the feature pool.

**S-158** [local_69b10fe4] — *An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms*

One row per participant. Thirty-seven kinematic input variables (nine features across four shapes plus one reaction time value), computed as residuals after controlling for age, depression and anxiety and averaged across trials and days; plus three questionnaire sets. A reduced discriminatory kinematic feature set was defined by retaining features, or feature-shape combinations, that showed significant group differences in the mixed models. That selection rule is stated precisely - including that a group-by-shape interaction yielding a difference on only one shape contributes only that shape's value - which is both good reporting and the point at which the design leaks, since the significance tests were computed over all participants including those later held out.

**S-159** [local_af9f4c12] — *An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data*

A 15-attribute harmonised row per participant after pruning, with continuous variables min-max normalised and categorical fields label-encoded. The predictor set contains the A1-A10 items and the composite Q_SCORE; the target is a four-level discretisation of a weighted sum of those same A1-A10 items. The label is therefore an arithmetic function of the inputs by construction, and the paper says so.

**S-160** [local_367db0b6] — *An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns*

224x224 images for the CNN backbones; the representation of questionnaire data is never specified, which matters because five of the seven named datasets are questionnaires and a 224x224 convolutional backbone cannot consume a checklist without a stated encoding. Aggregated feature vectors appear in the text as literal illustrative values such as [0.5, 0.6, ..., 0.8] and [0.45, 0.55, ..., 0.75].

**S-161** [local_8d43288c] — *Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos*

Cropped frame sequences from annotated behaviour segments, after region-of-interest detection to remove irrelevant background and augmentation to reduce overfitting. The ROI step is well motivated for uncontrolled home video, where background and framing differ systematically between recordings.

**S-162** [local_5f57ba19] — *Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension*

Eighteen AOI-based temporal gaze features per experimental instance, where an instance is one participant viewing one story under one modality in one speech phase. No clinical instrument score, demographic variable or diagnostic measure enters the feature set - the SCQ, KBIT-2 and PPVT-III are reported as sample characteristics and kept out of the model.

**S-163** [local_1d856900] — *Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare*

Dataset 1: a reduced tabular vector after correlation filtering above 0.90 and ANOVA F-test selection, drawn from 28 attributes that include the AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS scores alongside the ASD-traits target. Dataset 2: a 4,220-dimensional concatenation dominated by 4,040 image features, against 400 samples - a ratio of more than ten features per sample, and more than forty per original clinical sample.

**S-164** [local_7b19a959] — *Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis*

One row per participant containing 54 task-derived dependent variables, with AQ total and demographic variables added in specified configurations. No dimensionality reduction or feature selection is applied, and no clinical instrument is smuggled in - the AQ's presence is the explicit object of one of the three comparisons.

**S-165** [local_d7b6fa00] — *Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath*

One vector per participant, formed by aggregating nine scanpath descriptors across that person's trials via mean and standard deviation, after each scanpath was truncated or zero-padded to 20 fixations and before z-score standardisation. The 20-fixation cap is a substantive modelling decision - it discards everything after the twentieth fixation in longer scanpaths and pads shorter ones - and its effect is not tested.

**S-166** [local_e54c304c] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models*

640x640 RGB images with bounding boxes, preprocessed and augmented by Roboflow's export pipeline. Because augmentation is applied at export rather than at training time, augmented variants of an image may be distributed across the train, validation and test partitions - the paper gives no information that would exclude this, and gives no split ratio either.

**S-167** [local_e4c2a776] — *Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images*

Gabor-filtered facial images encoded as a concatenation of three backbone feature vectors. Neither the input resolution, the fused vector dimensionality, nor the wavelet basis is stated.

**S-168** [local_231757c7] — *SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers*

One 463-dimensional feature vector per child, pre-calculated by the dataset creators, z-score normalised, with timestamps omitted. Two aspects deserve note. The dimensionality is high relative to the sample - 463 features for 109 children, of whom roughly 87 are available for training - so the model operates in a regime where a random forest's variable selection is doing most of the work. And the repository's seven geometric augmentations (rotation, mirroring, scaling) were available and deliberately not used, a restraint that several studies in this corpus do not exercise.

**S-169** [local_1b457442] — *Screening autism spectrum*

Fifty-two tabular features per child spanning participant details, utterance statistics, stem words and parts of speech. The inclusion of age among the predictors is the study's principal unaddressed problem: the two groups in the Nadig corpus differ in mean age by roughly two years by the authors' own table, and age is reported as one of the four features that carry the result.

**S-170** [local_b26db2f2] — *Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches*

One row per game session, with fields covering session duration in seconds, game identity and task-performance variables, tabulated with data types and examples. The row is a session, not a child, and the paper does not remark on the distinction anywhere.

---

## RQ4.3 — Evaluation metrics

_170 of 170 studies charted for this question._

**S-001** [local_76fc33d0] — *Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers*

Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC. Headline: 97.7% / 95.6% / 100.0% / 0.97 (PNN, FC3).

**S-002** [local_0dbc5018] — *Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities*

Accuracy, specificity, sensitivity. Headline: 96.7% / 93.8% / 100% at seven features; mean across feature-subset sizes 84.9% / 89.1% / 82.2%. No AUC, F1 or confidence intervals.

**S-003** [local_dc5fc4bb] — *ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data*

Accuracy only - reported as best and mean across the three data types. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confidence intervals, which is a serious gap for imbalanced clinical classes.

**S-004** [local_863980f8] — *Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework*

Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, ROC curves and AUC - a fuller metric set than most corpus studies of this period. Headline: 88.51% accuracy / 93.10% sensitivity / 86.21% specificity / AUC 89.63%. No confidence intervals; a significance marker (p<0.001) is attached to the overall accuracy.

**S-005** [local_be8aa62f] — *Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder*

AUC (the primary metric), classification correct rate, sensitivity, specificity, ROC curves, and - unusually - the variance of performance across folds. Headline: AUC 0.82 for SVM (variance 0.12), 0.71 quadratic, 0.67 linear; sensitivity 0.50-0.52 and specificity 0.68-0.74 at the optimal threshold. Chance comparison by two-tailed t-test with Bonferroni correction.

**S-006** [local_e404a2a3] — *Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism*

AUC as the primary metric, reported with standard deviation across repetitions - a rarity in this corpus - plus sensitivity and specificity quoted at two explicitly stated thresholds (0.50 and 0.55) and full ROC curves. Headline: AUC 0.932 average, 0.926 Creativity, 0.848 Sharing; 83% sensitivity / 85% specificity at threshold 0.50 on Creativity. No accuracy figure is emphasised, though the abstract translates the result as 'up to 93% accuracy', conflating AUC with accuracy.

**S-007** [local_780141fc] — *Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study*

Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, reported per classifier with averages and standard deviations across methods; the true positive and true negative definitions and class sizes (P=14, N=16) are stated explicitly. Headline: 86.7% accuracy, 85.7% sensitivity, 87.5% specificity (linear SVM, nine features). No AUC, F1 or confidence intervals.

**S-008** [local_3a331973] — *Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data*

Classification accuracy only, supported by raw per-class correct/incorrect counts (which is at least transparent enough to recover the confusion matrix). No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confidence intervals - a significant gap given the 18-vs-37 and 11-vs-22 class imbalances, where the reported accuracies of 96.4% and 93.9% cannot be compared against the relevant majority-class baselines of 67% and 67% without recomputation.

**S-009** [local_7b3e6b3a] — *Earlier identification of children with autism*

Unweighted average recall as the primary metric with weighted average recall alongside, both reported with standard deviations across folds; full vocalisation-level confusion matrices for both classifiers; and subject-level accuracy at two explicitly stated thresholds. Using UAR rather than accuracy is the methodologically correct choice for the unbalanced 259-vs-425 vocalisation split, and this is one of the few corpus studies to make it.

**S-010** [local_36aa3ace] — *Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative*

Unweighted average recall only, chosen explicitly because the four-class task is imbalanced - the methodologically correct choice, and reported on both validation and test partitions. Full four-by-four confusion matrices are published for the best system under each feature set, which is unusually transparent and is what makes the near-floor autism-class performance visible. One-sided z-tests compare systems. No accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 or AUC, and no per-child metric.

**S-011** [local_44b58f21] — *ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces*

Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, reported for all four classifier configurations. Headline: 93.3% accuracy, 96.7% sensitivity, 90.0% specificity for the ANN. No AUC, F1, precision, confidence intervals or fold-level variance, despite averaging over ten folds and ten iterations where a standard deviation would have been readily available.

**S-012** [local_cb9a5b48] — *Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening*

Accuracy only, reported for five classifiers across three feature configurations, supplemented by narrative false-positive and false-negative counts (2 and 1 for the final model). No sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, AUC or confidence intervals, though the raw counts allow them to be derived: with 8 per group, 2 FP and 1 FN gives sensitivity 87.5% and specificity 75%.

**S-013** [local_40cd7d53] — *Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children*

Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, with a permutation-derived p-value establishing that accuracy exceeds chance. Headline: 85.1% / 86.5% / 83.8% (p<0.001). No AUC, F1 or confidence intervals. A contradictory second set of figures (82.8% / 79.3% / 86.2%) appears in the Discussion for what is described as the same analysis, and is never reconciled.

**S-014** [local_5b1d0b36] — *Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday*

Unweighted average F1-score as the primary metric, selected explicitly because the classes are unbalanced (18 ASD vs 9 TD) - the methodologically correct choice and one only a minority of corpus studies make. Accuracy (88.9%) and a confusion matrix are also reported, along with per-single-source F1 scores enabling the fusion ablation. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confidence intervals.

**S-015** [local_54954c19] — *Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching*

Classification accuracy, reported with 95% confidence intervals for every single configuration in every table - the only study in the corpus to do this systematically - plus confusion matrices for the two best results showing balanced per-class performance (0.722 control, 0.706 ASD for the best browse model). No sensitivity, specificity, F1 or AUC as such, though the confusion matrices permit their derivation.

**S-016** [local_d8dc996a] — *Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Per-subject averaged accuracy with standard deviation, detection accuracy at a stated threshold, a full confusion matrix with per-class precision and recall (ASD 83.33% precision / 78.95% recall; TD 80.95% precision / 85.00% recall), and a threshold sensitivity curve from 0.5 to 0.95. No AUC or confidence intervals, but the reporting is more complete than accuracy-only studies and the full per-subject accuracy table is published, which allows a reader to see the distribution rather than only its mean.
