**S-102** [local_0e476686] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts*

Accuracy and F1 for each model, together with full confusion matrices giving true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives - and the confusion matrices are the most valuable thing in the results, because they expose behaviour the summary metrics hide. The decision tree's counts (tp 11,229, fn 41, tn 2,540, fp 8,690) show a model that assigned almost every tweet to the autistic class: 99.6% sensitivity against 22.6% specificity, reported as 61.2% accuracy and F1 0.72, both of which make it look like a mediocre classifier rather than a near-degenerate one. BERT's counts give sensitivity 82.1% and specificity 86.5%, reasonably balanced. Publishing the raw counts for all four models is good practice and lets a reader recover what the headline numbers conceal. What is missing: sensitivity, specificity, precision and recall are never named or computed even though the counts are present; there is no AUC; there are no confidence intervals; there is no majority-class baseline, though the balanced tweet-level design makes it 50%; and there is no user-level metric, which is the only level at which the proposed application would operate. F1 is also computed with the autistic class as positive, which given the balanced tweet-level design is defensible but is never stated.

**S-103** [local_fbaf69bf] — *Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Two metric sets for two purposes, both appropriate. For the primary group comparisons: exact p-values with effect size r reported for every test at every scale and every movie, ANCOVA-adjusted significance after controlling for missing-data percentage and landmark variation individually and jointly, Spearman correlations for the redundancy analysis, and within-group Wilcoxon tests for the eyebrow-versus-mouth comparison. Reporting effect sizes systematically alongside p-values, and interpreting them (medium for non-social, large to very large for social), is better statistical practice than anything else in this corpus and is what allows the social/non-social gradient to be read as a graded finding rather than a binary significant/not-significant one. For the secondary classification: accuracy, precision and recall for three feature sets across four movies under leave-one-out cross-validation, ROC curves with AUCs compared by DeLong's method, and logistic-regression odds ratios. Gaps: no confidence intervals on any classification metric; AUC values are shown graphically but not quoted numerically in the retrieved text; no majority-class baseline, which at 9.2% prevalence would be about 91% and therefore above the reported accuracies; and no positive or negative predictive value at the study's own prevalence, which for a primary-care screening tool is the number that would matter most. The precision-recall combination reported (about 70% and about 89%) is also arithmetically incompatible with a 40:396 class ratio, implying an undisclosed balancing step.

**S-104** [local_74416ba7] — *Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders*

Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for four model variants across three classification problems - twelve complete metric triples, reported in a single table with the best in bold. Reporting all three metrics for every ablation condition rather than accuracy alone lets a reader see what the weighting actually does: for children it raises the baseline's sensitivity from 0.333 to 0.667 and the CNN's from 0.286 to 0.600, which is where the accuracy gain comes from, and the paper says so explicitly. The chance-level handling is the most straightforward in the corpus: group sizes were equalised so chance is approximately 50%, and each headline accuracy is tested against it with a binomial test, with all three p-values reported including the one that fails - schizophrenia at p = 0.052, described as marginally significant rather than rounded into significance. Feature importances from the random forest are averaged across cross-validation folds rather than fitted once. Missing: AUC or ROC, confidence intervals, and any precision or predictive-value figure. Given accuracies of 0.645 to 0.710 on samples of 30-31 participants, confidence intervals would be wide and their absence is the main reporting gap - a single participant moves accuracy by about 3 percentage points.

**S-105** [local_7c6a5aa4] — *Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders*

Average classification accuracy, and nothing else. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC, ROC curve, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears anywhere for any model - the thinnest metric reporting of any study charted in this review that reports quantitative results. Two consequences follow directly. Because the labelled set is 81 autistic against 99 non-autistic and bootstrapping was used for training-sample balancing, chance is approximately 50%, so the prior analysis's 47-61% range is at or barely above chance while the present 82% is a large gain - but the paper never computes or states the baseline, so a reader must infer it. And because no class-conditional metric is given, it is impossible to tell whether errors fall on autistic or non-autistic users, which matters especially here given that the comparison group is a heterogeneous aggregate of eight categories that the model may separate very unevenly. The one statistical analysis that is reported properly is the negative one: three simple usage measures compared with t-tests under Holm-Bonferroni correction, all non-significant, presented honestly as motivation for the modelling work rather than buried.

**S-106** [local_8a706eaa] — *Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder*

AUROC, accuracy, precision and recall, each with 95% confidence intervals estimated by the Hanley and McNeil method, reported for all three tasks in both the detection and severity problems - twenty-four interval-bounded estimates, and the most complete uncertainty reporting in this review. That completeness is a direct consequence of adopting the STARD reporting guideline and publishing in a journal that enforces it, and it makes the results checkable in a way that most of this corpus is not. The gaps are nonetheless significant for a diagnostic study. Specificity is never reported, which is an odd omission under STARD and matters because precision and recall alone do not characterise false-positive behaviour at a given prevalence; for the detection models precision is 95.5-98.9% at roughly balanced prevalence, so specificity is evidently high, but it should have been stated. No negative predictive value, no calibration, and no prevalence-adjusted predictive value are given, although the proposed use is referral support in a population where autism prevalence is a few per cent rather than 47%. For the three-class severity problem the class distribution is not reported, so the reader cannot compute a chance baseline, and no baseline is offered. And no permutation test or majority-class comparison accompanies the near-ceiling detection figures.

**S-107** [local_6b9484ce] — *Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking*

Better than the corpus norm for a paper of this scale. Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 are reported per class rather than only in aggregate, confusion matrices are given for the CNN, and ROC curves are plotted for both transfer-learning classifiers. The per-class reporting is what makes the study useful, because it reveals that the custom CNN's 71.9% accuracy conceals autism-class recall of 0.48 - fewer than half the autism images detected, which is below the 59.6% majority-class baseline implied by the confusion matrix. The authors explicitly justify reporting beyond accuracy on the grounds that it 'does not give much importance to the class imbalance in a dataset if at all it exists', which is the right reasoning. Gaps: AUC values are plotted but never quoted numerically; no confidence intervals accompany any figure, although a 57-image test set makes one image worth 1.8 percentage points and therefore makes the 81.0% versus 78.9% comparison uninterpretable; no majority-class baseline is stated; and no participant-level metric is possible given the splitting scheme.

**S-108** [local_c6a4ea7b] — *SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism*

Accuracy, macro precision, macro recall and macro F1, reported for every one of six classifiers and every one of seven feature-set configurations, with a majority classifier as the first row of both tables. Macro averaging suits the near-balanced 35:41 split, and including the majority baseline as a named comparator - with improvements quantified against it - is better practice than most studies charted here, particularly given the authors' explicit rationale that inconsistency in the datasets used across the literature makes cross-study comparison unreliable. The gaps are nonetheless serious at this sample size. No confidence interval is reported anywhere, and since every accuracy is an exact multiple of 1/17 the test set contains 17 items, so one child is 5.9 percentage points and the difference between the headline 94.1% and the next-best 88.2% is a single child. No confusion matrix, no AUC, and no sensitivity or specificity named as such. The majority-classifier figure of 56.4% also does not correspond to the 53.9% implied by the overall class ratio, so it appears to be computed on a particular split, which is not stated.

**S-109** [local_5c43dffa] — *Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths*

Training accuracy, test accuracy and AUC for every configuration across fourteen tables - and the decision to report training accuracy is worth crediting, because it makes visible what most papers in this corpus conceal: the models reach 100% training accuracy in essentially every experiment while testing between 67% and 81%. A reader can therefore see the overfitting directly rather than having to infer it. AUC is also reported throughout, which is better than accuracy alone, and the paper reasons about the gap between accuracy and AUC, correctly attributing the low AUC to class imbalance in the training data. Against this, no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1 or confusion matrix appears anywhere, so nothing is known about the error profile or about which class the models fail on. No confidence intervals are given; the temporal experiments are repeated three times and averaged, which gives some sense of stability, but the diagnosis and stratification headlines rest on single splits. And no chance baseline is stated, although after augmentation the classes are near-balanced.

**S-110** [local_32da8ede] — *A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths*

Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and a mislabelled F1, reported for the proposed model and all four comparators in both greyscale and colour conditions - and this fuller metric set is what exposes the paper's central problem. Reporting sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy is good practice, but here the three quantities cannot describe the same classifier: at 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images, the reported 77.60% sensitivity and 79.91% specificity imply an accuracy of about 79.0%, not the 95.59% claimed, and the multilayer perceptron shows the same pattern (94.69% claimed against about 73.6% implied). The discrepancy is not small and is not reconciled anywhere. Separately, Equation (4) defines F1 as 2 x (Sensitivity x Specificity) / (Sensitivity + Specificity), which is the harmonic mean of sensitivity and specificity - a balanced-accuracy variant - rather than the F1 score, so the column labelled F1 does not mean what its name implies. Also missing: AUC, confusion matrices, confidence intervals, and any majority-class baseline against an implied 60.0% floor.

**S-111** [local_15ed96cb] — *A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning*

Metric reporting is fitted to the epidemiological setting rather than borrowed from the classification literature, and this is one of the study's clearest strengths. Accuracy is not reported at all - correctly, since at 0.15% incidence a null model achieves 99.85%. What is reported instead: AUC with standard deviation across folds (0.86, SD 0.009), sensitivity (0.75, SD 0.03), specificity (0.81, SD 0.02), training AUC alongside test AUC with an explicit statement that the model is slightly overfit, full true positive, false positive, true negative and false negative counts for all four modelling methods, and the risk stratification expressed as enrichment - 0.006 incidence in the high-risk group against 0.001 in the cohort, a 4.3-fold increase. Supplementary material gives performance at multiple thresholds as multiples of the Youden threshold, with the trade-off against false positives described. The one omission is positive predictive value, which is not stated although the confusion counts make it computable: 874 of 144,632 flagged children, or 0.60%, meaning 165 flagged per recorded case. That figure is the single most important number in the review for understanding what a well-validated model at a realistic base rate delivers, and it is left for the reader to compute.

**S-112** [local_261afa51] — *AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: &#x201C;A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System&#x201D;*

Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for three models, plus a confusion matrix; precision and mAP50 for the expression module. Reporting sensitivity and specificity rather than accuracy alone is nominally good practice, and the discussion draws the correct general point that the choice between MobileNet and Xception depends on whether missed cases or false positives matter more. But three reporting problems undercut this. The confusion matrix reports 131 + 136 + 9 + 4 = 280 images, which matches neither the stated 200-image validation set nor the 100-image test set, and no explanation is offered. Sensitivity and specificity are written throughout as '0.97%' and '0.93%', conflating proportions with percentages. And no AUC, F1 or confidence interval is given, so a difference of one percentage point between MobileNet and Xception - on a partition of at most a few hundred images - is presented as a meaningful model ranking.

**S-113** [local_3e88f3ce] — *An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks*

Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC under two evaluation schemes, with ablation tables, ranked SHAP contributions and t-SNE visualisation. The metric set is adequate and the dual evaluation scheme is more than most of this branch reports. Three problems. The figures are internally inconsistent: the abstract and results report 99.40% accuracy with 99.99% ROC-AUC, while the contributions section reports 'up to 96.4% classification accuracy and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.92', and no reconciliation is offered. The split description is likewise inconsistent, given as 70:30 in the methods and as a 20% held-out set of about 247 subjects in the abstract, where 20% of 1,112 is 222. And no confidence intervals accompany any estimate, on a test set of roughly 247 subjects where a 95% interval around 99.4% would still span about a point and a half. A ROC-AUC of 99.99% on a diagnostic task is in any case a figure that should prompt a search for leakage rather than a claim of state-of-the-art performance.

**S-114** [local_5b5f2237] — *Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development*

Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for the best model in each of the two feature conditions, plus ROC curves for all four classifiers and Cohen's d for the derived features. Reporting sensitivity and specificity separately is what makes the study's key numerical detail visible: specificity is 95.24% in both conditions, identical to the decimal, so the entire improvement from 85.37% to 92.68% consists of sensitivity rising from 75.00% to 90.00% - that is, three more of twenty autistic children correctly classified, with no change at all in performance on the comparison group. On a sample of 41 where one participant is 2.4 percentage points, a three-participant difference obtained after selecting features on the outcome is not a stable result, and no confidence interval, permutation test or majority-class baseline is offered against which to judge it. AUC values are not quoted numerically despite ROC curves being plotted. The statistical analysis by contrast is properly equipped, with ANOVA across three groups including the surrogate control, Fisher's LSD post-hoc tests, and effect sizes.

**S-115** [local_13426811] — *Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning*

The best-calibrated metric reporting in the review after the population EHR study. Accuracy is reported with a 95% confidence interval for every one of sixteen conditions - four models by two tasks by two annotation methods - alongside precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC. Reporting confidence intervals is what makes the results interpretable at this sample size: the best interview model's interval of [0.75, 0.89] sits clearly above the 52.6% majority-class floor, while the weakest picture-book configuration at 0.60 [0.51, 0.69] does not. Model comparisons are then tested formally with McNemar rather than being asserted from point differences, and the results are tabulated with test statistics and p-values. Most importantly, non-significant comparisons are interpreted correctly: the authors state that non-significance 'does not definitively indicate the absence of a performance difference between models, particularly in the context of small sample sizes', citing the literature on statistical power. Across this corpus, model rankings resting on differences of one or two participants are routinely presented as findings; this is the only study that tests such comparisons and then declines to over-read them. Absent: confusion matrices, and any relation between predictions and the clinical severity variables collected.

**S-116** [local_948fa8d0] — *Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms*

Precision, recall, F1 and accuracy, reported as whole percentages for five classifiers across four feature conditions. The set is nominally adequate, but three problems undercut it. Precision, recall and F1 are reported as identical values to the percentage point in almost every row, which for a balanced binary problem is arithmetically possible but is presented without the confusion counts that would let a reader verify it. No AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears. And most fundamentally, no evaluation protocol is stated, so it is not determinable what population any of these numbers estimates - they may be held-out, resubstitution, or cross-validated figures, and the paper provides no basis for choosing between those readings.

**S-117** [local_893dfc22] — *Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed*

Accuracy 99.8%, precision 99.8%, recall 100% and specificity 94%, with t-values and p-values against three baselines at p < 0.01. Three problems. The combination is unusual for a balanced multi-class problem - perfect recall alongside 94% specificity - and no confusion matrix, per-class breakdown or definition of multi-class specificity is supplied to make it interpretable. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, and the number of runs behind the reported means is not stated, so the significance tests cannot be assessed. And no chance baseline is given, though six-way classification would place it near 17% under balance.

**S-118** [local_e7c16f2a] — *Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification*

Binary accuracy, reported as a distribution across cross-validation folds rather than as a single point, which conveys stability better than a bare figure; ROC curves for both models; and Pearson correlations with p-values for the acceleration analysis. Reporting the fold-wise distribution is good practice and is rare in this corpus. But the metric set is otherwise thin for a diagnostic claim: no sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1 or confusion matrix is given, so the error profile is unknown and it cannot be determined whether the models fail preferentially on autistic or comparison trajectories; no AUC value is quoted despite ROC curves being plotted; and no confidence interval accompanies either headline accuracy. No majority-class baseline is stated. Since the modelled unit is the trajectory rather than the child, no participant-level metric of any kind is available - which is the figure a clinical claim would require.

**S-119** [local_5a7ab52d] — *Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain*

Ten metrics defined by numbered equation - accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, false positive rate, false negative rate, negative predictive value, false discovery rate, F1-score and Matthews correlation coefficient - reported across two comparison tables to five decimal places. The precision of the reporting is inversely related to its informativeness: five decimal places imply a sample size in the hundreds of thousands, while the sample size is never stated. The metrics are also internally revealing in one respect: precision of 91% alongside sensitivity of 96.3% and specificity of 96.5% implies a positive class comprising roughly a quarter of the sample, information the paper does not supply directly. Three different headline figures appear - 96% accuracy with 93% F1 in the abstract, 96.44% accuracy with 91% precision in the conclusion, and 96.44886% with 91% in Table 3 - and the abstract's F1 value is not reproduced anywhere else. No confusion matrix, confidence interval or AUC appears.

**S-120** [local_8253c2ec] — *Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder*

Six metrics reported for baseline and optimised models across all four datasets - accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC-ROC. Including the Matthews correlation coefficient is good practice for imbalanced tabular data and is rare in this corpus, and class distributions are reported for every band so that majority-class baselines are computable at 69%, 52%, 61% and 73%. None of those baselines is stated or compared against, and no confidence intervals are given. The decisive reporting failure is not in the metric set but in its interpretation: six independent-looking metrics all reaching exactly 100% simultaneously, in four separate datasets, is a signature of a degenerate task rather than a converging body of evidence, and the paper reads it as the latter.

**S-121** [local_1e9d0b71] — *Machine learning’s effectiveness*

Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for each of three variable sets, reported alongside the named variables and cost parameter of each best model; SHAP values displayed for all participants; and correlations between SRS-2 total and predicted probability. Reporting sensitivity and specificity separately is essential at 15.1% prevalence and is done. But three gaps matter. No majority-class baseline is stated, so the reported 1.000 is not placed against the 84.9% floor that a trivial all-negative classifier would achieve - although sensitivity of 1.000 does establish that all 19 positives were caught, which a trivial classifier could not do. No AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears; on 19 positives, an exact binomial interval around a sensitivity of 1.000 would extend below 0.82, which is the figure a reader needs. And no positive predictive value is computed, despite the population-based design making it directly meaningful - at the observed 15.1% prevalence and perfect specificity it would be 1.000, but any realistic degradation in specificity would move it sharply, and that sensitivity analysis is exactly what a screening proposal requires.

**S-122** [local_b9e05a8f] — *Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network*

The broadest metric set in this branch: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Cohen's kappa, specificity, AUC and AUC-PR, with confusion matrices, ROC and precision-recall curves, means and standard deviations across runs, 95% intervals, McNemar's test and paired t-tests. The apparatus is well beyond what most facial-image papers in this review report, and the headline triple is internally coherent - 95.36% accuracy with 92.62% precision and 95.5% F1 implies recall 98.6% and specificity 92.2% at a 1:1 ratio, which reproduces the stated accuracy exactly. Two failures nonetheless undercut the reporting. The intervals are not compatible with the data: every one is the mean plus or minus 0.4 percentage points, accompanied by a standard deviation of 0.03, on test sets as small as 68 images where a single misclassification moves accuracy by 1.47 points; an exact binomial interval around 95% on 68 images spans roughly 87% to 99%. And no positive predictive value is computed for any realistic prevalence, despite a 1:1 class ratio that exists only because the datasets were assembled that way - at a population rate near 1-2%, a specificity of 92% would place the great majority of positive calls on non-autistic children.

**S-123** [local_0b0960c4] — *Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]*

Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 for all four architectures. Reporting specificity is appropriate at a 13:4 class ratio and more than several studies in this review provide. Three gaps: no confidence intervals on figures derived from 17 participants; no confusion matrices or class-wise breakdowns; and no chance or majority-class baseline, although the participant-level ratio places a trivial all-autistic classifier at 76.5%, so the reported 89-94% represents a much smaller increment over the trivial solution than the raw numbers suggest.

**S-124** [local_abad69fd] — *Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play*

The fullest metric reporting in the review's behavioural branch. AUC 0.826 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.776-0.877; sensitivity 85.4%; specificity 68.3%; positive predictive value 72.9%; negative predictive value 82.4%, all at a stated cut-off of 0.399; Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness of fit; a calibration curve relating predicted to observed probabilities; density plots for the retained indicators; and odds ratios with confidence intervals and p-values at both the univariate and multivariate stages for every indicator. Reporting discrimination, calibration, predictive values and per-predictor uncertainty together is what a prediction-model study should do and what almost no other paper in this corpus does. Three qualifications. The predictive values are computed at the 1:1 prevalence the matched design created; at a realistic screening base rate, a specificity of 68.3% would place the great majority of positive calls on non-autistic children, and this recalculation is exactly what the paper's screening proposal requires and does not perform. The reported AUC is apparent rather than optimism-corrected, despite a bootstrap having been run for that purpose. And the operating cut-off of 0.399 was chosen from the same ROC curve on which the sensitivity and specificity are then quoted, so that pair is a best-of-curve selection rather than a prespecified operating point.

**S-125** [local_cd7545e2] — *Predictive model using autism*

Well chosen for the question and honestly reported. Sensitivity and specificity of both published algorithms against clinical diagnosis, with the false-positive rates given as the headline numbers (45.0% original, 52.5% revised) rather than left to be derived. AUC for both algorithms and for the six-item model, with the interpretive bands stated in advance (excellent 0.90-1, good 0.80-0.90, fair 0.70-0.80, poor 0.60-0.70, bad 0.50-0.60) and DeLong's test for the paired comparison. Odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals for every domain and every retained item. Apparent classification accuracy of 86.6%. And both holdout figures - 85.4% training, 65.3% test. Reporting the drop is the single most valuable reporting decision in this record. Two gaps: the abstract and results present the apparent AUC of 0.938 as the model's discriminative ability without the held-out figure attached, so a reader who does not reach the limitations section will take away the wrong number; and no positive predictive value is computed for any realistic case mix, which for a differential-diagnosis aid would depend on the relative frequency of the two conditions among referred patients.

**S-126** [local_3ecb92bf] — *The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech*

Well chosen and honestly deployed. Unweighted average recall is the primary metric, which is the correct choice for imbalanced classes and sets chance at 50% and 25% for the two tasks. Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 are reported for every model and every partition - mixed-gender, female and male - for both tasks, alongside confusion matrices and sensitivity and specificity by gender for the equalised-odds analysis. Most valuably, two comparison tables place the results in context: one against a baseline and two published studies on the same corpus, the other against published Wav2Vec 2.0 implementations. Those tables show that the study's typicality result exceeds the baseline by 0.7 points, and that its diagnosis result of 60.9% falls below the baseline of 62.4% and below prior results of 67.1% and 69.4%. Reporting a table in which one's own method loses on the harder task is rare in this corpus and should be recorded as such. What is missing is any uncertainty estimate - no confidence intervals, no variance across runs, no significance testing - which matters when the typicality margin over baseline is 0.7 points and when the diagnosis test partition contains 26 samples per clinical class.

**S-127** [local_4b02df7c] — *Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism*

Accuracy, AUC and F1 for both classifiers, with 5-fold cross-validation accuracy for algorithm selection: 73% accuracy, AUC 0.728 and F1 0.71 at tweet level; AUC 0.78 and F1 0.805 at profile level. The figures are modest by this corpus's standards and are presented without inflation - the abstract, results and conclusion all carry the same numbers and none is described as high. What is absent is uncertainty and operating-point reporting: no confidence intervals despite a corpus that would support tight ones, no calibration, and no sensitivity or specificity at any threshold. For a paper that raises screening, the absent quantity is the positive predictive value at population prevalence - at roughly 1-2% base rate, a classifier with AUC 0.78 would place the overwhelming majority of its positive calls on non-autistic people. The authors reach a compatible conclusion by a different route, restricting legitimate use to cross-sectional rather than individual inference, but they do not compute the number that demonstrates why.

**S-128** [local_7d7f1fcc] — *Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children*

A complete confusion-matrix-derived set - accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, negative predictive value and F1 - reported for all five models in a single table, which is fuller than almost anything else in this corpus and unusual in presenting every ensemble variant rather than the best one. Reporting negative predictive value alongside precision is a further mark of care. Three gaps and two errors. No confidence intervals appear anywhere, on a test set of 80 children where a single case is worth 1.25 accuracy points and an exact binomial interval around 82.5% runs from roughly 72% to 90% - which means the ensemble's advantage over the video model alone, two children, is not distinguishable from noise. No positive predictive value at realistic prevalence is computed, although the paper is framed around screening and the balanced design makes the reported precision of 0.861 an artefact of the 1:1 construction; at a population base rate the same specificity of 0.875 would place the large majority of positive calls on non-autistic children. And the interpretive bands for what counts as good performance are not stated. The two errors are both in the abstract and neither affects the results section: the abstract describes 'higher specificity (92.5%, i.e., few false negatives) or sensitivity (90%, i.e. few false positives)', reversing the meaning of both terms, and gives the ensemble as 'Precision: 0.775, Recall: 0.861' where the table correctly has precision 0.861 and recall 0.775. Table 1 is internally consistent throughout.

**S-129** [local_5a331ffe] — *Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning*

Accuracy, F1 and recall for classification; mean squared error and concordance correlation coefficient for regression. The regression metric choice is well argued and the argument is worth recording: the authors note that a comparator 'did not report the performances of their approach according to the CCC despite it being the most popular metric for audio and visual affect recognition' and observe that 'it is possible that their approach is very accurate according to MSE but much less accurate according to CCC' - then demonstrate exactly that inversion in their own results, where Inception v3 beats the Perceiver on MSE while losing on CCC. Recognising that two metrics can rank models oppositely, and showing it in one's own data, is a level of measurement care rare in this corpus. The classification reporting is correspondingly weaker: no specificity, no confusion matrix, no confidence intervals, no positive predictive value, and - because the class balance is stated inconsistently - no determinable chance baseline for the reported 74.5%.

**S-130** [local_45ef7022] — *A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features*

A reasonable metric set applied at every stage - PSNR and SSIM for denoising, accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for both classification stages, ROC curves with AUC for severity (RF 0.9878, SVM 0.9865, KNN 0.9268), and computation time - with all formulae defined explicitly. What is missing determines whether any of it can be read. Class sizes across the three severity levels are never given, so neither the chance level nor the majority-class baseline is known and 98.33% has no reference point. There are no confidence intervals, on 1,500 images from 30 children where the effective sample is 30. There are no confusion matrices and no per-class breakdown, so whether the mild and moderate classes are distinguished at all - the clinically important discrimination for dosing - cannot be seen. There is no specificity, and the ROC description conflates specificity with the false positive rate. And the comparison table reporting that the classifiers exceed 'the clinical ABC method' has no stated criterion for either, so the numbers in it cannot be interpreted.

**S-131** [local_0f5a351e] — *Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

Per-class precision, recall and F1 with support counts, overall accuracy, weighted averages, confusion matrices for all three models, training and validation curves, an ROC figure for Inception-V3 and a comparison table against ten prior studies on the same corpus. That is a fuller presentation than several papers in this branch. Three defects undercut it. Every table is headed 'Validation results' and the confusion matrices are described as validation-stage, so no held-out test figure is reported despite a test partition being defined. The support counts of 294 per class - 588 in total - are 20% of the corpus rather than the stated 10% validation share, and are exactly balanced although the corpus is 1,327 against 1,613, so the evaluation partition's composition cannot be reconstructed and it is unclear whether augmentation reached it. And no chance baseline, confidence interval or prevalence-adjusted predictive value appears, so a 98% figure has no reference point - at the corpus ratio a trivial majority classifier scores 54.9%, and at a realistic population prevalence the reported precision would not survive.

**S-132** [local_786b6280] — *Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features*

Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC for all seven models, with ROC curves that plot the individual splits, the mean curve and a one-standard-deviation band. That variability band is worth singling out: on 64 children with 50 repeated splits it conveys the instability of the estimate more honestly than a point figure, and it is a form of uncertainty reporting that almost no other study in this review provides. Precision and recall are also interpreted correctly in clinical terms, with recall of 80-81% read as a low false-negative rate 'important for ensuring that children with ASD are diagnosed correctly' and precision of 84-86% as protecting children without autism from being misdiagnosed. Missing: confidence intervals, confusion matrices, calibration, and any positive predictive value at a realistic prevalence - the last mattering because the reported precision holds only at the near-balanced sample ratio.

**S-133** [local_879ec69b] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning*

Accuracy only, but reported with dispersion - average, maximum, minimum and standard deviation across repeated cross-validation cycles for every architecture on both datasets, plus per-epoch accuracy and loss curves. The dispersion reporting is a real strength and is what makes the architecture comparison interpretable: standard deviations of 0.71 to 1.82 on the Gait dataset against a 2.2-point spread between backbones show immediately that the architectural differences are barely larger than run-to-run noise, and the paper is able to note that ShuffleNet was more stable than MaxViT at the same mean accuracy. What is absent is everything a screening claim requires. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confusion matrix is reported for any proposed model, so the balance between missed cases and false alarms is unknown, and no positive predictive value at any realistic prevalence is computed. Accuracy on a 50:50 corpus tells a clinician very little, and on DREAM - where the class distribution is described as biased but never quantified - it tells them nothing at all.

**S-134** [local_93e5d23d] — *Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]*

A fuller metric set than most of this branch: accuracy 90.28%, AUC 90.83%, sensitivity 88.64%, specificity 88.64%, precision 95.12% and F-score 91.75%, with sensitivity and specificity reported separately and defined explicitly in the table as counts of autistic and typically developing instances. The statistical analysis reports means with standard errors and codes significance at three thresholds. Two problems limit what any of it means. Every classification figure is a validation-set value with no held-out test, taken at the best of 2,000 epochs, so all six metrics inherit the same selection optimism. And the instance-level definition of sensitivity and specificity means these are not per-child operating characteristics: a screening tool's sensitivity is the proportion of autistic children it flags, not the proportion of their individual cries, and with six cries per child the two quantities can differ substantially. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, on an effective sample of 62 children.

**S-135** [local_a0d73248] — *Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm*

Accuracy alone, at 0.9890. No precision, recall, specificity, F1, AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval is reported, and no class distribution is given, so the figure cannot be compared against the 73.2% majority-class baseline that the source dataset implies. For a screening application, sensitivity and specificity are the quantities that matter and neither is provided.

**S-136** [local_4ceee075] — *Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics*

Accuracy, AUC, precision and recall, with paired t-tests across the 5-fold results at p < 0.05 and 95% confidence intervals for accuracy, precision, recall and F1 stated to lie within plus or minus 1.5%. Reporting intervals and fold-level significance testing at all places the study above most of this corpus. Three problems limit the reporting. Specificity is not given, and with recall at 0.95 and accuracy at 85-90% on a balanced sample, specificity must be substantially below recall - roughly 75-85% by arithmetic - so the metric that a screening application most needs is the one omitted, and the model's error profile is asymmetric in a direction the reported figures obscure. No confusion matrix appears. And the stated interval of plus or minus 1.5% is narrower than 100 children in 5-fold cross-validation would normally support, with 20 children per validation fold meaning a single child moves fold accuracy by 5 percentage points; the derivation of the interval is not stated, so whether it describes across-fold variation or something else cannot be determined.

**S-137** [local_84bcd4ed] — *Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of*

Thin, and thinner still for the second target. For autism, accuracy alone is reported at 92%, described as holding 'across both training and testing datasets' - a formulation that conflates the two and gives no separate held-out figure, on a test partition of 279 images where a 95% interval would span roughly plus or minus 3 points before any leakage consideration. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears. For gelotophobia, no quantitative metric of any kind is reported: the results state that the system 'successfully classified gelotophobia in cases where facial expressions were clear' and that DeepFace alone was insufficient otherwise, neither of which has a denominator, a comparison or a ground truth. A paper whose stated objective is 'to develop a deep learning-based diagnostic system ... to detect gelotophobia' reports no number for that detection.

**S-138** [local_d97673f4] — *Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Accuracy of 88.33% with a confusion matrix presented as a figure. No precision, recall, specificity, F1, AUC or confidence interval is reported in the retrieved text, and no chance baseline is stated - although a confusion matrix at least permits per-class errors to be read off, which several studies on this corpus do not provide. Notably, no accuracy figures are broken out for the five extractors or the three preprocessing configurations individually, so the comparisons the study set up are not reported in a form that supports conclusions about them.

**S-139** [local_86a67a4f] — *Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children*

The fullest metric reporting of any Kaggle-corpus study in this review - accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, F1 and AUC for the autism model, six measures plus confusion matrices for emotion - and that completeness is what makes the problem visible. The autism figures are 'accuracy = 95, precision = 0.96, sensitivity/recall = 0.94, Specificity = 42.5, F1 = 0.95 and AUC = 78'. These cannot all be correct. On the stated balanced 280-image test set, a recall of 0.94 recovers about 132 of 140 positives while a specificity of 0.425 recovers about 60 of 140 negatives, giving 192 correct and an accuracy near 68%. The same figures imply about 80 false positives, so precision would be near 0.62 rather than 0.96. And an AUC of 0.78 is not compatible with 95% accuracy on balanced classes. Reporting specificity at all is what exposes this - the seven other Kaggle-corpus studies charted here that report accuracy alone would have concealed an identical failure. If the specificity of 42.5% is the accurate figure, the model correctly identifies fewer than half of non-autistic children, which is worse than chance and is the study's most important result. The emotion metrics, by contrast, are internally consistent and modest.

**S-140** [local_0a39cca9] — *Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy*

Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for each of the five pairings, with training and validation curves. The metric set supports one genuinely useful observation - that a pairing with higher precision but lower recall is 'less useful for finding all ASD cases', which is the correct screening-oriented reading and is articulated in almost no other study in this branch. What is missing is specificity, AUC, confusion matrices and confidence intervals, and no chance baseline is stated despite the exactly balanced construction placing it at 50%. The comparison table cites two prior studies at 0.7500 and 0.8050 rather than the high-nineties figures reported by other Kaggle-corpus work, so the study positions itself against modest comparators.

**S-141** [local_7432ffd7] — *Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models*

Accuracy, precision, recall/sensitivity, F1, per-class values and per-fold confusion matrices; means with standard deviations across the five folds. Missing: specificity as a separate figure, AUC or any threshold-free measure, calibration, positive and negative predictive value at a stated prevalence, and any participant-level metric. Because the analysis unit is the gaze sample, none of the reported numbers is a diagnostic accuracy in the clinical sense - not one figure in the paper describes how often a child would be correctly classified.

**S-142** [local_8ff20c48] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning*

Per-class precision, recall and F1 with support, macro and weighted averages, accuracy, a confusion matrix, micro-average ROC 0.87 and macro-average ROC 0.81, and PR values of 0.892 and 0.728. This is a fuller metric set than most of the corpus offers, and unusually the weaker class is reported honestly (non-autistic recall 0.53). Missing: specificity named as such, calibration, predictive values at a stated prevalence, and any confidence interval. The abstract's 78% does not match the 0.83 in the results and comparison tables - the 0.78 in the table is the weighted-average precision/F1 row, so the headline accuracy has been read off the wrong line.

**S-143** [local_986436f2] — *Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost*

Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, loss, AUC, detection accuracy (reported separately from accuracy and never defined), miss rate, fall-out, millimetre localisation error, and a confusion matrix. The abstract claims excellent specificity but no specificity value appears. The internal arithmetic does not hold: the confusion matrix reports 146 true non-ASD, 141 true ASD, 9 false positives and 4 false negatives, summing to 300 cases although the stated final evaluation set is 200 images and the test split is 506. Those cell counts give accuracy 287/300 = 0.957, precision 141/150 = 0.940 and recall 141/145 = 0.972 - none of which match the reported 0.985, 0.975 and 0.987. Separately, F1 is given as 0.925 while precision and recall are 0.975 and 0.987, whose harmonic mean is 0.981; no combination of the reported figures is mutually consistent.

**S-144** [local_bb4d1f7a] — *Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models*

Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, false discovery rate, false omission rate and AUC are all defined by equation, which reads as thorough; only accuracy, recall and F1 are then reported for the within-study experiments, and specificity, FDR and FOR appear as numbers nowhere. A four-class confusion matrix is shown and discussed sensibly - low and medium separate better than mild and high. The Saliency4ASD table reports accuracy and AUC together (95.93/95.82 and 97.95/97.84). The 25% four-class chance level is never stated, and no metric carries an interval.

**S-145** [local_13c1f46d] — *Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism*

Accuracy, precision, recall, F-score and G-measure, per class and averaged, at 500 through 2,500 epochs; ROC curves described qualitatively; a Gabor ablation with training time and a computational-cost index whose units are not given. No specificity, no numeric AUC, no calibration, no predictive values at a stated prevalence, and no confidence interval anywhere. The reported average of 96.43% is not one measurement but the best of five epoch settings, carried into both the abstract and the comparison table against baselines evaluated under unknown conditions in other papers.

**S-146** [local_e771fb69] — *Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data*

Accuracy, precision, recall and F1, reported per client, per feature subset, per local model and for the global model in both scenarios. No specificity, no AUC, no calibration, no predictive values and no confidence interval anywhere. The metric grid is dense and the reported values are internally revealing: they take only the values 0.11, 0.22, 0.33, 0.44, 0.55, 0.66, 0.77, 0.88 and 1.00, which are the achievable accuracies on nine test cases. The headline of 99.99% is that same 9/9 restated, and the paper describes it as flawless classification performance. One tabulated value, Client 3 on L_Attention at 0.01, is not a multiple of one ninth and is presumably a typographic corruption of 0.11.

**S-147** [local_945300a5] — *Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network*

Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and a confusion matrix, with sensitivity and specificity defined by formula but specificity never reported numerically. The reported figures reconcile exactly with the confusion-matrix cells - 92 of 102 correct gives 0.902; 47 of 51 predicted-positive gives 0.922; 47 of 53 actual-positive gives 0.887 - which is a level of internal consistency several other studies in this corpus fail to achieve. What is absent is any interval: with 102 test images the 95% confidence interval around 0.90 runs from roughly 0.83 to 0.95, so the comparison against the quoted literature figures of 87%, 88%, 89.2%, 90% and 92% is not discriminating. The abstract also describes the evaluation as using a nuisance matrix.

**S-148** [local_ed30e24c] — *Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI*

Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and log loss for all twelve configurations, plus a confusion matrix and SHAP plots for the best model. The log loss column deserves credit: it is the only calibration-sensitive measure reported by any study charted in this review, and it does real work here - Decision Tree posts 0.938 accuracy with a log loss of 2.223, exposing badly miscalibrated probabilities that accuracy alone would hide. Against that, no confidence interval accompanies any figure, and neither baseline is stated (50.7% on the balanced test set, 69.7% majority-class on the original data). The F1 score is also described as the geometric mean of precision and recall, when it is the harmonic mean.

**S-149** [local_b9de0d7f] — *Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques*

Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 across four feature conditions, seven classifiers and an ensemble; per-fold cross-validation values; Phase II results; and a state-of-the-art comparison. No AUC, no specificity, no calibration, no confidence interval, and no chance level for either the binary Phase I task or the seven-class Phase II task. Two internal inconsistencies matter. The 10-fold table prints an average accuracy of 0.986 while the ten listed fold accuracies average 0.9876, and it contains a fold reporting recall 0.999 against accuracy 0.988 and another reporting accuracy 0.999 - values out of line with their neighbours. More seriously, the comparison table credits the proposed approach with 99.99% accuracy, positioning it above four quoted literature figures (98.77%, 97.82%, 99.25%, 99.85%), when the study's own best tabulated result is 0.99 and its cross-validated average is 0.986. The headline claim of surpassing the state of the art rests on a number the paper never produced.

**S-150** [local_14df790d] — *Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach*

Accuracy, precision, F1, sensitivity, specificity, MCC and a confusion matrix for every model, plus per-subset comparisons and an iterative feature-addition curve. The metric set is the most complete in this branch: MCC is included deliberately because of the class imbalance, and its motivation - that incorrect diagnoses have significant implications for families - is stated. It also does real work, separating LR (accuracy 0.97, MCC 0.92) from ANN (0.98, 0.98). Two problems. No confidence interval accompanies any figure. And the confusion matrices are mutually inconsistent: LR, KNN and LR-KNN each have class totals of 105 and 212, while the ANN's are 110 and 207, so the four models were not all evaluated on the same 317-record partition.

**S-151** [local_4da2b941] — *Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study*

Pearson R between true and predicted scores, MAE, MAPE relative to the score range, and RMSE, per outcome and averaged across the four trials, with predicted-versus-true scatter plots against a perfect-agreement diagonal. Correlation magnitudes are interpreted against a pre-specified external criterion (Colton 1974), so strong and moderate are defined before the results rather than after. The tolerance analysis is the most practically informative reporting in the corpus: the best Aloofness model places 36.3% of predictions within 5% of the true score and just over 60% within 10%, which states plainly what the R=.85 does and does not deliver at the individual level. The paper also notes correctly that the lower MAE for Depression and Anxiety reflects their narrower score ranges rather than better prediction, and reads the MAPE accordingly. Two gaps: no confidence intervals or across-trial variance accompany the metrics, and no trivial baseline (for instance, predicting the sample mean) is reported against which the MAE and RMSE could be judged. A minor inconsistency: the abstract gives Rigidity R=.74 and Depression R=.60, while Table 3 gives .75 and .58 for the CAT-Q-ES-only configuration.

**S-152** [local_6e7174c0] — *A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach*

Accuracy, AUC, F-measure, G-mean, sensitivity, specificity, fall-out and miss rate, with formulae given, reported for both validation and test, plus a confusion-matrix figure. This is a fuller and better-chosen metric set than most of the facial-image branch offers - specificity and fall-out are reported as numbers rather than merely claimed, and the figures are internally consistent (sensitivity 94% with miss rate 0.06; specificity 88% with fall-out 0.12; their mean 91% matching the reported accuracy on a balanced test set). Two problems. No confidence interval accompanies any figure, and on 200 test images the 95% interval around 91% runs from roughly 86% to 95% - a range that contains almost every entry in the comparison tables, so the claimed ordering among methods is not established. And validation accuracy (86.5%) is lower than test accuracy (91%) by 4.5 points on 200 images each, which is reported without comment.

**S-153** [local_e04bcd32] — *Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network*

Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, a confusion matrix and an ROC curve for classification; percentage blur removed, PSNR, MSE and SSIM for deblurring. Specificity is not reported, no AUC value is given numerically, no calibration or predictive values appear, and no confidence interval accompanies any figure. The reported accuracy of 96.94% reconciles exactly with the confusion-matrix counts - 2,850 correct out of 2,940 - which is the problem rather than a reassurance, because 2,940 is the entire dataset and not the 400-image test set the methods section defines.

**S-154** [local_183eaef4] — *Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI*

Accuracy, F1, precision, recall and area under the precision-recall curve, per model and per fold, at four fold counts, with per-fold tables in an appendix. The choice of prAUC is thoughtful and explicitly justified by the expected class imbalance. Two absences matter. Specificity is never reported for any model, so the false-positive behaviour of a system proposed for paediatric screening is invisible; and the class balance is never given, so neither the prAUC baseline nor the majority-class accuracy can be computed. The reported neural-network figures are accuracy 1.0000, F1 1.0000, precision 1.0000 and recall 1.0000 - a model that misclassifies no child in any of ten folds - with prAUC 0.9601, a combination that is itself internally odd, since a classifier with perfect precision and recall should have a precision-recall curve area of 1.

**S-155** [local_b6ac2b98] — *Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks*

F1-score only, with precision and recall given by equation. The interpretive bands are stated in advance (0.0-0.5 poor, 0.5-0.7 moderate, 0.8-0.9 good, 0.9-1.0 excellent) and the results are then reported against them, so the descriptions excellent, good and moderate are pre-committed rather than chosen after the fact - a small but genuine discipline. Missing: accuracy, sensitivity and specificity separately, AUC, calibration, confidence intervals, across-fold variance, and any statement of the majority-class baseline. The last matters most for the ASD-versus-DLD comparison, where the classes are nearly balanced (24 versus 25) and F1 0.63 sits only modestly above chance, and for ASD-versus-TD, where the baseline is around 0.65 and the reported 0.86 represents a real but smaller gain than the number suggests in isolation.

**S-156** [local_44d3aef5] — *Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis*

Per-class precision, recall, F1 and support, overall accuracy, macro averages, ROC curves and training/validation curves. Specificity is defined by equation and never tabulated. No confidence interval accompanies any figure, and none is possible to infer without the split proportions, which are not stated. The support column is the only place the test-set size appears: 33 non-ASD and 22 ASD, 55 images in total. On 55 images the 95% interval around VGG19's 92% runs from roughly 82% to 98% and around DenseNet169's 78% from roughly 65% to 88%, so the reported ordering of the four architectures - and the ranking against the three prior studies at 87%, 90% and 79% - is not statistically distinguishable.

**S-157** [local_24fefc5f] — *A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection*

Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1, plotted against iteration count and training percentage. Two of the four definitions given in the text are wrong: accuracy is described as dividing the total number of instances by the number of correctly classified instances, which is the reciprocal of accuracy and would exceed 1; and specificity is described in words as dividing the total number of false positives and true negatives by the sum of both, which is identically 1. The accompanying equations for sensitivity and specificity are correct, so these are errors of exposition rather than of computation, but they appear in a section whose stated purpose is to define the evaluation measures. No confidence interval, no chance level and no class balance accompany any figure.

**S-158** [local_69b10fe4] — *An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms*

Test accuracy per algorithm and averaged across the three, with the full grid published as a heat map colour-coded against chance and ordered by mean accuracy - so the reader sees every configuration, including the two that performed at chance, rather than only the maximum. For the group-difference analyses the reporting is fuller still: F statistics, p-values, beta estimates with 95% confidence intervals, and Bayes factors quantifying evidence for the null with interpretive bands stated in advance. What is absent is any interval on the classification accuracies, which matters because the test partitions hold roughly 13 to 19 participants; the 95% interval around the 0.93 headline spans approximately 0.66 to 1.00, and around 0.73 approximately 0.49 to 0.90.

**S-159** [local_af9f4c12] — *An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data*

Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUROC per cohort and per ablation variant; per-class AUROC curves across the four severity levels and four age groups; Cohen's kappa with a confidence interval for label-expert agreement; and quantified stability under three separate perturbation analyses. The metric set is broad and the sensitivity reporting is a genuine strength. Two gaps. No confidence interval or across-fold variance accompanies any classification accuracy, despite ten folds having been run and despite intervals being reported for the kappa. And no class counts are given for either the binary or the four-level target, so no baseline exists against which a 99.10% can be positioned - which matters particularly for a four-class ordinal problem whose stratum boundaries the authors chose.

**S-160** [local_367db0b6] — *An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns*

The named metric set is clinically appropriate and unusually complete for this corpus - sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, ROC AUC and calibration, with thresholds set by the Youden index and significance assessed by paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. None of it is reported. No sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, AUC or calibration value appears in the extracted text, no test statistic or p-value is given, and the phrase all reported with 95 to 98% confidence intervals conflates a confidence level with an interval width. What is actually presented is bar charts of error rate, false-positive count and precision binned into low, medium and high before and after unlearning, plus a headline accuracy of 98% and a 23% error reduction with no denominator. If the stated class ratio of 25,000 positives to 1,200 negatives held, the majority-class baseline would be 95.4% and the headline would be 2.6 points above it.

**S-161** [local_8d43288c] — *Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos*

Validation accuracy and loss, precision, recall and F1 per architecture; per-fold means with standard deviations for every model and metric; per-class F1; two confusion matrices; learning curves; and paired t-tests with a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.0125. The statistical reporting is among the better examples in this corpus - the standard deviations are given rather than implied, and the multiple-comparison correction is stated explicitly. What is missing bears directly on interpretation: per-class sample counts are not reported, so the 25% chance level for a four-class problem cannot be checked against the actual class balance; the value of k is never given; and the very small per-fold standard deviations (under 0.004 across five architectures) are read as evidence that the model is robust and consistent across the folds when, over clips drawn from only 75 videos, near-identical fold results are equally consistent with folds that are near-identical resamples of the same recordings.

**S-162** [local_5f57ba19] — *Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension*

Macro F1 and AUC, chosen explicitly because the data are small and imbalanced, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every estimate; per-condition, per-phase and per-story breakdowns with standard deviations; paired t-tests between modalities within each phase with full statistics; and - critically - a per-fold majority-class baseline built into the design as a lower bound to test whether the gaze features add anything beyond class distribution. That last element is present in only one other charted study. The reported numbers are correspondingly modest and are described as such: about 55% F1 in the speech phase, 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC at best, with the paper noting where differences fail to reach significance and attributing that to the limited number of observations.

**S-163** [local_1d856900] — *Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare*

Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC for eight configurations on Dataset 1, plus accuracy and F1 for six ablation configurations on both datasets. Three problems. Precision, recall and F1 are omitted for both neural-network rows, so the two models carrying the headline figures are reported on accuracy and AUC alone. No confidence interval or cross-validation variance accompanies any value. And the reported logistic-regression row - recall 100.00%, precision 87.20%, ROC-AUC 1.000 - is the signature of a model that separates the classes perfectly on the test partition, which on a dataset containing four autism instruments as features is expected rather than notable, and which the paper reads as displaying more false-positive tendencies. The 63.28% majority-class baseline is computable from the paper's own table and is never stated.

**S-164** [local_7b19a959] — *Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis*

Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1 for both samples and each configuration, plus a label-randomised control model. The specificity/sensitivity split is reported rather than collapsed into accuracy (matched sample: sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 79.2%), which shows that the model misses roughly a third of autistic adults at the reported operating point - visible precisely because the paper reports it. Missing: confidence intervals, cross-validation variance on the final estimates, and calibration. The chance level is established empirically by the randomisation control rather than asserted.

**S-165** [local_d7b6fa00] — *Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath*

Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 with fold-wise means and standard deviations for all six models, plus a Friedman test on fold-wise F1 and a permutation-importance ranking. Reporting the standard deviations is a real strength and is also where the study's honest signal lies: an accuracy standard deviation of 0.0800 and an F1 standard deviation of 0.0952 on a five-fold split of 28 people means individual folds ranged widely, which is what five- or six-person test sets produce. On such folds, 0.9600 accuracy corresponds to roughly 27 of 28 participants classified correctly across the full cross-validation, and a single reclassification moves the figure by about 3.6 points. No confidence interval accompanies any estimate and the 50% chance level is never stated.

**S-166** [local_e54c304c] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models*

Precision, recall, F1, mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 for both models, with normalised confusion matrices, precision-recall curves and F1-confidence curves. The reporting looks complete and contains an impossibility. For YOLOv8n, mAP@0.5 is 94.76% and mAP@0.5:0.95 is 94.73%; for YOLOv9c, 93.32% and 93.21%. mAP@0.5:0.95 averages average precision across ten IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95, so it is bounded above by mAP@0.5 and in practice falls well below it - gaps of twenty to forty points are typical for face-scale objects. A gap of 0.03 points implies that localisation quality is perfect at every threshold up to 0.95, which no detector trained for 50 epochs on uncalibrated web photographs achieves. The two numbers are therefore not both genuine mAP values. No class counts, no split sizes, no chance level and no variance across the repeated runs the paper claims to have performed are reported.

**S-167** [local_e4c2a776] — *Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images*

Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure and AUC, per class and averaged, for both phases, with confusion matrices, precision-recall and ROC curves. The reporting is dense and contains one telling relationship: the 30% testing-phase average accuracy (98.42%) is higher than the 70% training-phase average accuracy (97.75%), and the per-class figures move in the same direction. A model that performs better on held-out data than on the data it was fitted to is normally a signal that the partition is not independent - shared or near-duplicate images across the split being the usual cause on this corpus - or that the reported training figure is not a resubstitution score. The paper reads the same inversion in its learning curves as good generalisation without overfitting. No confidence interval, no chance level and no variance across runs accompanies any value.

**S-168** [local_231757c7] — *SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers*

Accuracy with a fold-wise standard deviation (84.6 +/- 10.9%), held-out accuracy (86.4%), per-class results and, for the severe class, an exact binomial confidence interval (39.8%-100.0%) on a 4-of-4 result. Computing and reporting that interval is the single most useful reporting decision in this part of the corpus: it converts an apparently perfect result into a statement that the true accuracy could be anywhere above 40%, and the author draws exactly that inference. The fold standard deviation of 10.9 points is likewise reported rather than smoothed. What is missing: the three-class majority baseline (approximately 45.9%) is never stated, and no per-class sensitivity or specificity is given for the two real classes.

**S-169** [local_1b457442] — *Screening autism spectrum*

Six metrics per model per configuration - accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and p-values - with the rationale for each stated. The reporting is complete and the paper draws the right comparison from it: ROC-AUC 0.93 for ASD versus TD in Nadig, 0.87 in Eigsti, roughly 0.96 merged, and 0.71 for the three-class task including developmental delay. Missing: confidence intervals, fold variance, and the majority-class baselines - which matter particularly for Nadig, where 26 TD against 12 ASD gives a 68.4% baseline against a reported accuracy above 86%.

**S-170** [local_b26db2f2] — *Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches*

Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for all seven models, plus learning curves plotting training and cross-validation accuracy against training-set size. The learning curves are read carefully - training accuracy above validation accuracy is correctly described as expected, and the absence of an abrupt decline is noted - but the reading stops short of asking why validation accuracy is so high at all. No confidence interval, no fold variance and no chance level appears; and the 96% is not related to the effective sample of 12 children.

---

## RQ4.4 — Interpretability

_170 of 170 studies charted for this question._

**S-001** [local_76fc33d0] — *Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers*

Feature importance from the classifiers' inherent selection (DTREG). Most informative: vocal-quality measures H1*-A3* (selected by both classifiers) and H4, H1 variability, F0 range, shimmer, energy, jitter, A2.

**S-002** [local_0dbc5018] — *Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities*

Fisher discriminant ratio scores rank the features, and the full 17-feature ordering across the 30 LOO rounds is reported. Most informative: total duration, delta wrist angle and number of movement units of the transport sub-movement - interpreted as slower, more fragmented goal-directed movement with atypical hand inclination.

**S-003** [local_dc5fc4bb] — *ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data*

ReliefF weighting (k=10, Manhattan distance) selects informative images, and symmetric uncertainty quantifies feature-class correlation per grouping (highest for ADHD-vs-ASD: 0.336 on correctness, 0.449 on latency). The number of selected images is reported but not which images or emotions they were, so no interpretable behavioral feature emerges.

**S-004** [local_863980f8] — *Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework*

Interpretability by mean-histogram differencing: FeatDif = FeatASD - FeatTD, with the largest-magnitude bins visualised on the face and re-tested as a reduced feature set (top seven bins retain 79.31% accuracy). The informative regions are periocular and perioral, which the authors link to the eye-avoidance hypothesis. Direction of preference is reported but stated inconsistently across sections.

**S-005** [local_be8aa62f] — *Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder*

The 20 words contributing most to the LSI dimensions are visualised as two semantic networks (ASD vs typical), showing different hubs and markedly fewer connections in the ASD network. The interpretable finding is structural rather than lexical: mean local clustering coefficient 0.10 (SD 0.11) for ASD vs 0.32 (SD 0.15) for typical, p<0.001, robust to adjustment for gender, age, verbal IQ and vocabulary. Critically, no individual word frequency and no vocabulary-size difference reached significance, so the discriminative information lies entirely in word co-occurrence structure.

**S-006** [local_e404a2a3] — *Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism*

Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between group distributions, with the ten highest-distance features per game reported, described and boxplotted. Most informative: inertial force features dominate (all ten in the Sharing game), joined by touch-based gesture velocity, area, height and minimum duration in the Creativity game. The interpretation is substantive rather than decorative - greater impact force, altered angular force distribution, faster and larger, more distally placed gestures and faster taps - and is tied to a mechanistic account of disrupted prospective/feed-forward motor control.

**S-007** [local_780141fc] — *Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study*

Interpretability is the paper's core contribution rather than an afterthought. Four selection methods are compared (SVM weights, leave-one-parameter-out, PCA first-component loadings, and their combination) and benchmarked against nine standard Weka attribute evaluators, with agreement between methods reported (features 16, 29 and 37 recur across several). The nine selected features are all standard deviations from the two goal-less conditions, and their directions are interpreted substantively: higher variability in No-Target Fast, lower variability in No-Target Elevated, read as the autistic group failing to build a new sensorimotor plan for an unusual trajectory and instead retaining their habitual movement style - an interpretation supported by citation to the authors' own follow-up work.

**S-008** [local_3a331973] — *Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data*

Greedy forward feature selection identifies the discriminative features, with the top three per task visualised and the top 30 ranked by individual classification power. Informative features: head-motion speed (stories 1-2) and lip-corner depressor (story 10) for controls vs condition; inner-brow raiser (story 1), lip-corner puller (story 3) and head yaw (story 8) for comorbid vs ASD-only. Notably the features are segment-specific, implying that particular Strange Stories items carry the signal - an interpretable finding the paper does not pursue. The direction of each group difference is never stated.

**S-009** [local_7b3e6b3a] — *Earlier identification of children with autism*

Univariate Mann-Whitney U tests with effect size r, with the top ten features tabulated and the strongest visualised as per-group probability density estimates. Most informative features are voice-quality and spectral-balance measures over unvoiced segments - spectral slope 0-500 Hz and 500-1500 Hz, Hammarberg index, alpha ratio - together with MFCC variability, unvoiced segment length, f0 mean and range, and voiced segments per second.
