No model-internal importance (no SVM weights or BLSTM attribution) is reported, and the acoustic-phonetic interpretation of the differences is left undeveloped.

**S-010** [local_36aa3ace] — *Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative*

None. No feature importance, saliency, attention or attribution analysis is performed, and no acoustic property is identified as characteristic of any group. The only interpretability-adjacent result is which discriminator hidden layer produces the most useful representation, which speaks to network depth rather than to behaviour. This is one of the least interpretable studies in the corpus, and unusually the paper makes no interpretive claim it cannot support.

**S-011** [local_44b58f21] — *ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces*

Stepwise discriminant analysis with Wilks' lambda provides the interpretability, and the paper publishes the complete p-value distribution for all 20 candidate features - unusually transparent, since it lets a reader see exactly how sharp the separation between selected and discarded features is (three at p<=0.005, next best Fy1 at 0.084). The three retained features are interpreted anatomically as spanning loading response, mid-stance and terminal stance, and the altered second vertical peak is related to gait instability and body-weight support difficulties by analogy with cerebral palsy. The direction of each group difference is not reported.

**S-012** [local_cb9a5b48] — *Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening*

Interpretability comes from statistical comparison rather than model attribution. The Weighted Presence Vector similarity is shown to separate groups (p=0.001) while the binary Presence Vector does not (p=0.160), which is an informative negative result: the discriminative signal lies in how long a child stays near the robot, not in which regions they ever visit. The presence ratio in the robot-facing cell is directly interpretable as attraction to the robot. Importantly, the authors ran a permutation-style control - randomly regrouping the children and repeating the analysis, which produced no significant differences - a check almost no other study in this corpus performs.

**S-013** [local_40cd7d53] — *Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children*

Interpretability is handled better than in most of the corpus. SVM discriminative weights per AOI are tested by 1000-iteration permutation against the null that weights are arbitrary, so feature importance carries a p-value rather than a rank. Only mouth (p=0.008) and body (p=0.03) survive. The most informative result is a negative one: although fixation was globally reduced in ASD across seven AOIs, none of the eyes-to-face, mouth-to-face or nose-to-face ratios differed, so the group difference is in total looking rather than in the within-face distribution of attention - a finding that complicates the common eye-avoidance interpretation and which the authors report rather than suppress.

**S-014** [local_5b1d0b36] — *Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday*

Interpretability is handled through three complementary analyses. CFS selection reports exactly which features were chosen from which source. Per-source correlation coefficients with the diagnostic label are tabulated with the top five features per source. Single-source ablation quantifies each source's standalone contribution. The findings are substantive: acoustic features dominate, specifically high-order Mel cepstrum envelope and harmonic model phase distortion mean coefficients plus quasi-open quotient - all voice-quality measures; only one linguistic feature (LIWC_Interrog) survives CFS, and linguistic features appear in the top-five correlations of only the picture description test, leading the authors to conclude that linguistic features are discriminative mainly when speech content is not fixed. Directions of effect are not reported, only correlation magnitudes.

**S-015** [local_54954c19] — *Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching*

No per-feature importance ranking or saliency analysis. Interpretability instead comes from systematic ablation across design variables, which yields several substantive findings: gaze features alone outperform gaze plus contextual features; page-specific AOIs are necessary for search but not for browse, because search requires locating specific elements while browse treats all screen regions as equal; the Apple and AVG pages showed the largest between-group differences during browsing; and gender and visual complexity do not matter. The authors also connect back to prior analyses of the same data identifying longer scan paths, more transitions, shorter fixations and more fixations on irrelevant elements as the underlying behavioural differences.

**S-016** [local_d8dc996a] — *Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

A learned soft spatial attention map, generated per frame by the LSTM from its hidden spatio-temporal state and visualised superimposed on the video, is the interpretability mechanism - and it is designed into the model rather than applied post hoc. The maps concentrate on the hand and arm during reaching, which the authors read as the network attending to gesture kinematics, and they propose the maps as feedback clinicians could use in interpreting a diagnosis. The interpretation stops at localisation: no kinematic property (velocity, jerk, trajectory shape) is extracted or named, so the explanation identifies where the model looks but not what it sees there.

**S-017** [local_88ddfdd1] — *A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task*

No feature-level interpretation is offered, and this is a deliberate choice: the paper establishes that temporal ordering carries group-discriminative information without claiming to characterise what the ordering difference is. The illustrative hypothesis it uses to motivate the design - that TD subjects might look at the eyes before the mouth while ASD subjects do the reverse - is offered as a possibility to be tested, not a finding. The permuted-character control is the interpretive mechanism: because it destroys order while preserving AOI frequencies, any accuracy gain over it must come from sequence.

**S-018** [local_361110f1] — *Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features*

Two-stage and reasonably transparent: independent t-tests identify nine discriminative features from 18, and forward feature selection then builds up the model incrementally, with the accuracy-versus-feature-count curve published for all five classifiers. The substantive interpretation is developed - three of four selected features derive from the velocity distribution, connected to prior work showing velocity distributions characterise subtle individual motor differences, and greater maximal amplitude range in ASD is linked to reported macrographia and fine motor control deficits. However the direction of the velocity entropy and range differences is never stated, so the central claim that autistic children are more restricted is not directly evidenced for the features that matter most.

**S-019** [local_51533de4] — *Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations*

Well developed. Selection frequency across the 70 folds is reported per feature, distinguishing features chosen in all folds from those chosen occasionally, which is a more informative importance measure than a single ranking. Post-hoc linear regressions give directions and significance for key features. The substantive findings are specific: autistic children showed higher median HNR-delta, lower voicing-probability variability and reduced pitch dynamism (lower IQR of F0-delta); and confederates showed higher HNR-delta and lower jitter when talking to autistic children. The paper also collects qualitative human-rater justifications - flat intonation, long response latency, brief responses, frequent 'I don't know', topic changes, few follow-up questions - and uses them to diagnose what the automatic feature set is missing.

**S-020** [local_96c87d36] — *Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking*

Well developed and multi-layered. Random-forest importance values are averaged across all cross-validation runs and normalised, showing that coarse temporal measures (relative response time, fixation time, fixation frequency, response time) dominate while fine-grained spatial fixation statistics matter less. Face-feature channels are visualised by averaging network activations across frames and overlaying them on an average face, revealing that the informative channels correspond to distinct anatomical regions (forehead, eyes, cheeks, nose, ears). Separately, pixel-wise fixation density maps with t-tests localise where the groups differ - controls more on eyes and mouth, ASD subjects more on forehead, hair, ears and chin. This combination of model-derived importance, activation visualisation and independent statistical mapping is the most thorough interpretability treatment charted so far.

**S-021** [local_4b031d44] — *Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine*

Among the most thorough in the corpus. Shapley values are computed for all 159 videos in the second layer using the shap package, exploiting local accuracy so each video's predicted probability decomposes exactly into per-feature contributions with both magnitude and direction, and the same rater weights are applied to derive ensemble-level Shapley values. This permits interpretation at the level of an individual child's individual annotation. Separately, features selected most often during elastic-net tuning are compared across the US and Bangladeshi models, yielding the substantive cross-cultural finding that eye contact dominates for Bangladeshi videos while social participation and stereotyped speech dominate for US videos - with a plausible mechanism offered, namely that raters could evaluate language-based behaviours only when they shared the language.

**S-022** [local_05ef29e5] — *Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification*

None. No feature importance, saliency analysis or ablation is performed, and no behavioural feature is identified as informative - a notable gap given that random forests supply out-of-bag importance measures for free and the feature set is explicitly organised into three interpretable families. The paper's interpretive content is instead a literature-grounded argument about why the features should work and why age moderates them.

**S-023** [local_9528024b] — *Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol*

The model is inherently interpretable in structure - beliefs over named clinical states, observations tied to specific social cues, and reward rules stated in plain language (penalise name-call if the child is already engaged; penalise joint attention if the child is not engaged; reward play request if disengaged; reward imitation if engaged). But no analysis identifies which cues or tasks were most informative, and the observation probabilities encode clinician priors rather than empirical relationships, so nothing about autistic behaviour is learned from the data.

**S-024** [local_6230fe22] — *Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism*

None. No feature importance, ROI ranking or ablation is reported. The results assert that 'using ROIs as features for analysis prove clearly the levels of discrimination between ASD and non-ASD patients' but identify no specific region, direction or effect, so nothing interpretable about autistic visual attention emerges from the study itself.

**S-025** [local_785ba418] — *Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis*

No per-feature importance ranking from the final models. Interpretability comes from the group-level behavioural analysis, which reports the five most discriminative measures with means, t-statistics, p-values and Cohen's d, and from averaged velocity and vertical-amplitude profiles plotted across movement progression for both groups. The substantive finding is a speed-accuracy trade-off: autistic participants were slower but roughly twice as spatially precise (30.87 vs 64.01 mm2 scatter area), which is a difference in movement strategy rather than an impairment - a framing that contrasts with most motor studies in this corpus.

**S-026** [local_fea042be] — *Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual*

None quantitatively. Two example visualisations are compared qualitatively, with the observation that both show high-density central regions and that the ASD exemplar tended to look toward the bottom of the screen. The confusion matrix for the multi-label model does carry an interpretable finding - that non-ASD is discriminated well while ASD categories, especially severe ASD, are at least 20% worse - which suggests the representation captures the presence of atypicality better than its gradation.

**S-027** [local_ba5fbda7] — *Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD*

None from the model - no feature importance, SVM weight inspection or ablation is reported, which is a real gap given 4016 features reduced by PCA to an uninterpretable subspace. The only interpretive output is the per-participant decision-score plot, which shows the distribution of confidence and highlights that only one autistic participant fell on the wrong side of the boundary. Substantive behavioural interpretation is deferred to the companion manuscript.

**S-028** [local_7b468950] — *Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart*

Not addressed for the algorithm, which is applied as a commercial black box. The construct-level interpretability is nonetheless strong: the target is motor pattern rather than an aggregate behavioural impression, grounded in a specific and falsifiable hypothesis about movement disruption, so a positive result would be interpretable at the level of the construct even if not at the level of the model.

**S-029** [local_309e5baa] — *Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns*

None. No feature importance, saliency analysis or ablation beyond the small-versus-full model comparison, and no behavioral property is identified as characteristic of autistic gaze. The finding that the 7-feature model outperforms the 47-feature model on validation and nearly matches the 11.3-million-parameter CNN on the blind test is interpretable evidence that the aggregate statistics and deviation-from-typical distances carry most of the usable signal, but this is not developed.

**S-030** [local_a45f39e9] — *Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time*

No feature importance or saliency analysis, and no behavioural characteristic is identified as distinguishing atypical from typical episodes - so the study produces a classifier without a finding about autistic movement. Two ablations are reported and are informative in different ways: the pose-versus-RGB comparison supports the architectural claim that appearance-agnostic pose carries more signal than raw frames, while the imputation ablation inadvertently undercuts its own narrative by showing three conditions performing identically on three of four metrics.

**S-031** [local_d587f9cd] — *Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning*

High at the construct level, not applicable at the model level. Every measured quantity is a named nonverbal behaviour with a clinical referent, and the analytic unit is a joint-attention event of a specified subtype, so results are stated in the vocabulary a clinician uses. No classifier exists whose behaviour would require explanation; the neural components are perceptual instruments whose outputs - a face location, a gaze direction, an attention target - are directly checkable against the video.

**S-032** [local_08b8027d] — *SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths*

No feature-level interpretability - no saliency analysis, attention visualisation or ablation of the model itself. But the per-image accuracy analysis functions as a stimulus-level interpretability result and is a genuine contribution: accuracy varied from below 0.5 to above 0.8 across validation images, and inspection of the best and worst five showed that 'when there is a person, especially when the person is looking at the camera when the image was taken, the model performs better', while natural scenes without faces performed worse. This implies that reported aggregate accuracies on this benchmark are heavily dependent on stimulus composition.

**S-033** [local_c6f1209b] — *Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children*

Complete, because nothing is opaque: every value is a human rater's mark against a questionnaire item describing an observable behaviour. The interpretation offered is a psychological claim - a dissociation between automatic and intentional turn-taking - anchored to prior literature on automatic turn-taking deficits, rather than a statement about what a model responded to.

**S-034** [local_83b99e73] — *Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers*

Interpretability is inherent rather than post hoc: the features are named clinical behaviours, so the model operates on quantities a clinician already reasons about. Interpretation is supported by two separate analyses rather than by a model-explanation method - t-tests establishing which behaviours differ and in which episode, and Pearson correlations linking still-face behaviours to CSBS-DP symptom severity. The substantive interpretation is that the still-face episode's social challenge exposes communication impairment more sharply than ordinary interaction, evidenced by the SF episode both classifying better and being the only episode whose behaviours correlate with symptom severity. No feature importances, coefficients or ablations are reported.

**S-035** [local_638860ef] — *Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis*

Interpretability is pursued as an explicit design goal rather than a by-product: feature selection methods were chosen and developed 'aimed at selection stability to assure result interpretability', and the wrapped t-test runs until it converges on an identical feature set across 100 consecutive iterations. The resulting stable ten-feature set supports a specific behavioural interpretation - seven of ten features come from the elevated-amplitude condition, where autistic adults produced lower vertical amplitude and consequently earlier peak acceleration, indicating a failure to adopt the model's unusual movement style rather than a general motor difference. This is corroborated by conventional parametric tests showing significant group differences in the same condition.

**S-036** [local_7547db68] — *Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network*

No interpretability method - no saliency maps, no attention visualisation, no feature attribution. What the system exposes instead is a per-expression probability histogram shown to the user, with the maximum-probability bar taken as the prediction, and a per-expression breakdown of which categories failed. This is interface transparency rather than model interpretability: it shows what the model decided, not why. The clinical interpretation offered - that autistic children have facial expression recognition obstacles, so their expressions are harder to classify - is asserted from the prior literature rather than derived from the model.

**S-037** [local_878c259f] — *Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach*

No model-derived feature importance, but interpretability is supplied by a properly conducted univariate analysis that precedes and motivates the classification. The mixed-model ANOVA establishes that children with ASD sway significantly more in displacement, distance and area regardless of visual condition, with no group-by-condition interaction, and that both groups sway more with eyes closed. The negative result is equally informative and is reported plainly: sample entropy did not differentiate the groups, despite the introduction citing two prior studies reporting reduced COP complexity in ASD and interpreting it as 'a repetitive and restricted postural control pattern'. So the classification signal here is magnitude, not complexity.

**S-038** [local_1579c85a] — *Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through*

None. No feature importance, saliency or ablation analysis is performed, and no behavioral characteristic is identified as distinguishing the groups - so despite using Laban movement analysis, whose weight, space and time dimensions carry established interpretive meaning, nothing is reported about how autistic and typically developing children's movement qualities differed. The study yields a classifier without a finding.

**S-039** [local_157d6266] — *Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism*

Interpretability is architectural rather than post hoc. The three features have direct behavioural meanings (spatial deviation, lag, advance), joint importance is estimated automatically from the model's own displacement so that the score reflects the joints that actually matter for each movement, and the output is a bounded continuous score interpretable as 'how well the children performed with respect to a model'. The authors explicitly contrast this with methods that 'classify children into diagnostic groups based on broad differences in movement patterns', arguing those cannot distinguish general motor abnormality from imitation-specific impairment - a specificity critique that applies to several other motor studies in this corpus.

**S-040** [local_8be557e3] — *Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation*

No feature attribution or post hoc explanation. Interpretability is pursued at the representation level through t-SNE projections of the three feature spaces, which support a specific and testable claim: eGeMAPS-88 and eGeMAPS-54 are almost indistinguishable and heavily overlapped between classes, while the auto-encoder produces a more separable distribution. The authors offer a mechanistic reading - the bottleneck weights significant parameters up and ambiguous ones down - and a diagnosis of why statistical selection failed, namely that eGeMAPS contains temporal parameters relevant to vocalisation generally which confuse the ASD/TD distinction. The clinically interpretable layer is the vocalisation taxonomy rather than the model.

**S-041** [local_c79e100a] — *Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models*

No model interpretability method is applied, and neither the random forest nor the decision tree feature importances are extracted, which is a missed opportunity given both were trained. Interpretation is instead pursued through direct data visualisation: scatter plots of two features for three autistic and three typically developed subjects, before and after averaging, used to show that averaging compresses within-subject spread most for the subjects who varied most, and incidentally that autistic subjects vary more than typically developed ones. This is transparency about the data rather than about the model, and it is the source of the paper's only substantive clinical observation.

**S-042** [local_4fecbf6d] — *Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network*

No post hoc model explanation, but strong interpretability at the feature level and, unusually, at the symptom-domain level. Every feature's Pearson correlation against ADOS total, SA, RRB and age is reported with significance marking, sequential forward selection names the 15 features that minimise linear-model RMSE, and the resulting interpretation is specific: acoustic and prosodic features (pitch, formants, jitter, energy, ZCR) track restricted and repetitive behaviour, while conversational features (vocalisation rate, turn-taking, vocalisation count) track social affect. The authors correctly note why this matters - symptom heterogeneity means a single global severity estimate is less clinically useful than measures tied to specific domains. The age analysis serves a second interpretive purpose, showing that the severity-predictive features are largely distinct from the age-predictive ones.

**S-043** [local_95abe653] — *Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning*

No model-explanation method, but extensive experimental interpretation through ablation and design manipulation. The two substantive interpretive results come from controlled comparisons rather than from the model: capping browse time at 30 seconds isolates strategy from duration and shows the groups differ in how they scan, not just how long; and the AOI comparison separates the contribution of page structure from that of spatial granularity. The tentative behavioural reading offered - that autistic adults may scan elements in a different order or be drawn more to images than to text - is explicitly flagged as requiring further analysis rather than asserted from the classifier.

**S-044** [local_40168c96] — *Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based*

No saliency maps, attention visualisation or attribution over the model's decisions, and no directional characterisation of what distinguishes the groups. Interpretability is confined to the feature-family ablation, from which the authors infer 'the importance of semantic high-level attributes in ASD recognition' - a reasonable but indirect inference, since the high-level features are face, person and car detector responses and their removal costs 5.7 accuracy points. Because the model scores image content at fixated locations rather than gaze geometry, a per-category or per-region analysis would have been straightforward and would have connected the classifier to the reduced-social-attention literature the paper reviews at length; it is not performed.

**S-045** [local_d3852378] — *Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

No model-explanation method, but the factorial design itself is the interpretive instrument, and it yields anatomically specific conclusions: the head is the most consistently discriminative region and becomes more so under multisensory load, while arms and legs contribute less. This is supported independently by the joint-level statistical analysis showing more movement in autistic children at 13 of 15 significant joints, concentrated in head and legs, which the authors connect to documented stereotypies of head tilting and leg flapping. The interpretation is therefore anchored in observable anatomy rather than in abstract features - though the underlying group comparison uses an inappropriate paired test.

**S-046** [local_df438dd2] — *Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening*

No attribution or saliency method, but the pipeline is interpretable by construction: every intermediate output is a clinically meaningful quantity - stimulus onset time, face crop, smile or non-smile, per-stimulus score - so a clinician can inspect where a decision came from without any explanation technique. The failure case study is the interpretive high point, examining all 29 misscored trials and finding that most involve genuine smiles that clinicians attributed to spontaneous emotion rather than to the social stimulus, with four examples shown. This identifies a specific conceptual limit: the system measures whether a smile occurred in a time window, not whether it was caused by the stimulus, and closing that gap requires modelling attention or gaze direction rather than better expression recognition.

**S-047** [local_cd9e45eb] — *Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism*

Two complementary interpretability layers. At the paradigm level, bootstrap discard probabilities rank the six paradigms and reveal a surprise the authors flag themselves - Social Referencing, designed to probe automaticity of information-seeking from others, is the most discarded. At the feature level, SHAP values over the trained network yield a top-10 list spanning gaze duration to activities and to eyes, latency to biological and non-biological motion, exploration timing (start times of the 4th, 9th and 10th fixations or regions), and data quality. The interpretation offered for the quality feature is candid and important: autistic children 'can provide poorer quality data due to non-compliance and attention issues during presentation of socially-oriented scene content', so a variable normally treated as measurement noise is functioning as behavioural signal.

**S-048** [local_56237213] — *The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data*

No model-explanation method and no disclosure of which features mRMR selected, which is the paper's main interpretive gap - having established that fusion helps, it cannot say what the fused model is using. Interpretation instead comes from a parallel descriptive analysis: independent t-tests on each band and AOI, with the resulting differences read against established theory. The gaze findings are interpreted through the eye avoidance hypothesis, that autistic people avoid eye contact because they 'may consider it an unbearable social threat and experience uncomfortable physiological responses', making avoidance 'an adaptive strategy' that nonetheless degrades processing of facial identity and intention. The EEG findings are mapped onto cognitive functions band by band. Notably, the descriptive analysis found the strongest gaze effect on background fixation rather than on the eye region, and eye-region differences did not reach significance - a result that sits somewhat awkwardly with the eye-avoidance framing the discussion adopts.

**S-049** [local_f9a5195f] — *Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses*

No model-explanation method, but the ablation grid functions as a structured interpretability analysis at the block level, and its results are interpreted carefully. Two patterns are drawn out. First, discrimination is best in trial 1 - 'the first trial conducted which was before receiving any feedback or adjusting to the task' - implying the signal is strongest on first exposure and attenuates as children adapt, which has direct implications for protocol design. Second, emotion confusion matrices alone collapse to below chance in later trials, so the emotion-response signal is unstable. The behavioural interpretation is explicitly bounded: the authors note that classical eye-tracking studies have found subtler effects such as increased mouth relative to eye attention, and state that 'the gaze data collected by our system was too noisy to test for these subtler effects'.

**S-050** [local_16a77fb0] — *Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)*

Interpretability is designed in rather than added afterwards. Features were restricted to those with prior theoretical or EMG-based justification specifically 'for transparent and explainable diagnostic decisions', so every input has a stated behavioural meaning. Each is then reported as a univariate group comparison with effect size, so the multivariate result can be read against the individual behaviours: less social smiling in mouth and eye regions, reduced mimicry of the actress's cheek-raise, more intense frowning during negative content, higher fundamental frequency. The cost of this constraint is measured - all 17 action units reached AUC 0.74 against 0.65 for the selected subset. The clinical validity of the model's output is separately established by its correlation with ADOS score, and its principal bias by its correlation with age.

**S-051** [local_9c4af7a3] — *Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades*

The mutual-information filter is presented partly as an interpretability device - it 'communicates the attributes in the dataset which have the most predictive power in the model to drive future experimentation' - and three of the six retained features are named: mean amplitude of primary saccades, absolute saccade error and latency. The other three are never identified, and no model-derived importances, tree structure or decision rules are shown despite the classifier being a decision tree ensemble, which is among the more inspectable model families. The behavioural interpretation offered is that variability rather than central tendency distinguishes the groups, but the paper twice states that the implications are unclear - 'it is uncertain what further implications it has on sensorimotor activity' and 'it is still uncertain what the connections are between these dynamics and saccade error or latency'.

**S-052** [local_b70dae32] — *An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model*

The model is interpretable by construction: every input is a named clinical category, every hidden state is a severity level, and the posterior is an explicit product of two conditional probabilities that a clinician could in principle compute by hand. All 25 test cases are tabulated with their joint attention category, imitation category, actual category and predicted category, so every prediction and every error is individually inspectable - a level of transparency almost no other study in the corpus offers. What is missing is any account of the fitted probabilities, so the direction and strength of the learned relationships cannot be read, and no analysis of which of the nine input cells the model handles well or badly.

**S-053** [local_51a0af74] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data*

No model-explanation method, but the ensemble structure delivers interpretability at the level that matters clinically. Because each classifier corresponds to a specific video segment, the winning combination identifies which moments of the joint attention sequence carry discriminative information - here the gaze at rest, the gaze shifting to the object, and the gaze returning. The authors also report that regions containing the eyes outperformed regions containing the therapist's hand, which speaks directly to the gaze-versus-gesture distinction in joint attention. Both findings are interpretable and clinically legible; both are outcomes of an exhaustive search rather than tests of prior hypotheses, and no group-level feature statistics are reported to corroborate them.

**S-054** [local_d8d3037b] — *Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study*

Feature importances from the tree-based models identify continuousnum1 and continuousnum2 - continuous looking at figures and at the animal - as the most significant features, supported by density-distribution plots showing these features differing most between groups while others such as continuous landscape looking overlap closely. The interpretation offered is behaviourally specific and plausible: what distinguishes the groups is how long attention is sustained on social and animate content, not how much total time is spent there. What is missing is any directional statement or statistical test - no group means, no effect sizes, no significance testing for any feature - so the reader cannot tell whether high-trait participants sustained more or less continuous looking at figures.

**S-055** [local_991fe435] — *Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task*

No model-explanation method, and none is possible given the no-selection design - but interpretability is provided instead by an extensive parallel behavioural analysis with mixed-design ANOVAs, effect sizes and Bonferroni-corrected post hoc tests across four measures and four cue conditions. This establishes what the classifier is likely responding to: a strict group ordering in success rate and latency, longer dwell in confound and uninformative regions for both autistic groups, and a cue-type interaction present in the high-functioning group but absent in the low-functioning group. Scan-path visualisations for representative participants from each group make the qualitative differences legible. The interpretation offered - that low-functioning children's scan paths 'appeared to be more random and less purposeful' - is honest about being descriptive.

**S-056** [local_8692a64f] — *Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis*

Interpretability is the paper's organising principle rather than an afterthought. Every feature derives from a stated hypothesis, and the Pearson correlation heat map is used to test each hypothesis against the data and report the outcome - two supported, one refuted. The refutation is handled properly: head-eye co-movement correlated negatively with the label, so the conclusion states that autistic children 'show less head-eye co-movements than normal children (instead of positive correlation in the hypothesis 2)' while noting the feature remains diagnostically useful. The authors also draw a clinically directed conclusion, identifying which features 'doctors should pay attention to when diagnosing'. What is missing is any model-derived importance - the correlations are univariate and computed independently of the classifiers, so nothing establishes that the SVM actually uses the features the correlation analysis highlights.

**S-057** [local_4d6fac7e] — *Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network*

Interpretability is pursued at two levels and is the paper's strongest non-architectural contribution. Univariate t-tests establish which individual features differ between groups, with results interpreted against prior literature - reduced theta increase and stronger beta in autism for the comparator's band features, and greater differences in eye and body fixation. More distinctively, the adjacency matrix is analysed edge by edge to describe which features relate to which, both within EEG (mean value related to all but STFT; approximate entropy unrelated to sample entropy; STFT unrelated to entropy measures because 'entropy based features are calculated to measure the complexity of time series while STFT is a localized process in time and frequency domains') and across modalities. This turns the model's structure into a substantive claim about EEG-gaze relationships rather than leaving it as an implementation detail.

**S-058** [local_30c622f2] — *Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model*

Interpretability is the paper's organising purpose rather than an add-on. By fitting a separate attention model per severity group and comparing their retained feature sets, the analysis yields a directly interpretable dissociation - presence of face and presence of skin predict fixation for non-severe participants but not for severe ones - which is then connected to the wider literature on reduced face and eye-region looking in autism and on face perception relating to social-impairment severity. The authors correctly note the partial redundancy between skin and face features as reinforcing rather than duplicating the finding, and identify the single differing non-semantic feature as a steerable pyramid component that indexes edges, texture and orientation and 'is not related to object recognition'. The conclusion drawn - that top-down mechanisms differentiate severity more than bottom-up ones - is well supported by the structure of the result, subject to the caveat that the feature selection may not have been nested within folds.

**S-059** [local_bfc088c7] — *Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation*

Interpretability is served three ways. The forward selection ordering itself ranks features by contribution, showing that total session length alone reaches 79.49% and that only two fixation features are needed on top of it. The univariate table gives medians and effect statistics for every fixation feature, which is what reveals the eye-region null. And an error analysis examines the three misclassified autistic children individually, showing that on each of the three selected features they fell within the typically developing distribution - for instance, one had a total session length shorter than 75% of the typically developing group and mouth fixation higher than half of them. The authors read this as heterogeneity rather than model failure, which is the correct inference and is rarely drawn elsewhere in this corpus. The substantive interpretations offered - that the mouth matters because the task is conversational, and that longer conversations may reflect difficulty extracting social information - are plausible and appropriately hedged.

**S-060** [local_25e34bbd] — *Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification*

No model-explanation method and, more consequentially, no descriptive analysis of any group difference - no acoustic means, distributions, effect sizes or tests. The paper therefore establishes only that a classifier separates the groups, not what distinguishes them acoustically, which is a substantial gap for a study whose introduction reviews directional acoustic findings at length. The interpretation offered for why spectral-cepstral features win is at the level of feature family rather than individual parameter: they are Fourier-transform-based while jitter, shimmer, HNR and GNE are time-domain, and the result is said to be 'consistent with previous studies that, spectral and cepstral based features are best suited for discriminating voice with hoarseness from normal voice'.

**S-061** [local_4917150c] — *Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning*

No saliency or attribution analysis over the CNN, and the visual representation is not decomposed to show which regions of a scanpath image drive classification - a missed opportunity given that the images are directly human-interpretable and are reproduced in the paper for one participant from each group. Interpretability is instead pursued externally through the MIC analysis, which establishes that the velocity information encoded in colour correlates strongly with CARS severity and thereby argues that the model has something real to learn from. The authors connect this to the wider literature on saccade dynamics in autism, while noting honestly that the direction of the effect 'does not appear to be settled and seems to depend largely on the equipment and data used'.

**S-062** [local_241ec2c2] — *Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking*

Interpretability is delivered by the per-group feature comparison rather than by any post hoc explanation method, and it works well because the features are semantically meaningful image properties. Three findings are drawn out and connected to prior literature: the frame-centre feature entering only the autistic model matches reports of centre fixation 'even when there was nothing in the center'; Saliency Toolbox features entering both models is read as evidence of biologically general attentional mechanisms; and biological movement entering only the autistic model is explained by redundancy with face and person features in the typically developing model. The absence of any group-level statistics on the features themselves limits how far these can be pushed, and the interpretive claims rest on which features a genetic algorithm happened to retain, which is a noisier basis than a direct comparison would be.

**S-063** [local_36617ec5] — *Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis*

Interpretability comes from two complementary analyses rather than from any model-explanation method. Univariate testing with normality checking identifies 13 significantly differing features and localises them to specific scenes, and the eight hypothesis-contrast datasets rank feature families by discriminative value. Together these support a specific claim: coarse social-versus-non-social attention differentiates the groups while fine facial detail does not, at least at the area granularity used. The interpretation of the reversed direction is the most substantive interpretive work in the paper, connecting the finding to social-content level, to the static-versus-dynamic stimulus distinction, and to the argument that 'findings related to offline social cognition may not be generalizable across contexts'. The authors position their paradigm as 'an effective middle point' between contrived screen tasks and uncontrollable real settings.

**S-064** [local_d8e804d6] — *Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms*

Interpretability is strong because the features are physically meaningful angles and the mixed-effects analysis is conducted separately from the classification. Every feature is tested for group discrimination while controlling age, IQ and all three gesture-frequency measures as random factors, so the reported differences are adjusted rather than raw - a level of covariate control almost no other study in this corpus applies to its features. The resulting interpretation is concrete and clinically legible: autistic children move their heads through larger angles and accumulate more rotation per minute while making the same gestures with the same frequency. The blind human coding provides an independent check on the frequency null, with Spearman reliabilities of 0.787 for nodding and 0.895 for shaking.

**S-065** [local_712542ca] — *Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset*

None. No feature importance, no saliency, no cluster characterisation and no behavioural interpretation. The paper does not state what the four clusters correspond to - whether they separate stimulus types, participants, image quality or something else - which leaves its central claim uninterpretable: the reader cannot tell whether clustering identified clinically meaningful subgroups or simply partitioned the images in a way that happened to make one subset easier. Given that images from the same child are visually similar, one plausible explanation is that clusters partly track individual participants, which would make the within-cluster accuracy gain a direct consequence of increased within-fold similarity.

**S-066** [local_0ab41681] — *Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder*

Interpretability is the paper's organising purpose. Every feature is a physical quantity with a motor-control meaning, the group differences are reported with effect directions and interpreted against specific literatures on feedforward versus feedback control, and the synergy result is developed into an explicit mechanistic account - that impaired co-control forces either learning motor commands for each degree of freedom separately, which is prohibitively slow, or mapping each behavioural goal to a whole set of muscle activations, which prevents generalisation, with either extreme producing the idiosyncratic and fragmented motor strategies observed clinically. The correlation analysis then provides the discriminating evidence, showing that only the synergy measure tracks severity. Per-participant feature importance is computed and reported, and the authors verify that it agrees with the univariate findings.

**S-067** [local_9ca9b2cc] — *Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment*

Complete and by design. Every component of the score is a stated rule with a stated constant, adjustable per child by the operator, so a therapist can read the derivation of any score directly and can tune the measure to a particular patient. Against the learned models charted throughout this review, this is the opposite design point: nothing is fitted, so nothing requires post-hoc explanation, and the trade-off is that calibration is asserted rather than derived. For a system intended to run inside a clinical session and inform a therapist's next move, that trade is defensible.

**S-068** [local_02fa4215] — *Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning*

The paper's stated aim includes helping 'visualize common causes leading up to' autism, and interpretability is therefore central to its purpose - but no interpretability analysis is performed. No feature importances, no selected feature lists, no coefficients, no decision rules. What is offered instead is a list of narrative observations in the conclusion, each a frequency within the autistic group presented without the corresponding control-group frequency. Two of these are actively hazardous as written: 'most of the mothers were vaccinated during pregnancies' and 'almost 50 percent of the parents smoked before giving birth to children with autism' both appear in a list introduced as observations about autism, in a paper whose abstract promises to identify causes so that lifestyle changes can be made. Without a comparison rate these statements are uninformative, and in the vaccination case the juxtaposition risks reinforcing a well-documented and thoroughly refuted misattribution.

**S-069** [local_29a3fc54] — *Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism*

Interpretability is pursued through three complementary routes. Recursive feature elimination reduces the prosodic set to pitch and loudness, both physically meaningful. Those two are then correlated against four clinical measures using partial Spearman coefficients adjusted for WISC IQ, establishing that both track severity as rated by a professional (ADOS-2 CSS) and independently by a parent (SRS) - the authors note this is 'a noticeable result since it was established with separate informants', which is the right emphasis, since agreement across informant types is stronger evidence than a single-source correlation. Finally, the distributions of both features are plotted by group across all four activities and jointly in a two-dimensional visualisation, showing lower pitch with comparable dispersion and higher loudness with much greater variability in autism. The one interpretive gap is that the direction of the pitch effect is not reconciled with the prosody literature.

**S-070** [local_b7ec3755] — *Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images*

No model-derived interpretability method - no SHAP, no permutation importance, no tree-based importance despite using a random forest, where importance would have been available at no cost. In its place is a stimulus-level error analysis that turns out to be more informative: partitioning by classification accuracy shows that the five best images had autistic mean fixation duration of 213 ms against 574 ms for typically developing children, while the five worst had 318 versus 313 ms - so the model succeeds exactly where one feature separates the groups and fails where it does not. This localises the whole discriminative effect in mean fixation duration and simultaneously shows it is a property of particular stimuli rather than of the children. The dwell-time binning that follows (24% versus 15% of clusters under 100 ms; 21% versus 35% over 500 ms) links the finding to an existing reading-research framework in which sub-100 ms dwells indicate only partial information retention and dwells over 500 ms indicate further processing, giving the result a cognitive interpretation rather than leaving it as an unexplained numeric difference.

**S-071** [local_684969f6] — *Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data*

No formal interpretability method, and the authors say so: they 'have not conducted a full investigation to map these features back into explainable entities related to the scan-path data'. What they provide instead is more useful than a saliency map would have been. The ablation functions as an interpretability analysis by elimination, establishing which input families the model does and does not use - not the synthetic saccade, not the stimulus image, only the scanpath. That negative result then drives a direct distributional analysis: histograms of total scanpath duration by group, showing autistic scanpaths markedly shorter, with a one-sided two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of 0.278. The finding converges with the competing Startsev and Dorr entry, which independently identified total fixation duration as its most discriminating feature - cross-method agreement on the same benchmark, which is stronger evidence about what the signal is than any single model's attribution would be. The accompanying p-value of 4.09e-122 should be disregarded: it is computed over several thousand scanpaths treated as independent when they come from 28 children, which is precisely the non-independence the surrounding paragraph is arguing exists.

**S-072** [local_35004e74] — *Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children*

No internal interpretability - no attention, no saliency, no layer analysis - and the authors state the limitation plainly: 'the current level of analysis prevents us from drawing solid conclusions on what is represented in the NN'. What replaces it is external validation against clinical ratings, executed with more statistical care than any comparable analysis in the corpus. Correlations against ADOS severity, VABS-II and best-estimate IQ are Bonferroni-corrected at explicitly stated thresholds (p < 0.025, p < 0.013, p < 0.002 for the 27-item analysis). Recognising that ADOS items are collinear and that 27 separate tests would be the wrong instrument regardless of correction, the authors then run a Partial Least Squares Correlation with 1000 permutations to test the latent component and 1000 bootstrap resamples to establish salience stability - a multivariate treatment that yields a single significant component (p = 0.001) rather than a list of individually surviving items. The resulting picture is coherent: non-verbal coordination items load highest, verbal items lowest. The inference is nonetheless indirect - it establishes that model output covaries with clinically rated non-verbal atypicality, not that the network computes it, and the correlations are inflated by being taken across two groups whose severity distributions barely overlap.

**S-073** [local_fa91fc18] — *Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities*

Interpretability is pursued seriously and by an appropriate method. The stepwise-removal procedure of Olden et al. (2004) yields a complete importance ordering rather than a top-k list, and the accompanying curve shows how performance responds to progressive impoverishment of the input - more informative than a single importance ranking because it distinguishes redundant features from load-bearing ones. Boxplots of all twelve features by group then give the direction of every effect. The conclusions drawn are physically meaningful: speed and acceleration measures matter more than geometric straightness and directional coherence, and the movement picture that emerges - short, fragmented, non-straight trajectories with wide speed and acceleration excursions - is coherently linked to over- and under-compensation from disrupted prospective control, and cross-referenced to Anzulewicz's independent finding of greater impact force in autistic children's tablet interaction. There is one internal inconsistency: the Discussion's descriptive interpretation leads with STH, DC and MeanLength, but the study's own ranking removed STH second, sdDC fourth and DC sixth as the least impactful variables, while the acceleration measures the interpretation barely mentions were the last to be removed. The narrative therefore foregrounds the features the model found least useful. Both analyses were also run on the single best fold model rather than averaged across folds, so the ranking inherits that selection.

**S-074** [local_115dfe8d] — *A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children*

The weakest analytic dimension. There is no feature-level interpretability of any kind: no importance ranking, no per-family ablation, no group means, no effect sizes, no directional statements for any of the 221 features. This is a substantial loss because the feature set was designed to be interpretable - the ten brain regions, five frequency bands, four entropy scale ranges and seven graph metrics each correspond to a specific published hypothesis, and the eight areas of interest were constructed precisely to distinguish attention to eyes from mouth, to adult from child, and to joint-attention regions. A study that reported which of those differed would have contributed to the autism literature independently of its classifier; as written it contributes only a number. What interpretability exists is at modality level and is done well: the confusion-matrix decomposition establishing the EEG/gaze complementarity, and t-SNE projections of six feature spaces (raw EEG, raw gaze, raw concatenation, learned EEG, learned gaze, fused) showing progressive class separation. The t-SNE panels also surface an honest negative observation the authors do not hide - learned EEG features separate less well than expected, attributed to information loss in dimension reduction - though these projections are computed over the full dataset rather than per fold, so they illustrate rather than validate.

**S-075** [local_5b7ea7dc] — *AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

The strongest video-model interpretability analysis in the corpus, and the reason this short paper matters. Rather than presenting an attention heatmap and asserting that it looks sensible, the authors used the soft attention weights as a testable hypothesis about mechanism: they plotted the alpha values across all 300 frames for every clip and then checked each plot against the corresponding video to see whether a rise coincided with a specific social gesture. The finding is stated with appropriate precision - for typically developing children a distinct rise to at least twice baseline was 'invariably noted' somewhere in the sequence, though its onset and duration varied between children, while for autistic children attention weights 'did not change significantly throughout the duration of the video clip'. Crucially both directions are checked: every attention peak in a typically developing child coincided with an observed IJA behaviour, and across the whole dataset fewer than 1% of autistic children showed both an IJA behaviour and a corresponding peak. That establishes correspondence rather than mere plausibility, and it means the model's decision can be traced to the occurrence or non-occurrence of the clinically defined behaviour the protocol was designed to elicit - which is exactly the claim most deep-learning studies in this corpus make without evidence. The illustrative figure showing frames 80, 140, 180 and 240 for one child from each group makes the mechanism concrete. What is not done: attention is temporal only, with no spatial attribution showing which part of the frame is used, so it cannot be verified that the model is watching the child rather than the contingently responding examiner.

**S-076** [local_87fe26aa] — *Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Interpretability is strongest for EEG and absent for the behavioural modalities. The EEG t-test table is complete - all 30 region-band combinations with F, t, p, mean difference and standard error - and the directions and interpretations are given: theta power significantly higher in the autistic group in five of six regions with the largest effect at left frontal (t = 5.82), and interpretations offered for each band ('theta waves mainly reflect the emotional experience of individuals', 'the low-beta band is related to the capacity for concentration', gamma 'related to the abilities of learning, memory, and information processing'). Those band-to-function attributions are loose and would not survive scrutiny in the EEG literature, but the underlying statistics are fully reported and the theta finding is placed in the context of prior work. For gaze and facial expression there is nothing: no group means, no directions, no effect sizes, no indication of which clusters or which time windows differ. This asymmetry follows from the representations - clusters and frame counts have no semantic content to report - and it means the study, despite recording two behavioural modalities, contributes no behavioural finding beyond classification accuracy. The confusion-graph analysis is a genuine interpretability contribution at modality level, showing exactly which class each modality handles and which it fails.

**S-077** [local_893ce2fa] — *An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images*

None, and none is possible. There is no feature importance, attribution, saliency map or ablation, and the representation - individual pixels of a 28x28 downsampled plot - admits no behavioural interpretation even if attribution were computed. The paper offers no group difference, no effect direction and no descriptive statistic about gaze. Its one interpretive sentence, that 'the amount of information in the images and the use of space in the x and y coordinates are essential factors when classifying ASD', is a statement about how much of the frame the trace fills. Placed against the rest of this corpus, that is a meaningful observation in an unintended way: it is consistent with the classifier keying on trace density, which is a property of how much usable gaze data the tracker captured, and hence potentially on data quality rather than on viewing behaviour - the pattern seen in Li 2020's SHAP quality feature, Fang 2021's untracked-gaze 'area0' and Zhao 2021's differential OpenFace failure rates.

**S-078** [local_dffe4127] — *Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals*

Interpretability is pursued through study design rather than through model attribution, and is stronger for it. Four analyses jointly characterise what the gaze data contain. The effect-size profile across areas of interest, with bootstrap confidence intervals in both episodes, shows where the group differences lie and that they replicate. The reference-heatmap comparison establishes that the autistic and control group averages are nearly identical (r = 0.966) while individual autistic participants depart from both - which localises the phenomenon at the individual rather than group level. The fingerprinting analysis quantifies how much individually distinctive information the same features carry, and the four-versus-eight-feature comparison shows the information is distributed rather than concentrated. And the per-participant classification and clustering frequencies show which individuals the group-level model can and cannot place. The authors summarise the feature-level picture honestly as 'a rather distributed effect over heatmaps and facial features, with no single feature driving the effect', and note the caveat that their features were intercorrelated and their videos always contained people. The absence of a correlation between any gaze feature and ADOS severity is also reported, and is an important negative: the measures separate groups on average without indexing individual severity.

**S-079** [local_2b766683] — *Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech*

None. No feature importance, attribution, saliency, spectral analysis or group comparison of any acoustic quantity is reported, and no interpretation is offered of what distinguishes the classes. This is a substantial gap given that the paper's entire motivation is a specific set of prosodic claims - echolalia, monotonous intonation, atypical pitch, irregular stress - none of which is tested, measured or discussed after the introduction. The random forest's feature set would have supported at least a permutation-importance analysis at no cost, and mel spectrograms admit standard saliency methods. The consequence is that the study yields three accuracy figures and no knowledge about autistic children's speech, so it cannot be evaluated for construct validity: there is no way to tell whether the models are keying on prosody, on vocal-tract size, on recording distance, or on utterance length. The authors do gesture at interpretability as a future goal, proposing that combining audio features with computer-vision measures 'could possibly result in interpretable models', which acknowledges the present absence.

**S-080** [local_2895bdf0] — *Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection*

Interpretability is built into the design rather than added afterwards, and it operates at three levels. The features are individually meaningful by construction - mean length of utterance, filled-pause ratio, disfluency proportion, F0, shimmer, loudness - so any model weight is directly interpretable, in contrast to the learned representations used by the deep-learning speech studies elsewhere in this corpus. mSVM-RFE ranks them and identifies an optimal eight, evenly split between modalities, though the selection is honestly reported as producing no significant gain. And the misclassification analysis functions as the deepest interpretive layer, answering not 'which features matter' but 'which children does this measure see', which is the question that determines clinical utility. Its findings are specific and consequential: the language model is biased toward younger children with poorer language and less output; the voice model is unbiased with respect to language level; the residual misses have the highest IQ and most language output; and neither ADOS severity nor IQ predicts misclassification in any model - from which the authors draw the appropriately hedged conclusion that 'if replicated, this result could confirm that our voice and language measurement methodology specifically taps aspects of communication skills that are not confounded by autism severity or developmental delay'.

**S-081** [local_423b636b] — *Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers*

Interpretability is pursued through the design of the measures rather than through model attribution, and the analysis that carries most weight is the within-group contrast. Because the measures are three physically meaningful quantities, the finding can be stated directly in behavioural terms. The decisive analysis compares social against nonsocial movies within each group: neurotypical toddlers moved more, faster and less predictably during social content (r = 0.47, 0.62, 0.51), while autistic toddlers showed no content-dependent difference at all. That single contrast does three things a between-group difference cannot. It shows the effect is not simply 'autistic children move more' but that neurotypical children modulate movement by content and autistic children do not. It adjudicates directly against Martin and colleagues' published interpretation that increased head movement in autism serves to modulate perception of social stimuli, since on that account the difference should be confined to social content, and here it is not. And it rules out the reading that the measure indexes social engagement, since the group difference persists for nonsocial content. The paper then engages seriously with alternative mechanisms - general sensory modulation, postural control under multisensory demand, a regulatory function analogous to repetitive behaviour - rather than settling on one. The Mullen correlation analysis is the interpretively weakest element and contains an internal contradiction: the Results report positive correlations between Early Learning Composite and all three movement measures during social movies (r = .36, .39, .34), implying higher cognitive ability accompanied more movement, while the Discussion asserts that 'autistic children with lower cognitive abilities showed higher levels of head movement rate, acceleration, and complexity' and builds an interpretation on that reading.

**S-082** [local_ffa35101] — *Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study*

No feature-level interpretability, and none is possible given principal components of 8,640-dimensional envelope representations - the paper reports no group means, no effect sizes and no directional statements. What it provides instead is interpretability at the level of theoretical construct, which is the level its question operates at. The rhythm-versus-intonation contrast is itself the interpretive result, and the authors connect it to the existing descriptive literature ('the ML algorithms identified in this study appeared to capture patterns from acoustic features that were representative of these prosodic characteristics, paralleling such descriptive observations by clinicians and researchers') and to prior objective measures of speech rate, lexical stress and cross-syllabic durational variability. The Cantonese intonation failure is then given a mechanistic account grounded in phonology - pitch carries lexical meaning in tone languages, so f0 is under phonological constraint - and used to reconcile conflicting prior findings across English, Thai and Japanese. That is a stronger form of interpretation than a feature-importance ranking would have provided, because it generates a testable prediction: intonational differences in autism should be attenuated in tone-language speakers generally. The one interpretive overreach is the ASPM allele speculation, which substitutes a population-genetic explanation for a linguistic one that the paper has already established.

**S-083** [local_81ecbc6f] — *Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings*

None, and the authors treat this as the study's principal scientific shortcoming rather than a minor gap: 'Neural network encoders followed by classifiers can take into account a wide variety of utterance characteristics but does not help to identify which particular aspects of language are crucial.' They frame the remedy as a route to discovery rather than to trust, proposing LIME-style word-level attribution so that 'giving meaning to collections of important words may lead to discovering new dimensions of language relevant to ASD', and connecting it to their own prior work identifying sentiment and language abstraction as relevant dimensions - while noting 'it is very likely that this list is not exhaustive'. That framing is correct: for a study whose motivating literature is entirely about specific narrative constructs (coherence, causal connection, referential devices, internal state language), a classifier that cannot say which of these it is using contributes no linguistic knowledge. The one indirect interpretive finding is that skipped pages carry signal, inferred from zero-vector representation outperforming masking.

**S-084** [local_bc62bc4b] — *Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening*

Interpretability is pursued at two levels and both are useful. At feature level, the selections of all three algorithms are tabulated feature by feature and area by area for both datasets, with agreement across algorithms used as the criterion for calling a feature discriminative - a more conservative approach than trusting any single ranking. The resulting claim is specific and checkable: net dwell time, diversion duration and first fixation duration on the social area were selected by all three algorithms in both stimulus sets. The authors then situate this against their own published systematic review of eye-tracking features in autism, noting that fixation count, fixation time, average fixation duration and dwell time dominate the literature while diversion duration is essentially absent - so the finding is that the field's default feature set may not contain its most discriminative member. At model level, the decision tree is reproduced with its thresholds and its traversal explained in clinical terms, presented as a transparency argument rather than a performance one. What is absent is any link between model output and clinical characteristics: no severity measure was collected, so the authors' own proposal to examine the symptom profiles of false negatives cannot be executed on these data.

**S-085** [local_889d9bd6] — *Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children*

Interpretability is inherent in the design rather than added afterwards, since each feature is a named percentage on a named region and every group difference is reported with its direction and effect size. The per-area classification analysis then functions as a formal importance ranking, tested against permutation rather than asserted, and the finding that the rankings differ substantially between cohorts is the study's central claim. The eye-area result is the clearest example and is properly interpreted: comparison children's eye-looking rises from 17.6% at toddler age to 29.2% at preschool age while autistic children's stays flat at 15.4% and 15.1%, so the group difference emerges developmentally rather than being present from the outset. The authors offer a mechanistic account - that toddlers with typical development use visual mouth information for language acquisition, reducing eye attention, and that as language becomes more auditorily meaningful preschool attention shifts to the eyes - which is testable and which explains both the mouth and eye interactions coherently. Against this, the paper offers no interpretation at all of the finding that fixation is reduced on non-social areas, which is the observation most in tension with the social-attention framing it works within.

**S-086** [local_361b59fb] — *Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

No feature-level interpretability, and the algorithm and code are proprietary - so at the level of mechanism the Device is opaque. What the paper offers instead is case-level interpretability, and it is more clinically useful than a feature ranking would be. The indeterminate group is characterised diagnostically: 91.0% had at least one neurodevelopmental disorder, 71.0% were autism-negative with another condition, 20.0% were autism-positive and 9.0% had no developmental diagnosis - so the abstentions concentrate on the genuinely ambiguous rather than falling randomly. Output is cross-tabulated against DSM-5 severity, showing a clear gradient from 44 of 65 Level 3 children classified positive to 1 of 5 Level 1 children. Output is cross-tabulated against every comorbidity, showing for example that phonological disorder yields abstention 82.4% of the time. And specialist certainty is compared between cases the Device classified and cases it declined - 71% versus 64% completely certain, p = 0.40 - testing whether the Device abstains where clinicians are also uncertain, and finding no significant difference. Taken together these establish what the Device is doing at the level a clinician needs, even though they say nothing about how.

**S-087** [local_afdb603d] — *Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.*

The strongest part of the paper, and the reason it is worth charting despite its data problems. Every one of the 16 selected features is reported with group means, standard deviations, outlier counts and exact p-values, and then discussed individually against named prior work - with contradictory findings reported rather than suppressed. The pitch literature is described as containing 'opposite findings'; a proposed link between pitch excursions and 'motherese' speech is cited and then noted to have been 'disprove[n]' by later work; the loudness literature is enumerated as containing higher values, lower values, null results, and studies that avoided intensity entirely 'to avoid the risk of obtaining unclear results'; and the spectral findings are flagged as lacking comparators, with the authors stating plainly that 'we did not find any other relevant studies to confirm the importance of spectral features to detect ASD'. The jitter-shimmer-HNR discussion is the most substantive, correctly identifying the expected inverse relationship between jitter and harmonics-to-noise ratio, verifying it in their own data, and connecting it to the voice-pathology literature on breathiness and hoarseness. The interpretive irony is that this same literature supplies the reason to doubt the finding: harmonics-to-noise ratio is a signal-to-noise measure, and the two groups' signals were acquired through different chains.

**S-088** [local_4f7e7eb3] — *Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques*

None, and none is possible. There is no feature importance, attribution, saliency or ablation, and the representation - texture codes over a segmented, morphologically cleaned rendering of a gaze trace - admits no behavioural interpretation even in principle. No group means, effect sizes, directions or descriptive statistics about viewing behaviour appear anywhere.
