**S-161** [local_8d43288c] — *Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos*

No model interpretability, but a genuine and clinically sensible error analysis. Spinning is confused with the repetitive classes because of overlapping motion dynamics, and normal behaviour is confused with the repetitive classes in the independent test set - both of which are the errors one would predict from the physics of the behaviours, and both of which point at the harder discrimination (is this movement stereotyped or not?) rather than the easier one (is this flapping or banging?).

**S-162** [local_5f57ba19] — *Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension*

Two attribution methods - model feature importance and SHAP - applied convergently, and computed on each cross-validation fold's test set before averaging, which is the correct placement and is stated explicitly. The result is a ranked feature list dominated by eye revisits, mouth fixation count and mouth fixation-time percentage, interpreted against existing cognitive literature on social attention rather than presented as a novel discovery. The authors also note honestly where interpretation fails: for features beyond the leading ones no clear pattern emerged, which they attribute to the modest performance of the classifiers rather than explaining away.

**S-163** [local_1d856900] — *Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare*

SHAP and LIME are applied, and applied only to Dataset 1 - a choice the abstract states plainly. The consequence is that the paper's interpretability contribution covers the dataset where the answer is predetermined by the presence of AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS among the features, and omits the dataset where attribution would have been genuinely informative, namely which of four fused modalities carries the signal. No SHAP or LIME output is described in the extracted text.

**S-164** [local_7b19a959] — *Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis*

Feature importance is used as a scientific instrument rather than as decoration. The headline interpretive result is that several variables showing no significant group difference even under highly conservative Bonferroni correction nonetheless carried predictive value in combination - a finding that only a multivariate model can produce and that the authors read as evidence of complex latent relationships associated with autism rather than as a discovery of new markers. Reaction-time variables ranked consistently high; executive function was informative in this adult sample; and the near-identical importance profile with and without the AQ supports the claim that objective and subjective measures contribute differently. The authors also state the limit: the ranking may not generalise across ages.

**S-165** [local_d7b6fa00] — *Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath*

Permutation-based feature relevance, with an unusually precise statement of scope: the analysis was performed independently of model selection procedures and served solely as an interpretability tool rather than as a feature selection mechanism. That distinction matters and is drawn correctly - permutation importance computed for interpretation cannot leak into the model, whereas the same computation used to select features would. A full ranking is presented, though the extracted text does not name which descriptors dominated.

**S-166** [local_e54c304c] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models*

No formal attribution, but the paper contains an out-of-distribution probe that is the single most informative result in it and is presented only as a robustness comparison between architectures. Given a picture of a dog and a picture of a leaf, YOLOv9c classified the dog as Autistic and the leaf as Nonautistic, while YOLOv8n rejected both. The authors read this as evidence of YOLOv8n's superior filtering. The more important reading is what it reveals about the task: a model trained to detect autism from a photograph will assign an autism label to whatever is placed in front of it unless something else stops it, and the difference between the two architectures here is a difference in background rejection rather than in anything about autism. No other study in this fifteen-strong branch tests its model on a non-face input, and this one does so almost incidentally.

**S-167** [local_e4c2a776] — *Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images*

Grad-CAM++ is applied and a visual interpretation figure is shown, described as highlighting the most significant facial regions and improving model transparency. The description also calls this abnormality detection, which reframes model attention as pathology. No quantitative attribution is reported, no facial region is named as consistently salient across images, and no test establishes whether the highlighted regions correspond to anything anatomically meaningful rather than to image-provenance artefacts - the question the branch most needs answered and the one a saliency method is least able to settle on unlabelled web photographs.

**S-168** [local_231757c7] — *SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers*

SHAP applied per class with importance, summary and waterfall plots, yielding anatomically interpretable biomarkers (wrist, knee, elbow-to-foot) that the author relates to established motor findings in autism. The interpretation is properly bounded for the two real classes - the author states that for typical and moderate ASD the approach relies on biomarkers that are anatomically interpretable and reflect systematic motor patterns consistent with the literature - and implicitly withheld for the severe class, whose SHAP profile describes a distribution the author constructed. The reported axis gradient across severity is the clearest illustration: its severe endpoint (X-axis features 100%) is a property of the synthesis procedure rather than of any child.

**S-169** [local_1b457442] — *Screening autism spectrum*

Well executed. Logistic-regression coefficients were accumulated across all five cross-validation folds and averaged rather than taken from a single fit, and the resulting ranking was then tested by refitting on the top four non-part-of-speech features alone, which reproduced nearly the same 86% accuracy. That reduced-model check is a genuine validation of the importance ranking rather than an assertion, and it supports the paper's privacy argument directly - fewer features means less data collection. The named features are clinically interpretable, and their directions are stated. The one problem is that age is among them, and age is confounded with group.

**S-170** [local_b26db2f2] — *Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches*

None. Random forest was the best model and supplies feature importances at no cost, and none is reported. The study's entire justification is that specific executive functions are impaired in autism and that a game can measure them, so the identification of which game-derived variables carried the signal was both available and central - and it is absent.

---

## RQ4.5 — Validation strategy

_170 of 170 studies charted for this question._

**S-001** [local_76fc33d0] — *Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers*

10-fold cross-validation plus leave-one-out and grid search for hyperparameters, described as guarding against overfitting. No external or independent test set, no held-out site, no class-imbalance handling, no statistical comparison between classifiers, no deployment or real-time claim beyond 'may be used to assist clinicians'. Subject-independence of folds is not stated.

**S-002** [local_0dbc5018] — *Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities*

Leave-one-out cross-validation over 30 subjects, described as returning an almost unbiased error estimate. No external or independent test set (the authors explicitly name this as the main limitation), no held-out site, no class-imbalance handling (groups are balanced 15/15), no statistical test on classification performance, and no real-time or deployment claim - though practical feasibility is argued from the 15-minute session and 30-minute analysis time.

**S-003** [local_dc5fc4bb] — *ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data*

Effectively unaddressed. No cross-validation scheme, train/test split or repetition count is reported; no external validation; no held-out site; no statistical comparison between classifiers; no deployment or real-time claim. Class imbalance is handled by random oversampling to 30 instances per group, apparently applied to the full dataset before classification, which would leak duplicated samples across any train/test boundary.

**S-004** [local_863980f8] — *Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework*

Leave-one-participant-out cross-validation with participant-level aggregation - subject-independent at the decision level, which is better than the instance-level cross-validation common in this corpus. But K and the decision threshold are selected to maximise accuracy on the same data, K-means quantisation uses all participants' fixations, and there is no external or independent test set, no held-out site and no cross-cultural check. Class imbalance (29 ASD vs 58 TD) is handled by a tuned flexible threshold rather than resampling. Base-rate limitation on deployment is explicitly discussed; no real-time claim, though the authors note remote eye trackers make rapid data collection feasible.

**S-005** [local_be8aa62f] — *Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder*

10-fold cross-validation with random partitioning; performance tested against chance with Bonferroni-corrected t-tests; classifier variance across folds reported and explicitly interpreted as evidence of SVM overfitting. Covariate robustness is tested (age, gender, verbal IQ, vocabulary, WMS added to the model - no improvement) and the network result is re-tested under a generalized linear model with covariates. No external or independent validation, no held-out site, no class-imbalance handling despite a 27:132 split, and no deployment claim beyond a proposal for future real-time clinical visualisation. Whether LSI was refitted inside each fold is not stated.

**S-006** [local_e404a2a3] — *Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism*

10 repetitions of 10-fold cross-validation with AUC standard deviations reported, aggregating 740 predictions for the ROC; algorithm choice explicitly motivated by overfitting risk; redundant features (r>0.9) collapsed; a demographics-free model variant (RGF2) run to check that age and gender were not driving the result. Bias and generalisability are addressed narratively (selection bias, IQ confound, institution-specific sample, need for retraining on the general population) rather than by mitigation. No external or independent test set, no held-out site and no real-time/deployment evaluation, though commercial deployment as a screening device is an explicit ambition.

**S-007** [local_780141fc] — *Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study*

Robustness is handled better than anywhere else in the corpus at this sample size. A nested leave-one-out design places feature selection and hyperparameter tuning inside an inner training/development split, with the explicit statement that all selections are based on training-data performance and the test sample is treated as unknown. Feature-selection stability across iterations is examined and reported (SVM-weight features being more stable than leave-one-out features). The method is benchmarked against nine standard alternatives. What is absent: any external or independent dataset, any held-out site, any class-imbalance handling (14 vs 16 is near-balanced), and any deployment or real-time analysis. Generalisation across ASC heterogeneity is explicitly flagged as untested.

**S-008** [local_3a331973] — *Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data*

Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, which is subject-independent at the outer level. Overfitting is explicitly reasoned about in two places - rejecting raw-pixel deep learning, and motivating feature selection because 'any classifier trained directly on the entire feature-set is most likely to overfit'. But there is no statement that feature selection was nested within folds, no external or independent validation, no held-out site, no class-imbalance handling or metric, no statistical testing, and no deployment or real-time evaluation despite the time-saving clinical framing. The comorbid classifier is trained on 33 subjects total.

**S-009** [local_7b3e6b3a] — *Earlier identification of children with autism*

The strongest validation design among the early speech studies here: subject-independent 3-fold cross-validation with partitions matched for gender and diagnosis and balanced for vocalisation count, and a genuine three-way train/development/test split in which the SVM complexity parameter, the BLSTM architecture and the early-stopping point are all selected on development data only. Confusion matrices and fold standard deviations are reported. Weaknesses: the headline subject-level accuracy uses thresholds optimised on the merged training and development partitions of each fold, which is defensible but should be read alongside the 70% fixed-threshold result; there is no external or independent validation and no held-out site; class imbalance is handled by reporting UAR rather than by resampling; and no real-time or deployment evaluation is performed, though a paediatric-examination scenario is proposed.

**S-010** [local_36aa3ace] — *Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative*

Generalisability is addressed by design: partitioning is 'completely child independent', with all utterances from a given child confined to one partition, and a dedicated validation partition is used for all parameter optimisation while the test partition is 'solely used for the purpose of performance evaluation on unseen children'. This is the correct structure and better than most of the corpus. Class imbalance is addressed at the metric level (UAR) but not by resampling or class weighting, and the confusion matrices show the imbalance is not in fact overcome. No external validation on a second corpus, no held-out site, no bias mitigation, no calibration, and no real-time or deployment analysis.

**S-011** [local_44b58f21] — *ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces*

Weak. 10-fold cross-validation repeated over ten iterations is used and is explicitly motivated by small sample size, but both the label-using SWDA feature selection and the exhaustive hyperparameter grid search were performed on the complete dataset before the folds were drawn, so information from every test fold informed both the feature set and the model configuration. There is no external or independent validation, no held-out site, no class-imbalance issue (30/30), no statistical comparison between classifiers, no bias mitigation, and no real-time or deployment analysis - though clinical diagnosis and treatment evaluation are named as intended applications.

**S-012** [local_cb9a5b48] — *Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening*

Limited. 8-fold cross-validation is used and explicitly motivated by overfitting prevention, but with 16 children this leaves two per test fold, and neither the choice among five classifiers nor the two-layer stacking design is nested inside it. The random-regrouping control is a genuine robustness check on the statistical claim, though not on the classifier. There is no external or independent validation, no held-out site, no class-imbalance issue (8/8), and no real-time or deployment evaluation despite screening being the stated application. Generalisability is addressed only by the authors' plan to test more children, and the known failure mode (shy typically developing children) is handled by proposing combination with other methods rather than by any modelling change.

**S-013** [local_40cd7d53] — *Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children*

Five-fold cross-validation, with two separate permutation procedures - one testing whether classification accuracy exceeds chance (1000 label permutations) and one testing whether each AOI's discriminative weight is non-arbitrary (1000 permutations). Multiple comparisons across the ten AOI group tests are Bonferroni-corrected, and the correlational analysis with GDS subscores is likewise corrected, with the authors explicitly flagging which correlations did not survive correction. What is absent: external or independent validation, held-out site, any statement of whether AOI selection is nested within the folds, class-imbalance handling (not needed at 37/37), and any deployment or real-time analysis - though the authors explicitly position eye tracking as supplementary to clinical assessment rather than a replacement.

**S-014** [local_5b1d0b36] — *Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday*

Leave-one-subject-out with a genuine three-way split - one test subject, 18 training and 8 development subjects, with epochs and learning rate grid-searched on development only - which is subject-independent and separates model selection from performance estimation. Class imbalance is addressed at the metric level via unweighted F1. Robustness to real-world data corruption is a design goal rather than an afterthought: missing sources are explicitly encoded, error-correcting linguistic features are designed against the observed parent-prompting failure, and voice-activity segmentation adapts per recording to differing noise levels. Age and gender are deliberately excluded to prevent the model exploiting recruitment-correlated demographics. Absent: external or independent validation, any held-out site or device, calibration, and any deployment measurement despite the app being the contribution. Whether CFS is recomputed inside each leave-one-out fold is stated only as being 'conducted in the model training', which is suggestive but not explicit.

**S-015** [local_54954c19] — *Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching*

The strongest validation reasoning in the corpus. The background section explicitly critiques two prior studies (an EEG study reporting 94% and a French speech study reporting 93.5%) for partitioning data segments rather than participants, noting that this allows segments from the same participant into both training and test sets and produces 'potentially overoptimistic results' that do 'not account for real-world scenarios where the algorithm will have the task of correctly classifying a new person'. The study then adopts 100-fold cross-validation with strict participant-level partitioning (10 training and 5 test participants per group per fold) precisely to emulate diagnosing a new person, and reports 95% confidence intervals throughout. Class balance is enforced by design, including the random removal of one control. What is absent: external validation on an independent cohort, any held-out site or apparatus, calibration analysis, and any measurement of the proposed eye-tracker-free variant.

**S-016** [local_d8dc996a] — *Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Robustness is handled unusually seriously. Leave-one-subject-out with 39 independently trained models is used deliberately, with the authors stating that it is 'more challenging than the usual cross-validation whose classification scores are always higher' and that they consider it the correct procedure for a system meant to generalise. Appearance information is removed by Gaussian smoothing so the model cannot exploit incidental visual differences. A handcrafted state-of-the-art baseline is run and reported to fail at chance. A confidence-threshold sensitivity analysis shows detection accuracy degrading from 0.82 to 0.67 between thresholds 0.5 and 0.7 and dropping below chance above 0.9, with the authors stating plainly that the model 'is not more trustable after a threshold of 0.9'. What is absent: any external or independent dataset, any held-out site or camera viewpoint, any class-imbalance issue (19/20), and any real-time or deployment measurement despite clinical use being the stated aim.

**S-017** [local_88ddfdd1] — *A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task*

Among the best in the corpus. Subject-level partitioning is explicit and enforced, with both groups evenly split across folds and class priors set to 0.5. The 5-by-2 repeated cross-validation design is a recognised procedure for comparing classifiers. Both models are permutation-tested against chance (p < 0.001, k = 1000), which matters given accuracies near 50%. A benchmark using alternative standard techniques is run and reported as null, guarding against the conclusion being an artefact of the general pipeline. Sensitivity to algorithm settings is informally checked for both t-SNE and LightGBM. Absent: external validation on an independent sample, and any participant-level aggregation that would yield a diagnostic estimate.

**S-018** [local_361110f1] — *Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features*

Leave-one-out cross-validation is applied uniformly across all five classifiers, and the comparison across classifiers and feature counts is systematic. But the two selection stages are not nested: the t-test screen used the full labelled dataset, and forward feature selection optimised the same accuracy metric that is then reported, so the headline is a maximum over a search rather than an unbiased estimate - the same failure mode that Vabalas et al. (2019) in this corpus identify and correct. There is no external or independent validation, no permutation or significance testing, no class-imbalance handling (20 vs 23 is near-balanced), and no deployment analysis. Generalisability is addressed honestly in narrative terms - high-functioning only, unusable below age 2 - but not tested.

**S-019** [local_51533de4] — *Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations*

Feature selection is explicitly nested: univariate correlation filtering is performed 'within each cross-validation fold' (selecting 24-39 features per fold, 60 distinct features overall) and PCA is applied 'within each CV fold', with leave-one-out cross-validation over 70 children. This is the correct structure and avoids the selection leakage that affects most of the corpus. Robustness is further probed by testing whether demographic and IQ variables improve the model - they do not - which is a form of confound check. What is absent: external or independent validation, any held-out site, calibration analysis, and any real-world deployment test despite community prescreening being the stated goal. The human-rater comparison functions as an informal ceiling estimate rather than a validation.

**S-020** [local_96c87d36] — *Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking*

Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation repeated so each of the subjects is tested once, with balanced class weights addressing the 23-versus-35 imbalance, and results reported at three aggregation levels so the effect of the decision unit is visible rather than hidden. What is absent: external or independent validation, any held-out site despite multi-site collection, and any analysis of the apparatus confound. Most seriously, generalisability is undermined rather than tested by the design - the eye tracker is confounded with diagnostic group, and the model's most important features are sampling-rate-sensitive. No calibration analysis, no real-time or deployment claim beyond noting efficiency advantages over standardized diagnostic scales.

**S-021** [local_4b031d44] — *Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine*

The paper is unusual in this corpus for treating generalisation as an empirical question rather than an assumption. It applies previously published classifiers unchanged to a new cultural population and reports the resulting performance drop (92% accuracy on US videos to AUC 0.75 on Bangladeshi videos), then trains models on each dataset and tests on the other to compare feature reliance. Class imbalance is handled with balanced class weights. Three-fold cross-validation with reported training and test demographics gives some assurance of split stability. What is missing: whether cross-validation folds were partitioned at child level is not explicitly stated (though with one video per child this is largely moot); specificity is not reported; and no prospective or external validation of the retrained Bangladeshi models is performed.

**S-022** [local_05ef29e5] — *Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification*

Evaluation on an organiser-held-out test set with labels withheld is methodologically stronger than the internal cross-validation used by most of the corpus, and it makes the result directly comparable against other challenge entrants. But the design has a structural limitation the authors flag without connecting to validity: subject identity is randomised and inconsistent across images, so partitioning by subject is impossible and the same individual's scanpaths may fall on both sides of the split. Combined with per-image rather than per-person analysis, the reported figures estimate scanpath-level discriminability, not person-level diagnostic accuracy. No external validation beyond the challenge test set, no bias analysis, no class-imbalance handling, and no deployment or real-time consideration.

**S-023** [local_9528024b] — *Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol*

There is no validation in the machine-learning sense - no cross-validation, no held-out data, no independent test set. Robustness is addressed through two design decisions instead. First, the authors noticed that four tasks were driving belief close to certainty and judged this implausible given ADOS uses five modules of at least ten tasks each, so they introduced a confidence-scaling transformation and set it to 0.8 to deliberately reduce the information each task contributes - actively degrading apparent performance on principled grounds. Second, they validated against expert-assessed behaviour rather than diagnostic label, because they had observed the two diverging in their sample. Neither is a generalisation estimate. There is no external validation, no bias analysis, no class-imbalance consideration, and the system is not autonomous, so deployment readiness is explicitly not established.

**S-024** [local_6230fe22] — *Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism*

Leave-one-out cross-validation at the participant level is described and is an appropriate choice, with the rationale cited. Beyond that, nothing: no external or independent validation, no held-out site, no repetition, no permutation or significance testing, no class-imbalance handling or reporting, no calibration, no bias analysis, and no deployment or real-time evaluation despite clinical deployment in Saudi autism centres being the explicit goal. Generalisability is addressed only by the future-work statement that larger datasets are needed.

**S-025** [local_785ba418] — *Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis*

The strongest validation design among the motor studies here. Nested 10-fold cross-validation with normalisation, feature selection and hyperparameter tuning all performed inside each training fold, so test data never informs model development; the whole procedure repeated 100 times with random splits to yield performance distributions; and permutation testing with 1000 label shuffles to establish that accuracy differs from chance. The authors cite Varma and Simon on nested cross-validation giving 'almost unbiased' estimates and K-fold producing 'significantly overoptimistic results'. Absent: external or independent validation (explicitly named as future work), any held-out site, class-imbalance handling (24 vs 22 is near-balanced), and any deployment analysis. Outlier replacement with group means is performed before the folds, a small residual leakage path.

**S-026** [local_fea042be] — *Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual*

This is the study's weakest dimension. Ten-fold cross-validation is reported with AUC standard deviations, and dropout and augmentation are used as regularisers, but the fundamental question of what constitutes a fold is never addressed: 547 images derive from 59 children and 2,735 further synthetic images derive from those 547, so unless partitioning is by participant - which is never stated - the test folds contain images from children whose other images, and augmented copies of whose images, were used in training. Augmentation performed before rather than within the fold split compounds this. There is no external validation, no held-out site, no participant-level reporting, no class-imbalance treatment (328 non-ASD vs 219 ASD images), and no permutation or significance testing. The deployed web application demonstrates practical delivery but not validity.

**S-027** [local_ba5fbda7] — *Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD*

The methodological centrepiece. The paper argues explicitly that most autism machine-learning studies rely on simple cross-validation, which 'increases the likelihood of choosing an overly optimistic model', and that leave-one-out validation - used by several studies it names - 'creates overly variable test sets, rendering model outcomes unstable' given autism's heterogeneity. It implements repeated nested k-fold cross-validation instead: 10 outer folds with five permutations, a 5-by-5 inner cycle, participants shuffled before each fold definition, parameter optimisation confined to the inner cycle and performance evaluation confined to the outer, with PCA fitted inside each inner fold. It then presents 75.9% as a conservative estimate obtained under this regime, and codifies the standards in a Box listing minimum requirements. What remains absent: external validation on an independent sample (named as the immediate next step), transdiagnostic specificity testing, and any deployment analysis.

**S-028** [local_7b468950] — *Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart*

The methodological benchmark for this review, and the only design in the corpus that closes every failure mode the synthesis documents elsewhere. The algorithm is locked before the evaluation data exist, so no tuning to the labels is possible. The data are collected prospectively and 'independently of the Play.Care software engineers and commercial concerns', so the developers cannot influence the evaluation. Results are embargoed - 'the results are blind until data collection is complete' - so no interim selection can occur. Recruitment spans two countries and multiple streams, addressing the site-specific effects the protocol identifies in its own pilot. Sensitivity and specificity are prespecified as primary outcomes rather than accuracy. A non-autistic clinical comparison group of 200 children is recruited specifically to test differential diagnosis, prespecified as a secondary outcome. The trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov before results exist and the protocol is published in advance. And the sample size is justified with power calculations framed around detecting underperformance rather than demonstrating success. Most significantly for this review, the protocol states explicitly why the pilot's evaluation was insufficient despite using repeated cross-validation: it 'only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset'. That sentence identifies the exact inferential gap that most studies in this corpus leave open - cross-validation within a dataset establishes internal consistency, not generalisation - and the trial exists to close it. The one residual limitation is that recruitment through specialist services and existing diagnoses means predictive value at population prevalence will not be directly estimable even on completion.

**S-029** [local_309e5baa] — *Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns*

The paper's chief contribution to this review. Evaluation is performed twice: on an internal split partitioned by image (240 train, 60 test) and on an organiser-held blind test set of 100 images. The consistent 6-11 point accuracy drop and 0.09-0.14 AUC drop between the two regimes constitutes a direct measurement of internal-validation optimism on the same models and data. Overfitting is otherwise controlled by an extensive augmentation regime, dropout, L2 regularisation and batch normalisation, and the frozen pretrained image branch limits capacity. Absent: participant-level partitioning at any stage, cross-validation, permutation testing, class-imbalance handling despite the collapsing specificity, and any calibration or deployment analysis.

**S-030** [local_a45f39e9] — *Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time*

The weakest dimension. A train/test split is used but its partitioning basis is never stated, and with 8349 episodes derived from 555 videos - and an unknown but certainly smaller number of children - episodes from the same video and child will span the split unless deliberately prevented, which is not claimed. There is no cross-validation, no repeated splits, no permutation testing, and no class-imbalance handling despite a 5265-to-3084 imbalance that the recall-AUC divergence suggests is driving results. There is no external validation and no participant-level evaluation. The retraining of the pose estimator on the authors' own annotated child data is a sensible domain-adaptation step and is evaluated on its own terms (9-14% more annotated frames), which is a strength within the pipeline even though it does not address classification validity.

**S-031** [local_d587f9cd] — *Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning*

Not applicable in the classification sense, and the study does not claim otherwise. No classifier is trained, no held-out set exists, no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity or AUC is computed, and the evaluation is explicitly labelled a proof of concept. The two things it does validate are appropriate to its claims: the vision pipeline's technical performance is reported for the case study together with the occlusion failures encountered, and the behavioural observation is presented qualitatively as a pattern rather than as a discrimination. Four limits bound what can be taken from it. Six children in a single session each cannot support a behavioural claim, and no statistical test, effect size or uncertainty estimate is offered. Neither group has documented diagnostic status - the index group has no confirmed diagnosis and the risk factors are unenumerated, while the comparison group is asserted rather than screened - so the contrast is between two undefined populations. The mediator sequence is not counterbalanced, therapist always preceding robot, so the finding that at-risk children did not initiate joint attention toward the robot is confounded with order, accumulated fatigue and the novelty effect the paper elsewhere says it wishes to exploit. And the behavioural finding rests entirely on automated visual-focus-of-attention estimates from a pipeline whose occlusion failures the paper itself reports, with no reliability comparison against human coding of the same sessions - which the study's own tagged behaviour categories would have made straightforward and which is the single most valuable analysis it could have added.

**S-032** [local_08b8027d] — *SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths*

Evaluation on an organiser-held blind test set with labels withheld is a genuine strength and permits direct comparison against other entrants. Batch normalisation, dropout and a small architecture are used as overfitting controls, and the sensitivity of performance to visual feature dimensionality is explored empirically. But the internal split is partitioned by image rather than participant, model selection was performed on that same validation set across a six-configuration grid, and the resulting 17-19 point drop on the blind test is acknowledged by the authors as probable overfitting. There is no cross-validation, no participant-level partitioning, no permutation testing, no class-imbalance handling despite the precision-recall asymmetry, and no calibration or deployment analysis.

**S-033** [local_c6f1209b] — *Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children*

Not applicable in the machine-learning sense; no model is fitted and no individual receives a predicted class. The design's validity rests instead on the paired within-subject comparison, and this is its principal strength: because each child's instructed-behaviour rate is compared against their own spontaneous-behaviour rate, general ability, motivation, familiarity with the robot, session-specific factors and rater leniency are all held constant across the two conditions. That is a genuine methodological advantage at pilot scale, and it is why a study with no comparison group and an unreported sample size can nonetheless support a specific and interpretable claim. Three limits bound it. No between-group inference is possible, which the authors state as their first limitation. Inter-rater reliability is not reported here, although the competent-raters technique is the measurement instrument and the group quantified it in the 2022 follow-up at Kendall's W = 0.65. And no effect size or confidence interval accompanies the test statistic, so the magnitude of the dissociation is not characterised. Set against the modelling studies in this review, the design illustrates a point worth carrying into the synthesis: a within-subject contrast can extract an interpretable finding from a sample far too small for any classifier, and several of the between-group studies charted here with comparable sample sizes would have been better served by the same approach.

**S-034** [local_83b99e73] — *Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers*

Leave-one-out cross-validation over 83 samples, then an attempted verification on the 45 high-risk children. The verification is where the design breaks down: 40 of those 45 are the confirmed-ASD children the model trained on, so only the 5 N-ASD cases are genuinely unseen - and all 5 were misclassified. There is a further subtler problem: the ten features were chosen because t-tests on the full dataset showed them to differ significantly between groups, so feature selection preceded and stood outside the cross-validation loop, leaking label information into every fold. No independent site, no held-out cohort, no calibration analysis, and no comparison against the M-CHAT baseline that all high-risk children had already passed.

**S-035** [local_638860ef] — *Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis*

The strongest validation design in the corpus. Nested cross-validation at development, with feature selection performed inside each of ten nested folds; then a genuinely independent hold-out sample of 14 participants who took no part in development; then direct comparison of development and testing accuracies to verify that nesting controlled overfitting. Statistical significance is assessed. Feature selection stability is quantified with Kuncheva's index. The generalisation claim is additionally stress-tested by the incidental fact that the two samples differ substantially in sex composition, so the independent result holds across a demographic shift. What remains absent: external validation on a different site or protocol, sensitivity and specificity, and any deployment analysis.

**S-036** [local_7547db68] — *Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network*

The weakest validation in the corpus. No train/validation/test split, no cross-validation, no held-out set, and no reported performance on the source expression datasets. The clinical evaluation is a single pass over 20 children whose groups differ in age and recruitment site, with the decision threshold fitted to those same 20 results. There is no independent sample, no external site, no repeat measurement, and no comparison against the diagnostic scales the system is meant to support - which is notable given the paper analyses those scales item by item to justify its design but never compares its output against them.

**S-037** [local_878c259f] — *Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach*

Five-fold cross-validation with participant-level folds by construction, since each child contributes a single 12-feature vector - this avoids the window-level and image-level leakage that affects much of the corpus. Outliers were formally checked with Chauvenet's criterion because they 'could influence the classification accuracy', and none were found. Sample size was justified by a priori power analysis. What is absent: any nested structure separating algorithm selection from performance estimation, so reporting the best of six on the same folds carries selection optimism; no external or independent validation; no permutation testing against chance; no class-imbalance issue (25/25); no confidence intervals despite metrics of exactly 1.000; and no deployment or real-time analysis, though efficiency and minimal human intervention are cited as practical advantages.

**S-038** [local_1579c85a] — *Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through*

The weakest dimension. A single 80/20 split with no cross-validation, no repeated splits and no separation between validation and test sets, and - decisively - no statement that partitioning occurred at child level, when the discussion makes clear the unit is the 1-second data window with approximately 18,597 per subject. Dropout at 20% across four layers is the only overfitting control described. There is no external validation, no permutation testing, no class-imbalance handling despite 5 versus 7 children, and no calibration or deployment analysis. The authors do reason about deployment readiness qualitatively, correctly declining to claim diagnostic utility, but generalisation is addressed only through the aspiration to collect more data.

**S-039** [local_157d6266] — *Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism*

Strong. Three-fold cross-validation with class-balanced folds, and the metric-learning weights are learned only on training folds so that CAMI scores are computed 'completely independently from and without reference to' the HOC scores against which they are validated - an explicit leakage control on the validation comparison itself. The fold count is justified against the bias-variance literature and the analysis is replicated with ten folds in supplementary results. Test-retest reliability across repeated trials provides a form of stability evidence that cross-validation cannot. The small-sample concern is addressed with two quantitative arguments rather than dismissed. What is absent: external or independent validation on a separate cohort, sensitivity and specificity reporting, and any deployment evaluation - though the authors are candid that the current pipeline is not yet fully automatic.

**S-040** [local_8be557e3] — *Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation*

Five-fold cross-validation with a separate randomly selected 10% test set balanced across vocalisation categories, early stopping on validation loss, and best-model checkpointing - properly structured as a protocol. The defect is the unit of division: splitting is by utterance, not by infant, so with 1,125 utterances from 39 children the same speaker appears on both sides of every fold, and the models can exploit speaker identity rather than autism-related acoustics. Given that the two classes are also near-disjoint in age, speaker-level information is doubly informative about the label. No independent test cohort, no external site, no per-infant aggregation, and no comparison against the seven clinical instruments the labels came from.

**S-041** [local_c79e100a] — *Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models*

The weakest link, and knowingly so. Splitting is by gait cycle or by trial, never by participant, across 10 folds; the authors state outright that the same subject's and even the same trial's data can fall on both sides of a split, and proceed on the judgement that the effect is limited. With 21 subjects generating 278 cycles, and with the eight features being timing measures strongly determined by individual stature and habitual cadence, the classifiers can succeed by recognising people rather than by recognising autism - and the paper's own introduction concedes the premise, noting that gait analysis is used for 'person identification' and that 'gait representations are unique to individual people'. Compounding this, hyperparameters were grid-searched on the same cross-validation that produced the reported scores. There is no held-out participant set, no external cohort, no repeated cross-validation, and no significance testing.

**S-042** [local_4fecbf6d] — *Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network*

The strongest validation design among the corpus's speech studies. Splitting is at the participant level (51 train, 21 test), so the 100 sub-samples per child never cross the boundary - the leakage failure mode that undermines most segment-level work here is avoided by construction. The split is then repeated 50 times under explicit distribution-matching constraints (mean, SD and kurtosis of ADOS within +/-10% of the whole sample, skewness within +/-0.3), with rejection sampling until satisfied, and every model is run on all 50. Feature selection for the linear model is nested inside 5-fold cross-validation on training data only. What is missing: the architecture and hyperparameter search appears to sit outside the 50-split loop rather than nested within it, so the reported means retain some selection optimism; there is no external site, no independent cohort and no second language; and no test-retest or longitudinal reliability, which the intended use as a treatment outcome measure would require.

**S-043** [local_95abe653] — *Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning*

Participant-level splitting throughout, repeated 100 times, with per-participant classification by majority vote over that participant's AOI-level predictions - and the choice is argued for explicitly against the segment-level splitting the authors identify in prior EEG and speech work. Cross-study replication with different participants, stimuli and tasks provides a form of generalisation evidence stronger than repeated splitting alone. Two gaps remain. There is no external validation on independently collected data, which the authors address directly: it 'is currently not feasible for our approach due to the task-specific nature of the data, and the unavailability of comparable data collected independently' - an honest statement of a real constraint, and part of why they released their own data. And configuration selection sits outside the validation loop: task, AOI definition, feature set, split ratio and page subset were all chosen by their performance on the same 100 splits.

**S-044** [local_40168c96] — *Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based*

Participant-level splitting into disjoint training and testing sets, repeated over five random permutations with every permutation's result tabulated rather than only the best - a sound design, and better than most of the corpus. Two qualifications. First, the classification threshold is obtained by the maximum between-class variance method applied to the score distribution being classified, so at test time the boundary is set using the test subjects' own scores; this is transductive rather than inductive, and would not transfer to assessing an individual child, which is the deployment scenario the paper's cost and portability arguments envisage. Second, no independent cohort, external site or held-out stimulus set is used, and the cross-paper comparisons against 89% and 92% are drawn from studies on entirely different datasets and populations, so they establish nothing about relative performance.

**S-045** [local_d3852378] — *Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

The cross-validation architecture is correct: leave-one-subject-out folds, normalisation statistics computed on training folds only and applied to the held-out child, and SVM-RFE performed within each fold's training set with median ranks aggregated across folds. There is no participant-level leakage and no feature selection on the full dataset. What sits outside the loop is model selection - both the SVM hyperparameters ('the model was optimized to achieve best Cohen's kappa') and the choice of which of 24 configurations to headline were determined by the same leave-one-out estimate reported as the result. On 47 children this is a large source of optimism. The authors recognise the underlying constraint, noting that larger samples 'could allow validating the ML method, providing also the possibility to test the model' - an acknowledgement that no independent test was possible here.

**S-046** [local_df438dd2] — *Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening*

Leave-one-out cross-validation at both stages, with the autism classification held out at the child level. The perception module's training data is cleanly disjoint from the evaluation cohort - the fine-tuning database comes from 54 children with explicitly no overlap with the 41 participants - which prevents the most serious form of leakage in video-based work. Two weaker points: the stimulus scoring evaluation is at the trial level across 196 samples from 41 children, so the same child appears in training and test folds for that stage; and the decision tree was chosen as best of four on the same leave-one-out estimate reported as the result. There is no independent cohort, no external site, and no held-out test set, which the sample size precludes.

**S-047** [local_cd9e45eb] — *Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism*

10-fold cross-validation with identical splits across all methods and training-set-fitted normalisation per fold, plus 100 bootstrap runs to assess selection stability. Two limitations, one acknowledged and one not. Acknowledged: the authors state directly that validation performance may be over-optimistic and does not represent real-world performance. Not stated: the operating point on the sparsity curve, the hyperparameters and the conclusion that SGIN is best were all determined against that same 10-fold estimate, and no held-out cohort, external site or independent battery was used. The paper's own framing is careful about this - it describes the work as setting 'the stage for concerted techniques designed around engines to iteratively refine and define next-generation biomarkers' rather than as delivering a validated biomarker.

**S-048** [local_56237213] — *The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data*

The study's decisive weakness. No train/test split, cross-validation, held-out sample or repetition procedure is described anywhere in the methods or results. mRMR feature selection uses class labels and there is no statement that it was nested within any resampling scheme. The reported 85.44% is explicitly the maximum of a curve swept across one to forty-five selected features, so both the feature count and the reported figure were chosen against the same data. With 97 participants and an EEG feature pool potentially exceeding 300 variables, this is exactly the configuration in which unnested supervised selection produces substantial upward bias. There is no independent cohort, no external site and no replication. The accuracies should therefore be read as in-sample separability rather than as estimates of predictive performance.

**S-049** [local_f9a5195f] — *Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses*

Leave-one-participant-out cross-validation throughout, with Monte Carlo shuffling tests establishing significance against chance for every reported accuracy, hyperparameters grid-searched on training folds only, and Bonferroni correction applied when interpreting the grid. Most importantly, the design includes a null-model baseline using only age and gender, which is the element almost every other study in this corpus lacks and which is what converts a nominal 71% accuracy into an interpretable finding. What remains absent is an independent cohort or external validation, which the sample size precludes, and the acknowledged possibility that the mid-study chinrest change is confounded with group and could be exploited by the classifiers - a validity threat the authors identify but cannot remove.

**S-050** [local_16a77fb0] — *Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)*

Leave-one-participant-out cross-validation with nested three-fold cross-validation inside each training set for hyperparameter tuning, and an explicit assurance that no test-participant data entered training. The paper states directly that each participant contributes a single aggregate feature vector so that 'the data for the machine-learning analysis did not include any nested repeated measures' - an explicit repudiation of the segment-level splitting that inflates results throughout this literature. Beyond internal validation, the study adds two external reference points that most of the corpus lacks: a majority-vote baseline, beaten significantly, and eight practising clinicians rating the same videos, whose performance the classifier matched. What remains absent is an independent cohort or external site, and the age confound is detected but not corrected in the reported figures.

**S-051** [local_9c4af7a3] — *Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades*

k-fold cross-validation with k unstated, and with supervised feature selection performed on the complete dataset before the split. The paper sets out the sequence unambiguously - pass in data, select columns, apply filter-based feature selection, then split - and reproduces the Azure workflow confirming it. Because mutual information is computed against the class labels, every fold's feature set was chosen using information from that fold's test data, which biases the reported accuracy upward by an amount that cannot be estimated from what is reported. The paper's own description of cross-validation as a method that has 'been shown to lower bias and overfitting' sits directly alongside the step that defeats it. There is no held-out test set, no independent cohort, no external validation and no repetition.

**S-052** [local_b70dae32] — *An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model*

A held-out split by participant, with 8 children and 72 sessions for training and 4 children and 25 sessions for testing, and test participants selected randomly. Splitting by child rather than by session is the correct choice and is stated clearly. Two failures follow it, though. Prediction and evaluation both operate at the session level, so the 25 test observations are roughly six repeated measures from each of four children, and the kappa treats them as independent - the effective sample is 4 children, not 25 sessions. And the test set's composition is unbalanced at the child level (one mild, three minimal by Table 2), which cannot generate the 12-mild, 13-minimal distribution of actual categories reported in Table 4, leaving the evaluation internally inconsistent. There is no cross-validation, no repetition over alternative splits, no independent cohort and no confidence interval.

**S-053** [local_51a0af74] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data*

10-fold cross-validation with SMOTE correctly restricted to training samples - a detail explicitly stated and often got wrong elsewhere in this corpus. The problem is scale of selection: three ensemble strategies, all 511 classifier subsets, thresholds swept in fine increments, five SMOTE variants plus the unbalanced original, and a GridSearchCV over three hyperparameters for each of nine random forests, with the best result across all of that reported from the same 10-fold estimate. There is no outer cross-validation loop, no held-out set, no independent cohort and no repetition over alternative fold partitions. The consequence is that both the headline accuracy and the substantive claim about which segments matter are selection outcomes rather than validated findings.

**S-054** [local_d8d3037b] — *Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study*

A single 70/30 split of 107 participants with threefold cross-validated GridSearchCV inside the training portion, followed by application to a separate group of 22 diagnosed participants. The two-stage structure is the right instinct - fitting on one sample and testing on another population is more than most of the corpus attempts - but its execution defeats the purpose. The test sample contains only positive cases, so nothing about specificity or overall discrimination can be established. It differs from the training population by roughly twelve years of mean age and entirely in sex composition, both of which are model inputs. And the labels are not commensurable: the training positive class is above-median AQ in a non-clinical adult sample, while the test positives are clinically diagnosed individuals whose AQ scores were never measured. There is no repetition over alternative splits, no confidence intervals and no independent replication.

**S-055** [local_991fe435] — *Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task*

Subject-wise leave-one-out cross-validation with no feature selection and a hyperparameter fixed from external data - about as clean an internal validation as this sample size permits, and argued for explicitly against record-wise alternatives with citation to the methodological literature on accuracy inflation. Beyond that, the two cross-group tests constitute a genuine generalisation experiment rarely attempted in this corpus: an entire group is withheld from training and used as an unseen population. The resulting asymmetry - 100% correct on unseen low-functioning children from a model trained on typically developing versus high-functioning, against 53.85% on unseen high-functioning children from a model trained on typically developing versus low-functioning - is interpreted correctly as showing that 'a model trained with more similar groups can perform well with test data from a disparate group, and a model trained with data from more different groups will underperform with test data from an intermediate group'. What remains absent is an independent cohort, an external site and any replication.

**S-056** [local_8692a64f] — *Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis*

The weakest element. A single random split of 83 children into 43 training and 40 testing, with no cross-validation, no repetition over alternative splits, no held-out tuning set and no independent cohort. The two feature hyperparameters were set empirically with no procedure stated and an explicit acknowledgement that other values could improve performance, and the correlation analysis used to justify the feature design was computed across the entire dataset including the test half - so the features whose relevance is demonstrated on all 83 children are the same features evaluated on 40 of them. With a 40-child test set, the reported accuracies carry sampling uncertainty of roughly plus or minus 8 percentage points that is never quantified.

**S-057** [local_4d6fac7e] — *Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network*

The weakest element and the one that governs how the headline should be read. A single 8:2 split with no cross-validation, no repetition and no held-out tuning set. The unit of splitting is never stated, and the reported figures indicate it is not the participant: 42 children split 80/20 gives roughly 8 test children, on which 0.9500, 0.7368 and 0.7895 are unattainable, whereas they correspond precisely to 19/20, 14/19 and 15/19 samples. With EEG divided into 4-second epochs yielding roughly 90 segments per child, sample-level splitting would place segments from the same child on both sides of the boundary. Additionally, the t-tests and the covariance thresholding that determines the graph's edge structure were computed across the entire dataset, so the graph topology the network convolves over was constructed using test-sample information. There is no independent cohort, no external site and no replication.

**S-058** [local_30c622f2] — *Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model*

Five-fold cross-validation with splitting stated explicitly at the subject level, which is the correct unit and is clearly described. Folds were proportionally balanced. Two elements fall outside the loop. ReliefF feature selection is described once, per group, with no statement that it was repeated within folds - and since the group-specific feature sets are the paper's principal scientific claim, whether they were derived using all 88 participants or only training-fold participants materially affects their status. The 20-frame decision threshold was chosen by the Youden index applied to the ROC curve, which is the same curve used to characterise performance, so the operating point is fitted to the evaluation. There is no independent cohort, no external site and no held-out replication.

**S-059** [local_bfc088c7] — *Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation*

Leave-one-out cross-validation at the participant level, explicitly motivated as overfitting protection. The defect is that forward feature selection evaluates candidate features by their classification accuracy, and that accuracy is the leave-one-out estimate itself, so features were chosen to maximise the number subsequently reported. Compounding this, results are reported for every feature count from 1 to 21 across four classifiers and three feature sets - 252 cells - and the maximum is quoted as the headline. There is no outer validation loop, no held-out cohort and no repetition. The saving grace is that the paper prints the entire selection trajectory, so a reader can see that accuracy plateaus at 92.31% from three features through eleven and that the single-feature result is 79.49%, which makes the shape of the result assessable even though the peak is optimistic.

**S-060** [local_25e34bbd] — *Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification*

The decisive weakness. Partitioning is 70/15/15 with six-fold cross-validation, but over 255 voice samples drawn from only 19 children - roughly 13 phonations each - with no statement that a child's samples were confined to one partition. Repeated sustained vowels from one speaker constitute a speaker-identification problem, and MFCC, RASTA-PLP, jitter, shimmer and HNR are the standard feature set for exactly that task, so a classifier can achieve near-perfect accuracy by recognising individuals and mapping them to their known group. Six of 33 reported conditions achieve exactly 100% accuracy with AUC 1, which is what speaker-level leakage produces and which is otherwise implausible for a clinical classification from a single vowel. Additionally, the hidden neuron count was chosen by trial to maximise accuracy separately for each feature set and task, so every figure is a maximum over that search. There is no independent cohort, no external validation and no held-out speaker test.

**S-061** [local_4917150c] — *Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning*

The paper's most important element and the reason it matters to this review. Three-fold cross-validation is run twice on the same model and data under two splitting units. Pooling the 547 images regardless of origin gives approximately 90% accuracy. Splitting the 59 participants first and then assigning their images by ID - so that no child appears on both sides - gives approximately 71%. The authors describe the second explicitly as a further examination of model performance and note the decline as expected. With an average of 9.27 images per child, this constitutes a direct within-study quantification of segment-level inflation: roughly 19 accuracy points, on a design where images from one child are highly correlated. Residual issues: augmented samples presumably inherit their source image's participant, so the image-level figure may be further inflated; only accuracy is reported for the participant-level condition; three epochs is very few; and there is no independent cohort or external site.

**S-062** [local_241ec2c2] — *Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking*

Five-fold cross-validation over subjects, stated explicitly and unambiguously - 'no information of subjects used for testing is used in the learning phase, once the cross-validation was performed over the subjects' - which is the correct unit and is rarely stated this plainly. A second partition operates over frames, with 50 held out from model learning for diagnosis only, deliberately simulating stimulus independence. The authors also pre-empt and address the same-video contamination objection. Two elements nonetheless sit outside the loop: the genetic algorithm feature selection is presented as a single result per group with no indication it was repeated per fold, and the 28-vote decision threshold was chosen by Youden index on the cross-validated ROC. There is no independent cohort or external site.

**S-063** [local_36617ec5] — *Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis*

Five-fold cross-validation repeated four times with means and standard deviations reported, which is better practice than single-split evaluation and gives some sense of variability. The limitation is stated by the authors themselves - no independent sample exists and all participants contributed to validation - and compounded by the fact that both the feature subset and the model were selected on that same repeated cross-validation, across five algorithms and ten datasets. The reported per-dataset maxima are therefore optimistically biased, and the general-approach figure of 0.86 is the best of roughly fifty fits. The ten-feature cap on selection is a sensible guard against overfitting given 144 candidates and 55 participants, and using default hyperparameters removes one further source of selection. There is no external site, no independent cohort and no held-out replication.

**S-064** [local_d8e804d6] — *Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms*

Leave-one-out cross-validation at the participant level, correctly implemented and explicitly motivated as overfitting protection. The weakness is the search: the random feature combination approach deliberately tests every subset of the six features, and the authors justify it on the grounds that exhaustive search 'typically yields equal or higher classification accuracy simply owing to the fact that all features and feature combinations could be tested' - which is precisely the property that makes the resulting maximum optimistic. Sixty-three subsets across five classifiers gives 315 fits, all scored on the same leave-one-out estimate, with no outer loop and no held-out set. The mixed-effects feature screening also used all participants, though since all six features passed and all were retained, this contributed no additional selection. There is no independent cohort or external replication.

**S-065** [local_712542ca] — *Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset*

The decisive weakness, and unusually well documented because the source study performed the missing check. Ten-fold cross-validation is applied over 547 scanpath images drawn from 59 children, with no statement that a child's images were confined to a single fold. The study that released these images ran both configurations and reported approximately 90% accuracy pooling images against approximately 71% holding out participants - so the inflation attributable to image-level splitting on this exact dataset is known and is roughly 19 points. This reanalysis does not repeat that check. Separately, k-means clustering used the entire image set, so the partition determining each model's training and test pool was fitted on data including the test images. There is no held-out set, no participant-level analysis, no confidence intervals and no independent cohort.

**S-066** [local_0ab41681] — *Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder*

Leave-one-subject-out, correctly implemented and explicitly motivated as simulating 'the diagnosis of a new patient in everyday life clinical settings'. Normalisation is fitted on training folds and applied to test data using training statistics, and hyperparameters are grid-searched at each iteration rather than fixed globally. Two robustness analyses extend the validation usefully - varying the number of trials available in the test set, and restricting features to those derivable from the ulnar marker alone - both framed around deployment constraints rather than as statistical exercises. The residual issues are that the ROC operating point is chosen on the evaluation curve, and that no independent cohort or external site is tested, which the small sample precludes.

**S-067** [local_9ca9b2cc] — *Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment*

Not applicable in the classification sense - no model is trained, no individual is assigned a class, and no autism prediction is attempted. The relevant validation question is whether the automated attention measure tracks the construct it claims to measure, and the study answers it with concurrent validation against an independent human standard: agreement with the treating therapist's 0-100 attention ratings on 28 of 34 sessions, reported as 82.4%. That is the right design for the claim and it is described accurately, with the conclusion stating that the system matches 'over 80% of therapist assessments' rather than presenting the figure as diagnostic performance. Four qualifications bound it. The 34 sessions come from 6 children and are therefore clustered, with no adjustment reported, so the effective sample is closer to 6 than to 34. No chance-corrected agreement statistic is given, so how much of the 82.4% reflects the marginal distribution of the therapist's ratings is unknown. No reliability estimate exists for those ratings, so the ceiling on achievable agreement is unknown - and a measure agreeing 82.4% with a standard of unknown reliability could be tracking either the construct or that particular therapist. And the scoring constants are operator-adjustable per child, which is clinically sensible but means the score is not a fixed instrument and its agreement with a clinician may partly reflect tuning. The separate longitudinal claim - that attention rose across seven weeks - has no control condition at all, so it cannot be separated from familiarisation with a novel robot, practice on a repeated task, maturation, or the attention of being in a study; and with 5 of 11 children not completing and no reason given, the trend is computed on a self-selected subgroup. The authors label the causal claim a hypothesis, which is the correct standing for it.

**S-068** [local_02fa4215] — *Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning*

The weakest element. A single 80/20 split of 200 children gives a 40-child test set, with no cross-validation, no repetition across splits and no separate tuning set. SelectKBest's k was chosen as 17 'as it gave the best results', which tunes a selection parameter against the reported evaluation. Twenty-seven algorithm-by-selection combinations were evaluated and the maximum quoted in the abstract. There is no independent cohort, no external validation and no confidence interval, so the reported 95% cannot be distinguished from the 90% cells by anything the paper provides.

**S-069** [local_29a3fc54] — *Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism*

Five-fold cross-validation with training, development and test sets rotated and an explicit statement that model parameters were learned only from training examples and were 'totally blinded from the test examples'. Class imbalance is handled by iterative undersampling to 28 per class, repeated until scores converged at around 100 iterations - a substantially more rigorous treatment than a single balanced draw, since it averages away the randomness of which majority-class participants are selected. Confidence intervals are computed on every AUC. The IQ-matched subsample analysis functions as an internal replication under a controlled confound and returns a higher AUC (88.27%) than the main analysis, which is strong evidence that IQ was not driving the result. What remains: RFECV and the best-activity selection were both performed across the same cross-validation used for reporting, with no outer loop; and no independent cohort or external site was tested.

**S-070** [local_b7ec3755] — *Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images*

The benchmark's fixed 300/100 image split, with hyperparameters tuned by out-of-bag error on the training portion. Three weaknesses. The split partitions stimuli, not participants: all 28 children appear on both sides, so the model can learn subject-specific viewing idiosyncrasies from a child's training-image scanpaths and apply them to that same child's test-image scanpaths - the segment-level leakage pattern that recurs throughout this corpus, although here the low absolute performance suggests little was gained from it. Second, 23 classifiers plus a three-parameter grid were evaluated before one was chosen, and the resulting optimism is directly visible: the selection table reports 68.5% for TreeBagger while the test set returns 0.59, a nine-point gap that the paper presents without reconciling the two numbers. Third, no repeated splits, no cross-validation over participants, no confidence intervals and no significance test against the 0.59 competitor, so the claimed tie for first place rests on a single comparison of two point estimates on 100 images.

**S-071** [local_684969f6] — *Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data*

The strongest external evaluation arrangement in the corpus paired with the weakest partitioning principle. On the strong side: the test labels were withheld by the ICME 2019 organisers and all test performance was computed by them, so no amount of iteration could tune to the test set - the only genuinely third-party-scored evaluation here - and validation results are averaged over repeated runs with standard deviations reported. On the weak side: the partition is over images (240 train / 60 validation / 100 test), not over children, so all 28 participants appear in all three sets, and a model that learns a child's characteristic viewing tempo from their training scanpaths can apply it to their test scanpaths. The authors identify this mechanism themselves as the explanation for scanpath-only parity, which makes it the corpus's only self-diagnosed instance of the leakage pattern - but they do not draw the consequence that it bounds the 62.13%. The benchmark's fixed splits preclude re-partitioning without forfeiting the blind test, which is a real constraint rather than an oversight; the appropriate response would have been to state the resulting ceiling explicitly. A further diagnostic sits unremarked in the tables: validation-optimal and test-optimal configurations differ in both pipelines (LSTM 67.23% on validation but 60.40% on test; BrMLP-SP-F best on validation, BrMLP-SP on test), which the authors attribute to training and validation being 'more similar to each other than to the test dataset' without noting that this makes the validation set unfit for model selection.

**S-072** [local_35004e74] — *Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children*

The corpus's reference implementation of correct validation for a segment-generating modality. Three properties matter.
