Participant-wise partition: the 136 children are split 68/68 into training and Testing Set 1, matched on diagnosis, age, gender and ADOS module, so no child's frames appear on both sides - and matching the partitions on covariates, not merely the groups, is a refinement almost nothing else here applies. Participant-level aggregation: the network trains and predicts on 5-second segments (~505 per video, ~34,000 in training), but every segment prediction within a video is averaged into one ASD probability per child before any metric is computed, so the reported 80.9% is over 68 children and not over 34,000 clips. This is precisely the correction that Cilia had to apply retrospectively, watching image-level accuracy of ~90% fall to ~71% at participant level, and applying it by construction is what makes this figure comparable to a clinical one. Hyperparameter selection is confined to an 80-20 split inside the training set, with the least-validation-loss checkpoint carried forward. Two limits persist. Testing Set 2, though larger, contains only autistic children and comes from the same cohort, so it estimates sensitivity in a slightly older sample rather than replicating externally - no independent site or cohort is tested. And the covariate matching does not extend to cognitive level: best-estimate IQ is measured, differs between a typically developing and an autistic group as a matter of course, and correlates with the model's output at -0.283, so some portion of the separation may reflect general developmental level rather than autism specifically. No leave-one-site-out or examiner-held-out analysis addresses the parallel possibility that examiner behaviour contributes.

**S-073** [local_fa91fc18] — *Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities*

The study's decisive weakness, and the reason its numbers are not comparable to participant-level results elsewhere in this corpus. The dataset is 1,500 samples formed as 60 subjects x 25 tasks, explicitly 'randomized between subjects and tasks', and the folds are drawn so that 'for each fold, we take the 10% of the samples for testing and the remaining 90% for training, regardless of the number of ASD or TD subjects in the test or training set'. Every child therefore has roughly 22 or 23 of their 25 vectors in training whenever the remaining two or three are tested. Because each vector is an average of that child's habitual movement dynamics within a task, the network can identify the individual from their kinematic signature and recover the diagnosis from that identification rather than from any group-general motor property - the same mechanism Liaqat et al. diagnose explicitly in their own eye-tracking data and that Cilia quantified as a fall from ~90% to ~71% when the unit was corrected. No participant-held-out analysis is reported anywhere, so the magnitude of the inflation here is unknown. A second, independent issue concerns which number is reported: ten-fold cross-validation with five repetitions returned 88 +/- 3%, and the paper then states that 'for the successive analysis, we used the best trained model across the 10-fold', from which the 93% accuracy, 0.87 sensitivity, 0.98 specificity, ROC curve and complete feature-importance ordering are all derived. The best of ten is a maximum, not an estimate, and it is the figure carried into the abstract, the Discussion and the Conclusion while the cross-validated 88 +/- 3% appears once. Hidden-layer width was additionally selected on the same cross-validation. The compounded effect is that the reported operating characteristics come from a model chosen for performing best on data structurally related to what it was trained on.

**S-074** [local_115dfe8d] — *A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children*

Done correctly, and stated in terms that leave no ambiguity: 'we perform a 10-fold subject-independent cross-validation to evaluate the performance of the proposed model, where each subject is regarded as a sample', with stratified sampling to preserve the class ratio in every fold, each fold tested exactly once, and the average across folds reported with standard deviations. Because every child contributes exactly one feature vector - EEG features are averaged across that child's clean segments, gaze features aggregated across their two trials - there is no possibility of the segment-level leakage that inflates results throughout this corpus, and the 95.56% is a genuine participant-level figure. Feature normalisation is also fitted on training data only. Two gaps remain. The three network geometries, the noise level, both learning rates and both iteration counts are stated as given, with no description of how they were arrived at, so selection optimism cannot be excluded and may be substantial across four compared architectures. And there is no external validation - no second site, no held-out cohort, no replication sample - so the estimate, though internally sound, rests entirely on 90 children from two institutions in one city. The correct comparison for this study's 95.56% is therefore not the segment-level 90%-plus figures elsewhere in the corpus but the small set of participant-level results, against which it stands as one of the highest and, on validation design, one of the better supported.

**S-075** [local_5b7ea7dc] — *AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Correct in its most important respect and incomplete in a secondary one. The partition is subject-disjoint: 40 children in training and validation (16+16 and 4+4), 36 in test set #1, 18 in test set #2, accounting for all 94 participants with no child in more than one partition. This forecloses the identity-leakage route that inflates several other studies here, and it is the reason 0.916 can be compared to Kojovic's 80.9% and Han's 95.56% rather than to segment-level figures. Two independent test sets rather than one is a further strength, and making them differ in preprocessing turns the second into a domain-shift check rather than a redundant repetition. What is incomplete: the reported test metrics are clip-level, computed over 416 and 184 clips rather than over 36 and 18 children, so within-child correlation inflates the apparent precision even though it does not bias the point estimate; the paper describes per-subject probability averaging for training and validation but not for testing, and no per-child accuracy appears. There is also no cross-validation - a single fixed split with 32 training children - so the estimate carries no measure of split-to-split variability, and no external cohort or site. Finally, whatever architecture and hyperparameter selection occurred is undocumented, so it cannot be established that the validation set was used only once.

**S-076** [local_87fe26aa] — *Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Leave-one-out cross-validation over 80 children with the participant as the unit - structurally the right design, and it forecloses the within-subject leakage that inflates Simeoli, Liaqat, Mazumdar and Akter. But two selection steps precede it and contaminate it. The EEG feature set was determined by running independent-samples t-tests on band power across all 80 children and retaining the 12 region-band combinations reaching significance; only then was classification with leave-one-out cross-validation performed on those features. Every held-out child therefore contributed their label to the choice of features used to classify them - the classic selection-bias pattern, and one that inflates the EEG modality specifically, which is the modality the paper concludes is most discriminative and which anchors its central claim. Second, the number of gaze clusters was tested at four values and 'the final value of K was determined from the experimental results', so a preprocessing hyperparameter was also chosen on classification performance across the full sample. A third, milder issue is that the headline 87.50% is the best of three classifiers; the paper reports averages for single modalities but not for the fusion. There is no external validation, no independent cohort and no repeated-split estimate of variability. The correct reading is that the participant-level design is sound but that the reported figures - particularly for EEG and for the fusion that depends on it - are optimistic by an unmeasured margin.

**S-077** [local_893ce2fa] — *An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images*

The corpus's weakest evaluation design, and the weakness is threefold. First, no train/test split, cross-validation scheme, held-out set or partition of any kind is described anywhere in the paper; the only replication is 30 reruns of the optimiser. Second, augmentation preceded whatever evaluation occurred, and the authors state their purpose plainly: 'We included a data augmentation step to generate synthetic samples to enlarge the training and testing data.' Flips, translations and blurs of a source image are near-duplicates of it, so populating a test set with them guarantees that the model has effectively seen every test instance. Third, and independently of augmentation, the 547 source images come from a small number of children contributing roughly nine images each, and no participant identifiers exist in the released image set, so images from the same child necessarily span any partition. Layered on top, the metaheuristic optimises C and gamma against the KELM's mean squared error with the accuracy-versus-iteration curve in Figure 4 rising monotonically over ten iterations, which indicates the search is scored on the same predictions that are reported. The instructive comparison is with Cilia and colleagues, who built this dataset and reported that image-level accuracy near 90% fell to approximately 71% when computed per child. This paper reports 98.8% on the same images, cannot compute a per-child figure because it records no participants, and does not cite the correction. The gap between 71% and 98.8% is the measure of what these three compounding decisions add.

**S-078** [local_dffe4127] — *Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals*

The reference standard for this corpus, and the source of its most transferable methodological lesson. The classification procedure holds out a third of each group, samples a 10-minute epoch at random from the combined 43-minute dataset, trains on the remainder and repeats 10,000 times - so the estimate is not a single split and every participant is held out repeatedly. Decisively, the chance level is derived empirically from a null distribution and comes to 0.607 rather than the 0.500 that an imbalanced 48/105 design might naively suggest; the observed 0.618 therefore exceeds chance by about one percentage point at p = 0.039, which the authors correctly describe as 'only slightly greater than would be expected by chance' and as confirming that heterogeneity 'precludes diagnostically robust classification'. Had the same number been compared against 50%, it would have been reported as a 12-point improvement. Beyond classification, the validation apparatus includes: leave-one-participant-out construction of every reference heatmap 'to eliminate bias'; normalisation of area-specific gaze by successful on-screen frames so that tracking quality cannot leak into the behavioural measures; a partial correlation control confirming reliability is not driven by on-screen time; measurement of stimulus familiarity and verification that it affects no result; replication of every analysis across two distinct stimuli and across epoch durations from 10 minutes down to seconds; bootstrap confidence intervals on all effect sizes; permutation testing for fingerprinting; FDR correction throughout; and two independent sites with site membership displayed rather than pooled. The single most important output for this review is the fingerprinting result itself: gaze identifies an individual out of 153 at five to ten times chance from 2 minutes of data. That is a direct measurement of the individual-identity signal that any train/test split failing to separate participants will allow a classifier to exploit, and it explains quantitatively why studies here that split by image, segment, task or augmented copy report accuracies far above what participant-level designs achieve.

**S-079** [local_2b766683] — *Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech*

Correct on the dimension that matters most in this corpus and incomplete on a secondary one. The fold constraint is stated explicitly and reasoned exactly right: 'all clips spliced from a given child's video had to be included in the same fold to prevent models from learning from child-specific recording idiosyncrasies, including environmental background noise and audio quality'. That names both the mechanism and its two concrete forms, and it is the discipline missing from Cilia's image-level folds, Simeoli's task-level folds, Liaqat's image-wise splits and Gaspar's augmented copies. Fold composition is tabulated so the balance can be checked, all three models are evaluated on the same folds, and metrics are averaged with standard deviations. Three gaps remain. Metrics are clip-level rather than child-level, so 850 correlated observations from 58 children are treated as the effective sample and no per-child accuracy is available. There is no held-out test set beyond cross-validation, and the random forest's hyperparameters were 'manually chosen' with no procedure described, so some selection optimism is unquantified. And most importantly, no analysis addresses whether the classifier is separating diagnosis or separating age and sex - there is no age-matched subsample, no covariate adjustment, and no age-only or sex-only baseline, despite both variables differing markedly between groups and both directly determining child vocal acoustics. The validation protocol is therefore sound against leakage and silent on confounding.

**S-080** [local_2895bdf0] — *Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection*

Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, and uniquely in this corpus the choice is justified by citation to the methodological literature on exactly this issue - Saeb et al. (2017) on subject-wise versus record-wise validation - with the rationale that it approximates 'the clinically relevant use-case of diagnosis in unseen participants'. Because each participant contributes a single averaged feature vector, there is no possibility of the within-subject leakage that inflates results throughout this review. Robustness was checked against 10-fold cross-validation, giving 0.9235 against 0.9205 with p = 0.9219, confirming the estimate is not an artefact of the resampling scheme. Comparisons between models use DeLong's test rather than informal inspection. Sex-stratified models were fitted to test whether the sex imbalance drove the result. The confounding variables were tested rather than acknowledged. What remains: the soft-margin constants were chosen per model on performance and the linear configuration was selected for reporting over tuned non-linear alternatives, so some selection optimism is present though bounded by the small hyperparameter space; feature selection was performed under 10-fold rather than leave-one-out for software reasons; and there is no independent replication cohort - the sample is a single site and overlaps with the two prior papers whose findings are being replicated, so the 'replication' is of models rather than of data. The authors' own framing is appropriately cautious about all of this, describing the results as 'preliminary but very encouraging'.

**S-081** [local_423b636b] — *Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers*

Sound in every respect that this corpus commonly gets wrong, with the residual weakness being confounding rather than leakage. The unit is the participant, since all features are per-child summaries; leave-one-out cross-validation is used and justified by citation to Vabalas et al. on overoptimistic classification; AUCs carry Hanley-McNeil confidence intervals; and classifier configurations are compared by a formal criterion rather than by inspecting point estimates. Two further design properties strengthen the estimate beyond what the cross-validation alone provides. The class ratio of 41:416 approximates real screening prevalence, so the AUC is not estimated under an artificially balanced design - a distinction that matters enormously for translation, since the same AUC implies very different positive predictive value at 9% prevalence than at 50%. And diagnosis followed rather than preceded enrolment, so the sample is not conditioned on already being diagnosed, removing the referral filter that shapes almost every other study here. What remains unaddressed: age and missing data were covaried but sex was not, on stated power grounds; ethnicity and caregiver education differ significantly and are never revisited; cognitive ability differs and cannot be adjusted because Mullen data exist only for the autistic group; the 12 children with non-autism diagnoses were excluded, so the discrimination tested is against typical development rather than against developmental concern; and there is no independent replication cohort, though this study is itself a replication and extension of the group's earlier rate-only finding in a larger sample with redesigned stimuli.

**S-082** [local_ffa35101] — *Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study*

The strongest aspect of the study, and stated in the terms that matter: 'Several procedures were performed in the classification pipeline to further avoid overfitting and optimistic bias due to limited sample size and the high-dimensionality of data'. Three properties follow. Repeated 10-fold cross-validation is used rather than a single split. Dimensionality reduction into principal components and hyperparameter tuning are both performed 'in a nested fashion' inside the cross-validation, so neither the components nor the hyperparameters are informed by held-out data - the single most common source of optimistic bias in high-dimensional small-sample classification, and one that Liao and colleagues elsewhere in this corpus violate directly by selecting features on the full sample before cross-validating. Significance is established by permutation rather than assumed from a nominal chance level, with 5,001 iterations, and the resulting p values are what license the paper's negative claims. The unit is the participant throughout. What remains: no independent replication cohort, though the two-language design provides a form of internal generalisation test that is arguably stronger for the question at hand; no confidence intervals on the AUCs; no formal test comparing feature classes; and the unexplained 40% attrition from the English autistic sample, which is a selection concern that no amount of validation discipline can address. The combined-language model's validity also rests on the supplementary demonstration that language differences in the rhythm features do not account for the classification, a check that is performed but reported outside the main text.

**S-083** [local_81ecbc6f] — *Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings*

Leave-one-out cross-validation with the participant as the held-out unit, chosen deliberately for small-sample efficiency, and correctly described. Because each participant is represented by a single vector there is no possibility of utterance-level leakage. What is not controlled is selection: only the best classifier per input combination is reported, across three families and, for the masking configurations, a 27-point hyperparameter grid, all evaluated on the same folds that produce the reported numbers. With 50 participants and six reported configurations each maximised over several classifiers, the optimism is unquantified and could plausibly account for a substantial part of the 12-point gap between the best models (0.72) and the human raters (0.60). No permutation test, confidence interval or AUC is reported to bound this. Set against that, the study's benchmarking design provides a form of validation that internal resampling cannot: the human raters constitute an empirical performance floor obtained on identical input, and the standardised instruments an empirical ceiling obtained on identical participants, both of which anchor the model figures in a way no single-model study can achieve. The authors themselves qualify the ceiling, noting that their instruments exceeded their own published validation figures because the sample was selected for clear-cut cases while the validation sample included non-spectrum clinical participants.

**S-084** [local_bc62bc4b] — *Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening*

Two claims are made and both are the right ones to make, but neither can be verified from what is reported. The cross-validation is stated to be participant-based - 'the data is divided into ten subsets based on participants... ensuring that all participants' data appeared either in the training or test set' - which forecloses within-participant leakage, though since each child contributes a single feature vector the safeguard is structural rather than earned. Feature selection is stated to use training data only. Against these, three issues remain. The analysed sample cannot be reconciled with the 133 recruited: the accuracy grid across all six results tables is consistent with roughly 20 per class and inconsistent with 61 and 72, and the balancing statement acknowledges that classes were equalised without saying how or how much was discarded. The Wrapper feature-selection method is by definition driven by classification accuracy, and while WEKA's attribute-selection mode can be run under cross-validation, the description does not establish that selection was refitted inside each classification fold rather than performed once and then used throughout - a distinction that determines whether the reported figures carry selection optimism. And the headline 87.5% is the maximum over 24 reported configurations, with no correction, no confidence interval and no held-out confirmation. The public data posting is the mitigating factor: it is the only route by which an external reader could resolve the sample question.

**S-085** [local_889d9bd6] — *Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children*

Participant-level leave-one-out cross-validation, described in enough detail to confirm that each held-out child's classifier was 'determined using only the data from the other subjects, omitting the one predicted'. Cohorts were modelled separately, so no information crosses between them. Single-area classifications were tested against non-parametric permutation, which is what establishes that several areas do not exceed chance rather than leaving weak accuracies to be read as weak positives. The statistical analyses are protected by covariate adjustment, variance-assumption testing with an appropriate substitution, Tukey correction and multivariate-t adjustment for the interaction contrasts. Three gaps remain. There is no independent validation cohort, acknowledged. The two quality-control exclusions - calibration failure and off-screen fixation - are described but their counts are not reported, and both plausibly operate differentially by group, so the analysed sample is a compliant subset of unknown size and composition. And the reference standard is DSM-5 plus CARS without observational confirmation, which bounds what any validation can establish. The most valuable validation-adjacent contribution, though, is not internal: by calculating that 80% sensitivity and 82% specificity yields a 4.2% positive predictive value at 1% prevalence, the paper supplies the translation step that converts a cross-validated accuracy into a statement about deployment, and it is the only study in the corpus to do so numerically.

**S-086** [local_361b59fb] — *Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

The validation design is the study's principal contribution to this review and differs in kind from everything else charted here. Rather than resampling within a dataset, the model was locked with thresholds fixed on prior training and testing data, and then evaluated prospectively on consecutively enrolled children whose diagnoses were established afterwards by an independent blinded specialist consensus. All three Device inputs were blinded from one another and from the output; the specialists were blinded to the Device. The trial was registered before initiation, so the endpoints - PPV and NPV with FDA-agreed floors - were pre-specified rather than selected post hoc. Participant flow is fully documented with attrition causes including the COVID-19 disruption quantified. The two features that make this the corpus's benchmark are the population and the disclosure. The population is the referral cohort the tool is meant for, with 28.7% prevalence and only 9.4% neurotypical, so predictive values are directly deployable rather than requiring prevalence correction - the calculation Kong and colleagues perform hypothetically is here unnecessary because the design supplies it directly. The disclosure is the counterfactual: sensitivity 51.6% and specificity 18.5% without abstention, against 98.4% and 78.9% with it. No other paper in this corpus reports what its performance would be under a less favourable operating decision. What remains open is the temporal question the authors themselves identify - whether children given indeterminate or negative outputs at 18-72 months go on to receive autism diagnoses later - which the planned registrational study is designed to address and without which the NPV of 98.3% is a cross-sectional rather than a prognostic figure.

**S-087** [local_afdb603d] — *Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.*

The weakest dimension, and the authors say so more clearly than most. Feature selection by Mann-Whitney test was performed across all 28 samples before any split, so the 16 retained features are those that best separate the very children on whom the classifiers are then evaluated. The consequence is stated in advance and with a supporting citation: 'the feature selection operated on clinical recorded data can lead to high performances of the classifier, which are not reproducible on new data considering all the speech production. This aspect produces a bias in the results obtained by the classifier when used to create a tool able to distinguish the speech productions of the disease. For instance, while performing the same task on people with Alzheimer Dementia's speech, Luz et al. (2020) report that the performance evaluation metrics drop consistently if applied to the same dataset without performing the feature selection.' The scope is then narrowed accordingly - 'this work aims to test the feature extraction effectiveness and not automatically classify ASD from new speech data' - which is the right response to a known bias, though it does not remove it from the reported numbers. Three further limits compound it: an 80/20 split leaves six test samples; ten runs per method were performed with the best reported alongside the means; and there is no independent validation, no permutation test, no confidence interval and no baseline. The single most important validity threat, however, is not statistical at all: features selected for their ability to separate two groups recorded on different equipment will select for the equipment difference, and no amount of validation discipline within the dataset can detect that.

**S-088** [local_4f7e7eb3] — *Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques*

Two distinct problems, one shared with several studies in this corpus and one specific to this paper. The shared problem is the unit of analysis: 547 images come from 59 children at roughly 9.3 images each, and the 80/20 partition is by image with no participant grouping described, so images from the same child appear in both training and test. Cilia and colleagues, who produced this dataset, measured the consequence directly, reporting image-level accuracy near 90% falling to approximately 71% when recomputed per child; that correction is neither cited nor applied here. The specific problem is that the headline figure pools phases: the abstract and conclusion report 99.8% while the results text states the same model achieved 100% in training and validation and 98.7% in testing, and describes 99.8% as 'the overall accuracy'. One element is handled correctly and deserves credit - augmentation by flipping, rotation, displacement and shearing was applied only to the training and validation partitions, expanding them from 175 and 262 to 1,750 and 1,834 images, while the test set remained unaugmented at 44 and 66. This is the correct discipline and is precisely what Gaspar and colleagues violated on the same dataset by augmenting the testing data as well. Against that, there is a single fixed split with no repetition, no cross-validation, no confidence intervals and no external validation, so the reported differences among six configurations rest on one partition of 109 test images.

**S-089** [local_db6c2d7c] — *Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With*

The split is child-disjoint and stated as such, which is the single most important property and is applied correctly even under a feature construction that generates heavily overlapping windows: 324 videos to training, 71 to validation and 54 to a held-out test set, 'ensuring that all videos corresponding to a single child were assigned to the same set'. Hyperparameters were selected on validation and only the three best configurations evaluated on the test set, so the held-out estimate is not tuned. Group comparisons are protected by permutation testing with Bonferroni correction across both feature families. Three limits remain. There is no independent cohort. There is no baseline or null for the classification results, which matters acutely given a test set of 43 autistic and 11 comparison videos where the majority-class weighted-average recall of roughly 0.80 exceeds the reported 0.656 - a comparison the paper does not make. And the split is by video within child rather than being balanced on any covariate, so with an unreported age span of 2 to 15 years the training and test partitions could differ substantially in age composition without this being detectable. The overall picture is a study that validates its statistical claims rigorously and its predictive claim only loosely, while describing the latter as mild.

**S-090** [local_8b5fb23b] — *Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms*

This is simultaneously the study's weakest and its most valuable dimension, because it fails and then measures its own failure. Three separate contaminations affect the headline analyses. Rotation augmentation was applied to all 547 images before partitioning, so rotated copies of the same source image appear in training and test. Principal component analysis was fitted on the complete 547x10,001 array (and later the 2,566x10,000 array) before splitting, so the components for the conventional models are informed by test images. And images from the same child span the partition regardless of augmentation, at roughly 9.3 per participant. The authors identify the first of these explicitly - 'possible data contamination as similar replicates are entered into the training set, as seen in the testing dataset' - and respond by constructing a one-image-per-participant subset evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation, which removes both the augmentation and the within-child duplication. The result is 72.88% accuracy with 58.62% sensitivity, against 97.00% AUC in the contaminated condition. That within-study drop of roughly 24 points, produced by the same architecture on the same source images, is the cleanest quantification of validation-induced inflation available in this review, and its close agreement with the approximately 71% Cilia and colleagues obtained by the same correction on the same data amounts to an independent replication of the corrected figure. The remaining weakness is that the participant-level analysis itself is thin - 59 samples, one arbitrarily selected image per child, leave-one-out, no confidence interval - so 72.88% is 43 correct classifications and carries a wide interval.

**S-091** [local_6dcefc34] — *Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism*

Among the best-handled in the corpus on the dimensions the paper controls. Leakage is named explicitly and designed against: 'To avoid incorporating information from the distribution of the training data into the test set (i.e., data leakage), we carried out the following preprocessing steps separately for each test-train split of the data' - covering outlier removal, k-nearest-neighbour imputation, standardisation and SMOTE upsampling. Performing imputation and resampling inside the fold rather than on the full dataset is the correct handling and is violated by several studies here, including Liao and colleagues who select features on the whole sample and Kanhirakadavath and colleagues who fit principal components before splitting. The validation structure is genuine nested cross-validation - inner four-fold grid search selecting hyperparameters by AU-ROC, outer held-out fold estimating performance, repeated seven times for 28 estimates - so hyperparameter selection cannot contaminate the reported figures. Two residual issues. Feature selection was performed by inspecting importances across the 28 iterations and then retraining on the duration subset, so that selection used information from all folds; the effect is likely small since the selection is a binary family choice made on a large and statistically tested difference, but it is not nested. And the unit of analysis is not stated, so whether the folds are child-disjoint cannot be confirmed. Set against the corpus, the reported AU-ROC of 0.745 is modest precisely because these controls are in place, and the paper presents it as feasibility rather than accuracy.

**S-092** [local_65974fc7] — *Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction*

The weakest dimension, with three compounding problems. The split is by recording: 408 autistic and 428 comparison recordings train, the remainder test, described as randomly selected from 511 and 506 recordings originating in more than 80 and more than 60 children - so approximately six utterances per child are randomly assigned between the two sets and utterances from the same child appear on both sides. For one-second single-word samples from the same speaker in the same session, this approaches speaker identification rather than group classification, and it is the same failure that Kanhirakadavath and colleagues quantified on gaze images as a fall from 97% to 73% when the unit was corrected. There is no cross-validation of the classifier, no repetition and no confidence interval, so the reported figures come from one partition of 181 test recordings. And Method 2's headline of 59.71% is the best of 256 frequency sequences, chosen after inspecting all of them, with no correction and no report of the distribution across the other 255. Layered over all of this is the unresolved question of what the two ICA observation channels are: if the equations mean what they say, each unmixing matrix is estimated from a paired autistic and comparison utterance, so Method 1's features would be functions of a label-dependent pairing and the 98.51% would not measure classification at all. The paper provides no information with which to exclude that reading.

**S-093** [local_988c462e] — *The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation*

Among the better-designed validations in the corpus for a regression problem, with one important limitation that is interpretive rather than procedural. The split is by child and repeated 50 times, and - distinctively - each split is constructed so that the ADOS score distribution matches the full sample on four moments: 'we divided the children into training and testing datasets while balancing the distribution of ADOS scores (mean, standard deviation, kurtosis, and skewness) in each dataset'. Matching skewness and kurtosis as well as mean and variance is the right control for a bimodally distributed target, since an unlucky split could otherwise place most of the low-scoring comparison children on one side and inflate or deflate the correlation. Reporting means and standard deviations across the 50 repetitions rather than a single split follows properly. Hyperparameters were tuned by random search under five-fold cross-validation, though whether that tuning sat inside the 50 outer splits or was performed once beforehand is not stated - which leaves some selection optimism unquantified. The substantive limitation is what the correlation measures rather than how it was estimated: computed across a sample where the autistic group averages ADOS 14.6 and the comparison group 3.2, R = 0.606 conflates between-group separation with within-group severity grading, and no within-autism correlation is reported. That is the analysis that would distinguish a severity estimator from a diagnostic classifier expressed on a continuous scale, and it is the same conflation this review has flagged in Kojovic and colleagues.

**S-094** [local_76de1c03] — *The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children*

Not applicable in the machine-learning sense, since no model is fitted and no individual receives a predicted class - and the corresponding measurement-validation work is done properly. Six independent raters scored the same video material against definitions published in an appendix, inter-rater reliability was assessed with Kendall's W and reported at 0.65 (p < 0.001), and the Additional movements subscale returned an internal-consistency alpha of 0.77. Non-parametric tests appropriate to small ordinal samples were used throughout. The binding limitation is statistical power: with five children per group, only large effects are detectable, no confidence interval or effect size is reported, and nothing in the design supports individual-level inference - which is consistent with the study's own claims, since it asserts a group difference and a paradigm, not a classifier. Two internal-validity issues are unaddressed. Rater blinding to diagnosis is nowhere discussed, and since diagnoses were held in kindergarten records and every measurement is a human judgement, this is the study's main risk of bias. And no cognitive or language measure was obtained, so reduced turn-taking in a game requiring the child to understand the game cannot be separated from general developmental level. Set against the modelling studies in this review, however, the study has one structural advantage that no amount of downstream methodology can substitute for: its measurement instrument is published, its reliability is quantified, and its construct is named in advance.

**S-095** [local_3ba6d25c] — *Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach*

This is the paper's weak point and the reason its two headline numbers should be read very differently from each other. Segment level: tenfold cross-validation with random partition of segments. The text is unambiguous that the unit is the segment ('all behavior samples were randomly partitioned into 10 subsamples'), and there is no statement anywhere that a child's segments were kept together. With 19 + 20 children each contributing tens to hundreds of windows from one continuous recording, adjacent segments from one child are near-duplicates in feature space, and the classifier can exploit stable individual gaze idiosyncrasies - the exact leakage that Keles et al. in this corpus quantified directly by identifying individuals from gaze at 35.4% against 6.2% chance. So 74.15% is not an estimate of performance on an unseen child. Participant level: the aggregation is applied to those already-leaky segment labels, and then two further quantities are optimised on the same 39 children - the window length (10 candidates, Table 4 shows accuracies 0.77 to 0.87) and the threshold (a sweep whose grid is not specified, optimal values 0.40 to 0.56). Reporting the maximum of that joint search as the study's accuracy is best-of-many reporting; the median of Table 4 is 0.78. Feature selection is likewise unnested, run once on all data with the chosen subset reused in every fold. What the study does do right is the segment-level chance floor: the majority-class baseline is computed and plotted at every window length precisely because the class imbalance is group-linked, and the SVM beats it throughout. That is more care about chance than most studies here take, which makes the absence of the corresponding participant-level baseline or permutation test more conspicuous. A corrected design would partition the 39 children into folds, generate segments within folds, run forward feature selection inside each training fold, and select the window length and threshold on training children only - and would very likely report a materially lower number, as Cilia et al. found when they moved from image-level to participant-level evaluation of the same data.

**S-096** [local_70a30e2b] — *A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features*

Better than most on the split unit, weaker on everything downstream. The unit of splitting is the child - one aggregate feature vector per participant - so the segment-level leakage that inflates results throughout this corpus is impossible here by construction, and the paper deserves credit for that even though it is a consequence of the aggregate representation rather than a deliberate safeguard. The reported scheme is an 80/20 division with 5-fold cross-validation rotating which 20% is held out, giving fold test sets of about 9 children and averaged metrics. The problems lie elsewhere. First, feature selection: two consecutive rounds of backward elimination were run over the feature set, described in a section that precedes the results and with the surviving 10 features named as a fixed outcome, with no indication that the procedure was repeated within each training fold. Selecting 10 of 54 features on all 46 children and then cross-validating the chosen subset is a well-characterised source of optimism, and it is most severe exactly in this regime of many features and few samples - the regime the authors themselves identify as the reason feature reduction was needed. Second, model selection: three algorithms, three SVM kernels and four feature configurations were evaluated on the same 46 children, and the maximum of that grid is the abstract's claim. Third, no chance baseline: the majority class alone gives 60.9%, and no permutation test or confidence interval is reported, so with roughly 9 children per test fold a single child's label moves fold accuracy by 11 percentage points and the difference between the 78.61% and 85.56% configurations is a handful of children. Fourth, prevalence: 61% autism in the modelled sample against a population rate near 1-2%, with no prevalence-adjusted metric. The corrective design is straightforward and worth stating for the synthesis - move both backward-elimination rounds and the kernel/algorithm choice inside the training folds, report the mean and spread across folds rather than the best cell of the grid, add a majority-class and a permutation baseline, and retain the CP and fragile X children as a differential-diagnosis check.

**S-097** [local_a22f97df] — *A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities*

The critical weakness, and it is unacknowledged. The dataset is stated plainly: 60 participants x 25 tasks = 1,500 observations of 12 features, with a parallel 1,500-element label vector repeating each child's diagnosis 25 times. Cross-validation is 10-fold over that observation set, giving 91.2% +/- 5.6%. There is no statement that a child's 25 rows were assigned to a single fold, and the description ('we used the k-fold cross-validation with k = 10 and returning the average accuracy', applied to 'the collected dataset') implies observation-level partitioning. Under that scheme every test observation has roughly 22-23 siblings from the same child, same session and same hand in the training data, differing only in Leiter-3 subtest and difficulty level. Movement kinematics are strongly individual - speed and acceleration profiles are close to a motor signature - so a 12-input, 2-latent model can separate children rather than groups and score highly, exactly the leakage Keles et al. quantified directly elsewhere in this corpus by identifying individuals from behaviour at many times chance. Two internal signals support this reading: the authors themselves note that the clustering is 'even more evident' when participants are plotted as the mean of their tasks than task by task, which is what one expects when within-child consistency is high; and they never compute the participant-level accuracy that this observation invites. Secondary issues compound it. The choice of two latent dimensions was made from PCA on a latent space learned from the entire dataset. The class-conditional Gaussians used for the interpretability analysis and proposed as clinical thresholds are fitted to all 1,500 points. Only accuracy is reported. And the balanced 50/50 design, while making chance interpretable, is 25-50 times the population prevalence at which the proposed screening support would operate. The corrective is straightforward and would be a genuinely valuable result: split the 60 children into folds, train on one set of children and test on unseen children, report participant-level sensitivity and specificity as well as accuracy, and refit the latent Gaussians within training folds only. Given 60 children and a well-specified reference standard including ADOS-2, that study is within reach of this dataset.

**S-098** [local_c6853fe2] — *A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation*

There is no validation strategy, and this is the study's decisive methodological gap. No training/test split, no cross-validation, no development set, no held-out participants: the five decision constants were set by hand and are reported on the same 30 children and 109 calls used to define them, and the single trained component, YOLOv3, was retrained on more than 1,700 images drawn from those same 30 subjects, so the person detector has seen every child it is subsequently evaluated on. Nothing in the paper estimates how the pipeline would behave on a child it has never encountered. Compounding this, no chance-agreement floor is computed although the data make one essential: with 17 of 30 children scoring 5 and each of those children contributing five non-response events, a trivial always-predict-non-response rule would already agree with the clinician on well over half the participants and on a substantially larger share of the 109 calls, so the 98.2% event-level figure is being reported against an unstated and high baseline. For an ordinal agreement problem the correct summary is a weighted kappa or ICC; accuracy without chance correction systematically overstates agreement in exactly this configuration. The 109 events are also treated as independent although they cluster within 30 children and are serially dependent by the protocol's own logic. Finally, the reference standard against which all of this is measured is a single unblinded clinician with no second rater, so even a perfectly validated system could only be shown to reproduce one person's uncorroborated judgements. The corrective study is well within reach of this group and would be worth more than the current numbers: fix the thresholds on a development subset, evaluate on children whose images never entered detector training, add a second blinded rater and report inter-rater reliability, and report weighted kappa alongside accuracy at both aggregation levels.

**S-099** [local_f1b626c8] — *Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games*

The weakest element, and it fails on two counts that compound one another. First, the reported performance is not held-out. The abstract, results narrative and conclusion all quote 76.6% precision and 73.8% accuracy, which Table 5 identifies as the TOTAL column - the pooled figure across training, validation and test. The test column of the same table reads 66.7% precision and 58.3% accuracy, with sensitivity 57.1% and specificity 60.0%. The same pattern holds for every feature subset: total accuracies of 65.0-73.8% against test accuracies of 52.8-58.3%, with training accuracies of 67.9-78.6%. A roughly 20-point train-to-test gap in all four configurations is the signature of overfitting on a small dataset, and it is neither reported nor discussed. Second, the split is over observations rather than children. The paper says only that '70 percent of data ... were used for training and the remaining 30 percent for tests and validation', but the reported percentages determine the arithmetic exactly: with 240 rows split 168/36/36 in the MATLAB Neural Network Toolbox default proportions, 78.6% of 168 is 132, 66.7% of 36 is 24, 58.3% of 36 is 21, and (132 + 24 + 21)/240 = 73.75%, reproducing the reported total to the decimal, and the same reconstruction works for the other three subsets. Forty children therefore contribute six rows each, randomly scattered, so every test row has five siblings from the same child in the training set. Because the features are per-region fixation counts and durations - quantities that are highly stable within an individual and reflect that person's habitual looking style as much as their diagnosis - this is a direct channel for identity leakage, and it means even the 58.3% test figure is optimistic relative to a genuinely unseen child. Two further issues: four feature subsets were compared on the same data and the best reported, and no chance baseline, permutation test or confidence interval accompanies any figure, although the balanced design makes chance exactly 50% and the test partition is small enough that three observations separate the reported result from it. The corrective is available and would be worth doing: partition the 40 children, generate observations within partitions, tune the network on training children only, choose the feature subset on a development set, and report test-column figures with confidence intervals as the study's result.

**S-100** [local_6249bd63] — *Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior*

The strongest validation design encountered so far in this review, with one important caveat about how the result should be read. Each participant contributes exactly one feature vector, so the unit of splitting is the person by construction and the segment-level leakage that inflates most studies in this corpus is structurally impossible. Validation is nested cross-validation with a single tuned hyperparameter, the correlation window Tw over four candidate values, optimised inside the inner loop; the SVM's regularisation is left at its default rather than tuned, further reducing researcher degrees of freedom; and no feature selection is performed at all, so selection bias cannot arise despite 6,272 features. The outer evaluation is 10-fold cross-validation repeated 100 times with participant order shuffled between repetitions, which addresses fold-assignment variance - a source of instability that very few studies here even acknowledge. The identity-modelling step deserves separate credit as leakage control of a different kind: because the 3DMM estimates and removes facial identity, the representation is explicitly stripped of the individual-appearance information that, elsewhere in this corpus, silently drives high accuracy. The caveat is the base rate and the operating point. At 15 autistic and 27 neurotypical participants, majority-class prediction yields 64.3%, so 80.5% is a 16-point improvement rather than the 30 points a reader assuming balance might infer, and no permutation test or confidence interval is offered. The class imbalance also shapes the classifier: at sensitivity 0.55 and specificity 0.95 the model has learned to be conservative, so its accuracy is carried disproportionately by correctly identifying neurotypical participants. None of this undermines the study's actual claim - which concerns the non-overlap of AI and human errors, evaluated per participant - but it does mean the headline accuracy should not be read as evidence of a strong autism detector.

**S-101** [local_8b9e0e8a] — *Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas*

Among the stronger validation designs in this corpus at the level of splitting, with two specific weaknesses further down the pipeline. The split unit is the subject: 50% of the 333 children are held out, so all 82 stimulus-based patterns from a child stay together and within-child leakage is structurally impossible - which matters here more than usual, because the model scores individual stimuli and a naive pattern-level split would have placed 41 of each test child's own patterns in training. The procedure is repeated over five random permutations with the minimum reported (95.76%), addressing split-assignment variance. The semantic autoencoder is trained on MS COCO rather than on participant data, so the representation learning introduces no leakage. Two ablation baselines are implemented on the same data rather than cited from other papers. Against this: first, the decision threshold is fitted transductively. The paper states that subject average scores were computed 'for each subject in training and testing' and the Otsu maximum between-class variance threshold selected on that combined distribution, and the same is described for the stimulus-level threshold. Otsu does not use labels, so this is not label leakage, but the operating point is nonetheless chosen with sight of the test subjects' score distribution, and in a deployment where children arrive one at a time no such distribution exists - the threshold would have to be fixed in advance from training data alone, and no result is reported under that constraint. Second, several choices were compared on the evaluation data with no separate development set: LSTM hidden units and fully connected size, epoch count, mini-batch size, learning rate, and the minLength lower bound, all reported in a single results table with the best configuration carried forward. The stimulus-discriminability ranking used to argue that 60 images suffice was likewise computed on the same data, so the proposed shortened protocol is selected in-sample. Third, no majority-class floor (57.6%) or confidence interval is given. None of these undermine the subject-level split, which is the hard part and is done correctly; they mean the 96.73% is a mildly optimistic estimate under a transductively chosen threshold rather than a fully prospective one.

**S-102** [local_0e476686] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts*

The weakest validation design in the corpus, and the failure is structural rather than marginal. A single random 75/25 split was applied to 90,000 tweets, with the tweet as the unit. Those tweets come from 252 users, so every user is represented on both sides of the split, and the imbalance makes this acute for the negative class: 31 comparison users supply all 45,000 non-autistic tweets, roughly 1,450 each, of which about 1,090 land in training and 360 in test. A model needs only to recognise those 31 writing styles - vocabulary, topics, habitual phrasings, recurring names, professional jargon, regional idiom - to classify the negative test set almost perfectly, and BERT is exactly the kind of model that will do so. The positive class is less concentrated at roughly 200 tweets per user but is leaky by the same mechanism. Nothing in the paper estimates performance on a writer the model has never seen, which is the only quantity relevant to the stated application. Compounding this: there is no cross-validation and no repeated split, so the single reported figure carries no stability estimate; hyperparameters were grid-searched with no validation set distinct from the test set; no chance baseline or confidence interval is given; and no user-level aggregation is performed, so the study never reports the metric its own use case requires. The corrective is simple and would be a genuinely informative experiment: hold out entire users, expand the comparison group well beyond 31 people, mask autism-related vocabulary, and report user-level sensitivity and specificity. On the current design, the 84.3% cannot be interpreted as evidence about autism at all.

**S-103** [local_fbaf69bf] — *Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Sound at the level that matters most and loose at the margins. The classifier uses leave-one-out cross-validation over participants, so the split unit is the child and no within-participant leakage is possible - though this is easier to achieve here than elsewhere because each participant contributes a single feature vector per movie rather than many segments. More importantly, the paper's primary claims are not predictive at all: they are group comparisons with effect sizes, supported by ANCOVA adjustment for two prespecified confounds and by an internal control condition (non-social movies), which is a design where cross-validation is not the relevant safeguard and where the reported statistics carry their own uncertainty. Three looser points. The classification analysis was restricted to the four social movies because the group comparisons on the same data had shown larger effect sizes there, so that restriction is in-sample; the effect is modest, since the choice was made on a prespecified social/non-social distinction rather than by searching over movies individually, but it should be stated. No class handling is described for the decision tree, and reported precision near 70% with recall near 89% cannot be produced from 40 autistic against 396 typically developing participants - so an undisclosed balancing or subsampling step exists, and without knowing it the accuracy figures cannot be placed against the correct baseline. And no majority-class baseline is given, which at 9.2% prevalence would be about 91%, so the reported 76-79% accuracies would be below trivial on the unbalanced sample and are only meaningful under whatever balancing was applied. None of this affects the study's principal finding, which rests on non-parametric group comparisons with large effect sizes, confound adjustment and an internal control - a design that is more robust than a cross-validated accuracy figure and that this corpus contains too few of.

**S-104** [local_74416ba7] — *Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders*

One of the two or three soundest validation designs in this review. The scheme is nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation: in each outer fold a single participant is held out entirely, with all 21 or 32 of their trials excluded from training, and the inner loop with an 8:2 training/validation split is used to optimise the learning rate. Placing hyperparameter selection inside the outer loop is stated explicitly and is the correct construction; the great majority of studies in this corpus either tune on the test set or do not say. Because the split unit is the participant, the trial-level leakage that inflates results throughout this literature - where a person's own segments appear on both sides of the split - is structurally impossible here, and this matters more than usual because the per-trial classifier operates on individual FEIT images that would otherwise be trivially matched across folds. Class balance was engineered in advance by equalising group sizes, so chance is approximately 50% and is not an artefact of prevalence. And every reported accuracy is tested against that chance level with a binomial test, with the failing result reported as failing. The consequences are visible in the numbers: accuracies of 0.645 to 0.710 rather than the 90-plus figures common in this corpus, which is what a properly participant-disjoint, chance-tested evaluation of gaze features in 30 people looks like. Three residual weaknesses. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, and with 30-31 participants one person is roughly 3 accuracy points, so the 10-point gain from weighting in adults corresponds to about three people. The controls were selected from a larger pool by SRS-2 ranking, so sampling is conditioned on a construct-related variable. And the statistical analysis that motivates the whole approach - and that is used to validate the feature importances - treats trials as independent units when they cluster within participants, without any mixed-effects adjustment, so those p-values are anticonservative even after Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

**S-105** [local_7c6a5aa4] — *Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders*

The weakest element, with two problems either of which would be decisive on its own. The first is the pseudo-labelling. Only 180 users of approximately 5,372 disclosed a diagnosis; the remainder were assigned labels by k-means clustering seeded from the labelled cases, and the 70% and 82% figures are obtained on this enlarged corpus. So roughly 97% of the evaluation data carry labels generated by an unsupervised algorithm rather than reported by any person, and the reported accuracy is substantially a measure of how well a supervised classifier reproduces a clustering solution - a quantity that can be high regardless of whether the clusters correspond to diagnosis. The contrast with the same data before pseudo-labelling is stark and is visible in the paper's own Table IV: 47-61% across all three modelling views and six window sizes, at or barely above a 50% chance level. The second problem is the unit of cross-validation, which is never stated. The modelling operates on windows, each user generates many windows in proportion to their app use, and neither the earlier leave-one-out-with-100-bootstraps scheme nor the present ten-repetition 20-fold-with-ten-bootstraps scheme is described as partitioning users. If windows were partitioned - the natural reading - then every user's own data appear on both sides of every fold, and since key-press sequences from a customised icon layout are close to an individual signature, the classifier can succeed by recognising users rather than diagnoses. No user-level accuracy is reported anywhere, which is the number the stated research question requires. Compounding both: accuracy is the only metric, no chance baseline is computed, no confidence interval is given, window size was swept with the best reported, and tuning effort differed between the compared classifiers by the authors' own account. The corrective experiment is clear and would be worth more than the present result - partition by user, evaluate only on the 180 verified labels, report sensitivity and specificity at the user level, and adjust for or match on age.

**S-106** [local_8a706eaa] — *Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Correctly constructed at the split, and this deserves explicit credit: 'we used 10-fold group-wise (by individual) cross-validation', stated unambiguously, so all clips from a child fall in the same fold and no participant contributes to both training and testing. That is exactly the safeguard most of this corpus omits, and it matters here because each child supplies up to ten IJA and five RJA clips from a single continuous session, which under clip-level splitting would be near-duplicates. Confidence intervals are computed by a named method and reported for every metric, and the classification threshold is fixed at 0.5 rather than tuned. Within its own terms the evaluation is therefore sound, and the near-perfect detection figures cannot be attributed to participant leakage. The problem lies upstream, in what the evaluation is an evaluation of. The paper states that conservative criteria were used deliberately 'to select individuals belonging to clinically distinct groups to ensure development of an accurate and precise ASD vs TD classification model', and the participant table shows a 44-50 point IQ gap at p < .001 with an autism sample that is 62% preverbal or single-word. Separating those two groups is a far easier problem than the clinical question, and AUROCs of 99.5-99.8% are the expected result rather than a surprising one - so the honest reading is that the study demonstrates the protocol and pipeline work, not that the system would perform at this level on the children a referral tool would actually see. The severity analysis inherits the same issue in a specific form: its three classes include non-autism, so a large part of its 90.3% AUROC is the already-solved detection problem, and because no autism-only result is reported there is no evidence that the system grades severity within the spectrum. Further gaps: no external validation, which the authors acknowledge; no clinical comparison group; no specificity; no class distribution for the severity bands and hence no chance baseline; and no adjustment for the IQ difference despite ANCOVA being straightforward and the authors demonstrably comfortable with mixed ANOVA elsewhere in the paper. The corrective study is well specified by the authors themselves - an IQ-matched external cohort - and would be worth considerably more than the present numbers.

**S-107** [local_6b9484ce] — *Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking*

A single fixed 70/20/10 split of 547 images into 382 training, 108 validation and 57 test, with the image as the unit. Fifty-nine children produced those 547 images, so roughly nine images per child, and nothing in the paper indicates that a child's images were kept together - so on a random split each test image is accompanied by around eight siblings from the same child. This is the same design flaw that recurs across reuses of this dataset, and it is the reason the review treats the family of studies built on it as a triangulation problem rather than as independent evidence. What makes this particular paper informative is that the leakage does not produce a high number: 81.0% at best, against figures near 97-99% reported by other groups on the identical images. The most plausible reading is that generic ImageNet features plus a shallow classifier extract less individual-identity information from a rendered trajectory than an end-to-end network fine-tuned on the same data - so the gap between this study and the higher-scoring reuses is itself evidence about how much of those higher scores is identity rather than diagnosis. Read alongside the source authors' own participant-level correction to around 71% and another group's one-image-per-child leave-one-out result of 72.88%, this study's 81% sits closer to the honest end of the range than to the inflated one, despite sharing the flawed split. Other weaknesses compound the picture: a 57-image test set with no confidence intervals, so the three-way model comparison rests on differences of one or two images; no cross-validation or repeated splits; no chance baseline against an implied 59.6% floor; and one architectural choice (greyscale conversion) made with reference to observed accuracy on the same data.

**S-108** [local_c6a4ea7b] — *SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism*

The weakest dimension, and the problems compound. The reported scheme is a single 90:10 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation used inside the training data only for SVM hyperparameter selection - which is the correct placement for hyperparameter tuning and is stated clearly. But three issues sit above it. First, the arithmetic does not match the description: every reported accuracy is an exact multiple of 1/17 (64.7, 70.59, 76.5, 82.3, 88.2, 94.1 per cent), which fixes the test set at 17 items, roughly 22% of 76 rather than the stated 10%, and the discrepancy is unexplained. Whatever the intended design, a 17-item test set means one child is worth 5.9 percentage points, so the headline 94.1% is 16 of 17 correct and its margin over the next-best configuration is one child - a difference no confidence interval is offered for and none would support. Second, SHAP-based elimination from 77 to 63 features is described as performed on the initially extracted set with no indication of nesting inside the split, so the retained feature set was chosen with sight of the evaluation data; on 76 samples and 77 candidate features this is exactly the regime in which unnested selection produces substantial optimism. Third, six classifier families were compared and the best retained, with a 30-point spread between the worst and best, so the reported figure is the maximum of a search. Beneath all of this lies the pooling problem, which no amount of correct splitting would fix: because the Flusberg corpus contributes autistic children only and from a much younger age band, corpus identity partially predicts diagnosis, and a random split across pooled corpora cannot separate a linguistic signature from a corpus signature. The corrective design is available in the data and would be far more informative - leave-one-corpus-out validation, which would show directly whether features learned on Eigsti and Flusberg transfer to Nadig and vice versa, together with nesting the SHAP elimination and reporting the ablation ordering rather than point accuracies.

**S-109** [local_5c43dffa] — *Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths*

The weakest element, and the paper contains the evidence for its own strongest critique. The splitting unit is the scan-path image at 7:3 or 75:25, and no participant-level or subject-disjoint evaluation is reported anywhere in twenty pages. With 86 participants generating 1,414 clip viewings, each child contributes roughly sixteen images, so a random image-level split places about eleven of a test child's own scan-paths in training - and scan-paths from one child viewing different clips share that child's habitual gaze extent, saccade amplitude and scanning style. Rotation-based augmentation makes this worse rather than better, because augmented counts are quoted for the whole dataset rather than for training partitions, implying that rotated copies of a single scan-path can appear on both sides of the split. The sex-by-age experiment then supplies near-direct evidence of this: test accuracy rises monotonically with augmentation level, from 85.07% at 961/957 images through 85.81% at 1,276/1,259 to 98.84% at 3,121/2,905. A real signal does not strengthen when synthetic copies are added; a duplicate-leakage artefact does exactly this. The 98.8% is nevertheless reported as the paper's most striking stratification result. Training accuracy of 100% in almost every table confirms complete memorisation at every setting. Layered on top of the leakage is a confound the paper documents without recognising: it establishes that scan-path images predict age band at 80.5% and sex at 78.0% within the autistic group - both above the 74.4% achieved for diagnosis - while its diagnostic groups differ by 35 percentage points in sex composition and by a factor of two in the proportion aged 10 or over. Taken together these mean the headline diagnosis figure cannot be attributed to autism-related looking patterns rather than to age and sex. The corrective design is straightforward and would be genuinely valuable given the quality of the stimulus battery: split by participant, augment only within training folds, and evaluate diagnosis within age-and-sex-matched strata using the paper's own demographic classifiers as a check.

**S-110** [local_32da8ede] — *A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths*

Two problems compound, and a third makes the result difficult to interpret at all. First, cross-validation partitions the 547 images rather than the 59 children. With roughly nine images per child and no statement that a child's images were kept within a fold, each held-out image is accompanied by around eight siblings from the same child in training - the same route that has produced accuracies from 81% to over 99% across five reuses of this identical dataset, against the source authors' own participant-level figure near 71% and an independent one-image-per-child leave-one-out result of 72.88%. Second, the reported figure is the maximum of an extremely large hyperparameter search: separate sweeps over kernel size, stride, pooling, batch size, optimiser and thirteen architecture configurations, well over a hundred cells in total, every one scored on the same cross-validation with the best bolded and carried forward. No held-out confirmation of the selected configuration is performed, and the 35-point spread between optimisers on identical data shows how much room that search had to exploit. Third, and most consequentially, the headline accuracy cannot be reconciled with the sensitivity and specificity reported for the same model. At 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images, 77.60% sensitivity and 79.91% specificity give approximately 79.0% accuracy. That implied figure is strikingly consistent with the other honest estimates on this dataset - 81.0% from an independent transfer-learning study, 72.88% from one-image-per-child leave-one-out, and roughly 71% from the source authors' own participant-level correction - which suggests the class-conditional metrics may be the trustworthy ones and the accuracy column an artefact. Either way, the paper reports two irreconcilable characterisations of its own classifier and reconciles neither, so no single number from it can be carried into a synthesis without that caveat.

**S-111** [local_15ed96cb] — *A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning*

The strongest validation design in the review, and strong in ways that are structural rather than procedural. Four features stand out. The split unit is the child and the cohort is a whole population, so there is no possibility of within-participant leakage and no case-control sampling to inflate separation. Temporal leakage is controlled by design rather than by hope: predictors are capped at 24 months and outcomes restricted to diagnoses recorded after 24 months, adopted explicitly to prevent information flowing from diagnosis back to predictors - the only study here that faces this problem and the only one that solves it. Feature reduction from 100 to 59 was made a priori on clinical-relevance grounds, so no selection bias enters. And training AUC is reported alongside test AUC with the overfitting acknowledged in the text, rather than concealed. Three-fold cross-validation is modest but adequate at this sample size, and results are stable across folds (SD 0.009). Two internal checks add further confidence: a boys-only model tests whether performance depends on sex, given that sex is both a strong predictor and a strong group difference; and referral for developmental assessment, deliberately excluded from the feature set, serves as an external validity indicator, with high-risk children 3.29 times more likely to have been referred (95% CI 3.18-3.39). The residual limitations are epidemiological rather than methodological: no external cohort or health system has been tested, and the outcome label is substantially incomplete, with the authors estimating the true autism count at ten times the labelled figure - which biases sensitivity and specificity in directions the data cannot resolve.

**S-112** [local_261afa51] — *AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: &#x201C;A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System&#x201D;*

The design cannot support the claim, and the reasons are structural rather than procedural. A single fixed partition of 2,836 images into 2,536 training, 200 validation and 100 test provides no cross-validation, no repeated splits and no confidence intervals, and the test partition of 100 images makes each image worth a full percentage point. The order of augmentation relative to partitioning is ambiguous, with the text describing the partition and then the augmentation of the full 2,836-image dataset, which if taken at face value places transformed copies of the same photograph on both sides of the split. The number of distinct children behind the images is unknown, so participant-level splitting is not merely absent but impossible, and multiple photographs of the same child may straddle the split undetectably. Training accuracy reached 100%. The confusion matrix corresponds to no stated partition. But none of these is the decisive problem. Because the two classes were assembled from different internet sources, no split of these images - however careful - can distinguish a model that has learned facial morphology from one that has learned image provenance, and no result reported in the paper bears on which it is. The corrective is not a better validation scheme but a different dataset: photographs of diagnostically verified autistic and non-autistic children captured under matched conditions with the same equipment, which is what several other studies in this review provide and what this branch of the literature lacks.

**S-113** [local_3e88f3ce] — *An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks*

The subject is the analytic unit under both evaluation schemes, so the within-subject leakage that dominates the image, frame, EEG, thermal and cry branches of this review does not arise. What arises instead is target leakage of the most direct kind, and it operates through two channels simultaneously.
