First, the recorded values: ADOS_TOTAL, ADOS_COMM, ADOS_GOTHAM_SEVERITY, ADI_R_SOCIAL_TOTAL_A, ADI_R_VERBAL_TOTAL_BV and SRS_RAW_TOTAL are the scored output of the assessments through which the ABIDE-I sites established the diagnoses that constitute the label, and the study's own explainability analysis ranks them first and second among all contributors. Second, missingness: ADOS and ADI-R are administered to establish an autism diagnosis and are largely absent for control participants in ABIDE-I, so the presence or absence of a value on these fields carries the label independently of its magnitude, and no imputation or missingness-handling procedure is described that would neutralise it. A ROC-AUC of 99.99% is the expected consequence, and no partitioning scheme - subject-level, site-level or otherwise - could alter it. Three further issues are secondary but real. Neither evaluation is site-stratified, despite 17 sites with distinct scanners and protocols and a substantial literature documenting site as a confound for autism classification on this dataset; SITE_ID is label-encoded into the preprocessing, and no leave-one-site-out result is reported. Age and IQ, which differ between groups in ABIDE-I, are entered as predictors rather than adjusted for, so part of the residual signal is cognitive ability and developmental stage. And the reported accuracy and split descriptions are mutually inconsistent between sections. The remedy is straightforward and would make the study genuinely informative: refit with the six instrument-derived fields removed, run leave-one-site-out, and report an age-and-IQ-only baseline. The architecture is well enough constructed that the resulting numbers would be worth having.

**S-114** [local_5b5f2237] — *Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development*

Structurally sound at the level of splitting and compromised at the level of feature construction, and the two need to be separated. The splitting is correct and clearly described: leave-one-out cross-validation with each of 41 iterations training on 40 participants and testing on the remaining one, with each participant contributing a single feature vector, so within-participant leakage is impossible - the same standard achieved by the best studies in this review and not by most. The chance-level handling in the statistical analysis is better still: the pseudo-pair surrogate group, constructed by pairing a child's movement with an adult's from a different video, is an empirically derived null for a synchrony measure, which is the appropriate control because coherence between any two quasi-periodic signals is non-zero by default. Very few studies in this corpus construct a surrogate null of this kind. The compromise lies elsewhere. The 92.68% headline is achieved with features built by summing the six coherence values that a group comparison on all 41 participants had identified as significantly different. Leave-one-out cross-validation then evaluates those features on the same 41 participants. No participant's data trains the model that classifies them, but every participant's diagnosis determined which features the model could choose from, so the evaluation is not label-blind and the derived-feature result is optimistically biased by an amount the design cannot quantify. The paper's own explanation confirms the mechanism without naming it: the improvement is attributed to 'higher Cohen's d values' for the derived features, and higher effect sizes are exactly what selecting and summing on significance produces. The original-feature result of 85.37% is the more trustworthy figure, though even there four of the five selected features were among the significant ones and it is not stated whether forward feature selection was nested inside the loop. Two further points: four classifiers across two feature conditions and 63 candidate features were compared with the maximum reported; and no confidence interval accompanies a comparison in which the entire improvement is three children.

**S-115** [local_13426811] — *Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning*

Among the two or three soundest validation designs in the review, and sound in ways that require deliberate effort rather than good fortune. The split unit is the participant, with leave-one-out cross-validation formally specified: each of the 135 samples serves once as the test case with the remaining 134 as training data. The step that distinguishes it is the handling of the annotation model. Automatic tag annotation is itself a fitted component, and fitting it once on the whole corpus would leak information from held-out participants into their own annotations; instead the procedure trains the annotator on the training partition of each fold and then uses that fold-specific annotator to label the held-out sample. Very few studies in this corpus recognise that a preprocessing model is a fitted component at all, and none other nests one this carefully. Hyperparameters were adopted from standard values and deliberately not searched, removing the model-selection optimism that inflates most results here. Confidence intervals accompany every accuracy, and model comparisons are tested with McNemar rather than read from point differences, with non-significance correctly not interpreted as equivalence. Two residual concerns are not validation failures but bound what the result means. The comparison group's cognitive and educational level is unmeasured while the autistic group's full-scale IQ is 81-91, so an unquantified ability gap may contribute to the separation. And the transcripts come from the ADOS-2 sessions that produced the labels, so the language sample and the diagnostic judgement arise from the same encounter - which does not leak the label into the features but does mean the model is trained on speech elicited by an examiner who was assessing the participant for autism at that moment.

**S-116** [local_948fa8d0] — *Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms*

There is no validation strategy. This is not a case of an inadequate or leaky protocol but of no stated protocol at all: the words 'split' and 'validation' do not occur in the paper, no cross-validation is described, no holdout proportion is given, and no resampling scheme is mentioned, yet twenty accuracy figures are tabulated across four feature conditions and five classifiers. The methods section narrates the feature-extraction pipeline in step-by-step detail down to CSV export and then moves directly to results. Consequently none of the reported numbers can be interpreted as an estimate of performance on unseen data, and the comparison the paper is built around - handcrafted versus fused features, and among the three backbones - cannot be evaluated either, since a resubstitution comparison would favour the higher-dimensional representations regardless of their generalisation. Beneath this sits the same structural problem as in the companion study on this dataset: the two classes were assembled from different internet sources, so no split, however constructed, could separate a model that has learned about faces from one that has learned about photographs; and the number of distinct children is unknown, so images of one child may fall on both sides of any partition undetectably.

**S-117** [local_893dfc22] — *Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed*

Not assessable, because no validation scheme is described. The paper states no train-test split proportion, no cross-validation arrangement, no held-out set size and no partitioning unit anywhere. The one hint is that CK+ is used 'to test the WQPSO-FMRCNN model on unseen data' after KDEF, which would be cross-corpus evaluation - the design this review regards most highly, since it tests transfer across acquisition conditions and populations. It is not reported as a separate result, so what would have been the study's strongest methodological feature goes unquantified. Two further points bound the figures. CK+ contributes 327 peak frames from 118 individuals, roughly 2.8 images per person, and whether images of the same individual span any partition is unstated. And KDEF is geometrically standardised with eyes and lips at fixed coordinates, so a classifier operating on it faces none of the pose, scale or framing variation that any real deployment would present. A 99.8% accuracy on peak-frame posed expressions from geometrically aligned adult faces is close to the ceiling that this benchmark has long supported, and is not evidence about the harder problem the paper describes.

**S-118** [local_e7c16f2a] — *Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification*

The decisive weakness, and it is structural rather than procedural. The dataset is 738 trajectories from 20 children, roughly 37 each, and evaluation uses four-fold cross-validation with a 110-sample validation set described as 15% of the trajectory dataset. The unit is explicitly the trajectory: the validation size is quoted in samples out of 738, and nothing in the paper indicates that a child's trajectories were kept within a fold. Under a random trajectory-level split, each validation trajectory is accompanied by approximately 36 siblings produced by the same child in the same session with the same hand, differing only in which of eight targets was approached - and after rotation normalisation even that difference is removed. Fine motor kinematics at this granularity function close to an individual motor signature, so a model can separate children rather than groups and report high accuracy; the reported 0.90 is therefore not an estimate of performance on a child the model has not seen, and no participant-level figure appears anywhere. With only 20 children, a participant-disjoint scheme would have been straightforward - leave-one-child-out would give exactly 20 folds - and would have produced the number a clinical claim requires. Three secondary points compound this. No chance baseline, confidence interval or class-conditional metric accompanies either accuracy. The simulation and simplification analyses, which are the study's strongest contribution, are conducted on the same trained models and the same underlying trajectories. And the two feature sets were compared without model architecture being specified, so the 14-point difference cannot be checked against differences in capacity. The corrective is simple and the open data release makes it possible for others to perform: partition the 20 children, retrain, and report participant-level accuracy alongside sensitivity and specificity.

**S-119** [local_5a7ab52d] — *Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain*

Not assessable, and not assessable in a stronger sense than any other study in this review. The paper gives two accounts of its evaluation that are not reconciled: one describing a variable 'learning percentage' divided into five values with the complement used for testing, illustrated at 65% training and 35% testing; and another defining 5-fold cross-validation within the list of evaluation measures. Neither is linked to the reported figures, and neither states a unit of splitting - which is unrecoverable in any case, since the number of individuals contributing the data is never given, so it cannot be determined whether the rows being split are people or repeated measurements from people. Feature selection optimises a fitness function that uses inter- and intra-class similarity, and therefore class labels, with no statement that it was confined to training partitions. No chance baseline, class distribution, confusion matrix or confidence interval is reported. Underneath all of this lies the fact that the reported 96.44886% accuracy has no stated denominator: a reader cannot say whether it was computed on ten individuals or ten thousand, nor what proportion of them carried each label, nor what condition they were in when measured. The figure is not an estimate of anything that can be identified.

**S-120** [local_8253c2ec] — *Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder*

The mechanics are sound and irrelevant. Each respondent contributes one row, so the split unit is the person and within-participant leakage cannot occur; the 80/20 partition sizes are tabulated for all four datasets; class distributions are reported and the decision not to oversample is explained rather than assumed, which avoids the synthetic-minority inflation affecting several comparators in the paper's own literature review. All of this is better practice than much of this corpus. It has no bearing on the reported result, because the target in these datasets is computed from the predictors: the class is the summed A1-A10 score thresholded at the instrument's published cut-off, the ten items are model inputs, and the sum itself appears among the tabulated fields. A model with access to either can recover the label exactly, on any partition, under any validation scheme, with any architecture. Scores of 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC-ROC across four independent datasets simultaneously are the arithmetic consequence of that arrangement, and the paper's attribution of them to Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation misidentifies the cause. This is target leakage in its most complete form - more complete than the neuroimaging study charted alongside it, where the features summarised a clinical judgement, since here the label is a closed-form function of the inputs. The paper's own comparison table is the strongest available evidence that this is systematic rather than idiosyncratic: it places the subliterature on these datasets at 97.15% to 100%, and records one comparator using genuinely independent measurements - physical fitness tests, brain scans and severity assessments on recruited participants - at 77.99%.

**S-121** [local_1e9d0b71] — *Machine learning’s effectiveness*

Correct on the split unit and ambiguous on the step that matters. The evaluation is leave-one-out cross-validation over 126 participants, each contributing one 16-dimensional vector, so the unit is the person and within-participant leakage is impossible. The class imbalance is acknowledged and drives the choice of scheme, with the authors stating that with around 20 above-threshold samples they 'were forced to use LOOCV to avoid polarization of prediction toward the Low autistic trait group'. They then state the risk this creates in their own words - that leave-one-out 'can also produce optimistic performance estimates due to the small test set in each iteration' and 'can be unstable when the dataset contains noise or outliers' - and conclude that their results need cautious interpretation. That is the right instinct, but it does not reach the decisive issue. The methods state that the procedure 'simultaneously selected the 16 explanatory variables and optimized the hyperparameter', and three to five variables plus a cost parameter were retained per model from sixteen candidates on 126 participants of whom 19 are positive. Whether that joint selection was repeated inside each of the 126 folds is not stated anywhere in the main text. If it was not - and the sentence's placement before the description of cross-validation suggests it may not have been - then the selection saw every participant's label, and on this configuration that alone is sufficient to produce accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of exactly 1.000. Perfect scores on all three metrics for a behavioural measurement in five-year-olds are not a plausible property of the phenomenon, and unnested selection is the most parsimonious explanation. Three further points: no majority-class baseline is given against an 84.9% floor; no confidence interval accompanies a sensitivity estimated on 19 positives; and the three variable sets were compared on the same 126 participants. The corrective is straightforward and would leave the study's substantive contribution intact - nest the selection, report the resulting accuracy with an interval, and add the positive predictive value that the population-based design uniquely permits.

**S-122** [local_b9e05a8f] — *Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network*

The most developed validation section in the facial-image branch of this review, and worth recording carefully because it is the one place where a paper in that branch takes leakage seriously. The authors recognised that the video-derived corpus risks subject-level and temporal leakage under frame-level splitting, and rather than asserting the problem away they measured it: ResNet-50 features for all 1,163 images, maximum training-test cosine similarity of 0.9714, correctly interpreted as 'a substantial likelihood of leakage'. They then applied K-Means over the deep features, swept cluster counts from 30 to 150, split clusters rather than images 80/10/10, and reassigned test images exceeding 0.90 similarity to a training image back into the training set, adopting the 100-cluster configuration for its balance of test-set size (68 images), final similarity (0.8989) and reassignment count (28). The same check on the Piosenka corpus returned 0.90, and the original split was kept. Compared with the four other Piosenka-based papers charted here, all of which split images without comment, this is a substantial advance. Three qualifications bound it. Perceptual similarity is a proxy for identity and not a measurement of it - two images of one child under different lighting can fall below any threshold while two different children in matched conditions can exceed it - so the paper's claim to have confirmed 'the absence of subject- or frame-level leakage' asserts more than a cosine threshold can support. The reassignment step edits the test set using the model's own feature space, moving out precisely the images most similar to training data, which makes the reported performance conditional on a data-dependent curation rule. And the leakage machinery addresses only within-corpus duplication; it does nothing about the confound that determines what the labels mean, since a model that has learned to recognise images sourced from autism-related web content will do so equally well on perfectly disjoint subjects. The cross-dataset evaluation deserves the same reading. Training on one corpus and testing on the other reached 89-90% in both directions, which the paper offers as robustness. But both corpora were built by the same principle - autism-labelled material harvested from autism-associated online sources, controls from general online sources - so a confound common to both transfers exactly as a genuine phenotype would. Transfer between two datasets that share a construction bias is not independent confirmation; transfer to a clinically ascertained cohort would be, and is not attempted. The remaining gaps are the unstated evaluation partition for the hyperparameter fitness, the absence of any chance or prevalence baseline, and confidence intervals incompatible with the test set sizes.

**S-123** [local_0b0960c4] — *Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]*

The study reports no validation scheme at all, and the sample structure makes the omission decisive. With 13 autistic and 4 typically developing participants, accuracies of 89.02% to 94.02% cannot have been computed over people - 17 cases cannot produce those percentages - so they must be computed over EEG epochs or windows, and the paper never states how many segments were extracted, how long they were, how they distribute across participants, or how they were partitioned. With four control children, any participant-disjoint evaluation would place at most one control in a held-out set, which would make the reported specificity uninterpretable; the natural reading is therefore that segments from the same children appear on both sides of the boundary, and that the networks are separating individuals rather than groups. This is the same failure the review has documented for scanpath images, video frames, thermal images and cry instances, arising here in a fifth modality, and it is compounded by the absence of a stated majority-class baseline: at 13 against 4, a classifier that predicts autism for everything scores 76.5% at participant level, so the headline numbers represent a far smaller gain than they appear to. The paper's own comparison table is the most useful evidence in the study and it points the same way. It lists participant counts of 16/46, 10/5, 34/11, 10/10, 15/0 and 13/4 alongside accuracies of 92.9%, 93%, 72.77%-90.57%, 81%, 91.12% and 89.02%-94.02% - and one outlier at 212/199 participants reporting 56% to 64%. The single study in the table with a sample an order of magnitude larger than the rest reports by far the lowest accuracy, and the authors reproduce this pattern without comment. That inverse relationship between sample size and reported performance is the same one this review has traced through the behavioural branches, and its appearance in a table assembled by the authors themselves makes it the study's most transferable contribution.

**S-124** [local_abad69fd] — *Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play*

The weakest link in an otherwise carefully executed study, and instructive precisely because everything upstream is done well. Eighty-one indicators were reduced by group-difference testing and clinical judgement, then by univariate logistic regression, then by stepwise logistic regression, and the resulting five-predictor model's AUC, sensitivity, specificity and predictive values were computed on the same 246 children that drove every one of those selection steps. The operating threshold of 0.399 was likewise read off that same ROC curve. Selecting five predictors from 81 candidates on 123 events produces substantial optimism, and the standard remedy - bootstrap resampling that repeats the entire selection procedure within each resample to yield an optimism-corrected estimate - was partially performed but not reported that way: the bootstrap is described as validating the model, and the calibration curve and Hosmer-Lemeshow test address probability calibration and fit rather than out-of-sample discrimination, so no corrected AUC appears anywhere. There is no held-out set, no cross-validation and no external cohort. What makes this worth stating carefully is that the study's other validity properties are unusually sound - the split unit is the child throughout with no possibility of within-participant leakage, the diagnosis is a real clinical best-estimate judgement rather than a questionnaire threshold, the groups are matched and tested on age and sex, the comparison prediction about repetitive behaviour was made in advance and confirmed, and the authors themselves identify spectrum truncation as a source of performance inflation. The likely direction of error is therefore known and the likely magnitude is modest by this corpus's standards: an AUC of 0.826 with sensitivity 85.4% and specificity 68.3% is a plausible figure for this task, and the paper's own honesty about the CARS-2 floor points the same way. Two further items belong here. Coder blinding to group is not stated, and with autistic children recruited from hospitals and intervention centres and controls from a kindergarten, the recordings themselves may reveal group membership - which matters more in a human-coded study than in an automated one, because every one of the 81 indicators passes through a coder's judgement. And the predictive values that a screening claim depends on are quoted at the 50% prevalence of a matched design, with no recomputation for the base rate of any population in which the tool would be used.

**S-125** [local_cd7545e2] — *Predictive model using autism*

The clearest case in the review of a study whose validation honestly undercuts its own headline, and it deserves to be read as a model of reporting rather than as a failure. The six items were selected from 32 candidates using all 90 participants, and the apparent accuracy of 86.6% and AUC of 0.938 come from that same sample - so those figures are development-set performance, not estimates of generalisation. The authors then did what most of this corpus does not: they split the data into training and test samples and reported both results, 85.4% and 65.3%. A twenty-point drop on a single random split of 90 participants is what selection of six binary predictors from 32 candidates should produce, and the authors say so explicitly, naming the number of variables relative to the sample as the cause and concluding that external validation is required. The honest summary of the study's positive finding is therefore that a six-item ADOS-2 combination looks promising and has not yet been shown to generalise. Several further points bear on the validation. The split unit is the participant, so no leakage of the kind that dominates the image and frame-level branches of this review is possible. The comparison baseline is substantive rather than nominal - the instrument's own published algorithms on the same participants - which is more informative than a chance line and makes the negative finding robust to the selection problem entirely, since the algorithms were not fitted here at all. The holdout is a single random split whose proportions and repetition are unstated, and whether item selection was repeated within the training fold is not said; if it was not, the 65.3% is itself optimistic. Administrator blinding to diagnosis is not addressed, and every input is a clinician judgement made after diagnosis was established, so differential expectation is a plausible contributor to the item-level differences. Item-level inter-rater reliability was not computed within the study, although the instrument's published reliability concerns algorithm totals rather than individual items. And the exclusion of comorbid cases from both groups and of severe positive symptoms from the schizophrenia group means that the model was developed on the clean cases and would be deployed on the ambiguous ones. None of this touches the negative result, which is the study's durable contribution: the ADOS-2 algorithms, applied as published by certified administrators to verbally fluent adults with IQ above 85, misclassify 45% to 52% of schizophrenia patients as autistic and achieve AUCs of 0.562 and 0.569 against an independent clinical diagnosis.

**S-126** [local_3ecb92bf] — *The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech*

Genuinely mixed, with the best-stated splitting principle in this corpus sitting alongside an unexamined confound that undercuts the headline. On the credit side, the splitting is speaker-disjoint and the reasoning is articulated precisely: samples from each child belong to one fold only, 'to prevent the model from over-fitting by learning speaker or recording idiosyncrasies, and therefore deceptively excelling'. That is the leakage problem named accurately, and it is the failure mode this review has documented across the scanpath-image, video-frame and EEG branches where it went unaddressed. A separate development partition is maintained, the same folds serve both tasks for comparability, unweighted average recall is used throughout, minority-class upsampling is confined to training with development and test distributions deliberately left intact, and the results are benchmarked against a baseline and against published work on the same corpus. On the debit side, three problems bound what the 94.8% means. First, speaker disjointness cannot address a confound operating at the class level, and the corpus description states that atypical children were recorded in clinics while typically developing children were recorded in schools - so a model that has learned clinic acoustics transfers perfectly across any speaker boundary, and no acoustic normalisation is reported. Second, the number of children in each atypical class is never stated and the two participant counts given are mutually incompatible; if the diagnostic classes rest on very few speakers, the 26 test samples per class may effectively be one or two voices, and speaker-disjoint splitting offers little protection when class and speaker are nearly the same variable. Third, the development UAR of 78.0% against a test UAR of 94.8% is an inversion that the authors flag but do not explain, and a test score sixteen points above development usually indicates that the partitions differ in composition rather than that the model generalises unusually well - a reading supported by the fairness analysis, in which the same model's sensitivity falls to 43.6% and 61.5% on the female and male partitions. The fairness testing is the most valuable validation act in the paper and deserves emphasis: by evaluating on gender-specific held-out sets rather than only on a pooled test set, it exposes a fifty-point sensitivity gap that pooled reporting concealed entirely. That is a generalisation check almost no other study in this review performs, and its result is a warning about every pooled accuracy in this corpus. Finally, the four-class result is the study's most trustworthy number precisely because it is its worst: 60.9% against a 25% chance level, below the published baseline, on the task that requires distinguishing autism from dysphasia and PDD-NOS rather than from typical development.

**S-127** [local_4b02df7c] — *Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism*

Careful on the mechanics and unresolved on the substance, which is the reverse of the pattern in most of this corpus. The mechanics are good. Splitting is at user level with the reasoning stated explicitly - tweets from one user must not scatter across training and test, 'potentially leading to overfitting by the model due to learning user-specific patterns' - and applied to both tasks, 85:15 for tweet classification with a further 85:15 training-validation division, 80:20 for profile classification. Algorithm selection used 5-fold cross-validation with a held-out test partition maintained separately. And the sixteen-token removal list closes the most obvious inflation route, since the label is defined by a hashtag whose presence in the text would otherwise make the task a lookup. Together these are more deliberate leakage controls than most studies in this review implement, and the modest performance obtained is consistent with the controls having worked. What remains unresolved is the construct. The positive class consists of users who chose to participate in a hashtag community organised around autism advocacy; the negative class is a daily sample of general platform conversation. These populations differ in topic, audience, community membership, posting motivation, network position and - plausibly, though unmeasurably - in age, sex and geography. A model reaching 73% accuracy on that contrast may be detecting autistic language production, or the discourse register of self-advocacy, or the difference between a topically coherent community and a background sample, and the study provides no evidence separating them. The corpus construction adds a further asymmetry that is not discussed: the autism group's complete timelines were harvested while control tweets were drawn at 1,000 per day, so 17,323 users supply almost as many tweets as 171,273, and the two classes differ in how their material was sampled as well as in who wrote it. The authors reason carefully about label contamination in both directions and bound the control-group error at the population prevalence, but that bound assumes prevalence transfers to Twitter's user base and that non-self-identifying autistic users write like non-autistic ones. The honest reading is that the study demonstrates a detectable difference between two corpora whose separation has several sufficient explanations, and that its authors' decision to treat the result as a feasibility demonstration rather than a finding about autistic language is the correct one.

**S-128** [local_7d7f1fcc] — *Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children*

Among the soundest validation designs in the review, with two residual issues that bound rather than undermine it. The 160 children were split 50-50 into training and test halves of 80, each containing 40 autistic and 40 typically developing children matched for age, sex and ADOS module - so the held-out half is not merely participant-disjoint but constructed to be comparable to the training half on the three variables most likely to drive an artefactual result. That is stronger than a random split and stronger than anything else charted here. Within the training half, 80% trained and 20% validated, and every hyperparameter decision - segment length for both modalities, MFCC count, batch size, epoch count - was made on that validation set with the test children untouched; the authors even report the direction of the failures they observed while tuning, noting that larger batch sizes and epoch counts increased validation loss. Segments are nested strictly within participants, so although tens of thousands of 5- and 10-second clips were generated, none of the within-participant leakage that dominates the image and frame-level branches of this corpus is possible. The reported figures are computed on 80 children. The first residual issue is statistical: 80 test children is small, one case is worth 1.25 accuracy points, no confidence intervals are given, and an exact interval around 82.5% would run from roughly 72% to 90% - so the ensemble's 2.5-point advantage over the video model, two children, cannot be distinguished from noise, and the paper's framing of the ensemble as the best model rests on a difference the data cannot resolve. The second is the reference-standard circularity discussed above: the diagnosis was supported by 'gold standard diagnostic assessments' and the model input is the ADOS session, so unless the diagnostic ADOS was a different session from the recorded one, the label is not independent of the material. The severity of this is limited - the model receives raw pose and undiarised audio rather than coded items, so it must recover from signal what a clinician judged, which is a genuine inference rather than a lookup - but it is not zero, and a single sentence stating whether ADOS entered the diagnostic decision would settle it. Set against these, the design's positive features are substantial: matched recording context across classes, appearance stripped from the video representation by construction, participant-level matched splitting, tuning confined to a validation partition, a complete metric table for every model variant, and an interpretability analysis that identifies a plausible confound in the authors' own audio channel. The reported 78.8% to 82.5% is one of the more trustworthy performance figures in this review.

**S-129** [local_5a331ffe] — *Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning*

A study with better splitting practice than most of its branch and an unexaminable result, which is an instructive combination. The splitting is genuinely careful for the autism experiment: subjects are disjoint across partitions, the authors state why - 'in order not to distort the results or create overfitting' - and explain how it was achievable, since one child appears in one video. The partition is reported by child and by seconds of video rather than by frame count, which is precisely the disclosure the frame-level studies elsewhere in this review omit. Robustness is probed twice more, by varying the test proportion from 10% to 20% (74.5% to 74.8%) and by 5-fold cross-validation (75.2%), and the authors correctly note that a 5-fold arrangement approximates a 20% test split, so the agreement is expected rather than independent confirmation. All of this is sound. What defeats it is that the classifier's negative class is never described. For a two-class image model, the reported figure is a discrimination between two populations of images, and only one of those populations is characterised; if the non-autistic faces come from a curated corpus such as CK+ or AffectNet - both of which the study uses elsewhere - then the model may be separating home-video frames from studio or scraped photographs, and no splitting scheme could reveal it. The paper's own data-distribution table naming SSBD as the sole database across all three splits is incompatible with a second class existing, so the reporting is not merely incomplete but internally inconsistent. The class balance is likewise contradictory, called balanced in the methods and 'very imbalanced' in the results, which leaves the chance baseline for 74.5% undetermined. Two further points. The subject-disjointness argument rests on a property of SSBD alone, so whatever comprises the negative class has no stated leakage control - and the same corpus, under conventional splitting, was found by another study in this review to contain training-test pairs with cosine similarity up to 0.9714, indicating substantial near-duplication that subject-level splitting is designed to but may not fully address. And the 5-fold figure is reported as 'top-5 validation accuracy', a best-of-folds validation quantity rather than a mean held-out accuracy, so it is weaker evidence than it appears. Set against these, one part of the study's validation design is exemplary and belongs in the synthesis: the affect experiments constitute a true cross-population transfer test - train on neurotypical faces, evaluate on autistic children, then fine-tune - and the result, that the neurotypical-trained model transfers poorly and fine-tuning materially improves it, is both methodologically clean and substantively important.

**S-130** [local_45ef7022] — *A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features*

The single sentence describing evaluation is the study's undoing: '80% of the dataset was allocated for training purposes while the remaining 20% was used for performance validation'. The dataset is 1,500 images from 30 children, approximately 50 images each, and no participant-level partitioning is mentioned anywhere - the word 'split' appears nowhere else in the paper, and no cross-validation is performed for the severity task. On the natural reading, about 40 images of every child are in training and 10 in test. Severity is a fixed attribute of a child, so recognising the child suffices to recover the label, and thermal facial images of the same child in the same setting are near-duplicates of one another. A 98.33% three-class accuracy is therefore the expected arithmetic of the arrangement rather than evidence that thermal features encode severity, and the same is true of the AUC of 0.9878. This is the same failure the review has documented in the scanpath-image, video-frame and EEG branches, appearing here in a fourth modality, and it is compounded by four further problems. The severity labels have no stated source, so the quantity being predicted is undefined. The class distribution is unreported, so no baseline exists against which 98.33% could be judged even if the split were sound. The claim that the classifiers 'outperform the clinical ABC method' is incoherent if the ABC supplied the labels, and no alternative criterion is described. And skin temperature, the primary feature, was captured across outdoor play, classroom, dining and veranda settings with no ambient compensation, from overlapping groups of 10, 12, 4 and 4 children whose severity levels are not reported - so if severity is unevenly distributed across settings, thermal environment is confounded with the label in a way that no splitting scheme could remove. The remedy was available and unused: 20 videos were collected 'for real-time testing to assess the algorithm's performance in dynamic settings' and would have provided a genuinely held-out evaluation, but no result from them is reported. What makes this record worth stating at length is the destination of the number. A leaked accuracy in a diagnostic paper produces an overstated claim; here it produces a proposal to set the dose of psychiatric medication for disabled children, in a paper that itself lists cardiac arrest and kidney failure among the consequences of getting the dose wrong.

**S-131** [local_0f5a351e] — *Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

The weakest element, and it fails in three independent ways. First, the split is at image level - 80/10/10 with no mention of participant-level partitioning and no statement of how many distinct children the 2,940 images represent - so in a web-assembled corpus where one child may appear repeatedly, images of the same child can fall on both sides of the boundary. This is the standard failure of this branch and the review has documented it in five prior studies on the same corpus family. Second, and more unusual, every reported figure comes from the validation partition: all three result tables are headed 'Validation results', the confusion matrices are described as validation-stage, and the training curves report validation accuracy as the endpoint, while the 10% test partition defined in the methods section is never reported on anywhere. Model selection and performance estimation therefore share data, and the headline 98% is a selection maximum rather than a held-out estimate. Third, the evaluation partition cannot be reconciled with the described design: 294 samples per class totalling 588 is 20% of 2,940 rather than the stated 10%, and exact class balance is impossible under a random split of a 1,327-to-1,613 corpus - so either the evaluation set was stratified to equal size, or augmentation reached it, or the numbers are misreported, and the paper does not say which. Against all of this sits the confound that no splitting scheme could address: the paper states that the non-autistic images were 'randomly retrieved from web searches' while the autistic images came from an autism collection, so a model that has learned to recognise the photographic character of one source will succeed on perfectly disjoint subjects. The paper's own comparison table, listing ten prior studies on this corpus at 80.05% to 96%, is the most useful thing in it for the review: it shows a subliterature clustered below this study's figure, and the difference between them is a matter of evaluation protocol rather than of signal.

**S-132** [local_786b6280] — *Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features*

Sound on the mechanics for a study of this size, and unresolved on the confounds. Each child contributes one transcript and one feature vector, so the split unit is the person and no within-participant leakage is possible - which places this study among the minority in the review not exposed to the failure that dominates the image, frame and thermal branches. The evaluation is a 75/25 split repeated over 50 random draws with results averaged, and the choice is both explained and empirically justified: cross-validation was rejected because of small sample size, and 50 repetitions were selected because metrics stabilised, varying by no more than 1% as further splits were added. Stating a stability criterion for the number of repetitions is a level of care that very few papers in this corpus show, and the ROC plots with a one-standard-deviation band around the mean curve carry that honesty into the presentation. Three qualifications bound what this buys. Test folds contain sixteen children, so each averaged estimate rests on very small samples and no confidence interval is given; the headline 83-84% is stated elsewhere in the paper to have been obtained 'after the removal of certain features', a selection made on the same data, so it is a post-selection figure; and repeated random splitting addresses sampling variance and not the three confounds that determine what is being separated. Those are, in order of importance: that the top-ranked feature is a developmental language index with no independent language measure available and no age composition reported by group; that part of the typically developing class comes from corpora containing no autistic children, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class; and that the four source protocols differ in session length, structure and investigator role, while half the features are ratios to that investigator's output. None of these would be revealed by any splitting scheme, and none is addressed.

**S-133** [local_879ec69b] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning*

Two arrangements with materially different properties, reported clearly enough that both can be assessed. On the Gait Fullbody Dataset the split unit is necessarily the child, because each of the 100 children contributes exactly one sample, so 10-fold cross-validation partitions 90 children against 10; each configuration was run through five complete cycles giving 50 training runs, with mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation reported. That is sound practice and the dispersion reporting is better than most of this corpus. On DREAM, 1,833 samples from 61 children were split 1,650 against 183 per fold with no participant-level partitioning described - roughly 30 samples per child distributed across folds - so within-participant leakage is unaddressed. The instructive result is the direction of the difference: the leak-prone dataset produced the lower figure, 70.19% against 95.4%, which means the gap between them cannot be explained by leakage and must lie in sensor coverage, task, label structure or class balance. That inversion is worth carrying into the synthesis, because it is a counterexample to the assumption that leakage always explains the highest numbers in a branch. Three issues nonetheless bound the Gait figure despite its clean split unit. The single sample per child was chosen from ten trials 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', so the modelled data were selected with knowledge of the outcome - a threat that operates entirely upstream of cross-validation and that no splitting scheme addresses. The 95.4% is the best of six architectures whose spread is 2.2 points against run-to-run standard deviations reaching 1.82, on test folds of ten children where a single child moves accuracy by ten percentage points, so the difference between the reported winner and the reference implementation's 94.8% is not resolvable. And the DREAM experiment discards the non-spectrum class, making it a two-way discrimination among autism-related labels rather than an autism-versus-non-autism task, with the resulting class balance never quantified so that no chance baseline exists for its 70.19%. Finally, the paper transmits without comment the single clearest piece of evidence in this review for augmentation-driven inflation: the Gait dataset's own creators reported approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation and 92% after applying seven augmentation techniques including noise addition, scaling and flipping. A 32-point gain from augmenting a 100-sample dataset is a statement about the augmentation, not about gait, and it is quoted here as motivating background.

**S-134** [local_93e5d23d] — *Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]*

Three compounding failures make the reported 90.28% uninterpretable, and none is discussed. First, there is no test partition: accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F-score are all validation-set figures, and no held-out evaluation of any kind appears in the paper. Second, the final model was chosen as the epoch with the best validation accuracy out of 2,000 - so the reported number is a maximum over 2,000 draws taken on the very partition it is reported from, an optimistic selection whose inflation on a small validation set is substantial. Third, the evaluation unit is the cry instance rather than the child, as Table 1's own definitions confirm, and no participant-level partitioning is described anywhere; with roughly six instances per child from 62 children, cries from the same child will fall on both sides of the boundary, so the network can recognise an individual voice and recover that child's fixed label. This is the same failure documented in this review for scanpath images, video frames, EEG epochs and thermal images, appearing here in a fifth modality. Set against this, the statistical analysis is a separate and more defensible piece of work - a prespecified comparison of three clinically established measures, replicating a direction reported in prior cry research, with significance at p < 0.01 and p < 0.0001. But it faces its own confounds, all reported in the paper and none adjusted: the groups differ by 4.8 months in mean age during a period of rapid vocal maturation, using measures that change with that maturation; 87.10% of autistic recordings came from autism centres against a comparison group split between health centres and homes, and all three measures are sensitive to room acoustics and background noise, with harmonics-to-noise ratio - the strongest finding - being a direct measure of periodic-to-aperiodic energy that ambient noise depresses mechanically; the eliciting causes of the cries differ between groups; two device classes were used; and the tests appear to be computed over cry instances rather than per-child means, leaving their effective sample size unclear. The corrective analyses are all available from data the paper already reports - stratify by recording setting, adjust for age, aggregate per child, and correlate the acoustic features with the GARS-2 scores already collected.

**S-135** [local_a0d73248] — *Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm*

Sound mechanics on a task with no uncertainty in it. Each respondent contributes one row so the split unit is the person, and 5-fold cross-validation is appropriate for 704 rows - both better than several comparators in this branch. Neither bears on the result. The outcome variable 'Class/ASD' is the summed A1-A10 score thresholded at the AQ-10 cut-off; the ten items are inputs; and 'result', the sum itself, is printed among the paper's own enumerated feature list with no feature-selection step removing it described. A model with access to either the items or the sum recovers the label exactly, on any partition, under any resampling scheme, with any classifier - and 0.9890 accuracy is a figure a single decision stump on the 'result' column would reach or exceed. This is the third study in the review resting on the UCI-derived autism screening tables, and the pattern is identical across all three: careful analytic practice above a label that is a closed-form function of the features. The paper's own stated limitation, that reliance on a single dataset may limit generalisability, correctly names an external-validity concern while leaving the internal one entirely unaddressed - which is the characteristic failure of this subliterature, since diversifying the datasets would change nothing if each new dataset carries the same arithmetic relationship between its items and its label.

**S-136** [local_4ceee075] — *Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics*

Strong where this review's video branch is usually weakest, and unexamined where this particular sample is weakest. The splitting is subject-independent stratified 5-fold cross-validation, and the paper states both the mechanism and the purpose: 'To provide strong model validation and prevent data leakage ... The dataset was divided on a subject-independent basis such that data from the same participant was not included in both training and validation datasets.' In a corpus of frame-level data from 100 children, where naive splitting would place frames of the same child on both sides and produce a near-perfect figure, this is exactly the right control, and it is named as such - the clearest anti-leakage statement in this review's video branch. Stratification preserves class ratio across folds; four overfitting controls are specified with their parameters; and the resulting figure of 85-90% is modest and plausible, benchmarked against external comparators rather than presented in isolation. The remaining issues are of two kinds. Procedurally, all reported figures are cross-validation results with no independent held-out test, so architecture selection and performance estimation share the same folds; the reported accuracy is a range rather than a mean with fold-level detail; specificity is not reported although recall of 0.95 against 85-90% accuracy implies it is materially lower; and the stated plus-or-minus 1.5% intervals are narrower than 20-child validation folds would ordinarily support, with no derivation given. Substantively, and more importantly, subject-independence protects against recognising an individual across the split but offers no protection against a group-level confound, and this sample has a severe one: the autistic group is approximately 84% male and the comparison group 52%, while the model's inputs are 468 facial mesh points and 75 body and hand landmarks, all encoding sex-linked morphology and posture. A classifier that separates boys from girls would perform equally well on unseen children and would be entirely consistent with the reported figures. The study is therefore a clear illustration of a distinction the synthesis should draw: leakage control and confound control are different problems, and closing the first - which this paper does deliberately and well - leaves the second untouched.

**S-137** [local_84bcd4ed] — *Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of*

Two separate problems, of different kinds. For the autism task, the evaluation is a 90.48/9.51 image-level split into 2,653 training and 279 testing images, with 10-fold cross-validation on the training portion. The number of distinct children behind 2,932 images is never stated and no participant-level partitioning is described, so in a web-assembled corpus where a single child may contribute several images, images of the same child can fall on both sides of the boundary - the failure this review has now recorded for six other studies on this corpus family. The exposure is greater here than usual because DeepFace's features are optimised for face identity, so the representation is specifically good at the thing an image-level split leaves exploitable. Compounding this, the reported 92% is described as spanning 'both training and testing datasets', so no held-out figure is given separately, and no per-class metric or interval accompanies it. The authors do identify the absence of an external validation cohort, correctly noting that 10-fold cross-validation addresses overfitting but not generalisability. None of this touches the more basic issue that the autistic images were harvested from autism-related websites, so the label encodes provenance and no splitting scheme could separate that from a facial phenotype. For the gelotophobia task, the problem is not validation but the absence of anything to validate. The ethics section states that the GELOPH<15> 'was not directly administered to participants in this study' and that 'no direct contact with human participants occurred', which contradicts the abstract's assertion that it 'was administered to confirm the diagnosis' and means that no image in the corpus carries a gelotophobia label of any kind. There is therefore no ground truth, no held-out set, no metric and no result - and the conclusion nonetheless states that the study 'demonstrates the effectiveness of combining deep learning techniques with validated diagnostic tools for detecting gelotophobia'. Across this whole review, this is the only instance of a primary claim for which no measurement of any kind was performed, and it is worth distinguishing in the synthesis from the many studies whose measurements are confounded or inflated.

**S-138** [local_d97673f4] — *Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

No validation scheme is described anywhere. The retrieved text states no train-test split proportion, no cross-validation arrangement, no held-out set size and no partitioning unit, while reporting accuracy 'on test data' and presenting a confusion matrix - so a test partition existed and its construction is unstated. The number of distinct children behind 2,940 images is likewise unreported, so whether images of the same child appear on both sides of the boundary cannot be determined; this is the standard failure of the corpus family and is documented in this review for seven other studies on the same images. Augmentation compounds the concern: zoom and brightness variants of a single photograph are near-duplicates rather than independent observations, and the paper does not state whether augmentation preceded or followed splitting - a distinction that another study in this review makes decisive, reporting that its dataset's originators moved from roughly 60% to 92% accuracy by applying seven augmentation techniques to a 100-sample corpus. Two features nonetheless make this study's figure among the more plausible in its branch. Its 88.33% is the second-lowest of the eight Kaggle-corpus studies charted here, which span 81.0% to 99.8%. And its architecture is the one least able to memorise, since frozen pretrained extractors with a logistic-regression head fit only a linear function of fixed embeddings, whereas the higher-scoring studies on the same images fine-tune millions of parameters end to end. Neither observation can be confirmed without the split description, and none of it touches the provenance confound: a model that has learned to recognise images sourced from autism-related web content will perform identically on perfectly subject-disjoint partitions.

**S-139** [local_86a67a4f] — *Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children*

Two failures of different kinds, and the reporting quality that exposes the second is worth crediting. The first is standard for this corpus family: the split is at image level, 2,526 training against 280 testing and 80 validation, with the number of distinct children behind 2,886 images unreported, so in a web-assembled collection where a child may appear in several photographs, images of one child can fall on both sides of the boundary. Stratified random sampling was used and is correctly described as preserving class proportions across partitions - but stratification balances classes, not subjects, and the paper does not consider subject overlap. The authors do state candidly that 'the dataset was split only once, and the procedure was not repeated due to the high computational expense of training deep learning models', which names a real limitation with its reason and is more forthcoming than most of this branch. The second failure is arithmetic and more serious. The autism model's reported metrics - accuracy 95, precision 0.96, recall 0.94, specificity 42.5, F1 0.95, AUC 78 - are mutually incompatible on the stated balanced test set: recall 0.94 with specificity 0.425 gives roughly 68% accuracy, precision would be near 0.62 rather than 0.96, and an AUC of 0.78 cannot accompany 95% accuracy. No reconciliation is offered anywhere. The instructive point for the synthesis is that this inconsistency is detectable only because the study reported specificity and AUC alongside accuracy; the seven other studies charted here on the same corpus report accuracy alone or accuracy with precision and recall, and an identical internal contradiction in any of them would be invisible. If the specificity is the accurate figure, the model is below chance at identifying non-autistic children, and the paper's 95% headline conceals a result that would substantially undercut the branch's claims. The provenance confound in the corpus is untouched by any of this, since a model recognising autism-related web imagery would succeed on any partition.

**S-140** [local_0a39cca9] — *Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy*

An 80:20 image-level split with no cross-validation, no separately described validation partition, and no participant-level partitioning; the number of distinct children behind 2,936 images is never stated. Augmentation by rotation, flipping and contrast adjustment is applied without specifying whether it preceded the split, and such variants of a single photograph are near-duplicates rather than independent observations. These are the standard weaknesses of this branch. What is distinctive here is a confound the mixed corpus introduces and the paper leaves entirely unexamined. The images come from two sources - Kaggle and an autism centre in Semarang - and neither the proportion from each nor their distribution across the two classes is reported. If the clinic supplied predominantly autistic images while the comparison class came predominantly from the international web collection, the classes would be separable by ancestry, camera, lighting and photographic convention without any facial phenotype being involved, and the reported 0.8299 would measure source rather than diagnosis. The paper's own account of what the network extracts - face shape, expression and skin texture - is consistent with that reading. The remedy is available and unused: with two identifiable sources in hand, a source-held-out evaluation, or simply a source-by-class table, would settle the question directly. Two elements of the analysis nonetheless stand above the branch norm: the learning curves are interpreted for stability and overfitting rather than displayed without comment, and the precision-recall trade-off across pairings is read in screening terms, with a high-precision low-recall model correctly judged 'less useful for finding all ASD cases'.

**S-141** [local_7432ffd7] — *Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models*

Stratified 5-fold cross-validation on 1,048,575 gaze-sample rows, stratified by class only. This is the review's clearest instance of within-participant leakage at the finest possible granularity: with 59 children and roughly 17,800 rows each, every test fold is virtually guaranteed to contain samples drawn from the same recording session, the same child and the same stimulus presentation as the training rows, differing by fractions of a second. A model can reach 99.78% by recognising individual children rather than autism. Three further defects compound it. First, mutual-information feature selection was run on the whole dataset before cross-validation, so the folds were chosen using their own test labels. Second, mean imputation of missing values was likewise computed over the whole dataset. Third, early stopping restores the weights that minimise loss on the same partition whose accuracy is then reported. The 0.11% standard deviation across folds is presented as evidence of stability; it is better read as confirmation that the five folds are near-identical resamples of one recording set. No participant-level split, no external cohort, and no held-out site is attempted anywhere in the paper.

**S-142** [local_8ff20c48] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning*

A single random 80/20 split: 593 training, 149 test. No cross-validation of the final model, no repeats, no seed, no stratification statement, no interval estimate. TPOT's internal search cross-validates within the training portion, so the pipeline choice is not directly contaminated by the test rows - a cleaner arrangement than most of this corpus - and the manual re-fit with the reported parameters confirms the pipeline is what it claims to be. Two problems dominate nonetheless. First, the validation design cannot address the label's circularity: no split scheme can turn the reconstruction of a checklist threshold into diagnostic accuracy. Second, the test set is 71.1% positive and the paper never states the majority-class baseline, even though it prints it - the SVM comparator's recall of 1.000 at precision 0.718 and accuracy 0.71 is the all-positive classifier, sitting unremarked in the comparison table as though it were a genuine competitor. Read against that baseline, the AUTOML pipeline's contribution is about 12 accuracy points, and the non-autistic recall of 0.53 shows where its errors fall - on precisely the children a screening tool exists to reassure.

**S-143** [local_986436f2] — *Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost*

An 80-20 stratified image-level split (2,020 / 506) with 5-fold cross-validation inside the training portion. The cross-validation placement is correct in principle and better than most of this branch. Four problems undo it. First, the split is image-level, not child-level, on a corpus known to contain repeated faces, so the same child can appear on both sides. Second, augmentation by rotation and scaling is described as part of preprocessing rather than as applied within training folds only. Third, and most serious, the headline numbers do not come from the 506-image test set at all: 200 images (100 ASD, 100 non-ASD) were selected from the test set for the final evaluation, with no selection rule stated, which is the definition of a hand-picked evaluation subset - and the accompanying confusion matrix nonetheless totals 300. Fourth, every reported metric is presented as a monotone function of epoch count with the maximum always at the largest value tried (500), and no criterion determined where to stop, so the reported figures are the best point on a curve rather than the output of a prespecified procedure. The cross-validation folds, having been run, are never reported as a mean and standard deviation.

**S-144** [local_bb4d1f7a] — *Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models*

The design is a 70:15:15 partition of 4,000 eye images derived from 40 children at exactly 100 images per child (50 frames, left and right eye). Because the per-child image count is constant and the split is at the image level, every participant is present in the training, validation and test subsets simultaneously; more finely still, the left and right eye of the same video frame - two crops of one instant of one recording - can land on opposite sides. This is frame-level leakage of the same kind documented in the video, EEG-epoch, thermal, cry and facial-image branches, and it is sufficient to explain a 97% four-class result from 40 children. Three further weaknesses compound it. Augmentation by rotation and shearing is described as a dataset-preparation step applied before partitioning. Cross-validation is asserted four separate times as ensuring robustness, but no fold count, no per-fold result and no variance is ever reported, so it cannot be assessed and may not have been run on the final model. And the external comparison in Table 7 places this study's four-class severity accuracies (95.93%, 97.95%) beside Saliency4ASD entries (74.22%, 65.41%, 61.62%) that solve a different, binary ASD-versus-TD task on different data - the numbers are not commensurable, and the higher figure is not evidence of a better method. To the authors' credit, the abstract itself concedes that further evaluation on an independent dataset will assess the generalizability and precision of the model, which is the correct reading of their own result.

**S-145** [local_13c1f46d] — *Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism*

The validation account is internally contradictory, and this is the study's central defect. The experimental section reports confusion matrices at five epoch settings whose correct-classification counts - 1,338 normal plus 1,362 autism at 1,000 epochs, and comparable figures at the other settings - account for essentially the entire stated dataset. No train-test division is described anywhere in that section. If those matrices are computed over all available images, then every reported metric is a resubstitution figure on the training data. Separately and much later, the comparison discussion asserts that 5-fold cross-validation was applied with 80% training and 20% testing per fold, and that the model consistently attained elevated accuracy and F1 scores across all folds, exhibiting minimal variance - yet not one per-fold number, mean or standard deviation is given, so the claim cannot be checked and does not reconcile with the confusion-matrix counts. On top of that: the reported headline is the best of five epoch settings with no selection criterion or held-out basis; the Crested Porcupine Optimizer searched hyperparameters against an unstated objective on an unstated partition; augmentation is described before any split; and the split, whatever it is, is at the image rather than the child level on a corpus known to repeat faces. The comparison in Table 3 sets this study's figure against seven baselines taken from other publications on unstated data and protocols, which is a comparison of numbers rather than of methods.

**S-146** [local_e771fb69] — *Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data*

This is the review's clearest case of a metric grid resting on almost nothing. The entire empirical base is 44 examples. Those are divided among three simulated federated clients by a rule that is never stated, and each client's reported accuracy is computed on nine test cases - a number that appears nowhere in the text and must be reconstructed from the confusion matrices (6+2+1+0 = 9; 6+3 = 9) and from the quantisation of every tabulated accuracy to multiples of one ninth. On nine cases the standard error of an accuracy estimate is roughly 17 percentage points, so the difference between the paper's best result (1.00, reported as 99.99%) and its worst (0.11) is barely more than sampling noise, and the four-subset by three-client by two-scenario by two-model grid amounts to dozens of comparisons among estimates that cannot be distinguished from each other. Three further problems compound it. Class-conditional mean imputation was applied across the full dataset, writing outcome information into the predictor matrix. SHAP-based feature selection was likewise performed on the whole dataset before the federated runs. And no split ratio, seed, cross-validation or repetition is reported, so none of the figures carries a variance estimate. Finally, the headline itself is unstable across the paper: the abstract credits 99.99% to Client 2 and 88% to Client 1, the contributions list credits 88% to Client 3, and the results section reports the best configuration as accuracy 1.00 - three descriptions of the same experiment. The framing of nine correct classifications out of nine as flawless classification performance and as high diagnostic accuracy suitable for healthcare applications is not supportable at any sample size this study has.

**S-147** [local_945300a5] — *Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network*

A single 70/20/10 division at the image level - 369, 105 and 51 images per class - applied to 1,050 photographs from 70 children at exactly 15 photographs each. Participant separation is therefore impossible: five near-identical shots of the same child pulling the same expression, taken minutes apart under fixed lighting at a fixed one-metre distance with the same camera settings, are distributed across training, validation and test. This is the same frame-level leakage documented across the video, EEG-epoch, thermal, cry and facial-image branches of this review, and it is the study's decisive methodological failure - the more so because the acquisition protocol is so tightly controlled that the only systematic variation left between images of different children is the children themselves. Three further points. The split is unrepeated and unseeded, with no cross-validation and no interval on any figure. Training and validation accuracy are reported as reaching nearly 100% within the first few epochs with loss near zero, described as optimal and stable performance without signs of overfitting, while held-out accuracy is 90% - a gap the paper reads as success rather than as evidence about the split. And group membership is perfectly confounded with institution, since all autistic children were photographed at a special school and all comparison children at a state school, so any residual site difference in setup, operator or child preparation is available to the classifier. What would have rescued the design is available and unused: with 70 children, a participant-level split holding out, say, 7 autistic and 7 typically developing children entirely would have cost nothing and produced an interpretable, if less impressive, number.

**S-148** [local_ed30e24c] — *Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI*

The validation section is, in most respects, the most carefully constructed in this review's questionnaire branch. A stratified 70/10/20 split is used, the roles of the three partitions are stated explicitly (fitting, hyperparameter tuning and model selection, final reporting), Bayesian optimisation is cross-validated inside the training data only, the test set is described as never used during training or tuning, and the author pre-empts the overfitting objection directly, listing four mitigations. Two problems defeat all of that care. The first is ordering: SVM-SMOTE was applied to the whole 1,054-case dataset before partitioning, expanding it to 1,456 instances, and only then was the balanced dataset randomly partitioned. Synthetic minority instances are interpolations between real minority cases, so synthetic rows in the training set are constructed from real rows that ended up in the test set, and synthetic rows in the test set are constructed from real training rows. The hold-out is therefore not independent, and this alone can produce near-perfect minority-class recall. The second is the estimand: the label Class/ASD_Traits is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome, a deterministic threshold on the sum of ten items that are supplied as features. No split scheme can make the reconstruction of that threshold into a diagnostic accuracy. Together these explain a result that the paper instead attributes to methodological quality - 292 of 292 test cases correct, zero false positives and zero false negatives, reported as 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity and as confirming suitability for reliable clinical screening. The external comparison in Table III compounds this by ranking the 100% against literature figures of 97.15%, 97.82% and 93.69% from other datasets and protocols, presenting the gap as a methodological advance.

**S-149** [local_b9de0d7f] — *Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques*

Phase I follows the familiar pattern: an 80:20 split plus 10-fold cross-validation over data whose label is a threshold on the summed predictors, with SMOTE applied at an unstated point relative to the split and feature selection of unstated nesting. Row counts are absent at every stage, so no reported figure can be located to a sample. That much places the study alongside local_ed30e24c, local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 in the circular-label group. Phase II is a different and more serious matter, and it is the reason this record exists. The teaching-method target did not come from any school, therapist, assessment or record: the paper states that a new column named Teaching Method was added to the dataset using the numpy library, containing integers 1 to 6 for six specialised teaching methods plus 0 for no special education needed, and that these were assigned on the basis of severity as analysed from the Q-CHAT-10 score, which is the count of the A1-A10 values. The models are then trained to predict that manufactured column from the other columns - including A1 to A10 themselves. The reported 0.9917 accuracy therefore measures how well a classifier reproduces an arithmetic rule that the authors wrote, applied to the very features they wrote it from. It is not an estimate of anything about children, education or autism; a lookup table would score 1.00. Compounding this, the mapping from severity band to intervention (Pivotal Response Training for high-level, technology-aided instruction for moderate-to-high, PECS for moderate, task analysis for low-to-moderate, Intensive Behavioral Intervention for low) is asserted with no evidence base, no clinical input and no citation, and it inverts the usual intensity gradient by assigning the most intensive intervention to the least affected group. The results are then offered to educators and professionals as a basis for informed decisions about teaching methods that can have a significant impact on the children's learning and development. The merged two-region design offered a genuine external-validation opportunity - train on one cohort, test on the other - and it is not taken.

**S-150** [local_14df790d] — *Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach*

The validation design is under-reported - no split proportions, no value of k, no per-fold results, no statement of whether feature selection and tuning were nested inside the training partition, and a passage stating that the manually tuned model is then trained and evaluated on the dataset to ensure generalization, which describes tuning and evaluating on the same data. The confusion matrices imply a 317-record test partition but disagree on its class composition across models (105/212 for three of them, 110/207 for the ANN). Underneath that, the estimand is the branch's usual one: Class/ASD traits is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome and Q1-Q10 are its summands, so predicting the former from the latter is arithmetic recovery. What makes this study analytically valuable to the review is that its own feature-subset experiment maps the circularity almost completely without naming it. Subsets 3 and 4 retain the Qchat-10-Score and discard the items; Q1-Q10 retains the items and discards the total; Subset 2 retains both, and the author observes that this could sometimes mislead the model results.
