Five supplementary tables and figures carry the full feature list, per-fold training performance, multi-threshold performance and two sensitivity models. The three-week review period is short, though the study's design and reporting do not show the marks of it.

**S-112** [local_261afa51] — *AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: &#x201C;A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System&#x201D;*

Proceedings of ICMISI 2024, the International Conference on Machine Intelligence and Smart Innovation, IEEE, pages 87-91 - a five-page general machine-intelligence conference paper with no clinical or biomedical scope. The format accounts for the brevity but not for the absence of an ethics statement, of a limitations section, or of any check on what the classifier responds to. The paper carries internal inconsistencies - two input sizes, a confusion matrix matching no stated partition, sensitivity written as a percentage of a proportion - that a substantive review would be expected to catch.

**S-113** [local_3e88f3ce] — *An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks*

Diagnostics 15(17):2232, MDPI, open access under CC BY; received 26 July 2025, revised 30 August, accepted 1 September, published 3 September 2025 - a 39-day cycle. A diagnostics journal, and the review appears to have engaged with the architecture rather than the inputs: a paper reporting 99.99% ROC-AUC for autism diagnosis, whose own explainability figures name the ADOS total as the leading predictor, was accepted with an internally inconsistent accuracy figure (99.40% against 96.4%), an internally inconsistent split description (70:30 against 20%), and a subject count for the held-out set matching neither. The supplied metadata dates the article to 2024 while the article itself is a 2025 publication.

**S-114** [local_5b5f2237] — *Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development*

IRBM 45 (2024), article 100838, Elsevier - a biomedical engineering journal, published as an Original Article with a highlights list and graphical abstract. Received 22 February 2023, revised 15 January 2024, accepted 27 May 2024, available online 6 June 2024, so nearly sixteen months in review. The venue is a reasonable fit: the paper's substance is signal processing applied to a clinical question, and the reporting reflects that balance, with the motion energy and wavelet procedures specified carefully and the clinical apparatus - diagnostic procedure, demographics, ethics - reported to adequate but not detailed standards. The journal's declaration templates produce the unusual artefact of an animal-research statement in a study of children.

**S-115** [local_13426811] — *Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning*

PLOS ONE 19(9), article e0311209, published 27 September 2024; received 19 March 2024, accepted 15 September 2024, open access under CC BY, with a named academic editor. Twenty-nine pages, of which a substantial proportion is devoted to the linguistic theory, the annotation scheme and the interpretation of what the tags mean - so the balance is unusual for this corpus, with the machine learning occupying perhaps a quarter of the paper and the linguistic framework the rest. The venue's reporting requirements produce the data availability, funding and competing-interests statements, and the length permits the annotation scheme to be documented at a level that a conference paper could not accommodate. Two supplementary files carry the tag frequency comparisons between groups.

**S-116** [local_948fa8d0] — *Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms*

International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications 15(5), 2024, pages 566 onwards - a general computer-science journal published by The Science and Information Organization, outside the clinical and biomedical literature. The venue accounts for the reporting profile: extensive procedural description of feature extraction, a large comparison grid, and no ethics, funding, competing-interests or limitations statement. It does not account for the absence of an evaluation protocol, which is a scientific rather than a formatting omission.

**S-117** [local_893dfc22] — *Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed*

Traitement du Signal 41(6), IIETA, open access under CC BY, doi 10.18280/ts.410628; received 12 April 2024, revised 7 August, accepted 20 August, available online 31 December 2024. A signal-processing venue. The review process accepted a paper whose title and abstract promise autism facial expression recognition while its experiments use two general-population posed-expression corpora; whose class count differs across three locations in the text; whose architecture narrative refers repeatedly to physiological signals that are never collected; and which states no validation scheme of any kind.

**S-118** [local_e7c16f2a] — *Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification*

PLOS ONE 19(4), article e0302238, published 22 April 2024; received 9 January 2024, accepted 28 March 2024, open access under CC BY, with a named academic editor. The venue's requirements produce the data availability statement with its GitHub URL, the funder no-role statement and the competing-interests declaration - and the first of these is what makes this the only included study in the review with openly published data. Eighteen pages, with substantial space given to the theoretical framing, the task design and the preprocessing mathematics, and comparatively little to the model architecture, which is not specified.

**S-119** [local_5a7ab52d] — *Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain*

Intelligent Decision Technologies 18(1):533-559, IOS Press, 2024; received 26 September 2022, accepted 28 October 2023 - a thirteen-month review at a decision-technologies journal outside the clinical and biomedical literature. Twenty-seven pages, of which the great majority document the optimisation algorithm, the network architecture and the metric definitions, with a single paragraph and one five-row table describing the data. The venue explains the balance and the absence of clinical reporting conventions; it does not explain the absence of a sample size, which no venue's norms would require to be omitted.

**S-120** [local_8253c2ec] — *Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder*

Journal of Computational Mathematics and Data Science 13:100105, Elsevier, 2024. A computational mathematics venue, and the reviewing focus followed accordingly: the optimisation methodology, the architecture comparison, the class-distribution reporting and the metric set are all handled to a reasonable standard, while a paper reporting 100% on six metrics across four datasets - and deploying a public diagnostic tool on that basis - was accepted without the derivation of the class variable being examined.

**S-121** [local_1e9d0b71] — *Machine learning’s effectiveness*

Frontiers in Psychiatry 15:1464285, Original Research, open access under CC BY; received 13 July 2024, accepted 30 September 2024, published 17 October 2024. Editorial and review handling is disclosed by name as Frontiers requires, and the reviewers include a researcher whose own work on movement analysis in autism is cited in this review's corpus - an indication that the paper was assessed within the relevant specialist community. The venue's structure produces the ethics, funding, competing-interests and data-availability statements, and supplementary materials carry the per-variable rationale and calculation methods that would not fit the main text.

**S-122** [local_b9e05a8f] — *Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network*

PeerJ Computer Science 11:e3134, submitted 8 April 2025, accepted 29 July 2025, published 2 October 2025, open access under CC-BY 4.0, academic editor Davide Chicco, with subject areas listed as bioinformatics, algorithms, artificial intelligence and data science. The venue is a computer science journal, which shapes what the review process attended to: the paper's statistical comparison of model variants, its ablation design, its code archiving on Zenodo and its leakage analysis are all above the norm for this branch, while the absence of any ethics statement, any diagnostic reference standard and any demographic description passed without comment. PeerJ's declaration structure elicited funding, competing-interests, author-contribution and data-availability statements from these authors but has no field that would have prompted a human-subjects declaration. The bibliographic record also carries an inconsistency worth noting for the corpus: the supplied metadata dates the article to 2024 while the article itself is a 2025 publication.

**S-123** [local_0b0960c4] — *Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]*

Advances in Technology Innovation 9(4):287-300, 2024, doi 10.46604/aiti.2024.13951; received 1 July 2024, revised 31 July, accepted 2 August 2024 - a 32-day cycle. A technology-innovation venue, and the reviewing pattern is consistent with that: the acquisition chain, the feature families and the four architectures with their layer equations are all documented, while the complete absence of any validation scheme, of any majority-class baseline, of a limitations section and of any account of diagnostic ascertainment passed without comment, as did an ethics declaration stating in absolute terms that no human-rights statement or informed consent is required.

**S-124** [local_abad69fd] — *Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play*

BMC Psychiatry 24:799, 2024, open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; received 10 May 2024, accepted 30 September 2024, doi 10.1186/s12888-024-06129-9. A clinical psychiatry venue, and the difference from the engineering venues that dominate this corpus is visible throughout: the paper reports matching statistics and their tests, cites the psychometrics of its diagnostic instrument, describes coder training and inter-rater reliability, reports odds ratios with confidence intervals, tests calibration and goodness of fit, enumerates five limitations including its own selection bias, and supplies the full coding manual as supplementary material. It is comparably weak where clinical journals are typically weak: the statistical software is not named, the code is not available, the stepwise criterion is unstated and no optimism-corrected estimate is reported. The version under review is the blinded submission, with the recruiting hospital and ethics committee anonymised in the text.

**S-125** [local_cd7545e2] — *Predictive model using autism*

Frontiers in Psychiatry 15:1493158, Original Research, open access under CC BY; received 13 September 2024, accepted 19 November 2024, published 18 December 2024. Editorial and review handling is disclosed by name as the venue requires. This is a clinical psychiatry journal and the paper reads accordingly: the diagnostic process is described in detail with the explicit exclusion of ADOS-2 and ADI-R from it, the full clinical battery is reported for each group, sample size is justified against a comparable prior study, significance thresholds are stated including a stricter alpha for correlations, AUC interpretive bands are prespecified, effect sizes carry confidence intervals throughout, and the limitations section names overfitting as the explanation for the study's own validation drop. What a computational venue would have added is missing - no code, no data deposit, no statement of the holdout procedure's details - and what a computational venue would have missed is present in full.

**S-126** [local_3ecb92bf] — *The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech*

Frontiers in Digital Health 7:1274675, Original Research, open access under CC BY; received 8 August 2023, accepted 28 May 2025, published 18 August 2025, with editor and reviewers disclosed by name. The near two-year interval between submission and acceptance is unusual. The venue is a digital-health rather than a clinical journal, and the paper reads accordingly: the partitioning, metrics, benchmarking and fairness analysis are handled to a good computational standard while the clinical description of the corpora - diagnostic procedures, ages, per-class participant counts, recording conditions - is left almost entirely to the source datasets and is internally inconsistent where it is given. The supplied bibliographic metadata dates the article to 2024 while the article itself is a 2025 publication.

**S-127** [local_4b02df7c] — *Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism*

JMIR Formative Research 2024;8:e52660, Original Paper, open access. The record carries two notable annotations: the version retrieved is a corrected version, with the correction statement published at JMIR Formative Research 2024;8:e59349, and a formal comment on the article appears at JMIR Formative Research 2024;8:e59794. A published comment on a paper of this kind indicates that its approach was contested in the literature, which is itself part of the paper's significance for this review - it is the only included study whose ethics generated a documented scholarly exchange. JMIR's formative-research track is intended for feasibility and early-stage work, which fits a study whose conclusion is that the thing is possible and should not be done without consent. The venue's structure produced the ethical-considerations section with its IRB number, data-governance determination and description of measures taken beyond regulatory requirement - a section that has no counterpart anywhere else in this corpus.

**S-128** [local_7d7f1fcc] — *Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children*

PLOS ONE 19(10):e0308388, Research Article, open access under CC BY; received 30 April 2024, accepted 12 July 2024, published 3 October 2024. PLOS ONE's structural requirements produced the data-availability statement, funding itemisation and competing-interests declaration, and the venue's data-sharing policy is visibly what prompted the considered middle position adopted here - raw recordings withheld because they contain faces and voices, a de-identified pose subsample deposited on Zenodo with a DOI, and training code published on GitHub. That is the policy working as intended, and it is worth noting for the review that the same policy which cannot compel raw sharing of identifiable child data did elicit a genuinely useful partial release, made possible by the study's own choice of a skeletal representation.

**S-129** [local_5a331ffe] — *Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning*

Biomedical Signal Processing and Control 89:105712, Elsevier; received 24 February 2023, revised 18 October 2023, accepted 5 November 2023, available online 8 November 2023, with a 2024 issue date. A signal-processing venue, and the fingerprints are visible in both directions: the architectural detail, the metric definitions, the four-dataset comparison and the careful argument about MSE versus CCC are all to a good engineering standard, while the absence of any ethics or consent statement for identifiable children's home videos, the undocumented comparison class and the absent demographics passed review without comment. The journal's structure elicited funding, competing-interests, author-contribution and data-availability declarations but has no field that would have prompted a human-subjects statement.

**S-130** [local_45ef7022] — *A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features*

Biomedical Signal Processing and Control 100:107009, Elsevier; received 25 November 2023, revised 8 August 2024, accepted 30 September 2024, online 10 October 2024, with a 2025 issue date. The same journal published another study charted in this review, and the pattern is consistent across both: signal-processing components are held to a reasonable standard - denoising evaluated against alternatives on PSNR and SSIM, architectural choices supported by ablation, hyperparameters tabulated - while the clinical apparatus passes without scrutiny. Here that meant an article proposing automated psychiatric medication dosing for children was published with the declaration 'Ethical Approval. Not required.', with no stated source for its outcome labels, with no participant-level validation, and with no limitations section. The journal's declaration structure elicited statements on ethics, funding, data availability and authorship, so the ethics field was completed - with a denial of applicability that went unqueried.

**S-131** [local_0f5a351e] — *Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

Frontiers in Medicine 12:1569464, Original Research, open access under CC BY; received 31 January 2025, accepted 16 April 2025, published 21 May 2025, with editor and three reviewers disclosed by name. The venue is a general medical journal rather than an engineering one, which makes the pattern of what passed review notable: a physiognomic premise asserted without measurement, a corpus whose comparison class is described in the paper's own methods as web-search results, no demographic information of any kind, results reported from a validation partition while a defined test partition goes unreported, support counts inconsistent with the stated split, a claimed feature-importance analysis that does not exist, and an introduction that contradicts the abstract and the results tables about which models were compared. The retrieved text ends mid-discussion at Table 8, so the declarations could not be assessed.

**S-132** [local_786b6280] — *Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features*

2024 IEEE 3rd International Conference on Computing and Machine Intelligence (ICMI), doi 10.1109/ICMI60790.2024.10585946. A short computing-conference paper, single-authored by a student at The Harker School in San Jose - a secondary school - which is worth recording factually because it contextualises both the scale and the character of the work. The paper is careful where a beginner might not be: it splits by participant, justifies its repeated-split design with a stated stability criterion, documents its token-cleaning rules against TalkBank's transcription guide, plots ROC variability bands, compares its feature findings explicitly against three named prior studies including where it contradicts them, and reports modest accuracies without inflation. It is weaker on the clinical reasoning that a conference in computing and machine intelligence would not have prompted: no independent language measure, no age composition by group, a non-autistic clinical comparison deliberately discarded, and a recommendation about clinical model choice resting on a one-to-two-point margin. Set beside several journal papers in this review that report 98-100% from image-level splits on web-scraped corpora, its 84% from a participant-level split on a consented research archive is the more informative result.

**S-133** [local_879ec69b] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning*

Electronics 14(11):2231, MDPI, open access under CC BY; received 26 April 2025, revised 21 May, accepted 26 May, published 30 May 2025 - a 34-day review cycle. An electronics and computing venue, and the profile matches: the software stack is versioned to nine packages, the hardware is specified, the cross-validation scheme is stated separately for each dataset with fold sizes and repetition counts, and every architecture is reported with mean, max, min and standard deviation. What a clinical venue would have required is absent: no sensitivity or specificity, no demographic composition, no examination of the outcome-informed trial selection quoted in the methods, and no discussion of what the 25-point gap between the two datasets implies about the construct being measured.

**S-134** [local_93e5d23d] — *Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]*

Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, Brief Report, accepted 18 March 2025, open access under CC BY-NC-ND, doi 10.1007/s10803-025-06811-1. A clinical autism journal, and the venue's influence is visible in what is reported well: the four-stage diagnostic procedure with clinician qualifications, the explanation of why ADOS was unavailable in Farsi, the ethics and consent statements, the exclusion rules, the per-group recording-setting and cry-cause distributions, and above all a competing-interest declaration that itemises employment, founder status, equity holding and advisory compensation by individual. The brief-report format constrains length, but the omissions that matter are not length-related - a test partition, a participant-level split and a model-selection rule that does not maximise over the evaluation set are design decisions rather than reporting ones, and the same journal's structure that elicited an exemplary conflict declaration did not elicit any account of how the 90.28% was obtained.

**S-135** [local_a0d73248] — *Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm*

Procedia Computer Science 258:1576-1585, Elsevier, 2025, open access under CC BY-NC-ND, doi 10.1016/j.procs.2025.04.389, peer-reviewed under the scientific committee of the International Conference on Machine Learning and Data Engineering. A conference-proceedings venue with a short review cycle, and the reviewing engaged with the modelling rather than the data: a paper whose own methods section prints a feature list containing both the summed screening score and the thresholded outcome derived from it was accepted reporting 0.9890 accuracy without that relationship being examined.

**S-136** [local_4ceee075] — *Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics*

Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics 14(5):3985-4000, October 2025, open access under CC BY-SA; received 20 March, revised 8 August, accepted 1 September 2025. An electrical engineering and informatics venue, and the profile of what was and was not scrutinised follows: the acquisition protocol, the feature construction, the validation strategy, the regularisation parameters and the architecture are all specified in detail, while the absence of any diagnostic ascertainment procedure and of any ethics or consent statement for a prospective study recording 100 children passed review without comment. The journal's structure elicited conflict-of-interest and data-availability declarations - the latter citing 'privacy and ethical considerations' - but has no field that would have prompted a human-subjects statement.

**S-137** [local_84bcd4ed] — *Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of*

JMIR Formative Research 9:e72115, 2025, Original Paper, with a companion article listed at formative.jmir.org/2026/1/e91833. The formative-research track is intended for early-stage and feasibility work, which fits a study proposing a diagnostic architecture ahead of collecting the data to evaluate it. The venue's structure produced the ethics, funding, data-availability and competing-interest declarations, and the ethics statement is more detailed than most in this branch - it is also the statement that reveals the contradiction with the abstract about whether the GELOPH<15> was administered. That a paper whose abstract, objective and conclusion all centre on gelotophobia detection was published while its own ethics section records that no gelotophobia assessment took place is a reviewing gap that the structured declarations made visible rather than concealed.

**S-138** [local_d97673f4] — *Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Cognitive Models and Artificial Intelligence Conference (AICCONF '24), Istanbul, 25-26 May 2024, ACM, doi 10.1145/3660853.3660888; five pages. A short conference paper from an artificial-intelligence venue, and the profile follows: the preprocessing and augmentation are documented carefully, the software and hardware are versioned, and the five-extractor comparison is set up systematically, while no validation scheme, no class distribution, no per-configuration results, no ethics statement and no limitations section appear.

**S-139** [local_86a67a4f] — *Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children*

Pattern Recognition 173:112906, Elsevier; received 13 June 2025, revised 11 November 2025, accepted 8 December 2025, online 9 December 2025, with a 2026 volume date. A pattern-recognition venue, and the profile is characteristic: the partition sizes, stratification procedure, quality filter, architectures and metric tables are all documented, while a metric set that is arithmetically impossible on its own stated test set was published without reconciliation, alongside no ethics statement, no diagnostic ascertainment and no chance baseline. The limitations section is nonetheless one of the better ones in the branch, which suggests the shortfall is in verification rather than in candour.

**S-140** [local_0a39cca9] — *Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy*

International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications 16(7):229ff, 2025. An open-access computer science venue, and the profile follows: the ensemble pipeline, augmentation, split ratio and metric tables are documented, while the corpus's dual provenance is left unquantified, no ethics statement appears despite clinic-sourced images, no limitations section is provided, and the conclusion repeats the results paragraph verbatim. An unedited template placeholder survives in the keyword list.

**S-141** [local_7432ffd7] — *Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models*

Frontiers in Medicine 12:1690177 - an open-access general medical journal, not a computing venue. This matters for the review's venue analysis: the paper's audience is clinical, its abstract advises healthcare professionals, and no clinical reviewer flagged the absence of an ethics statement, the absence of a limitations section, or the use of a diagnostic instrument as a model input.

**S-142** [local_8ff20c48] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning*

Diagnostics 15(15):1859 (MDPI) - an open-access clinical diagnostics journal, with academic editors drawn from the biomedical signal-processing community. The venue's clinical framing did not surface the label circularity or the abstract/table accuracy mismatch in review.

**S-143** [local_986436f2] — *Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost*

Sadhana 51(1):30 - the Indian Academy of Sciences' general engineering-sciences journal, not a clinical or specialist vision venue. This is relevant to the review's venue analysis: the mismatch between a 2D Kaggle photo set and a paper about 3D scanning, the unsourced demographic table, the absent ethics statement and the internally inconsistent confusion matrix all survived a 324-day review cycle at a general engineering journal.

**S-144** [local_bb4d1f7a] — *Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models*

Neural Computing and Applications 37(33):27631-27654, in a special issue drawn from the 2023 India International Congress on Computational Intelligence. Special-issue routing is relevant to the review's venue analysis: the impossible CARS bands, the absent TD group behind a TD claim in the abstract, the surviving x placeholder in the participant count, and a literature review containing building-energy and distributed-generation citations all passed review in 53 days.

**S-145** [local_13c1f46d] — *Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism*

Computers, Materials & Continua 83(2) (Tech Science Press) - a broad-scope open-access computing journal covering materials, computing and engineering. This is the review's clearest venue-mismatch case: a diagnostic claim about children, resting on unlabelled web photographs and an explicit ethics exemption, published in a journal with no clinical review capacity, with no limitations section and no future work, in 81 days.

**S-146** [local_e771fb69] — *Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data*

Complex & Intelligent Systems 11:173 (Springer) - a computational-intelligence journal. Relevant to the review's venue analysis in a specific way: this is a privacy-and-governance paper by construction, invoking GDPR and HIPAA, published without an ethics statement of any kind, and its headline accuracy of 99.99% on nine test cases passed review over 126 days.

**S-147** [local_945300a5] — *Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network*

2025 10th International Conference on Computer and Communication Engineering (ICCCE), IEEE, pages 351-355. A short engineering conference paper. The venue explains but does not excuse the asymmetry between a fully specified acquisition protocol and a completely unspecified model, and the survival of unrelated stunting terminology in the workflow description.

**S-148** [local_ed30e24c] — *Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI*

Engineering, Technology & Applied Science Research 15(5):27954-27959 - an open-access general engineering journal. A 100% diagnostic accuracy claim, a hold-out contaminated by pre-split synthetic oversampling, and a label that is a threshold on its own predictors passed review there in 48 days including a revision round.

**S-149** [local_b9de0d7f] — *Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques*

IEEE Access - a high-volume open-access multidisciplinary engineering journal. The published PDF is the unedited accepted version, retaining template placeholders in the header (Date of publication xxxx 00, 0000; DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2017.DOI) and a VOLUME 4, 2016 footer throughout. No reviewer questioned a fabricated educational-placement target, a 99.99% figure absent from the results, or the absence of any ethics statement in a paper recommending educational interventions for individual children.

**S-150** [local_14df790d] — *Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach*

Engineering Research Express 7(2):025269 (IOP Publishing) - an open-access general engineering journal. A 132-day review including one revision round did not surface the mutually inconsistent confusion matrices, the missing split proportions and cross-validation k, the unstated chance level, or an ethics statement that treats absence of direct human interaction as constituting ethical approval.

**S-151** [local_4da2b941] — *Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study*

Research in Autism 128:202712 (Elsevier) - a specialist autism research journal rather than an engineering or general-science venue, and the difference is visible throughout: dimensional outcomes, in-sample psychometrics, effect sizes with confidence intervals for group comparisons, a self-critical limitations section, an ethics analysis of algorithmic screening in mental health, and deposited code. It is the only paper in the corpus published in a venue whose reviewers are subject-matter specialists in autism, and it is also the only one to release code, report internal consistencies, or discuss stigma.

**S-152** [local_6e7174c0] — *A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach*

International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems 18(3):312-319 - an open-access computing journal. Review appears to have been rapid (received 17 January 2025, revised 4 February 2025) and did not surface the absent ethics statement, the unreported class counts, the 200-image test set behind a four-way ranking claim, or the mismatch between a movement-based biomarker rationale and a still-image input.

**S-153** [local_e04bcd32] — *Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network*

International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems 18(4) - an open-access computing journal, the same venue as local_6e7174c0. Review did not surface the mismatch between the stated 400-image test set and the 2,940-image evaluation, the absent ethics statement, or the reporting of reference-dependent image-quality metrics for photographs that have no sharp reference.

**S-154** [local_183eaef4] — *Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI*

Diagnostics 14(22):2504 (MDPI) - an open-access clinical diagnostics journal, with paediatric and psychiatric clinicians among the authors. The clinical involvement is real and shaped the feature selection; it did not surface that four instrument measurements of the target condition were sitting in the predictor set, which is precisely the observation clinical expertise is best placed to make. The paper cleared review in 40 days.

**S-155** [local_b6ac2b98] — *Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks*

Frontiers in Neuroscience 19:1558621 - an open-access neuroscience journal, with a 127-day review. The venue's disciplinary fit shows in the reporting: matched group characteristics with ANOVA and chi-squared tests, a standardised language measure, a pre-specified interpretive scale for F1, an ethics reference number, and a limitations paragraph that includes the provisionality of early diagnoses.

**S-156** [local_44d3aef5] — *Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis*

Frontiers in Medicine 11:1436646 - an open-access clinical journal, accepted in 44 days. A 100% diagnostic accuracy claim, an abstract that reports image counts as child counts, an absent ethics statement, an unstated test-set size and no limitations section all passed clinical review.

**S-157** [local_24fefc5f] — *A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection*

Computational Biology and Chemistry 120:108619 (Elsevier), 2026 issue. A computational-biology venue, and the mismatch shows: a paper with no sample size, no validation protocol, no reported class balance, two incorrect metric definitions, image architectures applied to binary questionnaire responses, and author statements referring to co-authors of a single-authored manuscript.

**S-158** [local_69b10fe4] — *An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms*

Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders 18:8, a specialist neurodevelopmental journal, with a 180-day review - the longest among the charted 2026 studies. The disciplinary fit is visible throughout: formal group matching with equivalence tests, mixed models with appropriate random-effect structure, Bayesian evidence for the null, pre-specified interpretive thresholds, deposited data and scripts, complete ethics reporting including participant remuneration, and a limitations section that reasons about cohort effects in ascertainment.

**S-159** [local_af9f4c12] — *An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data*

Discover Applied Sciences 8(4):363 (Springer) - an open-access multidisciplinary applied-sciences journal. The venue is not clinical, yet the paper is the most careful in the branch about the boundary between computational and clinical claims, which suggests the discipline of the authors rather than of the reviewers is doing the work here.

**S-160** [local_367db0b6] — *An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns*

Alexandria Engineering Journal 145 (2026) 164-181 (Elsevier) - a general engineering journal. Review did not surface a sample description in which 25,000 positive cases are drawn from 10,000 samples and a 21-to-1 ratio is called balanced, three incompatible age ranges for the study population, partition counts differing between sections, a named metric set none of whose values are reported, cybersecurity vocabulary about malicious and fraudulent events in a paper about infants, or a surviving response-to-reviewers sentence in the body text.

**S-161** [local_8d43288c] — *Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos*

Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience 20:1626315, with a 174-day review including a substantial revision. The review did not surface the absent ethics statement for reuse of identifiable children's home videos, the unreported number of distinct children, the absence of a non-autistic comparison behind a screening claim, or the reading of near-zero fold variance as robustness.

**S-162** [local_5f57ba19] — *Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension*

Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 10(3), Article ETRA012, the ETRA eye-tracking venue. The disciplinary fit shows in the reporting: participant-independent nested cross-validation, bootstrap intervals, a majority-class lower bound, paired significance testing between conditions, fold-level attribution computation, and an explicit comparison of the achieved performance against published clinical-viability thresholds.

**S-163** [local_1d856900] — *Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare*

Computer Modeling in Engineering & Sciences 146(1):41 (Tech Science Press), 55 days from submission to acceptance. A modelling and engineering venue; review did not surface an entirely unsourced clinical dataset carrying an IRB claim with no committee or institution, a split performed over augmented copies, a four-class severity result reported alongside a binary detection result, or four autism instruments sitting in the predictor set.

**S-164** [local_7b19a959] — *Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis*

Translational Psychiatry 16:129 (Nature Portfolio) - a clinical and translational psychiatry journal, and the only such venue in the charted corpus. The disciplinary fit is evident throughout: matched-subsample analysis, Bonferroni-corrected group comparisons, a label-randomisation control, sensitivity and specificity reported separately, deposited analysis code, documented data-access procedures, an explicit language statement citing community preference, and a discussion that diagnoses the methodological failures of the prior literature it is compared against.

**S-165** [local_d7b6fa00] — *Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath*

Array 30 (2026) 100753 (Elsevier) - an open-access computer science journal. The author list spans engineering and clinical institutions including a psychiatric hospital, which makes the absence of any description of the source cohort's diagnosis or demographics more notable rather than less. The paper discloses an editorial conflict of interest for one author, which is good practice and uncommon in this corpus.

**S-166** [local_e54c304c] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models*

Journal of Pioneering Medical Sciences 15(1):137-145, a medical sciences journal, 90 days from submission to acceptance. Clinical review did not surface the absent class counts and split ratios, the mAP inconsistency, or the reported finding that one of the two models labels a dog as autistic.

**S-167** [local_e4c2a776] — *Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images*

Multimedia Tools and Applications 85:300 (Springer), 218 days with a revision round. A multimedia and computing venue. Review did not surface an ethics declaration stating that no human participants were involved in a study of 2,940 children's photographs, a data-availability statement denying that any dataset was analysed, a test accuracy above training accuracy read as good generalisation, or the mismatch between the stated 50 epochs and the 25-epoch learning curves.

**S-168** [local_231757c7] — *SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers*

Frontiers in Psychiatry 17:1751654, 107 days with a revision round. A psychiatry venue, and the fit shows in the reporting - confidence intervals on a small-sample result, an explicit statement that held-out sets are not external validation, full provenance for a secondary analysis, and a limitations discussion that identifies the study's own most striking result as uninterpretable. The revision round appears to have strengthened rather than softened these statements, since the synthetic-data caveat appears in the abstract itself.

**S-169** [local_1b457442] — *Screening autism spectrum*

Scientific Reports 15(1):34134 (Nature Portfolio). A multidisciplinary venue. The reporting reflects it: demographic tables by group and sex, six metrics with stated rationales, a quantified overfitting check, KS validation of the oversampling, and a limitations section that names the information cost of the privacy choice.

**S-170** [local_b26db2f2] — *Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches*

Expert Systems With Applications 295 (2026) 128884 (Elsevier) - an applied AI journal. Review did not surface that 640 analysis rows come from 12 children with no participant-level partitioning, nor the Phishing keyword.

## RQ5.3 — Year and framing

_170 of 170 studies charted for this question._

**S-001** [local_76fc33d0] — *Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers*

2013 - the earliest study in this corpus. The paper characterises the field as having focused on verbal children over age three and positions itself as pushing the age range down to 18 months; it does not otherwise analyse field-level trends.

**S-002** [local_0dbc5018] — *Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities*

2015. The paper characterises prior pattern-classification work in ASD as dominated by neuroimaging (structural MRI, DTI) with only isolated behavioral examples (automated vocal analysis), and positions kinematics as a cheaper, less intrusive alternative - an explicit statement of the field's shift from neuroimaging toward behavioral signals.

**S-003** [local_dc5fc4bb] — *ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data*

2016. The related-work section positions the study against neuroimaging-based ADHD classification and against kinematic ASD classification in 2-4 year-olds (Crippa et al.), explicitly noting that its own high-functioning, older ASD participants are harder to separate from controls - an early acknowledgement that sample severity drives reported accuracy across this literature.

**S-004** [local_863980f8] — *Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework*

2016. The paper characterises machine learning in autism research as so far dominated by feature selection to shorten diagnostic instruments (ADOS/ADOS-G item reduction) and by neuroimaging, with behavioral classification only just beginning (citing Crippa et al. 2015 as the motivating precedent) - documenting the field's pivot toward behavioral prediction that this corpus goes on to record.

**S-005** [local_be8aa62f] — *Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder*

2016. The paper positions data mining of language production for psychopathology as previously proposed but never demonstrated quantitatively across diagnostic groups, presenting itself as a first step - an early marker of the linguistic-content strand that grows later in this corpus (social media text, picture-book narratives, conversation transcripts).

**S-006** [local_e404a2a3] — *Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism*

2016. The paper positions itself as the first to use smart-device serious games to study motor patterns in autism, and notes only one prior machine-learning study of autism-specific motor patterns (Crippa et al., optical motion capture, n=30) - which it critiques directly for SVM plus leave-one-out cross-validation being 'prone to over-fitting'. This is the corpus's clearest early example of methodological self-correction within the field, and it documents the shift from laboratory optical motion capture to consumer-device sensing.

**S-007** [local_780141fc] — *Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study*

2017. The paper surveys the emergence of machine learning in autism research across neural markers, cognitive scores, diagnostic-instrument item reduction and pregnancy risk factors, and notes that 'to date, there have been few studies that have applied machine learning to autistic motor data', naming Crippa et al. (2015) as the only prior motor example. It positions itself as the first to apply machine learning to imitation kinematics and, unusually, contrasts its own design against that predecessor on specific methodological grounds - less constrained task, exploration of which test conditions discriminate, and adults rather than children where group differences should be smaller.

**S-008** [local_3a331973] — *Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data*

2017. The paper characterises computer vision for ADHD and ASD as 'still in its infancy', with prior work confined to detecting predefined behavioural markers (AOSI markers, self-stimulatory behaviour, social games, engagement) whose 'effectiveness in predicting the actual ADHD and ASD diagnosis still remains to be seen'. It positions itself as one of the first to pose diagnosis directly as a machine-learning problem and, unusually for this corpus, targets adults rather than children.

**S-009** [local_7b3e6b3a] — *Earlier identification of children with autism*

2017. The paper notes that early speech-language development in ASD has repeatedly been characterised as delayed and deviant but that only a few studies examine vocalisation specificities at the feature level, and that most of those assessed crying with single acoustic features such as fundamental frequency or duration. It positions itself as one of the first to explore ASD-related pre-linguistic vocalisation specificities across a wide standardised parameter set - documenting the shift from single hand-picked acoustic measures to standardised high-dimensional feature sets that characterises the speech strand of this corpus.

**S-010** [local_36aa3ace] — *Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative*

2017. The paper characterises the field as showing that 'high levels of accuracy can be achieved' for discriminating typically developing children from children with ASC, but immediately qualifies that these results come from 'rather small datasets, and may lead to potential confounds', naming corpus size as 'a major obstacle in the development of robust models which are sufficiently reliable for clinical practice'. It positions itself as the first application of GAN representation learning in computational paralinguistics. This is one of the corpus's most explicit internal critiques of its own literature's headline accuracies.

**S-011** [local_44b58f21] — *ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces*

2018. The paper notes that machine learning has been proven effective for automated gait recognition in cerebral palsy, post-stroke and Parkinson's disease, but that 'research in the area of automated recognition of ASD gait using machine learning techniques based on GRFs gait features is less prevalent' - positioning autism gait analysis as lagging behind other clinical gait populations, and its own contribution as an incremental extension of the authors' prior KNN study on the same data.

**S-012** [local_cb9a5b48] — *Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening*

2018. The paper situates itself against traditional questionnaire-and-expert screening (3DI, ASD-OC), noting clinical guidance that no questionnaire can be recommended as a diagnostic test and that a combination of direct behavioural observation and caregiver report is recommended instead - then frames robot-based screening as 'a new trend'. Its own contribution is explicitly the automation of a previously manual feature-extraction step in an existing robot protocol, illustrating the corpus-wide progression from manually coded behavioural observation to automated sensing of the same behaviour.

**S-013** [local_40cd7d53] — *Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children*

2018 (published online August 2018, in the 2019 volume). The paper documents the field's trajectory in some detail: eye tracking as 'one emerging objective tool increasingly being applied in ASD clinics and research', machine learning recently applied to behaviour, brain activity and eye tracking with 'encouraging results', and ASD biomarker research having 'grown exponentially' with integration into future risk assessment 'almost certain'. It also situates itself against three specific predecessors (Shic et al. on infants, Liu et al. on face-scanning machine learning, Fujioka et al. on adults), comparing accuracies directly - one of the more explicitly cumulative papers in the corpus.

**S-014** [local_5b1d0b36] — *Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday*

2018. The paper characterises prior speech-based autism work as demonstrating that vocalisations contain usable biomarkers across infants, young children and teenagers, but criticises it on two specific grounds: recordings are 'mostly based on audio data obtained in very controlled environments' and are 'often manually reviewed, segmented, and processed by speech experts', which limits both practicality and recording length. It positions the emergence of affordable child-specific smart devices (Amazon Echo Kids Edition at $79, Xiaomi Kids Smartwatch at $45) as the enabling shift - documenting the corpus-wide movement from laboratory instrumentation toward consumer hardware and naturalistic settings, and framing it explicitly as a global health-equity argument.

**S-015** [local_54954c19] — *Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching*

2018. The paper surveys autism classification from fMRI (71-86.7% across several studies) and EEG (94%), and argues that eye tracking 'has not been used to investigate whether it is suitable to detect autism by considering atypical visual attention patterns', claiming to be the first study to test gaze data for autism screening. It also documents an important methodological trend critically rather than approvingly - noting that several high-accuracy results in the literature rest on partitioning by data segment rather than by participant - and situates eye tracking as moving from research equipment into consumer hardware (Samsung Galaxy S4, Tobii gaming trackers, Acer notebooks), anticipating the consumer-device turn this corpus records.

**S-016** [local_d8dc996a] — *Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

2018. The paper surveys machine learning applied to autism across quotient-based diagnostic tools, MRI, kinematic data, eye tracking and language acoustics, and argues that these modalities are 'quite invasive or require specialized personnel, often affecting the behavior of the subjects under study', and that most rely on 'handcrafted features and simplified linear models that often fail to handle the complexity of human behaviors in less controlled settings'. It positions itself as the first to cast autism diagnosis as a video-based computational problem and as part of the shift toward deep learning - a shift this corpus documents accelerating sharply from 2018 onward.

**S-017** [local_88ddfdd1] — *A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task*

2019. The paper's field characterisation is methodological rather than clinical: it observes that 'most related studies rely on spatial information about which different areas of visual stimuli were looked at, without considering the order in which this occurred', and that 'even state-of-the-art analyses of this type are typically based on spatial but not temporal eye movement information'. It also criticises the prevailing stimulus convention - that existing studies 'typically use facial images with cropped peripheral regions... and such that the locations of the key facial regions are the same across images', which 'facilitates the analysis but can be seen as somewhat unrealistic'. Both observations identify structural simplifications in the gaze literature that this corpus otherwise leaves unexamined.

**S-018** [local_361110f1] — *Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features*

2019. The paper characterises machine learning in autism as having concentrated on two things: shortening existing diagnostic instruments by removing redundant ADOS and ADI-R items (citing a claimed 100% accuracy from an 8-item ADOS subset, later above 95% on a larger sample), and classifying from neuroimaging, eye gaze and kinematic data - with only 'a handful' of kinematic studies, none of which targeted restricted and repetitive behaviour. Its closing argument that integrating genetic, neurological, psychological and kinematic features 'might pose a considerable challenge to the current diagnostic criteria of ASD' is one of the corpus's more ambitious claims about where the field is heading.

**S-019** [local_51533de4] — *Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations*

2019. The paper characterises the speech-and-autism literature as drawing overwhelmingly on either highly structured elicitation (reading sentences or word lists) or semi-structured clinical interviews with an autism expert, chiefly ADOS evaluations, and argues these 'produce results that may not generalize to the everyday conversations that impact the lives of children on the autism spectrum'. It cites specific prior accuracies for calibration - roughly 74% from pitch features on 146 children, roughly 69% from speech rate and rhythm on 69 children - and identifies interlocutor speech features as an emerging and underused signal, noting prior findings that psychologists' speech predicted children's symptom severity better than the children's own features. This move from clinical-elicitation corpora toward naturalistic interaction is one of the clearest trend statements in the corpus.

**S-020** [local_96c87d36] — *Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking*

2019. The paper surveys the eye-tracking-plus-machine-learning literature specifically, citing SVM classification of children from face-recognition scanpaths, deep-learning extraction of fixated-region features achieving 92% in adults, and gaze-plus-demographics classification across ASD risk levels. Its critical observation is that 'these studies only considered the eye-tracking data, mainly what was looked at, without jointly taking into account the task performance', which it attributes to behavioural tasks being 'general but not specific enough' - identifying the integration of task performance with gaze as the field's next step. It also cites a systematic review noting that eye-tracking results have varied across studies and are sensitive to sample size, age, developmental level, IQ and stimulus variation.

**S-021** [local_4b031d44] — *Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine*

2019. The paper documents the field's cross-cultural blind spot directly: empirically validated tools like ADOS and ADI-R 'are not always used in different countries, particularly in developing countries, as these tools are expensive, require trained clinicians to administer, and may be limited by available translations and cultural adaptations', and it notes that global autism prevalence is 'largely unknown' with estimates of 0.15-0.8% in Bangladesh and around 3% in Dhaka, most cases in semiurban and rural areas going unnoticed. It situates itself in a programme of prior work on rapid mobile ASD detection from short home videos, and its central empirical contribution - measuring how far those US-validated classifiers transfer - is the kind of external validation this corpus otherwise almost entirely lacks.

**S-022** [local_05ef29e5] — *Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification*

2019. The related-work section surveys the eye-tracking-plus-machine-learning turn in some breadth, citing web-browsing gaze classification, saccade-based classification on six subjects, and a 700-image saliency study finding stronger centre bias and reduced saliency for faces in ASD. It also cites contrary evidence - that social orienting is 'not qualitatively impaired' in ASD and that the excess-mouth, diminished-eye gaze hypothesis has poor support - making it one of the few corpus papers to acknowledge that the underlying behavioural claims are contested. The existence of a dedicated Grand Challenge with a shared dataset is itself evidence of the field's move toward benchmark-based evaluation around 2019.

**S-023** [local_9528024b] — *Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol*

2019. The paper positions itself as 'one of the first applications of humanoid robots in the diagnostics procedure', distinguishing diagnostic from the much commoner therapeutic robot applications and noting that diagnostic use 'brings forth some additional requirements and challenges, especially in terms of data acquisition and reasoning'. It observes that the complexity of the diagnostic process 'imposes constraints on the robotic applications in form of the need for efficient processing and reasoning algorithms', which results in a 'low number of robotic applications in ASD diagnosis'. It also documents that most robot-autism research still uses 'some form of Wizard-of-Oz approach with various degrees of autonomy', and that observations are typically 'collected through analysis of video recordings, which is a common technique in this field' - an accurate characterisation of the robot strand of this corpus.

**S-024** [local_6230fe22] — *Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism*

2019. The literature review is the paper's strongest section and characterises the field carefully: screening has 'evolved recently from subjective clinical assessments to objective metrics acquired from sensing devices such as gaze-tracking, motion sensors, and speech analytics'; machine learning in autism has 'largely focused on how to select the most effective features from a large feature set on the clinical diagnostic tools to shorten the diagnosis time'; and, most pointedly, 'all presented studies adopted machine learning differently yet there is no automatic prediction model integrated within a screening tool to be used in clinics'. It also documents a geographic gap - a shortage of Arabic-language autism research and uncertain prevalence estimates of 1.4, 29 and 59 per 10,000 children in Oman, the UAE and Saudi Arabia - which is a dimension of coverage bias not raised elsewhere in this corpus.

**S-025** [local_785ba418] — *Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis*

2019. The paper explicitly characterises the state of kinematic autism classification: three prior studies using tablet gameplay sensors, reach-and-throw tracking and movement imitation achieved 'high classification accuracy rates of 86.7% to 96.7%', but 'these studies used K-fold Cross-Validation, which was demonstrated to produce overoptimistic performance estimates, especially when a sample size is small' and did not test significance against chance. This is the corpus's most direct statement that its own literature's headline accuracies are methodologically inflated, and the paper's 71% is offered as the corrected estimate for a comparable task.

**S-026** [local_fea042be] — *Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual*

2019. The related-work section surveys the eye-tracking evidence base - shorter and less frequent saccades in high autistic traits, longer fixation on dynamic geometric images in ASD toddlers, declining eye fixation in infants aged 2 to 6 months who later developed ASD, and cohort evidence for eye tracking as an objective measure of autism risk and severity - and then the machine-learning turn, citing RNN classification of Fragile X from gaze during conversation (86-91%) and the authors' own earlier saccade-feature model on 17 children. It positions the visual-representation approach as novel: 'It is claimed that such approach has not been applied before in the context of ASD, to the best of our knowledge'. The accompanying dataset release and deployed web service also document the field's move toward shared benchmarks and demonstrable tooling around 2018-2019.

**S-027** [local_ba5fbda7] — *Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD*

2019. The paper provides one of the corpus's most explicit critical surveys of its own field. It notes that early machine-learning work in autism aimed at shortening ADOS and ADI-R administration by item reduction, 'yielding a classification accuracy of autism vs. typically-developing individuals of up to 99.9%', but warns that in such studies 'the features utilized for classification are still highly subjective and not independent of the respective clinician who bases the diagnostic decision on just those features (circularity)'. It catalogues the kinematic strand (96.7%, 92.5%, 93% from staged movement tasks) and observes that 'the movements under investigation were staged, thus, highly unnatural', arguing for a move to naturalistic interaction. And it identifies simple cross-validation and leave-one-out as sources of unstable and optimistic estimates. Together these amount to a diagnosis of three distinct methodological problems in the 2015-2019 literature that this corpus documents.

**S-028** [local_7b468950] — *Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart*

Published July 2019 by a collaboration between the University of Strathclyde, the University of Glasgow, the University of Aberdeen, the Gillberg Neuropsychiatry Centre at Gothenburg, and Harimata sp. z o.o., funded through a Horizon 2020 SME Instrument subcontract. For this review the article is the methodological benchmark against which the rest of the corpus can be read, and it earns that position on six counts. The algorithm is locked before the evaluation data exist and applied by investigators separate from its developers, with results embargoed until collection closes - so none of the tuning, selection or leakage mechanisms documented across the other 130-odd included studies can operate. Sensitivity and specificity are prespecified as primary outcomes rather than accuracy. A 200-child cohort with other neurodevelopmental disorders is recruited to test differential diagnosis as a prespecified secondary outcome, making this the only powered study in the corpus to address the question the free-play and robot studies name as the hardest and that the ADOS-versus-schizophrenia study shows the field's gold-standard instrument failing. The sample size is justified with power calculations framed around detecting underperformance, with the protocol stating that 'if the Play.Care assessment is underperforming, which is the major concern of healthcare services, this study has a high probability of detecting it'. The commercial interest is managed structurally, with academic investigators holding no equity, company board members with vesting options identified individually, and the analysis blinded to the developers. And the protocol is registered and published before any result exists. Beyond the design, one passage deserves to be carried into the synthesis verbatim, because it states the inferential problem that most of this corpus leaves unexamined: the pilot 'employed the same dataset to train and test the machine learning algorithm. It did so with 10 repetitions of a 10-fold cross-validation procedure that is not prone to overfitting. Nevertheless, it only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset.' Repeated cross-validation establishes consistency within a dataset and not generalisation beyond it - and the entire trial exists because its authors took that distinction seriously about a 93% figure of their own. What the article cannot supply is a result: it is registered as NCT03438994 with status 'Pre-results', and no participant data are reported.

**S-029** [local_309e5baa] — *Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns*

2019. The paper documents the state of gaze-based autism classification concisely: atypical visual attention 'sometimes emerged even before the onset of the disorder', with delayed attentional disengagement in infants correlating with later toddlerhood diagnosis, but 'a holistic automated diagnosis tool remain elusive'. It cites the 92% accuracy reported for deep-network gaze classification in 20 high-functioning ASD and 19 typically developed adults and immediately qualifies that this 'may not be directly applicable to gaze patterns from children' - one of the few instances in the corpus of a paper explicitly discounting a headline result it builds upon. The existence of the Saliency4ASD challenge itself evidences the field's move toward shared benchmarks with blind evaluation around 2019.

**S-030** [local_a45f39e9] — *Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time*

2019. The related-work survey characterises the field as having grown 'in the last couple of decades' around home-video behaviour analysis, infant observation scales, facial expression quantification with IQ-matched controls, caregiver-child interaction analysis, and multimodal eye-movement classification - and then identifies a specific gap: 'none of them focused on studying full body pose movement over time as an indicator of atypical behaviors', with most work 'focusing on specific body parts of children (e.g. face)'. This is an accurate characterisation of the corpus, where face and gaze dominate and full-body pose is rare. The commercial NODA platform also documents the emergence of remote video-based autism assessment as a deployed service by 2019.

**S-031** [local_d587f9cd] — *Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning*

Published 2019 by a group at the Universidade Federal do Espirito Santo in Brazil. The framing identifies the problem precisely: autism signs may be observable before ten months while reliable diagnosis is only possible at 18 to 24 months, diagnosis 'is usually performed through several sessions of behavioral observation, exhaustive screening, and manual coding behavior', and automated video coding could 'help the clinicians to reduce the delay'. For this review the study contributes three things, none of them a detection result. It builds the most developed measurement infrastructure in the corpus - an unstructured, scalable multi-camera RGBD network on ROS in which each node performs local face analysis and a fusion node computes visual focus of attention through a Hidden Markov Model - and it does so from cited open-source components, addressing directly the occlusion problem that limits single-camera gaze measurement with a moving child in a room containing two adults and a robot. It specifies its construct more precisely than anything else here, decomposing joint attention into initiation, response and request-initiation subtypes and reporting its finding at that level rather than in aggregate. And it closes the loop between measurement and robot behaviour, with the reasoning module modifying the robot's gaze, expression and rewards according to the child's performance - a design the introduction motivates by observing that earlier robot-assisted diagnostic systems 'have primarily been open loop and remotely operated' and 'are unable to perform autonomous feedback to enhance the interaction'. Its behavioural claim, however, cannot be relied on: six children in single sessions, no documented diagnostic status in either group, no ethics approval reported, an uncounterbalanced mediator order that confounds the key finding with order and novelty, no developmental measure in three-year-olds, and no reliability check of the automated attention estimates against human coding. The paper's own framing is appropriately modest - 'a proof of concept', a group 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis', and a conclusion that the observed pattern 'can be used as evidence to improve the ASD diagnosis' rather than that it discriminates.

**S-032** [local_08b8027d] — *SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths*

2019. The paper documents the intersection of two technical trends: deep saliency prediction models (EML-Net, SalGAN, SAM with attention mechanisms) that have displaced conventional saliency models since 2014, and the application of those models to autism classification. It notes that a saliency prediction dataset for children with ASD exists but comprises only 13 children over 500 images, and cites a prior deep architecture performing ASD classification from sets of images along with an algorithm for selecting the most discriminative image contents. The existence of the Saliency4ASD challenge with a blind test track is itself evidence of the field's move toward benchmark evaluation, and the fact that two entries in this corpus independently report the same validation-to-test collapse makes that benchmark unusually informative.

**S-033** [local_c6f1209b] — *Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children*

Presented in 2019 at an automation and robotics conference by a Polish collaboration between the Department of Cybernetics and Robotics at Wroclaw University of Science and Technology and the Research Unit for Cognitive and Applied Psychology at the University of Lower Silesia - the same group whose 2022 follow-up is charted separately in this review. The framing is distinctive: rather than presenting a method, the paper presents a stage in an interdisciplinary development process, arguing that diagnostic human-robot interaction 'implies the need of close cooperation between psychologists and engineers' and delivering both a psychological result and a set of engineering requirements as co-equal outputs. For the synthesis the study contributes three things. Its finding is a within-construct dissociation rather than a group difference: autistic children performed significantly more behaviours when instructed than spontaneously in imitation (W = 21, p = 0.028), which the authors read as a deficit in automatic rather than intentional turn-taking. That is a claim about the structure of the difficulty, and the measurement principle behind it - separating prompted from unprompted performance to distinguish capacity from spontaneous deployment - has wide application in a corpus where most behavioural measures collapse the two. Its design demonstrates that a paired within-subject contrast can extract an interpretable result from a sample far too small for any classifier, which several similarly sized between-group studies charted here might usefully have adopted. And its stated future direction identifies the field's hardest problem correctly: 'the especially challenging task is to differ autism from other similar disorders', with a commitment to observe robot interactions with children who have other developmental conditions. Almost no study in this review makes that commitment, and the one included study that does test autism against another clinical group found the field's gold-standard observational instrument achieving an AUC of 0.562 - which is the evidence that this priority is the right one. What the study cannot supply is any detection result: no comparison group, no model, no classification, no accuracy, an unreported sample size and no diagnostic ascertainment described.

**S-034** [local_83b99e73] — *Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers*

2020. The framing is the diagnostic delay gap: autism can currently be diagnosed at 2 years but 'age at ASD diagnosis is still 40 months or even later', and Chinese prevalence estimates rose from 0.07% to 1.8%. The authors position video-based behavioural coding as the objective alternative to the retrospective parent interviews and rating scales that dominated earlier work, which they characterise as 'highly subjective and unfavorable for widespread promotion'. They also note that machine-learning screening had by then reached over 80% accuracy using EEG and brain imaging, and argue that combining social behavioural indicators with biological indicators is the necessary next step - positioning this paper as supplying the behavioural half of that combination.

**S-035** [local_638860ef] — *Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis*

2020. The paper gives one of the corpus's sharpest field characterisations. On the clinical problem: UK average waiting time between initial concerns and clinical diagnosis exceeds three years, adult diagnostic instruments 'have only been validated for use with children', and adult diagnosis is 'less accurate, more subjective and lengthier'. On the methodological problem: 'only a handful of ML studies used kinematic data for autism prediction. All studies had small sample sizes and achieved high classification accuracy', but such models 'are prone to fit noise', and to the authors' knowledge those studies 'did not avoid pooling training and validation data', were not tested with independent data, and did not assess statistical significance. This paper is the corrective demonstration that follows from that diagnosis.

**S-036** [local_7547db68] — *Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network*

2020. The framing is epidemiological and economic rather than methodological: prevalence rising from 3-5 per 10,000 in the 1980s to 2.76% among US children aged 3-14 by 2016; an estimated 10 million people with autism in China including 2 million children, growing by nearly 200,000 annually, with no national statistical survey; 33% of parents reporting that caregiving seriously affected their careers with an average annual income loss of 30,957 yuan. Against that, the paper identifies the bottleneck as clinical throughput and subjectivity - one to two hours per diagnosis, results 'easily disturbed by external factors such as hospital level, physician's subjective level, patient's education level, age' - and positions an app-deliverable CNN system as the answer, with explicit emphasis on remote and underdeveloped areas. The paper is a clear marker of the corpus's deployment-first strand, in which access and cost arguments substitute for validation.

**S-037** [local_878c259f] — *Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach*

2020. The paper situates itself carefully in two literatures. On postural control it notes that reduced postural stability in ASD is 'well-established', with prior force-plate studies reporting greater sway displacement, areas, standard deviations, velocities and root mean square, and two studies reporting decreased COP complexity. On machine learning it observes that classifiers have already distinguished impaired postural stability in multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease and vestibular dysfunction, and have been applied in autism to eye gaze, cognitive function, pregnancy risk factors and hand movements - but concludes that 'to our knowledge, there has been no study that utilized machine learning approaches to study postural control features in children with ASD'. It thus documents the transfer of an established clinical-biomechanics method into the autism domain.

**S-038** [local_1579c85a] — *Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through*

2020. The brief related-work statement characterises prior machine-learning approaches to ASD diagnosis as based on standardised assessment data, brain imaging datasets, and kinematic analysis of upper-body movement during specialised tasks. The paper positions its own contribution against these as using 'only behavioral data captured through video recordings of a naturalistic interaction with social robots' with unrestricted movement and no obtrusive sensors - articulating the corpus-wide trend away from constrained laboratory tasks and toward naturalistic, sensor-free observation.

**S-039** [local_157d6266] — *Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism*

2020. The paper characterises the field precisely along two axes.
