On imitation assessment, it notes that human observation coding remains the standard but is 'subjective and time-consuming and requires intensive coder training', rendering it 'impractical for use in clinics and home settings', and that prior automated approaches are either rule-based with 'very limited generalizability' or DTW-based but reduced to dichotomous or categorical outputs that waste the continuous distance metric. On machine learning it makes a specificity critique that bears directly on this corpus: prior studies classifying autism from motor patterns 'did not directly assess imitation ability even when some tasks involved imitation', so 'it is unclear if the observed differences represent general motor abnormalities or specific imitation impairments' - a limitation that 'restricts the use of these methods for intervention purposes'.

**S-040** [local_8be557e3] — *Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation*

2020. The framing cites prevalence rising from 1 in 150 children in 2000 to 1 in 54 in 2016, and identifies the bottleneck as the gold-standard behavioural assessments themselves - time-consuming, requiring multidisciplinary teams, and unstable because of accessibility, subjectivity and 'interpretive bias between professions'. Its most distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is a data-availability argument: it names infant anonymity requirements and parental non-recognition at early developmental stages as the structural reasons the field's data is small, dispersed by sex, age and vocalisation count, and unrefined, and it observes that 'these problems were typically overlooked by previous research with controlled and small amounts of data'. The method is then designed for those conditions rather than assuming they will be solved.

**S-041** [local_c79e100a] — *Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models*

2020. The framing is a shift in the field's evidential basis: research on autism detection 'traditionally focused on behavioural aspects' but has moved toward 'more objective alternatives' such as gait analysis, on the argument that instrumented measurement 'can identify ASD with more confidence when compared to behavioural assessments recorded by human beings'. The paper situates itself against a set of prior results it reports at face value - 95%, 89% and 100% for random forest, KNN and SVM on adolescent scan data, 96.2% for a PART classifier on gaze and demographic data - and against gait datasets of 60 subjects (30/30) and 44 subjects (12/32). Its own contribution is to notice that these studies differ in how each subject is represented and that this choice has not been examined, which makes it one of the few papers in the corpus whose motivation is a defect in the literature's methodology rather than a clinical need.

**S-042** [local_4fecbf6d] — *Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network*

2020. The framing is unusual in this corpus for arguing about tooling as much as about clinical need. It identifies LENA as the dominant platform for automated speech analysis in autism and objects on methodological grounds - LENA 'is not an open-source software and it is, therefore, not possible to further develop the LENA algorithms nor assess their utility in estimating ASD severity' - making open, inspectable pipelines part of the paper's motivation. It also notes that only a few studies had attempted severity estimation rather than binary classification, citing one that explained about 40% of the variance in Social Affect scores from 33 English-speaking children, and positions itself as the first application of these features and deep learning to Hebrew, arguing that the results 'highlight the utility of speech analyses for estimating ASD severity at very young ages, regardless of the child's spoken language or their cultural environment'.

**S-043** [local_95abe653] — *Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning*

2020. The framing is unusual in taking the measure of its own field before contributing to it. It positions resting-state fMRI as the state of the art for adult autism detection from behavioural data, quoting 79-86% under leave-one-out and 71-83% on unseen data, and notes the practical objection that fMRI is expensive, obtrusive and unsuitable for pregnant women or people with sensory issues, metal implants, claustrophobia or head trauma. It then singles out the EEG (94%) and speech (93%) results as 'potentially overoptimistic' for segment-level splitting, and observes of a comparable child eye-tracking study reporting 85.1% that there was 'no note on how the data was split'. Against that background it positions its own 74-75% as comparable to fMRI at far lower cost, and frames the adult high-functioning population as the underserved case: symptoms are less obvious, lifelong coping strategies mask presentation, and 'unlike for children, critical incidents with adults are not monitored by school staff or parents'.

**S-044** [local_40168c96] — *Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based*

2020. The framing combines an access argument with a methodological one. On access: autism diagnosis 'usually relies on a multidisciplinary team of experts, which is relatively difficult to achieve, especially for economically underdeveloped areas', and eye trackers are 'affordable, portable, and easy to operate' so 'they can also be used in poor and remote areas'. On method: the paper's specific criticism of the existing eye-tracking literature is that models 'have usually utilized statistical analysis to discover the differences between the two classes' and so 'have high requirements for selecting the stimuli and indicators of eye movement for analysis', and that they analyse static fixations while 'the actual eye movement is a dynamic process'. Protocol duration is treated as a competitive dimension in its own right - the paper contrasts its short recording against comparators needing 10 or 10-45 minutes - reflecting a field increasingly aware that attention span, not accuracy alone, bounds what is deployable with young children.

**S-045** [local_d3852378] — *Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

2020. The framing is a critique of the gold standard on two grounds simultaneously - objectivity and ecological validity. On objectivity: 'since in ADOS examiner has to judge a child's performance giving scoring and rating, evaluation relies on the examiner's expertise and subjectivity; likewise, in ADI-R ASD diagnosis is based on caregivers' reports rather than on objective evaluation'. On ecology: the limitation is 'the absence of both objective assessment methods and the ecological validity of the setting'. Virtual reality is offered as addressing both at once - a controlled, repeatable environment that is nonetheless a simulated real-life scene, with sensory content that can be manipulated in ways a clinic room cannot. The paper positions itself as 'the first attempt to discriminate ASD children from children with typical neurodevelopment using body movements parameters of an imitation VR task and machine learning', and situates repetitive behaviour as an under-studied criterion domain relative to social communication.

**S-046** [local_df438dd2] — *Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening*

2020. The framing is about clinician workload and the limits of subjective scoring in a specific, unusually difficult case. The paper argues that the responsive social smile differs from other screening indicators because it lacks clear benchmarks and is 'evaluated by emotion description', that assessing 'children's emotions on small faces' while simultaneously running the experiment is error-prone, and that 'remembering every score for different social stimuli during the screening or perform the behavior scoring after the test is very subjective and labor-intensive'. Its comparison table is a useful snapshot of the 2020 field - eye movement at 88.51%, hand imitation at 86.70%, prosody at 76.00%, neuroimaging at 70.00% - and its accompanying observation is that 'cost and age requirements prevent some accurate ASD screening methods among children', with neuroimaging singled out as both expensive and impractical for young children who cannot stay still. Its own cohort at 12-32 months is the youngest in that table.

**S-047** [local_cd9e45eb] — *Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism*

2020. The framing is explicitly regulatory and infrastructural rather than clinical-need-driven: it situates itself among 'large-scale ongoing efforts in progress to develop next generation biomarker applications', cites the FDA-NIH Biomarker Working Group, and identifies validation studies aimed at markers of treatment response, predictors of later outcomes and subgrouping for intervention response. Its diagnosis of the field's practical bottleneck is precise and rarely stated elsewhere in this corpus: 'the longer the session associated with a biomarker, the more burdensome that biomarker becomes, and the less likely it will be to see practical implementation', with long batteries 'often stressful for young children and infants' and shorter sessions reducing burden, improving data quality and requiring less staff time. It also criticises current selection practice - 'straightforward winnowing of experimental batteries based on independent trial discriminability' - for ignoring interrelationships between trials that machine learning can capture, while warning that overfitting risk in the large-p small-n regime demands specialised techniques.

**S-048** [local_56237213] — *The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data*

2020. The framing is the standard objectivity argument - 'clinical diagnosis is mainly based on behavioral scale tests including the autism behavior checklist and Childhood Autism Rating Scale' and 'due to subjectivity, evaluation results may not be very accurate' - but with a more specific biomarker orientation than most: biomarkers are defined as objective indicators of biological processes used 'for diagnosis, outcome predictions, and treatment prediction', with high accuracy, reliability and validity named as prerequisites for clinical use. The paper's distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is its argument for why single-modality approaches fail: it cites a review finding a U-shaped profile of EEG power alterations in autism (excess low- and high-frequency power, deficient alpha), then notes that other studies found no EEG differences at all, particularly in high-functioning autism, and concludes that heterogeneity makes EEG alone insufficient. Eye tracking is added specifically because 'atypical face processing' has been found across all presentations. That is a heterogeneity-driven rationale for fusion rather than a generic more-data-is-better argument, and it is unusual in this literature.

**S-049** [local_f9a5195f] — *Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses*

2020. The framing is the gap between where social skills are practised and where they are measured: emotion recognition and eye contact skills 'are important to improve social functioning, but the methods currently used to measure and track such skills are delivered in clinical settings or via trained administrators outside the social context where these skills are practiced'. The proposed remedy is mobile and wearable machine learning platforms enabling continuous phenotyping during natural social interactions. The paper's most valuable contribution to the field's self-understanding is its retraction of a prior assumption, stated explicitly: 'The prevailing belief in the literature was that facial attention differences are very clear in ASD, so we hypothesized that distraction ratios across an emotion recognition task alone were enough to distinguish ASD vs NC reliably. We now believe that integrating further subtlety through robust gaze-tracking hardware will be required to design a phenotyping marker from this effect.' It also reports that later generations of the same research group's system abandoned the eye tracker entirely because of bulkiness and calibration problems - a rare disclosure of a technology's practical failure trajectory.

**S-050** [local_16a77fb0] — *Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)*

2020. The framing is distinctive in locating the problem in the measurement instrument rather than in access or cost alone. For general cognition, standardised tests exist - the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, the Mini Mental State Examination - but 'quantifying social interaction deficits is still in its infancy', so clinicians rely on the clinical gaze, which 'practitioners need many years of training to acquire' and which is 'difficult to verbalize, teach, quantify, standardize, and validate'. The paper's own expert-rating data then substantiate this claim empirically: eight experienced clinicians rating the same videos ranged from 0.56 to 1.00 accuracy, with performance correlating with months of experience. The population argument is equally specific - adults with average or above-average intelligence are diagnosed late because they develop camouflaging strategies, and 'to the best of our knowledge, no existing approach focuses on adults with ASD and normal intelligence levels despite the high need for access to diagnosis'. The paper is also careful about its own claim, stating that the SIT 'is not meant to substitute traditional clinical assessment but rather to allow additional information about the client's social communication abilities at an early stage of the diagnostic process'.

**S-051** [local_9c4af7a3] — *Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades*

2020. The framing is access and throughput: CDC prevalence of 1 in 54, an estimate of 'two undiagnosed cases for every three accurately diagnosed', and a description of comprehensive developmental evaluation as requiring 'a multidisciplinary team consisting of a psychologist, neurologist, psychiatrist, speech therapist, and may include others' conducting in-depth neurological, cognitive and language testing, with no single medical test available. Two framing points are distinctive within this corpus. First, the sex argument - girls with subtler presentations who are 'better at copying stereotypical social patterns' go undiagnosed into adulthood - correctly identifies camouflaging as a diagnostic failure mode, although the study then reports no sex data. Second, the rationale for choosing saccades over social gaze is temporal rather than practical: sensorimotor abnormalities are said to be present 'prior to the identification of social and cognitive deficits', which would make an oculomotor marker earlier-detectable in principle than the social behaviours clinical diagnosis relies on. The paper also states that saccades in autism are an under-researched area, which is broadly consistent with this corpus, where gaze studies overwhelmingly examine where people look rather than how their eyes move.

**S-052** [local_b70dae32] — *An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model*

2021. The framing combines prevalence growth (CDC estimates moving from 1 in 59 to 1 in 54) with a claim that autism is 'the fastest-growing developmental disorder in the USA with a 6% to 15% increase in rate per year'. Distinctively for this corpus, it invokes COVID-19 as a driver: 'especially under the current COVID-19 situation, the current research trends are focusing online for technology-based therapies', which situates robot-mediated intervention within a pandemic-era shift toward remote and technology-delivered care. The rationale for robots is given as controllability, accuracy, low cost and adaptability, plus the claim that autistic children are drawn to robots because of their predictable behaviour. The specific gap claimed is that existing robot therapies improve skills but cannot label severity, and the authors note a prior HMM attempt that 'failed to produce hidden Markov models that are indicative of a person's level of autism'.

**S-053** [local_51a0af74] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data*

2021. The framing identifies a specific methodological gap rather than a general access problem: joint attention is 'an important marker to differentiate children with ASD from 12 months onwards', its verification 'requires the therapist's experience, attention and time spent, considering that the specialist's observation not using any tools is the most common practice', and the obstacle to automating it is technical - 'the studies cited in the literature that use ET signals combined with computational methods do not process trajectory data or ignore that the paradigm involves the displacement of regions of interest'. The developmental grounding is unusually explicit for this corpus, linking gaze-following to inferences about intentions and motivations and framing anticipation as 'the action of providing a view of the immediate future based on the immediate past', which 'appears to be difficult in ASD'. That framing directly motivates the anticipation feature, giving the paper a rare coherence between construct, feature design and analysis.

**S-054** [local_d8d3037b] — *Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study*

2021. The framing is unusually specific about health-system context in China. It describes the two-stage screening structure recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics, notes that 'approximately 50% of the time is carried out with staff assistance' even for parent-completed tools, and that assessment can 'continue for months if the symptoms are not sufficiently obvious'. On China specifically it observes that 'the study of mental diseases used to be marginalized due to the conservative culture and weak science consciousness', that 'a majority of child health care institutions in China have not incorporated early ASD screening into their daily work', and that parents and primary health care staff lack awareness of early behavioural characteristics. It also positions itself against two named Chinese eye-tracking studies reporting 88.51% and 85.1%, criticising both for using only a face on a computer screen, and grounds that criticism in a substantive claim from the literature - that social attention in autism appears normal when social information is presented statically or in isolation, which is the argument for immersive scenes.

**S-055** [local_991fe435] — *Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task*

2021. The framing is a systematic critique of three methodological patterns in the existing literature, each with a named remedy. First, that behavioural features in prior work 'often relied on manually labeled features such as the retrospective coding of children's behaviors in videotapes' which 'were essentially based on subjective ratings, which reduced the appeal of using machine learning algorithms' - remedied by using raw gaze samples. Second, that most studies performed binary classification, which 'fails to take into account the heterogeneity in the ASD population' - remedied by three-class classification including functioning level. Third, that brain-imaging classification 'is generally limited to adults or older children (over 7 years)' so that 'the application of machine learning to young children or infants, who are arguably in more need of automatic classification, is challenging' - remedied by a 15-minute child-friendly eye-tracking task. To these it adds the selection-inflation critique, singling out a named study reporting 96.7% after selecting an optimal feature set from 15 participants per group and noting that such practice 'is currently prevalent among medical studies with the machine learning techniques, and its overestimation of prediction accuracy should be cautioned'. That is the most precise methodological self-awareness in the corpus.

**S-056** [local_8692a64f] — *Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis*

2021. The framing is the standard subjectivity argument - diagnosis 'mainly relies on experts' comprehensive clinical analysis of children, which is usually subjective and highly dependent on doctors' individual professional skills' - with an added emphasis on pre-verbal assessment, aiming to 'diagnose children without linguistic ability in an early stage'. Its distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is a preference for structured over unstructured data: it observes that 'most of the studies focus on unstructured data, which has complicated correlations among numerous parameters' and argues that 'it is highly desired to develop an effective auxiliary diagnostic method for ASD with the utilization of structured data'. That is an argument for interpretability over raw predictive power, and it is one of the few places in this corpus where the trade-off is stated as a design principle rather than discovered after the fact. The biological motion rationale is also well grounded, citing the classic finding of strong visual sensitivity to biological movement in typical viewers against reports of abnormal gaze to point-light displays in autism.

**S-057** [local_4d6fac7e] — *Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network*

2021. The framing is a two-stage critique. First, that single-modality analysis is inherently limited because 'the bio-marker information carried by the bio-signal of a single-modality is likely insufficient or distorted' - an argument for fusion on information-theoretic rather than merely empirical grounds. Second, and more specific, that existing fusion work 'mainly rely on feature-level fusion or decision-level fusion' and that 'these simple kinds of fusion strategies may not make full use of modality-cross information, thus the performances are largely limited'. The paper then demonstrates this empirically by implementing both a feature-concatenation baseline and a deep network over concatenated features, and showing the latter performs worst. It also grounds the cross-modal premise in developmental neuroscience, citing work linking frontolimbic connectivity at 6 months to responding-to-joint-attention at 9 months, and studies finding eye-tracking and EEG measures correlated during social stimulation - so the fusion argument rests on a claimed functional relationship rather than on an assumption that more data helps.

**S-058** [local_30c622f2] — *Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model*

2021. The framing is that severity classification is under-explored relative to diagnosis - 'although we know little about its potential use in severity classification, in literature there are some important clues about the use of eye tracking in symptom severity' - and it assembles those clues carefully: a reported correlation of r = -0.52 between fixation on social stimuli and ADOS social scores; evidence that geometric preference predicts later symptom severity and joint-attention gaze shifting; and a finding that autistic children preferring the geometric side scored worse on ADOS, Mullen and Vineland alike. Its methodological argument is that region-of-interest analysis, which dominates the field, discards information: 'although using all the image information and visual attention models... could be more informative'. It builds directly on a 2015 three-level saliency study that found semantic features important in characterising autistic viewing and 'suggesting top-down impairments', and extends that from diagnosis to severity - which is a genuinely incremental and well-posed research question rather than a reapplication of an existing method to a new dataset.

**S-059** [local_bfc088c7] — *Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation*

2021. The framing is a specific critique of ecological validity in the existing eye-tracking literature. The paper observes that prior data 'were primarily obtained by having participants watch images (ie, videos, pictures, web pages)' but that 'human gaze behavior is highly context-sensitive', that experimental setting and cognitive load influence visual attention, that face-to-face interaction is 'much more perceptually and cognitively difficult' than image watching, and that 'the presence of the social partner elicits a different pattern of both neural response and gaze behavior' - concluding that image-viewing findings 'could not be directly generalized to the scenario of natural social interaction'. It also situates itself on age, noting a meta-analytic mean diagnosis age of 60.48 months and arguing that future work should examine younger children than its own 6-13 range. And it is unusually explicit that the field has not yet addressed differential diagnosis: 'our study and most others only classified individuals with ASD and TD... More scientific endeavor is certainly required before a practical ML model that could detect ASD from different conditions is established.'

**S-060** [local_25e34bbd] — *Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification*

2021. The framing is unusual and revealing: autism is introduced not as a neurodevelopmental condition but as one of two 'voice disabilities' within a paper about pathological voice detection, alongside Down syndrome, in a context where '1.2% of the world's total population is facing some type of voice disability'. Prevalence figures are given for both conditions in the United States and India (1 in 59 and 23 per 10,000 for autism; 1 in 700 and 1 in 1250 for Down syndrome). The critique of existing diagnosis is brief - ADOS-R and ADI-R 'require standardized structures for capturing the behaviors and found to be very difficult' - and the paper's real intellectual investment is in the acoustic literature, which it reviews carefully across five prior Down syndrome voice studies with their specific findings on fundamental frequency, jitter and shimmer. Its stated novelty is the differential task: prior work 'analyzed the variability of acoustic features in the voice produced by children with ADS, DS and normal children' but 'there has been no attempt to classify both'.

**S-061** [local_4917150c] — *Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning*

2021. The framing is conventional on diagnosis - hours of clinical examination, symptom variation, susceptibility to human bias - but two observations are distinctive. First, an unusually frank statement of how service capacity shapes research: the sample is school-aged rather than preschool because 'in our region there were not enough diagnosed children younger than 6 years, and the time it takes to consult a doctor to make a diagnosis can be as long as 2 years', so the very diagnostic delay the tool is meant to address prevented studying the age group where it would matter most. Second, an argument about acceptance rather than accuracy: 'parents seem to have high acceptance of eye tracking as part of the clinical evaluation because the visual results are easier to understand than is the ADI cutoff', and 'for some parents, a lack of an objective measure can lead to delayed or diminished acceptance of the clinical diagnosis'. That reframes the value of objective measurement as communicative as well as diagnostic, a consideration essentially absent elsewhere in this corpus. The paper also identifies the absence of a benchmark dataset as an obstacle to comparing methods, and responds by releasing its own.

**S-062** [local_241ec2c2] — *Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking*

2021. The framing is a precise methodological critique rather than a general appeal to objectivity. Region-of-interest methods carry two costs: annotation burden, since every ROI must be marked on every frame of every video, and information loss, since aggregating within a region discards 'which visual features of sub parts of an image had a more fixed gaze'. The paper grounds its alternative in attention theory, distinguishing bottom-up circuits driven by image properties from top-down circuits using prior knowledge and social rules, and traces the computational lineage from the Koch model through Itti's implementation to the supervised saliency models of Borji and Judd. It positions its own advance as extending these from static images to video, citing the argument that video 'can contribute with more discoveries because the videos have temporal information'. It also situates itself quantitatively against prior work, tabulating AUCs of 0.71, 0.71 and 0.86 from three published studies against its own 0.82, and noting that its sample is larger and more heterogeneous in age, sex and severity than the comparators.

**S-063** [local_36617ec5] — *Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis*

2021. The framing combines three arguments. On objectivity, that assessment 'relies on children's observable behaviors and parents' interview responses, which clinicians rate according to their expertise and subjectivity', with the specific addition that 'social desirability bias has been found to affect the veracity of parents' responses'. On ecological validity, that assessment 'occurs in laboratories or clinical settings lacking ecological validity that could offer a deeper understanding of real-life abilities'. And on timing, that 'many ASD dimensions are internal and do not manifest until 2-3 years of age', lengthening diagnosis. Its most valuable contribution to the corpus's framing is a careful review of the inconsistency in the social-attention literature: it catalogues studies finding reduced social attention, four finding increased social preference, and eight finding no difference, and identifies the moderators as static versus dynamic stimuli and level of social content - citing meta-analytic evidence that autistic children attended less to social stimuli specifically 'when the social content was higher (i.e., the number of people exceeded one)'. Its own contrary result is then argued within that framework rather than against it.

**S-064** [local_d8e804d6] — *Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms*

2021. The framing combines diagnostic delay with a specific argument for motor markers. On delay, it cites more than a year on average between initial screening and confirmed diagnosis in the United States, and a 35-country meta-analysis giving a mean diagnosis age of 60.48 months, falling to 43.18 months among children aged ten or under. On motor markers, it assembles evidence of atypical motor function in postural control, gait stability, arm movements and gross and fine motor control, and of delayed motor development in infancy that 'could subsequently contribute to the social impairments' - so motor features are argued to be developmentally upstream of the social criteria, not merely correlated with them. It then identifies head movement specifically as documented but unexploited, citing stereotyped head rolling, shaking and banging, greater head turning displacement and velocity when viewing social stimuli, and slower and less frequent head turning in response to name. Its closing claim is notably strong: 'the current diagnostic system of ASD, which are established on behavioral evaluation of social communication and restricted and repetitive behavior, would be greatly challenged' by combining features across neuroimaging, eye tracking, EEG and motion capture.

**S-065** [local_712542ca] — *Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset*

2021. The framing is brief and largely a literature enumeration, cataloguing prior eye-tracking autism work including the source dataset's own publications, web-page gaze studies, video-based screening paradigms, geometric-preference subtyping and autism risk indices. Its stated motivation is that 'there are needed a elaborated work that can explore significant factors of eye-signs for detecting autism', though the analysis performed does not in fact explore any factors. Its most interesting incidental observation is the honest one that motivates the clustering: 'these scanpath images were almost similar for normal and autistic children', which is a candid statement that the raw visual difference between groups is small - consistent with the source study's finding that participant-level accuracy sits near 71%.

**S-066** [local_0ab41681] — *Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder*

2021. The framing is developmental and causal rather than diagnostic-efficiency driven. It argues that 'low-order impairments of sensory processing and motor coding during the early stages of life may impact the acquisition of more complex abilities, including socio-communicative skills and cognitive functions', and assembles evidence of pervasive sensorimotor impairment across posture, balance, gait, aiming movements, eye-hand coordination, force control and handwriting - proposing that these 'scattered disturbances presumably arise from a limited number of common dysfunctional mechanisms'. Its most distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is a methodological criticism aimed at its own field: that standardised symptom assessments 'are often only used to assign group labels (i.e. ASD vs. neurotypical)', and that 'this approach has prevented understanding the impact of motor differences in the heterogeneous expression of ASD symptoms'. The paper then acts on that criticism by correlating every kinematic measure against ADOS totals within the autistic group, which is what yields its central dissociation.

**S-067** [local_9ca9b2cc] — *Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment*

Published 2021 by a group at United Arab Emirates University with Al Ain Hospital, and collaborators at RIKEN, the University of New South Wales, Western Sydney University and the University of Malaya. The framing separates it from most of this corpus: the problem identified is not detection but the cost of repeated assessment during therapy - assessment 'is typically performed at the time of enrollment and repeated during long-term therapy to measure progress', and if it 'could be repeated more frequently to trace the severity and development of symptoms, then therapists could implement more efficacious diagnostic and therapeutic options, and patients and their parents would be better motivated to withstand long, repetitive therapy sessions'. For this review the study contributes three things that the detection-oriented literature does not. It closes the loop: the automated attention measure feeds back into the interaction scenario, which adapts to each child's score history across sessions, so measurement serves intervention rather than terminating in a classification - no other study in the corpus implements this. It demonstrates what is achievable without any learned model: three transparent rules with operator-adjustable constants, running at 1 Hz on a phone camera mounted to the robot the child is attending to, agreeing with the treating therapist's judgement on 28 of 34 sessions. And it is longitudinal, tracking six children across a seven-week course, in a corpus that is otherwise almost entirely cross-sectional. Its evidential weight is nonetheless limited in ways that should be stated: there is no comparison group and no control condition, so the observed rise in attention cannot be separated from familiarisation, practice or maturation; 5 of 11 children did not complete and no reason is given; the 82.4% is an uncorrected agreement rate over sessions clustered within six children, against a therapist standard of unknown reliability; and the population is narrow - male, mild to moderate, verbally capable - despite the abstract describing the target as children with minimal verbal capabilities. The authors' own restraint is worth noting: the causal claim is presented as a hypothesis, and the system is positioned as a tool for therapists rather than as a diagnostic instrument.

**S-068** [local_02fa4215] — *Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning*

2021. The framing is about data absence rather than methodological gap, and on that point it is informative and specific. The authors note that 'no reliable epidemiological data on the prevalence of autism exists' for South Asia, that Pakistan does not track or report autism cases, that the country's only government-run child psychiatry department averages two patients a day, and that 'even in that department, no such reasonable measures have been taken to store data in any format', so data 'had to be collected from scratch'. That account of health-system data infrastructure is a genuine contribution to the corpus's picture of where this research happens and under what constraints, and it distinguishes the paper's problem from the throughput and objectivity arguments that dominate elsewhere. The scientific execution does not match the framing: the stated aim of identifying causes for lifestyle modification is beyond what a 200-child cross-sectional questionnaire without diagnostic ascertainment can address, and the conclusions drawn from it are single-group frequencies presented without comparison.

**S-069** [local_29a3fc54] — *Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism*

2021. The framing is the most precisely targeted in the corpus. Rather than arguing that clinical assessment is subjective in general, it identifies exactly where prosody falls through the diagnostic net: ADOS-2 Module 3 contains one item rating 'Speech abnormalities associated with autism (Intonation/Volume/Rhythm/Rate)' on a 0-2 scale where an abnormal score 'represents a composite of abnormal features crudely lumped together'; the SRS contains one item on unusual tone of voice; and 'there is no reference to speech or voice quality in any of the 7 diagnostic criteria laid out in' DSM-5. It also identifies a technical rather than clinical obstacle - that existing pitch detection algorithms produce octave errors on quasi-periodic disordered speech and lack the resolution to capture fine perturbation - and addresses it with a model previously validated on other clinical populations. Its account of why prior pitch findings conflict is likewise specific, attributing heterogeneity to variation in voice sampling context, from home recordings to structured caregiver interactions to professional evaluations 'with varying social and cognitive demands', and then testing that account directly by comparing four conversational contexts within one dataset.

**S-070** [local_b7ec3755] — *Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images*

2021 (submitted 2020, revised December 2020). Framed as early detection enabling early intervention, with the standard supporting claim that symptoms appear in the first two years and that early programmes let children enter kindergarten alongside typically developing peers - though the model is applied to school-age children of unstated age and could not address toddlers, whose viewing behaviour the paper's own Discussion says differs qualitatively. The more distinctive feature of the framing is what surrounds it: this is a challenge paper, so its comparative claim is against seven named competitor methods on a shared test set rather than against the literature at large, and its headline number is a modest 0.59 stated without inflation. The corpus contains few papers that report a result this weak, and its presence is a useful corrective - the same modality that yields 90%-plus in single-laboratory studies yields 0.53-0.59 across all eight entries when the data are fixed and shared.

**S-071** [local_684969f6] — *Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data*

2021 (submitted May 2020, revised January 2021), extending a 2019 ICME Grand Challenge submission. The framing is the standard early-detection argument, sharpened by specific epidemiological figures on the diagnostic delay and by the claim that scanpath-only classifiers would be computationally light enough for mobile deployment. What distinguishes this paper's position in the literature is not its framing but its evaluative stance: it is one of the few here written in explicit competition with named alternatives on a shared blind test set, reporting its own prior submission's weaker numbers alongside the improved ones, and it treats the failure of its own central idea as a finding rather than an embarrassment. Its related-work section is also unusually careful about generalisation, noting that a 92%-accuracy adult study 'may not directly translate to ASD diagnosis among children' because children's and adults' gaze patterns differ - a caution that other papers in this corpus citing the same adult results do not observe.

**S-072** [local_35004e74] — *Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children*

2021 (received March, accepted July). The framing is the standard early-detection argument but stated with unusual precision and with quantities attached: autism is detectable at 14 months and with high certainty before two years, yet over 70% of affected children are not diagnosed before 51 months; children diagnosed before age two can gain up to 20 IQ points over the following year, while those diagnosed after four 'will not show any substantial cognitive gain even with adequate intervention'. That last figure converts the diagnostic delay from an inconvenience into a quantified loss and is the strongest version of the early-detection premise in this corpus. The critique of existing tools is equally specific - most screening tests are questionnaire-based, perform with low to moderate accuracy, and are 'prone to recall and subjectivity bias'. What most distinguishes the paper's positioning, though, is its critique of the prior computational literature rather than of clinical practice: it names the field's dominant paradigm - single-feature extraction from controlled prompts - as the limitation to be overcome, and argues that a construct defined by the decoupling of behaviours from one another cannot be measured by indexing those behaviours one at a time. The Discussion is also careful about scope in a way few papers here are, stating that diagnosis 'is unlikely to be set on the track of automated performance before long' and positioning the contribution as screening that catalyses referral.

**S-073** [local_fa91fc18] — *Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities*

2021 (received November 2020, published May 2021). The framing is the standard critique of observational diagnosis - it 'requires a lot of time', relies on 'the interpretative skills of clinicians', and 'take a long time without being able to deliver an objective and shareable result' - but the paper adds a more specific diagnosis of the field's problem: 'one of the main gaps in the diagnosis of autism is related to the lack of a quantitative evaluation of the disorder; in fact, although the variability within the disorder is known, there is still no valid method to recognize and categorize these differences'. The target is therefore the absence of graded measurement rather than subjectivity as such. A second framing move is methodological and unusual for this corpus: the authors argue explicitly that classical group-difference statistics are the wrong instrument here, 'since several interactions of motion variables could, actually, affect the presumed typical autistic motor pattern, we cannot assume that there must necessarily be movement variables typical of autism', and cite Yarkoni and Westfall to justify a predictive rather than exploratory approach. That is a considered epistemic position rather than a default. The paper also positions itself in a specific lineage - Anzulewicz's iPad gameplay study with 262 features reaching 'up to 93% accuracy', Crippa's upper-limb kinematics at 96.7% - and its own 93% lands squarely on the number it cites, which the Discussion treats as convergent confirmation rather than as an occasion to ask whether the two studies share a validation design.

**S-074** [local_115dfe8d] — *A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children*

2022 (submitted September 2021, published July 2022). The framing combines the standard prevalence appeal (1 in 54 per US CDC) with two more specific claims: that 'there is limited understanding of the neural patterns behind ASD and the severity of the disease', and that 'there is a lack of experienced experts for ASD diagnosis' - the second being a workforce argument that is more concretely relevant in the Chinese context the study is situated in than the objectivity arguments that dominate elsewhere in this corpus. The paper's distinctive positional claim is methodological: that 'most existing methods mainly rely on a single modality with limited information and often cannot achieve satisfactory performance', and that since autism has 'abnormal manifestations from the cellular level to the behavioral level' no single level of measurement can suffice. Its related-work section is unusual in citing single-modality accuracy figures from both literatures side by side - 92.34% and 96.44% for EEG, 88.51% and 85.1% for eye tracking - which sets up the fusion argument but also, unintentionally, shows that the highest reported unimodal figures already exceed this study's own unimodal results (81.11% and 86.67%), a discrepancy that goes unremarked and that most likely reflects differences in validation design rather than in signal quality.

**S-075** [local_5b7ea7dc] — *AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

2022. The framing combines the usual prevalence and early-intervention arguments (1 in 59, billions in socio-economic burden, improved outcomes from early detection) with a workforce argument that is more specific and more relevant to the deployment claim: early detection 'does not appear to be feasible, especially in regions where there is a scarcity of mental health specialists'. What distinguishes this paper's positioning is its critique of the immediately preceding work rather than of clinical practice in general. It observes that the Cognoa system, which obtained FDA marketing authorisation, 'may be considered not fully automated as it uses as input for the machine learning model not the actual videos, but human ratings corresponding to the quality of behavior conveyed in each video' - a precise and correct distinction between automating inference and automating measurement that no other paper in this corpus draws. And it criticises Zunino's grasping-kinematics classifier on the ground that 'the targeted gesture is not generally considered an indication of ASD behavior by most mental health specialists', which is a criterion of clinical construct validity rather than of accuracy. Those two criticisms jointly define the paper's design: raw video in, and a behaviour clinicians already accept as diagnostic as the target. The conclusion's comparative claim - higher accuracy and F1 than prior models reporting 0.70-0.80 - is asserted without statistical test and across studies with different populations and IQ distributions, which sits oddly against the care of the critique that opens the paper.

**S-076** [local_87fe26aa] — *Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder*

2022. The framing is standard in its premises - 1 in 54 prevalence, 'a tremendous economic and mental burden to society', existing methods 'depend on the assessment of experts, which are subjective and costly' - but two elements are distinctive. The critique of current tools is concrete rather than generic, citing the M-CHAT as a case where a parent questionnaire 'is administered by specialists in rigorously controlled clinical settings, usually taking hours to complete', so the objection is to throughput rather than to validity. And the aetiological framing is unusually non-deterministic for this literature: the paper cites 'an emerging view is that the atypical behavior of ASD children may be caused by early brain adaptation to an adverse environment, rather than a result of ongoing neural pathology', which recasts early intervention as preventing maladaptive adaptation during a period of plasticity rather than as treating a fixed pathology. That framing then does argumentative work, supplying the paper's justification for including EEG at all - that 'atypical brain development in children with ASD appears earlier than atypical behavior, and the critical period of early intervention will be missed if the detection is based on behavioral data'. The claimed contributions are explicitly comparative: that prior work has applied each modality separately, that 'studies on data fusion are few', and that 'the discriminative powers of different data modalities are unclear' - a gap the study does address, and the modality-ranking result is its most transferable finding whatever the absolute accuracies are worth.

**S-077** [local_893ce2fa] — *An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images*

2022 (received October 2021, revised February 2022). The framing is the standard objectivity argument in a strong form: 'the accurate diagnosis of ASD is usually affected since it is linked to the judgment of an expert, which produces biases related to the lack of objectivity', with the gold standard characterised as requiring 'multiple sessions and a qualified professional', hence 'time and... high cost'. The proposed role is appropriately modest - 'automatic screening tools can accelerate the diagnosis by identifying which individual require a complete autism assessment' - and the discussion repeats that the method 'permits the experts to provide a preliminary overview that guides diagnosis to more complex stages and tests'. Two features of the background are worth noting against the corpus. The clinical description is the least accurate here, framing autism as a condition from which children 'deteriorate' without early medical prescription and cataloguing 'red flags' at 12, 14 and 18 months. And the paper's positioning of its own novelty - 'to the best of our knowledge, this is the first time KELM is used for ASD classification by using gaze tracking images' - is a claim about the pairing of an algorithm with a dataset rather than about any question concerning autism, which is a fair statement of what the study contributes.

**S-078** [local_dffe4127] — *Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals*

2022. The framing is a deliberate inversion of the rest of this literature. Rather than arguing that clinical diagnosis is subjective and that automated classification would be objective, the paper starts from the premise that autism 'has so far defied any simple diagnostic markers or cognitive mechanisms' and asks what property of the data would have to hold for classification to be possible at all. It then names the field's characteristic omission precisely: 'Across ASD eye tracking studies, this is a major unanswered question: what portion of the variance in findings can be assigned to between-individual variability, and what portion can be assigned to within-individual variability?' - and observes that 'individual-level reliability is a prerequisite for successful classification and prediction'. That reframing converts a methodological question into a substantive one and produces a result the accuracy-maximising literature could not have produced: a demonstration that the measurement is reliable, the group difference is real and replicable, and the classifier nonetheless fails, because reliability and classifiability are different properties. The paper's positioning of eye tracking is correspondingly measured - it emphasises the modality's practical advantages, its applicability from infancy to adulthood, its resistance to volitional control and its emerging feasibility on phones and over the internet - while directing those advantages toward subtype discovery, longitudinal monitoring and intervention assessment rather than toward diagnosis.

**S-079** [local_2b766683] — *Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech*

2022. The framing combines the usual epidemiological appeal with two access statistics that are more concrete than the corpus norm: 83.86% of American counties have no autism diagnostic resources at all, and the delay from first consultation to diagnosis averages over two years, pushing typical diagnosis past age four with documented downstream consequences including higher psychotropic medication use, lower IQ and reduced language aptitude. The distinctive positioning, though, is a critique of the immediately preceding speech literature on deployability rather than on accuracy. The authors name two studies achieving comparable or better results - one using 'a specialized biosensor device with 4 directional microphones', another 'multiple wireless microphones, providing high purity recordings at a central recording location (a hospital)' - and argue that such work 'does not accelerate the process of autism detection' precisely because the conditions that produce clean data are the conditions that prevent scaling. They then add a validity argument alongside the logistical one: recording in unfamiliar settings with unfamiliar adults may itself alter the behaviour being measured. That pairing - that laboratory control buys signal quality at the cost of both reach and ecological validity - is the sharpest statement of the deployment-versus-fidelity tradeoff in this review, and it is the axis along which this study should be compared with Asgari and colleagues, who took the opposite position and gained interpretability, clinical characterisation and confound control in exchange for requiring a clinical ADOS session.

**S-080** [local_2895bdf0] — *Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection*

2022. The framing is unusual for this corpus in three respects. First, it declines the diagnostic frame outright: 'This work (past and current) is not currently intended to be employed for diagnostic or screening purposes. Rather, our methodology uses already-established diagnosis as an external criterion against which we can validate (in the sense of discriminant validity) these voice and language measures.' The target is outcome measures for trials and longitudinal studies, and the paper closes on that application. Second, the critique of existing instruments is specific rather than generic - conventional tests like the CELF-4 and PPVT 'evaluate structural aspects of language' and must be augmented by natural language sampling; parent-report instruments such as the CCC-2 have validity limits 'as illustrated in treatment studies that have shown caregiver reports to be susceptible to the placebo effect'; and, echoing the group's companion paper, the ADOS and SRS 'include only one item each on voice quality' despite prosodic difference being a cited characteristic of autism. Third, the epidemiological framing is calibrated rather than alarmist, citing a worldwide prevalence range of 0.043% to 2.68% and noting that 'reasons for the increasing prevalence rate are uncertain' - written by an author who has published extensively on exactly that question. The comparison against prior work is likewise careful, noting that Tanaka et al.'s sample of four autistic and two typically developing participants made its findings 'unreliable', and that the sampling contexts of the compared studies differed from this one so that 'examination of contextual effects should be vigorously pursued'.

**S-081** [local_423b636b] — *Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers*

2022-2023. The framing is developmental and mechanistic rather than diagnostic, positioning head movement as 'one of the early sensorimotor signs associated with autism' and situating it within an established literature on motor differences - stereotypies, fine and gross motor impairment, motor planning and coordination, asymmetry in home videos of infants later diagnosed, and documented difficulties in gait, balance, postural control, movement accuracy, manual dexterity and praxis. What distinguishes the positioning is that the paper engages directly with a competing published interpretation and produces evidence against it: Martin and colleagues found head movement differences only during social stimuli and proposed that autistic children use head movements to modulate their perception of social scenes, whereas this study finds differences during both content types and states plainly that 'our data do not support the hypothesis that the head movements of the autistic toddlers were used to modulate the perception of social stimuli, per se'. It then offers alternatives without overclaiming, noting that 'the nature of these differences in head movement dynamics is not fully understood'. The translational claim is correspondingly modest - computer vision 'offers a scalable means of detecting subtle differences' that 'may be helpful in identifying early behaviors associated with autism' - and the stated endpoint is a multimodal digital phenotyping tool combining this channel with gaze, facial dynamics and response to name, not a standalone diagnostic. Given the disclosed commercial interest in the app, that restraint is notable.

**S-082** [local_ffa35101] — *Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study*

2022. The framing is unusual for this corpus in being about scientific generalisation rather than about diagnostic deployment. The stated problem is not that clinicians are subjective or that diagnosis is slow, but that 'most studies have concentrated on studying prosody in English-speaking groups' while 'language is fundamentally cultural, and how specific aspects of prosody are used can vary substantially across languages' - so the field's evidence base may describe an English-specific phenotype without knowing it. The paper documents the concrete consequence: higher f0 and larger f0 range are reported repeatedly in English-speaking autistic groups, yet a Thai study found lower f0 range and a Japanese study likewise, and the existing cross-linguistic comparisons have all been between closely related languages (English and Danish, both Germanic; Cantonese and Mandarin, both Sinitic). The clinical implications drawn are correspondingly framed around intervention and cultural sensitivity rather than screening - that cross-linguistic differences 'may also help to optimize culturally sensitive diagnostic and intervention practices', and that if extensive pitch experience ameliorates intonational differences then pitch is 'a fruitful target for speech interventions in ASD for those who do not speak a tone language'. Diagnostic application is mentioned only in the conclusion and hedged: 'although further study with larger samples, and with additional language comparisons, is needed to support adaptation of the current models into clinical use'. The methodological argument against scalar summaries - that averaging or taking extreme values discards the dynamics that constitute prosody - is also a positional claim about how the field measures, and it is the study's most transferable methodological contribution.

**S-083** [local_81ecbc6f] — *Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings*

2022 (submitted October 2020, accepted April 2022). The framing is unusual in this corpus for beginning from the strength of existing practice rather than its weakness: 'the validity and reliability of diagnosis of ASD improves considerably when diagnostic evaluation is carried out using standardized tools with good psychometric properties', and computational models are positioned as tools that 'may provide tools that, similarly to psychological testing, support clinicians in their decision-making'. The limiting statement follows immediately - 'due to the multidimensionality and complexity of the diagnosis problem, the role of such automatic analyses of narratives may only be complementary or supportive' - and the paper then proves its own point by measuring the gap between its models and the standardised instruments. The specific clinical gap it identifies is narrower and better argued than the usual appeals to cost or delay: hand-coding of narratives 'is time and labour intensive, and requires extensive training for coders to achieve reliability', which 'limit[s] sample sizes and may be difficult to implement across different research sites', while 'objective, valid and reliable measures of narration ability among individuals with ASD with no clear structural language deficits are limited' and 'standardized tests often miss evident-in-naturalistic-settings differences'. The target population is therefore explicitly the group for whom current instruments are least sensitive - 'participants with less severe autism spectrum-related symptoms, more advanced language, and no intellectual disability' - and the sample is constructed to match, with non-verbal IQ of 80 or above and fluent speech required.

**S-084** [local_bc62bc4b] — *Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening*

2022. The framing is the standard early-screening argument but with more specific and better-sourced grounding than most in this corpus. The clinical problem is stated in concrete terms: 'many clinicians adopt a wait and see approach during the early years, delaying their diagnosis'; assessments are 'time-intensive processes that make many children are waitlisted for a long time'; and access depends on 'financial resources available to a child, the number of clinicians in a region, and governmental policy around access to resources'. The instrument critique is quantitative rather than rhetorical, citing the M-CHAT-R/F's reported positive predictive value of 54% for autism against 98% for developmental delay in a low-risk group, and noting that 'currently, no screening instrument can identify young children with ASD from non-ASD peers with high accuracy'. What most distinguishes the framing, though, is a genuinely critical reading of the machine-learning literature the paper is contributing to. The introduction surveys eight prior studies with their reported accuracies and then observes that 'the results of the reviewed studies indicated a large variance in prediction of ASD diagnosis', attributing it to 'the age of the participants, validation methods, and sample size but also... processing of noise, training dataset imbalances, feature selection, ranking, and data cases that overlap in features', and concluding that 'the variability of ASD classification performance require a careful reading of improvements in ML research related to ASD classification'. The discussion goes further, noting that many machine-learning studies in autism are 'limited by diverse methodological problems such as unreliable evaluation measures, small sample size, class imbalances in data, and invalid diagnostic procedures', citing Frazier's meta-regression that poorly designed and poorly reported studies overestimate group differences, and dissecting Pierce's geometric-preference finding to point out that only 40% of the autistic participants actually showed the preference and that the number of repeated trials was never reported. That level of critical engagement with the surrounding literature is unmatched in this corpus - which makes the study's own unreported sample reduction and unaddressed developmental confound the more striking.

**S-085** [local_889d9bd6] — *Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children*

2022. The framing is the standard early-detection argument, but the paper's positioning is developmental rather than translational. Its motivating observation is that 'few studies have investigated the eye tracking differences across different chronological age groups' despite evidence that brain alterations in autism differ across ages, and its specific clinical rationale for the 3-year boundary is that 'a proportion of the children identified with possible autism before age 3 do not meet criteria for autism at later follow-up' while 'many children are not diagnosed with ASD until age 3 or older despite displaying symptoms much earlier'. The literature review is unusually careful about what is and is not established, reporting Frazier's meta-analysis of 122 studies as finding a reliable pattern of gaze abnormality that 'persists across ages and worsens during perception of human interactions' while also noting that 'adding perceptual complexity to stimuli or increasing cognitive load during attention-heavy tasks does not increase gaze abnormalities in autism', and citing a review concluding that 'the excessive mouth and diminished eye gaze hypothesis of ASD is not generally supported'. The comparative claims are likewise measured: rather than asserting superiority, the authors situate their 80% and 71% against a meta-analysis of MRI-based classification reporting sensitivity 0.83 and specificity 0.84 for structural and 0.69 and 0.66 for functional imaging, concluding only that 'our findings based on the eye tracking are comparable with results obtained from sophisticated brain imaging tools' - a comparison whose point is cost and accessibility rather than accuracy.

**S-086** [local_361b59fb] — *Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

2022. The framing is a health-systems argument rather than a technical or clinical-deficit one, and it is the most concretely evidenced in the corpus. The problem is specified with figures at each link in the chain: US prevalence 1.9%; mean age of diagnosis over 4 years despite reliable diagnosis being possible at 18 months; an estimated three-year delay between first caregiver concern and diagnosis, longer for children who are non-white, female, of lower socioeconomic status or rural; 27% of autistic children still undiagnosed at age 8; waits of up to 18 months between primary care screening and specialist diagnosis; only about 1% of autistic patients diagnosed by primary care clinicians; roughly 60% of children who fail a screen neither referred nor diagnosed; and 61% of 454 children with an eventual autism diagnosis having screened negative on a common screener in a cohort of over 20,000. The barriers to primary care diagnosis are then named specifically - low confidence with diagnostic tools, lack of specialist training, insufficient time to administer or to review results, and inadequate reimbursement - as is the observation that existing instruments risk overdiagnosis 'in populations with a lower prevalence of ASD, as is the case in primary care' and lose reliability when combination instruments are used stand-alone by time-pressured clinicians. The proposed role follows from this analysis and is correspondingly bounded: not to replace specialist assessment but to let primary care resolve the straightforward cases so that specialist capacity concentrates on the complex ones, with the authors observing that 'reducing tertiary referral loads by even a third could significantly shorten wait times for interventions to begin'.

**S-087** [local_afdb603d] — *Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.*

2022. The framing is linguistic rather than translational: the motivating gap is that 'there are already many English contributions showing abnormalities of autistic speech at the prosodic level' but 'few studies on this promising field in Italian', so the question is whether findings established in one language transfer to another - the same question Lau and colleagues address between English and Cantonese, approached here for a language typologically closer to English but still untested. The historical framing is distinctive and well handled, quoting Crystal's characterisation of prosody research as 'the Cinderella of speech' that remains 'in the cellar, with few visitors', and tracing the neglect back to Kanner's original 1943 description, which described a child for whom 'it made no difference whether one spoke to him in a friendly or a harsh way' - an observation the authors note 'the researchers ignored... in the decades that followed'. The clinical ambition is stated modestly and consistently: the aim is a tool that 'may evolve, through further studies' and could 'support clinicians in diagnosing the disorder', with the classification component explicitly disclaimed as not intended for use on new speech data. That restraint distinguishes the paper from most in this corpus and makes its data problems more regrettable rather than less, since the scholarship would have supported a stronger study.

**S-088** [local_4f7e7eb3] — *Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques*

2022. The framing is the standard early-detection argument with the usual supporting claims: prevalence of one in 160 per WHO, diagnosis typically delayed to age 4 despite symptoms appearing earlier, and eye tracking recommended as 'fast, inexpensive, easy to analyse and applicable to all ages'. The related-work section is a list of prior studies with their reported accuracies and no critical assessment, and it includes an error that indicates limited engagement with the clinical literature - the ADOS is attributed to Lord et al. as 'a method... for assessing autism' consisting of 'unstructured observational tasks', when the instrument is explicitly semi-structured and standardised, and the CARS is described as being 'based on the doctor's assessment of children's behaviour through two scales, a social communication questionnaire and a social responsiveness scale', which conflates three distinct instruments. One passage is worth noting because it states a caveat the paper then ignores: 'evidence regarding positive eye-tracking outcomes as a strong predictor of long-term outcomes in children with ASD is lacking'. Having noted that the predictive validity of the modality is unestablished, the paper proceeds to report 99.8% accuracy and to propose the systems as aids for diagnosis and early detection without returning to the point.

**S-089** [local_db6c2d7c] — *Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With*

2022. The framing is the standard access and delay argument - 1 in 44 prevalence, lengthy parent questionnaires and clinical observation producing 'long waiting times for results', and a goal of 'mitigating the problems associated with limited diagnostic resources for neurodevelopmental disorders, especially in regions where access to care is limited'. What distinguishes the positioning is the structure of the related-work critique, which sorts prior video-based work into three categories and identifies a specific cost for each: manual annotation 'require[s] large numbers of trained annotators when implemented on a large scale, which is expensive and time-consuming' and 'may compromise the privacy of participants'; eye trackers 'require custom hardware that can often be expensive and inaccessible, especially for individuals living in resource-limited regions'; and structured-environment studies controlled 'room lighting and distance of the camera from the participant's face', leaving translation to natural settings untested. The study then removes all three constraints simultaneously and reports what remains, which is a small but statistically defensible difference and a weak classifier. Read that way the paper is a deliberate test of how much signal survives the removal of every experimental control - and the answer, reported without inflation, is not much.

**S-090** [local_8b5fb23b] — *Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms*

2022. The framing is the standard screening argument with the usual claim that current procedures 'are highly subjective, leading to misdiagnoses or missed diagnoses' and that an objective biomarker 'would substantially impact current diagnosis practices'. Two features of the positioning are better than that suggests. The scope is explicitly bounded - a dedicated Clinical Implications subsection states that 'rather than being a diagnostic tool, the research model we proposed in this work is meant to be used for ASD screening using ET data' - which is the correct claim for what the evidence supports and is stated before any results are discussed. And the literature review engages with prior figures specifically rather than generically, comparing its own augmented AUC of 97.00% against 'the performance (AUC: 90%) reported in the research work on the same dataset with augmentation' - that is, against the source authors' own result on the same images. What the paper does not do is carry its own contamination diagnosis into that comparison: having established that the augmented condition is contaminated, it compares its contaminated 97% favourably against another group's similarly obtained 90%, when the informative comparison is between its own participant-level 72.88% and the source group's participant-level result of approximately 71%.

**S-091** [local_6dcefc34] — *Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism*

2022. The framing is a health-equity and access argument built around the COVID-19 transition to remote care, and it is more specific than the corpus norm at each step. Prevalence is similar in rural (0.9%) and urban (1.0%) areas, but rural communities face limited access to identification and intervention, and 'up to 80 pct. of counties in the U.S. lack sufficient diagnostic resources'. The critique of existing screening is where the paper is sharpest, and it is a critique this review should record: caregiver-report questionnaires 'require literacy and perform worse with non-white and lower education caregivers', so 'naively deploying digitized versions of diagnostic questionnaires risks exacerbating current disparities in the early identification of ASD'. That argument - that digitising an instrument inherits and can amplify its demographic bias - is made by no other paper here, and it motivates the study's choice to derive signal from a child's behaviour rather than a caregiver's report. The paper also engages with adoption as a design problem, noting that 'delays in the adoption of telehealth have been attributed to unengaged and resisting users' and that 'simply providing the current physician interaction through a smartphone may not be the best way of providing remote care', which is why the data collection is embedded in a game with progression mechanics rather than an assessment. Whether the resulting AU-ROC of 0.745 supports the deployment ambition is a separate question, and the abstract is appropriately hedged, claiming feasibility and 'potential' rather than accuracy.

**S-092** [local_65974fc7] — *Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction*

2022. The framing is a comparative argument for acoustic screening over the alternatives, and it is made concretely: methods based on eye movement, EEG and gut microbiome analysis 'all require expensive equipment, and the detection process is complex', while 'the scale based method highly depends on the subjective experience of doctors', so acoustic analysis 'provides a new path which is more simple and reliable for autism screening'. The related work is engaged specifically rather than generically, contrasting the study's use of speech against a prior study using infant cry - 'they focused on cry which is more random than the speech voice' - which is a reasonable methodological distinction. The paper also identifies a genuine infrastructure gap that this review can corroborate: 'currently, there is no available public speech dataset for ASD children, which creates a big obstacle for related research', a statement consistent with the fact that no speech study in this corpus shares its recordings, in contrast to the eye-tracking literature where a single public image dataset supports at least three of the charted studies. The paper's own corpus, roughly 7,000 recordings from over 140 children, would have been a substantial contribution to that gap had it been released.

**S-093** [local_988c462e] — *The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation*

2022. The framing is unusually precise about what the field has and has not done. Prior speech studies 'reported high classification performance' but 'did not estimate the severity of autism symptoms in individual children', and the two exceptions are named and characterised - one on Japanese-speaking adolescents using support vector regression, one on English-speaking children reaching a correlation of 0.634 in 33 participants. The paper also identifies the specific practical dependency it is removing: the earlier acoustic findings on prosody, pitch variability and speech rate all 'used manual annotation and inspection of the audio recordings', which is what makes them non-scalable. Its comparative positioning is likewise concrete rather than promotional: it acknowledges achieving worse diarization error than a four-microphone beamforming study, explains why, notes that a prior 499-hour corpus comprised verbally fluent children whereas this cohort 'mostly do not speak fluently or use little or no phrase speech', and describes its own correlation as 'similar' to the 0.634 of a smaller study rather than as an improvement. Adding a Hebrew-language cohort also extends the linguistic coverage of this corpus, which is otherwise dominated by English with single studies in Italian, Polish, Cantonese and Chinese.
