**S-094** [local_76de1c03] — *The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children*

Published August 2022 by a Polish-British collaboration spanning robotics, cognitive psychology, education and rehabilitation medicine. The framing is a well-informed critique of existing assessment: parent- and caregiver-report screening instruments have limited reliability, ADOS is the exception because it is 'enriched with interactive protocols', and diagnostic effectiveness is compromised by the difficulty of differentiating autism from sensory integration disorder, dysphasia and ADHD - so assessment often depends on long-term observation and 'often leading to ambiguous diagnostic outcomes'. For this review the study is valuable in four respects, none of which is a performance figure. It is the corpus's clearest example of construct-first design: rather than collecting a behavioural stream and asking what separates the groups, it names turn-taking as the target, builds two contrasting game scenarios to dissociate command-response from imitation, publishes the observational scale that defines the measurement, and quantifies its reliability across six raters. It brings the assessment to the child - both groups were seen in their own kindergartens under an identical protocol - so the recruitment and setting asymmetry that this synthesis has documented across the photograph, audio and thermal branches does not arise. Its translational claim is the best-calibrated in the corpus: the robot is 'a supplementary tool, thanks to which specialists can acquire additional diagnostic intuition to be used with standard tools', and the mechanism is described as a specialist learning what typical play with NAO looks like and thereby seeing deficits by observation - a proposal to calibrate human judgement rather than to replace it, which no other study here entertains. And its future-work section names children themselves among the target users whose cooperation is required to improve the games, the only participatory-design commitment in this review. What it cannot supply is evidence about detection: five children per group, no model, no individual-level prediction, no accuracy, no rater blinding, and no developmental-level covariate. Its role in the synthesis is therefore as the upstream complement to the modelling studies - a demonstration that a robot-delivered paradigm elicits a measurable group difference on a defined construct, which is the prerequisite that most of the automated work in this corpus assumes rather than establishes.

**S-095** [local_3ba6d25c] — *Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach*

Published online 2022, issued 2023, from Shenzhen University's Institute of Human Factors and Ergonomics with the Shenzhen Guangming District Center for Disease Control and Prevention and Shenzhen Kangning Hospital - an engineering-plus-public-health-plus-psychiatry collaboration, funded by eight Chinese grants including the National Natural Science Foundation, the Shenzhen Science and Technology Innovation Committee and a Guangdong Key Realm R&D Program. The framing is incremental and explicitly novelty-staking: the authors argue that all prior eye-tracking classification work has used visual fixation patterns and that 'no study has been found to identify ASD with oculomotor behavior', then draw a conceptual distinction between where attention is directed and how the eyes move in the sockets. The clinical motivation is the standard one for the period - diagnosis depends on clinician experience and caregiver report, is time-consuming and may be biased by subjective factors - and the proposed role is complementary, that eye tracking 'might be incorporated in clinical practice to complement existing diagnostic procedure'. The paper is unusual for 2022 in explicitly flagging that the whole eye-tracking classification literature, its own work included, has only ever tested against typical development.

**S-096** [local_70a30e2b] — *A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features*

Published 2023 from the University of Tehran (Mechanical Engineering and ECE) with co-authors then at the University of Minnesota and UC Riverside, with no external funding. The framing is health-equity engineering rather than diagnostics: the opening premise is that many cases remain undiagnosed 'due to the limited access to experts, especially in low and middle-income societies', and the proposed answer is a device cheap enough to deploy in homes and daycares. Version 2 of an existing platform, so the framing is explicitly incremental - the contributions are stated as introducing a new modality and suggesting new features, and the authors state that they do not wish to compare their accuracy against other modalities in the literature but only against their own version 1. That restraint is unusual and appropriate. The paper is also of its moment in treating multimodality as an answer to within-spectrum heterogeneity - different autistic children show different symptoms, so a comprehensive screen needs several sensing channels - an argument that recurs across the 2022-2023 papers in this corpus.

**S-097** [local_a22f97df] — *A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities*

Published 2023 from the Department of Humanistic Studies, University of Naples Federico II, in collaboration with the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, where two of the four authors were employed and from which the autistic participants were recruited - disclosed appropriately in the competing-interests statement. No funding is reported. The framing is a critique of existing assessment: the authors list four specific constraints of gold-standard tools - no explicit sensory-functioning assessment, dependence on examiner expertise and subjective evaluation, limited ecological validity, and the time demanded - and position quantitative motor measurement as the remedy. The paper is explicitly a second pass at the group's own earlier dataset, whose descriptive analysis had failed to separate the groups significantly, which makes it an unusually transparent instance of a common pattern in this corpus: conventional statistics find nothing, a deep model is applied to the same data, and separation appears. The stated ambition is to move eventually to unsupervised latent organisation so that the model no longer depends on clinical labels for ground truth - a 2023-era aspiration that the paper's own sample size prevents it from testing.

**S-098** [local_c6853fe2] — *A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation*

Published 2023 by Jilin University's School of Communication Engineering with the Department of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics of The First Hospital of Jilin University, funded by the Science and Technology Development Plan of Jilin Province and the National Natural Science Foundation of China. The framing is capacity-driven and quantified: the opening cites autism prevalence rising to 1-2%, more than 10 million diagnosed people in China of whom about 3 million are children, and the striking statistic that 'globally, less than 5% of assessments use the ASD gold standard diagnostic tool, which is mainly due to the long test time, complex training of evaluators and high cost'. That last figure is the clearest statement in this corpus of why instrument automation, as opposed to diagnosis replacement, might matter. The paper positions its own contribution against three named prior response-to-name systems (Bidwell, Petric, Liu, Wang), arguing that all previous work relied on face, head pose and gaze while ignoring body pose - so the framing is incremental within a small, well-identified subliterature. Its most creditable move is the methods-section disclaimer that the work assesses response to name and not autism risk, which sits in unresolved tension with the abstract and conclusion.

**S-099** [local_f1b626c8] — *Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games*

Published 2023 from the Islamic Azad University Science and Research Branch and Tabriz Branch, with the Institute for Cognitive and Brain Sciences and the Faculty of Education and Psychology of Shahid Beheshti University, Tehran; no funding received. The framing is workforce scarcity: 'since the proper diagnosis of this condition depends on the correct and accurate decision of the specialist, the availability of adequate specialists in this area seems necessary. Unfortunately, the number of these specialists is low with respect to the growing autistic population', leading to the goal of a system 'easily applicable by not-so-expert users'. That is a task-shifting rationale rather than an accuracy-improvement one, and it recurs across the Iranian and Chinese papers in this corpus. The introduction is unusually wide-ranging for a short engineering paper, surveying therapeutic games, socially assistive robots, brain-computer interfaces and fuzzy learning before arriving at its own design, and it conspicuously cites work on same-race versus other-race face processing in autism without applying that literature to its own choice of Japanese stimuli for Iranian children. The conclusion's call to include 'conditions overlapping with autism for differential diagnosis' is a 2023-typical acknowledgement that the case-control geometry is the field's binding constraint.

**S-100** [local_6249bd63] — *Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior*

Published 2023 (author manuscript available in PMC from November 2023), from the Center for Autism Research at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the University of Pennsylvania, funded by four NIH grants (R01MH118327, R01MH122599, 5P50HD105354-02, R21HD102078). The framing is deliberately corrective rather than promotional. The opening premise is that psychiatry, unlike the rest of medicine, relies almost exclusively on observational and paper-and-pencil instruments, and that computational behaviour analysis could supply the missing instrumentation - with the explicit acknowledgement that clinical assessment reliability is currently limited, citing the DSM-5 field trial kappa of 0.69 for autism. The central rhetorical move is to identify a gap the field has left open: 'to our knowledge, no study has directly compared AI algorithms and human raters with respect to overall predictive capacity or specific decisions on individual cases'. That reframing - from 'can AI classify autism?' to 'does AI tell a clinician anything they did not already know?' - is the paper's real contribution and is the question most of this corpus does not ask. The positioning is consistently augmentative: AI as an assistive tool that could prompt a clinician to re-evaluate when the two disagree, with the caveat that this is only workable if the algorithm can say why.

**S-101** [local_8b9e0e8a] — *Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas*

Published 2023 by Northwestern Polytechnical University's School of Automation with the Institute of Artificial Intelligence at the Hefei Comprehensive National Science Center, in collaboration with the Children Healthcare Department of the Affiliated Hospital of Northwest University, the Children Rehabilitation Center of Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital, Beijing University of Chinese Medicine and Nanchang University - a broad engineering-clinical consortium, funded by three National Natural Science Foundation of China grants. The framing is health-equity infrastructure and is stated with more precision than most: the introduction identifies three specific barriers to screening in remote areas - affordability, child-friendliness and the availability of professionals - and every subsequent design choice is justified against one of them, including the explicit contrast with fMRI as an unaffordable alternative and the proposal that storage and analysis run on a cloud computing centre. The prevalence trajectory is cited precisely (1/68 in 2014, 1/59 in 2018, 1/44 in 2021 per US CDC), with the claim that developing-country prevalence is comparable. Two aspects of the positioning are notable for the synthesis. The paper explicitly criticises the small-sample norm in this literature, arguing from its own visualisation that 'when the number of subjects is less than 100, the test cannot accurately reflect the performance of the model' - a methodological argument that a 333-child multi-site study is entitled to make and that indicts much of the surrounding corpus. And the burden framing in the opening paragraph ('most patients diagnosed with ASD cannot independently live, study and work when they grow up, which places a heavy burden on their families and society') is the starkest deficit language encountered in this review, sitting uncomfortably beside an otherwise child-centred and access-oriented design.

**S-102** [local_0e476686] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts*

Published 2023 by the SALBIS and SECOMUCI research groups in the Department of Electric, Systems and Automatics Engineering at Universidad de Leon, Spain, partially supported by a university internal research programme. The framing is the familiar access-and-scarcity argument - diagnosis 'remains a challenge due to the resources and specialized professionals needed', existing methods rest on interviews and questionnaires that 'take too much time' - combined with a strongly stated case for early diagnosis occupying most of the introduction. The positioning within the field is explicitly as a gap-filler: the authors note that prior autism machine-learning work has used images and eye tracking, that 'few have focused on detecting ASD using text as input', and that there is 'a notable gap in research utilizing the information found in Twitter users' biographies'. That gap is real, and social-media language is a legitimate and under-explored modality. What makes the paper a cautionary case for this review is the distance between its framing and its evidence: a study motivated in its opening pages by identifying autistic children before the age of three, using adult self-disclosure on a platform with a minimum age of 13, claiming to 'pave the way' for diagnosis on the basis of a tweet-level classification whose validation design cannot distinguish autism from authorship. It is also the only study in the corpus that builds a health classifier from identifiable individuals' public disclosures with no ethics approval, no consent and no discussion of either.

**S-103** [local_fbaf69bf] — *Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Published 2021/2023 by the Duke University Electrical and Computer Engineering department with the Duke Center for Autism and Brain Development and Duke Children's Primary Care - an engineering-psychiatry-primary care collaboration, funded by an NIH Autism Center of Excellence award, two further NIMH R01s, the Marcus and Simons Foundations, NSF, ONR and NGA, plus Apple, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services and Google. The framing is scalability of assessment: standardised observational assessment requires highly trained clinicians, manual facial coding from video is complex and time-intensive, and neither deploys at scale, so computer vision is proposed to make quantification universal. The positioning within the group's own programme is explicit and unusually candid - the paper states that it replicates the affect-related analysis of its own prior work on a larger dataset with redesigned stimuli, and then argues that the new complexity measure is 'an independent and more powerful measure' than the group's earlier one. Self-supersession of this kind is rare in this literature. The paper also carries an internal methodological critique of its own field, noting in a footnote that multiscale entropy is widely used in health research without addressing the across-subject comparability problem, with the result that 'often authors report lower MSE for data that is clearly more complex and vice-versa'. Commercially, this is one of the most conflicted studies in the corpus - several authors have licensed the underlying app technology to Apple and benefited financially - and it is also the only one to describe a structural mitigation, with data analysis independently reviewed throughout by a named conflict-free co-author.

**S-104** [local_74416ba7] — *Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders*

Published 2023 by the Augmented Human Communication Laboratory at Nara Institute of Science and Technology with the Department of Psychiatry at Nara Medical University School of Medicine and Osaka Psychiatric Medical Center, funded by a single JST CREST grant (JPMJCR19A5). The framing is diagnostic refinement within psychiatry rather than population screening: the opening premise is that experienced psychiatrists identify autism and schizophrenia through interviews, responses and neuropsychological tests, and that 'the discovery of disorder-specific biomarkers and behavioral indicators with sufficient sensitivity is important' to improve that process. Two aspects of the positioning are distinctive for this corpus. The paper's central concern is differentiation between two conditions rather than detection of one - 'since ASD and Sz are often difficult to differentiate, we propose to examine eye movement differences during facial expression recognition for the distinction' - which puts it among the very few studies here that treat the clinically realistic problem. And its contribution is framed as a modelling gap rather than a performance gap: prior basic research had established that gaze differences vary by presented emotion, but 'machine learning models that take this into account have not been examined', so the paper's claim is that a known behavioural fact should be built into the model architecture. The resulting accuracies are modest and are reported without inflation, with binomial tests against chance and a failing result left visible - a tone that stands out against the corpus's prevailing register.

**S-105** [local_7c6a5aa4] — *Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders*

Published 2023 by a distributed group spanning University of Colorado Colorado Springs, Yale, University of Virginia, University of Miami, University of Washington, Seattle Children's Research Institute, Microsoft Research and Van Robotics, funded by NSF and NIH grants, with data provided by the GiveSpeech Foundation. The framing is a data-availability argument rather than a clinical one: the authors contend that AAC research is dominated by single-subject designs and expensive clinical trials requiring 'specialized infrastructure and a great deal of clinical expertise', while the dense telemetry that digital AAC systems generate has been almost entirely ignored - 'with the exception of one prior report, no efforts have been made to use the dense streams of data collected by digital AACs to derive insights of clinical importance'. That is an accurate observation and the study's real contribution is to demonstrate the point. Its positioning within this review is distinctive in three ways. It is the only study whose participants are AAC users, so its autistic sample comes from the minimally verbal end of the spectrum that the rest of the corpus systematically excludes. It is one of very few that pose the differential question explicitly - autism versus others who also need AAC, not autism versus typical development. And it is the only one whose data were generated as a by-product of people using a product for their own purposes, which gives it unmatched ecological validity and simultaneously removes every control that makes a finding interpretable. The paper is also unusual in reporting a null result prominently: three simple usage measures showed no group difference at all, and this is presented as the motivation for the modelling rather than concealed.

**S-106** [local_8a706eaa] — *Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder*

Published 2023 by the Department of Biomedical Systems Informatics at Yonsei University College of Medicine with the Division of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry at Seoul National University College of Medicine and LumanLab Inc, funded by an MD-PhD Physician-Scientist Training Program grant from the Korea Health Industry Development Institute. The framing is a critique of the existing computational literature rather than of clinical practice, and it is one of the sharpest such critiques in the corpus: prior autism-detection models are said to be unsuitable for tool development because of 'a lack of automation, the requirements for specialized and expensive equipment, calibration, trained personnel, dependence on human rating of autistic behaviors, and low precision and recall', with the low performance attributed to the absence of targeted behavioural biomarkers and of methods for quantitatively measuring hallmark autism behaviours. The response - instrument an already-validated clinical construct with a replicable protocol and a consumer camera, rather than search for a statistical signature in whatever data are available - is the study's real contribution and is a template the rest of this literature could usefully follow. Two contextual features should be carried into the synthesis. This is one of very few studies here whose autistic sample is predominantly minimally verbal with mean IQ in the 50s, a population systematically excluded elsewhere by paradigms requiring screen attention or conversation - and simultaneously the study whose groups differ most on IQ, so the two facts are the same fact. And the method is patented by its authors with a commercial entity involved in data management, disclosed fully but without the independent-analysis safeguard reported by the Duke group elsewhere in this corpus.

**S-107** [local_6b9484ce] — *Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking*

Published 2023 by the Department of Computer Science at Vellore Institute of Technology, India, with no reported funding. The framing is the standard workload-and-subjectivity argument: there is no definitive biological test for autism, diagnosis depends on a chain of specialist referrals and subjective instruments, and 'the process of diagnosis itself consumes a lot of time and energy of both the children and parents', so computer-aided methods offering a reliable 'second opinion' are attractive. The paper positions itself within an eye-tracking-for-diagnosis literature that it surveys across several conditions - Parkinson disease, dementia, dyslexia, schizophrenia - before turning to autism, which is a useful reminder that the same modality and often the same architectures are being applied across diagnoses, and that a scanpath classifier reported at 95% for dyslexia and 78.85% for schizophrenia in the cited work is not obviously measuring anything condition-specific. For this review the study's value is not its result but its position: it is the fourth independent reuse of the 547-image dataset encountered here, it applies a different modelling family from the others, and its comparatively modest 81% - obtained under the same image-level splitting that has yielded 97-99% elsewhere - is a useful data point on how much of those higher figures is attributable to method rather than to signal.

**S-108** [local_c6a4ea7b] — *SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism*

Published 2023 by the Human-Machine Interaction Lab at IIIT Delhi, funded by an Indian government Science and Engineering Research Board start-up grant with partial support from a TCS Foundation centre and the Infosys Centre for Artificial Intelligence. The framing is the standard objectivity argument - autism diagnosis depends on behavioural assessment because 'the unavailability of genetic tests or biological markers' leaves no alternative, and 'quantifying these behavioural traits is cumbersome, and the efficacy of such methods primarily depends on the evaluators' expertise'. What distinguishes the paper's positioning is the specificity of the gap it claims: prior computational work on semantic-pragmatic language in autism has examined individual features such as echolalia or pronoun use in isolation and 'focused only on smaller feature sets', so 'the cumulative effect of the features and how they complement the lexical, syntactic and other text-based features in the diagnosis of autism has not been analysed'. That is a well-identified and genuinely open question, and the feature-family ablation is a direct answer to it. The paper's other distinctive commitment is to interpretability as a design constraint rather than a reporting nicety - features are specified against ADOS so that predictions can be explained in clinically recognisable terms - which puts it in the same small group as the joint-attention and facial-complexity studies charted here. For this review its main value is as the corpus's clearest demonstration that pragmatic language measures carry as much discriminative signal as lexical ones and combine with them additively; its main caution is that this was established on three pooled corpora, one of which contains autistic children exclusively.

**S-109** [local_5c43dffa] — *Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths*

Published 2023 by a seven-institution United States consortium including the Yale Child Study Center, Seattle Children's Research Institute and the University of Washington, funded by an NIH K01 award and a Simons Foundation grant, with a first author who also leads the AAC-telemetry study charted elsewhere in this review and a senior author (Shic) whose eye-tracking work recurs throughout this literature. The framing is heterogeneity rather than detection, and it is argued rather than asserted: clinical assessment is subjective and expert-dependent, autism heterogeneity has 'led to the presumption of the presence of multiple etiologies rather than a single disorder', and the quest for personalised medicine is obstructed by it - so a method that can parse subgroups is more valuable than one that only separates cases from controls. The literature review is the most thorough of any study in this corpus on the specific question of scan-path classification, surveying Carette's LSTM work (83% on 32 children), Li's oculomotor behaviour framework (80% on 49 children), Elbattah's autoencoder clustering, the Saliency4ASD grand challenge submissions of Tao and Shyu (74.22% validation falling to 55.66% on test, attributed to overfitting) and Wu (65.41% and 55.13%), and Pusiol's Fragile X work - and it criticises several of them on exactly the right grounds, noting where validation-to-test performance collapsed and where the stratification comparisons needed to support a heterogeneity claim were not reported. The paper's own most valuable contribution to this review is an unintended one: by demonstrating that scan-path images classify age at 80.5% and sex at 78.0% within a single diagnostic group, it quantifies how much demographic information this widely used representation carries, and therefore how much caution the many scan-path autism classifiers in this corpus require.

**S-110** [local_32da8ede] — *A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths*

Published 2024 by the Department of Artificial Intelligence at the University of Jordan with Princess Sumaya University for Technology, Amman. The framing is the familiar cost-and-expertise argument, developed at unusual length: diagnosis requires specialised professionals using observation, interviews and questionnaires; current tools are time-consuming because of 'the extensive number of items that need to be checked by the specialist' and rely on 'static human-embedded rules'; and because 'each specialist relies on their own expertise and experience to diagnose autism spectrum disorder', the process suffers 'inconsistencies and a lack of reliability'. The introduction also engages with delayed diagnosis and its causes - limited resources in rural areas and low-income families, shortage of specialist referrals, parental awareness - which locates the work in the access literature. For this review the study's value is as the fifth reuse of the 547-image dataset and as the clearest instance of a specific reporting hazard. It is the only reuse to report sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy, and those class-conditional metrics imply roughly 79% - close to the independent transfer-learning reuse at 81%, to the one-image-per-child leave-one-out figure of 72.88%, and to the source authors' own participant-level correction near 71%. The 95.59% headline is irreconcilable with them. Whichever number is correct, the paper illustrates why a review of this literature must recompute rather than accept reported accuracies, and why the near-ceiling figures that dominate this dataset's reuse literature should be treated as claims requiring arithmetic verification.

**S-111** [local_15ed96cb] — *A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning*

Published 2024 by the University of Haifa's occupational therapy department with Maccabi Healthcare Services, Tel-Aviv University and the Keshet Autism Center, funded by the Gertner Institute of Health Policy and Epidemiology. The framing is health-services and equity oriented rather than technological: autism diagnosis typically occurs after age three despite behavioural markers being observable in the first two years, the barriers are heterogeneity in presentation, subtlety of early signs during short visits, and 'disparities in healthcare screening resources and in provider awareness', and the proposed remedy is to exploit data a universal surveillance system already collects. The paper is unusual in this corpus for treating the health system as the unit of intervention - its contribution is an alerting layer for a national programme that currently contains no autism-specific screening instrument, not a new measurement device. For the review its importance is threefold. It is the only study reporting performance at a genuine population base rate, and its numbers make the prevalence problem concrete in a way no other study does: an AUC of 0.86 with 75% sensitivity yields a high-risk group of 144,632 children containing 874 recorded cases, a positive predictive value of 0.60%. It shows that on real population data with clinically chosen features, logistic regression matches gradient boosting exactly, which reframes the algorithmic arms race visible across the rest of this corpus. And its limitations section models the standard the field should meet, quantifying its own label noise at a factor of ten and stating the cost of its own representational choices in the same breath as their rationale.

**S-112** [local_261afa51] — *AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: &#x201C;A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System&#x201D;*

Published 2024 by the Department of Computer Engineering at the Arab Academy for Science, Technology and Maritime Transport, Alexandria, with no funding statement. The framing is access and speed - traditional manual assessment is time-consuming, AI 'offers expedited decision-making' - and the deliverable is a consumer mobile application 'designed to be user-friendly for families and psychiatrists alike'. For this review the study functions as a negative exemplar marking the boundary of the field, and it is worth setting out precisely what it exemplifies. First, a label derived from image provenance rather than diagnosis: an image is autistic because it was found on an autism website. Second, class-confounded data collection, in which the two classes come from different sources so that every photographic property distinguishing those sources is available to the classifier - the same failure mode this review has recorded in an acoustic study where autistic and comparison children were recorded on different devices, but here operating on the entire dataset rather than one feature family. Third, a physiognomic premise adopted from a single citation without engagement with the history of inferring conditions from facial structure. Fourth, a proposed consumer deployment - parents photographing their children to receive an autism determination - advanced without diagnostic validation, without any interpretability check on what the model uses, and without ethical consideration of the photographs of identifiable children on which it is built or of the consequences of a false result delivered to a family by an app. The review should record that this branch of the literature exists, that it reports accuracies comparable to or higher than the most carefully conducted studies charted here, and that those accuracies carry no evidential weight.

**S-113** [local_3e88f3ce] — *An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks*

Published September 2025 by computer science groups at Lahore College for Women University and The Superior University in Pakistan, with collaborators at the University of North Dakota and King Saud University. The framing is the branch standard: ADOS and ADI-R are 'subjective, time-consuming, and largely impossible in low-resource environments', so objective neuroimaging biomarkers combined with automated classification should replace them. For this review the study earns extended treatment for three reasons, none of which concerns its accuracy. It is the corpus's clearest and most instructive case of target leakage, and its mechanism is distinct from the questionnaire-dataset studies charted alongside it: there the label was an arithmetic function of the features, here the features are the scored output of the clinical assessment that produced the label, which is less mechanical and equally circular - and compounded by the fact that ADOS and ADI-R are largely absent for controls in ABIDE-I, so missingness carries the label as well. Second, the leakage was made visible by the study's own interpretability apparatus. GAMI-Net's additive decomposition ranks ADOS_TOTAL first at 0.278 and the final SHAP analysis ranks ADOS_Gotham_Total first at 0.234, and the paper reports both transparently while reading them as clinical alignment. That is the strongest argument in this review for interpretable-by-design architectures: a black-box model on the same inputs would have produced the same 99.99% with nothing to reveal why. Third, its own Table 1 tabulates recent comparators in the neuroimaging branch at 80.2% to 97.1% accuracy, so figures in the high nineties are that branch's norm rather than an outlier - and if phenotype fields are commonly used alongside imaging, those figures require the same provenance and arithmetic scrutiny this review has had to apply to the scanpath-reuse and facial-image literatures. Two structural notes complete the picture. The study has the richest clinical phenotype of any in the review - ADOS, ADI-R, SRS, FIQ, VIQ, PIQ across 1,112 subjects at 17 sites - and reports none of it as sample description, having converted it into features; and its motivating argument, that the standard instruments are impractical in low-resource settings, is contradicted by a proposed alternative requiring both an MRI scanner and those same instruments as input.

**S-114** [local_5b5f2237] — *Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development*

Published 2024 by Shenzhen University's Institute of Human Factors and Ergonomics with the Shenzhen Guangming District Center for Disease Control and Prevention and Shenzhen Kangning Hospital - the same engineering-plus-public-health-plus-psychiatry consortium, the same cohort and the same recordings as the group's oculomotor paper charted elsewhere in this review, funded by seven Chinese sources including the National Natural Science Foundation. The framing is the familiar objectivity-and-efficiency argument, but it is developed with more precision than most: the paper distinguishes two separate deficiencies in current practice, lack of objectivity and excessive time cost, and observes that machine-learning work which merely shortens ADOS or ADI-R by pruning items addresses the second while leaving the first untouched, because 'the issue of lack of objectivity remains if individuals' behavior is rated by experts'. That is a sharper diagnosis of what automation is for than most papers in this corpus offer. Its distinctive scientific contribution is to target a dyadic construct - coordination between two people - rather than a property of the child, and to control it with a surrogate-pair null. Its distinctive cautionary contribution, for the review's purposes, is that it is the clearest available demonstration of how much analytic choice determines outcome: the same recordings analysed by the same group with complexity matching yielded no significant coordination difference, and with cross wavelet analysis yield both a significant difference and a 92.68% classifier. The paper reports both facts and reconciles neither.

**S-115** [local_13426811] — *Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning*

Published 2024 by the Department of Neuropsychiatry at Hirosaki University with Aomori Chuo Gakuin University and the Natural Language Processing Lab at Tohoku University, funded by two JSPS KAKENHI grants. The framing is diagnostic supplementation grounded in a specific, well-evidenced critique of the gold standard rather than in generic complaints about subjectivity: ADOS-2 does not clearly differentiate autism from ADHD or from the negative symptoms of schizophrenia and other psychiatric comorbidities; masking, compensation and camouflaging can conceal impairment; and adult diagnosis is further hampered because caregiver developmental reports are usually unavailable while self-insight is unreliable. That is a more precise diagnosis of what automated assessment is for than any other paper in this corpus offers, and it leads to a correspondingly bounded claim - language analysis as one input among several, not a replacement. Four features make the study particularly valuable to this review. It is the only one that applies a gold-standard instrument to both groups, so its comparison group is screened rather than assumed. It is the only one that nests a fitted preprocessing component inside its cross-validation. It is the only one that tests model comparisons statistically and then declines to over-read non-significant differences. And it is the only one that refuses to rank its models by accuracy, retaining an interpretable linear model on the explicit ground that interpretability is not commensurable with accuracy in clinical use. Set against these, its unmeasured comparison-group IQ is a real limitation, and its reliance on ADOS-2 transcripts means the speech analysed was produced inside the diagnostic encounter itself - a form of dependence between sample and label that no other language study here faces and that the paper does not discuss.

**S-116** [local_948fa8d0] — *Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms*

Published 2024 by the Department of Computer Science and Systems Engineering at Andhra University with the Department of Applied Psychology at GITAM Deemed to be University, Visakhapatnam. The framing is early detection and parental support, with the observation that diagnosis 'depends predominantly on the aberrations in the functioning of the brain that may not surface in the very early stages' and that technology has been 'a blessing to the parents who are clueless about managing the condition'. The presence of a psychology co-author makes the absence of any diagnostic verification, demographic reporting or ethical consideration more striking rather than less. For this review the study's value is entirely as a second data point on the facial-photograph branch of the literature, and it strengthens three observations already recorded from the companion study on the same dataset. The branch is not small - two independent groups publishing in the same year on the same scraped collection, with a literature review here citing at least half a dozen further examples using facial images, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet and hybrid vision transformers at accuracies from 88% to 92.5%. Its reported accuracies are comparable to or higher than the best-conducted studies in this review, so accuracy in this literature does not order studies by evidential quality. And its methodological reporting can omit the evaluation protocol entirely without that omission preventing publication - which is the strongest available evidence that peer review in this branch is not filtering on the properties that determine whether a number means anything.

**S-117** [local_893dfc22] — *Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed*

Published December 2024 by a computer science and engineering group at R.M.D. Engineering College, Thiruvallur. For this review the study's value lies in what it illustrates rather than in what it measures, and two lessons carry into the synthesis. The first concerns the boundary between autism-framed and autism-evidenced work. Every framing element here - title, keywords, abstract, introduction, problem statement, conclusion - is written in terms of autistic people and the failure of conventional systems to read their faces, which is a real and under-addressed problem stated with some sympathy; and the entire experimental content is six-way emotion classification on posed expressions from non-autistic adult volunteers, evaluated at peak frames on a corpus whose images are geometrically standardised. A reader relying on title and abstract would record 99.8% as an autism result. The second concerns what such figures mean. The paper's own introduction notes that 'staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones' and that the field lacks work on spontaneous stimuli, which is precisely why 99.8% on peak-frame posed adult expressions is near the long-established ceiling for that benchmark and carries no implication for autistic children in spontaneous distress - the application the conclusion invokes. Another study charted in this review tests exactly that transfer and finds that affect models trained on neurotypical faces perform poorly on autistic children and improve materially only after fine-tuning on autistic data. Read together, the two studies make the point cleanly: the emotion-recognition benchmark is solved, the autism-relevant problem is not, and the two are frequently reported as though they were the same. Three further defects should be recorded: no validation scheme, split or partitioning unit is stated anywhere; the reported metrics (100% recall with 94% specificity across six classes) are presented without confusion matrices or class-wise results; and the number of emotion classes is given as six, seven and five in three different places.

**S-118** [local_e7c16f2a] — *Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification*

Published 2024 by the Natural and Artificial Cognition Lab in the Department of Humanistic Study at the University of Naples Federico II with the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Research and Rehabilitation Center, funded by a PNRR MUR project and a University of Naples internal line. Three of the five authors also appear on the variational-autoencoder study charted elsewhere in this review, and both studies recruit autistic participants from the same rehabilitation centre - though the samples, tasks and analyses differ, so this is a related programme rather than a reanalysis. The framing is a clinical-gap argument rather than an accuracy claim: motor differences are prevalent in autism and appear before language and social difficulties, yet they are treated as secondary symptoms and 'there are no adequate tools available to accurately assess motor function in children with autism' - so the contribution sought is an instrument for something currently unmeasured, not a replacement for something already measured. That is a more defensible position than most in this corpus and it is grounded in embodied-cognition theory rather than in appeals to objectivity. For the review the study's value is threefold. It is the only included study to publish its data openly, at a stated GitHub URL, which makes its central claim independently checkable and sets a standard the rest of the corpus does not meet. Its causal-manipulation interpretability method - generating synthetic trajectories with systematically varied acceleration and measuring how predictions respond - is a template other studies could adopt in place of post-hoc attribution. And its incidental finding that a model without acceleration as an input still correlates with acceleration at r = 0.69 is a useful counterweight to the assumption, common across this literature, that a feature-engineering gain means additional information rather than easier access to information already present. Set against these, its 738 trajectories come from 20 children and are partitioned by trajectory rather than by child, so the headline 0.90 is not an estimate of performance on an unseen child - and with only 20 participants, leave-one-child-out validation would have been trivial to perform.

**S-119** [local_5a7ab52d] — *Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain*

Published 2024 by computer science and engineering departments at MIT-ADT University and the Vishwakarma Institute of Information Technology, Pune, with no funding statement and no clinical collaboration. The framing is the economic-burden argument in its strongest form in this review: undetected autism 'may create more economic pressure, affect the family relationship, and also become a burden in social and medical care', and the condition 'has brought a large economic and mental burden to society'. For the review the study is worth recording for three reasons, none of them to do with its result. It is the only included study that reports no sample size at all, which marks the outer limit of what this literature will publish. Its target conflates autism with visual sensory processing disorder into a single binary label, which no other included study does and which makes even a valid result uninterpretable clinically. And its one worked data table shows the three 'Detected' individuals carrying body temperatures of 100.4, 95.5 and 103 and heart rates of 102, 62 and 133 against 98.5 and 99.5 with heart rates of 85 and 89 for the two 'Not detected' - so in the only data the paper displays, the label separates abnormal from normal vital signs. Read alongside the facial-photograph studies charted here, it indicates that the segment of this literature driven by algorithmic novelty rather than by a clinical question can reach the high nineties on data it does not describe, with a target it does not define, and pass peer review at a journal with a thirteen-month review period.

**S-120** [local_8253c2ec] — *Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder*

Published 2024 by mathematics and computer science departments at four Nigerian universities. The framing is an access argument stated with more precision than anywhere else in this review: over 125,000 individuals were reported waiting for a mental health service examination in England in July 2022 against a recommended three-month wait, so 'parents and caregivers [do] not have the necessary support and services early'. That problem is real, quantified and correctly identified, and it is why work of this kind is written, published and cited. For the review the study contributes three things, all cautionary. It is the corpus's most complete instance of target leakage: the class variable in the UCI and Kaggle autism screening datasets is the summed A1-A10 item score thresholded at the instrument's published cut-off, the items are the model's inputs, and the sum is itself among the tabulated fields - so the outcome is a closed-form function of the predictors and 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC across four independent datasets is the expected arithmetic, obtainable by a summation and a comparison. Second, the paper's own literature review documents that this is systematic rather than isolated, tabulating the subliterature on these datasets at 97.15% to 100% while recording one comparator that used independent measurements - fitness tests, brain scans and severity assessments on recruited participants - at 77.99%, roughly twenty-two points below. Third, and most consequentially, the study does not stop at reporting: it deploys. An interactive web-based diagnostic tool was built, illustrated in the paper, and described as routing user input through age-specific pre-trained models to give 'immediate diagnostic feedback', 'accessible for clinical and at-home use'. A parent using it answers the Q-CHAT-10 or AQ-10 items and receives back, presented as an artificial-intelligence diagnosis, the output of those instruments' own scoring rule - with no positive predictive value computed at any realistic prevalence, and with the training data drawn from screening-app users whose positive rates run to 69%. What should be said in the study's favour is that its analytic reporting is careful where the corpus norm is not: class distributions are given for every band, the decision not to oversample is explained, split sizes are tabulated in full, the Matthews correlation coefficient is included, and the methodological critique of grid-search hyperparameter tuning is well reasoned. The gap between that care and the unexamined provenance of the label is the review's clearest illustration of how rigorous analysis above a corrupted target produces a confidently wrong deployment.

**S-121** [local_1e9d0b71] — *Machine learning’s effectiveness*

Published 2024 by informatics and engineering groups at Shizuoka and Gifu Universities with neuropsychiatry and medical sciences at Nagasaki University, funded by two JSPS Grants-in-Aid together with JST MIRAI and JST CREST. The framing is a timing gap stated with unusual precision: autism can be detected at 14 months and diagnosed with high accuracy by two years, yet more than 70% of affected children are not diagnosed until after 51 months, so identifying autistic traits before elementary school entry is the target. The chosen route is to instrument an assessment that already happens - the one-legged standing test within a routine preschool medical examination - which is why near-complete population coverage was achievable. For this review the study is valuable on four counts. It is one of only two with genuinely population-based sampling, and the only one whose comparison group is simply the rest of the same age cohort, so the spectrum-truncation problem that inflates the diagnostic studies does not arise at all. Its measurement is embedded in an existing examination with a consumer webcam and a single pressure mat, so the deployment claim is credible rather than aspirational. Its cross-sensor fusion is constitutive rather than additive, with the discriminative features being correlations between body movement and base-of-support movement that neither sensor could produce alone - and the ablation shows those features outperforming the conventional sway measures drawn from prior literature. And it correlates its model's output with the continuous SRS-2 score, testing whether the prediction tracks the trait dimension rather than only the imposed threshold. Against all this stands a single unresolved question: whether the joint feature-selection and hyperparameter-optimisation procedure was nested within the leave-one-out loop. On 126 children with 19 positives, selecting three to five of sixteen variables plus a cost parameter would by itself explain accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of exactly 1.000, and the paper does not say. The authors' own warning that their validation scheme 'can produce optimistic performance estimates' should be read as applying with more force than they intend.

**S-122** [local_b9e05a8f] — *Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network*

Published 2025 by information systems and computer science groups at Al Yamamah University Riyadh, Minia University and King Faisal University, funded by King Faisal University grant KFU250488. The framing is the standard early-detection appeal - screening is subjective, expertise is scarce, and a facial-image classifier would be objective, scalable and non-invasive - built on a physiognomic literature the introduction reviews approvingly and the conclusion endorses, telling clinicians that facial traits 'indicate the condition'. For this review the paper occupies an unusual position, and its value lies in the tension between its two halves. Methodologically it is the best-executed study in the facial-photograph branch: it is the only one to test for leakage rather than assume its absence, and it found a maximum training-test similarity of 0.9714 in the video-derived corpus, which is direct evidence that the naive frame-level splitting practised by the papers it draws on does leak; it is one of the few in the whole corpus to archive its code with a DOI; it reports a full metric suite with significance testing; its ablation honestly records that its own architectural contribution underperforms without the accompanying hyperparameter search; and it evaluates across datasets in both directions. Substantively, none of that reaches the problem, because the labels in both corpora encode where an image was found rather than any assessment of the child in it - a fact the paper states in its own methods and never revisits. The cross-dataset result sharpens rather than resolves this: two corpora built by the same principle, autism-labelled material from autism-associated online sources against controls from general online sources, will share their confounds, so 89-90% transfer between them is what a provenance-driven model would produce as readily as a phenotype-driven one. The lesson the review should carry from this paper is that methodological rigour applied downstream of a corrupted label does not repair it, and can make an uninterpretable result look better validated than the less careful papers alongside it. Two further points belong in the discussion: no ethics or consent statement appears anywhere in a paper whose training data are identifiable photographs of children scraped from personal websites, Facebook pages and YouTube; and the reported confidence intervals of plus or minus 0.4 percentage points on a 68-image test set are narrower than a single test image, which is a reporting failure that the journal's statistical framing did not catch.

**S-123** [local_0b0960c4] — *Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]*

Published 2024 by the School of Computer Engineering and Mathematical Sciences at the Defence Institute of Advanced Technology, Pune, with a collaborator at Manipal University Jaipur, using data provided by the brain-computer interface group at King Abdulaziz University. The framing is identical to that of the behavioural studies charted throughout this review - diagnosis 'predominantly depends on subjective and time-consuming behavioral assessments', so a 'reliable and non-intrusive biomarker' is needed - which is itself worth recording, because the two branches share a motivation while differing entirely in what they measure and in what they require. For the synthesis the study contributes three things. It is the review's representative of the electrophysiological branch, and it makes clear both that branch's advantage - a purpose-built corpus with both groups recorded on identical equipment under an identical protocol, removing the acquisition confound that undermines the scraped-image and clinic-versus-school studies - and its cost, since a research EEG amplifier, a gel cap, a trained operator and a child who will sit still is precisely the apparatus that the webcam-and-toys approaches exist to avoid. Second, it reproduces the methodological pattern the review has traced across five behavioural modalities: 17 participants, accuracies necessarily computed over epochs, no stated partitioning rule, and a majority-class baseline of 76.5% that goes unmentioned. Third, and most usefully, its own comparison table supplies independent evidence for the review's central quantitative observation. The table lists six prior studies with participant counts from 15 to 80 reporting accuracies of 81% to 93%, and one study with 411 participants reporting 56% to 64% - so within a table the authors assembled themselves, the single study with a sample an order of magnitude larger than the rest reports by far the lowest performance. The inverse relationship between sample size and reported accuracy that this review documents in the scanpath, facial-image and speech branches is therefore visible in the electrophysiological branch too, and visible in a summary constructed without any intention of demonstrating it.

**S-124** [local_abad69fd] — *Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play*

Published 2024 by the Peking University Sixth Hospital group - NHC Key Laboratory of Mental Health and the National Clinical Research Center for Mental Disorders - together with authors from ALSOLIFE, a Beijing autism-services company, with no external funding and two patent applications declared by six of the eleven authors. The framing is developmental and clinical rather than technological: play is introduced as a meaningful activity in its own right that supports quality of life, social inclusion and later friendships, and the argument for using it as a measure is that the core traits of autism naturally manifest there. The intended contribution is a time- and cost-efficient screening aid that could 'remove the geographic barriers' to early identification. For this review the study is valuable on four counts. It has the most complete clinical characterisation of any behavioural study charted here - real DSM-5 best-estimate diagnosis by psychiatrists, CARS-2 corroboration with cited psychometrics, deliberate matching on age and sex with tests reported, and comorbidity and medication handled by explicit exclusion. It demonstrates what a brief observation can and cannot access: the social-communication and play dimensions separated the groups while the restricted-repetitive indicators were statistically degenerate in 90 seconds, confirming a hypothesis the authors stated in advance and bounding what every short-observation study in this corpus can claim. It reports honest and modest performance - AUC 0.826, sensitivity 85.4%, specificity 68.3% - with calibration, predictive values and per-predictor confidence intervals, in a literature where accuracy alone above 95% is the norm. And its limitations section contains the clearest statement of spectrum truncation and its effect anywhere in this review: children below CARS-2 30 were excluded, 'consequently, the performance of the clinical prediction model may be overestimated'. Two cautions travel with it. The five predictors were selected from 81 candidates and the operating threshold from the same ROC curve, all on the development sample, so the reported figures are apparent rather than validated, and the bootstrap that was run is not reported as an optimism correction. And the screening claim rests on predictive values computed at the matched 50% prevalence; at any realistic base rate a specificity of 68.3% would make most positive calls false, which is the calculation that determines whether this tool is deployable in the settings its authors envisage.

**S-125** [local_cd7545e2] — *Predictive model using autism*

Published December 2024 by psychiatry departments at Showa University and Teikyo University in Tokyo, with no funding of any kind declared and no competing interests, acknowledging a named colleague for teaching the team ADOS-2 administration. The framing is entirely clinical: the two conditions overlap in symptoms, co-occur, cluster in families and share genetic risk, while the features clinicians use to separate them become unavailable in exactly the cases where separation is hardest - when verbal expression is poor, when symptoms are concealed, or when an autistic adult's characteristics did not surface until adolescence. For this review the study is important out of proportion to its size, for four reasons. It is the only included study whose comparison group is another clinical population rather than typical development, and it therefore supplies the evidence that the free-play study charted alongside it identifies as missing when it observes that distinguishing autistic from other non-typically-developing children is the harder and more clinically relevant problem. Its central result is negative and well established: the ADOS-2 - the instrument this literature routinely calls the gold standard and against which computational models are benchmarked - achieved AUCs of 0.562 and 0.569 for autism against schizophrenia in verbally fluent adults, misclassifying 45% to 52% of schizophrenia patients as autistic, with no domain score carrying significant predictive value. That figure should sit beside every high accuracy in this review, because those accuracies were obtained against typically developing comparison groups and none of them has been tested against the discrimination that actually matters in a clinic. Its explanatory finding names the mechanism: what the ADOS-2 detects in schizophrenia is negative-symptom severity, evidenced by correlations across all domains with the PANSS negative scale, by markedly higher negative-symptom scores in cut-off-positive patients, and by a regression in which cut-off positivity is predicted by the negative scale alone - so a measure of social-communication atypicality behaves, in this population, as a measure of negative symptoms. And its own positive contribution is reported with a candour that is rare here: a six-item model reached an apparent AUC of 0.938 and 86.6% accuracy, then fell to 65.3% on a held-out split, and the authors attribute the gap to having six variables in a sample of ninety and conclude that external validation is required. A study that publishes the number that undermines its own headline is a useful counterweight to a corpus in which perfect scores are reported without any held-out check at all.

**S-126** [local_3ecb92bf] — *The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech*

Published 2025 by speech and behaviour-analysis groups at Imperial College London, the University of Augsburg and University Grenoble Alpes - the GLAM and iBUG laboratories, whose senior authors are central figures in computational paralinguistics and automatic behaviour understanding - with no funding and no declared conflicts. The framing is data-scarcity-driven: obtaining child speech data is hard because ethics committees rightly restrict it, so transfer learning is offered as a way to build usable models from small corpora. For this review the study earns its place on four counts, none of which is its headline. It is one of only two included studies whose comparison groups include another clinical population, and the only one to attempt a four-way separation of autism from dysphasia and PDD-NOS - the discrimination that clinical practice actually requires. It names the leakage problem precisely and splits by speaker to address it, in language sharper than most papers in this corpus manage. It performs equalised-odds fairness testing on held-out gender partitions and publishes a result that undermines its own headline: D-FT sensitivity falls from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls and 61.5% for boys, and W2V2-FT from 92.3% to 24.4% and 53.8% - which should be read as a general warning that pooled accuracies in this literature may conceal large subgroup deficits that nobody has looked for. And it benchmarks itself against a stated baseline and prior work on the same corpus, showing its four-class result at 60.9% against a baseline of 62.4% and prior results of 67.1% and 69.4%, so its own model loses on the harder task. Two cautions travel with it. The binary result rests on a corpus in which the atypical children were recorded in clinics and the typical children in schools - a recording-setting confound perfectly aligned with the class label, stated in the paper's own dataset description and never revisited - so 94.8% may be substantially a measure of room acoustics, and no normalisation is reported that would rule this out. And the participant accounting is internally contradictory, with the number of children in each diagnostic class never stated, which leaves the protective value of the speaker-disjoint splitting unquantifiable. The general lesson matches the one drawn from the multiscale-attention facial study charted nearby: careful validation methodology applied above a confounded data layer produces a well-validated uninterpretable number, and the review should treat the two together.

**S-127** [local_4b02df7c] — *Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism*

Published 2024 by the Department of Information and Computer Sciences at the University of Hawaii at Manoa. The framing is the standard access argument - limited availability of standard tests, misdiagnosis, delayed services, negative outcomes later in life - applied to a data source of unprecedented scale and zero collection cost, with the stated aim of 'enabling support for communities with limited access to diagnostic resources'. For this review the study matters on four counts, only one of which is its performance. It is the only included study whose behavioural data are naturally occurring and unelicited, at a scale - 6.5 million posts from 188,596 people over nine years - that no laboratory design can approach, which makes it the clearest available test of whether ecological validity and scale can substitute for measurement control. The answer it returns is instructive: 73% accuracy and AUC 0.728, modest against the 90-plus percent figures obtained elsewhere in this corpus under laboratory conditions with clinical ascertainment, and obtained despite the vastly larger sample. It implements two deliberate leakage controls - user-level splitting, with the reasoning stated, and removal of the sixteen autism-related tokens that define its own label - which places it among the more careful studies here on mechanics. It is the only paper in this review to discuss its own label honestly enough to state in its conclusion that the model predicts hashtag use rather than autism. And it is the only paper anywhere in the corpus that argues against the deployment of what it built: having demonstrated feasibility, the authors restrict legitimate use to population-level inference, enumerate the misuse scenarios an individual-level classifier would enable - insurance profiling, university admissions, hiring, government surveillance of citizens - delete the dataset and the models, note that the data were never shared outside the author team, and caution researchers against building comparable systems without explicit consent and participatory community-centred design. Set beside the studies charted nearby that scrape identifiable photographs of children from support pages with no ethics statement at all, or that ship an 'AI-driven assistive diagnostic tool' for at-home use on the strength of a model that recomputes a questionnaire's own scoring rule, this paper is the corpus's clearest demonstration that the ethical questions raised by this literature are tractable when researchers choose to engage with them. The substantive caution that travels with it is that its positive class is a self-selected advocacy community and its negative class a background platform sample, so the 73% has several sufficient explanations and the study does not distinguish them - a limitation the authors partially anticipate by declining to treat the result as a finding about autistic language at all.

**S-128** [local_7d7f1fcc] — *Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children*

Published October 2024 by the Psychiatry Department of the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Geneva with the Geneva School of Economics and Management, funded through a Swiss National Science Foundation Sinergia grant for digital phenotyping of autism, NCCR Synapsy, two further SNSF grants, the Private Foundation of the HUG, a university equipment grant and Fondation Pole Autisme. The framing is clinical and the argument for automation is stated without disparaging existing practice: the gold-standard diagnostic procedure is credited as 'the product of convergent clinical and research work over the past four decades', existing screening questionnaires are described as 'highly valuable' while varying in validity and replicability, and the gap identified is the years-long latency between first observable signs and diagnosis. For this review the study is one of the most useful included, for four reasons that are largely independent of its accuracy. Its recording context is matched across classes - both groups assessed with the same protocol in the same setting - which removes at a stroke the acquisition confound that this synthesis has had to record against the photograph, video-frame and clinic-versus-school audio studies. Its video representation strips appearance by construction, rendering pose as skeleton-on-black, so identity and setting cannot contribute to the classification; that is a designed answer to the confound rather than an assertion that none exists, and it also made partial data sharing possible. Its splitting is participant-level and matched on age, sex and ADOS module, with tuning confined to a validation partition carved from the training half. And its interpretability analysis, which regresses model confidence on all 27 ADOS items across both modalities with a normalisation model to make them comparable, produces the review's clearest demonstration that a modality label does not determine the construct measured: the audio model's most predictive items are showing, pointing, sensory exploration and hand mannerisms rather than anything vocal, and the authors conclude in their own voice that ambient non-vocal sound from object manipulation, and possibly the examiner's prosodic adaptation to the child, contributed to what they had labelled a speech-based classifier. That finding generalises to every study in this corpus using undiarised interaction audio. The performance itself - 80.0% video, 78.8% audio, 82.5% ensemble, on 80 held-out children - is modest, honestly reported, and roughly what one should expect from an unconfounded design, which is itself the most useful calibration this review can offer against the 95-100% figures reported elsewhere. Two cautions travel with it: no confidence intervals on an 80-child test set, where the ensemble's advantage over video alone is two children and cannot be distinguished from noise; and no statement of whether the ADOS sessions used as model input contributed to the diagnoses used as labels, which would take one sentence to resolve.

**S-129** [local_5a331ffe] — *Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning*

Published 2023-2024 by the LISSI laboratory at Université Paris-Est Créteil with the Faculty of Computer Science and Information Technology at the University of Malaya, funded by a Malaysia-France bilateral research grant. The framing is affective computing rather than diagnosis: the goal is a platform for longitudinal monitoring that could alert clinicians and parents to deterioration, and the motivating claim is that affect measures developed on neurotypical people do not work for autistic people. For this review the study's value is concentrated in one finding and one contrast. The finding is that a model trained on AffectNet - a large in-the-wild corpus of neurotypical faces - performs poorly at estimating arousal and valence in autistic children, and that fine-tuning it on autistic data produces noticeably better results, from which the authors conclude that data relating to autistic children rather than to neurotypical subjects is what such a task requires. That is a clean empirical demonstration, in a corpus otherwise short of them, that emotion-recognition technology built on general populations does not transfer to autistic faces - which bears on the several studies in this review that apply generic affect models to autistic children, and on any deployed system that would do so. The contrast is between this study's modest, stable, subject-disjoint 74.5% on SSBD face crops and the 94.6% that the authors themselves cite from a study using the Kaggle facial-image corpus, noting only that it was 'on another dataset' whose 'data distribution' the comparator exploited. This review has charted five studies on that Kaggle corpus reporting 81.0% to 99.8% under image-level splitting, against the present study's mid-seventies under subject-level splitting on a different in-the-wild corpus - and the pattern is the one the synthesis has documented throughout: figures in this branch track the splitting and labelling scheme rather than any property of the children. Three cautions travel with the study. The autism label rests on the authors' stated confidence in parents who posted videos of their children stimming, with no clinical ascertainment of any kind. The composition of the non-autistic class is never disclosed, so the classification result cannot be interpreted, and the paper's own data table contradicts its existence. And there is no ethics or consent statement anywhere, in work that crops faces from identifiable children's home videos and has five non-expert raters annotate their emotional states frame by frame - a gap made more conspicuous by the fact that the paper does discuss the trustworthiness of its data, but only as a question about label accuracy.

**S-130** [local_45ef7022] — *A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features*

Published 2024-2025 by the Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering at Vignan's Foundation for Science, Technology and Research in Andhra Pradesh, with data collected at a special school in Chennai and no funding. The framing is pharmacological rather than diagnostic, and this makes the study unique in the review: its output is not a diagnosis or a screening flag but a psychiatric medication dosage level, mapped from a predicted severity grade across a named list of agents including metformin, arbaclofen, cannabidiol, oxytocin, bumetanide, lovastatin and trofinetide. Two things about it deserve to be carried into the synthesis, one positive and one cautionary. The positive: the modality argument is the best-reasoned sensor-level answer in this corpus to a problem the review has documented repeatedly in visible-spectrum facial analysis, since thermal imaging requires no illumination and, as the authors correctly note, 'is not affected by lighting conditions or skin tone' - so a face-based method is proposed that is structurally immune to the demographic fragility that undermines the photograph studies charted here. The clinical motivation is also the sharpest statement of the continuous-monitoring case anywhere in the review: a 15-minute checklist 'does not capture the full range of daily behavioral variations in children', and the children were accordingly imaged during play, lessons and meals rather than in a clinic. The cautionary point is that neither strength is realised. The 80-20 split is over images rather than children, with about 50 images per child, so the classifiers can identify individuals and thereby their fixed severity labels, and 98.33% is what that arrangement produces; the severity labels themselves have no stated source, making the predicted quantity undefined; the claim to outperform the clinical ABC is incoherent if the ABC supplied those labels; class sizes are unreported so no baseline exists; skin temperature was measured across indoor and outdoor settings with no ambient compensation, confounding environment with any physiological signal; no feature importance distinguishes temperature from mood; the 20 videos reserved for real-time testing are never analysed; the sample is entirely male; current medication, which itself alters thermoregulation and correlates with severity by construction, is unrecorded; and there is no limitations section. Above all, the study was conducted on 30 disabled children at a named residential special school under the declaration 'Ethical Approval. Not required.', with no consent or assent statement of any kind, and offers its identifiable thermal images to anyone on request. For a review assessing what this literature does with its findings, this is the clearest case of a leaked accuracy attached to the highest-stakes recommendation in the corpus - a paper that lists cardiac arrest and kidney failure among the consequences of imprecise dosing, and then proposes that an image-level-split classifier of unstated provenance should inform the dose.

**S-131** [local_0f5a351e] — *Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder*

Published May 2025 by groups at the King Salman Center for Disability Research in Riyadh together with King Faisal, Prince Sattam Bin Abdulaziz and Al-Baha Universities. The framing is the standard access argument - conventional diagnosis is time-intensive and costly, creating barriers 'particularly in resource-limited settings' - combined with a physiognomic premise about distinct facial morphology in autism. For this review the paper is the sixth built on the Kaggle facial corpus and adds three things to the record.
