It states the provenance confound more plainly than any of the others, in its own methods: the autistic folder holds images of autism while 'the non-autistic subfolder had images randomly retrieved from web searches'. It supplies, in its Table 1, the most complete catalogue of the subliterature in the corpus - ten prior studies on the same images reporting 80.05%, 84.66%, 86%, 87.9%, 89%, 89.87%, 90.5%, 90.67%, 91.3%, 92%, 93.24% and 96% - which makes visible both the scale of the effort invested in this dataset and the fact that its reported accuracies cluster below the figure claimed here. And it contains, in its introduction, the only passage in this branch that names the harms of autism identification as such: labelling that 'may impact the child's self-esteem and social relationships', and 'a risk of overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis, leading to unnecessary interventions and therapies'. That the paper then proposes artificial intelligence as the mitigation for those very risks, without explaining how a classifier trained on web-scraped images with no diagnostic ascertainment would reduce mislabelling, is the clearest illustration in the review of how the access argument absorbs its own counterarguments. Three cautions travel with the study: all reported figures are validation-partition results while the defined test partition is never reported on; the evaluation support counts are irreconcilable with both the stated split and the corpus class ratio; and the abstract, introduction and results tables disagree about which architectures were compared and which performed best.

**S-132** [local_786b6280] — *Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features*

Presented at an IEEE computing conference in 2024 by a single secondary-school author in California. The framing is the standard early-detection argument, stated accurately: 1 in 36 children affected, no medical test, professional diagnosis reliable from age 2, and many children diagnosed late or never. For this review the study is valuable on four counts that have little to do with its accuracy figure. It is one of a small number of included studies whose split unit is the participant and whose evaluation design is both explained and empirically justified - 50 repeated 75/25 splits chosen because metrics stabilised within 1% - and it reports estimate variability through ROC standard-deviation bands rather than a bare point figure. Its features are named psycholinguistic constructs with an established literature, so its results are directly comparable with prior findings, and it makes those comparisons explicitly, confirming one study's mean-length-of-utterance result and contradicting another's on total word count. Its accuracy of 83-84%, benchmarked against three prior studies at 70-80%, sits in a credible range for a genuinely hard task and provides a useful calibration point against the 95-100% figures produced elsewhere in this review by leaked or confounded designs. And its sex-stratified feature analysis reports a diagnosis-by-sex interaction - mean length of turn lower in autistic boys than typically developing boys but higher in autistic girls than typically developing girls - which, if real, means a classifier trained predominantly on boys would misread girls, exactly the failure another study in this review demonstrated empirically with sensitivity falling from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls. Three cautions travel with it. The top-ranked predictor is mean length of utterance, a canonical index of expressive language development that the paper's own analysis shows rising with age, and with no independent language measure and no age composition reported by group, language delay and age cannot be separated from autism as explanations. Part of the typically developing class was drawn from corpora containing no autistic children and using different recording protocols, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class, and the four protocols differ in session length, structure and investigator role while half the features are ratios to the investigator's output. And the developmentally delayed children present in one source corpus were deliberately excluded to keep the task binary, discarding the non-autistic clinical comparison that would have made the study far more informative and that the review has found almost nowhere else.

**S-133** [local_879ec69b] — *Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning*

Published May 2025 by the School of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Aizu, Japan, funded by the university's Competitive Research Fund. The framing is screening-oriented and modest in its target: because 'deciding to visit a hospital often requires recognising signs within the household', a video-based assessment could give families 'a clearer motivation to visit a hospital' - an aim scoped as prompting help-seeking rather than replacing assessment, which is among the better-calibrated translational positions in this review. For the synthesis the study contributes four things. Its modality argument fills a real gap: diagnosis 'often requires speech-based tests' yet 'many young children may not yet be able to speak', so a movement-based measure reaches the youngest and least verbal children whom the language-based studies charted elsewhere here cannot assess. Its skeleton representation is a designed confound control, discarding face, appearance, clothing, room and lighting entirely, and the paper argues the accompanying privacy advantage explicitly against the anonymity concerns raised for eye-tracking and video data - the same reasoning that led the Geneva group to render pose as skeleton-on-black. Its architecture comparison produces a valuable negative result: across six image backbones the accuracy spread is 2.2 points on one dataset and 1.3 on the other, against a 25-point gap between the two datasets, so in this branch the data determine performance and the architecture barely matters - a corrective to a literature organised around architectural novelty. And the direction of that 25-point gap is instructive, since the corpus with unaddressed within-participant leakage produced the lower figure, which is a counterexample to the assumption that leakage always explains the highest numbers. Three cautions travel with it. The Gait dataset's single modelled trial per child was chosen from ten 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation' - selection on the outcome, quoted in the methods and never examined. No sensitivity, specificity or confusion matrix is reported for any model, and no demographic data exist for either corpus in a domain where gait varies strongly with age and sex. And the paper transmits, as motivating background, the clearest evidence of augmentation-driven inflation in this review: the Gait dataset's own creators went from approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation to 92% with seven augmentation techniques applied to 100 samples.

**S-134** [local_93e5d23d] — *Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]*

Published 2025 by a group spanning Zoundream AG in Basel, the Barcelona Center for Maternal-Fetal and Neonatal Medicine, and the University of Bologna, funded by Zoundream AG together with Swiss and Spanish innovation agencies, with two authors employed by the company, one of them a co-founder holding stock, and a third compensated as a scientific advisory board member. For this review the study occupies a position no other paper does. Cry is the earliest behaviour any included study measures: it is present before language, requires no cooperation, no task compliance, no social engagement and no cognitive floor, and it can be captured on a phone at home and repeated indefinitely at no cost. That combination reaches a population - pre-verbal infants, and children whose developmental level precludes the tasks used everywhere else in this corpus - that nothing else charted here can assess, and the physiological rationale is coherent, since jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio index the stability of laryngeal control rather than any social or communicative construct. The diagnostic ascertainment behind the corpus is also among the better ones in the review, with four stages culminating in independent confirmation by a child psychiatrist in a separate setting, and the authors explain rather than conceal the absence of ADOS. And the competing-interest declaration is the most complete in the corpus. Against all of this, the evidential yield is limited by three things the paper reports and does not examine. The classification figure has no held-out test, was taken as the best of 2,000 epochs on the validation set, and is computed over cry instances with no participant-level split from 62 children contributing roughly six cries each - so it says nothing about performance on a new child. The recording settings are strongly imbalanced, with 87.10% of autistic cries captured at autism centres against a comparison group split between health centres and homes, and all three significant acoustic measures are sensitive to the acoustic environment, with the strongest finding being the one ambient noise would most directly produce. And the groups differ by 4.8 months in mean age, untested and unadjusted, in a window of rapid vocal maturation using measures that change with it. The study's most useful contribution to the synthesis is therefore its construct rather than its numbers: it demonstrates what a pre-linguistic, task-free, physiologically interpretable behavioural signal would look like, and simultaneously how easily such a signal is confounded by where the recording was made.

**S-135** [local_a0d73248] — *Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm*

Published 2025 by computer science and electrical engineering departments at Alliance University, Bengaluru, with a collaborator at Nitte Institute of Professional Education, Mangalore. The framing is the standard access argument - conventional diagnosis is subjective and time-consuming, so machine learning should make it faster and more accurate. For this review the study's value is corroborative rather than novel: it is the third built on the UCI-derived autism screening tables, and it makes the leakage visible in a way the others do not, because it prints its complete feature list including both 'result' - the summed A1-A10 score - and 'Class/ASD', the outcome that is that sum thresholded at the AQ-10 cut-off. The relationship between the two is a matter of arithmetic, and the reported 0.9890 accuracy is its consequence rather than a measurement of detection. Two features of the study make the case more useful than the bare finding. Its analytic practice is otherwise unremarkable but adequate - 5-fold cross-validation, one row per respondent, a stated preprocessing and feature-engineering pipeline, a reasonable classifier and a reasonable optimiser - which is the same pattern the review has now recorded across five modalities: rigour applied above a corrupted target produces a confidently wrong result. And its single stated limitation is diagnostic of how the subliterature understands itself: 'heavy reliance on a single public Kaggle dataset, which may limit the model's generalizability', with the remedy proposed as incorporating diverse datasets. That names an external-validity problem while leaving the internal one untouched, and would not help, because every dataset in this family carries the same closed-form relationship between its items and its label. The one analysis that would have settled the matter - a Random Forest feature-importance plot, available at no cost - is not reported.

**S-136** [local_4ceee075] — *Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics*

Published October 2025 by information systems and sociology groups at L.N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University in Astana, with collaborators at Esil University and the National University of Uzbekistan. The framing is health-systems oriented and accurate for the region - a shortage of qualified specialists and a high burden on healthcare systems - with the technology positioned as a route to 'earlier identification and timely referral to specialists' rather than as a substitute for diagnosis, which is among the better-calibrated translational positions in this review. For the synthesis the study contributes three things. Its acquisition design is one of the strongest here: both groups were recorded under an identical purpose-built protocol in the same controlled environment, so the acquisition confound that undermines the photograph, video-frame, thermal and clinic-versus-school audio studies charted elsewhere cannot operate; the protocol actively elicits both social and motor behaviour in 8 to 10 minutes; and the landmark representation discards appearance, clothing, skin tone, lighting and background before any learning, removing a further class of confound by construction. Its validation is the most explicitly reasoned anti-leakage design in the video branch, naming subject-independence and data leakage directly and specifying four overfitting controls with their parameters - and the resulting 85-90% is modest and credible, benchmarked against external comparators. And it is a clean illustration of a distinction worth stating in the synthesis: leakage control and confound control are separate problems. The autistic group is approximately 84% male against 52% in the comparison group, a 32-percentage-point gap, and the model's inputs are 468 facial mesh points and 75 body and hand landmarks that encode sex-linked morphology and posture; a classifier separating boys from girls would produce exactly these figures under perfectly subject-independent cross-validation. No stratified or adjusted analysis addresses this, and no stream-wise ablation shows whether the signal lies in facial geometry or in hand motion, which would bear directly on the exposure. Two further gaps: no diagnostic reference standard of any kind is described for a prospectively recruited sample, so the predicted label is undefined; and no ethics approval or consent statement appears anywhere, in a study that recorded over 16 hours of video of 100 children including 50 autistic children.

**S-137** [local_84bcd4ed] — *Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of*

Published 2025 by the Information Systems department at Mansoura University, Egypt, with no funding and no declared conflicts. The framing identifies a genuinely under-researched problem: gelotophobia, the fear of being laughed at, affects around 6% of neurotypical people but up to 45% of autistic people, reaching 41.98% in adolescents with high-functioning autism, and the paper's account of the condition - internalised belief, heightened rejection sensitivity, shame, social withdrawal - is written from the experiencing person's perspective in a way that little else in this corpus manages. Identifying a comorbidity that shapes autistic people's social participation, and proposing to route ambiguous cases to a validated self-report instrument rather than forcing a facial judgement, are both good instincts. For the review the study contributes three things, all cautionary. It is the seventh built on the Kaggle facial-image corpus family, and its own description - images 'collected from platforms such as Kaggle and ASD-related websites' - restates the provenance confound that makes every figure in that branch uninterpretable, while its choice of DeepFace, a face-recognition library whose embeddings encode individual identity, maximises the exposure that an image-level split with an unreported number of distinct children creates. It applies an emotion classifier trained on neurotypical faces to autistic children without fine-tuning, which a study charted elsewhere in this review shows empirically to degrade substantially. And it is the only paper in the corpus whose headline contribution rests on no measurement at all: the abstract states that the GELOPH<15> 'was administered to confirm the diagnosis' while the ethics section states it 'was not directly administered to participants in this study' and that 'no direct contact with human participants occurred', so the gelotophobia system was never evaluated against any ground truth, no metric for it appears anywhere, and the conclusion nevertheless claims its effectiveness has been demonstrated. That distinction matters for the synthesis: most of the problems documented in this review concern measurements that are confounded or inflated, whereas here a diagnostic claim is advanced for a construct on which nothing was measured. The paper's own limitations section, which names uncontrolled demographics, the absence of external validation and the fact that its proposed architectures were never implemented, is candid enough to make clear that the authors understood the work as preliminary; the abstract and conclusion do not.

**S-138** [local_d97673f4] — *Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection*

Published 2024 by a group at Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology in Dhaka. The framing is physiognomic - autistic children are said to show wider eyes, a larger mouth, a shorter mid-face, a broader upper face and a pronounced philtrum, with the abstract asserting that 'differentiating facial features from normally developing children is a clear way to identify children diagnosed with ASD' - and the abstract also attributes diagnostic delay to families 'in denial and superstition', which is the least sympathetic characterisation of parents in this review. For the synthesis the study is the eighth built on the Kaggle facial-image corpus and contributes three observations. Its reported 88.33% is the second-lowest of those eight, which span 81.0% to 99.8%, and its architecture is the one least able to memorise - five frozen ImageNet extractors feeding a logistic-regression head, fitting only a linear function of fixed embeddings against the millions of end-to-end parameters used by the higher-scoring studies on the same images. That pattern is consistent with the review's broader finding that figures in this branch track model capacity and evaluation protocol rather than any signal in the data. Its preprocessing comparison is the most thoughtful in the branch, contrasting three configurations of which one strips colour and normalises local contrast - removing exactly the appearance cues most likely to differ between two image sources - though the per-configuration results are not broken out, so the comparison's answer is not reported. And its accessibility argument is the clearest statement of why this branch exists: 'since capturing a facial image is simpler compared to other detection methods, we anticipate a significant reduction in the difficulty of ASD detection', with the whole pipeline running on a laptop GPU and a public dataset. Against all of this stand the branch's standing problems, none addressed here: no diagnostic ascertainment for any image, no validation scheme or partitioning unit described anywhere, the number of distinct children unreported, augmentation applied without stating whether it preceded splitting, no demographic data in a study whose premise is morphometric, only accuracy reported, and no ethics or consent statement for identifiable photographs of children taken from the internet.

**S-139** [local_86a67a4f] — *Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children*

Published 2025 by the Department of Computer Science at Bharathiar University, Coimbatore. For this review the study contributes three things. It is the ninth built on the Kaggle autistic-children facial corpus, using the standard 2,526/280/80 partition, and it reports the fullest metric set of any of them - which is precisely what makes its central problem visible: the autism model's figures cannot all be true, since accuracy of 95% is incompatible with the specificity of 42.5% and recall of 94% reported beside it on a balanced 280-image test set, and precision of 0.96 is incompatible with that specificity at a 1:1 ratio. The seven earlier studies on this corpus report accuracy alone or accuracy with precision and recall, and an identical contradiction in any of them would have been undetectable. The lesson for the synthesis is that specificity is not merely an additional metric but an arithmetic check, and its near-universal absence from this branch removes the field's simplest defence against inconsistent reporting. If the 42.5% is the accurate value, the model identifies fewer than half of non-autistic children correctly - below chance, and a finding that would tell against the whole branch. Second, the study's emotion component is genuinely well motivated and its result is instructive. The stated rationale is that existing emotion models are 'primarily trained for healthy ones and consequently missing abnormal facial movements', so a recogniser trained on autistic faces is needed - correctly identifying a real problem - and the resulting 73.33% on six classes sits far below the 98-99% that posed neurotypical benchmarks support, which corroborates the independent finding elsewhere in this review that affect models transfer poorly to autistic children. Third, its limitations section is among the more candid in the branch, naming missing gender and ethnicity data, small sample size, the restriction to static images, the absence of external clinical validation, the absence of any explainable-AI component despite having argued for one, and CPU-only training - and the methods separately state that only a single split was performed and why. That candour makes the unreconciled metric table the more conspicuous. What remains unaddressed throughout is the corpus's provenance: the autistic class was harvested from autism-related online sources, so the label records where an image was found, and no diagnostic ascertainment exists for any child depicted.

**S-140** [local_0a39cca9] — *Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy*

Published 2025 by an electrical engineering group at Universitas Semarang with collaborators at Institut Kesehatan Indonesia and a Jakarta stem-cell laboratory. For this review the study is the tenth built on the Kaggle facial-image corpus family and the only one to supplement it with images from a clinical service - an autism centre in Semarang - which makes it both the branch's most interesting variation and its clearest missed opportunity. Mixing a web-scraped collection with clinic photographs could have anchored part of the corpus in real diagnoses; instead the paper reports neither the proportion from each source nor how they distribute across the two classes, so a reader cannot tell whether the addition reduces the provenance confound documented across the other nine studies or replaces it with a sharper one, in which Indonesian clinic photographs and international web images are separable by ancestry, camera and setting alone. The paper's own description of what the network extracts - 'the shape of the face, the expression on it, and the texture of the skin' - is unusually candid about the range of information a whole-image CNN receives, and names skin texture, which is exactly the kind of property that tracks image source rather than the child. The remedy was in the study's hands: with two identifiable sources it could have trained on one and tested on the other, and that single experiment would have been the most informative result in the entire facial-image branch of this review. Three further observations. The reported 0.8299 accuracy with precision 0.8514, recall 0.8182 and F1 0.8344 is internally consistent and among the branch's lower figures, and the study benchmarks itself against comparators at 0.7500 and 0.8050 rather than against the high-nineties claims elsewhere. Its precision-recall discussion is the branch's best, correctly judging a high-precision low-recall model 'less useful for finding all ASD cases'. And its account of rising prevalence is accurate where most of this corpus is alarmist, attributing the change from 1 in 150 to 1 in 36 to diagnostic criteria, awareness and broader age-range detection. Against this: no ethics or consent statement anywhere, despite identifiable photographs of children attending a clinical service; no diagnostic ascertainment described even for that portion; no demographic data; image-level splitting with the number of children unreported; no specificity or confusion matrix; and no limitations section.

**S-141** [local_7432ffd7] — *Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models*

2025, published 9 October, 32 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is unqualified diagnostic replacement: the system successfully diagnosed ASD, the approach shows promise for clinical application, assisting healthcare professionals in diagnosing ASD more accurately through advanced artificial intelligence technology. The comparison table positions the contribution purely as a higher accuracy number than nine listed predecessors, with no comparison of study design, split scheme or sample. It belongs to the review's leaderboard genre, in which the reported figure rather than the estimand is the unit of scientific progress.

**S-142** [local_8ff20c48] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning*

2025, published 24 July, 46 days from submission to acceptance including one revision round. Framing is assistive and comparatively restrained: an encouraging approach to improve detection, a first step towards early diagnosis within a few minutes saving time and expense. The novelty claim is placed on the population rather than the accuracy - unlike prior work relying on publicly available datasets from high-income countries, this study uses a locally developed dataset reflecting regional demographics and clinical practices - and that is the paper's real contribution to the corpus. The overreach is concentrated in one sentence claiming the system differentiates intellectual disability disorder from ASD using DSM-5-TR-derived questions, which nothing in the study tests.

**S-143** [local_986436f2] — *Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost*

Received 4 October 2024, revised 13 March 2025, accepted 24 August 2025 - the longest review cycle among the recently charted studies, and by far the least effective. Framing is diagnostic-replacement with an explicit efficiency argument: enabling more accurate and automated ASD screening, reducing reliance on subjective assessments, and facilitating timely interventions. Positioning is entirely comparative against numbers quoted from a single prior paper, with the contribution expressed as a higher AUC (0.98 against 0.74, 0.66 and 0.64) rather than as an estimate of anything.

**S-144** [local_bb4d1f7a] — *Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models*

Received 12 August 2024, accepted 4 October 2024, published online 4 December 2024, issued 2025. Framing is assistive-to-transformative: the work is said to show how ML and eye tracking can transform the diagnosis and treatment of autism and to set a new standard in the field, with the method described as capturing spatial and temporal dynamics with unprecedented accuracy. Set against that rhetoric, the paper is also one of the few in the corpus whose abstract states outright that generalisability has not yet been assessed, and whose introduction motivates the work partly by stigma reduction, inclusion and long-term quality of life rather than solely by detection throughput.

**S-145** [local_13c1f46d] — *Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism*

2025, published 16 April, 81 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is unqualified computer-aided diagnosis, with an unusual and revealing justification: early recognition is said to be significant to aid families and parents in superstition and denial, and AI is credited with aiding the treatment and reintegration of autistic patients. The contribution is expressed purely as a higher number than seven quoted baselines. There is no limitations section, no future work, and no acknowledgement that any part of the claim is provisional - the paper's closing position is that the method is superior, full stop.

**S-146** [local_e771fb69] — *Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data*

2025, published online 19 February, 126 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is infrastructural rather than clinical - the contribution is offered as a viable solution for healthcare applications involving sensitive data that preserves privacy and security while maintaining high diagnostic accuracy. The claim of high diagnostic accuracy rests on nine test cases; the claim of privacy preservation rests on a federated architecture simulated over a single downloaded file; and the paper's own governance obligations - stating an ethical basis for reusing 44 people's behavioural recordings - go unmet. It is the corpus's clearest example of privacy engineering standing in for research ethics.

**S-147** [local_945300a5] — *Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network*

2025 IEEE conference proceedings. Framing is optimistic but hedged more than most: the study is said to pave the way for further application of facial recognition technology in clinical contexts and the potential development of automated detection systems that can be used in daily diagnostic practice. The novelty claim is placed on the dataset rather than on the accuracy - the paper's stated purpose is to remedy the poor representativeness of existing autism face datasets, and it does so by actually recruiting and photographing 70 children under a controlled protocol rather than by downloading images. That is a real contribution to a branch of this literature that has otherwise recycled the same web-scraped corpus twelve times over.

**S-148** [local_ed30e24c] — *Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI*

2025, accepted 14 August, 48 days from submission. Framing is screening-tool improvement rather than diagnostic replacement, and is comparatively measured: integrating robust feature selection with explainable ML models can significantly advance the reliability of early ASD screening tools. The overreach is concentrated in one sentence - that 100% sensitivity and specificity confirm the model's suitability for reliable clinical screening applications - and in a comparison table that ranks the perfect score above three published figures from unrelated datasets. The paper's genuine contributions are its hyperparameter transparency, its inclusion of log loss, and a limitations paragraph that correctly identifies single-dataset dependence.

**S-149** [local_b9de0d7f] — *Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques*

2025 (accepted version, citation DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2024.3349988). Framing moves beyond diagnosis into intervention allocation: the aim is personalised educational approaches for individuals with ASD, harnessing machine learning to enhance precision in addressing their unique needs, with results said to help educators make informed decisions. The paper opens by insisting that no two autistic children are alike and closes by assigning them to six intervention categories on the basis of a ten-item checklist total that the authors themselves binned. It is the corpus's clearest example of a pipeline whose output is an action taken on a child rather than a probability, built on a target the authors wrote with numpy.

**S-150** [local_14df790d] — *Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach*

2025, published 28 May, 132 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is screening-support rather than diagnostic replacement and is among the most measured in the corpus - the title claims to predict autism traits, the abstract offers a scalable and cost-effective approach for early detection and personalized intervention strategies, and the discussion admits that results across subsets were not entirely satisfactory. The overreach is confined to the closing claim of facilitating the way for integrating ML techniques into clinical settings. Its distinguishing contribution is analytical rather than predictive: by systematically varying which parts of the Q-CHAT arithmetic enter the feature set, it produces the branch's most complete map of why these accuracies are what they are.

**S-151** [local_4da2b941] — *Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study*

2025, accepted 15 September, 133 days with a substantive revision round. Framing is deliberately bounded: the results show the viability of machine learning to predict traits and symptoms and suggest potential for developing a tool that may improve screening in individuals whose diagnosis is unclear or not yet established. The discussion then constrains that further - algorithms should be extensively cross-validated against health records before implementation, should be used as screeners to accelerate referral rather than replace clinical evaluation, and should be applied within a personalised-medicine approach respecting autonomy. Where the rest of this corpus claims diagnosis and delivers checklist arithmetic, this study claims correlation between self-reports and delivers exactly that, with the error bars in view.

**S-152** [local_6e7174c0] — *A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach*

2025. Framing is diagnostic and confident: the model is a pioneering approach contributing significantly to early diagnosis and intervention strategies, and a powerful tool to enhance ASD diagnosis and improve outcomes for individuals with ASD and their families, hedged only by a clause acknowledging that further validation on larger, diverse datasets is needed. The contribution is expressed as a position in a leaderboard over one public image corpus, and the paper is explicit that this shared corpus is what makes the comparison solid - which is the clearest statement in the review of how this branch understands evidence.

**S-153** [local_e04bcd32] — *Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network*

2025 (received 26 October 2024, revised 1 March 2025). Framing is diagnostic and efficiency-oriented: the model is offered for screening and detection of ASD in children, as computer-aided diagnosis, and as achieving higher accuracy with reduced model complexity and less execution time. There is no limitations section and no future work; the contribution is stated entirely as a position above five quoted figures on the same public image corpus, and the paper's own account of why ASD diagnosis is difficult - that there is no blood test or scan and that developmental history and behaviour must be assessed - is not reconciled with what it then does.

**S-154** [local_183eaef4] — *Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI*

Published 8 November 2024 (indexed here under 2025), 40 days from submission. Framing is translational and confident: the integration of ML and XAI promises to revolutionize intervention strategies, the study successfully developed highly precise and interpretable ML models for ASD diagnosis, and the findings support the adoption of AI-driven diagnostic tools by healthcare professionals and contribute to personalized intervention strategies. The paper positions itself in a comparison table against ten prior studies, with the distinguishing contribution in every row being the absence of XAI in the others - so novelty is claimed on the explanation layer while the estimand goes unexamined. Its most interesting feature is that a team including practising clinicians, applying correct cross-validation, formal statistical testing and three explanation methods, arrived at accuracy 1.0000 and treated it as a result to be defended by resampling rather than as a signal to inspect the feature list.

**S-155** [local_b6ac2b98] — *Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks*

2025, published 24 June, 127 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is deliberately restrained and, unusually, becomes more restrained as the paper proceeds: the abstract reports the ASD-versus-DLD F1 of 0.63 alongside the higher figures rather than burying it, and the conclusion states that the approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis. The clinical claim is limited to a preliminary step toward computer-aided diagnosis. Its contribution to the review is not a performance number but a controlled contrast: by running the same pipeline against a typically developing group and against a second clinical group, it converts the corpus's ubiquitous ASD-versus-TD figure into an interpretable quantity.

**S-156** [local_44d3aef5] — *Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis*

Published 19 July 2024 (indexed here under 2025), 44 days from submission. Framing is unqualified diagnostic assistance: the classifiers are said to demonstrate the potential of eye-tracking data to aid physicians in efficiently and accurately screening for autism, and users and healthcare professionals can utilize these classifiers to enhance the accuracy rate of ASD diagnosis. The contribution is stated as a leaderboard position - 100% against 87%, 90% and 79% on the same public dataset - and attributed to preprocessing. There is no limitations section, no future work and no hedge of any kind.

**S-157** [local_24fefc5f] — *A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection*

2026 issue. Framing is early-detection and cost-saving: initial identification and treatment can diminish the need for wide examinations and expensive medical procedures, and prolonged effects and severity can be avoided at a timely determination of ASD. The contribution is expressed as architectural novelty - a named hybrid (MEResNeXt) built from two named components, fed by a named metaheuristic (DeSEHO) built from two further named components - with the accuracy figure as its warrant. It is the corpus's clearest example of method-naming as the unit of contribution: four new acronyms are introduced, forty equations specify borrowed architecture internals, and the number of children behind the result is never mentioned.

**S-158** [local_69b10fe4] — *An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms*

2026, accepted 15 December 2025 after 180 days. The framing is unusual for this corpus in that its primary contribution is negative and clinically protective rather than a performance claim. The motivating concern is that PD assessments are primarily movement-based, so autistic people may score highly on PD diagnostic criteria because of autism-related movement differences - a differential-diagnosis risk that matters given rising PD diagnosis rates in autistic populations. The study then finds no kinematic similarity between autism and PD that is also distinct from controls, which addresses that concern directly. The classification work is labelled proof-of-concept, kinematics are proposed for use in conjunction with clinical assessments rather than instead of them, and the applied suggestion - that a tablet-and-stylus protocol could support community-scale assessment without laboratory equipment - is proportionate to what was demonstrated.

**S-159** [local_af9f4c12] — *An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data*

2026. The framing is the study's principal contribution to this review. Where the rest of the questionnaire branch presents reconstruction of a checklist threshold as diagnostic accuracy, this paper presents the same task as what it is - approximation of a deterministic behavioural scoring function - and repeats that restriction in the abstract, the contributions, the methods, the results and the conclusion. It describes its own labelling as a heuristic with internal consistency but no external diagnostic validity, bounds its SHAP interpretation against causal claims, calls external validation against clinician-annotated data necessary rather than desirable, and requires human oversight for any deployment. The overreach that remains is modest and confined to the discussion, which speaks of diagnostic precision and of stratifying ASD into four functional levels, and to the clinical-integration proposal for electronic health records and e-learning platforms. It is the only study in the branch whose stated conclusions a reader could act on safely.

**S-160** [local_367db0b6] — *An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns*

2026. The framing rests on a genuinely important and under-addressed problem: that once a newborn's data enters a training set there is usually no mechanism to remove it when parents withdraw consent, and that this is a live obligation under GDPR and HIPAA. That argument is correct and is made nowhere else in this corpus. What follows it does not support any of the claims made from it - accuracy improved to 98%, error rates reduced by 23%, false positives reduced, and a framework said to be able to validate itself in real-world clinical implementations and to be implementable in hospital settings. The study reports no confusion matrix, no metric values from its own named metric set, no consistent sample size and no ethics approval, in a paper whose organising principle is the ethical handling of newborns' data.

**S-161** [local_8d43288c] — *Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos*

2026, published 18 March, 174 days from submission with one revision round. The framing is internally split. The objectives section states that the system should be used as a clinical decision support system and not an independent diagnostic system - an accurate and unusually explicit limit. The title, abstract and conclusion pull the other way, placing the work in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder, claiming it facilitates the quick, accurate, and effective screening of ASD, and asserting tremendous potential for real-world clinical implementation. What the study actually demonstrates is that a CNN-GRU distinguishes four movement categories in home video at about 93% under a clip-level split, which is a behaviour-recognition result and a useful one; the screening language is added on top of it.

**S-162** [local_5f57ba19] — *Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension*

2026 (May). The framing is the most disciplined in the review. The abstract concedes in its own body that performance remains modest; the results section opens by observing that the modest overall performances underscore the inherent challenges of detecting ASD from gaze-based features in data-scarce naturalistic settings; and section 7.3 states that roughly 64% F1/AUC positions the work as a research exploration rather than a deployable diagnostic tool, given benchmarks for clinical viability often exceed 80-90%. Value is claimed only for preliminary screening as a complement to human judgement, and the proposed future work includes defining, by cost-benefit analysis, what performance threshold would count as meaningful for low-stakes screening. Set beside the studies in this corpus reporting 99% and 100% from checklist thresholds and web-scraped photographs, its contribution is not a method but a demonstration of what the honest number looks like.

**S-163** [local_1d856900] — *Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare*

2026, published 29 January. The framing is trust-centred - the stated goal is a model that is not only good at predicting ASD but also clear in its reasoning, with the title promising to enhance trust, interpretability and reliability in AI-driven healthcare. Against that, the paper reports a 98.2% figure from a dataset it does not source, whose split partitions augmented duplicates, and whose task is not the one the abstract implies; it applies its interpretability methods only to the dataset where they are least informative; and it reproduces the branch's characteristic overreach in describing machine learning as a suitable replacement for routine and expensive screening tests. Its genuine methodological contribution - explicitly confining SMOTE to the training partition and publishing the whole pipeline as an algorithm - is real and is the part of the paper most worth borrowing.

**S-164** [local_7b19a959] — *Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis*

2026. The framing is screening-support and is bounded at every point: the measures may be a promising means of predicting autism, providing complementary information to existing screening questionnaires; the value proposition is triage for expedited assessment given protracted diagnostic wait times, not replacement of clinical assessment; and the reported gain is stated as 9 percentage points over the most popular adult screening questionnaire, with the authors noting that this matters in the context of an estimated 1% population prevalence. The paper is also unusual in reporting a result that undercuts its own headline - that the same models reach 81.8% on the unmatched sample and 74.0% once age and gender are matched - and in choosing the lower figure as its primary estimate.

**S-165** [local_d7b6fa00] — *Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath*

2026. The framing is proportionate and, on the point that matters, correct: the reported results should be interpreted as a proof-of-concept demonstration, pending validation on larger and more diverse populations. The claims that go beyond that are about engineering rather than clinical accuracy - reduced preprocessing overhead by eliminating scanpath-to-image conversion, suitability for real-time screening environments, and a more direct and deployable solution bridging the gap between research prototypes and practical clinical tools - and even those are asserted without any timing measurement. Its contribution to the review is as the eye-tracking branch's demonstration that participant-level evaluation is achievable in this modality and that when it is applied, the resulting figure comes with a standard deviation of eight accuracy points on 28 people.

**S-166** [local_e54c304c] — *Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models*

2026, published 5 February. Framing is real-time clinical screening: the study is said to facilitate real-time ASD screening, providing healthcare professionals with timely and effective interventions in clinical environments, with mobile and web deployment proposed to reach remote areas. There is no limitations section and no future work, and the contribution is expressed as a position above one quoted prior YOLO result. Its distinguishing features within the branch are two: an ethics paragraph that at least names the sensitivity of children's facial data before proceeding, and an out-of-distribution test that inadvertently shows the model assigning an autism label to a photograph of a dog.

**S-167** [local_e4c2a776] — *Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images*

2026. Framing is diagnostic-aid: the technique is offered as a promising diagnostic aid in clinical settings for the early and non-invasive detection of autism, and the stated research gap is a computationally efficient, privacy-preserving and accurately optimised framework - with no privacy mechanism described and no runtime measured. The contribution is expressed as a position above seven quoted figures. Its one substantive merit within the branch is its limitation paragraph, which states plainly that the dataset's lack of demographic information prevents any assessment of how facial morphology and expression vary across populations, and commits future work to demographically diverse data - the clearest statement of the branch's central problem made by any of its sixteen members, sitting alongside declarations asserting that the study used no data and involved no human participants.

**S-168** [local_231757c7] — *SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers*

2026, published 23 March. The framing is the most restrained in the charted corpus relative to the numbers reported. The abstract states 100% accuracy for the severe class and, in the same sentence, that this represents a methodological proof-of-concept rather than clinical validation because the features were synthetically generated; the discussion adds that a single misclassification would reduce recall to 75%; the conclusion describes the work as proof-of-concept demonstrating methodological feasibility pending validation on independent datasets; and future work is specified with a minimum sample target. Its contribution to this review is therefore not its accuracy but its demonstration that an author can report a perfect score and simultaneously explain, in the abstract, why it means nothing - the exact move that the corpus's fifteen facial-image studies and seven checklist studies do not make.

**S-169** [local_1b457442] — *Screening autism spectrum*

Framing is screening-support and privacy-forward, and both claims are qualified in the abstract itself - the models are described as a foundation for future applications in clinical and educational contexts, and the privacy claim is explicitly limited to the absence of biometric data rather than to any cryptographic guarantee, with the authors stating that they have not implemented differential privacy or encryption. The paper's contribution to this review is twofold. It is the only study in the corpus to make privacy the design criterion and to argue explicitly that facial-image approaches invade the privacy of minors - a critique that applies directly to the sixteen facial-image studies charted here, several of which reuse web-scraped photographs of identifiable children with no ethics statement. And its three-class result (ROC-AUC 0.71 including developmental delay, against 0.87-0.93 against typical development) joins local_b6ac2b98 and local_69b10fe4 as the review's differential-diagnosis calibration points.

**S-170** [local_b26db2f2] — *Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches*

2026. The framing is the most appropriately bounded in the primary-data group: the tool is offered as laying the groundwork for future research and practical applications to screen for suspected ASD among children in school settings, and the discussion states explicitly that screening should be understood as an initial support for identifying warning signs and guiding the search for specialised clinical evaluation, not as a definitive diagnosis, with professional training required to reduce misinterpretation and the risk of stigmatisation named. Its contribution to this review is a study that gets almost everything right about design, ethics, transparency and scope - primary collection in the real setting, matched groups, published code and data, a full hyperparameter grid, enumerated criteria, dual consent, and an unprompted discussion of screening ethics - and then reports a 96% that its own validation design cannot support, because 640 game sessions from 12 children were split by session rather than by child.
